Level Z

107 books · 10 pages each

1. 1865 and the Close of the Civil War

1A map can show the Union states and the Confederate states in 1865. The end had come. Early spring of 1865 was the season. General Robert E. Lee realized a hard truth. His exhausted Confederate Army could do no more. Lee had said that dying a thousand deaths would be better than surrender. He now saw no choice. The cause of the South had been crushed. On April 9, Lee dressed in a fresh uniform. Wearily, he rode his horse to a meeting. He went to meet U.S. General Ulysses S. Grant. The place was a private home in the town of Appomattox Court House, Virginia. He arrived at the house. He sat down to wait. Half an hour later, Grant made his appearance. Grant was clad in an old uniform. The uniform was muddy. The two generals had a friendly conversation. Then they got down to business. The business was ending the war. A side note belongs with that meeting. When the Civil War broke out, President Lincoln made Lee an offer. The offer was command of the Union armies. Lee declined. He said he could not fight against his beloved state. That state was Virginia. Lee left in order to join the Confederacy. After that departure, the government of the United States took his estate. The estate was Arlington. It lay across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. The grounds of the estate became Arlington National Cemetery. In the decades leading up to the Civil War, the North and the South were already divided. Slavery was one important difference. The North was a region of growing industry. It was also a region of small farms.

2Large-scale agriculture played a lesser part in the Northern economy. Slavery had existed in the North. By 1804, all Northern states had outlawed the practice. The South was a much different world. Its economy was built on cotton. Southern plantation owners had made a choice about labor. They chose the labor of enslaved people to plant cotton. They used that labor to harvest cotton too. Nearly four million Black people were held in slavery in the Southern states by the middle of the 1800s. They were forced to do many jobs. Most lived on cotton plantations. Most worked there as well. A picture shows members of an enslaved family. Their enslavers could separate that family at any time. During those same years, abolitionists in the North worked to stop slavery in the South. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 was a federal law. It made a fugitive from one state a fugitive in every state. It required people in free states to return anyone who escaped slavery. The return was to their enslavers. Even so, help came from some people in the North. They helped escapes from slavery. The Civil War might never have happened under one condition. The United States would have had to remain a small group of states in the eastern part of the continent. Instead, during the 1800s, the nation was expanding. It moved into huge areas of land. That land had been forcibly taken from Native peoples to the west. Those territories were becoming states. Congress had to decide a question about each new state. The question was whether the state would allow slavery. The Southern states wanted a rough balance.

3They wanted balance between states that allowed slavery and free states. If free states outnumbered states where slavery was legal, a shift would follow in Congress. Southern representatives would be outnumbered. Representatives from free states would not share the interests of the South. They would likely vote against Southern representatives on various issues. That balance on slavery was maintained for several decades. Tensions between North and South were still growing. The country reached a breaking point in November 1860. The event was the U.S. presidential election. To the South's dismay, Abraham Lincoln was elected president of the United States. He was the candidate of the Republican Party. That party was antislavery. The Southern states felt fear about a Republican-led government. They feared it would destroy their economy. They feared it would put an end to their practice of slavery. After the election, seven Southern states seceded from the Union. The seven were South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas. In February 1861, they officially formed the Confederate States of America. They hoped it would be a permanent nation. They hoped it would stay separate from the United States. A photograph shows Abraham Lincoln in 1865. The war began just two months after the new nation formed. The place was Charleston, South Carolina. On April 12, 1861, a Union commander refused to surrender the Union fort there. Confederate forces opened fire. Four other Southern states were forced to choose sides. Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee also seceded. They joined the Confederacy. How terrible the war would become was beyond anyone's guess. In the first two years of the war, little went well for the Union.

4President Lincoln was failed by his generals. The failures came one after another. A Union victory in 1862 opened a door for Lincoln. He could issue the Emancipation Proclamation. That order granted freedom to slaves in the Confederacy. When the war began, Lincoln's main goal had been to save the Union. Now he began to think about slavery. He thought about how to end it once and for all. The North felt its cause was just. Union losses were still horrible. In one battle, a Union survivor recalled a terrible sight. Men fell as leaves fall in autumn. He said it seemed miraculous that any of them escaped at all. Another man spoke about the cries of the wounded. He said the cries were weird. He said they were unearthly. He said they were terrible to hear and bear. Frederick Douglass was a famous speaker. He was a formerly enslaved person. Like many free Black Americans in the North, he celebrated news of the Emancipation Proclamation. He said all of us are liberated by this proclamation. He said everybody is liberated. He said the white man is liberated. He said the Black man is liberated. He said the brave men now fighting are liberated. Those men were fighting the battles of their country against rebels and traitors. Douglass also recognized a limit. The proclamation was only the first step on a long road. The road led toward freedom and equality for all Black Americans. On its own, the Emancipation Proclamation did not end slavery in the United States. It only freed enslaved people in certain places. Those places were the portions of Confederate states not already under Union control.

5This allowed enslaved people in Confederate areas to fight for the Union. The North badly needed those soldiers. The order also redefined the war. It made the war a crusade against slavery. Two more years would have to pass before slavery finally ended. An amendment to the Constitution would be needed as well. During the Civil War, nearly 200,000 Black Americans fought on the Northern side. Northern feeling against the fighting grew while the war dragged on. Democrats did not take the Republican view. Democrats called for an end to battle. They called for a negotiated end to the war. The 1864 election would determine the whole direction of the war. Lincoln believed he would lose. He won instead. Reelection gave him strength to continue the war. He wanted to reunite the country. He wanted to end slavery. In January 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment. That amendment is an addition to the Constitution. It ended slavery in the United States except as a punishment for crime. Lincoln also finally had the generals he needed. One was Ulysses S. Grant. The other was William Tecumseh Sherman. Those two commanders were professional. They were also effective. They sought to destroy the Confederacy. They sought to end the war as quickly as possible. Sherman's campaign carried him into the deep South. In late 1864, his men burned much of Atlanta. Then they marched across the state of Georgia. They tore up rail lines. They destroyed bridges. They set fire to many homes. Women took part in the Civil War in more than one way. More than four hundred women disguised themselves as men.

6They fought in the Union army or the Confederate army during the Civil War. Tens of thousands of other women worked behind the lines. Those women were white and Black. They worked as laundresses, as cooks, and as nurses. Susan Baker King Taylor was born into slavery in Georgia in 1848. At age fourteen she became a schoolteacher. She taught other newly free Black Americans. She also worked as a laundress for Black Union soldiers. She worked as a nurse for them too. Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland. She escaped North at age twenty-seven. Over many trips, she helped other family members escape North. Then she guided dozens of others to freedom. She worked for the Union Army as a cook. She also worked as a nurse, a scout, and a spy. She led an armed raid in South Carolina. That raid liberated more than seven hundred enslaved people. Meanwhile, farther north, Grant had been waging a campaign against Lee. The campaign was grim. It was also steady. One horrible battle took place in mid-1864. The place was Cold Harbor, Virginia. Grant ordered an attack on the Confederate lines. The attack caused some seven thousand Union casualties. Those losses came in twenty minutes. One Union soldier later said the scene was not war. He called it murder. Such bloodshed gave Grant a nickname. The nickname was the Butcher. Lee's army was still being worn down by Grant. By early 1865, Lee was stopped outside Petersburg, Virginia. His men were in trenches there. A later chapter of Grant's life began with his war record. In the western campaigns of the Civil War, Grant showed what he could do.

7Lincoln placed every Union force under Grant's command in March 1864. Five years later, Grant became president. He was the eighteenth president of the United States. The fifty-dollar bill carries his picture. Before dawn on April 3, Lee fled Petersburg. He knew that staying any longer would doom his army. Union forces doggedly pursued his retreat. Lee's escape was not something Grant would accept. On April 6, about eight thousand Confederate soldiers were killed or wounded. Grant's army did that harm. Lee saw only one reasonable option left. That option was surrender. The Civil War had lasted four bloody years. The finish was close. Grant's offer for the South's surrender used generous terms. All Confederate soldiers were permitted to return home. He also agreed that Lee's troops could keep their horses. They could keep their mules too. Lee's men were nearly starving. For that reason, Grant ordered food for thousands. Other Confederate forces in the South had not yet given up the fight. They all soon surrendered. On April 2, Confederate President Jefferson Davis fled Richmond. Richmond was the Confederate capital. On May 10, he was captured. He would spend two years in prison. The Civil War was over. A poster announced that end. The date it gave was April 9, 1865. The United States remained united. Joy in the North over victory in the war did not last. The joy soon turned back to mourning. On April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth gained entrance to a private box. It was the Lincolns' box at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C. The president sat watching a play. His wife, Mary, sat with him.

8Booth fired a single shot into Lincoln's head. Then he jumped down to the stage. The unconscious Lincoln was carried across the street. He was taken to a private house. Early the next morning, death came. Booth was an actor. He was fiercely opposed to Lincoln. He was fiercely opposed to abolition too. He was part of a group that sought revenge. The group wanted revenge for the defeat of the Confederacy. They planned more than one killing. They planned to kill Lincoln. They also planned to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson. They planned to kill Secretary of State William Seward as well. As it turned out, only Lincoln was killed. Seward still received serious knife wounds. Union troops tracked Booth and another man. They tracked them to a farm in Virginia. Booth was shot to death. Trials for their crimes came later for the other people in his group. A court found four men guilty. Those four were hanged. Lincoln's body was sent on a funeral train. The train went back to his home state of Illinois. Lincoln was gone. He had lived long enough to achieve his main goals. He saved the Union. He ended slavery. The end of the Civil War also began the next chapter in United States history. By December 6, 1865, enough states had ratified the Thirteenth Amendment for it to become law. That amendment ended slavery. Within the next five years, two more amendments were passed. They were the Fourteenth and the Fifteenth. They gave formerly enslaved people civil rights. They gave them voting rights too. In 1870, Hiram Revels of Mississippi took a Senate seat.

9He was the first Black American elected to the U.S. Senate. After the war, the U.S. government protected formerly enslaved people. The system was called Reconstruction. After Reconstruction ended in 1877, the Southern states found ways around two amendments. They got around the Fourteenth. They got around the Fifteenth. They created new rules. The rules were known as Black codes and Jim Crow laws. The rules enforced racial segregation. They diminished the power of Black voters. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was passed. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was passed too. With those laws, Black Americans finally obtained the rights the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments had intended. Those rights are still under attack. Advocates continue to strive for equality. They continue to strive for protection under the law. The Civil War did something beyond ending slavery. It established a principle. The United States is an indivisible nation. States do not have the right to secede from the Union. Their feelings about their country do not create that right. Other times of great strain have come to the nation in the years after the Civil War. Americans continue to be divided today. The divisions cover many issues. They take many forms. Yet we remain one nation. That nation is the United States of America. A timeline keeps the dates in the order they were listed. On December 20, 1860, South Carolina seceded from the Union. It was the first of eleven Southern states to do so. On November 6, 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. On June 8, 1861, Tennessee seceded from the Union. It was the last of eleven Southern states to do so.

10On April 12, 1861, the Civil War began. On January 1, 1863, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. On November 8, 1864, Lincoln was reelected. On January 31, 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment. On April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln. On April 9, 1865, General Robert E. Lee surrendered. He surrendered to General Ulysses S. Grant. On December 6, 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment was ratified by Congress. Hard words from the story can be stated in plainer lines. Abolitionists means people who fought to make slavery illegal. Fugitive means a person who is running from something, usually from legal authorities. Amendment means a change or an addition to a document or a law, such as the U.S. Constitution. Indivisible means not able to be separated. Mourning means the act of expressing grief, especially for someone who has died. Campaign means a planned series of actions designed to reach a certain goal. Representatives means people chosen to speak, to vote, or to act on behalf of a person or a group. Casualties means people injured, killed, or missing during a war or a disaster. Confederate means having to do with the Southern states that separated from the United States during the Civil War. Seceded means formally withdrew from membership in an organization or a group. Union means the group of states that fought against the Confederacy during the American Civil War. It also means the United States. The Emancipation Proclamation means an order issued by President Lincoln in 1863. That order freed all the slaves under Confederate authority. The story closes on the same nation the war refused to split.

2. A Fish That Strikes with Electricity

1A legendary shocker opens this book, from old reports to newer science. The animal is shown to be a fish. Its electricity is explained. A stunning attack is described. A warning says where not to swim. A last question asks if the animal could supply energy in the future. Special words close the pages. The year 1800 found the German naturalist Alexander Humboldt hunting electric eels. The search was in the land now called Venezuela. He believed the eels, and the shocks they make, could help his work. Catching some alive had to come first. Electricity as a force was poorly understood then. Mysteries about that force might be solved with living eels. Bare hands were too dangerous, and Humboldt knew it. Severe pain through a whole body can follow a shock. Local fishermen were asked for help. Five years of his life, from 1799 to 1804, were spent exploring South America. The eel hunt was one piece of that journey. Living animals were what he needed. Pain from a shock was already known. The cause of the force was still unclear. Fishermen who knew the water could bring him close enough to learn. The five-year journey covered a wide part of South America.

2Eels were not the only thing he studied, but their shocks were a special prize. A living eel could be tested. A dead story could not. Pain was the warning that kept his own hands off the animals. Help from local people was the safe path he chose. Humboldt watched the fishermen guide about thirty horses into a pond. The pond was murky and shallow. His description says what followed. Eels as thick as snakes rose out of the water. Hundreds of shocks hit the horses. Five eels could be caught only after that. Study of the eels taught Humboldt a great deal. A picture drawn from his writing shows the horse method. Horses stand in the pond while eels rise, and the power of the animals is clear. Modern gear that would have made the catch safer was not his to use. Scientists came to know his horse-fishing account widely. Doubt lasted a long time. Some thought the tale was stretched, the way fish stories often are. A scientist confirmed a key point only in recent years. Eels do rise from the water to protect themselves, matching what Humboldt saw.

3The body is long and shaped like a tube. Color is gray-brown. Yellow or orange often shows under the head and on the throat. Catfish are closer relatives than other eels are. The shape still looks more like an eel. Knifefish is the common name of their scientific order. Every knifefish can use electricity to some degree. Length can reach 2.1 to 2.75 meters, or 7 to 9 feet. Weight can reach 20 to 22 kilograms, or 44 to 48.5 pounds. Thickness can match an average adult human thigh. Color is much the same for males and females. Size is much the same too. Telling the sexes apart can be hard for scientists. Electrophorus electricus is the scientific name. The animal type is fish. Fish, crustaceans, and amphibians are the diet. Air is breathed through the mouth, which sets electric eels apart from most other fish. Gills are present, as in other fish. Breathing out is mostly what those gills do. The mouth opens at the surface. Special organs in the mouth take oxygen from the air into the body. Used air leaves through the mouth and the gills.

4A breath of air is needed every few minutes. Trapping an eel underwater can drown it. Fins are present, as in most other fish. Small fins sit on either side of the head. One long fin runs along the belly. That belly fin stretches the length of the body. A backbone also runs the full length and helps the eel move. Swimming uses an S-shape wave of the belly fin. Slow movement is the usual pace. An attack is when the pace quickens. A cut-off tail can grow back. Worms can regrow parts as well. Sea stars can. Certain lizards can. The mouth breath is not optional. A few minutes is the longest usual wait between breaths of air. Gills do not do the main job of taking air in. They help send used air out. Surface visits are therefore constant. Fins on the head are small. The belly fin is the long one, and the S-shaped wave is the swimming stroke. Speed stays low until an attack starts. A lost tail is not a permanent loss, because that part can return. Worms, sea stars, and some lizards share a similar power to replace a missing part.

5Electricity is what sets an electric eel apart from other fish. No fish on Earth is more electric. Protection is one known use of the power. Finding the way, or navigating, is another. Hunting is another. Prey can be stunned or killed. Bioelectricity is the tool. Electric currents acting inside a body are what bioelectricity means. Weaker electrical skills show up in other fish. Other knifefish have them. Some skates, rays, and catfish have them. Navigation, communication, or self-protection can be the use. None of those fish matches the attack shock of an electric eel. Headaches once brought a risky treatment from ancient Greeks and Romans. A live electric ray was held to a person's forehead. Numbness in humans can follow a ray's shock, so the treatment might have helped. This is not something to try at home. The electric ray, the clearnose skate, and the electric catfish are other electric fish. Three electric organs fill most of the inside of an electric eel. Their names are the main organ, Hunter's organ, and Sachs' organ. Shocking power comes from these organs. They begin just behind the head. They continue down the back.

6They run along both sides into the tail. Two-thirds of the body is electric organ. Shocks leave the body from these organs. A battery with a positive end and a negative end is a fair comparison. The head is the positive end. The tail is the negative end. Curling the body around prey can make the shock stronger. Head and tail have to touch for that boost. Prey can be hit with as many as 650 volts from the electric organs. Small animals can be killed by that. Large animals can be stunned. Water within 8.5 meters, or 28 feet, carries a shock that can be felt. A typical wall socket in the United States is already dangerous to people. Five times the volts of that socket is what an eel can produce. Their own shocks do not harm them. The reason is not settled. Size of the eel compared with size of the prey might matter. Speed of the shock moving away from the body might matter. Inner structures that are not fully understood might matter too. Electrocytes are known. They are special cells inside the electric organs, and they help create the shock.

7Long rows are how the electrocytes line up. Each one gives a tiny shock when bioelectricity is used. The tiny shocks come at nearly the same moment. Stacking the cells and timing the shocks together makes the tiny shocks larger. One big stunning zap is the result. Prey must be found before that zap. Murky water is home. Eyesight is poor. Night is when they are most active. Eyes are not the hunting tool. Bioelectricity is. Bats and owls locate prey from sound that bounces off objects. Electricity gives eels a similar skill. About fifty low-volt pulses go out every second. A pulse is a beat of electricity that repeats. Plants, animals, and nearby objects break into those pulses. The breaks reveal what is around the eel. A short burst follows when prey seems close. Two or three high-volt pulses make that burst. Muscles clench because of the shocks. Muscles twitch even though the animal does not choose to move. Exact location of the prey shows up in that movement. A high-volt shock comes next. Twitching stops. Sometimes the prey dies. The eel moves fast. Prey is sucked through the mouth straight into the stomach.

8Recovery and escape do not have time to happen. Small fish, crustaceans, and amphibians are the usual food of adults. Worms, insect larvae, and small fish are the usual food of the young. Top predators is the rank of electric eels. They are common where they live. Muddy or sandy rivers that move slowly are the usual places. The Amazon River holds them. The Orinoco River holds them. Tributaries of both rivers in northern South America hold them. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean border that continent. Swamps, creeks, and ponds can hold them too. Lake edges in tropical plains or forests can hold them. Low-oxygen water is survivable because they breathe air. Hours out of water are possible if the skin stays wet. Mating mostly happens in small ponds. Males make nests from bubbles of their saliva. Hundreds of eggs are laid in the bubbles by females. Males guard the nests. They guard the babies after hatching until the young are about 10 centimeters long, or 3.9 inches. Self-defense must start then. Shocks from the young are weaker than adult shocks. Animals that will risk a bite threaten the young. Crocodiles are one threat before the eels grow.

9Black caimans are crocodile relatives. Few predators will risk eating an electric eel, and black caimans are among those few. Slow rivers with mud or sand bottoms are the common home. Northern South America is the region, along the Amazon, the Orinoco, and the streams that feed them. Air breathing lets an eel stay in water that holds little oxygen. Wet skin is enough for hours on land. Bubble nests in small ponds are where most mating happens. Males both build the bubbles and guard what hatches. At about 10 centimeters, the young must shock for themselves, though the shock is weaker than an adult's. More is known about electric eels now than Humboldt knew. Learning is not finished. Electrocytes are being studied at Yale University as a model. The hope is cells that could stand in for batteries inside medical devices. A pacemaker is one device. It keeps a human heart beating. Chemicals inside a pacemaker battery could poison a patient if the device broke. A safer battery is the goal, one that will not harm the inside of a body. A battery that does not run out of power is the other goal.

10A line Humboldt set down over two centuries ago still fits. He wrote that people remained a long way from knowing every secret of how fishes act through electricity. The next secret these eels will open is still unknown. Words from this account are gathered here. To amplify is to increase amount, strength, or importance. Electric means charged, powered, or producing energy from moving particles that carry charge. Electric currents are electric charge moving through matter. Immune means shielded from something, or able to resist it. Internal means inside, or happening on the inside. To navigate is to find a way across a long distance, or to steer toward a place. Organs are body parts with set jobs, such as kidneys or lungs. Shocks are sharp jolts felt when electric current touches a body or passes through it. To stun is to knock a creature out, or into a daze. Top predators stand at the top of a food chain, where no other animal eats them. Tributaries are rivers or streams that join a larger river. Volts measure the force that starts an electric current moving.

3. A Flight Along Sixty Degrees North

1Girls try new winter boots in a picture. The place is a factory that makes boots, close to Russia's St. Petersburg. Sixty degrees north is introduced first. Wildlife of the subarctic comes next. Anchorage, in Alaska, comes next. Oslo, in Norway, comes next. Helsinki, in Finland, comes next. St. Petersburg, in Russia, comes next. The same trip in winter comes next. A summing up closes the trip. A glossary ends the book. Summers are short at 60 degrees north latitude. Winters are cold there. A map asks where the labeled spots sit. Find the places named in this book. Welcome onto a flight that circles the world. The line followed is 60 degrees north latitude. The subarctic region is the land below. South of the Arctic Circle is what subarctic means. Long winters that are cold mark this region. Short summers that are cool mark it too.

2The matching line in the Southern Hemisphere is not on this trip. Sixty degrees south has no airports. Land is missing there. Glaciers sometimes sit in subarctic mountains. Ice in these giant sheets has piled up for a very long time. Hundreds of years may pass during the buildup. Thousands of years may pass. Bears live in the subarctic. Wolves live there. Caribou live there. Moose live there. Inland parts of continents at this latitude often wear huge forests. The trees stay green all year. Taiga is the name, said TIE-guh. Winter cold in these forests can drop to −65 degrees Fahrenheit. That is −54 degrees Celsius. Trees must survive that cold. June is when this trip happens. June is summer north of the equator. Warmth is the rule. Daylight is plentiful. Southeast Alaska holds Mendenhall Glacier. Tourists like to visit it.

3Among major cities of the United States, Anchorage is the one farthest north. The trip begins there. The latitude is 61 degrees north. June 21 brings the Summer Solstice Festival, and the timing matches. Summer solstice means the year has no longer day. Daylight in Anchorage then lasts from about nineteen hours up to twenty-two. An imaginary circle around Earth is called the Arctic Circle. It lies near 67 degrees north latitude. It is the southern edge of a special zone. Inside that zone, the summer solstice sun never sets. Water balloon volleyball appears in a picture. The game is part of the Annual Heroes Games. Those games sit inside Anchorage's Summer Solstice festival. Cook Inlet is where Anchorage stands. The inlet is a narrow channel. The Gulf of Alaska holds it. Dena'ina Athabascan people call this area home.

4Say the name in two beats: deh-NYE-nah, and then a-thuh-BA-skuhn. Water nearby makes the climate milder than inland places. Winters stay warmer beside large bodies of water. Summers stay cooler beside them. On a summer day, Anchorage often reaches a high near 65 degrees on the Fahrenheit scale. That is 18 degrees Celsius. Winter highs average 20 degrees Fahrenheit. That is −7 degrees Celsius. Outdoor festivals draw many Alaskans at the summer solstice. Night does not stop the parties. The midnight sun is still shining. Oslo's harbor, in Norway, appears in a picture. The flight turns east toward northern Europe. Oslo is the landing. The city stands on an inlet. That inlet opens into the North Sea. The North Atlantic Drift is a warm ocean current. Mild weather for 60 degrees north is the result. Summer can reach 70 degrees Fahrenheit.

5That is 21 degrees Celsius. Winter can sit in the mid-20s Fahrenheit. That is −4 degrees Celsius. Oslo is incomplete without one museum. The Viking Ship Museum is the place. Vikings were people who lived by the sea. About 1,000 years ago they lived in this region. Their ships were sturdy. Their sailing skill was strong. Coastal Europe was in their travels. Iceland was in their travels. Greenland was in their travels. North America was reached too. A Viking ship in a picture was found in Norway. The find was inside a large burial mound. Constitution Day in Oslo brings children into the streets. Traditional clothes are worn. Flags are carried. Helsinki sits at 60 degrees north. Arrival matches Nightless Night. Bonfires mark the summer solstice. Sunset waits until almost 11:00 pm. A sea fortress called Suomenlinna can be toured before dark.

6Sweden built it in the 1700s. The goal was to guard the way into the Baltic Sea. Russia, next door to Finland, conquered it later. Finland holds the fortress again today. Old cannons can be seen on the grounds. History of the place can be learned. Outdoor cafes come after the tour. Mild summer weather is there to enjoy. Six islands carry the fortress of Suomenlinna. Venice of the North is a nickname sometimes given to St. Petersburg. Beautiful canals are the reason. The flight continues east to that city. Some canals were made by nature. Some were made by people. Peter the Great founded it. He was a czar, meaning a ruler, of Russia. The 1700s were the years of the founding. City land stretches across the Neva River. It also stretches to Finsky Bay. Swamp covered that land at the start.

7Peter the Great changed the swamp. Canals were built on his orders. Soil was filled into the wet ground. White Nights is the June celebration. Walks last all night. Canals are the path. Drawbridges are part of the path. Dogsledding began with Indigenous Peoples thousands of years ago. Ice-packed land was the road. Snowy land was the road. Dogs and humans move the sled together. They steer it together. Cold weather suits these dogs. Snow suits them. A high-fat diet is what they are bred to eat. Wooden sleds once crossed vast distances. Teams held from two dogs to twelve. Hunted game was carried. Supplies were carried. Inuit scouts later used sled teams in World War II. Mail has been carried by famous sled teams. Trade goods have been carried. Medicine has been carried. People of every background now honor that history.

8The Iditarod is the yearly race. The distance is 1,000 miles. That is 1,609 kilometers. Anchorage is the start. Nome, in Alaska, is the finish. Now imagine these cities in midwinter. December 21 is that date in the Northern Hemisphere. Conditions would feel very different. Winter solstice means the year has no shorter day. Daylight along this latitude shrinks to about five hours. Darkness fills the rest. Cold fills the day. Coastal cities see highs in the 20s Fahrenheit. That is about −4 degrees Celsius. Each of the four cities sits near a large body of water. Winter there stays much warmer because of the water. Inland towns are colder. Far from the coasts, a winter afternoon may reach only about 5 degrees on the Fahrenheit scale. That is −15 degrees Celsius. Cold lasts so long that summer cannot fully thaw the ground.

9Permafrost is the result. Roads are very hard to build on it. Buildings are very hard to build on it. A tilting telephone pole appears in a picture. Melting permafrost under it is the cause. Winter also offers the aurora borealis. Northern lights is the other name. Evening skies fill with natural light. The cause is strong bursts of electricity, high up in the air. Farther south, the same kind of show has another name. Aurora australis is that name. Night sky grows brighter under the northern lights. A blanket toss appears in a picture. Inupiat people take part. Visitors take part. Kotzebue, in Alaska, is the place. Hunting once used this technique. Celebrations use it now. Competitions use it now. Warm temperatures marked the summer trip along 60 degrees north. Days were long. Summer tilts the Northern Hemisphere toward the Sun.

10Sunrise and sunset move farther apart because of that tilt. Cultures in the four countries of this trip differ widely. Each place still celebrates the summer solstice. That day holds the most sunlight of the year. Glossary Aurora borealis names the northern lights. Charged particles are the cause. Earth's magnetic field pulls them into the atmosphere. Canals are dug waterways across land. Transportation uses them. Irrigation uses them. A hemisphere is half of Earth. The equator can split Earth into north and south. A line through the poles can split Earth into east and west. An inlet is a narrow water strip running from a larger body into the land. Latitude tells how many degrees a place sits above or below the equator. A solstice is one of the two yearly times when the Sun stands farthest from the equator.

4. A Living Sea of Grass

1Sections of this book follow. A Sea Made of Grass. Three Prairie Kinds in North America. Why Fire Matters. How the Prairie Works Together. Keeping Prairies Alive. Plants You Can Find. Animals You Can Find. Words and Topics. A question opens the topic. Picture a ship with open sea in every direction. Or picture a boat with a large lake stretching all around. Every direction shows water. Now picture a different sea. This one is grass. Waves of green surround you. Gold is there. Brown is there. Reddish grass is there. Flowers of many colors run as far as sight can go. Hundreds of species of plants live in this grassy sea. Hundreds of animal species live there too. Birds of different kinds fly overhead. Some swoop. Some dive. Their prey spends most of life hidden in the grasses. The land is flat, or it rolls gently. Names change by continent. South American grasslands are called pampas. Asian grasslands are called steppes. South African grasslands are called veld. A large natural grassland is not the turf in a yard. Yard turf is mostly one color. It stands about 2 inches tall. Little hides there beyond insects. Grasslands are not all the same. They grow in North America and in South America. They grow in Europe and in Asia. They grow in Africa and in Australia. Every continent has them except Antarctica. Rainfall sets the pattern. Grasslands usually grow where rain is too much for a desert. The same places have too little rain for a forest. Grasses, of course, are the main plants. Not every grass is the same grass. Hundreds of species fill the world's grasslands. Most share one trait. They are tough. They are hardy. Fire can be survived. Heat can be survived.

2Freezing can be survived. Drought can be survived. Grazing can be survived. What else could live through all of that? Roots grow deep underground. Water is found there. Nutrients are taken in there. Stems and leaves above ground may die. Fire can burn them. Animals can eat them. New plants can still rise from those roots. A note on size: More than 140 million acres of North America once lay under tallgrass prairie. That area is 56.7 million hectares. About 10 percent of it remains. A map shows the old area of each prairie type. Three Prairie Kinds in North America. Prairies is the name used for grasslands of North America. Rainfall amount makes each prairie different. Soil type makes each one different too. Three main types exist. Tallgrass is one. Mixed-grass is one. Shortgrass is one. The main difference is easy to guess. Height of the grasses is the answer. Travel starts in the east of North America's prairie region. The direction is west, the way many European settlers went in the 1800s. Tallgrass prairie comes first. Much of Illinois is included. Iowa is included. Minnesota is included. North Dakota and South Dakota are included. Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas are included. Yearly rain is 30 to 40 inches. That is 76 to 102 centimeters. Some grasses there grow taller than an average human. Big bluestem is one. Indian grass is one. Height reaches 8 feet or more. That is 2.4 meters. Roots can go even deeper, to 9 feet. That is 2.7 meters. Soil in a tallgrass prairie is deeper than soil in other prairie kinds. It is darker. It is richer in nutrients. Walking through on foot would make it easy to get lost. A photo shows Pembina Trail Preserve in Minnesota.

3Westward travel reaches mixed-grass prairie. Parts of North Dakota and South Dakota hold it. Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas hold parts of it too. Yearly rain is between 15 and 25 inches. That is 38 to 64 centimeters. Little bluestem grows here. Sideoats grama grows here. Height falls between 2 and 3 feet. That is 61 to 91 centimeters. Soil is usually dark brown. A photo shows mixed-grass native prairie in South Dakota. East of the Rocky Mountains is where shortgrass prairie sits. Yearly rain is only about 10 inches. That is 25 centimeters. The prairie spreads onward from there. A photo shows shortgrass prairie in Montana. States in this shortgrass region include Montana. Wyoming is included. Colorado is included. New Mexico is included. Texas is included. Little rain falls because the mountains make a rain shadow. Warm, dry winds blow down from the mountains and dry the land. Most grasses here grow between 8 and 18 inches tall. That is 20 to 46 centimeters. Buffalo grass is one example. Bunch grass is another. Roots reach about 3 feet deep. That is 91 centimeters. The soil is light brown. A chart title mentions prairie plants and uses feet as the measure. People who manage prairies start fires on purpose. The fires are called controlled burns. Trees and shrubs are kept from growing. Why Fire Matters. Most things cannot live through fire. A prairie can. A prairie grows stronger because of fire. Deep roots are the reason. New stems grow from those roots with ease. Flames in a fire may pass 400 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 204 degrees Celsius. Underground, the temperature rises only a few degrees. Once the fire stops, roots quickly send up new stems. Young trees on the prairie face a different fate.

4Shrubs do too. Flames will probably kill them. Without fires, those trees and shrubs would keep growing. The prairie would become a forest. Until the 1800s, Lightning hit the ground and started prairie fires. Fires were also set by Native American people. The Sioux did. The Pawnee did. The Cheyenne did. A ring of fire was sometimes set around bison. Buffalo is another name for those animals. The herd was forced to run past one chosen spot. Hunters killed the bison there. Food came from the animals. Clothing came from them. Shelter came from them. Burning had another purpose. Burnt plant material decomposed and added nutrients to the soil. Americans whose ancestors came from Europe entered the prairie region during the 1800s. Putting fires out was their usual choice. Danger was what they saw. Because of that choice, many prairie places became forests. A note on herds: millions of bison once lived in huge groups on the prairies. New settlers did not want the animals where farms and towns would rise. The killing was huge. Bison did not make a hard target. Flight was not their response. Circles formed around the young so the young stayed protected. About 500 bison were all that were left when 1890 arrived. Some people then began breeding the survivors. Zoos held some. Ranches held some. Today about 200,000 bison live in protected areas. Yellowstone National Park is one of those places. How the Prairie Works Together. Plants, animals, and nonliving things all interact. Fire is included. Together they make the prairie ecosystem. Six main parts form it. The Sun is part one. Producers are part two. Primary consumers are part three. Secondary consumers are part four. Decomposers are part five. Nonliving substances are part six. Light and heat from the Sun supply energy for everything else.

5That energy flows through the whole system. Producers are the grasses and the other plants. They build their own food. Sun energy is used. Water is used. The air supplies carbon dioxide gas, and that is used too. Nutrients from the soil are used. Primary consumers eat the plants. Jackrabbits are an example. They eat grasses and clover. Herbivores is another name for these animals. Nutrients and energy come straight from plants. Secondary consumers eat meat. Carnivores is their other name. They eat the animals that eat plants. A fox that eats jackrabbits is an example. A jackrabbit is pictured. Prairie potholes are a special case. Some prairie areas hold water for part of the year, or for all of it. Those areas are prairie wetlands. If the water lasts only part of the year, the name is prairie pothole. Ducks rest there. Other birds rest there. They also breed there. These birds migrate, which means they travel long distances in spring and in fall. Rainwater is taken in by prairie potholes, the way a sponge takes water in. Flooding is reduced. Decomposers are organisms in the ecosystem. Dead plants and dead animals are broken down. Chemical substances left in the soil are the result. Bacteria are included. Fungi are included. Mushrooms are a kind of fungus. Nutrients form from those chemical substances. Plants use the nutrients to grow. The chemical substances, Water joins those substances as the part of the ecosystem that is not alive. Keeping Prairies Alive. North America has little natural prairie left. Most were changed into farms long ago. Cities replaced others. Some places still let you sense what early settlers saw. They saw a sea of grass. Prairie preserves are those places.

6Scientists work there. Volunteers work there. People like you can join. The aim is to restore prairies to a natural condition. A state department of natural resources can tell you whether a prairie is near you. Ask if any task needs a volunteer. Seed collecting is one task. Bird counting is another. Few lessons about North America's great grasslands are better than these tasks. A photo shows cord grass seeds gathered so the prairie could be restored. A note on deep time: where prairies stand today, a warm, shallow ocean once lay. The span runs from about 440 million years ago back no farther than about 410 million years ago. Fossils tell scientists this. The region also holds further traces of sea animals from that ancient time. Plants You Can Find. A few examples follow. Grasses come first. On the tallgrass prairie, few grasses stand taller than big bluestem. Height reaches 8 feet or more. That is 2.4 meters. Early summer is when new shoots appear, and only then is the color blue. Red shades come afterward. Brown shades come too. Long clusters hold the flowers. Those hairy clusters are called spikelettes. A bird's foot has three toes in front. The clusters copy that shape. Extra names follow from that shape. Turkeyfoot is one. Beardgrass is one. Drier ground suits little bluestem better than it suits big bluestem, the larger relative. Height can reach about 4 feet. That is 1.2 meters. Short hairy clusters, called spikelettes, hold the flowers. The stem tops arrange those clusters in a zigzag. Seed heads look fluffy. Thin stalks carry the flowers of sideoats grama, all hanging toward one side. Usual height is 32 inches. That is 81 centimeters. Mixed-grass prairies hold it. Shortgrass prairies hold it too. This grama grass, and other types, were important forage.

7Large bison herds of earlier times grazed on them. A reddish tint on the prairie comes from sideoats grama flowers. Bison also relied on buffalo grass as forage. Height is about 6 inches. That is 15 centimeters. In the 1800s, settlers cut slabs of sod formed by this grass. They used the slabs like bricks to build houses. A lawn in central Texas would suit buffalo grass well. Other plants come next. Composites: The composite family includes a large share of prairie plants. Sunflower is another name for that family. Each large flower is really many tiny flowers. Tiny flowers in the center are called disk flowers. A ring of other flowers surrounds them. Those are called ray flowers. Blazing stars are composites. Bright pink flowers appear. Red flowers appear. Purple flowers appear. Colorful shooting stars are what they resemble. Large leaves mark the compass plant, and it too is a composite. Edges of those leaves always point north and south. Goldenrods carry bright yellow clusters of flowers. Late summer brings them. Fall brings them too. Legumes: The legume family includes a large share of prairie plants. Pea is another name for that family. Flowers on these plants have complicated shapes. Say the family name leh-GYOOMZ. Wild indigo is one picture subject. Clovers of several kinds are prairie legumes. Flower colors include white, yellow, red, and purple. Wild indigos are included too. Their flowers can be white or cream-colored. Stems of wild indigos hold a blue dye. Early settlers used that dye to color clothing. Animals You Can Find. A wide variety lives on prairies. A few examples follow. Grouse are brown birds that look like chickens. They live on the prairie ground. Seeds are on the menu.

8Leaves are eaten. Grains are eaten. Berries, buds, and flowers are eaten too. A male who wants a female dances. He makes cooing sounds. His neck carries a purple sac. It swells until it looks like a balloon. Flocks of grouse are called coveys. A sharp-tailed grouse is shown proving he fits his name. Snakes include a large prairie reptile, the bullsnake. It is brownish. Length can reach 8 feet. That is 2.4 meters. It slithers through the grass. Rodents are food. Birds are food. Eggs are food. A loud hiss is part of its warning. The prairie kingsnake lives here too. So does the massasauga. Timber rattlesnake is another name for it. The fox snake is included. A bullsnake hisses loudly. The hiss warns others to stay away. Western prairies are home to prairie dogs. Dogs they are not. Barking is the doglike habit of these rodents. Towns are their groups. Hundreds of animals share one town. Large systems of underground burrows are dug. Hawks send them running to hide. Coyotes do too. Other enemies do too. Burrows can be 16 feet deep. That is 5 meters. Dirt mounds ring the entrance holes. Daytime hunters overhead include several kinds of hawks. They search for rodents, for songbirds, and for other prey. At night, owls take over that hunting role. The northern harrier is also called the marsh hawk. It stands about 2 feet tall. That is 61 centimeters. Hunting flight glides low over the ground. The call is kee kee kee. Speed can reach 40 miles an hour. That is 64 kilometers an hour. Chicks share a prairie nest with an adult hawk. Coyotes are sometimes called prairie wolves. Size is about that of a medium-sized dog. Usual weight is between 20 and 50 pounds.

9That is 9 to 23 kilograms. Rodents are eaten. Rabbits are eaten. Dead animals are eaten. Fruit is eaten. Howls sound spooky. Night is when they can be heard. A coyote mother is shown with a squirrel she has caught. Coyotes outweigh foxes. Usual weight is between 8 and 15 pounds. That is 4 to 7 kilograms. Like coyotes, Almost any catch can become a meal. Gray foxes live on prairies. Red foxes live there too. North America has few foxes smaller than the swift fox. No animal in North America outruns the pronghorn antelope. It is a long-legged mammal. It eats plants. Home is the shortgrass prairie. Running speed can reach 60 miles an hour. That is 96 kilometers an hour. Most highways set a lower speed limit. Shoulder height is about 40 inches. That is 102 centimeters. Males have two black horns. Hooklike prongs mark those horns. A photo shows a female pronghorn on the left and a male on the right. Other animals pictured include a gray fox, a fox snake, a massasauga, and a northern harrier. Preserves of tallgrass prairie include these places. Flint Hills National Wildlife Refuge stands with Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in Kansas. The preserve named Goose Lake Prairie stands in Illinois. It is a state natural area. Living Prairie Museum is in Manitoba, Canada. Tewaukon National Wildlife Refuge is in North Dakota. Waubay National Wildlife Refuge is in South Dakota. Preserves of shortgrass and mixed-grass prairie include these places. Caddo National Grassland and Lyndon B. Johnson National Grassland are in Texas. Comanche National Grassland is in Colorado. National Bison Range is in Montana. Prince Albert National Park is in Saskatchewan, Canada. Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge is in Oklahoma. Words to Know. Bacteria are organisms of one cell.

10Some of them cause infections and disease. Fungi are small organisms. They grow on material that once was living, and they make spores. Burrows are holes or tunnels. An animal digs them in the ground and uses them as shelter. Grazing means animals feed on field grass. Animals that eat only plants are herbivores. Plants are their only food. Carnivores are animals. Meat is their only food. Interactions are the relationships that link living things with things that are not alive. A drought is a long stretch of time. Very little rain falls. An ecosystem is a biological community. Organisms live there together with their habitat. A mammal is warm-blooded. Hair or fur covers it. It nurses its young. Its babies are born live. Forage is food for animals that eat plants. Hay can be forage. Grain can be forage. Grass can be forage. Nutrients are substances in food or in soil. Organisms need them to live, to stay healthy, and to grow. Rodents are small mammals. Large gnawing teeth keep growing for the animal's whole life. A species is a group of animals. Members are similar. They can breed with one another. Topics include indigos, bacteria, legumes, and bamboo. Little bluestem and big bluestem are listed. The massasauga is listed. Bison and the northern harrier are listed. Blazing stars and prairie dogs are listed. Buffalo grass and the prairie kingsnake are listed. Carbon dioxide and preserves are listed. Clover is listed. Prairie types listed are mixed-grass, shortgrass, and tallgrass. The compass plant and the pronghorn antelope are listed. Composites and coyotes are listed. The Rocky Mountains are listed. The ecosystem and sideoats grama are listed. Fire, the fox snake, the fox, and soil are listed. Fungi and grouse are listed.

5. A Marble Memorial in Agra

1A map shows Agra in India beside the Yamuna River, and it also marks Burhanpur, the Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal. The Mughal dynasty created the Taj Mahal, and the result is magnificent. Picture yourself drawing something to honor a person who mattered deeply to you. A starting point would be needed. Whatever you chose, you would likely fill the drawing with the most beautiful things you could imagine. India holds a place made for that purpose. It remembers someone who was loved very deeply. The 1600s were the time of building, under the Mughal dynasty. Say Mughal as MOO-guhl. Rich works of art made the Mughals famous. Beautiful architecture did too. Their family name, Mughul, led to the word mogul. A mogul matches the richest king in wealth and in power. The Taj Mahal is their most famous creation. Shah Jahan, the fifth Mughal ruler, had it built. Most people, hearing Taj Mahal, picture the mausoleum and its huge white dome. The whole place is larger than that building. It covers 16 hectares, or 42 acres. The design stands for a home in paradise.

2That home was for Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan's favorite wife. Buildings, walls, gates, and gardens follow one plan. The plan reflects the Islamic picture of a perfect heaven. Grass covers the grounds now. Flowers once suggested the gardens of paradise. Fruit trees once did the same. The garden is split into four equal parts by four channels of water. A pool at the center is where the parts meet. The channels stand for four heavenly rivers named in the Koran. The Koran is the holy book of Islam. Today's visitors enter through the Great Gate. Red sandstone and marble make this striking building. Words from the Koran greet people as they come in. Inlaid flowers decorate the Great Gate. Two towers of eight sides stand on either side of it. A plan of the complex names the pieces. A tower is one. A riverfront terrace is one. The mausoleum is one. An assembly hall called the jawab is one. A mosque is one. A central pool, a water channel, and gardens are included. The Great Gate and a forecourt are included.

3Every path leads visitors toward the large mausoleum. Mumtaz Mahal's burial is there. Looking out from within the Great Gate, a visitor sees the dome, shaped like an onion, set in the arch. The framing looks perfect. Out in the gardens, the channels of water shine with the mausoleum's reflection. Visitors' first view, once they pass the Great Gate, is that perfectly framed mausoleum. A raised platform of marble holds the building. That platform dominates the grounds. Four tall towers stand around it. Each tower rises more than 40 meters, or 130 feet. Red sandstone is the material of most structures on the grounds. White marble covers the mausoleum. It covers the platform. It covers the towers around them. In Islam, white is the color of mourning. White on a tomb tells the faith of the one resting there. Emperor Shah Jahan's public tomb lies beside another. The second belongs to Mumtaz Mahal, his third wife. Carved screens of marble cover the windows. The building was meant to be Mumtaz Mahal's mansion. That mansion was pictured in paradise's gardens. From outside, the marble seems to shift color.

4Light causes the shift. Weather causes it too. Sometimes the whole building seems to glow. Eight sides shape this mausoleum, as they shape many Mughal tombs. Four outer walls are the long ones. Four are the short ones. Huge arches open the four long walls. Smaller arches sit to either side. Mumtaz Mahal's coffin is at the center inside. The room has eight sides. It occupies the middle of the building. A second coffin beside hers marks where her husband was buried. Carved marble screens of great beauty surround both coffins. The coffins visitors see are not the real burial places. Downstairs, a room kept private holds the true burial places. They lie directly under the coffins above. No other structure in the Taj Mahal is decorated as richly as the mausoleum. Some experts think it stands for Mumtaz's crown in heaven. The Persian word for crown is the source of taj. Designs of geometry cover almost every inch of the floor. Vines run over the walls. Flowers do too. Butterflies do too. Precious stones and semiprecious stones make the designs bright.

5Jade is one stone. Jasper is one. Turquoise is one. Lapis lazuli is one, said LAP-is LA-zuh-lee. Artisans set thousands of gems into the patterns. Diamonds are among them. Rubies are among them. Amethysts are among them. Other gems are among them too. Every day, thousands of people come to the mausoleum. Mughal rulers had built tombs before this one. Few of those tombs were for a woman. Unmarked tombs hold Shah Jahan's other two wives. Why build so magnificent a memorial for Mumtaz? He met her when he was a prince of fifteen. She was fourteen. Her name then was Arjumand Banu. An engagement followed soon after. Marriage came five years later, in 1612. Mumtaz Mahal was the title he bestowed on her. The words mean Chosen One of the Palace. She became the companion who stayed with him always. Travel took her everywhere he went. War was no exception. His battle camp was where she was when life ended. In 1631 she died as their fourteenth child was born. Her age was only thirty-eight. Heartbreak followed for Shah Jahan.

6The court historian said the shah's beard turned white. Crying was so constant that he needed glasses. Jewelry was given up. Fancy clothes were given up. Music was given up. Celebrations were banned every Wednesday. Wednesday was the day Mumtaz died. On each yearly anniversary of her death, the court had to wear white. The white clothing was for her memory. He picked the memorial's site soon after he returned to the capital. Agra was that capital city. The land he chose lay beside the Yamuna River. Say Yamuna as YAH-moo-nah. Garden mansions of Mughal royalty already lined that river. A bend in the river was chosen for the mausoleum. The slower current stopped the banks from being washed off. The river worked as a natural mirror. Light bounced from the water onto the white marble walls. He placed the Taj Mahal along the Yamuna, on its west side. River water feeds the channels in the gardens. Building began in 1632. About a year had passed since Mumtaz Mahal's death. The labor lasted nearly twenty-two years. No Mughal building project was larger.

7Workers numbered more than twenty thousand. A thousand elephants took part. Architects came from all over the world. Stoneworkers came. Painters came. Gems arrived from China and from Tibet, and also from Afghanistan and further countries. They supplied semiprecious stones. They supplied marble in different colors. Some white marble slabs that covered the mausoleum were enormous. The haul covered hundreds of miles. Carts carried the stone. Each cart was pulled by oxen in teams of twenty, or as many as thirty. Scaffolding, ropes, and pulleys formed a system. That system moved the marble into place. The mausoleum rises about 70 meters, a height of 240 feet. The dome is 44 meters, or 144 feet. Weight is estimated at 11,000 metric tons, or 12,000 tons. Twenty-two years went into the Taj Mahal. The cost in 1632 was about 32 million rupees. Today the same project would need about 1.6 billion dollars. That sum is four times the cost of building Disney World. Sunrise to sunset is the daily opening, on every day but Friday. Friday is the Muslim holy day. Moonlight visits are also allowed.

8The nights are the full moon and the night before and the night after. The holy month of Ramadan is the exception. The place is not the one Shah Jahan finished in the seventeenth century. After the shah died, the site was practically abandoned for years. Thieves took many gems. They took many semiprecious stones. Gold lamps vanished. Persian carpets vanished. Other decorations vanished. By the late nineteenth century, Britain's rulers had replaced the Mughals in India. Restoration of the Taj Mahal began under them. Neat lawns took the place of gardens that had grown wild. Damaged marble was repaired. Missing screens were replaced. Missing lamps were replaced. The gardens now resemble the restored look they had in 1899. New threats have appeared since the nineteenth century. Air pollution harms the soft face of the marble. The pollution comes from iron foundries and from factories, along with other industries. A yellow fungus called marble cancer adds more harm. It also discolors the stone. More visitors mean more wear and tear. India's government has set measures to protect the monument. A zone without traffic now surrounds it.

9The zone reaches 2 kilometers, or 1.2 miles. Polluting vehicles stay out. A wider protected zone bans polluting industries. Public groups and private groups are working as partners. Their work repairs and restores the structures. Challenges remain. Earthquakes have already been survived. Lightning has been survived. Wars have been survived. Floods have been survived. Luck, together with a great deal of hard work, may carry it through the centuries ahead. Artisans are restoring marble artwork of great beauty. That artwork was made hundreds of years ago. Morning light on the Taj Mahal gives visitors a view they do not forget. Later light does the same. Thousands of visitors come each day. They arrive from every part of the world. World Heritage Site is the title the United Nations gave the Taj Mahal. A vote across nations added another honor. Voters added it to the New Seven Wonders, a set honored across the world. Shah Jahan wanted a memorial for the wife he loved. He wanted the whole world to admire it for all time. Forever may be too long for the building to last.

10Centuries after the work, it is still among the most beautiful memorials ever made. Some words in this book have special meanings. Artisans are people skilled at a craft or a trade who make things by hand. Banned means something was no longer allowed. Dominates means someone or something keeps a strong, commanding hold. A dynasty is a line of rulers in one country who come from the same family. Geometric belongs to the math that studies angles and points, and also lines, surfaces, and solids. Islamic describes Muslims' monotheistic faith. Marble is a hard stone often used for statues and buildings. A mausoleum can be one large tomb. It can also be a structure that holds several tombs. A memorial stands for the memory of a person, a place, a thing, or an event. Restoration is the act of bringing something back to its first condition. Symbolize means an object, a picture, or a sign stands for an idea. A tomb is a vault, a chamber, or a grave for someone who has died.

6. A Run Called Hope

1Reporters listen as Terry talks, and his parents stand beside him. The moment is the end of his run. Contents. A hard road starts. School, then college. A crash, then cancer. Still an athlete. The plan. Across Canada. Support grows. The worst news. The race continues. Words to know. A hard road starts. Spring of 1980 is when Terry Fox set off to run the length of Canada. The effort would be historic. The goal was bold. He wanted money that could help people find ways to treat cancer. He also wanted ways to cure it. Doctors had amputated his right leg when he was eighteen. A prosthetic leg let him run. It attached above the knee, on the residual limb. Day two of the journey covered 32 kilometers, or 20 miles. A blizzard was blowing. The wind was fierce and full of ice. His plan was the whole width of Canada. This single day was already brutal. More than 8,000 kilometers still lay ahead. That distance is 5,000 miles. A family photo shows them resting together.

2From the left, beside Terry, are his father Rolly, his brother Darrell, his mother Betty, and his sister Judith. Childhood was spent in big cities. Winnipeg was one. Vancouver was the other. He loved inventing sports. He loved games so complicated they could run for days. Projects, once started, got finished. He was persistent that way. A run the length of a nation could therefore look possible. It would still be a very long project. As a boy he loved baseball. He loved soccer. He loved riding a bike. His little brother Darrell often played along. So did his best friend, Doug Alward. Love of sport showed when he tried out for basketball in eighth grade. Practice lasted hours. Many sessions started early in the morning. Commitment and effort won him a place on the team. High school and after. By high school he was in games on a regular basis. In time the coach put him in the starting group. During the last year of high school, the school picked a top athlete.

3He and his buddy Doug shared that honor. Classrooms went well too. He graduated with grades of A and of B. College came next. The future job was unclear. Maybe he would teach gym. Basketball, he knew, had to continue. Simon Fraser University took him in during 1976. That school had the strongest team in British Columbia, the province where it sits. Focus and determination were his tools. He meant to make the roster and play basketball in college. When things broke. He did make the Simon Fraser team. Then life shifted. Freshman year brought a car crash. The month was November. Serious injury passed him by. Afterward his knee felt sore. He told no one. Basketball practice, he thought, explained the pain. Late winter changed that picture. He was limping badly. His mother took him to a doctor. The diagnosis was not the sore knee people expected. A rare cancer was the source of the leg pain. Its name is osteogenic sarcoma. Nobody knows the cause. It spreads fast. It can threaten life.

4What cancer is. The word covers related diseases. Body cells start growing with no control. Almost any site can be the start. Bone can. Soft tissue can. Blood can. Cancer cells may travel through the body. Lumps called tumors often form. Normal tissue is destroyed. Only one cause of death ranks higher than cancer worldwide. A diagram shows a tumor, a cancer cell, a healthy cell, and the way cancer cells double. His first feeling was anger. He was only eighteen. None of this matched his plans. Treatment started as he worked through those feelings. A hospital ward became his room. Surgeons amputated the right leg above the knee. Doctors hoped the cut would stop the cancer from moving through his body. Nothing guaranteed it would stay gone. After surgery he learned to walk on a prosthetic leg. Chemotherapy followed for months. His body weakened. His hair fell out. The drugs were treating the cancer even so. Other patients filled the hospital. Cancer treatment was their reason for being there as well.

5He saw that his days looked like theirs. He met a boy of ten named Greg Scott. Cancer had taken one of Greg's legs as well. Life as an athlete, still. Sports remained open to him. Play continued, with some changes in method. Summer 1977 made him a basketball player in a wheelchair. He trained hard, building strength the way he always had for sports he loved. Running came next. An artificial leg felt awkward at the start. He adjusted. His first race was a mini-marathon of 27 kilometers, or 17 miles. He finished last. Contentment stayed with him, because he had completed the distance. The plan takes shape. Like many people who survive cancer, he lived with a chance the disease would return. He designed a way to help the search for cures that would last. Different cancers would be included. He would run the full span of Canada. People would learn more about the disease. Money would be raised for research. At each stop he would ask for donations. A journey of 8,000 kilometers, or 5,000 miles, would feel daunting.

6That difficulty was part of the point. More attention meant more money. The route was planned with care. Marathon of Hope would be the name. Doug, his friend, would come along and drive a van. Terry's stride was a hop. Springs in the artificial leg could reset after every step. Running the country. Training covered more than 4,800 kilometers, or 3,000 miles. Then he was ready. April 12, 1980, opened the Marathon of Hope. The start was St. John's. That city is in Newfoundland, the province farthest east in Canada. From the first day the work was incredibly hard. Days ran long. Spring in the maritime provinces can still be freezing. At breaks, Terry and Doug crowded into the van. They cut oranges. They cut other snacks. Highways in the countryside were dangerous. Trucks at high speed nearly forced him off the pavement. Legs ached every day. Wind burned his skin quickly. Sun burned it too. Some towns found him exhausted, with nobody waiting and nobody giving.

7Other towns met him with warmth. Whole communities lined up to cheer. A picture shows him studying a map during a van break. Support widens. Four maritime provinces of Canada were behind him before Quebec began. Each day he covered about a marathon's distance. Every week left him exhausted. Spirits rose when Darrell, the younger brother, joined the trip. As the country passed slowly under his feet, the crowd of followers grew. Late June brought him into Ontario. Dozens of television stations were covering the run. Newspapers were covering it. Soon it was obvious that attention had widened. The whole nation seemed to be following, and Canada's prime minister was among them. In Toronto, thousands stood along the streets while he ran. Money for cancer research poured in. Toronto City Hall gave him a roaring welcome on July 11, 1980. A map traces the Marathon of Hope across Canada, with North America around it. The start is marked at St. John's on April 12, 1980. Newfoundland is on the route. So is Prince Edward Island, with Charlottetown.

8Nova Scotia is on it. Quebec is on it, including Montreal and Quebec City. Ontario is on it, including Ottawa, Toronto, and Thunder Bay. The finish mark reads September 1, 1980. The United States and Mexico appear beside Canada on the wider map. The worst news. On September 1 the run stopped without warning. By then he had covered 5,300 kilometers, or 3,300 miles. He had been feeling sick. He had been coughing. Chest pains had started. Doctors in Thunder Bay, Ontario, were his next stop. They found that the cancer had come back. He asked to take treatment and keep running. Doctors said no. The run he called the Marathon of Hope had to stop. He flew home for care. His death would shock people. It would sadden people across Canada and far beyond. A large crowd later filled his funeral in Vancouver. The race goes on. Eight further months of treatment followed. The cancer kept advancing. He died on June 28, 1981. A few days later the funeral was held in Vancouver.

9Hundreds of letters of condolence reached the family. Poems reached them. Gifts reached them. Hearts around the world had been touched. He never completed the cross-country run. Even so, the Marathon of Hope met his aims. Millions of people learned why more research must be funded. Treatments were the goal. Cures were the goal. His wish to end cancer did not stop when he died. Family members founded the Terry Fox Foundation in 1988. It still raises money for cancer research. Each year, people join Terry Fox runs. A run lasts one day. Participants collect money to fight cancer. Cities all over Canada host them. Countries as distant as New Zealand have hosted them. Zimbabwe has hosted them. To date, the sum raised has passed 800 million dollars. It has not stopped growing. No complete cure for every cancer has been found yet. Progress has still been huge. New treatments have lifted survival rates for different kinds of cancer. Donations from groups like his have mattered a great deal.

10The run taught people something large. One person can change the world. Runners in Stanley Park, in Vancouver, appear in a picture. They honor his memory. They raise money for research. Words to know. Amputated means cut off. Limping means walking unevenly, often because a leg or a foot is hurt. An athlete is a person trained for sports, games, or other tests of speed, strength, and skill. A marathon is a long running race of 26 miles, about 42 km. Chemotherapy uses chemicals as medicine. The usual aim is to destroy cells that are cancer. Maritime describes the sea, sailing, or jobs done on the water. A condolence offers comfort after a death among family or friends. Prosthetic describes an artificial stand-in for a body part that is gone. Research studies a subject in detail so that new facts can be learned. A diagnosis is the naming of an illness or an injury. A disease is an illness. A residual limb is the part of a limb still there after amputation.

7. A Voice for the Living World

1Contents. A warning that came early. First steps. Writing beside the ocean. The book that moved a nation. A model for now. Words to know. A warning that came early. For months, reports had crossed Rachel Carson's desk, and she read them. The year was 1945. She worked as a scientist. She was also editor in chief. Her agency was the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Editing the department's reports was her job. Other biologists who studied wildlife were worried. The worry centered on a pesticide in common use. Its name was DDT. Mosquitoes died when it was sprayed. Other pests died too. Birds died in those same places. So did other wildlife. Tests also raised worry about humans over the long term. Officials in government ignored what the tests said. That July she offered an article. The magazine was Reader's Digest, popular across America. She wanted to explain DDT and the harm it did. The magazine said no. She turned to different work. Twelve years passed. DDT was being used more heavily than before. It reached her attention again. By then her books were best sellers. Fame was a new tool. She would spend it protecting the natural world she loved. Her method was simple. She would tell people what was true. First steps. Rachel Louise Carson kept happy memories from childhood. Exploring outdoors was one of the first. Those memories stayed among her happiest. Birth came in 1907. Home was a large homestead in the west of Pennsylvania. Three children shared the house, and she was the youngest. Her mother, Maria, walked the land with her for days at a time.

2Wildlife was what they watched. Reading was another love. Soon the girl was making picture books of her own. Birds filled them. Other animals filled them. She drew the pages as well as writing them. A popular magazine for children even printed her stories. At ten she already knew the work she wanted. She would be a writer. A photo shows her young. Maria Carson was determined. A bright daughter who worked hard should reach college. Money was always short. Robert Carson, the father, had trouble holding a job. Piano lessons taught by Maria brought cash. Odd jobs brought cash. She even sold her china dishes. The money went to Rachel's schooling. Enrollment at a nearby college came in 1925. English was the plan. A biology class changed the plan, and it changed her life. The professor became a mentor. The friendship lasted for good. She moved her degree to zoology. That field is the study of animal life. She excelled. High honors marked graduation in June 1929. Books had already made her love the sea, back when she was a teen. The summer after the diploma, the sea was new to her eyes. A lab on the Massachusetts coast invited her to do research. The lab studied marine biology. She went to the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. Marine science is what that place is built to study. Up close, she studied creatures of the sea. She also met them in the habitats where they lived. The summer felt like bliss. Aquatic scientists were all around her. Later she called that season an inspiration for the work ahead.

3A place at Johns Hopkins University was already hers. The school is in Baltimore, Maryland. More zoology was the aim. Family money trouble did not let up. Her parents moved to Baltimore and lived with her. Lab assistant pay made her the household's main support. Studies continued anyway. The master's degree was finished in 1932. She hoped next for a doctorate, the highest degree a school can give. Two years later, money forced her to leave the program. Writing, which she loved, soon mattered again. A photo shows her in 1932. Women in environmental science. Women who work as ecologists have frequently been denied respect. Recognition has been hard to win. Even so, women have added a great deal to the environmental movement. A few of them follow. Marjory Stoneman Douglas lived from 1890 to 1998. Florida's wetlands had a fierce defender in her. Her 1947 book took up the Everglades. She pictured that ecosystem as a river made of grass. The book helped keep development from destroying it. Margaret Thomas Murie lived from 1902 to 2003. For nearly forty years she studied wild country and wild animals. Alaska was one field. Wyoming was another. She helped create the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. She also campaigned so other wild areas would get federal protection. A photo shows her in 1974. Wangari Maathai lived from 1940 to 2011. She was a biologist from Kenya. She founded the Green Belt Movement. Kenyan women learned, through that program, to plant trees. Cut-over land could be restored. Conservation was part of her work. Women's rights were part of it.

4The Nobel Peace Prize came to her in 2004. Jane Goodall, whose years are given as 1934 to 2025, opened the study of chimpanzees living wild in Tanzania. She championed wildlife and animal habitats in front of the world. Greta Thunberg was born in 2003. This young activist stirred students across nations. Their demand is that governments face climate change. A photo shows her in 2019. The sea, and the woman writing about it. During 1936 she took part-time work in Washington, D.C. The office would later be known as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, or FWS. Her first task was short scripts for radio. The subject was life in the sea. A year on, the title changed. She became an assistant aquatic biologist. Science and writing could now live in one job. She could explain hard environmental science. An ordinary reader could understand the result. The reader could enjoy it too. She excelled again and rose. Soon she was editor in chief over every publication. On the side she sold science pieces to magazines and to papers. Extra cash was the reason. Death had taken her father in 1935. Mother and other relatives still depended on her. The first book appeared in 1941. Its title was Under the Sea Wind. A poetic voice described animals in the water and animals along the shore. Critics praised the beauty of the writing. They also praised the scientific accuracy. Sales disappointed her.
