Americans were fixed on World War II, fought from 1939 to 1945. She did not see it yet, but the job was the right ground for her life's work.

5Projects sharpened the writing until it cut clean. During those same years, the newest studies from expert scientists were in her hands. When a vacation opened, she and her mother fled to the shore. Birds held her attention. Tide pools held it. She tramped mud flats looking for natural wonders. A second book appeared in 1951. Its title was The Sea Around Us. Like the earlier book, it carried readers over the ocean and down into it. The language stayed clear. It also stayed graceful. Specialists loved it. So did everyone else. Critics praised it in warm, bright terms. This time the success was huge. Buyers kept it among top books for eighty-six weeks, according to the New York Times. Prizes followed, including a National Book Award given for nonfiction. A photo shows her receiving that award in 1952. Those earnings let her resign from the FWS in 1952. Writing could be the whole job. She built a cottage on Maine's rugged coast. The ocean sat just outside the door. Other subjects waited. One of them would become the most important work she ever did. A photo shows her in 1952. Her refuge. A wildlife refuge bearing Rachel Carson's name was established in 1966. It lies near the cottage of her summers. Along the coast by Kennebunkport, Maine, it runs for 50 miles, or 80 km. Wetlands of importance are protected. Birds that migrate use the shore habitat, and that habitat is guarded. Other wildlife uses it too. About three hundred thousand visitors come each year. Bird-watchers come. Other lovers of nature come. The book that started a movement.

6After World War II, science and technology looked bright. Atoms had been unlocked. Atomic bombs came from that power. Nuclear energy came from it. In medicine, antibiotics killed infections and saved lives past counting. No challenge seemed beyond science. Destructive insects were one of those challenges. DDT and similar pesticides were the chief weapon. Trucks rolled along neighborhood streets. The chemical sprayed houses. Gardens got the spray too. Planes released it over forests. They dropped it on fields. Officials told the public there was nothing to fear. A photo from July 1945 shows a young person at the beach. A new machine, on its first test, sprays that person with DDT. Salmon died because of DDT. Butterflies died too. They were only some of the victims. By 1957 her doubts about pesticides had returned. She remembered the DDT reports from her FWS years. Fresh reports were arriving from biologists. Naturalists sent them too. Where DDT was used, bird populations were dead or dying. Poison was reaching fish. Helpful insects were dying, butterflies among them, and bees among them. She started gathering notes for another book. The research pointed to a grim likelihood. Chemicals inside pesticides could make people seriously ill. Chemicals inside herbicides could do the same. Cancer was among the illnesses. She knew the proof had to be solid as rock. She would be asking whether giant chemical firms were poisoning wildlife. She would be asking whether they were poisoning people. Friends warned her. Those huge businesses would do all they could to wreck her reputation. Drafts went, chapter by chapter, to experts.

7The experts checked the facts. Personal blows landed while she worked. In 1957 a niece died. A young great-nephew needed care, and Carson took that duty. Twelve months afterward, her deeply loved mother died. In 1960 she learned she had cancer. Surgery slowed the book. Treatments slowed it. Spells of intense pain slowed it. Release came in September 1962. The title was Silent Spring. It pictured a world gone quiet. Birds no longer sang. Insects no longer buzzed. Chemicals had wiped them out. Inside, she set out the scientific case with care. Pesticides were shown affecting the environment. Herbicides were shown doing the same. Questions rose about harm to human health. The best-seller list held the book for over a year. A national argument ignited. The question was whether chemicals were a safe way to control nature. A chickadee is one bird the book discusses. Translators have carried this third book into over thirty languages. A photo shows her speaking to a Senate subcommittee. The month is June 1963. She did not demand that every such chemical be banned. She did urge tighter testing by government. She urged closer rules. She asked readers to think about long-term danger. Poisoning the environment was that danger. Again she showed a gift. Hard science became clear to people who were not scientists. Makers of the chemicals attacked, as friends had predicted. They tore at her research. They tore at her qualifications. Some attacks rested only on the fact that she was a woman. Critics called her hostile to business. They called her a fanatic about nature. They said she would accept starvation before she would accept chemicals that kept food on the table.

8In the months after, she answered calmly. Speeches carried her case. Interviews carried it. Other scientists stood up for the research. They stood up for the conclusions. Health was failing, yet she testified in front of U.S. Senate members. President John F. Kennedy pointed to Silent Spring. Other political leaders did too. To them it proved a need. Government had to study environmental policy with greater care. Summer 1963 brought her back to the Maine coast. Her great-nephew came too. They needed the rest. Of every place she knew, the cottage was her favorite. She would not visit it again. A 1961 photo shows her looking along that coast. Why DDT caused trouble. In 1939 a scientist in Switzerland, Paul Müller, built what looked like a miracle spray. The long name is dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane. DDT is the short name. Insects died. Birds and other animals seemed unhurt. Insect-spread disease could be stopped when outbreaks grew large. Malaria was one such disease. Typhus was another. A Nobel Prize rewarded his research. Through the 1940s and the 1950s, DDT was spread widely against insect pests. Biologists later found the poison gathering in animal tissues. The process is called biomagnification. Harmless at first glance, the chemical made trouble as years passed. Bird eggs turned brittle. They broke easily. For some birds, the drop passed 80 percent. Bald eagles were among them. The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States. Silent Spring turned a bright light onto DDT and what it did. Further research followed. In 1972 the U.S. government banned this use.

9Bald eagles rebounded. Other species rebounded too. How the poison climbs. Picture an eagle, then a big fish, then a small fish, then plankton. An animal that eats animals under it in a food chain also eats the DDT stored in their tissues. The chemical piles higher as it climbs the chain. That piling is biomagnification. One path through an ecosystem is shown this way. On land the same climb happens, except plants sit at the bottom. A model for today. In a 1963 speech she said conservation is a cause without an ending. There is no moment, she said, when anyone may claim the work is done. Death came the following year. Her vision of guarding the natural world did not die. The idea kept moving without her. Silent Spring helped start the environmental movement that followed, and that claim is fair. More Americans began to question pesticides. They questioned pollution that nobody controlled. Her writing fed new laws. Wilderness gained protection. Wildlife gained it. People gained it. The Clean Air Act dates to 1963. The Wilderness Act dates to 1964. The Clean Water Act dates to 1972. The Endangered Species Act dates to 1972. DDT drove bald eagle numbers in the continental United States into a plunge. By 1963, nesting pairs found there numbered just 417. Today the count is nearly 10,000. Rachel Carson is part of the reason. Love of nature was the root of her environmentalism. Ecosystems fascinated her, both for their beauty and for their science. She spent her working life passing that joy along. She believed people guard what they have learned to love.

10Humans, in her view, belong inside the natural world. They are not its enemies. A 1961 photo shows her at the Maine house, keeping company with a cat. Wild land is still shrinking today. Wildlife populations are still shrinking. Threats to the environment are larger than before. Climate change is a global danger among them. Awareness has grown at the same time. Activism has grown. Determination marked her. Courage marked her. Passion marked her. For the hard problems in front of us, she is still a hero. She is still a role model. Words to know. Activism is the effort, or the belief, that works toward social or political change. Inspiration is a good influence, or a spark that leads to a new idea or a new act. Aquatic describes plants and animals that live in water or near it. Marine describes whatever has to do with the sea. A movement is a shared push by many people toward a goal or a change, and it includes the people and groups inside that push. Conservation here means guarding wild land and the living things on it. Environmental describes whatever has to do with the natural world. A naturalist pays close attention to wild plants and to wild animals. Excelled means the work was done very well. A pesticide is a chemical or a biological substance that kills animals or plants seen as harmful. A herbicide is a chemical mix, or a biological one, used so unwanted plants die. Testified means gave answers while sworn to tell the truth before a judge.

8. A Voice Named Ella Fitzgerald

1The parts of this book come in this order. Spotlight Night. Growing Up Ella. A Band Takes a Chance. Hard Miles on Tour. A Singer Who Set the Style. After the Curtain. A List of Words. Performers point to the Apollo Theater as the room where Fitzgerald's career got going. Spotlight Night. Tellings of that evening mostly match. Called up to perform, Ella could not move. The light held her in place. Along one cheek, sweat began to run. Her gaze dropped. She wore boots made for work. Those boots felt heavy. Scuff marks covered them. Seats creaked as listeners grew impatient. A performance was what they had come to see. Nothing about this scared teen promised that any performance would start. Ralph Cooper was running the contest. Off to the side, he hissed a warning. His order was simple. His order was that she act. Frustration made his head shake. The show that night was called Amateur Night. Its stage was the Apollo. Harlem was the neighborhood around that theater. The city was New York. Cooper felt the whole evening sliding downward, and he blamed this girl. Ella then bent toward Benny Carter. A well-known band of his was playing behind every contestant. Cold air filled the room. The year was 1934. Her request was the song Judy. Carter said yes. He called her kid. Dancing to a piece like that one seemed unlikely to him. He told her to choose it anyway. She moved once more to center stage.

2As the band began, she cleared her throat. Nerves had not left her. The opening note broke in her throat. Together the crowd moaned. Booing started. Shouts told her to get off. Her heartbeat raced. She feared it might burst. In one picture, Benny Carter holds his trumpet. Panic showed on her face, and he noticed. The players halted and waited. Thanks showed in the look she gave Benny. A long breath came next. Then she nodded. Music began a second time. Her eyes shut. Boos no longer reached her. Only one song stayed in her ears. It was the favorite of her mother. Memory carried her home to the kitchen. In that memory, her mother lived. Young Ella danced there while her mom's voice filled the room. The final note drifted away. Ella's eyes opened. Nobody in the seats was moving. She believed the song had failed them. Panic climbed through her throat. She spun, ready to run off. Clapping began with a single person. A second person joined. A third followed. All at once the Apollo roared with applause. Ella turned toward Benny. His news was happy. The crowd was hers. They were calling for another song. He wanted to know what she would offer next. No time remained for an answer. Carter turned from her. The band jumped into a new piece. Its title was The Object of My Affection. Ella stayed right with the beat. Her grin was wide enough to split her face.

3She sang once more. Years later, the reason stands out. During her lifetime, Grammy Awards came to Ella Fitzgerald 13 times. A title stuck to her. People call her the First Lady of Song. One photo catches her just a few years past that Apollo evening. Growing Up Ella. April 25, 1917, was her birth date. Ella Jane Fitzgerald was her full name. Newport News, Virginia, was the town of her birth. William was her father. Temperance was her mother. Friends shortened Temperance to Tempie. Not long after the birth, the parents went separate ways. Yonkers, New York, became the next home for Ella and her mother. Tempie later had a boyfriend named Joe Da Silva. The household included him. Part of Joe's work was driving people. Tempie's job was at a laundromat. Extra money came from food she prepared for events. A child arrived in 1923. They named her Frances. Across their whole lives, Ella and Frances stayed close. One photo shows Ella while she was still a girl. Third grade was when she chose a future. Professional dancing was the dream. Street corners became her stage, and passersby got a show. Singing mattered to her just as much. Classmates turned into friends when she copied famous singers in a lifelike way. One singer she loved to copy was Louis Armstrong. Another was Connee Boswell. Dancers knew the Savoy Ballroom as the place to be. Its doors stayed open for that kind of night until 1958.

4Then the ballroom closed. A bit later, Ella and a friend named Charles often slipped away. Harlem's Savoy was where they went. Newest dance steps got practiced there until the pair could do them cold. Age fifteen found Ella and Charles taking those routines into clubs. The clubs were spread through Yonkers. Money came to Ella for the dancing. She was a paid dancer. Tragedy arrived next. Life shifted hard in 1932. A heart attack killed Tempie, Ella's mother. Only a few months passed. Then a heart attack killed Joe as well. An aunt in Harlem took in Ella and Frances. Grades sank during those months. Day after day, she was missing from class. Officers who track students away from school caught her. Their work was to see that children showed up. Those authorities placed her at a reform school. Its name was the Riverdale Children's Association. Rigid rules there met her rebellion. Suspicion remains that teachers beat her. Abuse is part of that same suspicion. Autumn of 1934 was when she ran. Housing was something the teen did not have. Tips from songs and dances were how she tried to live. The stretch of Harlem where she worked had a nickname. People called it Black Broadway. Come the 1930s, Black residents were most of Harlem. Stages such as the Apollo hosted entertainers who were already known. Out on the sidewalk, lesser-known acts played for anyone walking by.

5A picture shows Harlem during the 1930s. Nightclubs in Harlem were filling with talent tryouts in those days. Ella sent her name to more than one contest. Organizers chose her for a special night at the Apollo. That night was for amateurs. Dollars in the prize purse totaled twenty-five. About five hundred dollars is what the same prize would be now. November 21, 1934, was the date. Seventeen was Ella's age. Fitzgerald learned her real calling on that night. Dancing was not it. Singing was. Love went both ways between her and the listeners. She left a saying behind her. The road ahead, she said, counts more than the road behind. Winning that amateur contest did not convince everyone. Some doubted she could last as a singer. Appearance was the likely cause. Plain clothes meant for work were what she wore. Boots were on her feet. Glamour of the kind people expect from a star was missing. Months had passed with no home, while she cared for herself. Different clothes were beyond her means. A poster promotes a show she did with Chick Webb and his orchestra. A Band Takes a Chance. Chick Webb led a band and was still rising. At their first meeting he refused to hire Fitzgerald. A player from Webb's own band had brought her over. That player said he would leave the group if Webb would not listen to her. Webb backed down. A two-week job at the Savoy was the offer.

6She could sing with them there. Dislike from the crowd would end it. Pay would not follow her out. One detail is easy to miss. Age 21 brought Ella her earliest major hit. Chick Webb's orchestra was behind that record. Playfulness filled the tune. Wording came out of a nursery rhyme from the 1800s. A-Tisket, A-Tasket is the name of that rhyme. A photo catches Fitzgerald mid-song, with Chick Webb beside her. Crowds took to her at once. Affection grew inside the band as well, Webb included. Sis became their name for her. The Braddock Hotel is where they rented her a room. Clothes fit for a stage act came with help from some bandmates. Touring found her among the singers whose outfits drew the most notice. Inventing a look of her own became a joy. Records followed, made by Fitzgerald with the Webb orchestra. Decca was the company on the label. Several of those songs climbed all the way up the charts. Travel took the group around the country. Death came for Chick Webb in 1939. Leadership of the band passed to Fitzgerald. A split ended the band after three more years. World travel did not stop for her. Hard Miles on Tour. Moving from city to city was harsh for Black musicians, Fitzgerald among them. Racism met them often. One flight crew made her surrender a seat. White passengers took that seat. A booked show in Sydney, Australia, then fell through.

7Three days passed before any flight could carry her to Australia. Earlier years held a similar wound. She was aboard a train. Hours went by on her feet. Black riders were limited to one section, and that car was jammed. A free seat finally appeared. It sat in the section saved for white riders. She took it. Right away the conductor scolded her. He commanded her to leave. Outside a station in 1956, a photo shows a white officer of the police. He sets out a sign. Words on it reserve the waiting room for white people alone. Black passengers were not to share that room. An extraordinary voice let Fitzgerald do astonishing things. A Singer Who Set the Style. Popularity still found her, even with the racism in her path. Jazz singing had few bigger names in the world. She also helped polish a fresh branch of that singing. Scat is the name for it. Orchestra instruments got copied by her voice alone. Made-up speech sounds joined that copying. Bo-dube-be is one of those sounds. Rebop is another. Many scat singers slip off pitch. She did not. Scales could rise or fall, and her tuning stayed exact. Musicians call this gift relative pitch. Hear any note, and she could judge how every other note sits beside it. The sung result stayed in tune each time. Perfect pitch is a narrower gift. It lets a person name one note after hearing it, then sing that note.

8Relative pitch serves a singer far more. Respect arrived from other headliners because of the art she gave to scat. Frank Sinatra was one of them. Bing Crosby was another. Nat King Cole stood with them. Louis Armstrong did too. Mel Torme was on that list as well. A private title came from Torme. He named her High Priestess of Song. Celebrity fans were part of her public. Marilyn Monroe, the actress, was among the keenest. Peggy Lee, the singer, was another. A photo places Fitzgerald with Monroe at a jazz gathering. Hollywood's Tiffany Club was the room. A second photo shows a duet with Frank Sinatra. Louis Armstrong and Fitzgerald share a studio picture. They are recording a song. Her album count passed 200 during her career. Phoebe Jacobs was on Fitzgerald's staff. Fame, Jacobs said, never pulled Fitzgerald away from ordinary life. She stayed grounded. One tale got told often. A television interview had brought both women to New York City. Hunger made Jacobs want a stop for food. She urged Fitzgerald to continue without her. Hunger had Fitzgerald too. A street seller's hot dog was all Jacobs planned to grab. Fitzgerald chose to come along. Mid-meal, a man approached. His comment was that the woman facing him matched Ella Fitzgerald. Eye to eye, she met his look. Her reply was calm. People said that to her constantly, she told him. Off she walked, the hot dog still held in one hand.

9Confidence and a grounded air show in a picture from 1961. Care for others ran deep in her. Time and money both went to children who had less at school and less at home. Day programs for children opened with her help. Fundraisers for children drew her again and again. Ray Brown was her second husband. Together they adopted a boy. Ray Brown Jr. was his name. Later life found her devoted to a granddaughter. Alice was that child's name. A picture seats Fitzgerald next to her son. Song Requests. Guests at one private party got a question from her. Did anyone want a particular song? Rap was the request from a young man. Laughter rolled through the room. Her reply came right back. Word-play like that, she told him, had been hers since before his birth. Scatting started on the spot. Delight took the listeners. A photo shows the song she gave a cheerful crowd. Recognition followed the talent in her voice. After the Curtain. Death came in 1996. Her age was 79. Sales of her records had passed 40 million. Carnegie Hall had presented her 26 times. Movies had included her. Guest spots on television shows had been numerous. Headline status at the Copacabana belonged to her before any other Black artist. That New York club was famous worldwide. America's president placed the National Medal of Arts in her hands. France offered a matching honor. People know it as Commander of Arts and Letters.

10Music doctorates of the honorary kind came from noted universities. Yale was one. Princeton was one. Dartmouth was one. Yonkers was the town that raised her, and she lost her mother while still young. Racism stood in the way. Sexism stood in the way. Classism stood in the way. She continued. Few artists have reached what she reached. Legend is the word that fits. Every age claimed her as a fan. Every race did too. Every background did too. Those fans remain. A 1988 photo catches her in performance. A List of Words. Auditions are tryout performances. Actors give them. Musicians give them. Dancers give them. A compassionate person notices suffering. That person wants to help. Engagements are entertainment jobs. Each one lasts only a short time. Frustration is a heavy disappointment. It grows strongest when nothing you do can fix the problem. A gig is stage work. It does not stay for long. Impersonations copy another person. The copy may be a voice, a look, or a set of actions. The aim is to entertain. Improvised work is invented while it happens. Jazz keeps a strong rhythm. On top of that rhythm, players invent as they go. Petrified means deeply scared. Racism judges people by race. It treats some races as lesser. A reform school houses young people. Its aim is to change behavior that breaks the rules. Scat belongs to jazz singing. Nonsense syllables stand in for words. The voice copies an instrument.

9. A Water Road Across New York

1Contents. A blocked road west. A plan across New York. Digging the waterway. A project people mocked. Boats, wheat, and travelers. A change that lasted. Words to know. The United States near 1800. A blocked road west. During the 1600s, colonists who had come from Europe mostly kept close to the Atlantic shore. The 1700s brought little change in that pattern. Home for most of them lay between the ocean and a line about 400 miles inland. 640 km is the same distance. There the Appalachian Mountains stand up. They make an enormous wall. That wall is a barrier. It runs north and also south. The stretch is longer than 1,500 miles. In kilometers, that stretch is 2,400. Easy travel stopped at those peaks. People on the coastal side could not treat the range as an ordinary road. The transportation problem in this book starts with that wall. Later pages follow a New York plan for a canal. They follow the digging. They follow the critics and the opening trip. They follow boats, crops, and passengers. The close of the book tells why the waterway still matters.

2A list of words comes last. By the first years of the 1800s, people in America were living inside states. Some lived in territories instead. A growing number wanted land west of the Appalachians. That soil was fertile. Resources there were rich. Indigenous people already held those lands. Settlers still meant to colonize them. First they had to cross the mountains. They had to carry themselves. They had to carry freight too. Europe offered a model. People there traveled on canals. A canal is an artificial waterway. Those canals were popular. They moved people and freight in an efficient way. Could the United States copy that idea? An early 1850s painting shows Daniel Boone. In the picture he guides settlers through an Appalachian pass. Planning the route. New York set up a Canal Commission for the state. That group drew a route running across New York. Lake Erie would meet Albany by water. Lake Erie belongs to the Great Lakes. It sits in the Midwest of America. Albany is the capital of the state. The Hudson River runs past it. Boats leaving Albany could follow the Hudson south.

3New York City stood at the end of that river trip. Beyond the city lay the Atlantic Ocean. Buffalo would sit on the canal. So would Syracuse. So would New York City. Smaller places would prosper from their spots on the route. Rome was one. Lockport was another. Little Falls was a third. A map traces the first Erie Canal route. The waterway would help many people in New York succeed. Members of the five Haudenosaunee Nations suffered greatly because of it. Say their name ho-dee-no-SHO-nee. They were made to leave for reservations. Nothing was allowed to block the canal path. The route crossed land the Haudenosaunee had held first. Another name for them is the Iroquois. DeWitt Clinton gave the canal its strongest support. Voters chose him as New York governor in 1817. His campaign carried a promise. Jobs would come to places along the path. Money would come too. New settlers would come as well. Some people did not believe the canal would work. Indigenous land lay under the path. Communities of the Haudenosaunee depended on that land.

4Settlers would earn money from the trade route. The land would be harmed. The water would be harmed too. Thomas Jefferson was president then. He refused Clinton's plea for federal money. Clinton then paid for the canal with tax money from New York State. Art made in the 1800s shows crews at work on the ditch. The job started in 1817. Its first depth was 4 feet, or 1.2 m. Its first width was 40 feet, or 12.1 m. Beside the bank, crews made a towpath. That path was 10 feet across, or 3 m. Horses would walk there and pull the boats. Mules would do the same. The task was hard. No school in the country then taught engineering. The engineers mostly taught themselves. They had to navigate ground that was not level. Water had to flow the whole length without a break. Crews started in the middle section. That section was the flattest. Moving east, they changed how high the land sat. Moving west, they did the same. Sometimes they dug the ground down. Sometimes they piled soil to lift it.

5One picture shows an aqueduct beside the canal. Soil was not the only thing crews had to deal with. They built eighteen aqueducts. Each one carried the canal above a river. Some carried it above a ravine. Locks were needed at eighty-three places. A lock raises a boat. A lock can also lower a boat. For hard stretches, the lock technology was cutting-edge. Here is how a lock acts. A boat comes to water that sits higher than the water it is on. Or the water ahead sits lower. The boat goes in through a gate. Inside, the water is lifted or dropped. The change follows the level in the direction of travel. Once the levels are the same, the far gate opens. The boat sails on. A tour boat is shown entering a lock. It is on its way to a lower stretch. Mocking names. Clinton's rivals in New York kept joking as time passed. One joke name was Clinton's Folly. Another was Clinton's Big Ditch. The bill came to 7 million dollars. Around 130 million dollars is what that bill would be in 2019.

6People called the cost expensive. In 1822, Clinton would not seek another term. Talk spread that the work would go on forever. Crews reached the end in 1825. In that same year, voters made Clinton governor once more. October 1825 brought the big opening celebration. Clinton led officials along the route. Supporters came on that first festive trip. The boats left from Lake Erie. They followed the canal until Albany. Then they took the Hudson as far as New York City. At the ocean, Clinton held a barrel. Lake Erie water filled that barrel. He poured it into the Atlantic. The act was symbolic. Two bodies of water were now officially joined. A picture marks the celebration in New York City. The day is November 4, 1825. Farm fields and the canal appear together in artwork dated 1829. Westward travel for people was no longer the same. Westward travel for goods changed too. A crossing from Albany to Buffalo once needed two weeks. With the canal, that crossing needed five days. Settlers in greater numbers headed for the Midwest. Ohio, as it is today, received some of them.

7Michigan received some. Indiana received some. Illinois received some. Farming became the main work for most of those settlers. Sending freight east from the Midwest turned easy. It also turned cheap. Lumber was one natural resource there. Gravel was another. Soil good for crops was another. People began calling the Midwest America's breadbasket. Wheat leaving the Midwest was measured in bushels. The export count for 1826 was fourteen thousand. The export count for 1840 was eight million. Little Falls, New York, appears in an 1890 view of a barge on the canal. Freight could also move from the east toward the west more easily. Midwest families gained access to goods they had been unable to get. Stoves were among those goods. Nails were among them. Cloth was among them. Other basic supplies came from factory towns on the East Coast. Before any canal, Ohio wheat cost 100 dollars for each ton sent to New York City. Once the canal existed, the price for that same load fell to about 10 dollars. Seven tons would have cost 700 dollars before.

8Seven tons cost 70 dollars after. The extra cost before the canal was 630 dollars. Shipping was not the only use. Travel inside the country changed as well. Pleasure trips drew tourists onto the canal. Packet boats let them lounge. The same boats let them dine. The same boats let them sleep. Along the towpath, horses led the boats. Mules led them too. The pace was slow. It was about 4 miles in an hour. That is 6 kmph. A passenger could step off and walk a while. The boat could be caught again later. The charge was four cents for each mile. A mile measures 1.6 km. Tolls were part of the price. Meals were part of it. A bed was part of it. Those tolls helped repay what the canal had cost to build. An 1884 painting sets a packet boat near Little Falls, New York. Success brought a wider cut. In 1862 the width grew to 70 feet, or 21 m. The depth grew to 7 feet, or 2 m. Early in the 1900s, a larger canal was built.

9Giant barges could use it. Those barges hauled tons of freight. Pieces of the first route were reused. By the 1950s, other ways to move goods had appeared. Trains on railroad tracks were faster. Trucks on highways were faster. Both were cheaper. The old waterway turned into a place tourists liked. Leisure boaters became its main users. Museums now stand on the banks. Educational sites there welcome guests. A 2009 picture shows a tugboat at work. It is pushing two barges on the widened barge canal. South Street in New York City appears in a picture of the docks from the 1870s. Why the work still matters. From 1820 until 1850, New York City grew until four times as many people lived there. That change is what quadrupled means. The canal was a main cause of that growth. Before the waterway, the city's port was smaller than the port of Baltimore. It was smaller than Philadelphia's port. It was smaller than the port of New Orleans. Today this city is the biggest in the United States. The story does not stop at the state line.

10Indigenous land in the West was opened to American settlers. The look of the nation changed. Merchants could send freight across the country at a low cost. The trip was also easy. Among large building jobs of the nineteenth century, this canal had huge impact. As engineering, it remains exceptional. Words to know. Access is a way of getting or using a thing. An aqueduct is a channel people build so water can travel from place to place. A barrier is something natural, or made by people, that stops movement. Efficient describes a good use of time or of resources. Exceptional describes something unusually fine. Expensive describes a high price. Navigate means finding a way across a long distance. Prosper means reaching success with money. Quadrupled means a rise to four times the old amount. Symbolic describes an object, a picture, a sign, or an act that stands for an idea. Tolls are fees paid for the right to use a road, a bridge, or a waterway. Transportation is the moving of people or of things from one place to another.

10. Adaptive Sport and the Paralympic Games

1Japan's Chiaki Takada is mid-contest in a long jump final. Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, hosted those 2016 Paralympic Games. The Chinese swimmer is He Junquan. Say the name HU, then jin-CHEN. His Paralympic medals include nine gold, six silver, and six bronze. He has set several world records. All of this was done without arms. Beijing, China, in 2008 looked ready to yield him one more gold medal. He led the 50-meter backstroke final as he neared the last wall. The crowd was screaming. A reporter who was there put the excitement this way. Anyone present who had feet was up and using them. A short side note belongs here. A child who fell into a river was once saved by He Junquan. The child was in danger of drowning. His legs were what kept the boy from sinking. He used them to push the boy to safety. A photograph shows him competing at the 2008 Paralympic Games. The names Special Olympics and Paralympics can be confused. They are very different. Only athletes with intellectual disabilities may enter the Special Olympics. Age six is old enough to take part. Elite athletic competition is the focus of the Paralympics. The Special Olympics uses sport another way. The aim is to help every participant fulfill their potential, whatever their skill level. Washington State in 2016 is the setting of a photograph of Special Olympics participants. A swim race ends when a swimmer touches the final wall.

2He Junquan had to slow down. The only body part he could use to hit the wall was his head. That slowdown let Daniel Dias of Brazil tap the wall first. Dias reached it with an outstretched arm. He Junquan finished second. Silence fell on a stunned crowd. Dias had won the race. Junquan had won their hearts. At the medal presentation, a silver medal went around his neck. He accepted the medal with his teeth. He accepted the flowers with his teeth. A bow showed his respect. He had proved himself an amazing athlete. He had also proved himself a good sport. The Paralympic Games are about that spirit. Adaptive athletes are competitors who have one or more disabilities. The disabilities may be physical. They may be intellectual. Arms or legs are missing for some adaptive athletes. Others use a wheelchair. Others have limited vision. Many disabilities are not obvious, yet they affect life in important ways. A disability may have been present from birth. An injury or an illness may have changed that athlete's life instead. These competitors enjoy the contest. What their bodies can do is amazing. Desire plus hard training has let them compete at the highest level. From 1960 onward, adaptive athletes have entered the Parallel Olympics, another name for the Paralympic Games. Ancient Greece is where the Olympic Games first took shape. Athletic contests there were held every four years.

3Those ancient contests stopped in the fifth century of the common era. The modern Olympic Games started again in 1896. About fifty years after that restart, the first Paralympics got underway. British war veterans with injuries to the spine were the first group in the program. The idea belonged to a British doctor, Sir Ludwig Guttmann. His name is said LOOD-wig GOOT-muhn. Doctor Guttmann wanted his competition to grow as famous as the Olympic Games. Worldwide, nations joined the Paralympic movement, and his hope came true. The first official Paralympic Games took place in 1960. The city was Rome, Italy. About four hundred athletes came. They represented twenty-three nations. Eight events were on the program. Archery was one. Fencing was one. Swimming was one. Basketball was one. The first Winter Paralympic Games came in 1976. The host was Sweden. Nordic skiing was among the winter events. Amputees could compete. Visually impaired athletes could compete. Both the summer Games and the winter Games have followed a four-year rhythm ever since. A change arrived in 2001. The city that hosts a Summer or Winter Olympic Games must also host the matching Paralympics. A side note tells more about Doctor Guttmann. He was Jewish, and Germany was his original home. Sixty other Jewish people were saved from certain death while he still lived in that country. German officers were told the patients could not leave, because he described them as too sick.

4Just before World War II started, he and his family left Germany. Nazi persecution was the reason. A portrait shows Ludwig Guttmann. Today's Paralympic Games welcome athletes in ten categories. The categories cover physical disabilities. They cover visual disabilities. They cover intellectual disabilities. Relative ability in the sport is what sorts athletes inside each category. Organizers group athletes whose disabilities affect performance to a similar degree. A swimmer with a spinal cord injury may share a race with swimmers who have cerebral palsy. Athletes with missing limbs can share that race. Team sports use a points system. Wheelchair basketball is one example. Disability determines the points assigned to each player. A team may put on the field only a group whose points stay at or under a maximum. Perfection is not what the classification system achieves. Mistakes are sometimes made. Fairness is the goal that keeps the International Paralympic Committee at work. A 2016 photograph shows Great Britain and Spain in a wheelchair basketball match. Many Paralympic events match events in the Olympic Games. Cycling is one shared event. Rowing is one. Swimming is one. Alpine skiing is one. Snowboarding is one. Other sports belong only to the Paralympic Games. Football 5-a-side is one of those. Goalball is one. Sitting volleyball is one. Para ice hockey is one. The unique events are worth a closer look. In sitting volleyball, a player must stay seated whenever the ball is hit.

5The net stands 1.15 meters high for men, which is 45 inches. For women it stands 1.05 meters high, which is 41 inches. Several groups of athletes may compete. They include athletes with spinal cord injuries. They include athletes with amputations. They include athletes with cerebral palsy. They include athletes with brain injuries. They include athletes who have had a stroke. A full list of Paralympic events splits by season. Summer events include judo and wheelchair fencing. They include powerlifting, archery, and wheelchair rugby. They include rowing, athletics, and wheelchair tennis. They include shooting and badminton. They include sitting volleyball and boccia. They include swimming and canoe. They include table tennis and cycling. They include taekwondo and equestrian. They include triathlon and football 5-a-side. They include wheelchair basketball and goalball. Winter events include Alpine skiing and biathlon. They include cross-country skiing and Para ice hockey. They include snowboard and wheelchair curling. Para ice hockey is played by athletes with physical disabilities in the lower body. Sticks drive a rubber puck into the other team's goal. Players do not wear ice skates. Each player sits on a sledge. One blade or two blades run beneath the sledge. Two sticks serve each player. The sticks handle the puck. They also push the player around the rink. The five-player form of football, also called soccer, is full of excitement.

6Every player except the goalies has a visual impairment. Outfield players wear blackout masks so the match stays fair. A noisemaking device inside the ball lets players find it by sound. The playing field has walls. Tackles occur. Fouls occur. Penalty kicks occur, as in other football. Sighted guides stand on the sidelines for each team. They shout instructions. Goalball was created specifically for Paralympians with visual disabilities. Events for those athletes show how many ways a contest can be adapted. Three players make up a goalball side. The aim is to send a big rubber ball into the other team's goal. Jingling bells inside the ball tell players where it is. Every competitor must wear a blackout mask. Vision is completely obscured. A football match from the 2012 Paralympic Games shows the play. Blind athletes on the track, and partly sighted ones, also get guidance from sound. Spoken information gives cues. Clapping gives cues. Electronic signals give cues. The cues serve competitors who cannot see. While such sounds are in use, spectators must stay absolutely silent. A guide runner uses the lane beside the athlete. A tether, fastened loosely around both wrists, usually links the pair. During a race the guide may give verbal cues. A 2008 photograph shows Australia in a cycling event at the Paralympic Games. Visually impaired cyclists ride a bicycle with two seats. A pilot sits in front. The athlete pedals.

7The pilot steers. Swimming uses helpers called tappers. A tapper stands at each end of the pool. Each one holds a long pole. The pole taps a swimmer who is nearing the wall. Every swimmer must wear blackened goggles. The rule stops a partly sighted swimmer from gaining an advantage. One challenge for the Paralympics is wider participation. A wider set of countries still needs a route onto the athlete list. High-income economies send more than their share of athletes to the Games. Equipment is easier for those countries to provide. They are often better able to supply training. Success for Paralympic athletes depends on both. The problem is not limited to the Paralympics. The Olympic Games show the same imbalance. It is true of many other international sporting competitions. In many countries, prejudice still blocks athletes who have disabilities. Support for adaptive athletes is steadily growing. Support for Paralympic competition is growing too. Five athletes from around the world show the range. A 2016 photograph shows shot put medalists celebrating. Iran is one of the countries. Great Britain is another. South Africa is the third. Chantal Petitclerc is from Canada. Her name is said SHAWN-tel PE-tee-klair. A photograph shows her winning gold in 2008. At thirteen, she lost the use of both legs. She was struck by a barn door of great weight. She was visiting a friend's farm. After the accident she could not attend gym class.

8A different plan came from the physical education teacher at her high school. She swam during the school's lunch hour. At eighteen she entered her first wheelchair race. She finished last. She did not stop. Barcelona, Spain, hosted the 1992 Paralympic Games, where wheelchair racing brought her two bronze medals. Further Paralympics followed. Her career ended with fourteen gold medals. She had twenty-one medals in all. She set five world records. After she retired from sport, she became a senator. The seat represents the Canadian province of Quebec. Ntando Mahlangu is a runner from South Africa. Say the first part n-TAHN-doh. Say the second part mah-LAHN-goo. His nickname is Blades. From birth, a condition stopped development of the legs under the knees. Childhood was spent in a wheelchair. He could not walk. At age ten he chose amputation at the knee. The surgery let him wear prosthetics. He could walk. He could even run. Running blades reached him for the first time before that year ended. Jumping Kids, a charity in South Africa, was the source. Catching him has been difficult from then on. His first Summer Paralympics was in 2016. The city was Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Silver was his medal in the men's race over 200 meters. In the Paralympic running community he is seen as an up-and-coming star. He was only fourteen at that first Paralympic Games. Terezinha Guilhermina is from Brazil.

9She and her guide appear in a photograph after gold at the Paralympic Games of 2012. Say te-re-ZEE-nyah for the first name. Say geel-air-MEE-nah for the last. Several of her siblings shared a rare genetic disease. She was born with it too. The disease left her completely blind. Running began at age twenty-two. She had borrowed running shoes from her sister. Starting in 2004, she entered four Summer Paralympic Games. Her medals include four gold. They include four silver. They include three bronze. Colorful blindfolds in her races are a known part of her style. Momoka Muraoka is a skier from Japan. Say MOH-moh-kah for the first name. Say moo-rah-OH-kah for the last. At age four she was diagnosed with a condition. The condition causes swelling in the spinal cord. A wheelchair became necessary for mobility. Sit-skiing began at age nine. Paralympic training began at fourteen. Her first Winter Paralympics was in 2014, in Sochi, Russia. She entered three events. She fell in one. She did not medal in the others. The 2018 Paralympics were held in Pyeongchang, South Korea. There she won one gold medal. She won two silvers. She won two bronzes. The 2014 Paralympic Winter Games include a photograph of her sitting super-G run. Devendra Jhajharia was born in India. Say de-VEN-drah for the first name. Say JAH-jah-ree-ah for the last. At eight years old he was climbing a tree.

10He grabbed a branch that touched a live electric cable. The shock nearly killed him. Doctors could not save his left hand. Former playmates shunned him after the accident. They taunted him. They ridiculed him. He locked himself in the house rather than face the other children. Sport entered his life because his mother insisted. He made a javelin at home. He practiced with it on his own. At fourteen he won a district championship. He had no formal training. His first Paralympic gold came in 2004. The Games were in Athens, Greece. A second gold came in 2016. Those Games were in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. India had never had a Paralympian with two gold medals before him. Both gold-medal performances set world records. Mike Schultz, a snowboarder from the USA, competed at the 2018 Games. He won a gold medal. He won a silver medal. The leg he used was a prosthetic he had designed himself. The Paralympics began in a humble way in 1948. They have grown into a huge sporting event. They have grown into an important one. They, like the Olympic Games, show the human spirit when it is at its best. Top athletes are on display. They achieve excellence in the sports they have chosen. They are strong examples of competitors who worked hard to reach greatness. Years ahead will still see that spirit on display at the Paralympic Games.

11. Africa's Heavyweight Beetles

1In the wild, a Goliath beetle is about to eat part of a banana. Black bands and white bands cross its body, much as they do on a zebra. This beetle is as agile as an acrobat. It is one amazing insect. Adult Goliath beetles grow as big as sparrows. They weigh nearly twice as much as those birds. Their larvae grow even bigger than the adults. That size is why Goliath beetles count as giants of the insect world. A chart can set a human hand next to one beetle and one larva. A human hand can measure 7.44 inches in length. That length equals 18.89 centimeters. The same hand can measure 3.3 inches across. That width equals 8.4 centimeters. One Goliath beetle can measure 4.33 inches in length. That length equals 10.99 centimeters. That beetle can weigh 1.7 ounces. That weight equals 48.2 grams. A Goliath larva can measure 5 inches in length. That length equals 12.7 centimeters. A larva can weigh 3.5 ounces. That weight equals 99.2 grams. The hand in the chart is longer than the adult beetle. The larva is longer than the adult. The larva is also heavier than the adult.

2Length and weight together make the larva the larger animal. The banana shows a wild beetle at a meal. The stripes make the insect easy to see. Agile movement means a big body can still move quickly and with accuracy. Giant is a fair name for an insect of this size. A picture can place a rhinoceros beetle, a Hercules beetle, and a Goliath beetle side by side. Beetles come in many shapes. They also come in many sizes. Goliath beetles outweigh every one of them. Fossils from three hundred million years ago show ancient dragonflies. Those dragonflies had wingspans as wide as a hawk's wings. Scientists think modern insects have a size limit. They think Goliath beetles have already reached that limit. Earth's atmosphere holds less oxygen now than it held millions of years ago. With less oxygen in the air, monster insects belong to the past. No monster bigger than a Goliath beetle is expected now. A few beetles alive today are longer than the Goliath. Rhinoceros beetles carry massive horns. Those horns nearly double the full length of the body. Horn length is not the same as body size. It is not the same as weight either.

3Rhinoceros beetles cannot match Goliath beetles on body size. They cannot match them on weight. Goliaths win the title of heavyweight champions. The name Goliath beetle covers six separate kinds. Those six kinds are related. Most show black stripes on all of the body or on part of it. Early British scientists saw the stripes. They called the insects zebra beetles. No two beetles carry the same markings. That is true even inside one Goliath species. Different markings make the kinds hard to identify. Over the years, insect scientists thought they had found more than two dozen kinds. Experts today agree on a smaller number. They agree there are only six types. Each type has a scientific name. Each type also has a way to say it. Goliathus cacicus is said go-LY-uh-thus KA-sih-kus. Goliathus goliatus is said go-LY-uh-thus go-LY-uh-tuhs. Goliathus regius is said go-LY-uh-thus REJ-ee-us. Goliathus albosignatus is said go-LY-uh-thus al-bo-SIG-nuh-tuhs. One name is written with quotation marks around the second word. That name is Goliathus atlas, said go-LY-uh-thus AT-luhs. Goliathus orientalis is said go-LY-uh-thus or-ee-en-TAH-lis. Ladybugs show up in many neighborhoods. Other beetles show up there too.

4They may not look much like Goliath beetles. They still share several features with those larger insects. Every beetle has two pairs of wings. The hind wings are large. They are softer than the front wings. Beetles use the hind wings for flying. The front wings are smaller. They are harder than the hind wings. The front wings act like sturdy armor. They protect what sits underneath. When the beetle is not flying, the front wings cover the hind wings completely. The hind wings are the more delicate pair. Insect mouths have adapted for different jobs. A butterfly's mouth is suited for sipping nectar. A mosquito's mouth is suited for piercing skin. Beetles do sip tree sap. Even so, their mouths are especially well suited for chewing. Many kinds of beetles can be found on flowers. On flowers, some eat pollen. Others eat flower petals. Goliath beetles probably do not feed on flowers. Scientists think these supersized insects are too heavy. Flowers could not support that weight. A male Goliath beetle has horns shaped like the letter Y. He uses those horns for battle. Antennae on the head can unfold. Unfolded antennae improve how well the beetle senses its environment.

5Sharp claws give a Goliath a strong grip. That grip helps it climb. Hardened front wings protect the delicate wings used for flight. All insects have wings. Most insects have six legs. Those legs have joints. The body has three main parts. The parts are the head, the thorax, and the abdomen. An outside skeleton covers the body. Those traits are what make a Goliath beetle an insect. There are more than one hundred different families of beetles. In science, an animal family is a group that shares similar features. Goliath beetles belong to the scarab beetle family. That family also includes rhinoceros beetles. It also includes dung beetles. All beetles use their antennae to detect odors. They also use antennae to detect chemicals in the environment. Scarab antennae have a special shape. Separate plates overlap on them. The plates can open like a fan. Opening the antennae increases their size. Scientists believe the larger size makes the antennae more sensitive. Goliath beetles use their antennae to detect food. Rotting fruit is one food they can detect. Males use those same antennae when they search for mates. A diagram can show the antennae closed.

6It can show them half open. It can show them fully open. Expanding antennae help scarab beetles sense their environment. A cold case comes from a museum. Workers at London's Natural History Museum found a Goliath beetle in the collection. Several holes had been punched through its body. A scientist recently showed what made the holes. They were gunshot wounds. X-rays revealed a shotgun pellet still inside the beetle's body. The scientist studied where the wounds sat on the body. He reported that the beetle was shot while flying. He reported that it was upside down at the time. You might think giant beetles would be slow. You might think they would be clumsy. Goliaths are not. They are so skillful at flying that early insect collectors had a hard time. Those collectors had to shoot Goliath beetles out of the sky to catch them. Scientists today still have trouble getting near them. Scientist Dr. Brett Ratcliffe explains the problem. He says they are very difficult to observe in nature. Much of what scientists know comes from studying captive insects. Insect fans supply many of those captives. Quite a few of them like to raise Goliath beetles as pets.

7Goliath beetles live in Africa. Tropical rainforests are one home. Dry grasslands are another. These areas are warm through the whole year. A dry season there lasts for several months of the year. Wild Goliath beetles feed on fruit. That fruit grows during the wet season. They have mouths for chewing. They also feed on tree sap. Sap is most common during the wet season. Warm, humid conditions mark that season. Sharp claws help them scratch through bark. Under the bark they reach the sweet sap. Goliath beetles sometimes gather on trees. They gather where food is plentiful. Most of the time they stay on their own. Dr. Ratcliffe says they are not social insects. Male Goliath beetles defend the best feeding sites. They defend those sites against intruders. The head of every male Goliath has Y-shaped horns. He uses those horns to push other males away. Scientists think a claim on the best feeding site may help a male. It may help him attract females. When a female is ready to lay eggs, she digs deep into the soil. One laying can hold as many as one hundred eggs.

8The eggs hatch after about two weeks. Then the young larvae come out. The larvae are eyeless. They are wingless too. They spend all their time eating. They also spend that time growing. Rotting plant matter in the soil is what they eat. They may also eat smaller beetle larvae. They may also eat adult insects. About four months is enough time for these larvae to reach full size. The larger species can grow up to 5 inches in length. That length is 12.7 centimeters. A dollar bill is about that long. A large larva can have a weight as high as 3.5 ounces. That weight is 100 grams. Five mice together weigh about the same. After an egg hatches, a Goliath beetle still has four more stages ahead. Those stages lead to the adult. When the wet season ends, the larvae burrow deeper underground. They continue until they reach sandy soil. There they build cells with thin walls. The cells are similar to butterfly cocoons. Inside each cell, several months pass. In that time a larva's body goes through changes. It turns into its adult form. Wings grow and fold into place.

9Legs do the same. The outside of the body hardens into a protective shell. The adult Goliath beetle then stays in hibernation. It remains inside the earthen cell until the dry season ends. The wet season begins again. Moisture then seeps down through the ground. When the moisture reaches the cell, the hibernating beetle wakes. The cycle begins again. Adults in captivity can survive about eight months. Life in the wild is different. Goliath beetles must find food there. They must also escape enemies. For these reasons, life in the wild is probably much shorter. Scientists think monkeys might eat Goliath beetles. Large birds might eat them too. First those animals would have to catch them. Goliath beetles do a very good job of hiding in treetops. Because of that hiding, no one knows for sure. Inside the cell, a developing Goliath grows legs. It also grows an outer skeleton. The life cycle drawing shows the path from egg to adult. In Cameroon, in Africa, a male Goliath climbs on a human hand. Most of us have probably never seen an insect larger than a grasshopper. Picture the reaction in 1766. A navy doctor fished the first known Goliath beetle from an African river.

10Since then, these giant beetles have drawn insect fans everywhere. Enormous size makes them a sight to behold. Flashy stripes add to that sight. Goliaths are speedy flying machines. They are heavyweight champs. They are awesome insects in every way. A rare shot shows a Goliath beetle in flight. The place is the Ituri Rainforest Reserve. A few words help readers follow this subject. Adapted means changed to fit a new situation or a specific environment. Agile means able to move quickly and accurately. Burrow means to dig a tunnel or a hole. Captive means confined, or without freedom. Features means traits, characteristics, or parts of something. Larvae means baby animals that go through major body changes before they look like adults of their kind. Scarab means a type of large beetle with a hard shell that is often black. Social means naturally tending to live in a group. Species means a group of living things that are physically similar. Those living things can reproduce. No new animal enters the story here. The same giant beetle simply remains worth a long look.

12. Africa's Tallest Free-Standing Mountain

1A line of climbers goes up the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro. They are heading for the peak covered in snow. The mountain stands in Tanzania, in Africa. Africa's highest peak has earned a nickname. People call it the roof of Africa. Its altitude is 5,895 meters (19,341 ft.). It rises 4,877 meters (16,000 ft.) above the land around it. No freestanding mountain on Earth rises higher. A freestanding mountain does not belong to a mountain range. Tanzania is the country that holds Mount Kilimanjaro. The name is said tan-zuh-NEE-uh. It sits close to Tanzania's border with Kenya. Kilimanjaro National Park is a World Heritage Site. Officials established the park in 1973. The goal was to protect the mountain above the tree line. In 2005 the park grew larger. The added land protects forest lower on the slopes. Park status shields the habitats on the mountain. Its life forms stay under protection too. The government of Tanzania provides that protection. Mount Kilimanjaro began as a volcano. The buildup began roughly 750,000 years ago. The cause was eruptions along East Africa's Great Rift Valley. The Great Rift Valley is an enormous crack in Earth's crust. It lies in East Africa. Those eruptions built Shira. Shira is Kilimanjaro's oldest volcano.

2Eruptions at Shira ended about 500,000 years ago. After it collapsed, a huge caldera remained. During the next forty thousand years, two more volcanoes formed. Their names are Mawenzi and Kibo. Eruptions kept happening across a long span of time. Kibo's summit grew taller than the other two peaks. The eruptions also shaped many features on all three peaks. The latest strong eruption took place about two hundred years ago. Outside South America, Kilimanjaro is the tallest volcano. Shira is extinct. Mawenzi is extinct as well. An extinct volcano is not expected to erupt again. Kibo is dormant. A dormant volcano might erupt again someday. Black rock set against white glaciers is part of the mountain's beauty. Glaciers have helped shape Mount Kilimanjaro too. Their great weight cut into the rock below. Moving downhill, the ice carved ridges. It carved valleys as well. Glaciers on Kilimanjaro may seem surprising. The peak is only about 322 kilometers (200 mi.) from the equator. Lower slopes have warm weather through the whole year. Sunlight that hits the pale ice is mostly bounced away. That bounce of light lets the ice stay cool. People believe the name Kilimanjaro comes from two words. In Swahili, kilima means mountain. Kichagga uses njaro for the pale color of those snowy summits.

3The ice on the mountain is still shrinking, little by little. Global warming is one reason. Cutting down nearby forests is another reason. Cut trees leave the air beside the peak with less moisture. Fewer clouds form. Less rain falls nearby. More moisture then leaves the glaciers by evaporation. The glaciers were first measured in 1912. More than four-fifths of that ice mass has disappeared. Some researchers predict they may be gone completely by 2060. Glacier ice stores important information from the past. The record concerns Earth's atmosphere and its climate. For the whole of Africa, Kilimanjaro's ice is the only record of this kind. If the ice melts, that record will be gone forever. A large share of the mountain's beauty will be gone too. An ice core is a cylinder of ice. Scientists drill it from an ice sheet or from a glacier. Bubbles inside the ice hold bits of Earth's old atmosphere. Some bits are thousands of years old. Others are hundreds of thousands of years old. Scientists study these pockets of air. They measure how the mix of gases has shifted across long periods. Old temperatures leave clues inside ice cores too.

4They hold clues about other parts of the environment. Around Kilimanjaro's foot live the Chagga people. Small villages keep traditional Chagga culture alive. For centuries, human communities have stayed on these slopes or close by. Large groups entered northern Tanzania early in the eleventh century. They came from places across Africa. Many belonged to various Bantu tribes. They made homes on the southern slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro. They made homes on the eastern slopes too. They also settled Mount Meru. They settled the nearby town of Moshi. Together they became a new community, the Chagga people. Several other tribes already lived there when the Chagga arrived. As time passed, only the Chagga remained. The Chagga are Tanzania's third-largest ethnic group. They have remained speakers of a Bantu language. That language has several dialects. A dialect can sound like a fully separate language. German colonists arrived in the late 1800s. Missionaries arrived then too. Before that arrival, Chagga chiefdoms often fought one another. German colonial rule then forced order on the region. Afterward, the Chagga banded together. They built advanced methods for farming the slopes. They prospered. Tanzania became independent in 1961. After independence, the Chagga kept improving how they farmed. Today they are the wealthiest communities in Tanzania.

5They are also the most highly organized. Bananas are their main crop. In the rich volcanic soil they also raise yams. They raise beans. They raise maize. A coffee grown by the Chagga is famous far beyond Tanzania. That coffee now matters to Tanzania's national economy. As years passed, older Chagga ways of daily life shifted. Pride in their cultural identity is still strong. Moshi Town in Tanzania looks out on a beautiful view of Kilimanjaro. On the rim of Kibo's crater, the top spot is Uhuru Peak. Climbers from many nations try this mountain each year. The number is at least twenty-five thousand. It is the tallest mountain in Africa. It is one of the Seven Summits. One peak from each of Earth's seven continents belongs to that group. Many mountaineers set a goal of climbing all seven. Among them, Kilimanjaro is one of the easier climbs. Most paths to Kibo's peak do not call for special training. On Mount Kilimanjaro, the top of Kibo is the highest spot. Climbers do not need ropes. They do not need mountaineering gear. Good hiking boots are enough, along with camping equipment. Even so, the climb is not easy. Air grows thinner on the way up.

6Climbers must get used to it slowly. That care helps them avoid altitude sickness. A climb up and back usually takes from five to nine days. Success comes to roughly two in every three people who try. Reaching Kibo's summit is not the only reason to visit. Many nature walks suit guests with smaller plans. Day trips go to Lake Chala, a beautiful lake in a crater. Day trips also go to Shira Plateau. That plateau formed when the first volcano on Kilimanjaro collapsed. Trout fishing is popular in the mountain's rivers. The whole district is excellent for taking photos. Visitors add over $20 million a year to the economy nearby. Climbing and other activities create work. Guides find jobs. Porters find jobs. Hotel staff, food growers, and travel agents find jobs. Construction workers and still more people find jobs too. The whole region's economy gets a lift. Lake Chala can look blue. It can look turquoise. It can look green. The shade depends on the time of year. A striking part of a Kilimanjaro climb is the changing view. Climbers move through several ecosystems on the way up. Sea level sits far below the cultivated zone, which runs from 800 meters to 1,800 meters (2,625 to 5,906 ft.).

7This zone receives the most rain. Melted ice from glaciers forms many rivers there. Water is plentiful, so the zone holds farmland. Small villages stand there too. This zone circles the base of the mountain. The montane forest begins at 1,800 meters and reaches 2,800 meters (5,906 to 9,186 ft.) over the sea. Climbers start in this forest. Plants grow thicker on the south side. They grow thicker on the east side too. Those sides get the most rain. Monkeys live in the forest, along with elephants, leopards, giraffes, and rhinos. Other animals live there as well. The animals are hard to see. Cool forest slopes higher up are home to elephant's trunk flower. The flower is a semiofficial symbol of Mount Kilimanjaro. Above the trees lies the heather and moorland zone. Heights here run from 2,800 meters up to 4,000 meters (9,186 to 13,123 ft.) past sea level. Some lists split this belt into two zones. The zone is drier than the forest under it. It is windier too. Daytime heat can reach 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees F). At night the temperature can fall below freezing. Climbers often see clouds level with their eyes. Wild grasses are a main plant here.

8Giant heathers are the other main plant. The animal seen most often is the four-striped grass mouse. Bigger animals sometimes wander uphill. They do not remain for long. Giant groundsels grow in the moorland zone. They belong to the sunflower family. They can live where the air is thin and the land is high. From 4,000 meters to 5,000 meters (13,123 to 16,404 ft.) over the sea lies the alpine desert. Yearly rain there is less than 20 centimeters (8 in.). Few plants can live at this height. Survivors must handle strong sunlight. They must also handle cold below zero. Animals include birds that hunt. A spider that lives at high altitude is here too. The summit belt of Kibo reaches from 5,000 meters to 5,895 meters (16,404 to 19,341 ft.) over the sea. Almost no life stays here. Water is missing. Lichens are the main living things. The country that holds Mount Kilimanjaro once had another name. People called it Tanganyika (tang-guh-NYEE-kuh). It became free of British rule in 1961. Two years before that, Julius Nyerere (nih-RAIR-ee) spoke about the future. He later became the country's president. He said the people of Tanganyika wished to light a candle. He wanted the candle set on the top of Mount Kilimanjaro.

9He imagined its light reaching past the borders. The light would stand for love in a place that had known hate. It would stand for hope and respect in a place that had known neither. Nyerere's words turned Kilimanjaro into a sign of independence for all of Africa. The summit of Kibo is called Uhuru Peak. Uhuru is Swahili for freedom. Julius Nyerere was president of Tanzania from 1964 to 1985. The writer Ernest Hemingway pictured Mount Kilimanjaro in a famous description. He said the mountain seemed as wide as the entire world. He called it great. He called it high. He said the sun made it look astonishingly white. Nature on this peak is rich. Many kinds of plants live there. Many kinds of animals live there too. Some of those living things exist nowhere else on Earth. The mountain is a dramatic sign of what volcanoes can create. It is a fascinating piece of Earth's geologic past. Travelers arrive from every corner of the world. For them, Kilimanjaro is a peak to climb. It is a personal goal to meet. For people who live nearby, it brings prosperity. It brings pride. It is a strong sign of freedom.

10It is a strong sign of self-government. People of many different lives sometimes get to see it. For them, the mountain is a place of stunning beauty. These words help with the topic. Geologic describes land, rocks, soil layers, or minerals. Altitude sickness is how the body reacts when oxygen is short at a great height. A headache can be one sign. Vomiting can be another. Glaciers are big masses of ice piled with hard-packed snow. They last through every season. They creep downhill. A caldera is a wide basin with a bowl shape. The ground there fell into a magma chamber that had emptied. Montane describes cool country in the mountains. Evergreen trees and other plants grow in that country. An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the places they live. A plateau is high, flat land spread across a wide area. The equator is a made-up line circling Earth. It lies midway between the North Pole and the South Pole. A porter carries goods, gear, or bags for someone else. Evaporation happens when water turns from liquid into gas. Heat brings on that change. A summit is a mountain's topmost point. A tribe shares both customs and a homeland.

1Pages ahead: Jim Thorpe, 1887 to 1953, ranked above every other athlete of that century. His move into paid sport. Mildred Didrikson Zaharias, 1911 to 1956, sometimes called the other Babe. Play that seemed to have no limit. Jackie Robinson, 1919 to 1972, bold on a baseball field. Althea Gibson, 1927 to 2003, who went first. Jesse Owens, 1913 to 1980, quicker than the field. He kicked placements too. The school's baseball team starred him. So did the basketball team. Golf suited him. Tennis suited him. Swimming suited him. Give him a sport and he usually excelled.

What the king told him was plain. No athlete alive, the king said, stood higher than Thorpe. Another picture freezes his long jump at those same 1912 Games. Skill of many kinds is required. A run of 200 meters comes next. A run of 1,500 meters closes it. Ten events, kept in this order. The decathlon opens with a run of 100 meters. A long jump is second. A high jump is third. A shot put is fourth. A run of 400 meters is fifth. Hurdles of 110 meters are sixth. A discus throw is seventh. A javelin throw is eighth. A pole vault is ninth. The official record still does not hold his scores. Paid sport came next After the Games, the whole world knew his name. Congratulations arrived in a letter from the White House. Pro teams offered contracts that would make him rich. He said no. College football at the old school got one last season. Touchdowns that season numbered twenty-five. Points totaled 198. Marriage came too, to Iva Miller, the girlfriend from his college years. The year was astonishing. Baseball paid him starting in 1913, on the New York Giants. Swinging a bat, he was great. Covering the outfield, strength and speed made him great as well. Skill in baseball was real. Preference still bent toward football. That pro game was young in 1915, and Ohio is where he joined the Canton Bulldogs. Championships arrived three times: 1916, then 1917, then 1919. Baseball filled the summers in between. Leadership followed in 1920. The American Football Association made him its first president. Years later that group was the National Football League. He wanted the game loved by more people. Halftime was his stage. From the 50-yard line he drop-kicked a ball through the goalposts. Facing the opposite end, he did it once more. A statue of him greets people at the Football Hall of Fame. The figure honors pro football's founding father and the game's earliest true star. Across the twentieth century, no athlete ranks above him. A 1925 picture shows a Giants game, with Thorpe fielding.
