Mildred, called Babe, ruled women's basketball. She ruled track and field. She ruled golf. The decades were the 1930s, the 1940s, and the 1950s.

4Competition from her was serious and rough-and-tumble. Women of that time were expected to stay modest and polite. Texas is where 1911 brought her into a family of seven children. She was number six. High school showed her off in volleyball. Baseball did too. Swimming did too. Tennis did too. Basketball did most of all, and it was then the women's sport with the biggest following. Loss never touched her high-school team. Thirty points from her alone was a normal night. Twenty points from an entire team was what people called respectable. A picture shows free throws leaving Babe's hands. Track and field pulled her interest next. Lifting weights was a belief she held firmly. Few women trained that way. Work that serious, plus ability she was born with, showed up at a national meet during July of the year 1932. Eight events received her name. She won five. She also won the whole meet with no teammates. Squads of twenty stood on the other side. The Summer Olympics came weeks afterward. Gold and world records arrived in three tests: hurdles of 80 meters, the javelin, and the high jump. Golf is where wider fame waited, and no game stayed out of her reach. She did not pick up a club until she was twenty-one. Focus and determination then drove the swing. A thousand balls a day raised blisters. Tape went over the blisters. Hitting continued. Her first championship arrived a year on, in 1935. George Zaharias, a pro wrestler, became her husband in 1938. Golf is where they had met. Twenty years after the wedding produced eighty-two tournament victories. Seventeen arrived back to back in 1946 and again through 1947. The LPGA, short for Ladies Professional Golf Association, was founded with her help in 1949. The year 1953 found her at the peak of her play, and the diagnosis was cancer. Surgery followed. Doctors believed she would not play again.

5Four months was all it took for a return to the pro tour. Cancer took her life the year after that. She was forty-five. Family grieved. Millions of fans grieved. Achievements across a life in sport put her into a Hall of Fame for golf. A second hall, for track and field, took her too. Six times voters named her Woman Athlete of the Year. Nobody else has been honored on that scale. A picture puts Babe Didrikson at the far right of the frame. Hurdles of 80 meters took her 11.7 seconds, and that sprint broke yet another world record. Rights for female athletes had a fierce advocate in her. The push for equal treatment stopped short of every peer. Remarks she made about people of color were sometimes racist. One infamous moment went past words. Water from a pitcher was dumped on two teammates as they slept. Those two women were the earliest Black women on the Olympic track team of the United States. Athletic greatness here is beyond doubt. Character did not rise to the same prowess. Jackie Robinson lived from 1919 to 1972, and baseball had never seen a bolder player. Try to picture today's Major League Baseball with no Frank Thomas. Take away Derek Jeter. Take away Alex Rodriguez. Try the Hall of Fame with no Hank Aaron. Take away Willie Mays. Take away Roberto Clemente. Take away the many other brilliant players who are Black or Latino. The blank spaces are hard to picture. They might have stayed blank. Courage from Jackie Robinson blocked that. Determination from him blocked it too. Major League Baseball had its first Black player in 1947, and that player was Robinson. A picture shows Jackie Robinson. Discrimination pressed on people of color in many parts of life then. Sport was one part. Big-league clubs fielded white players only. Black players who loved the game built leagues apart from those clubs.

6Stars of real talent came out of those leagues. Large crowds came too. The Brooklyn Dodgers had a general manager named Branch Rickey. Keeping talent out struck him as wrong. Players were harmed. Baseball was harmed. Integrated clubs were his aim. He knew the person who faced racism and crossed the color line would need to be unusual. Jackie Robinson was the person he found. A picture remembers the U.S. Army in World War II, when Black officers were few. Robinson was one of them. Any hitter would respect his bat. Any runner would respect his legs. Any fielder would respect his glove. Base running of a daring kind excited crowds. Players on the other side felt unsteady. He competed with a fierce edge. A soft bunt could beat you. A hard blast could beat you. Character could beat you, and that mattered most. Minor-league ball filled a year. That year he owned the top batting record. His club won a championship. Age twenty-eight is when the Brooklyn Dodgers added him. Rookie life was hard. Opponents shouted insults. Pitchers aimed the ball at his body. Boos came from the stands. Teammates, some of them, treated him badly. April 15, 1947, was the first official day he spent in the Major Leagues. A picture shows him that day with other Dodgers. Dignity stayed quiet, and it stayed with him. So did determination. Temper did not win. Fists did not answer. The diamond did the talking, through his skill. Hitting in that rookie year was solid. Stolen bases led the league. Rookie of the Year was the prize. A batting title in the National League arrived in 1949. The Most Valuable Player award, the highest honor, arrived the same year. Pay in 1950 made him the Brooklyn Dodger with the largest salary. Leadership of the club was his as well. The lesson was about ability. Perform at that pro level and the major leagues were where you belonged.

7Black players soon found jobs on other clubs. Latino players did too. Players in this country's national pastime now come from every race. They come from every nationality. So does management. Integration of modern baseball is complete. Talent of every player is celebrated. A scholarship had come from UCLA. The letters name a university in Los Angeles, a city in California. Four sports produced varsity letters: baseball first, then basketball, then football, then track and field. Pressure later, as the first Black player in this league, was easier to carry because of that leadership. Althea Gibson lived from 1927 to 2003 and led others through a closed door. Baseball's color line may have broken under Robinson. Tennis needed a Black woman before the door would open. Sharecropper parents in South Carolina had her in 1927. At age three the family shifted to Harlem. That neighborhood sits inside New York City. She grew tall. She grew athletic. Street games around home were hers to rule. City paddle tennis, across the whole city, was a title she took at twelve. School lost hours because she wanted more play. By seventh grade she had left school. A picture shows the hard work she put into skills on a court. Tennis skill drew two young Black doctors. One was Dr. Robert Johnson. The other was Dr. Hubert Eaton. They were hunting young Black talent in tennis. Her game improved with their help. High school was finished with their help too. She climbed to the top rank of the ATA. That group, the American Tennis Association, was entirely Black. Competition at the National Indoor Championships came in 1949, and no Black woman had entered before her. Race barred her, that same year, from the U.S. National Championships. Today's name for that event is the U.S. Open. Twelve months later, an invitation to that Open arrived. Round two was close, and she lost.

8Respect remained. A year later, Wimbledon in the United Kingdom invited her, a first for a Black player. Few tennis championships in the world are bigger. One picture from the year 1956 shows her rushing the net at the National Championships held in the U.S. Study did not stop away from the court. An athletic scholarship came from Florida A&M. That campus stands in Tallahassee. She played tennis there. She played basketball. She played golf. Physical education was the degree, finished in 1953. The year 1956 was the breakthrough. A Grand Slam means the world's four leading tennis tournaments, all inside one year. No Black player had won one until she did. Wimbledon doubles, on the women's side, was also hers that year. Wimbledon singles followed in 1957. The trophy came from the hands of Queen Elizabeth II, ruler of the United Kingdom. New York welcomed her home with a parade of ticker tape. The U.S. Nationals fell to her before that year ended. Both of those titles were hers again the next year. Sports Illustrated put her on its cover. Time magazine did too. Female Player of the Year was the Associated Press choice, two years straight. The 1957 Wimbledon trophy passes from Queen Elizabeth II to Althea Gibson in one picture. A legacy as a top athlete was already safe because of tennis. More was coming. Membership in the LPGA, the Ladies Professional Golf Association, opened to her in 1964. No Black golfer had been a member before. Clubs across the country often refused Black golfers both membership and the chance to play. Where Gibson was allowed on the course, the clubhouse was often closed. Bathrooms were often closed. Threats said she might be killed. Insults from crowds were racist. She did not bend. Certain tour courses turned events that had been open into invitation-only events, hoping to keep her out. Players in the LPGA voted. They would boycott any tournament that did not welcome every player.

9Clubs gave way. Two sports lost a color line because of her talent and her determination. Black tennis stars who came later walked a road she had cleared. Arthur Ashe walked it. Venus Williams walked it. Serena Williams walked it. Golf events on her schedule from 1963 through 1977 numbered 171. Jesse Owens lived from 1913 to 1980, and people called him the fastest man. Junior high in Cleveland, Ohio, is where this sprinting legend first burst into view. His age group lost a world record in the high jump. It lost one in the long jump. A high-school coach wanted him on the track team. Work after school helped his family, so afternoon practice could not happen. Morning training with the coach began at 5:00 a.m. Stories about him grew. A national meet for high-school track saw the teenager tie a world record in the dash of 100 yards. The long jump gave him a world record that was new. One picture shows him leading at the Olympic Games of 1936. College athletes met in 1935, and more world records fell. The dash of 220 yards was one. The long jump was one. Low hurdles of 220 yards were one. The dash of 100 yards, at 9.4 seconds, was a world record he tied. Track and field had never seen one athlete do so much. An hour, more or less, held all of it. His back was hurt the entire time. Triumphs greater than the records were still waiting. His parents had named him James Cleveland Owens. Jesse was what people called him. An Olympic name that stays Berlin, Germany, held the Summer Olympic Games in 1936. The Second World War had not started. Owens made the trip, and the hosts did not want him. Germany's ruler was Adolf Hitler, leader of the Nazis. Their belief set non-Jewish white people above everyone else, a so-called master race.

10Black people, in their words, were primitive. Attitude from Hitler did not make Owens feel small. Threats did not either. Berlin's track was the proof. Gold medals numbered four. Olympic history had not seen that before. Home from Germany meant a parade of ticker tape and cheers full of admiration. Playgrounds in Cleveland later had him as director. Speeches made his name familiar. Young people, in this country and abroad, heard him tell them to give their best. America's Ambassador of Sports was a title the government gave him. The Presidential Medal of Freedom arrived in later years. Home in 1953 is where one picture finds Jesse Owens. Names that stay An amazing stretch of time, the twentieth century, built the pro sports world familiar now. It also produced athletes who rose out of a field already full of huge talent. Ability of a rare kind left the world astonished. Their sports were changed forever, and changed for the better. Their societies were changed the same way. Competing at the very top became possible for everyone. Memory will keep each of them as a legend of American sport. Words to know Accomplished: managed to do a thing, or to reach a goal. Dominated: stood ahead of others in success, influence, or power inside a sport or a contest. Achievements: results that effort made real. Integrate: to join separate ideas, or separate groups of people. Astonishing: able to surprise you. Intimidated: pushed into fear, or into a sense of being overwhelmed. Determination: resolve, the commitment that keeps you on a hard goal. Legend: someone famous for one special talent, or for one special deed. Dignity: a state in which respect and honor are deserved. Omissions: people or things that were not included. Revolutionized: changed something on an enormous scale. Discriminated: acted unfairly toward someone over race, over age, over sex, over religion, or over some other difference.
