Furry animals follow the frogs. Invertebrates have their own part. Life under the water has a part too. One part is about animals that stayed hidden in open view. A closing part asks what may lie ahead. Important words are explained at the end.

2Tamoya ohboya is the scientific name of the Bonaire banded box jellyfish. The name came from a contest. The winner expected a common reaction. Most viewers, the winner said, would blurt Oh boy! Imagine that you hope to find an animal species no one has named. Which place would you choose? Choose a place that no one has searched. Trips to far corners of Earth produce many of the new species. A microscope can reveal still more. DNA can separate two animals that look alike. They can still be different species. Busy places hold some new life forms as well. People walk past those spots every day. A single year can bring more than 15,000 new animal species. Set beside species already known, that yearly haul is about 1 percent. Known species already number past 1.5 million. Species are also vanishing. The pace is a record one, and it reaches around the globe. A newly named species gives scientists a thrill. It also matters a great deal. The year 2007 brought a newly identified monkey. Its forests are remote. Democratic Republic of the Congo is the country that holds them. Large eyes give the lesula a look full of feeling. Observers call it shy. They call it quiet too.

3The first animal scientists saw was not wild at that moment. A girl was keeping it as a pet. Twenty-eight years had passed with no new monkey species. The lesula broke that gap. The year 2010 brought yet another new monkey. Scientists found it through its calls. The calls were complex. Colombia’s Amazon jungle is home to the Caquetá titi monkey. About twenty other titi species share that jungle. A bushy beard of red fur sets this monkey apart. Its forehead has no white bar. Babies of this species make a soft sound. The sound is a purr, like the purr of a cat. Thousands of these monkeys would mean a healthy population. The number thought to be alive today is smaller. It is fewer than 250. The titi that was just discovered is already listed as endangered. A pea is about as big as the Matang narrowmouthed frog. Few frogs anywhere are known to be smaller. The discovery year was 2010. The place was the island of Borneo. Borneo lies in Southeast Asia. Museums already held examples. Those collections were a century old. Staff had treated the tiny frogs as young of a different species. Calls heard at dusk changed that idea. The sounds came from inside pitcher plants.

4Calls are made only by adult frogs. Full-grown animals, then, could be this small. The frog depends on pitcher plants. A female places eggs along the pitcher’s sides. Young tadpoles live in liquid that collects inside. Spike-nosed tree frog is a second name for the long-nosed tree frog. A herpetologist found the species during a 2010 expedition. The route led into New Guinea’s Foja Mountains. Few people had explored that country. Its distance from other places earned a nickname. People call it the Lost World. Size is not what makes this tree frog stand out. A long nose does. No other frog has a nose quite like it. A calling male lifts the nose. The nose then looks like a spike. The call ends, and the nose drops. The reason is unknown. The long nose also earned the nickname Pinocchio frog. Discovery happened at a campsite. The frog sat on a bag of rice. The same 2010 Foja Mountains trip produced the blossom bat. A bat is a mammal. Even so, people compare this one with a hummingbird. The nickname is hummingbird of the bat world. Nectar is its drink. A long tongue reaches the nectar. Rainforest trees supply the flowers. Feeding does a second job. The bat pollinates the flower.

5Seeds can form after that. New plants can grow from the seeds. Madagascar was the site of an expedition in 2005. That trip revealed Goodman’s mouse lemurs. A mouse is close to their size. Night is when these tiny lemurs move. They jump from tree to tree. Daytime rest sometimes happens in a nest. The nest is a vacant one that birds once used. Madagascar is the only place where lemurs live. Brazil’s tabletop mountains are the only home of Sazima’s tarantulas. Climate on those heights is not the climate of the land below. Animals with backbones are called vertebrates. Scientists think vertebrates are a small slice of life. Their share of all species is only 3 percent. The familiar animals sit in this group. The ones most similar to people sit here too. Amphibians belong in the group. Reptiles belong in it. Birds belong in it. Fish belong in it. Mammals belong in it. Animals without backbones are called invertebrates. They make up the other 97 percent of animal species that science knows. Some invertebrates frighten people more than others. Tarantulas can be in that group. Their bodies are big. Hair covers them. About nine hundred species exist. They hunt other animals. Small mammals can be killed by the largest species.

6Lizards can be killed by them. Birds can be killed by them. Sazima’s tarantula looks different from a typical fright. Beauty is its special trait. Dark blue covers the body. The color almost seems to glow. The habitat of this arachnid is extremely small. High mountains in Brazil are the only place it lives. Insects usually pass through several stages as they grow. Planthoppers do the same. Wings on a young planthopper are only starting to form. South America’s rainforest hid the troll-haired planthopper until 2013. Good looks may not be its strength. Its hair, at least, is striking. The strands are not true hair. Wax leaves the insect’s belly as secretions. Those secretions become the wild coat. One idea explains the coat. A predator grabs, and the coat breaks away. The planthopper then leaps clear. That idea is still only a theory. Scientists have not confirmed it. Greek stories tell of the Gorgons. Hundreds of snakes covered each Gorgon’s head. Hair was absent, and snakes stood in its place. Those beings gave this starfish the Gorgon’s head name. The year 2010 is when scientists found this starfish. It lives far below the waves. The depth is about half a mile. In meters, that depth is 800.

7The ocean there is the North Atlantic. This animal is a basket star. Five appendages leave the body. They curl, and they branch, and they look like arms. Tips on those five appendages can number five thousand. Plankton is part of the diet. Shrimp drifting in the water is part of it too. The tips gather that food. Walking is another use for the appendages. The animal moves along the seabed on them. Danger brings a third use. The appendages wrap the body. A tight ball is the result. The ball is a shield. Much of Earth’s ocean is still unknown. The seas are simply huge. The walking bamboo shark was not unknown for that reason. People did not name it until 2013. Spots and bands on its body do not match other bamboo sharks. Humans have little to fear from it. That is true of most sharks. Indonesia’s coast is where it lives. Color is what revealed the new species. Scientists saw that its coloration was not the same. Experts expect a length of about 30 inches. That is about 80 centimeters. Fins push the body over the ocean floor. The shark is hunting while it moves. A wiggle makes the motion look like walking. Rarity is a problem for these sharks.

8Indonesia’s government has begun steps that protect them. An olinguito can be confused with an olingo. The olinguito face is smaller. It is also rounder. The tail is shorter. Say the name as oh-lin-GEE-toh. For a long time, nobody noticed the olinguito as its own animal. People kept treating it as something else. Researchers caught the error in 2013. The wrong name had stuck past a hundred years. A teddy bear is a fair comparison for this mammal. Night is when it travels. It leaps among the trees. Raccoons have a family of relatives. This animal is the smallest member of that family. Ecuador is one place it lives. Colombia is the other. Thirty-five years had passed since the Americas gained a new species of this type. The olinguito was that next species. A species can stay unnamed even while people see it. They may file it under a species they already know. Similar looks are the usual reason. The match is on the outside, at least. Science calls these cryptic species. Genetic code is what finally separates them. DNA tools are spreading. Distinct species are being reported more often because of those tools. Dense brush hides the Cambodian tailorbird. New birds are nearly as seldom found as new mammals.

9A find inside a major city is rarer than that. The year 2009 brought this bird to researchers. They found it in Phnom Penh and in the area around the city. One bird turned up amid a road construction site. Tests, taken as a full set, showed a species of its own. Genes were part of the study. Feathers were part of it. A pretty song was part of it too. Warbling is something every tailorbird does. The songs are never quite the same from one species to another. This bird’s song marks it off from every other tailorbird. From 2000 to 2009, finds can be sorted by type. Insects lead, at 88,598. Plants come next, at 23,604. Arachnids total 12,751. Fungi total 11,984. Crustaceans total 7,070. Mollusks total 5,949. Bacteria total 4,417. Fish total 3,587. Everything else totals 18,351. International Institute for Species Exploration gathered the figures. A review is where the count was published. The title reads Retro SOS 2000–2009: A Decade of Species Recovery in Review. New species still surprise people. How many animal species share the planet? The estimates do not agree. They spread across a wide range. Experts do share one view. Discovery has not yet reached most species. Known animals also show hard problems.

10Populations of many species are tiny. People change the land. Habitats become small because of that activity. They become smaller still as time passes. Hope sits beside those problems. A new find can restart work to protect a habitat. It can also restart work to bring a habitat back. Rare animals in that place can be saved. Surprising animals can be saved too. Some of them are already known. Some are not known yet. DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is the code that holds genetic information in a living thing. An endangered living thing is in danger of vanishing completely. Extinction means a full group of animals or plants is gone. A gene is a basic piece of heredity. Traits move from parents to offspring through genes. Habitat means the natural home of a plant or an animal. A herpetologist studies reptiles and amphibians. A juvenile is a young person or a young animal. Maturity has not arrived yet. Population means every member of one species inside a set area. Something rare does not happen often. Another word for it is uncommon. A remote place is distant or cut off. A secretion is a substance, often a liquid. A plant or an animal makes it and lets it out.

15. Animals on Long Seasonal Journeys

1Caribou cross a river inside Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. African elephants move through Kenya on migration. A severe dry season can push their travel past 100 kilometers (62 mi.). A trip of a thousand miles, people say, starts with one step. It might also start with a swish. It might start with a flutter. Many animals travel by land. Many travel by sea. Many travel by air. Each year they go hundreds of miles in order to eat and to raise young. Some go thousands of miles. This move, made each season or each year, is called migration. The distance makes the trips impressive. The exact paths make them impressive too. The many hardships along the way make them amazing. In much of the world, seasons are marked by which wild animals are present. A summer forest full of birdsong grows quiet in winter. Early spring feels still. Then tiny frogs begin to chirp as the air warms. Some animals that seem to vanish are only dormant. They rest when food is scarce and life is harsh. Frogs, for example, dig underground for the winter. They dig down during a severe dry spell too. Plenty of other animals do not become dormant. They do not shrink their need for food. They do not shrink their need for water. The journey leads to habitats with enough food and water for adults and for young. In Australia, burrowing frogs leave the ground after the first rains of winter.

2Winter sends many animals southward on the northern half of Earth. In the Southern Hemisphere they do the reverse. They go north. Seasons on the lower half of the globe run the other way. A closed road helps red crabs of Christmas Island cross in safety. The crossing is part of their yearly migration. Some migrating animals cover a fairly short distance. Those red crabs walk 8 kilometers (5 mi.) each year. They leave the island's forests for beaches nearby. They breed there when the rainy season begins. Set that walk beside the flight of monarch butterflies in North America. These bright insects fly as far as 4,800 kilometers (3,000 mi.) in autumn. They fly that far again in spring. Monarchs pollinate many kinds of wild flowers. Milkweed is what they need in order to reproduce and lay eggs. Every animal migration returns at set times of the year. Exactly how an animal knows the moment to leave is still a bit of a mystery. Leaving before the food is gone is essential. What, then, sets a migrator in motion? For some birds, the length of the day is the cue. These birds are called obligates. Their bodies are set to depart at a fixed time, whatever else happens. The semipalmated sandpiper is one example. Arctic coasts are where these birds nest and raise young in summer. They feast there on life from the sea along the shore. They store fat. Extra weight matters on a flight this long.

3When days start to grow shorter, the sandpipers leave. The flight covers an astonishing 4,000 kilometers (2,500 mi.) with no stop. They head south to winter homes in South America. Most of the path lies over open water. No place offers a rest or a bite of food. Sandhill cranes on migration, about half a million of them, often appear when spring is just starting. They gather along the Platte River in Nebraska. Other birds seem to time spring and autumn trips by temperature and by weather. The sandhill crane is one of them. Their long route runs between the Arctic Circle and Mexico. The start may slip by days. It may slip by weeks. It may also come early by that much. The cranes ride tailwinds. They ride thermals, which are rising columns of warm air. On a good day those aids can carry them 650 kilometers (400 mi.). Waiting for the best weather lowers the effort. The journey crosses North America. Gray whales mate in warm water off Mexico's Baja Peninsula. They give birth there too. A mother waits until her calf is strong enough. Then the pair swims the long way back toward cold Arctic seas. Food is abundant there. No other mammal on Earth makes a longer trip every year. Good conditions can also start a migration in other species. Gray whales spend summer in cold water between Siberia and Alaska. They may eat for as many as twenty hours a day.

4In fall, ice spreads over the sea, and the whales turn south. They look for warmer water. A pregnant female can give birth safely there. On the journey they eat very little. The route covers 16,000 to 23,000 kilometers (10,000 to 14,300 mi.). Summer blubber, rich in fat, keeps them alive. People find their way with memory, with maps, and with technology. Animals on long migrations use several navigation tools as well. Birds and insects in the air carry a sense of direction inside them. Celestial bearings are the base of that sense. In daylight they judge where they are by where the Sun sits. Birds that migrate at night use the stars. Warblers do this. Blackcaps do this. One scientist cast pictures of a night sky onto a ceiling shaped like a dome. He wanted to learn how some night fliers pick a direction. Caged indigo buntings sat under the star display. They fluttered and faced the way they would normally fly. When he turned the star picture, the birds turned too. The test showed that star positions guide these birds. Cloudy skies hide the stars. What do birds use then? Birds can steer by Earth's magnetic field. Some other animals can too. Earth behaves a bit like a huge magnet. A magnetic field wraps around it. Certain animals feel the pull of that field at their own spot. The pull helps them choose a path. Researchers still do not fully know how this sensing works.

5One idea says sockeye salmon carry a compass inside the body. The compass aims them at their goal. At birth, a salmon can somehow tell its exact place in the magnetic field. That place is imprinted in memory. The Gulf of Alaska may hold sockeye salmon for up to four years. After that they go back to the fresh water where they were born. The swim covers thousands of kilometers. They release eggs, which is called spawning, at that exact point. They can sense the spot while coming in from the sea. In British Columbia, sockeye salmon return to the birthplace to spawn. Monarch butterflies raise a harder question, because the trip spans more than one lifetime. A full loop from Hudson Bay to Mexico lasts longer than one monarch lives. Butterflies born in Mexico must find a region they have never seen. Some animals are born ready to leave on certain days. In a similar way, monarchs are born ready to follow routes used by earlier generations. A magnetic map kept inside their genes may explain the instinct. Genes are the basic units of heredity. A trait moves from parents to offspring by means of a gene. In monarchs, genes somehow write the destination into memory. Thousands of monarchs can blanket one tree. The tree stands in an oyamel fir forest in central Mexico. They crowd together so they stay warm. They wait through the winter. In spring they fly north.

6Late November brings wildebeest onto Serengeti plains where the grass is short. Calves are born in February. In April the herd begins the great move back toward the north. September is when the herd fords the Mara River. By October they are turning south again. Many mammals on the move trust landmarks. A keen sense of smell guides them too. Two mammal migrations among the biggest ever recorded happen in Africa. Each year 1.5 million wildebeest take part in the great Serengeti migration. They travel between feeding lands in Tanzania and in Kenya. The route covers 2,900 kilometers (1,800 mi.). Grassy plains lie on the way. So does the rushing Mara River. The herds follow rain and greener grass toward the north. Zebras often join them. Gazelles join them too. Bats arriving at Kasanka National Park each autumn come hungry. By late December, when they leave, they have eaten more than a billion fruits. The bat gathering at Kasanka is just as astonishing. It is the largest mammal migration on Earth. Ten million straw-colored fruit bats come from nearly every part of Africa south of the Sahara. Northern Zambia's swamp forest is the patch where they gather. For several weeks they feast. The fruit appears after rains begin. By day they cover the tree trunks. At dusk they fly out to feed. Sooty shearwaters are dark birds that live by the ocean. It migrates vast distances over open ocean. A single path may cover 14,000 kilometers (8,700 mi.).

7New Zealand lies at one end of the path. The North Pacific Ocean lies at the other. If the bird needs 29 days, a typical day covers 483 kilometers (300 mi.). Choosing the right time is only one problem for animals that migrate. Choosing the right direction is another. A still larger problem is getting past hazards. Some hazards come from nature. People build others. A jackal is one hunter these travelers may meet. Many migrators are animals that other animals eat. They must watch for predators the whole way. Lions rely on Serengeti wildebeest as a chief food. Jackals eat them too. Crocodiles wait in lagoons and in rivers. Hawks hunt the fruit bats of Africa. People hunt those bats as well. Dates and figs make the bats plump. Hawks also hunt songbirds along their migration paths. Those paths are the flyways of North America. Bad weather adds more trouble. A sudden storm can wreck a bird's flight plan. A big flock may be forced down in an odd place. People call that event a fallout. One fallout of songbirds struck south Texas in April 2013. Thousands of tired, hungry birds landed on South Padre Island. The island sits off the Texas coast. People who lived there set out fruit. They set out worms. The food gave the birds strength to fly north again. Changing weather has also broken migrations on land. It has broken migrations in the water.

8A warm spell can melt snow early. Floods then make travel harder for animals such as elk. A flooded river can spill over its banks. Salmon on the move can be pushed off their route. When the water drops, they can be left on dry ground. A drought can leave little food. It can also start wildfires that threaten herds on the move. Barriers made by people threaten long trips too. A dam blocks a waterway that fish once followed. A highway across a migration path puts animals and drivers on a crash course. A fence stops range animals that are migrating. They cannot follow old trails to feeding grounds that matter. In Wyoming, migrating pronghorn meet a wire fence. The lower wire, seen up close, has no barbs. A pronghorn can slip under it and not get cut. Structures that people value can still harm animals on the move. Giant turbines turn wind into clean electric power. Their huge blades kill migrating birds. They kill migrating bats. Big solar farms kill birds as well. The Ivanpah plant in the Mojave Desert of California is one example. Thousands of birds fly into tightly focused beams of sunlight. The beams burn them to death at once. Researchers answer these problems with tracking devices. They follow migratory animals. The records go into studies. The studies show how building projects change the environment. The facts can help planners keep new buildings off migration routes. Knowing the routes has moved people to help rather than harm.

9Knowing how the animals behave has done the same. In Florida, a scientist tags a young loggerhead sea turtle. After the tag is on, the young turtle begins a 7,250-kilometer (4,500 mi.) swim. More amazing still, the turtles finish in only seventy days. If one species earned the title of grand champion of migration, the arctic tern would earn it. Tiny trackers let scientists follow this bird. It flies between the North Pole and the South Pole. The finding stunned the researchers. The trip was twice as long as people had thought. The distance was an incredible 70,800 kilometers (44,000 mi.). Many Arctic terns do not fly a straight line from north to south. The route bends back and forth between Greenland and Antarctica. Swirling winds are the reason. The winds carry them along. The added miles spare the birds a huge effort. They avoid flying straight into the wind. Some areas now build wildlife bridges over roads. They build tunnels under roads. The crossings sit where a road meets a land migration route. Bridges and tunnels keep animals and drivers apart. Both stay safer. Engineers are improving energy machines that hurt migrators without meaning to. Vertical wind turbines are being developed. Someday they may take the place of the huge horizontal blades on wind farms. Fish ladders, built for this purpose, now stand beside certain dams. Those dams lie on routes salmon use. The ladders let the fish reach spawning grounds without harm.

10Pollution weighs on animals already tired from a long trip. Facts about that harm could lead to rules that protect them. In Alaska, a salmon leaps up a fish ladder. What stands out most is that the journeys continue. Year after year, the animals set out, even with every obstacle. Trips across land, through the air, and under the sea keep these species alive. Seeing why the trips matter can move us to act. We can help the journeys go on for many years. These words help with the topic. Celestial bearings are a sense of place in space and in time. The Sun, the Moon, the stars, and other sky bodies are the guides. Dormant means not active now, but able to become active later. A hazard is a possible danger or risk. Imprinted means planted in memory so it stays. A magnetic field is the space around a magnet, an electric current, or a moving electric charge. Magnetic force fills that space. To monitor is to watch how something proceeds over time. A multigenerational event covers several generations. It can cover more than one life cycle. Navigational describes the work of steering toward a destination. An obligate animal must repeat a set behavior in order to survive. It may also need a set kind of living place. Optimal means best, or most fitting. Relocation means moving from one place to another. To trigger is to make something start.

16. Animals with Two Parents' Traits

1Long ago, Greeks pictured living things that joined two animals in one body. Centaurs were one imagined kind. Minotaurs were another. Griffons were another. Manticores were another. Those pictured beings may not be real. Real animal hybrids are. A hybrid brings together traits from different species. Hybrids show up more often than people expect. Two parents of different species make a hybrid animal. A horse is one species. A donkey is another. Their looks are close enough for mating. Their behavior is close enough too. The baby is a mule when the mother is the horse. The baby is a hinny when the mother is the donkey. A cross of species does not always yield hybrid young. Parents that differ too widely may produce no live offspring. The young may be weak instead. They may be unhealthy. Healthy young from two species usually mix what each parent is like. The closer the parent species are, the better the chance of healthy hybrid young. A chart gives the baby's name from which parent is female and which is male. A horse mother and a donkey father produce a mule. A donkey mother and a horse father produce a hinny. Names of hybrids often change with which species was the mother and which was the father. Characteristics of the hybrid often follow the mother's species.

2Among these mixes, mules are generally larger than hinnies. Mules are generally hardier than hinnies too. Most hybrids cannot reproduce. Eggs and sperm are reproductive cells, and they are harder to make than ordinary body cells. Consider the mule. Every body cell takes half its DNA from the mother, a horse. The other half comes from the father, a donkey. DNA molecules store the instructions a cell follows. Hair color is one such instruction. Ear shape is another. The same molecules carry what makes a horse a horse. They carry what makes a donkey a donkey. Horse DNA and donkey DNA share a great deal of that information. Mules can survive because so much information is shared. Their cells lack a complete horse DNA set. They also lack a complete donkey DNA set. What they need in order to function is still all there. The arrangement of that information differs between horse DNA and donkey DNA. Reproductive cells fail to form properly when those mismatched molecules are used. Parent species must be closely related if mating is to produce hybrid young. They must be related even more closely if those young are to make healthy reproductive cells. Breeding of hybrids, including mules, goes back to ancient times. A mule handles hardship better than a horse.

3A mule keeps its feet better than a horse. Heat affects a mule less. A mule is hurt less often. Zebroids are a later hybrid, sometimes the name for zebra mixes. A wild zebra is extremely hard to train. Many diseases of horses and of donkeys leave wild zebras unharmed. The zebroid takes a gentler personality from the domesticated parent. Fighting off disease comes from the wild parent. A hybrid of zebra and donkey shows marks of both parents. Beefalo is another mix from recent times. It joins bison, also known as buffalo, with domesticated cattle. Bison handle hardship much better than cattle do. Their meat carries less fat than standard beef. Handling bison is hard, which is also true of many wild animals. They can be dangerous. A beefalo is as easy to manage as ordinary cattle. The hardiness of bison is in the beefalo. The independence of bison is in it too. Beefalo can take extreme heat, as bison can. They can take extreme cold too. The meat is low in fat. It is low in the bad type of cholesterol. It holds more protein than beef. The father of a liger is a male lion. The mother of a liger is a female tiger. Ligers grow to about twice the size of either parent species.

4Nearly 1,200 pounds, equal to 544 kilograms, is the weight of the heaviest healthy male on record. Their usual color is yellowish-brown, the lion color. Bellies are pale. Stripes are faint, the tiger pattern. Ligers do not appear in nature. Lions live in one habitat, and tigers live in another. Accredited zoos refuse to interbreed these big cats. Some independent breeders still raise big-cat mixes as curiosities. A leopon comes from a leopard crossed with a lion. A jagulep comes from a jaguar crossed with a leopard. A lijagulep comes from a lion crossed with a jagulep. Hercules, known as the world's biggest cat, poses beside his little brother Aries. Both cats are ligers. Until not long ago, people could get hybrids only from species close enough to mate. Some species are somewhat alike but cannot mate. Some will not mate. Hybrids of those species did not exist. Camels and llamas are an example. Given the chance, they would still rarely mate. Medicine can now fertilize an egg inside a test tube. That step made a camel-llama hybrid possible. The hybrid is called a cama. Scientists hope it will carry the camel's strength. They hope it will carry the camel's hardiness. They hope it will carry the llama's sweeter disposition. Hybrids can appear whenever related species interbreed.

5Sharing an environment is enough to make that possible. Spotting a hybrid can be surprisingly hard. It is also hard to say when two animals are separate species. Scientists often define a species by two traits. The animals must have the potential to interbreed out in nature. If they do interbreed, the offspring must be healthy and fertile. Fertile means those offspring can reproduce. Looks by themselves can confuse the question. Dog breeds can look very different and still be one species. A Great Dane is one breed in that pair. A Chihuahua is the other. Fruit flies can look like twins and still belong to different species. Ring species make the border between hybrids and separate species hard to see. Picture preschoolers sitting in a circle to understand a ring. Each child stands for a separate species. Each child can reach two others. Seven salamanders illustrate the idea. One is picta, said PIK-tuh. One is oregonensis, said or-e-guh-NEN-sis. One is platensis, said plah-TEN-sis. One is xanthoptica, said zan-THOP-ti-kuh. One is croceater, said KROH-see-ay-tur. One is eschscholtzii, said es-SHOHLT-zee-y. One is klauberi, said KLOU-bur-y. These salamanders began as one species. Their traits split as they traveled south. The San Joaquin Valley sits inside the ring these salamanders formed. San Joaquin is said wah-KEEN. Each can still interbreed with the neighbor beside it.

6Where the extremes overlap, that stops. The pair in southern California does not interbreed. At that point the ring is broken. Now picture the children in a game of telephone. A whisper starts with the opening child and moves to the next one. The whisper continues from child to child. The last child usually hears something unlike the starting words. Change around a ring of species works in that same way. Each species is like the species on either side. The likeness is enough for interbreeding. This holds until the circle comes back to the start. The starting species and the ending species differ the most. Those two cannot interbreed. Ensatina eschscholtzii is the salamander in this ring. Evidence points to slow change in the members of a ring species. They change while they adapt to particular conditions around them. In some regions, the ranges of separate species overlap. Hybrids arise in those overlaps. Animals of each parent species greatly outnumber the hybrids. Parent populations therefore stay mostly the same. Species that had been isolated are sometimes pushed together all at once. Hybrids can then cause trouble for the parent species. They may compete for food. They may compete for territory. They may compete for other resources. They may compete for mates. Genes of the original species can shift when hybrids rival the parents for mates.

7Over recent decades, many species that had been apart have been brought together. Climate change is behind that contact. The Arctic has felt the greatest effects. Some native species there are shifting the ranges they naturally use. Rising temperatures are one reason. Melting sea ice is another. Animals from farther south used to find northern lands too cold. Those animals now stretch their ranges toward the north. Species once separated by geography now interbreed. Grizzly bears and polar bears are one pair. In 2006, people spotted one of the first hybrids of those bears. The animal is called a grolar bear. Its fur was thick and white. Its legs were brown. Its paws were brown. Its head was wide, in the grizzly shape. More grolar bears have been found since then. The finds suggest that grizzlies and polar bears interbreed regularly in the wild. One bear in a picture is not confirmed as a grizzly-polar hybrid. Its body shape still suggests that mix. Its short neck suggests the same. Its face looks odd beside other polar bears, and that suggests the same. Cubs from this pairing might show brown together with white. Is the result a serious matter? A world full of polar bears might make the answer no.

8Polar bears, however, risk extinction. Every birth of a polar bear counts. The issue turns into a numbers game. Genes specialized for the harsh Arctic get diluted as polar bears interbreed with grizzlies more often. Grizzly genes cause that dilution. Polar bears might, at last, simply be gone. A grolar bear may also fit poorly in either parent's environment. At a zoo in Germany, grolar bears still seem drawn to hunt seals the way a polar bear is. They do not seem to keep that bear's powerful swimming. No one yet knows whether wild hybrids last as well as animals that are not hybrids. Suppose the wanted traits come from species too different for mating even in a test tube. Spider silk is one trait, and only spiders can make it. Lots of milk is the other trait, and only mammals can make it. Spider silk outmatches steel in strength. It also outmatches steel in flexibility. Bacterial growth has trouble taking hold on it. Those qualities suit many medical jobs. Researchers hope to form artificial ligaments from the silk. They hope for stitches nearly impossible to see, for people having eye surgery. One ounce of silk takes fourteen thousand spiders. A spider often eats the spider living beside it. A big spider farm is impossible for that reason.

9Scientists instead used genetic engineering, direct work on an animal's genes. Goat DNA was given the proteins that build spider silk. Milk from those goats then carries the spider silk proteins. Milk is simple to collect. Researchers hope one day to engineer goats that produce spider silk in amounts useful to sell. The transfer of spider genes into goat cells happened in a laboratory. For that reason, spider goats are transgenic animals, not hybrids. In earlier years, scientists treated animal hybrids as a dead end in evolution. Sterile was the state of most hybrids. Even hybrids able to reproduce usually carried a blend of the parents' traits. Each parent was probably a strong fit for its own environment. Blending the traits would fit the young to neither environment. What we usually find in nature matches that expectation. A hybrid species is usually a weak fit for the place it lives. Survival often does not follow. Reproduction often does not follow. Drastic change in the environment can face a species. The species may be unable to adapt quickly enough to stay alive. Hybrids offer two species a way to exchange genetic information. Traits gained by a hybrid might let it live where one parent could not. They might let it live where both parents could not. Might hybrids put at-risk species, polar bears among them, in danger?

10Or are hybrids a natural help when environments change quickly? A share of both may be true. Time alone will answer. Some words in this book have special meanings. Offspring are a person's children, or the young of another animal, and the word can also mean descendants. Adapt means to change so that a living thing fits a new situation or a particular environment. Reproduce means to make young that are like the original living thing. DNA works as a code that stores genetic information for a living thing. A species is a group of living things that look alike in body and can reproduce. Fertilize means to join male and female reproductive cells so a new animal or plant can begin. Sterile describes a living thing that cannot produce offspring. Genetic describes heredity and the differences passed through living things. A test tube is a narrow glass tube shut at one end, a common tool in science labs. Offspring count as hybrids when the parents differ in type, in breed, or in species. Transgenic describes an organism whose DNA was changed by genes brought in from another species or breed. Interbreeding is mating across two species so the young combine traits from each parent, also called crossbreeding.

17. Anne Frank’s Hidden Years

1Today the Anne Frank House is a museum. The rooms have been restored. The rooms match their look from the time the family was hiding. Yearly visits to the site pass one million. July 5, 1942, in the afternoon, was when the bell at the door sounded. Anne Frank was thirteen years old. She expected the caller to be a friend. The postman instead carried a letter meant for Margot, the older sister. The letter told Margot to report for transport. The letter called the destination a work camp. Edith Frank, mother of both girls, was badly shaken by that news. Almost three years of World War II were already behind the family. Much of Europe was already under German control. Jewish families such as the Franks were being gathered in growing numbers. They were sent to concentration camps. Otto Frank arrived home. He reassured his daughters. He promised the family would not be split apart. Secret plans were already in place, made by Otto and by Edith. Both girls were told to fill their school bags. A diary was the first object Anne placed inside her bag. The diary had a red-and-green checkered cover. She had already begun to fill it with her private thoughts. The next morning, the Franks left their home. Heavy rain was falling. A small warehouse was where they went. That building was part of a company Otto had owned before German troops invaded. An apartment hidden upstairs swallowed them from public view.

2They would hide there for more than two years. During that time, Anne poured her thoughts onto paper. She poured her feelings onto paper too. The account ahead follows the family into hiding. It follows the storm of hate and war. It follows life under Nazi occupation. It follows Anne's escape into her diary. It follows the day they were caught. It follows a tragic end. Family pictures show Edith Frank. They show baby Anne with Edith. They show Otto Frank. They show Margot Frank. One picture shows Margot, Otto, and Anne together. Otto Frank was an officer for Germany during World War I. Those fighting years ran from 1914 to 1918. Frankfurt, in Germany, was where he made his home once the fighting stopped. Everyone who described him called him kind. He was smart. He was hardworking. Edith's family was Jewish, and it was wealthy. Before she met Otto, she worked for her family's business. She married Otto in 1925. They soon had two daughters. Margot was born in 1926. Annelies Marie Frank was born on June 12, 1929. People called her Anne. Germany's loss in World War I left the country in deep trouble. The country was left broke. Many Germans felt angry. Many felt desperate. Rival political groups fought one another for power over the government. Germany felt the Great Depression with special force starting in 1929. Adolf Hitler used that public desperation for his own gain. Hitler had also served during World War I, just as Otto had.

3Hitler was antisemitic. In his telling, Jewish people inside Germany had caused the nation's loss. A picture shows Adolf Hitler at the center of a group in 1933. The party under Hitler's lead was called the Nazis. More Germans looked to that party, and its power grew. Those Germans wanted the Nazis to solve their problems. Full command of Germany's government passed to Hitler and his party in 1933. Otto and Edith Frank saw the danger at once. Law followed law under Nazi rule. The laws took away the property of Jewish citizens. The laws took away their rights. Both parents knew their children must leave Germany. They needed to leave before the situation grew worse. The Netherlands became their new country during 1933 and 1934. Many thousands of other Jewish people from Germany departed as well. The move to Amsterdam came before Anne's fifth birthday. No Dutch city is larger than Amsterdam. Anne was outgoing. She was curious about people. She was curious about the world around her. She liked school. Friends filled her days. She went to Ping-Pong parties. She ate ice cream. She had the love of her family. A picture shows Anne in 1939. Poland was attacked by Nazi Germany on the first day of September 1939. That attack started World War II. German forces entered the Netherlands in May 1940. By the end of that year, Germany's powerful army controlled most of Europe. Its air force did too.

4The Frank family had already fled Nazi Germany. Many other Jewish families had fled it too. Many of those refuge countries were now in Nazi hands. Otto searched for a path that would carry his family to safety across the ocean. Each try was stopped or turned down. Under those German occupiers, freedom for Jewish residents of Amsterdam kept shrinking. They did it through a series of anti-Jewish decrees. Radios owned by Jewish people had been taken by 1939. Jewish people had to obey a curfew. Phones were taken from them during 1940 as well. A badge became required in 1941 for every Jewish person older than six. The badge was a yellow Star of David. The word Jew was written on it. Bicycles had to be handed over. They were forbidden to use trams. They were forbidden to ride in cars. The ban included their own cars. Keeping a pet was not allowed. They were forbidden to leave the country. Jewish children lost every school in 1942. Many Dutch people protested. Protecting Jewish friends meant real danger, and many Dutch people accepted it. They were often arrested for trying to help. They were often imprisoned. The situation grew worse. The four Franks began their hiding in July 1942. Hermann van Pels soon joined the family. He was Otto Frank's business partner. His wife, Auguste, joined them. Their son, Peter, joined them too. Peter was sixteen. That November, dentist Fritz Pfeffer moved in. He became the eighth person in the hideaway.

5A picture shows Peter van Pels. Visitors can still see that bookcase at the Anne Frank House. It once hid the way into the rooms Anne named the Secret Annex. In her diary, Anne called their hiding place the Secret Annex. The annex was livable. It was cramped. It included a kitchen. It included a bathroom. It had cold running water. Each room served as a living area. Each room also served as a bedroom. There was a single entrance. A bookcase hid that entrance. They covered the windows in every room. Covered windows kept lamplight from leaking out after dark. The people in hiding got great help from their helpers. Anne's word helper meant the friends, not Jewish themselves, who had promised support. Those friends would supply food. They would supply other things the family needed. The helpers included Miep Gies. They included her husband, Jan. They included other friends. People who used to work for Otto Frank were among the helpers. So were people who used to work for Hermann van Pels. The helpers risked imprisonment. They risked execution. They were helping to hide Jewish people. A 1935 picture shows Otto Frank seated at the center of his office workers. Miep Gies appears in that office photo with Otto. Johannes Kleiman is in it too. Victor Kugler and Bep Voskuijl are also there. A few years later, those workers labored to keep Otto and his family alive. Anne wrote that the helpers never complained.

6Each day they came upstairs with a smile. They brought newspapers. Best of all, perhaps, they brought conversation. On weekdays, employees worked on the floor below the secret apartment. Perfect quiet was required of Anne and of every person with her. Tiptoe was the only safe way to walk. They had to whisper. No one could run water. No one could flush the toilet. They feared someone would hear them. A reward was offered for reporting any Jewish person. Finding the family would have meant instant arrest. Anne used those silent hours for writing in the diary. She told about her family. She told about her housemates. She glued in old family photos. She wrote about how it felt to be growing into a young woman. The circumstances were grim. Many times she expressed despair. She expressed a great fear that they would be caught. The first diary ran out of space quickly. She moved on to notebooks. She moved on to sheets of loose paper. Writing made the fear easier for Anne to bear. It helped her cope with boredom. It let her shake off her cares. It let her shake off her sorrows. One hope she wrote down was work as a journalist. She also dreamed of becoming an actress. Pictures of film stars went up on a wall in the small room she used. Downstairs opened to them only after every worker had left. They could never go outside.

7The radio was a spot where they often sat together. They listened to broadcasts. June 1944 brought news they were glad to hear. A very large Allied army had come ashore in France. To the east, Soviet troops were pushing German forces backward. Otto started following how the fighting moved. He marked it on a wall map. People in the annex began to hope the Nazis would lose before long. Freedom might then return for the Franks and for the friends beside them. One photograph shows Germany's secret police. Their name was the Gestapo. The scene is 1940, with Jewish men marched out of Warsaw, a city in Poland. Hidden rooms were stormed by that secret police on August 4, 1944. How those rooms were found is still not certain. No action was open to the Franks or to the others with them. They raised their hands at gunpoint. Police looked through every part of the Secret Annex. One officer of the Nazis dumped out the briefcase Otto carried. Anne's writing was inside it. The officer wanted the briefcase so he could carry the Franks' valuables. Pages from the diary lay spread on the floor. Helper Miep Gies picked the pages up afterward. A drawer in a desk was where she stored them. She wanted Anne to have the pages again once peace returned. Early in September 1944, the family was sent to the camp called Auschwitz. Auschwitz was a concentration camp in Poland. Once inside, the family was separated.

8Otto was placed in the men's camp. The camp for women received Edith, Anne, and Margot. The winter cold took a terrible toll. Tiny amounts of food took a toll too. Backbreaking work took a toll as well. Edith tried with all her strength to aid the two girls. She even gave them all of her food. November 1 was the day the girls were taken away from Edith. The two sisters were moved to another concentration camp. That camp was in Germany. A picture shows women prisoners packed into barracks at Auschwitz. People labeled inferior were the ones Hitler and his party wanted gone from Europe. Those people included Jewish people. They included Romany people. They included gay people. They included people with disabilities. Pushing Jewish citizens out of Germany was their first effort. They made life so miserable that people fled the country. Mass killing had become the plan by 1942. Across Europe, Jewish people were seized and taken away. They were sent to concentration camps. Most of those camps were in Poland and Germany. When the war stopped, Nazi murder had taken six million Jewish lives. Five million people from further groups were killed as well. Germany surrendered in May 1945. That surrender ended World War II in Europe. What the freeing soldiers saw inside the camps filled them with horror. They found stacks of bodies. People still alive looked like skeletons that could move. Trainloads of children had been killed there.

9Trainloads of women had been killed there. Trainloads of men had been killed there. Otto Frank survived. He returned to Amsterdam. He already knew starvation inside Auschwitz had killed Edith. He still hoped that Margot and Anne were alive. Soon a friend brought horrible news. That friend had met both girls inside the camps. Illness had struck Anne. It had struck Margot too. They died in February 1945. Her age was only fifteen. A picture shows Otto Frank in 1976. Miep Gies gave Otto Frank five notebooks. Loose pages of Anne's writing, more than two hundred of them, came with those notebooks. He was struck at once by Anne's talent. He later said he had not known how deep her thoughts went. He had not known how deep her feelings went. Seventy years of readers have opened this diary. Translators have put the text into more than sixty languages. Buyers around the world have taken more than thirty million copies. Anne's work has been adapted into a play that won awards. It has been adapted into a film. It has been adapted into two television miniseries. In the United States, schools have read the book for decades. Teachers have taught it for decades too. Anne's writing offers keen insights. Readers meet the inner life of a teenager trapped in a terrible time. Her story warns every age about hatred. It is a warning against extremism. Printers in the Netherlands produced the book first. Its title is Diary of a Young Girl, under Anne Frank's name.

10That was two years after the war. In time the book sold widely, as a best seller, in many countries. Through Anne, a great many readers see a single person inside the Holocaust's terror. She was a young writer. She was a talented writer. The years she should have lived were taken away. The world also lost how far her talent might have gone. Her potential was stolen from the world too. A picture shows Anne at age twelve. The Allies were the countries that aided one another in World War II. Together they defeated Germany, Italy, and Japan. An annex is a building added to a larger building. Antisemitic means feeling hatred toward the Jewish people or acting with hostility toward them. Decrees are official orders or decisions. Despair is a deep feeling of hopelessness. To emigrate is to leave one country and settle in a different country. The Great Depression was an international economic crisis. It ran from 1929 through the 1930s. In World War II, the Nazis carried out an organized killing of people, above all Jewish people, and history calls it the Holocaust. The word Jewish relates to Jews as a people, a culture, or a religion. From 1933 until 1945, Nazi members belonged to the party that ruled Germany. An occupier is part of an invading force that has seized a place. To restrict is to limit, control, or confine.

18. Beasts in the Myths of Old Greece

1A map of ancient Greece around 750 bce marks Macedonia and Troy. It marks Asia Minor, Greece, and the Aegean Sea. It marks Delphi, Athens, and Mycenae. It marks Europe, the Mediterranean Sea, and Sparta. It marks Africa and Crete. Coming pages open with an introduction. Centaurs come next. Sirens come after them. Medusa follows. The Minotaur follows her. Typhon follows him. A conclusion comes last. Useful words close the book. A greeting appears on one vase made in the fifth century bce. Heracles, said HAIR-uh-kleez, is the Greek hero. Cerberus is the dog he meets. That dog guards the underworld. It has two heads, or sometimes three. Myths appear in many cultures. A myth is a story that explains a big idea in a way people can grasp. Good and evil are ideas of that kind. A myth can take more than one shape. It can be a lesson. It can explain a historical event. It can explain a natural phenomenon. It can be a warning. In ancient Greece, religion and myth were tightly joined. The stories were not told for entertainment. Gods and goddesses carried deep meanings.

2Greek people used those meanings as guidelines for living. Heroes and villains share the spotlight with the gods. Fantastic creatures often stand at the center too. Another vase shows the goddess Athena. She helps Heracles attack the Hydra. That monster is made of many snakes. A Centaur had a human head and a human chest. The rest of the body was a horse. These creatures were violent. The animal part ruled the human part. Their weapons came from nature. Giant stones were one weapon. Wooden sticks were another. Greeks met them with metal shields, with spears, and with swords. Greeks saw the untamed Centaurs as their culture's opposite. Centaurs seemed animal-like. Emotion drove them. Greeks saw themselves as civilized. Reason drove them. Ixion, a king from Greece, is where the Centaur story starts. Zeus allowed him a life beside the gods and the goddesses. That home was Mount Olympus. What reached Zeus next was a rumor. Love for Hera, his own wife, had supposedly seized Ixion. Zeus tested Ixion. He made a cloud. The cloud looked exactly like Hera. Ixion did fall in love with that cloud.

3He believed he had found Hera. Birth came from the cloud. The child was the first Centaur. Anger drove Zeus to a punishment. Ixion had to spin forever. The spin was on a wheel of blazing fire. A sculpture from the Parthenon shows Centaurs winning a fight with Greeks. The Parthenon is a temple in Athens from the fifth century bce. Pictures of these battles were common all over ancient Greece. Drinking cups carried them. Stone temples carried them. Current events rarely appeared in Greek art. Myth pictures were how Greeks showed their feelings about the world around them. One great enemy was the Persians. Greeks tied the Persians to how wild the Centaurs were. Battle scenes of Greeks against Centaurs displayed Greek superiority over the Persians. Guest and host had a bond that ancient Greek culture treated as important. That bond is the lesson inside Ixion's tale and the birth of the first Centaur. Ixion showed disrespect to Zeus. Zeus was his host. The punishment taught what follows when that accepted custom is broken. Sirens, like Centaurs, were hybrid creatures. A Siren was a woman.

4She also had the wings of a bird, the legs of a bird, and the body of a bird. The story stands for self-control. Home for the Sirens was an island. Sea lay on every side of that island. Beautiful songs went out to sailors. The sailors lost control of their ships. The ships crashed on the island's rocky shores. Myth says a human life came before the Sirens' winged one. They served the goddess Persephone as maids. Say her name pur-SE-fuh-nee. Hades ruled the underworld. He carried Persephone away. He wanted her as his wife. Wings let the Sirens search for her. The search failed. They settled on the island. Many sailors died there, caught by surprise. A few sailors went past and lived. Orpheus, said OR-fee-uhss, was a famous Greek musician. He played so loudly that the Sirens' song could not be heard. Odysseus was a Greek king. He was sailing home from the Trojan War. He told his sailors to tie him tightly to the boat's mast. The sailors blocked their own ears. They would not be tempted to stop rowing.

5Greeks were proud of their restraint. Getting past the Sirens' song stood for a strength of will. Ancient Greeks valued that strength. Odysseus appears lashed to the mast on a Greek vase made in the fifth century bce. He could hear the song. He could also stay alive. The mythological Sirens connect to an everyday word. A siren, the device, blasts a warning that is loud. The same stories gave us siren song as an idea. That is something so appealing that you want it. The want remains even when the thing is dangerous. Beauty was what the Sirens were known for. Medusa was famous for a look that frightened people. Greek artists usually drew the Gorgons a certain way. The Gorgons were Medusa and her two sisters. The heads were large and round. The eyes were huge and staring. Hair was absent. Snakes grew from the skulls instead. Pointed tusks finished the face. Flared nostrils finished it. Tongues stuck out of the mouths. Medusa's sisters were immortal. Medusa herself was mortal. Humans could therefore harm her. She still had a defense. A direct look into her eyes turned a person to stone.

6The myth begins with an evil king. The woman he loved was mother to a boy, and the boy was Perseus. He wanted Perseus out of the way. He tricked the boy into a promise. Whatever the king named, Perseus had to fetch it. The wish was Medusa's death, and her head as proof. The king believed the deed could not be done. Gods and goddesses helped Perseus. He cut off Medusa's head. Two creatures sprang from her body. One was Chrysaor, said kriss-AH-or. He was a giant. His name means golden blade. The blade may refer to grain. The other was Pegasus, a horse with wings. Springs of water are what the name points toward. Some people read the killing as the end of a drought. Chrysaor and Pegasus then stand for the good that followed. Thriving crops are one part of that good. Flowing water is the other. Ancient Greeks trusted a frightening Gorgon face. They believed it would protect them. They believed it would ward off evil. Gorgon pictures went everywhere. Shields carried them. Another creature of mixed parts was the Minotaur.

7A bull's head sat on a man's body. The name joins two sources. Minos was the king of Crete, and the monster lived there. In the Greek language, taurus means a bull. Destruction followed the monster, so it was locked away. A maze held him, twisted in its paths, and people called it the Labyrinth. The maze lay beneath the king's palace. Athenian boys killed the king's son. Minos wanted revenge. He attacked the city of Athens. Athens wanted the attacks to end, so it made a deal. Every year it would send seven boys. It would also send seven girls. The Minotaur would receive them. Theseus was a brave boy from Athens. He volunteered to be one of the victims. In Crete, he was put in a cage. The other victims were in that cage too. Ariadne, said ah-ree-AHD-nee, was the princess of Crete. Love for Theseus struck her as soon as she saw him. She did not want the Minotaur to kill him. She asked the man who had built the Labyrinth. She wanted to know how Theseus could get out.

8The answer was a ball of yarn. Theseus should unwind it as he walked the maze. She also gave him a sword. The sword was for killing the Minotaur. After the kill, Theseus followed the yarn trail. The trail led him out of the maze. Once Greece ruled Crete, this myth became popular. Centaurs often stood for the Persians. In a similar way, bulls could stand for Crete. An important goddess in Crete held bulls as sacred. Theseus beating the Minotaur could stand for something larger. It could stand for the Greek conquest of Crete. The fierce Minotaur was tiny next to Typhon, said TY-fon. Typhon was a giant. Wings grew on him. One hundred heads grew on him. He stood for the destructive forces of weather. One head was human. Ninety-nine heads belonged to other creatures. Lions were among them. Bulls were among them. Boars were among them. Snakes were among them. Dragons were among them. From the knees downward, giant snakes took the place of legs. Fingers were missing. Fifty serpent heads coiled out of each hand instead. Fire flashed in his eyes.

9Flames whipped from his mouth. Only Zeus could match Typhon in battle. Zeus was the king of the gods. Rule of the whole world was what Typhon threatened to seize. Zeus answered with thunder and lightning. Typhon fought with fire and wind. The whole world shook from their battle. Zeus set fire to every one of the hundred heads. He then locked the monster under Earth. Ancient Greeks blamed Typhon for fierce winds. In great storms, those winds ran across land and across sea. Lava was blamed on him too. The lava poured from volcanoes. Comfort came from one idea. Zeus was able to beat the wrecking forces of nature for which Typhon stood. Ancient Greeks did not keep these creatures only to be entertained. They did not keep them only to be terrified. The creatures and their myths carried deep meanings. The meanings helped people understand the world of their own time. Challenges they faced were easier to cope with because of those meanings. A large place in ancient Greek culture belonged to these mythical creatures. They are still popular now. Children stay fascinated by the amazing stories.

10Adults stay fascinated too. Famous business marks borrowed pictures from these old creatures. A fashion label uses the head of Medusa. A fuel company uses Pegasus. A coffee company uses a Siren. To cope is to handle a difficulty with success. It can mean to overcome that problem. Hybrid means made from a mix of different things. Immortal means living forever. Death does not apply. A creature, in this book, is an animal. The word fits best when the animal is strange or unusual. Myths are traditional stories. They explain historical events, natural happenings, or social customs. Supernatural elements often appear. A culture is a particular society. It has its own ideas and customs. Defeating means winning a victory over someone else. A phenomenon is an event or occurrence that stands out. Dominated means controlled. It can mean overpowered. Restraint is control over one's actions. It is also control over one's emotions. A drought is a long dry spell. Little rain falls, or none. A water shortage can follow. Symbolized means an object, a picture, or a sign stood for an idea.

19. Bonfire Night and Guy Fawkes

1Pictures of the day often show masks of Guy Fawkes. An old nursery rhyme in the United Kingdom tells people to keep the fifth of November in mind. The rhyme names gunpowder, treason, and a secret plot. It says there is no reason this gunpowder treason should ever be forgotten. Adults and children across the United Kingdom meet each November 5. They come for fireworks. They come for bonfires. Friends and families shout with joy when flames take the figure on the fire. People call the dummy a Guy. People call this old festival Guy Fawkes Day. People also call it Bonfire Night. The day celebrates an event in 1605. King James I, together with his ministers, halted a secret plan that day. The plot would have blown up Parliament. Lewes, England, holds the largest Bonfire Night gathering anywhere. The account ahead asks who Guy Fawkes was. It tells the story of the Gunpowder Plot. It tells how the plotters were caught. It asks whether another conspiracy was involved. It follows the legacy of the plot. It then closes the story. York, England, in the year 1570, was his birthplace.

2Queen Elizabeth I was reigning then. Catholic lands and Protestant lands in Europe were fighting one another then. Struggles over power between the two faiths fed those wars. Under Elizabeth, practicing the Catholic faith was against English law. A fine was a common punishment for Catholics found at worship. They were often killed. Guy's grandparents were Catholic. His parents were Protestant. After his father's death, his mother took a Catholic husband. When Guy was a teenager, he decided to convert to Catholicism. Violence aimed at England's Catholics filled him with anger. He was angry about the cruelty too. England was behind him once he reached his early twenties. He traveled to the Netherlands. He joined the Catholic Spanish army. That army was fighting the Dutch Protestants. Twelve years of his life went to soldiering in Spain's army. He became an expert with explosives. A picture of the Gunpowder Plotters shows their leader, Robert Catesby, second from the right. In 1603 Elizabeth I, who was queen, died. King James I took the throne after her. He said Catholics would find him more welcoming. What followed instead were laws that pressed Catholics even harder.

3Many English Catholics had stayed loyal to the king. Other English soldiers in Spain's army crossed his path. Violence against England's Catholics angered them just as deeply. Spain was his destination in the year 1603. He described the hard situation of England's Catholics to Spain's king. No help would come from that king. Fights between the armies of Spain and England already stretched back many years. A recent agreement had stopped that fighting. At the same time, Robert Catesby was shaping a revolt in England aimed at King James I. Thomas Wintour, his cousin, was brought into the plan. Fawkes received their invitation in April 1604. They needed his skill with gunpowder. They needed that skill to make explosives. Fawkes did not hesitate. May 1604 found him back in London, meeting fellow conspirators inside a nearby inn. Secrecy was the promise they swore. Many women were part of the wider movement. Anne Vaux was one of them. Men alone took part in the plan itself. Their aim was an explosion at Parliament on the day it opened. All the ministers would be there.

4The king would be there too. The plotters would then place King James's daughter on the throne. Her name was Princess Elizabeth. Nine was Elizabeth's age then. The plotters believed they could shape her reign if they raised her Catholic. The sworn group numbered thirteen people altogether. Lambeth was where Robert Catesby kept a house. The Thames flowed between that Lambeth house and the Parliament buildings. Extra gunpowder was on hand because Spain and England were at peace. The plotters bought thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. They stored the barrels in Catesby's house. A royal bodyguard post went to the plotter Thomas Percy. His new house stood close to Parliament. By chance, he heard that a cellar under the Parliament buildings was available to rent. By night, the conspirators moved the gunpowder. They used a rowboat. The boat crossed the Thames, leaving Catesby's house for the cellar. Guy Fawkes took a false identity. He called himself John Johnson. Thomas Percy's servant was the part he played. That disguise let him walk inside Parliament's buildings without alarm. He did not raise suspicion. Watching those thirty-six barrels, kept under the building, was the task given to him.

5November 5, 1605, was the date chosen for Parliament to open. The plotters were ready. Some historians believe the powder he had was no longer fresh. They think it would not have exploded. A few days before Parliament opened, Lord Monteagle received an anonymous letter. He was a Catholic nobleman. He was loyal to the king. Stay away from Parliament on November 5, the letter told him. A dreadful event was coming, the letter said. The king's leading helper was the person who next saw that letter, from Lord Monteagle's hand. After the king learned of the plot, he ordered a full search of Parliament. Stacked wood filled much of the cellar when the first searchers looked. A second search was ordered. This time the searchers found Fawkes in the basement. He had fuses with him. He had matches that he was hiding. The searchers looked through the cellar more carefully. At last they found the thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. The guards caught Guy Fawkes in the act. He struggled against the men who had seized him. They tied him up. Questions waited in the king's own rooms, and that is where they led him.

6Fawkes told the king's guards what he had meant to do. Destroying the king had been his goal. Destroying Parliament had been his goal as well. He claimed that nobody else had taken part. He told the king he was sorry only because the plot had failed. The Tower of London became his prison. Exactly what he suffered inside that prison has never been proved. His last confession carried his signature by November 9. By that date he had given out the rebellion's full details. He had named his fellow plotters. News of the arrest reached the other plotters on November 5 in the morning. Giving up was not the choice of Robert Catesby or of several partners. A rising against the government was still their aim. Horses were taken at Warwick Castle by Catesby's small rebel band. The authorities chased them. The king's soldiers closed around the rebels on November 8. They fatally wounded Robert Catesby. They fatally wounded three others. The men still alive were locked inside the Tower of London. English courts heard treason cases against all eight plotters who were still alive.

7The courts sentenced them to death. January 1606 brought Guy Fawkes and three partners out to the yard. The place was the yard outside Parliament. They were executed there. The harshness of the punishment was a warning. Anyone else thinking of treason was meant to take that harsh end as a warning. Later, King James I spoke well of how loyal Fawkes had been to his cause. An inside scheme is what some experts think this powder plot may have been. In that view, the king's own ministers planned it. They hoped he would accept rules against Catholics that were harsher still. In that telling, the note of warning to Lord Monteagle may have been drafted by the king's top minister. Their work happened very near the king's own guards, which is hard to explain any other way. Some readers ask if the plotters served only as scapegoats. Did leaders want more support for a king who was unpopular? Clear proof for this idea has not been found. Once the plot came to light, the public felt relief.

8Knowing the king had survived eased people's fear. His survival, the king declared, counted as a miracle. He treated that survival as proof that divine right put him on the throne. Gunpowder Treason Day was the first name of the holiday. Church bells were rung, according to writings from those years. They lit bonfires. England already liked to burn models of disliked people on outdoor fires. Evil spirits, people thought, would leave if those figures burned. From November 5 onward, the figure on the bonfire was made to look like Guy Fawkes. Newer pictures sometimes put fireworks in his hands and set Parliament behind him. Local customs for this night survive in parts of Britain. Bonfire societies exist in Lewes, a town of southern England. Those societies date back to 1679. The participants wear elaborate costumes. They carry torches through the streets. Some towns now burn images of well-known people the public dislikes. They burn those figures instead of the traditional Guy Fawkes.

9Late in the nineteenth century, grand shows of fireworks grew very popular in towns and in cities. Torch-lit processions had become popular too. The processions led to the place where the bonfire was held. They led to the firework displays. Today, local charities usually organize the bonfires. Municipal organizations organize them too. What this day marks is that the powder plot failed. Their goal had been the death of England's king. That attempt was more than four hundred years ago. Millions across the United Kingdom still gather around bonfires each November 5. They still enjoy fireworks that night. Some people see Guy Fawkes in another way. To them, he is someone who defended his own beliefs. They see a person who fought against oppression. Parliament's buildings get a traditional search by guards once each year. That search happens ahead of Parliament's State Opening. They make sure no would-be plotters are hiding in the cellars. A calculation was worked out by scientists at the Institute of Physics. The conspirators hid 2,500 kilograms of gunpowder. That weight equals 5,512 pounds. They figured harm could have reached about 490 meters out from the blast's middle.

10That distance equals 536 yards. Guards prepare for their yearly search of Parliament. Guy Fawkes has an island named after him. The island is in the Galapagos Islands, in Ecuador. People call it Isla Guy Fawkes. Anonymous describes a thing with no known name, no known identity, and no known origin. Large outdoor fires made for a celebration are called bonfires. 2His shows on television captured the thrill of scuba. They captured its grace. They captured its freedom. Adventurous people felt moved to try scuba themselves. 3It let them work more easily too. Some worked as salvagers. They raised valuables from ships that had sunk. Air still had to be pumped down from the surface.
