The great step forward was a regulator designed with care. The diver held it in the mouth. Fixed to the tank, it fed high-pressure air to the diver. The air arrived at a pressure the body could use. Breathing felt natural. For the first time, a diver could swim easily while carrying the air supply. The gear opened paths into the undersea world. People who were not professional divers could enter too. A photo from California in 1950 shows Cousteau on the right. He wears a dive suit of fabric and rubber.

4He is trying an early Aqua-Lung. For a person who likes snorkeling or other fun in the water, scuba adds a real extra depth. Study is part of learning to dive. Training is needed to dive safely and well. Most people begin with Open Water Certification. A scuba shop can provide it. A training center can provide it too. Classes meet in a classroom. Students also train in a pool with an instructor. A written test must be passed. Four practice dives must be done in a lake or in some other open water. New divers must show the instructor a set of skills. They must put scuba gear together and use it the right way. They must go down safely and come up safely. They must deal with gear that fails. Most Open Water courses last two weeks or longer. At the end, the diver gets a certification card. One of several approved training groups issues the card. With the card, a certified diver can rent gear. The diver can dive in places around the world. An instructor shows junior divers what to do if a mask comes off underwater. Junior Open Water Certification is open to children aged ten through fourteen. A junior diver must stay with an adult who is already certified.

5For safety, training for ages ten and eleven stops at 12 meters (40 ft.). Groups that train divers usually tell adult beginners to stay above 18 meters (60 ft.). A shallower dive makes the surface easier to reach if trouble starts. Training gets divers ready for conditions that are unlike anything on land. It gets them ready for surprises. The gravest hazards come from breathing air that has been compressed. Pressure grows as a diver goes deeper. Every dive needs a careful plan for depth. It needs a careful plan for time. Nitrogen narcosis is one risk. Deeper dives raise that risk. Air holds nitrogen, which is a gas. Under the water, nitrogen from the compressed air leaves body tissues more slowly than it does at the surface. Bubbles can form. The bubbles affect the nervous system. Narcosis can weaken vision. It can make a diver feel light-headed. It can cause confusion. Signs of nitrogen narcosis are not the same for everyone. Depth matters. The dive site matters too. Decompression sickness is another grave danger. People also call it the bends. It can strike if a diver stays down too long. It can strike if the trip upward is too fast. Dives past 30.5 meters (100 ft.) raise the risk in particular.

6As with nitrogen narcosis, gas bubbles are the cause. The bubbles form and then swell inside muscles and other tissues. The pain can be severe. The sickness can kill. Divers learn to rise slowly so they can avoid it. They may pause at set depths on the way up. The pauses are decompression stops. During each pause, risky gases can exit the body. A diver who gets the sickness can be treated. A decompression chamber is used when one is nearby. Divers are not the only people who have suffered this sickness. Work on New York's Brooklyn Bridge started in the 1870s. Laborers went down into huge underwater boxes called caissons (KAY-sahnz). Pumps kept air pressure high inside the boxes. The pressure held the water out. The laborers dug into the bed of the East River. They were making the base of the giant bridge. Back on the surface, many of them reported headaches. They reported pain in their joints. At least five of them died. Each death was later tied to decompression sickness. A barracuda may swim near a diver. Someone new to diving may fear sharks. Stingrays may seem just as frightening. In truth, these animals rarely threaten a diver. Attacks by sharks or by other sea animals are extremely rare.

7Divers are taught to treat every wild animal with great respect. They keep a safe distance. The gap protects ocean life. It protects the diver. Scuba training can also open jobs. Extra certificates often prepare a diver for harder work. A salvage diver is a specialist. This diver finds cargo lost at sea. This diver brings that cargo up. An offshore diver or a water welder works in construction. The job is building and fixing oil rigs and other platforms at sea. A police diver is an officer. The work includes search and rescue. It includes investigations under the water. An underwater photographer runs a camera. The specialty is pictures and films made below the surface. A scientific diver is a scientist. Geology is one field studied this way. Archaeology is another. Marine biology is another. Further fields use scuba too. Once training and a certificate are in hand, a diver can go exploring. Wonderful dive sites exist all over the globe. Four places show different kinds of diving done for enjoyment. Reef diving is one kind. The Great Barrier Reef is a famous site for that kind. Coral reefs are the finest places to see bright fish and other sea life.

8This reef system is the largest on Earth. It stretches some 2,300 kilometers (1,400 mi.) beside the coast of Australia. Visitors can swim beside whitetip reef sharks. They can swim beside potato cod. They can swim among many forms of coral. Wreck diving is another kind. Biscayne National Park in Florida is a site for it. The marine park holds more than one hundred places of archaeological interest. Forty-three of them are shipwrecks. One ship was the Guerrero. It went down in 1827. It was carrying Africans who had been enslaved against the law. Young divers get training in a program called Diving with a Purpose. They study the Guerrero site and other sites. They hope to find ships wrecked during the Atlantic slave trade. They hope to record those ships. Freshwater diving is a third kind. Riviera Maya in Mexico is a site for it. Eastern Mexico holds many caverns underground. Pools of fresh water in them are called cenotes (sih-NOH-teez). Clarity is usual in this water. It is cool. Dos Ojos ranks among the most impressive cenotes for diving. It is a large underground web of caverns and caves. Cold-water diving and drift diving form a fourth kind. The Channel Islands of California are a site for both. Ocean water off California is cold.

9Warmth comes from a thick wet suit or from a dry suit. A dry suit lets in no water at all. Many divers choose dry suits for cold water. They choose them for diving under ice. Channel Islands dives also call for drift-diving skill. Ocean currents carry the divers from place to place. A chase boat follows behind. The boat picks them up when the dive ends. Divers can see forests of kelp under the sea. Around the Channel Islands, those forests shelter many kinds of marine animals. Lobsters live there. Bat rays live there. Sea lions live there. Otters live there. A dive into a lake or an ocean feels like a drop into a different world. Life under the surface does not match life on land. Scuba lets a diver see that strange, beautiful place up close. Divers often say that gliding underwater is an awesome feeling. It is like hovering. It is like flying. In Mexico's Sea of Cortes, a diver takes a photo of a sea lion. Scuba is an enjoyable skill to learn. Training plus good judgment makes it very safe. It is thrilling as well. It is a bold way to visit places that few people ever see. Advanced divers who dive for fun may go no deeper than 30.5 meters (100 ft.).

10To avoid the bends, training says a diver should rise no faster than 9 meters (30 ft.) each minute. A diver at 30.5 meters (100 ft.) needs a set time to reach the surface at that rate. The time is 3 minutes and 20 seconds. These words help with the topic. Air pressure is the push of air in the atmosphere. Nitrogen narcosis is a confused state of mind. It happens when nitrogen enters the blood while pressure is high, as in a deep dive. An ascent is a move upward. A certification is an official paper. It proves that a goal was met. Recreational describes rest or an activity done for enjoyment. Compressed describes something squeezed tightly. A regulator may be a device. It may be a person. Either one controls how much of something flows, or how fast. Decompression sickness is a dangerous illness. Staying down too long can cause it. Rising too fast can cause it. A salvager recovers pieces of a ship after it has wrecked. A valve opens and closes. It manages the flow of a liquid, a gas, or some other material. A descent is a move downward. 22. Children Who Marched for Rights

1On May 5, 1963, a group of Black girls sits inside a fairgrounds building. The city is Birmingham, Alabama. Arrests during civil rights demonstrations had brought them there. Contents. A day that mattered. A long fight. Young people step up. The commissioner. Pressure at work. What the march won. Words to know. A day that mattered. May 2, 1963, arrived in Birmingham, Alabama. School was skipped by over 1,000 Black children. The plan was to gather at 16th Street Baptist Church. They did. At one in the afternoon the march started. Groups held about fifty children each. Pairs stepped out of the church doors. Hands clapped. Voices laughed. Songs rose. Lessons of nonviolent direct action were already in them. Their target was racial segregation. That system forced Black people apart from white people. Some people ranked this city as the most divided by race in the United States. Police in the city were all white. They waited with batons. Dogs waited with them. Fire hoses waited too. The days that followed became one of the movement's most dramatic confrontations. Through the Children's Crusade, the nation watched anti-Black racism show its ugliness. The world watched too. Fresh energy entered a long struggle. Black people were demanding equal rights in the country that was theirs. Young marchers appear in a picture from the Crusade. The long fight. Separation by race still happens in many American cities. In the early 1960s the separation was law.

2The name for those policies was Jim Crow. Under them, Black people were treated as second-class citizens in the towns where they lived. Whites Only signs turned Black people away from restaurants. Other public places did the same. Terror kept many Black citizens from casting votes. To stand up was to risk being killed. Violent supporters of segregation were the danger. The White Citizens' Council was one group. The Ku Klux Klan was another. Local officers often pretended not to see. Sometimes they aided the white groups. Racial violence took thousands of lives. Men died. Women died. Children died. A growing share of Black Americans was ready to resist. About that hate group. Members who join the Ku Klux Klan share a racist belief. It claims white people are superior to every other race. Founding came after the Civil War, fought from 1861 to 1865. Violence and terror were the tools. The goal was to seize white control again in Southern states. Lynchings, which are hangings, numbered in the thousands. Black Americans have been the chief targets. Hatred is also aimed at Jewish people. It is aimed at Catholics. It is aimed at members of the LGBTQ+ community. It is aimed at immigrants. Across generations, Black people had built a large part of American life. Work was hard. Taxes were paid. Military service was given. Equal rights were still refused. Justice was still refused. In 1954 the highest court in the land ruled on schools.

3It said separating students by race broke the Constitution. The year 1955 brought another shock. Two white men killed a teenager who was Black. His name was Emmett Till. A jury of white men only found them not guilty. Equal rights suddenly felt more urgent. Justice did too. The civil rights movement gained supporters. Momentum grew. Reporters paid attention. The best-known leader to emerge was Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He served as a Baptist minister. He headed the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. People shorten that name to SCLC. He and others built a plan called nonviolent direct action. Big demonstrations would test laws that were unfair. Segregated towns would be disrupted. Police would face more arrests than they could handle. Training taught marchers to keep the peace no matter the blow. Even an attack was not a reason to strike back. The belief was this. Once more Americans who were not Black saw the cruelty, more would back the cause. Seeing the injustice would move them. A portrait shows Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. By 1963 some of that momentum had slipped away. Fewer bodies showed up to demonstrate. Papers sent thinner crews. TV networks sent fewer cameras. White officials were also learning. Softer attacks meant kinder headlines. SCLC leaders wanted a win too large to ignore. A new protest campaign was the answer. They aimed at Birmingham, Alabama. Many already treated its segregation as the worst in the nation.

4After-dark towns. Tellings of this history often stay on the South. Discrimination was widespread in the North as well. It was widespread in the West. Black people met it. So did other minority groups. Unofficial rules called sundown laws set a curfew. People who were not white had to be out of the city limits. Homes there were forbidden. After dark, being caught could turn dangerous. Such sundown towns existed by the thousand. The map ran from Darien in Connecticut, to La Crosse in Wisconsin, to Glendale in California. Segregation signs used wording that readers today call offensive. Young people step forward. Early in 1963 Fred Shuttlesworth invited guests to his city. He preached as a Baptist minister in Birmingham. He was a cofounder of the SCLC. The guests were Dr. King and other organizers from that group. Their name for the effort was Project C. The letter C meant confrontation. Birmingham already had a grim name among Black people. Bombs had destroyed Black houses. Bombs had destroyed Black churches. Some called the city Bombingham. Attempts on Shuttlesworth's life had failed more than once. He was still alive. Not everyone welcomed Dr. King. Some Black residents did not. Most white residents did not. Atlanta, Georgia, was his base, so they labeled him an outsider. Trouble in their streets was not wanted. Nationally, though, he pulled attention the way lightning pulls the eye. The press arrived wherever he arrived.

5Project C opened in a slow, heavy way. Church rooms filled when he spoke. Asked to march, people paused. Most Black households in the city were working class. Pay was low. A lot of Black providers worked for white bosses. Jail might mean a lost job. Something worse was easy to imagine. Children had been watching the whole time. They had been listening. Workshops had also trained them in civil rights. Nonviolent direct action was part of that training. Youth organizers inside the SCLC suggested a dangerous shift. The idea drew on leaders from SNCC. The long name is Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee. Let students stand at the front of the protests. Excitement ran through the young people. Jobs they might lose were rare. Putting children in jail would stain the city badly. The protests needed exactly that stain. Groups from churches supplied a key part of the stand against segregation. A picture shows them gathered. Argument followed. The plan was controversial. Dr. King refused at first. So did other leaders. Harm to children and to teens was not acceptable to them. Most parents refused too. Safety worried them. The youth still pushed to join. Discrimination was the air they had grown up in. They had seen parents humiliated. They had seen grandparents humiliated. Pools open to the public, but marked Whites Only, barred them from swimming. A lunch counter would not serve them a hamburger. A chance had come to speak.

6Inhumane treatment could be protested out loud. Word spread among Black students about a day called D-Day. One reading was Demonstration Day. Another was Ditch Day. On the local station aimed at Black listeners, DJs slipped hints between songs. The clock time was eleven in the morning. The calendar day was May 2, 1963. Grade-school children were included. Teens were included. College students were included. Pack a toothbrush, they were told. The meaning was clear enough. Night might not find them in their own beds. The hour struck. At one Birmingham high school, youth held a sign outdoors. It read It's Time. Minutes later, hundreds aimed for the doors. Classroom windows became exits for some. The jail letter. Police in Birmingham seized Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. on April 12, 1963. They said he had been parading without a permit. Eight days in jail followed. From that cell he answered white clergy of the city. Their plea had been patience. Their plea had been less disruption. He wrote that patience across centuries had gained Black people nothing. He told white religious leaders to quit offering excuses for discrimination. He told them to stand with civil rights for Black Americans. Readers know the piece as the Letter from Birmingham Jail. Few arguments for racial justice have ever hit harder. The young people met at 16th Street Baptist Church. From there, they marched straight into history. The man in charge of safety.

7Voters chose Eugene Bull Connor as commissioner of public safety. They did it seven times. His racism was vicious. It was aggressive. Public safety, in his hands, served white residents. Black people, children included, were abused to keep that order. Officers and firefighters held the front. Their job was to block young Black marchers. Downtown lay several blocks off. That was the marchers' goal. A photo shows Connor in those days. By three in the afternoon on May 2, more than 600 young people were behind bars. Prayer kept them going. Songs kept them going. The march was working as planned. National eyes were on the scene. Friday was May 3. Students skipped class again and tried for downtown. Connor prepared force. News writers were in place. Camera crews were in place. He ordered arrests to start. Batons shoved bodies. Batons struck them. Next he ordered hoses onto clusters of marchers. Streams hit with high power. Heads took the blast. Chests took it. Legs took it. The pain was sharp. Some people were thrown off their feet and sent rolling down the pavement. Trees became shelter. Buildings became shelter. Police dogs were brought in to attack and to scare. One picture freezes a firefighter aiming a firehose. High-pressure water slams into protestors. Before night, about two thousand more young people had been taken in. Local jails could hold no one else. Buses carried children and teens to the fairgrounds.

8Lockup waited there. Some cells were animal pens, and they stank. Plenty of marchers were not finished. Released prisoners turned around and got arrested once more. Courage like that pulled adults in. Ranks swelled. The city started to stop. How pressure worked. Saturday made Birmingham the lead story nationwide. TV pictures caught firefighters blasting water at young bodies. Newspaper fronts showed dogs. The dogs ripped clothing on marchers who had not fought back. Kennedy, the president, was in the capital. Reports said the pictures made him ill. He called SCLC leaders. He called Birmingham officials. A truce was his request to all of them. People he sent tried to help both sides negotiate. A settlement of some kind was the hope. His televised talk on civil rights came later, on June 11, 1963. A picture marks that speech. Protests, meanwhile, picked up again. Terror in Connor's style was biting less. Fear dropped among Birmingham's Black citizens, young and old alike. White owners of businesses had enforced segregation by choice. Now they counted what the trouble cost in money. Civic leaders counted the damage to the city's name. May 8, 1963, brought a pause. King and fellow leaders chose a pause. Marching would wait while talks went on. Tension filled the talks. May 10 produced a cautious deal. Public restrooms would lose their color line within ninety days. Drinking fountains would too. Downtown shops promised open lunch counters. They promised open rooms for trying on clothes.

9Young people still jailed would be let out. Arrangements covered that release. Bias in hiring was postponed to future meetings. So were other disputes. The drive had begun to desegregate a city long ranked among the most separated in the land. Young activists of a new generation had inspired the win. Another bombing. September 15, 1963, fell on a Sunday. Services were being held at 16th Street Baptist Church. A bomb went off. Robert Chambliss was named. Thomas Blanton was named. Bobby Cherry was named. The dead were four girls. One was Denise McNair, age eleven. Cynthia Wesley was fourteen. Addie Mae Collins was fourteen. Carole Robertson was fourteen. New support grew for the civil rights law that Congress would pass in 1964. What the march of children achieved. Energy from that march carried the wider movement forward. In hindsight, Birmingham was a turning point of real weight. One month later, Kennedy addressed the country by television. Birmingham was in the speech. He dared the nation to finish segregation completely. Federal laws on civil rights were promised. Black Americans would be protected. Tears came to many Black listeners. At last the president was backing their cause. Later years turned many movement aims into statutes. Congress acted the next year. The Civil Rights Act carried the date 1964. Segregation was outlawed. So was discrimination tied to race. Color was covered. Religion was covered. Gender was covered.

10National origin was covered. The Voting Rights Act came in 1965. State policies that had stopped Black Americans from voting were struck down. New laws did not erase racial prejudice. They did not erase discrimination. Fair treatment and equal treatment, though, opened doors that had been shut. Black Americans gained chances they had been denied. The United States entered a different chapter. Words to know. An activist works to change social life or political life. To negotiate is to seek a formal deal by talking it through. A confrontation is a clash, in words or in blows, between opposing sides. Nonviolent direct action stays peaceful on purpose. A strike can be the tool. A boycott can be the tool. A group, a company, or a government is pushed to change. Controversial means a matter that splits people into strong disagreement. Racism ranks one race above another and treats people unequally for that reason. A demonstration lets a crowd show that it supports something, or that it opposes something. Discrimination treats a person or a group unfairly over gender, race, age, faith, or some other difference. Segregation is a rule for keeping groups apart, and race is a common reason. To disrupt is to block the usual way a thing happens, or to slow it. Urgency is the sense that a problem must be handled at once. Momentum is the force that keeps a movement going, or growing, over time.

23. Come Explore Mexico

1A copper sculpture shows a mariachi player. The parts of this guide come in this order. First comes a travel brochure. Next comes the land. Then comes the best time to visit. The story of the country follows. Mexico City comes after that. The center and the south come next. Then come the Gulf Coast and the Yucatán Peninsula. Northern Mexico follows. Quick facts about Mexico come near the end. A word list closes the guide. A mariachi band plays together. This travel brochure is by Juan Rodriguez. It comes from Ms. Brown's Fifth-Grade Class. Welcome to Mexico. I love this beautiful country. I am glad we can explore it together. The history here is rich. The culture here is rich too. People who live here are very kind. Their hospitality feels out of this world. There is a great deal to see. There is a great deal to do. The real question is whether you will have enough time. You might rest on the shore of a beach. Mexico has many beaches for that. You might visit wonderful museums. You might see historic sites. You might walk through ancient ruins. A horseback ride in the mountains is possible. A boat ride through the wetlands is possible too. You could listen to mariachi music played nearby. Whatever you hope to do, Mexico has something for you. The Land. Let us start the tour with the geography of Mexico. Mexico lies in the southern part of North America. The neighbor to the north is the United States. Guatemala is a neighbor to the south. Belize is a southern neighbor too. Mexico is divided into a north and a south. The Americas are divided in that same way. In southern Mexico, most states have wide rural areas. A large farming population lives in those areas. Northern states are wealthier than southern states. The northern states are mostly urban. They are mostly industrialized as well. The central part holds more than half of the people. That central area is called the Valley of Mexico.

2The capital is Mexico City. Mexico City sits in the valley. Lists of world cities place it among the twenty largest. The Mexico City area is home to about 22 million people. The whole country of Mexico has about 130 million people. A map names the states and the federal district. The names include Baja California Norte, Sonora, Zacatecas, and Chihuahua. They include Coahuila, Nuevo León, Sinaloa, and Tamaulipas. They include Durango, San Luis Potosí, Baja California Sur, and Querétaro. They include Nayarit, Campeche, Hidalgo, and Yucatán. They include Jalisco, Distrito Federal, Aguascalientes, and Tabasco. They include Veracruz, Colima, Guanajuato, and Quintana Roo. They include Oaxaca, Chiapas, Michoacán, and México. They include Morelos, Tlaxcala, Guerrero, and Puebla. The Gulf of Mexico is marked along the east. A picture shows the Mexican flag. A seal is shown with it. Mexico's land covers 756,066 square miles, which is 1,972,550 sq km. How large is that area? The United States has room for about five Mexicos inside its borders. Mexico has states, just as you might not have guessed. There are 31 states, plus a federal district. Every one of these areas has cool places to visit. The blue water is as varied as the people. The landforms are as varied as the culture. Mexico has many landform regions. Very few of those names sound like one another. One region is the Mexican plateau. Another is the central plateau. The Gulf Coastal Plain is a region. The Pacific Coastal Lowlands are a region. The southern highlands form a region. The Chiapas Highlands form a region. The Tabasco Plain is a region. The Yucatán Peninsula is a region. Say Yucatán as yoo-kah-TAHN. The Sierra Madre Occidental is a mountain region. The Sierra Madre Oriental is a mountain region too. The Sonoran Desert is a region. A map adds more names to the picture. The Gulf of California lies to the west. The Pacific Ocean borders the western side. The Gulf of Mexico borders the eastern side.

3Mesa Central sits in the middle. Volcán Pico de Orizaba is marked on the map. Sierra Madre de Chiapas rises in the south. Rivers on the map include the Yaqui and the Conchos. The Fuerte and the Lerma-Santiago are rivers too. The Montezuma, the Balsas, and the Suchiate are rivers as well. The Chihuahuan Desert covers dry ground. Baja California stretches as a long peninsula. Mexico City is marked on the map. A wider view shows North America and South America. Asia appears on the Ring of Fire map. Australia appears on that map too. Do You Know? Volcán Pico de Orizaba last erupted in 1687. Nobody reached the top until 1848. Only two peaks in North America stand higher. Do you know those two highest points? Mexico is a diverse land. For varied plant and animal species, it ranks third in the world. Mexico also lies in the Ring of Fire. That name means a Pacific zone where volcanoes are very active. I hope you will visit Volcán Pico de Orizaba. This dormant volcano is fascinating to see. No point in the country stands higher. The top reaches 18,406 feet, or 5,610 m. Mexico has cities. Mexico has rural areas. Mexico has deserts. Mexico has rainforests. Mexico has wetlands. Mexico has canyons. Every kind of environment you might want is here. Let us look further into my country. When to Visit. Keep the coastal climate in mind. Along the coast, the weather is hot. The coastal weather is humid too. If hot, humid days do not suit you, travel from October through May. Inland temperatures are almost always milder. Mountain temperatures are milder as well. Travelers who love dry weather should try Baja California. Say Baja as BAH-hah. The Sonoran Desert stays dry all year. The Chihuahuan Desert stays dry all year too. A picture shows desert cacti growing in Baja California's Sonoran Desert. My Country's History. The Spanish conquered the Aztecs in 1521. Before that year, Mexico was part of Mesoamerica.

4The Olmecs lived in Mesoamerica. The Maya lived there. People of Teotihuacán lived there. Say Teotihuacán as tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN. The Toltec people lived in Mesoamerica. The Aztec peoples lived there too. All of these groups were here long before the Spanish arrived. Buildings they left can still be visited. Those buildings include temples. They include pyramids. They include ball courts. Among Mesoamerican civilizations, the Aztecs held the most power. The Spanish invasion changed the people. The invasion changed the land as well. Some people from Spain came here to live. Spanish colonizers forced many Indigenous peoples to leave their own religions. Those peoples were made to become Catholic. Learning Spanish was also forced on many Indigenous peoples. Many Indigenous languages are no longer spoken. Náhuatl is still spoken by about 1.5 million people. That language belonged to the Aztec Empire. The official language in Mexico today is Spanish. Until 1810, Spain held Mexico as a colony. A revolt by many Mexicans rose against Spain. Official independence came to Mexico in 1821. The country is a republic today. A picture shows the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlán. Tenochtitlán was the capital of the Aztec Empire. Mexico City. Now the tour turns to great cities. We start in the heart of Mexico. That heart is Mexico City. Under Aztec rule, this city was called Tenochtitlán. Say Tenochtitlán as tay-nohch-teet-LAHN. Aztec builders made many ancient ruins in the city. They made ruins around the city as well. Templo Mayor means Great Temple. That temple marked the site of the Aztec capital. Workers built it during the 1300s and the 1400s. The Spanish tried to bury the temple. In 1978, the amazing ruins were uncovered. The site is a museum now. Many cathedrals stand in Mexico City. Other Spanish architecture stands here too. Catedral Metropolitana is the largest cathedral in all of Latin America. Would you believe the building took nearly 300 years? Famous Mexican artists left painted art across the city.

5They left sculpted art as well. One of the best known is the muralist Diego Rivera. His murals of Mexican history date from 1929 to 1935. The murals are in the courtyard of the Palacio Nacional. Say Palacio as pah-LAH-see-oh. Say Nacional as nah-see-oh-NAHL. Many rulers have lived on the palace site. Moctezuma was an Aztec emperor. Before the Spanish conquest, Moctezuma lived on this same site. After the conquest, the site became home to Hernán Cortés. Cortés was a Spanish conquistador. Say his name as air-NAHN kor-TESS. Today the president's offices are inside the palace. Plaza de la Constitución is the square in front of the palace. People often call that square the Zócalo. It is one of the largest public squares in the world. Another major stop is the city's largest park. Aztec people used to spend summer vacations there. You can spend part of a vacation at Bosque de Chapultepec. Say Bosque de Chapultepec as BOHSS-keh DEH chah-pool-teh-PEK. A zoo is inside the park. A botanical garden is inside the park. You can buy a balloon there. You can buy a snack there. Museums are inside the park. Art galleries are inside the park. You can do all of this and never leave the park. More art museums and centers fill the city. One is the Palacio de Bellas Artes. Another is the Museo Dolores Olmedo Patiño. The Museo Mural Diego Rivera is here. The Museo Frida Kahlo is here. Many further museums wait as well. Frida Kahlo taught herself to paint. She is known for bold self-portraits. The painting of hers that I like best has a monkey in it. A picture shows Frida Kahlo's painting Self-portrait with Monkey. Shoppers in Mexico City will not leave disappointed. Visit the Bazar del Sábado in the Plaza San Jacinto. Bazar del Sábado means Saturday Market. The market sits in the San Ángel neighborhood. Mexican fruits are for sale at the Mercado de la Merced. Vegetables are for sale there. Candy is for sale there too.

6A picture shows candy sold at that Saturday market. The Center and the South. Northwest of Mexico City, buildings from the Spanish colonial years still stand. People sometimes call this area the Colonial Heartland. Rich farming has its center in this same area. The Spanish built many cities and towns in this area. They built them to use the silver deposits. Taxco lies southwest of Mexico City. Taxco has many beautiful silver shops. Farther west, the coast has many beaches. Acapulco is known for those beaches. Say Acapulco as ah-kah-POOL-koh. Decades ago, Puerto Vallarta grew into a popular beach resort. Hollywood stars came there to stay. A picture shows Spanish colonial architecture. Travelers who tire of the beach can visit Colima. Colima has been rebuilt again and again. Earthquakes hit often and keep damaging the city. After Mexico City, Guadalajara is the country's second largest city. Say Guadalajara as gwahdah-lah-HAH-rah. Many great places wait in Guadalajara. The famous Cathedral took more than two centuries to build. A short walk from the Cathedral passes a lot of Spanish colonial architecture. A picture shows the Cathedral at Guadalajara. Like much of Mexico, this region is a pleasure outdoors. Lago de Chapala is the country's largest lake. Boating there is a fine plan. Fishermen on Mexico's Lago de Chapala appear in a picture. Huasteca Potosina offers waterfalls, tropics, and mountains. Say Huasteca Potosina as wahss-TEH-kah poh-toh-SEE-nah. It lies in the state of San Luis Potosí. I also suggest a boat ride to Tamul waterfall. The water drops 344 feet. It falls into a canyon. Central and southern Mexico hold many ancient ruins. The ruins come from Mesoamerican civilizations. Teotihuacán may be one of the greatest Mesoamerican cities of all. Two great ancient temples stand there. They are the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. Visitors come here more than to any other Mesoamerican site. A picture shows Teotihuacán's Pyramid of the Sun. So what was Teotihuacán? In about ce 400, about 125,000 people lived there.

7The name Teotihuacán stands for the place where gods were created. Residents were called Teotihuacanos. Many different Indigenous peoples lived in Teotihuacán. At that time it ranked among the largest cities in the world. Monte Albán was a city of the Zapotec people. Say Monte Albán as MOHN-teh ahl-BAHN. It is in the state of Oaxaca. Say Oaxaca as wah-HAH-kah. Their ceremonial site can be visited on a mountaintop. For a time, the Olmec used this place as a cultural center. The Teotihuacanos used it as a cultural center too. A picture shows Teotihuacán's Pyramid of the Moon. A picture shows El Tajin in Veracruz. Coast of the Gulf and the Yucatán Peninsula. The tour now reaches the tropical plains of the Gulf Coast. Jungle covers much of this land. Several Mesoamerican cultures once lived here. The Maya were one of them. The Olmec were one of them. The Totonac were one of them. Olmec artifacts turn up all over the region. A rich share of them is in the Parque-Museo de La Venta. A picture shows Mayan hieroglyphics. Ancient pyramids can be visited at El Tajin. For the Totonac, El Tajin was a major center of religion. Totonac people lived here between ce 900 and 1150. Quiahuiztlán is another place to see. Say Quiahuiztlán as kee-uh-weet-ZLAN. It was a city on a hilltop. Some 15,000 Totonac people once lived there. A picture shows an ancient Mayan ball court. Chichén Itzá holds the best preserved ruins the Maya left behind. Temples stand at Chichén Itzá. Mexico's largest ancient ball court is there. An observatory is there too. The Maya loved to study the stars. I love looking at the stars too. The Maya had a writing system of their own. Uxmal is another Mayan site worth a visit. Most Spanish cities in the Yucatán were built on top of Mayan ruins. Most Spanish towns there were built the same way. What else can a visitor do on the Gulf Coast?

8Almost anything. Museums are plentiful. Cathedrals are plentiful. Churches are plentiful. Do not skip the city of Veracruz. The waterfront promenade is a lot of fun. The arcades are a lot of fun too. Like the Colonial Heartland, this region grows a great deal of food. Sugarcane is grown here. Cacao is grown here. Cacao tastes wonderful. Coffee is grown here. A picture shows coffee beans. White sand beaches make the Yucatán Peninsula famous. The peninsula has plenty of those beaches. Water wraps three sides of it. Baja California is wrapped by water in that same way. A barrier reef near two islands is the world's second longest. Australia's reef is the longest one. The islands are Cozumel and Isla Mujeres. Say Isla Mujeres as EES-lah moo-HEH-ress. People like to snorkel at the reef. People like to scuba dive there too. Cancún is probably the favorite place for a suntan. This region is known for natural wells called cenotes. The wells are breathtaking. The Cenote de Dzitnup is probably the one people visit most. Say Cenote de Dzitnup as si-NOH-tee day ZEET-nup. It lies near Valladolid. Say Valladolid as bah-yah-doh-LEED. Can you believe the well was found only a half century ago? A picture shows scuba lessons. A picture shows that long reef beside the islands of Cozumel and Isla Mujeres. People call the reef the Great Mesoamerican Reef. A picture shows the deep northern canyon known as Copper Canyon. Northern Mexico. Many Mexican deserts lie in the north. Many mountains lie here. Many canyons lie here too. You may know the Grand Canyon in the United States. Copper Canyon is even bigger. The canyon is more than one mile deep. It belongs to the Sierra Madre Occidental range. A train can take you close to the view. From the train you see the deep canyon. You see waterfalls. You see lakes. The Rarámuri people live in this canyon country. Say Rarámuri as rah-RAH-moo-ree. They are famous for drums they make.

9They are famous for violins they make. For beaches and resorts such as Cabo San Lucas, choose Baja California. Baja California is a peninsula. Water lies along three sides. In winter, whales swim along the shore. The whales are migrating south. A picture shows Cabo San Lucas along the Baja California shore. Baja has no Aztec ruins. The reason is that the Aztecs never lived here. Ancient cave paintings can be found instead. Many people believe ancestors of the Cochimi made the paintings. The pictures show people. The pictures show animals. The colors used are black and red. Baja California's cave paintings appear in a picture. The most amazing ancient ruins here may be the adobe buildings at Paquimé. Say Paquimé as pah-kee-MEH. Adobe is brick made from mud and grass. Builders often stacked many of these bricks. The finished buildings look like apartment buildings of today. More than 3,000 people made those adobe buildings their home from the 900s through the 1300s. The buildings stood near the Casas Grandes river. The fate of the people who lived there is still unknown. A picture shows ancient ruins at Paquimé. A picture shows a whale diving in the Sea of Cortés. The tail is above the water. Visitors who skip ruins and beaches may still like whales. A boat is one way to watch them. At Guerrero Negro, blue whales are often seen. They swim along the Sea of Cortés. People who get seasick can watch from land. Many other sea mammals can be seen on land too. The nearby places are Laguna San Ignacio and Bahia de Magdalena. Mexico has a vibrant culture. The land is breathtaking. The waters are beautiful. The history is abundant. The food is delicious. You will have to agree that Mexico offers a great deal. So come for a visit. A picture shows the cultural center of San Miguel de Allende. Quick Facts About Mexico. Among ethnic groups, Mestizo people are both Indigenous and Spanish.

10Mestizo people make up 62 percent. Indigenous people make up 28 percent. Other groups, mostly European, make up 10 percent. Roman Catholic followers make up 78 percent. Protestant followers make up 11.2 percent. Other religions make up 0.2 percent. People listed as unaffiliated make up 10.6 percent. Languages include Spanish, Mayan, and Náhuatl. Other languages are spoken as well. In government, the executive branch has a president and cabinet members. The legislative branch has a Senate with 128 seats. The Chamber of Deputies has 500 seats. The judicial branch is the Supreme Court of Justice. That court has 11 judges. The currency is the peso. Natural resources include petroleum, silver, antimony, copper, and gold. They also include lead, zinc, natural gas, and timber. In the workforce, agriculture accounts for 13.4 percent. Industry accounts for 24.1 percent. Services account for 61.9 percent. Industries include food and beverages, tobacco, chemicals, and iron and steel. They include petroleum, mining, textiles, and clothing. They include motor vehicles, consumer durables, and tourism. Exports include cars, vehicle parts, computers, and delivery trucks. Exports also include crude petroleum and insulated wiring. Word List. Cathedrals are large churches. Geography means the natural features on the surface of Earth. A century is a span made of one hundred years. Indigenous describes people who are native to the place. Civilizations are societies that are organized and developed. A landform is a physical feature on Earth's surface, such as a mountain. A colony is a land ruled by a different country. Mariachi is traditional music of Mexico. That music goes back to the 1800s. Conquered means one group attacked another and took control of the land. Murals are pictures painted on walls. A republic is a country with a president and with representatives the people elect. A conquistador was a conqueror who came from Spain. Dormant means not active. Ruins are what remains after a place is destroyed or damaged. An empire is land controlled by one ruler. That ruler is an emperor.

24. Condors, Birds of Enormous Wings

1A rare California condor holds its enormous wings open to the sun. This book begins by meeting the condor. Life on wind and rock comes next. A closer look at the body follows. A nest with one egg has a part. Trouble for condors has a part. A closing part calls the condor a truly giant bird. A glossary explains key words. South America’s Andes Mountains rise in majesty. High above them, a huge bird takes off. Weight is over 30 pounds, or 13.5 kilograms. Powerful wings measure an amazing 10.5 feet across, or 3.2 meters. The climb reaches a dizzying 15,000 feet, or 4,600 meters. No flying bird on Earth is larger. This is the giant Andean condor. Gliding along, it searches for food far below. A huge wingspan helps. Extra-keen eyesight helps too. A size chart compares three bodies. An Andean condor can stand up to 4 feet, or 1.2 meters. Wingspan can reach 10.5 feet, or 3.2 meters. Weight can reach 33 pounds, or 15 kilograms. A California condor can stand up to 4.6 feet, or 1.4 meters. Wingspan can reach 9.7 feet, or 3 meters. Weight can reach 25 pounds, or 11 kilograms.

2A person in the chart is 6 feet tall, or 1.8 meters, and weighs 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. The opening bird is the Andean condor, already past 30 pounds with a 10.5-foot wingspan. The chart’s top weight for that species is 33 pounds. California birds are a little taller in the chart and a little lighter. Eyes and wings work together while the bird glides and hunts the ground far below. A map of condor homes shows South America and the Andes Mountains. It shows the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean. One shaded area is the California condor range. Another is the Andean condor range. Western South America is home to Andean condors. The American Southwest is home to California condors. Every condor needs a wide-open habitat. When food appears, there must be room to drop down on huge wings and land. Wind currents must be strong enough too. Those currents let the birds climb high. They also let the birds cover long distances. A single day of travel can reach 150 miles, or 240 kilometers. Speed can reach 50 miles per hour, or 80 kilometers per hour.

3The sea is home for some of these birds. High cliffs are their perches. The shoreline is easy to see from there. Most condors, though, live where the land is dry. They soar over rocky canyons. They soar over deserts and mountains. Nests are preferred on elevated landforms. A lofty nest helps keep eggs safe from predators that walk on the ground. Twigs and feathers are not gathered into a cozy nest. The birds settle on rocky cave floors instead. Jagged outer ledges are used too. Large holes are nests for some California condors. Those holes sit high in California redwoods. Those trees tower over every other kind. The year 2006 revealed nests in redwoods near Big Sur. The Andes Mountains gave Andean condors their name, and that range is their home. Open ground matters because the wings are too broad for a tight landing. Wind does the heavy work of the climb. A day can cover 150 miles. Cliffs, dry canyons, deserts, and mountains are all part of the picture. Eggs stay safer when the nest is high, whether the floor is a cave, a ledge, or a redwood hole.

4Andean condors eat many kinds of animals. Llamas are among them. Alpacas are among them. One day of feeding can reach 4 pounds, or 1.8 kilograms. After that, days may pass with no meal. The diet is carrion only. Carrion means animals that are dead and decaying. You would not find it tasty. Rabbits can be a meal for California condors. Gophers can too. Both are small mammals. Larger mammals are preferred. Deer are preferred. Cattle are preferred. Near the ocean, condors clean beaches of seafood. Small fish are included. A stranded whale of great size can be included. A dead animal can be full of harmful bacteria. Those bacteria can cause disease. Condors are not in danger from them. Special digestive systems are the reason. Nature gets an important service. Rotting flesh is swallowed. Ecosystems stay a little more free of germs. Smell is not a strong sense for condors. Eyesight is excellent, and it is the tool used to find food. Even a great height does not hide a meal from those eyes. Other birds that eat carrion may circle nearby. That circle is a sure sign of a meal.

5The condor swoops in and eats what those birds have found. A beak that is sharp and curved tears the flesh. Food is shared. One picture shows a California condor about to eat what remains of a whale. Llamas and alpacas show how wide the Andean menu is, yet every meal is carrion. Four pounds can be enough for one day, and then the bird may fast. Bacteria in rotting flesh do not sicken a condor. Other scavengers circling overhead often reveal the next meal, and the condor simply drops in to share it. Strength and a sharp edge mark the bill. Width across the wings can hit 10.5 feet, or 3.2 meters. Feathers cover the body. The head does not have them. Legs are strong. Talons are wide. Every bird has a backbone. Every bird has feathers. Every bird has wings. Every bird has a bill. Every bird lays eggs. Every bird is warm-blooded. Adult California condors, male and female, share clear likenesses. Both have black feathers. A fluffy black ruff circles the neck like a collar. Andean birds, whether male or female, wear black body feathers. Necks on those birds are white.

6Males of that species also grow large fleshy lumps on the head. Those lumps are called combs. California condors do not have combs. A comb, if you see one, means the bird is a male Andean condor. Excitement or anger changes the head color. The head turns deep pink or deep orange. Storks are among the closest relatives of condors. The two birds do not look alike at all. Condors stay very clean. After a meal, the head is rubbed clean on rocks. Tree branches are used the same way. A bath in water follows. Hours can then go to smoothing feathers. Black feathers and a black neck ruff mark both sexes of the California bird. White necks mark Andean birds, and only the Andean male adds a comb. A head that flushes deep pink or deep orange is showing excitement or anger. The bill, the wings, the feathers, the legs, the talons, and the eggs all fit what makes a bird a bird. A bald head is shared by all condors. The bare skin is a useful adaptation. No feathers from the neck upward makes grooming simpler. That matters after the head goes into a decaying animal.

7Messy bits have almost no feathers to cling to. Two years pass between eggs, and only one egg is laid. Protecting that egg is crucial. The female sits on it. The male sits on it too. About fifty-six days pass before hatching. Growing up changes the feathers step by step. Gray yields to black. Flight begins around six months of age. Luck in the wild usually means a life of about sixty years. Zoos and refuges can stretch life past seventy-five years. Most animals live longer in captivity, and condors do too. Protected places pamper them. The wild holds many hazards. People have done some of the greatest harm. An Andean condor chick waits in one picture. Parents are on the way with food. A bare head keeps the mess of a carcass from sticking. Two years is a long wait for a single egg, so both adults take turns sitting. Fifty-six days is the usual wait until hatching. Gray feathers darken toward black, and flight comes near six months. Sixty years is a lucky wild life. Past seventy-five years is possible in a zoo or a refuge, where the birds are protected and even pampered.

8People remain a major hazard outside those safe places. Andean condors are endangered. California condors are endangered. Two centuries ago, far more of these birds were alive. Trouble started when people moved into condor country. Many people in North America disliked the big birds. Many people in South America disliked them too. They shot the birds. Coyotes were disliked as well. Wolves were disliked. Poison was left out to kill them. Condors ate those dead animals and died from the poison too. Lead poisoning killed many more. People had shot an animal. A condor feasted and sometimes swallowed lead bullets by accident. Electrical power brought a newer danger. Eyesight is sharp, yet power lines are not always seen. A strike on the wires kills the bird. Extinction was frighteningly near for California condors in 1987. Wild survivors numbered only about ten. Scientists caught those wild birds. Refuges became their new home. There the birds could be protected. Scientists could also help them raise young. Five hard years of dedication passed. Releases back to the wild then began. May 2013 found over 230 California condors free in the sky once more.

9Andean birds have had a rescue of their own since 1973. Groups in South America have reserved land for them. Numbers are rising. A few thousand are estimated to live in the wild. Rescued birds in one picture were later released. Numbered tags let researchers keep track of them. Shooting, poison set for coyotes and wolves, lead from bullets, and unseen power lines all cut the numbers down. About ten wild California birds remained in 1987. Capture, refuge care, and a five-year effort made release possible. By May 2013 the free count was over 230. Andean numbers, helped since 1973 by land set aside, are climbing toward a few thousand. Utah is the setting of one picture. A canyon there holds a California condor in flight. Picture a bird that gigantic passing overhead. The sight is amazing. An eagle’s wings would have to double to match this span. A falcon’s wings would have to be multiplied by five. Protected reserves now shelter many California condors. Little other land still gives these huge birds a sky. Serious dangers have not gone away.

10Continued protection of the birds can keep them with us. Protection of their environments matters just as much. If that care continues, wonder at these giant high fliers can last for centuries. An adaptation is a shift in a living thing or in its species. Survival in that home becomes easier. Captivity is a life shut in, without freedom. Carrion is meat left after an animal dies and begins to rot. A current is moving air or moving water that keeps one direction. Decomposing means rotting, or falling apart into tiny pieces. An ecosystem binds living things to the habitats around them. To propel is to drive a person or an object ahead. A refuge is a place that offers safety, ease, or protection. Wingspan is the measure from one wingtip across to the other. A canyon flight in Utah shows the scale. Set against an eagle, the wings are twice as wide. Set against a falcon, they are five times as wide. Reserves are among the last skies these California birds still use. Dangers remain, yet steady care for the birds and their homes can keep that awe alive for centuries.

25. COVID-19 and a Worldwide Health Crisis

1An employee at an elementary school in Orlando, Florida, takes a student's temperature. The check comes before the student may enter the school. An artist's rendering shows particles of COVID-19. Spikes cover the particles. The spikes help the particles bind with host cells and invade them. December 2019 brought alarm to doctors in Wuhan, China. A new illness had appeared. Shortness of breath was one symptom. Fever was another. Fatigue was another. Some patients struggled so hard to breathe that a hospital stay was required. Good medical care let many patients recover. Not every patient survived. A new coronavirus caused the illness. The illness was named COVID-19. Spread came quickly. The World Health Organization, known as the WHO, issued a declaration in March 2020. The status of COVID-19 was now a pandemic. A pandemic is a disease that has raced across the whole world. Daily life is shaken hard by a pandemic such as COVID-19. All of us have to put in effort if a pandemic is to be beaten. Scientists have a part. Students have a part. Each of us has a role when a pandemic crisis must be solved. A chart of history's deadliest pandemics lists several outbreaks and their dates.

2The Plague of Justinian is marked 541 to 542. The Black Death is marked 1347 to 1351. Smallpox is marked 1520. The Spanish Flu is marked 1918 to 1919. Pandemics reach back to ancient times. One example is the Plague of Justinian. Around 541 of the common era, it moved across Europe, Asia, and Africa. Thirty to fifty million people died. That toll was about half the world's population then. After about eight hundred years, the Black Death left Asia and entered Europe. Fifty million people died. Bacteria were behind the Plague of Justinian. Bacteria were behind the Black Death too. Drugs called antibiotics now kill many bacteria that cause disease. Bacteria therefore start fewer pandemics. Viruses are the more common cause of modern pandemics. Viruses have driven deadly pandemics many times. Smallpox, a viral infection, moved around the world for centuries. It caused blindness. It caused death. Scientists in 1981 identified AIDS, a viral disease new to them. The death toll from AIDS around the world is thirty-two million. Viral influenza in 1918 reached five hundred million people across the world. Influenza pandemics returned in 1957.

3They returned again in 1968. A 2009 flu called H1N1, also known as swine flu, reached 1.4 billion people. Masks were on people's faces during the Spanish Flu pandemic of 1918. What turns a disease into a pandemic? A new disease such as COVID-19 tends to spread easily. Bodies have no defenses against it yet. Contagion is far stronger in some diseases than in others. Danger is far greater in some diseases than in others. A pandemic usually requires both traits at once. The disease must be very contagious. It must also be very dangerous. A dangerous disease does not always become a pandemic. A contagious one does not always become one either. Ebola is deadly, yet fairly rare. Africa has seen several terrible Ebola outbreaks. A worldwide spread has not happened for this disease. The common cold is very contagious. It usually is not deadly. Colds do not cause pandemics either. Medical help today is far stronger than it was in earlier pandemics. Disease can also travel faster now than ever before. On every continent, city life packs people close together. Those cities are larger than cities of the past. Where people live and work in tight quarters, sickness passes easily.

4More of the planet is now home to humans. Contact with wildlife has grown closer. Viruses that live in animals can infect humans more readily because of that contact. Travel spreads disease as well. Hours are enough for a flight to reach any region on Earth. Sickness can ride along. A timeline tracks how fast COVID-19 moved in early 2020. On January 20, 2020, five countries had cases. On February 3, 2020, the count was twenty-eight countries. On February 29, 2020, it was sixty-four countries. On March 20, 2020, it was 184 countries. Five countries had the disease, and nearly every world region had it only two months later. One photograph shows a COVID-19 patient leaving a hospital in Wuhan, China. The patient had received a lung transplant. Early signs of a new disease, even one that might turn into a pandemic, are often easy to miss. Understanding how it behaves takes time. Doctors and nurses need training so they watch for new diseases. A doctor in Wuhan, China, named Li Wenliang sounded a warning late in 2019. His warning described a new illness aimed at the lungs.

5The illness he warned about was COVID-19. A few months later, Doctor Li died of it himself. Quick cooperation among countries is required once a new disease is spreading. Detection and a halt to the spread both depend on that speed. The World Health Organization helps countries talk to one another. Scientists around the world can then share what they learn. A test worked out in one country can be used in others. During the COVID-19 pandemic, scientists in China identified the new virus very quickly. What they learned about the virus went to the WHO. The WHO shared it so that COVID-19 tests could be developed everywhere. Some countries could test huge numbers of people at once. Others struggled. Preparation was strong in South Korea, to take one example. After COVID-19 arrived, that government managed daily tests in the tens of thousands. The United States struggled to produce enough tests for a large population. Personnel there made a first batch of tests. A flaw made those tests useless. Testing delays let the virus spread unseen for several months. The United States then had many more cases than South Korea.

6Early testing helps a government control a disease. When large numbers of people can be tested, medical workers can act quickly. Sick people can be treated. They can be kept from passing the illness on. Rapid spread in the United States was fed by several local issues. First, the country chose to build its own test. A German lab had the earliest test on offer, and the country did not use it. Faults spoiled the earliest tests that the United States government supplied. Rapid testing became impossible. COVID-19 moved through the population without being detected. Many people already carried the disease when working tests finally arrived. Making enough tests for everyone grew very hard. Mask-wearing was not a social custom in the United States at the pandemic's start. In many Asian countries, a sick person customarily wears a mask in any public place. Most people in Japan covered their faces once COVID-19 showed up. China did too. South Korea did too. That habit helped slow the virus early. Few masks were worn in the United States, and that gap helped the virus move. No single national plan covered closing schools or businesses. Some states temporarily shut businesses and public spaces.

7That procedure is known as a lockdown. Other states did not lock down. The virus spread more easily where lockdown rules were less strict. A COVID-19 test kit is part of this picture. Everyone has to contribute if a pandemic is to be contained. People in every part of society must work together. The goal is safety for themselves and for others. One government task is to stop people from passing the infection along. Officials might temporarily forbid travel. They might temporarily close businesses. They might tell people to stay home. A sick person might need to quarantine, which means staying away from others for a time. Officials might also require quarantine before a person enters a country. The aim is to keep illness from spreading. Hospitals and officials track where the disease is moving. Governments and hospitals share the latest information so people can protect themselves. Care for sick people depends on hard work by doctors and by nurses. The work can be very dangerous. Some medical professionals picked up COVID-19 from the patients they treated. Some of them died. Doctor Li in China was one of those deaths.

8Other workers keep going during a pandemic. Farmers do. Postal workers do. Grocery store clerks do. Firefighters do. Police officers do. Schoolteachers do. These people, and many others in important jobs, are called essential workers. Society keeps functioning for everyone because of the work they do. Citizens must also protect one another. Public health orders can be obeyed. Masks can be worn. Hands can be washed often. Large gatherings can be avoided. Trips away from home that are not needed can be skipped. Schools may close. Offices may close. School may shift online. Jobs may shift online. Time with friends may shift online. New ways to connect have to be found. During COVID-19, people in Italy began a daily routine. Each afternoon, singing rose from the windows of their homes. Alertness from governments and from scientists has to continue even when a pandemic seems over. They must keep sharing information. A very contagious disease can return with ease. Control often happens in cycles. Final defeat usually comes only after the disease has been fought again and again. Control means slowing the spread, then stopping it. Countries around the world take up that work.

9Hospitals keep treating sick people at the same time. Scientists race to discover a vaccine. Immunity to a virus is what this substance, a vaccine, is meant to create. Once vaccinated, the body can repel the disease and stay well. Finding an effective vaccine, testing it, and making it available worldwide usually takes years. Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine in 1796. People gained protection from the deadly smallpox virus. Some viruses still have no known vaccine. The virus that causes AIDS is one of them. For a disease like that, communities must contain the virus together. The aim is to keep it from spreading through the whole population. A picture shows a volunteer receiving a shot. The injection, part of a medical trial, is one possible vaccine against COVID-19. Countries share the work of seeking a vaccine able to stop COVID-19. In 2020, scientists tested dozens of possible vaccines. The work went on in the United States. It went on in China. It went on in the United Kingdom. It went on in Germany. Other countries took part as well. A vaccine for this disease will require the sharpest thinking scientists can offer, in every country.

10Two rankings use figures dated November 5, 2020. One ranking orders countries by how many COVID-19 cases they had. The United States leads that case list. India comes next. Then Brazil. Then Russia. Then France. Then Spain. Then Argentina. Then Colombia. Then the United Kingdom. Mexico is last. A second ranking orders countries by COVID-19 deaths. The United States leads that death list. Brazil comes next. Then India. Then Mexico. Then the United Kingdom. Then Italy. Then France. Then Spain. Then Iran. Peru is last. Cheers greeted healthcare workers outside hospitals in New York City in 2020. They were met with thanks. The scene belongs to the COVID-19 pandemic. A pandemic can strike at any time. It can spread with lightning speed. Travel, work, and shared living all help it move. During a pandemic, every person has a role in stopping the spread. A child may stay home from school. A store clerk may put on a mask before work. A nurse may help a sick patient breathe. A scientist may study vaccines in a lab. Each of these acts is a way to keep one another safe and healthy.

26. Desert Animals That Bite and Sting

1Sections follow this order. A Child in the Emergency Room. Bites and Stings That Can Kill. Bites and Stings That Do Not Kill. Final Advice. Words and Topics. A map marks California, Arizona, and New Mexico. Tucson and Mexico are marked too. Jude McNally holds a tarantula in a photo. He uses the spider to teach people how spiders behave. A Child in the Emergency Room. A girl of two years arrives at the emergency room. A red mark shows on her leg. She is too young to tell anyone what happened. Her parents believe an animal bit her or stung her. How can a doctor in that room name the animal that caused the injury? Jude McNally is managing director of a center in Tucson. The state is Arizona. His workplace is the Poison and Drug Information Center. He studies things that poison the body or harm it. A talk with Jude will explain desert bites and desert stings. Bites and Stings That Can Kill. Question: A young girl like this one reaches the emergency room. What is the first step? Jude: Doctors search for signs of bites and stings that can threaten life.

2Four possible animals are in mind. Black widow spiders are one. Scorpions are one. Insects that fly and sting are one. Rattlesnakes are one. Question: If the animal is a black widow, what do doctors watch for? Jude: Venom is made by every spider. Most spiders cannot push that venom into a person. The black widow can. The female black widow is the one to watch most closely. A bite from her injects venom. Muscle cramps follow a black widow bite. Burning, stinging pain starts where the bite landed. Swelling stays small. Major puncture wounds cannot be seen. Muscle cramping begins, usually near the sting. Small children suffer that cramping worst of all. A child may cramp in muscles all over the body. Sometimes the belly turns stiff, like a board. Sometimes breathing grows difficult. Puffy eyes can appear in children too. No muscle cramping means the case is not a black widow bite. Doctors set that animal aside. A note: many insecticides fail against black widow spiders. Those chemicals are made to kill insects. Remember a key difference. Spiders are arachnids. They are not insects. A bark scorpion is pictured.

3Tail included, it is about two inches long. Question: A scorpion sting would show which signs? Jude: Arizona holds over thirty kinds of scorpions. Only the bark scorpion can threaten a life. A two-year-old stung by one will be restless. Sitting still will be impossible. Muscle twitching is common. The mouth area shows it most. Another clear sign is roving eye syndrome. The eyes cannot focus. Movement disorders appear too. The child may look caught in a strange dance. Stings from other scorpions bring swelling in one local spot. The bark scorpion brings almost no reaction where it stung. With a two-year-old, a tap test is used. Fingers run up and down the body. A scream marks the sting site, because the pain is so sharp. Careful looking sometimes finds a single puncture wound. Three signs have to show up. Restlessness is one. Twitching is one. Roving eye syndrome is one. If they are absent, scorpions are ruled out. Homes sometimes get visits from scorpions. Dark places are where they hide. Question: Flying insects that sting leave which clues? Jude: Bees raise a worry about allergic reactions. Wasps do too. Ants do too.

4Most people see some redness where they were stung. Itching appears. Swelling appears. Those signs fade in a couple of days. A reaction somewhere other than the sting, inside the first hour, is different. It is called a type 1 allergic reaction. Life can be threatened. The window is described as an hour. Usually you know within 20 to 30 minutes if allergy is the problem. Unless allergy is present, discomfort from a wasp sting or a bee sting usually fades in a few days. Breathing trouble is a major warning. Another warning is an itch in the hands after a sting on the back. Trouble swallowing after a sting on the leg is a warning too. Each of these means the whole body is reacting. Emergency medical care is required for this type 1 reaction. The patient can die. A note for readers: a bite or sting problem should lead to a call. Phone a center that handles poison. The center for your region knows which animals in your area deserve concern. A doctor in a photo checks a girl's blood pressure. Deaths from insect stings outnumber deaths from a combined group.

5That group is black widows, scorpions, and rattlesnakes. Ruling out allergy to flying, stinging insects is that important. Breathing ability is checked to rule allergy out. Blood pressure is tested too. An allergic reaction drives blood pressure down in an extreme way. Question: A rattlesnake bite shows which signs? Jude: Ruling a rattlesnake bite out right away is harder. The illness moves in stages. It starts with a puncture wound. Some bleeding is possible. Swelling then shows at the bite. Discoloration shows there too. Hours later, the skin may blister. Tissue destruction can follow. Skin around the site dies. Muscle tissue dies too. A photo shows a western diamondback rattlesnake. When bruising travels across the body is a definite sign of a snakebite. Blood is drawn. Parts of the blood that handle clotting are measured. Snake venom destroys those parts. The patient starts bleeding on the inside. Tissue dies because of that bleeding. The whole process covers 24 to 36 hours. Antivenom is given the entire time. The goal is to halt how the body reacts once venom is inside. A math note gives costs. Each vial of rattlesnake antivenom bills a patient about 3,000 dollars.

6One patient stayed in the hospital 10 days. He received more than 50 vials. Other hospital costs sat on the same bill. The total was 326,000 dollars. How much of that bill was the antivenom? How much was everything else? Small, sharp teeth fill the mouth of a Gila monster. The name is said HEE-luh. Bites and Stings That Do Not Kill. Question: Some animals do not cause signs that threaten life. A bite from a Gila monster would look like what? Jude: Teeth marks usually form a little row. Sometimes they form a circle. A single puncture is not the pattern. Teeth remain in the wound in about one case out of three. Pain is severe. The lizard hangs on a long time after biting. Half a minute is common. Longer is possible. Most people bitten by a Gila monster, Jude says, brought the bite on themselves. The animal is very docile. Harassment is what most victims were doing. A note: this venomous lizard lives mostly in Arizona. Northern Mexico is the other main home. Question: What about scorpions that are not bark scorpions? Jude: Swelling often starts at the site when the scorpion is some other kind.

7The start comes minutes after the sting. Pain is felt there. Tingling may occur. Numbness may occur. Hours are usually enough for it to fade. Swelling is the clue that bark scorpion is the wrong answer. A bark scorpion causes no swelling. Fine hairs cover the body of the desert hairy scorpion. Question: Spider bites other than the black widow show which signs? Jude: Venom from most other spiders causes local inflammation. Full-body signs usually do not follow. Brown recluse spiders are the other bites watched closely. Often the bite itself is not felt. Hours pass, and a blister rises where the bite landed. The blister later breaks open. A scab forms. Tissue dies. A large area can be involved. Weeks can pass. Months can pass. A brown recluse is pictured. A bite from this spider may need months before it fully heals. Emergency-room diagnosis rarely includes brown recluse bites at the start. The signs need time to develop. Set aside the black widow. Set aside the brown recluse. Other spider bites cause no serious problem unless infection sets in.

8Harm to humans is absent in most spiders. Some spiders eat common pests. Houseflies are one example. Mosquitos are another. A common garden spider is shown. A garter snake is shown. A note on deaths: snakebite death is rare in the United States. Worldwide, it is common. India is one example. An estimate says 40,000 people die there from snakebites each year. Deadlier kinds of snakes are one reason. Less access to health care is the other. Question: What about snakes besides the dangerous ones already named? Jude: Nonvenomous snakes far outnumber venomous ones. Plenty of snakes called nonvenomous do carry venom. A bite from them is still not a serious health risk. Soreness can follow. Once in a while, blisters develop at the site. Swelling can develop too. Nothing serious follows. Estimates for the United States pass 35,000 snakebites each year. Of that total, 6,000 to 8,000 carry venom. A bullsnake is pictured. Final Advice. Question: What guidance do you have for readers? Jude: Rattlesnakes are the exception. Almost every other bite and sting we treat happens in homes or near them. Night is when spiders are active. Night is when scorpions are active.

9By day they look for a dark crack or a crevice. Meeting them is more likely at night, while they are active. Lights switched on at night lower the risk. Nighttime lighting is a useful safety step. The picture makes that point. See something dangerous, and one step backward usually does the job. You leave the reach of the danger. Leaving the animal alone lowers risk further. More than half the rattlesnake patients we treat had already seen the snake. They knew the danger. They still put themselves at greater risk. Smart choices make safety much more likely. Pictures show a raccoon, a bat, a fox, and a skunk. Rabies cannot be carried by cold-blooded animals. Many smaller mammals cannot carry it either. Skunks can carry rabies. Bats can. Raccoons can. Foxes can. Coyotes can. A county health official should hear about bats inside your house. Time around any of these animals is a reason too. Any risk means you need a series of vaccines. Full-blown rabies has been survived by only one known person. Words to Know. Antivenom is a medicine. It stops the damage a venom would do.

10Discoloration is a shift in color. Disorders are ways a body works that are not normal. Assessing means evaluating. It can also mean measuring. Docile means peaceful. Aggression is absent. Blood pressure tells how strongly the heart pushes blood. Embedded means stuck firmly in place. Harassing means bothering someone. Tormenting is another word for it. Clotting means parts stick together so bleeding stops. Inflammation is redness that hurts. Swelling comes with it. A culprit is whoever caused an injury or a crime. The cause can be a person or another animal. Local means limited to one particular body part. A diagnosis names an illness or an injury. A puncture is a tiny opening through the skin. A site is a location. Symptoms are signs. They point to an illness or an injury. A syndrome is a group of symptoms. They show up together. Venom is a poisonous liquid from an animal. A snake can make it. A spider can make it. An insect can make it. Topics include antivenom, insects, a lizard, mammals, and rabies. Reactions listed cover blood, breathing, movement, sight, and skin. Scorpions, snakes, and spiders are listed too.

27. Earth's Highest Mountain

1What this book covers: a beginning. The mountain itself. Getting ready to climb. The route up. The Sherpa people. The first to arrive on top. Later climbers. Dangers. A closing word. Places to learn more. Words to know. A beginning Each year, when the weather allows it, hundreds of people begin a brutal climb. They bring a powerful hunger for adventure. They hope the climb will place them at the highest spot on Earth. That spot is the summit of Mount Everest. It is the tallest mountain in the world. Strength plays a part in a successful summit. Careful planning plays a part. Good weather plays a part. The right equipment plays a part. A share of luck plays a part too. The mountain itself Mount Everest stands in Asia. Nepal lies on one side of its border. On the other side is the Tibet Autonomous Region. That region is part of China. The peak is sixty million years old. Among a chain of peaks that rise extremely high, this one stands tallest. People call that chain the Himalayas. A map shows where this peak and the Himalayas are found. Both the range and the peak sit near a fault. Two plates meet there. A plate is a moving piece of Earth's crust. One plate slides beneath the other. The upper plate is pushed up. Mountains rise from that push. The peak is still growing. Each year it adds about 6 centimeters. That gain is 2.4 inches. The summit stands 8,850 meters over the level of the sea. In feet, the height is 29,035. A passenger jet flies at nearly that height. K2 is the second-tallest mountain on Earth. This peak rises almost 305 meters above K2. Those 305 meters equal 1,000 feet. A chart lines up several famous mountains for comparison. Many people call the highest point on Earth the ultimate challenge. The way up is filled with danger. Steep cliffs of rock stand in the way.

2So do cliffs of ice. Deep crevasses stand in the way. So do slabs of ice and snow that shift. Air near the top holds much less oxygen than air lower down. Breathing is very hard. Climbers tire easily. High winds may blow. Temperatures may fall below zero. With all of that, the highest place on Earth can seem almost impossible to reach. How the peak got its names In English, the peak is called Everest. The name honors Sir George Everest. He was Surveyor General of India during colonial rule. The Nepali have a much older name for it. They say Sagarmatha. That word is Sanskrit. It means peak of heaven. People in Tibet say Chomolungma. That name means Mother Goddess of the World. Blocks of ice keep moving in the Khumbu icefall. On the path up from the south, this icefall ranks with the worst hazards. Getting ready A person who wants to climb this mountain must be in excellent shape. The work is very strenuous. The body faces huge demands. Most climbers train for years. They build skill on other hard mountains. They also stay extra days at high elevation. That time lets the body acclimate to thinner air. The trip costs a great deal. A trip run by seasoned leaders may be priced as high as 65,000 U.S. dollars. Personal gear is extra. Air fares are extra. Insurance is extra.
