The lowest price people estimate is around 30,000 dollars. Oxygen costs 300 dollars for one bottle. A climber may need up to twenty bottles. That oxygen bill is 6,000 dollars. Nepal's government charges 10,000 dollars just for a permit. Gear and preparation can save a life. A climber here must stay warm. The climber must stay dry. The climber must rest. The climber must drink enough water. Staying alive here calls for piles of special clothes. It also takes climbing gear, camping gear, and food made for high altitude. Some of those supplies are listed below.

3Clothing: pants and a jacket that keep water out. A lightweight coat filled with down. Warm covering for the head. A heavyweight suit filled with down. Several pairs of socks that hold heat. Dark glasses for bright sun, and goggles as well. Gloves that keep water out. Heavy mittens filled with down. A fleece top and fleece pants. Climbing gear: a harness. Heavy boots for climbing, chosen two sizes too large so more socks will fit. Crampons, the metal spikes worn on shoes. An ice ax. A face mask. Maps. A compass. Oxygen in 20 canisters. A rope 15 meters long. Camping gear: bottled gas. A large tent for Base Camp. A stove for cooking. Smaller tents of high quality for the higher camps. A tool that purifies water. Down sleeping bags, two or three of them. Pads to sleep on. The route up The safest seasons are spring and fall. May draws the most climbers. A climb can last two months. The dates must be planned so that dangerous weather is avoided. In winter, the temperature can drop to −50 degrees Celsius. That reading is −58 degrees Fahrenheit. In summer, enormous storms lay meters of snow on the slopes. Climbers often visit old temple sites before the trek starts. The sites are in Kathmandu. That city is Nepal's capital. Advance Base Camp stands on the northern slope. It sits at 6,400 meters. That height is 21,000 feet. Up to fifteen routes reach the top. Base Camp is the start for most of those routes. The camp's height is almost 5,500 meters above the sea. That is 18,000 feet. The summit is still 3,219 meters higher. That remaining gap is 11,000 feet. Reaching Base Camp on foot may use up ten full days. Once there, climbers rest for about a week. Their bodies adjust to air that is thin. For the next few weeks they walk toward camps that sit higher. They also walk back down.

4They go to each camp and return several times before they move on to the next camp. Those trips let them practice hard work in thin air. After the highest camp becomes home for a while, weather news is what they study. They look at the sky. Several tries over several days may be needed. Conditions must be favorable. Wind should be no stronger than 32 kilometers an hour. That limit is 20 miles an hour. Snow should not fill the sky. Weather that turns harsh and inhospitable can hold them inside the tents. Several days may pass that way. They may even return to Base Camp. Climbers need about twelve hours to leave the top camp and touch the summit. They usually set off near the middle of the night. Climbers can then come back before dark the following day. The last 100 meters are the hardest. Those meters equal 300 feet. This stretch includes the Hillary Step. The step is a cliff made of ice and of rock. Sir Edmund Hillary gave it his name. A map shows the path followed by Edmund Hillary together with Tenzing Norgay. Once climbers are on top, they may stay about an hour. They take in the view. They take in the feeling of sitting at Earth's highest point. Then they try to head down before the sun sets. The return down to that top camp lasts about four hours in most cases. Some climbers do not take a slow path to the top. In 2003, two sherpas each made the trip on a different day. Each one left Base Camp and stood on the summit in less than thirteen hours. One of them returned in 2004. That climb took eight hours and ten minutes. It was a record. Few visitors can match a Sherpa's speed on the climb. Their bodies are already adjusted to thin air at high altitude. A picture shows sunset from the highest point.

5Climbers have little time to look at the view. The Sherpa people The earliest Sherpas entered Nepal some five centuries back. They crossed over from a region called Tibet. In the beginning they herded animals and traded goods. After they settled beneath this mountain, they became famous for leading climbers upward. Their bodies have adapted to the small amount of oxygen in the Himalayas. They easily outperform visitors from lower regions. Most climbers could not reach the top without sherpas. Sherpas serve as guides. They also serve as porters, and they carry most of the gear. A load can weigh more than the carrier's own body. Loads past 150 pounds are common. The capital letter matters. Sherpa names an ethnic group of people. Written with a small s, sherpas are the guides for trips on this mountain and for other climbs. Some members of the Sherpa people become those guides. A guide is not always a member of that people. A picture shows two Sherpa girls. They are at a festival in Nepal. Guides from Nepal, and the people who plan the routes, are necessary on every climb here. Sherpas are strong. They know a great deal. They adjust to what the mountain demands. For many listeners, their work and the climb are one and the same. What they understand, and what they can do, is a vital service. They lead the way. They give advice. They haul gear. They cook. Their pride in a mountaineering heritage is easy to understand. The legend around that heritage is part of the pride. Names in this community follow a pattern. A boy's name frequently matches the weekday of his birth. A name may also honor a particular virtue. That custom explains why so many share one first name. Most people here use a single name only. Names you will often hear are Tenzing, Ngawang, Tashi, and Dorje. Who stood there first Climbers from Great Britain were the first to attempt the top.

6They started toward the summit in 1921. The attempt failed. George Mallory had been on that 1921 trip. In 1924 he tried again, with Andrew Irvine. Someone saw them for the last time above Camp VI. That camp is also called Camp 6. Many years passed with their fate unknown. In 1999, a group came upon Mallory's body. It lay 305 meters short of the summit. That gap is 1,000 feet. No one can say for certain that he had made the top and was heading down when he fell and died. Success on his part is doubtful. Another team tried in 1953. On May 29 of that year, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay moved slowly up the icy face. They were the first to stand on the summit. Seven weeks had gone by since they reached Everest Base Camp. Back home in New Zealand, Hillary kept bees. The climb brought him a knighthood. From then on, people said Sir Edmund Hillary. Norgay was a Sherpa. The whole world celebrated what the two had done. A photograph places Sir Edmund Hillary on the left. Tenzing Norgay stands with him on the summit. The photo marks their historic climb in 1953. Fame was not what either man was seeking. Fortune was not the goal either. They still used their fame to help people in Nepal. Sir Edmund Hillary started a foundation. Hospitals have been built through it. Medical clinics have been built. Schools have been built. Bridges have been built. The same foundation has planted trees across the Himalayas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands. Tenzing Norgay started a school for climbing. Dozens of the students there have reached this summit. Like Hillary, Norgay used what he had achieved to open more schooling for Sherpa children. The climbers who followed Once those two had been to the top, plenty of people expected that nobody else would bother. What happened was the reverse.

7From the 1920s onward, thousands have attempted the summit. By 2010, the number who had succeeded was over 3,300. Every age group is represented. Attempts arrive from every region of Earth. Climbers who have summited include people from Austria. Bosnia is on the list. China is on the list. Germany is on the list. Great Britain is on the list. Canada is on the list. Italy is on the list. Japan is on the list. Mexico is on the list. Russia is on the list. The United States is on the list. Many further countries are on it too. A picture shows Takao Arayama, a mountaineer from Japan. He was seventy at the time. In May 2006 he was nearing the summit by the Tibetan route. The years have brought many firsts. In 1975, Junko Tabei came from Japan and was the first woman on this mountain. A 1978 summit was done with no oxygen carried in bottles. During 2000, one person skied the full descent from the peak. The next year, a different climber came down from the summit on a snowboard. Blindness did not stop Eric Weihenmayer in 2001. He was the first person without sight to stand there. Future firsts are still unknown. Peter Hillary is Sir Edmund Hillary's son. He took up the same climb his father had made. Peter has been to the top twice. One climb was in 1990. The other was in 2002. Apa Sherpa, who is a Sherpa, holds the record for visits to the summit. He has been there twenty times. The twentieth visit came in May 2010. That same month, Jordan Romero was thirteen. He became the youngest to make the climb. The record he broke belonged to a Sherpa who was fifteen. That earlier climb was in 2001. Over the same weekend in May 2010, the summit saw more than two hundred climbers. As of May 2008, the oldest summit climber was a Nepali man of seventy-six.

8A timeline of major feats 1921: the first attempt, by a British team. 1924: George Mallory vanishes. 1953: Hillary, called Sir Edmund, stands on top with Tenzing Norgay. 1975: a woman reaches the summit for the first time. 1978: a climber gets there with no bottled oxygen. 1980: the first climb made alone, by Reinhold Messner. 1996: a storm takes 15 lives, the largest one-year toll known then. 1999: the body of George Mallory is discovered. 2001: a person who is blind reaches the top for the first time. 2004: the quickest climb on record, 8 hours and 10 minutes. 2008: the oldest summit, at age 76. 2010: Apa Sherpa sets a new personal record of 20 summits. 2010: the youngest summit, at age 13. 2015: a quake strikes Nepal. At South Base Camp, 18 people or more are killed. 2020: the government of Nepal stops issuing climbing permits for a time. The pause came from concern about the COVID-19 pandemic. A picture shows Apa Sherpa, a Nepali guide who works at high altitude. May 2010 was his twentieth time on the summit, a record. Dangers Death comes to nearly one climber in every ten who try. In 1996 the mountain was especially deadly for climbers. Fifteen people died in that one storm. Between 1922 and 2009, deaths on the climb passed 220. Avalanches kill more people here than any other cause. Many routes follow glaciers. Those glaciers are rivers of ice, and the ice moves. While the ice creeps downhill, enormous pieces can break away and collapse. The ice also opens huge cracks. Those cracks are crevasses. Snow may cover them. A single misstep can drop a climber to death. Climbers have to handle air that lacks oxygen. Trouble can start above just 3,000 meters. That line is 10,000 feet. The body may feel nausea. Headaches may come. Confusion may come. Muscle coordination may be lost. Hallucinations may appear. Still higher, edema can strike. The condition can kill.

9Fluid gathers in the brain. It can gather in the lungs instead. Breathing grows harder as a person climbs. At 5,500 meters, only half the normal oxygen is available. That camp height is 18,000 feet. Near the summit, breathing capacity is down to 30 percent of what is normal. The heart pounds. Each breath is a struggle. Even pulling on boots forces a stop for rest. Thin air at these heights screens out fewer harmful rays from the Sun. Skin left bare can be burned severely. Eyes without proper cover can be burned within minutes. White snow throws the light back. That glare can leave a person unable to see for a while. Covering the eyes matters even under cloud. Winds here can reach hurricane force. They can exceed 161 kilometers each hour. That speed is 100 miles each hour. The cold wind can freeze bare skin in under a minute. Frostbite is a grave danger. Some climbers have had fingers removed. Toes have been removed. Noses have been removed. Doctors amputated those parts. Crowds are a problem even in this harsh place. A picture shows lines of people gathered to go up. Climbers also face serious dehydration. Drinking plenty of water is important. Because the temperature is so low, water freezes. It must be melted again before anyone can drink. Crowding has turned dangerous. As many as 354 people have aimed for the summit on one day. Some died in the line because their spare oxygen was used up while they waited. Trash has collected. Bodies are sometimes met on the way up. They are met on the way down as well. Inexperience brings huge risk. Nothing requires a climber to prove past experience. Novices who attempt the trek are unprepared. Injury is more likely for them. Death is more likely for them. A picture shows a porter bearing a basket woven from straw. An injured climber rides in that basket. The pair will travel hard for two days.

10Only then can a helicopter fly the injured man to a hospital. A closing word This mountain is no place for a faint heart. Look at the dangers and you may ask why anyone comes. Cold that freezes is a threat. Wind at high speed is a threat. Snow that blinds is a threat. A shortage of oxygen is a threat. Avalanches are a threat. Crevasses are a threat. Slopes of ice are a threat. People come anyway. Adventure thrills them. Finishing the climb fills them with pride. Standing at the top of Earth fills them too. Those feelings draw thousands here. A picture shows Jordan Romero at age thirteen. May 2010 was when he set the mark as the youngest climber to finish this ascent. If you want to know more Libraries keep many books about this mountain. Some tell the lives of famous climbers. Some tell true stories of climbing trips. Some explain how a person can start climbing mountains. Other useful subjects are mountain climbing, exploration in the arctic, and the Himalayas. Films, movies, and television programs about the peak can be found at a library or a video store. Some reports even follow climbers while they are still going up. Words to know Acclimate: to adjust when the climate is new, or when a situation is new. Amputated: cut off. Crevasses: deep cracks in the ice of a glacier. Dehydration: a dangerous shortage of water in the body. Edema: a condition in which fluid gathers in organs or in body tissues. Fault: a crack in Earth's crust. The crust moves along that crack. Hallucinations: sights or sounds a person experiences that are not really there. Inhospitable: harsh and unwelcoming, and hard to live in. Nausea: the feeling of being sick in the stomach. Porters: workers who haul supplies and gear. Strenuous: needing a lot of hard work and energy. Summit: the highest point on a mountain.

28. Egypt's King for Sixty-Six Years

1A carving on an Egyptian temple shows Ramses II. The British Museum holds a huge statue of him. Weight is 6.58 metric tons, or 7.25 tons. Ramesses II is another spelling of King Ramses II. His reign fell in the New Kingdom. Five hundred years is the length of that period. People call it the golden age of ancient Egypt. Third king of the Nineteenth Dynasty is the place he held. The years 1279 to 1213 BCE are his reign. Sixty-six years is how long he ruled. Most people in that era died before age forty-five, so a reign this long was unusual. Egypt gained one of its most powerful pharaohs, or rulers, across those years. Ramses the Great is the title he earned. In ancient times he was almost certainly the most famous pharaoh. Fame's beginning is the subject of this book. A royal surprise, childhood training, and a warrior's rise to king are covered. Battles are covered. The name Ramses the Great is covered. Special words close the account. A temple carving is the first picture of this king. A huge statue in the British Museum is another. Two weight figures describe that statue, 6.58 metric tons and 7.25 tons. Ramesses II is simply another way to write the same name. Pharaoh means the ruler of ancient Egypt.

2The New Kingdom, about five hundred years long, is remembered as a golden age. His seat was third in the Nineteenth Dynasty. The throne years run from 1279 to 1213 BCE. Sixty-six years on that throne was rare, because most people then died before forty-five. Power grew across those years, and the title Ramses the Great followed. Ancient fame belongs to him more than to other pharaohs of his world. The pages ahead stay with the surprise of his family line, his training, his wars, and that famous name. Birth came around 1303 BCE. Seti I, a military commander, was his father. Mut-Tuy was his mother. Say her name MOOT TOO-ee. At least one older sister, named Tia, is what experts think he had. Another sister, Henutmire, may have existed. Say that name he-nuht-MEE-ray. Pharaoh was probably not the future his parents expected. The royal family did not even include them. Tutankhamun died with no heir. A short reign as pharaoh went to one of his officers. Horemheb replaced that officer a few years later. Army command under Tutankhamun had been Horemheb's post. An army general named Paramessu was Ramses II's grandfather. Service beside Horemheb was part of Paramessu's past. Heir was the role Horemheb gave Paramessu after becoming pharaoh. Several years later, Paramessu himself became pharaoh. Ramses I was the name he took.

3A new royal line was what he made of his family. Seti I, father of Ramses, became pharaoh only a few years after that. The throne's line then included Ramses. Tutankhamun's funeral mask is a famous object from the earlier king. A map of Egypt in the reign of 1279 to 1213 BCE names many places. The Orontes River and Kadesh are named. The Mediterranean Sea, Pi-Ramesse, and the Nile River Delta are named. The Nile River, Abydos, Thebes, the Ramesseum, and Karnak are named. The Red Sea, the Egyptian Empire, Abu Simbel, the Hittite Empire, and Nubia are named. Artwork and carvings found in buildings he raised are the source for his early life. Successor to Seti I was a title given at a young age. Watching his father do a pharaoh's work supplied much of the education. Wild birds are offered to Amun, a god, in one scene of father and son sharing a religious duty. Two carved scenes show Ramses with Seti I. A bull is roped in one scene. An offering to the god Amun is made in the other. Egypt's army would one day be led into battle by the crown prince. Strength and endurance had to be built. Training probably started while he was still a small child. Fighting's demands were the point of the physical tests.

4Bulls to be roped were one test. Wild horses to be ridden were another. Captain in the army was a title given early. The rank may have been a name only. A title and authority in the boy's hands helped Seti prepare the nation for the coming rule. Adulthood, in that time, arrived with the teenage years. Military campaigns were shared with his father. Diplomacy and war were learned on those trips. Pharaoh's work would need that practice. A household of his own was already his. Nefertari became his first wife when he was about fifteen. Many wives were common for rulers then. Ramses followed that custom. Eight or more royal wives is the number historians think he married. Several minor wives were married as well. Favorite status belonged to Nefertari. He wrote that his love for her was unique. He wrote that nobody could rival her. The most beautiful woman alive is what he called her. Chief wife is the place she kept until she died. An elaborate temple at Abu Simbel was dedicated to her after her death. Colossal statues decorate it. Nefertari, Ramses, and their children are the figures. A pharaoh's image is usually larger than the rest. Her statue matched his in size. Solid sandstone is the rock her temple was carved from.

5Battle is the subject of a scene at the Nubian temple of Beit el-Wali. Ramses and his two sons appear in the fight. A large role filled much of his father's reign. Military campaigns were his to direct. Courage as a warrior became his reputation. The artwork puts him in a charge, and his two oldest sons ride with him. A rebellion in Nubia is where historians place this fight. South of Egypt is where the country of Nubia lay. Gold and riches came from Nubia. Control of it was fought over by Egyptians and Nubians. Thirteen years was the length of Seti I's rule. About twenty-five was Ramses's age when Seti died. Pharaoh was the result of that death. Several building projects of his father were restarted early in the new reign. An immense hall at Karnak had been ordered by Seti I. Stoneworkers and artisans were to build it. Tall columns numbered 134. Raised relief, also called bas-relief, decorated the walls. Background of a scene is cut away in that process. The images stay raised. Honor for Ramses II was the aim of the Ramesseum. Memory of him was meant to last for eternity. Five thousand square meters, or 53,820 square feet, is the area of the Great Hypostyle Hall of Karnak. A different cut was ordered before long.

6Images were carved straight into the stone. Speed improved, and detail fell. Sunk relief is the name of those less detailed images. Temple building moved at double the earlier rate. More temples were built by him than by any other pharaoh. Many new projects were commissioned. A second temple at Abu Simbel, larger than the first, was one. His mortuary temple, the Ramesseum, in Thebes, was another. A new capital city was another. Pi-Ramesse was the name he chose. Ramsesopolis is a loose translation of that name. Closer reach to old enemies was the gain. The Hittites were those enemies. East of Egypt, in a region now called Syria, was their home. Hittite armies were beaten by Ramses with success. Many small provinces they had taken were reclaimed. Some of those provinces were ones his father had failed to win back. Kadesh was attacked and captured by the Hittites soon after Ramses II became pharaoh. Trade made Kadesh important. About twenty thousand soldiers were led by Ramses to retake it. The fifth year of his reign was the time. Fame of this battle is among the highest of his reign. A record belongs to it once Hittite chariots are counted. About 4,500 chariots make it the largest chariot battle the world has known. The first military ambush on record was part of the battle.

7Temple walls across Egypt and Nubia carry the story in pictures, which is another reason for the fame. Ramses is drawn larger than every other figure. Total defeat of the enemy is how he appears. A large Ramses II beating the Hittites is repeated in many similar images. The victory people were meant to believe was not quite real. Death nearly took Ramses. A draw is a fairer word than a clear Egyptian win. Egyptian records have been read by scholars. Hittite records have been read too. Separation of the army as it neared Kadesh is their conclusion. Scouting ahead was the job of Ramses's division. A day behind came another division. A third group swung wide to strike from the far side. Two local people told Ramses where the Hittite army was. Many miles to the north was their report. The truth arrived quickly. The Hittite army was much closer. An attack was already being prepared. One carving places Ramses II inside a chariot during the fight at Kadesh. Around 2,500 chariots belonged to the Hittite army. Three men rode in each one. Word was sent by Ramses to his other divisions. Reinforcements that were coming still met a Hittite ambush. Chariots in that ambush numbered 2,500. The small force that had gone ahead with Ramses was attacked next.

8His own account says he held the enemy off alone. Flight of the rest of the army is what he claimed. A different rescue appears in other records. The Ne'arin, an elite division, arrived just in time. The pharaoh was saved by that division. Heavy losses hit both sides. A truce was then declared by the two leaders. Forces were pulled back to Egypt. Poems were commissioned over the next year. Wall carvings were commissioned too. Every one of them told the battle. Every one of them cast him as a hero. History's first propaganda campaign, some experts say, had begun. Fifteen years later, war again seemed close. Distance from his base made fighting hard. Peace was chosen instead of battle. Ramses II and the Hittite king joined to write a peace treaty. Pieces of that treaty still appear in peace treaties of modern times. One piece was a promise not to attack each other's lands. Allies for years to come was another result. A copy of the treaty hangs on a wall today. The United Nations General Assembly building is where that wall stands. Giant sculptures of Ramses II stand at Abu Simbel. They flank the entrance of the larger of two sandstone temples. Rule lasted until 1213 BCE.

9Natural causes ended his life that year. Ninety-one was his age. His oldest son, the first heir, died before him. The next eleven sons in the line died before him too. The thirteenth son became pharaoh next. Decline of the dynasty started soon. One hundred fifty years after the death, the New Kingdom ended. Fame in ancient Egypt was so great that later kings borrowed the name. At least nine later pharaohs were named for him. Ramses the Great is the name used today. Monuments built by him outnumber those of any other pharaoh in history. Temples built by him do the same. Art, architecture, and historical records are the legacy. People and culture of his time can be understood more clearly because of them. A timeline can mark the life of Ramses II. The scale notes 1310 BCE and 1210 BCE. Birth was in 1303 BCE. Ramses I became pharaoh in 1298 BCE. Seti I became pharaoh in 1291 BCE. A first two wives were married in 1289 BCE. A revolt in Nubia was put down in 1281 BCE, and his two oldest sons went into battle with him. The throne was his in 1279 BCE, and work on the Ramesseum began around then. Kadesh was fought in 1274 BCE. Work at Abu Simbel began around 1264 BCE.

10The Ramesseum was finished in 1259 BCE. Peace with the Hittites was signed in 1258 BCE. Nefertari died in 1252 BCE. Isetnofret, the second wife, died in 1244 BCE. A first Hittite princess was married that same year. Abu Simbel's construction was finished around then as well. A second Hittite princess was married in 1231 BCE. Death at age ninety-one came in 1213 BCE. Words from the reign are gathered here. An ambush is a surprise attack launched from a place of hiding. Campaigns are series of planned actions aimed at chosen goals. Diplomacy is the skill, or the practice, of bargaining between people who speak for different countries. A dynasty is a run of rulers from one family inside a country. A legacy is a thing passed from earlier times into the present. Mortuary describes what belongs to burial, or what relates to it. Pharaohs were the rulers of ancient Egypt. Propaganda is news, art, or other media that often uses false or stretched information to sway people. A rebellion is a fight against authority or power, also called an uprising. Reigned means held rule over an area as its leading person. A successor is the person who comes next in a job or in a post won by election. A truce is a promise to stop fighting.

29. Elephants, Huge Mammals of Land

1Big and brainy elephants open this book. A closer look at the body comes next. African elephants and Asian elephants are compared. Places they gather come after that. Their plant diet has a part. Family life has a part. A closing part calls them giant friends. A glossary explains key words. Size can be set beside a person. An African elephant’s shoulder stands 13 feet high, or 4 meters. Weight can reach 14,000 pounds, or 6,350 kilograms. A human example is 6 feet tall, or 1.8 meters, and 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. An Asian elephant’s shoulder stands 10 feet high, or 3 meters. Weight can reach 11,000 pounds, or 5,000 kilograms. No land animal alive today is more gigantic than an elephant. A walking creature of still greater size would have to be sought in dinosaur times. Huge is not the whole story. Intelligence is high. Messages pass between elephants in many ways. They are clever enough to join forces and finish a task. The size chart is there so a reader can compare. Shoulder height is the measure for both elephant species.

2Weight is listed beside it. A person is drawn into the same comparison so the giant scale is clear. Land life today has no bigger walker. Brains and teamwork sit beside that size. A touch can carry a message. A sound can carry one. A shared job can too. The same animal that far outweighs a person can also plan with the herd. A stately elephant has no real match. The body is giant. Skin is thick and gray, or thick and brown. Legs are round and sturdy. The strangest part is the trunk. It is long and shaped like a snake. Nose and upper lip are joined in that one appendage. Feeling at the tip is very sharp. Several big jobs belong to the trunk. Breathing is one. Lifting food is one. Lifting water is one. A blast of air makes a trumpet call loud enough to hurt ears. Touch is a language too. Trunks meet other elephants in different ways. Two elephants often wind their trunks together. Affection is the message. A mother may stroke her calf gently with the trunk.

3The stroke can calm the calf. It can also scold a calf that misbehaves. Ears on an African elephant are twice the size of ears on an Asian elephant. Milk from the mother feeds a young elephant for as long as three years. Breathing, drinking, and picking up food all use the trunk. More jobs use it too. Feet are big and round. Soft pads cover the bottoms. Elephants are mammals. Every mammal has a backbone. Every mammal has hair at some point in life. Every mammal is warm-blooded. Every mammal makes milk for its babies. Gray skin and brown skin can both appear. The trunk stays the tool for the loudest call and for the gentlest touch. Pads under the feet soften each step. Those pads, the hair, the warm blood, and the milk all fit the mammal pattern. African and Asian are the two main elephant species. The continent under your feet is a simple clue. Other clues exist too. African elephants are the larger relatives. A male can stand 13 feet, or 4 meters, and weigh up to 14,000 pounds, or 6,350 kilograms.

4Females are shorter and lighter. Height is around 9 feet, or 2.7 meters. Weight goes up to 10,000 pounds, or 4,540 kilograms. An Asian male is shorter than an African male by around 3 feet, or 0.9144 meters. He is lighter by about 3,000 pounds, or 1,360 kilograms. Asian females are smaller still. Tusks are often missing on them, which is not the usual case for African females. More differences show in the body. Floppy ears on an African elephant are often double the Asian size. The African back sinks in the middle. An Asian back does not. Look closely at the trunk tip. Two finger-like flaps are there. Food and small objects can be grabbed by those flaps. Tusks dig. They also fight. They also shift objects around. African elephants use them to dig for water as well. Asian elephants keep smaller ears. Large round bumps sit on top of the huge head. Those bumps are a clear mark of the species. Often they are the tallest point on the animal.

5The back is flat, or it arches. The trunk tip has a single finger-like flap, not two. Knowing the continent helps, yet the ears, the back, the head bumps, and the trunk tip can settle the question alone. Tusks on an African elephant do extra digging when water is the goal. Asian females often show no tusks at all. Many habitats can hold elephants. Food must be enough. Water must be enough. Africa gives them hot, dry grasslands. It gives them rainforests. It even gives them deserts. Sea level is possible. High mountains are possible. Asian elephants use wet rainforests and swamps. They also use drier forests that face long seasons without rain. Lions are fierce. Tigers are fierce. Even they seldom threaten an elephant, because the elephant is so massive. Humans are the greater danger. Ivory tusks are taken in illegal hunts. Elephants that harm crops are shot. More people mean less wild land. Roads keep being built. Crops keep being planted. Trees keep being cut. Animals that need huge amounts of food and space lose ground fastest. Elephants once walked across almost all of Africa and almost all of South Asia.

6Today those habitats are much smaller. A range map names Asia and the Bay of Bengal. It marks the Equator and the Asian elephant range. It names Europe and the Mediterranean Sea. It names Africa, the Equator again, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean. It marks the African elephant range. Food and water decide whether a habitat will do. Dry grass, wet forest, desert, and mountain can all work in Africa if those needs are met. Asia adds swamp and long dry seasons. People remain the serious threat, both through ivory hunts and through land taken for roads, farms, and cut trees. Killing for ivory breaks the law. So does shooting an elephant over damaged crops. The old spread across Africa and South Asia is no longer whole. Plants are the only food elephants eat. That makes them herbivores. Inside that limit they are not choosy. Grass is eaten. Leaves are eaten. Bark from trees is eaten. Seeds are eaten. Fruits are eaten. Quantity matters most. An adult can put away more than 300 pounds of food in a day.

7That is 136 kilograms. Water intake is about 20 to 60 gallons. That is 75.7 to 227.1 liters. The trunk works like a giant straw. Water then sprays from the trunk’s end into the mouth. Digestion uses only about 44 percent of what was eaten. A pregnancy lasts eighteen to twenty-two months. No other animal carries young longer. One close living relative is the hyrax. It is small, cute, and furry. A family link is easy to miss. Woolly mammoths are close relatives too. More than ten thousand years have passed since those mammoths died out. An Asian mother in one picture sprays water with her trunk. A sunny day may send her rolling in sand or dirt. The roll helps her avoid a sunburn. Plants of many kinds fill the menu, yet the daily pile must be huge. The trunk lifts the drink and then sends it into the mouth in a spray. Less than half of each meal is actually digested. The long pregnancy and the links to hyraxes and woolly mammoths show how unusual this animal’s family line is.

8Eighteen months is the short end of that wait. Twenty-two months is the long end. At a water hole the trunk acts like a straw. Social life is strong in elephants, and strongest among females. Adult females share family groups. The oldest female usually leads. A herd may include a grandmother. It may include her grown daughters. It may include the calves of those daughters. Care is shared. Meals are shared. Baths and play are shared. A newborn weighs 250 pounds, or 110 kilograms. From the first moment, every member of the herd gives the mother help. Predators are driven off by adults working as a team. A hungry calf may even be nursed by another adult. Childhood lasts a long time. Nursing can go on until three years have passed. Across that time, and across several later years, vital skills are learned. The young elephant learns where food is. It learns where water is. It learns how the trunk works. Full maturity waits until age ten to fifteen.

9Males and females then split. Males leave the herd. They live alone, or they live with other males. Females remain. In time they raise calves of their own. A life without serious trouble can last sixty to seventy years. Teeth are limited. Only six sets grow in a lifetime. After the last set is gone, chewing becomes poor. Marshes are a common home for older elephants. Softer plants grow there. Family groups of females stay tight. The oldest female sets the lead. Calves, daughters, and a grandmother may share one herd. Play, baths, and meals happen together. Males head out once maturity arrives. A full life can cover sixty to seventy years if serious trouble stays away. Six tooth sets are all the animal gets. A bond with these king-sized elephants is hard to avoid. They are brainy. They are caring. Fun matters to them. Size is awesome. Personalities are distinct. Ignoring them is nearly impossible. Protection from all of us can keep these giants roaming Earth for a long time still. Kenya, in Africa, holds the Samburu National Reserve.

10African elephants in one picture stand on that reserve. Affection is a caring or loving feeling. An appendage is an outside body part that juts away from the body. An arm is one example. A leg is another. A habitat is the natural home of a plant or an animal. Herbivores are animals whose food is plants alone. Immense means very large. Ivory is the white material in the tusks of elephants and of other animals that have tusks. Mature means developed in body or in mind. To nurse is to give milk made by a mother. A baby may drink it. A young animal may drink it. Tusks are large teeth that stick out past the closed mouth of some mammals, including elephants and wild boars. Care, play, and sharp minds make these animals easy to feel close to. Distinct personalities match their huge size. Guarding them now can leave them walking the Earth far into the future. Twisted trunks show affection that is easy to spot. Ivory is still a reason some people hunt them against the law.

30. Elizabeth Tudor Rules England

1A map of the 1500s shows three kingdoms: Scotland, Ireland, and England. Wales is marked on the same island. London is shown with a star. The Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea border the land. France lies across the water, and the wider map also shows Asia, Europe, and Africa. This book follows Elizabeth from her world and her youth to her last years. It tells about Mary and Elizabeth, her early challenges, and a threat from Spain. It tells about the Elizabethan Age, and a word list closes the book. Elizabeth Tudor may have been England's greatest monarch. To understand her, a reader first needs her family story. Her father was Henry VIII, king of England. Before Elizabeth was born, Henry married Catherine of Aragon. They had a daughter named Mary. Henry wanted a son. While he was still Catherine's husband, he came to love Anne Boleyn. He wanted Anne to be his wife. He asked the pope, leader of the Catholic Church, to annul the marriage to Catherine. The pope refused to grant that wish. Henry then formed a separate church. He made himself its supreme ruler on Earth. The Church of England was the name of the church he had formed.

2Next he declared that his first marriage had no legal force. Free from the pope, Henry married Anne in secret. Anne became queen of England. Greenwich, England, was the place of Elizabeth Tudor's birth on September 7, 1533. Henry felt affection for Elizabeth and favored her over Mary. He still wanted a son who could inherit the throne. Henry started to lose interest in Anne Boleyn. It seemed she, too, would not give him a son. In time he accused Anne of treason and had her executed. He declared that their marriage had no legal standing. He declared Elizabeth illegitimate, a child of parents who were not married. That ruling meant she could not inherit his throne. In 1537 Jane Seymour, Henry's third wife, gave birth to the son he wanted. The boy was named Prince Edward. Jane was already weak and exhausted. She caught a high fever and died soon after the birth. By then Elizabeth had begun her schooling in a serious way. Private tutors taught her math, history, geography, architecture, and needlework. She learned to speak and write fluent French, Italian, Greek, and Latin. She was an excellent student, and her tutors regarded her highly.

3Elizabeth was intelligent, and she relished her schoolwork. Her manner was witty and captivating. She charmed every person she met. In her free time she enjoyed riding horses, dancing, and playing the lute. She rarely saw her father. She often spent time with her older sister and her younger brother. Henry married three more times, but none of those marriages produced another child. His sixth and final marriage, in 1543, was to Catherine Parr. Catherine Parr pushed him hard to set a line of succession. A Tudor family portrait lines up five figures from left to right. They are Lady Mary, Prince Edward, Henry VIII, Jane Seymour, and Lady Elizabeth. At Catherine's urging, Henry restored Mary and Elizabeth as heirs. Their brother Edward still stood first in line. Henry VIII died in 1547, and Prince Edward became king at the age of nine. Under Edward, the Church of England leaned toward Protestantism, a newer kind of Christianity. His reign was short. Edward died in 1553, and Mary, Elizabeth's older half sister, became queen. Mary was the daughter of Henry and his first wife, Catherine. Mary was Catholic and held that faith strongly. A growing number of people were turning toward Protestantism.

4Mary's goal as monarch was to stop every Protestant practice. She believed that people who rejected Catholic teachings were heretics. During her reign she ordered the execution of about three hundred people. Those people had been found guilty of standing against the Catholic Church. The killings earned her the nickname Bloody Mary. Elizabeth had been raised as a Protestant, and she valued that faith. She did not trust Mary. She believed she had to look Catholic if she wanted to stay alive. She attended mass in public and studied the Catholic religion. Artwork of the sixteenth century shows the Tower of London. People were sent to that tower to be locked up. Many of them were tortured or killed. Mary still believed that Elizabeth followed Protestant ways in secret. When people tried to overthrow Mary, Mary thought Elizabeth was behind the plot. Mary had Elizabeth arrested and sent to the Tower of London. Elizabeth said she was innocent. She was kept in the tower for two months. She was then released and kept under house arrest for a year. Mary married Prince Philip of Spain and hoped for an heir. She wanted England to remain Catholic. She wanted to block Elizabeth from the throne.

5Mary had no children. She had to accept that Elizabeth, next in line, would lawfully follow her. Mary died of an illness in 1558. The crowning of Elizabeth as queen took place on January 15, 1559. At that moment her age was twenty-five. She quickly showed that she would rule as a Protestant, yet she tolerated Catholics. From the start of her reign, some advisors tried to find her a suitable husband. A marriage could create new alliances between England and other countries. A child would also give England a sure heir. Elizabeth saw the danger in a foreign king. England might then fall under another country's rule. An English husband would rank beneath her royal status. She might also lose power as queen. Many proposals came to her, and she rejected all of them. Elizabeth had fair skin and fair hair. People in Tudor England considered her beautiful. Once she was queen, she dressed in a very elaborate way. She favored bright oranges and bright reds, with jewels as accents. She exuded power and authority. One famous image shows her in coronation robes. More urgent problems pressed on her. Early in the reign, Catholic and Protestant faiths split Europe.

6Elizabeth worked to stop Catholic Spain and Catholic France from invading England. An invasion might aim to defeat Protestantism. She also watched Scotland, the neighbor to the north, so it would not join her enemy. Mary, Queen of Scots, was Elizabeth's cousin and the Catholic queen of Scotland. Mary posed a grave threat. Many English Catholics tried to depose Elizabeth. They wanted Mary to ascend the English throne and restore Catholicism. Some of those threats were linked to Mary. When Mary came to England, Elizabeth imprisoned her for nineteen years. In 1586 Elizabeth's patience came to an end. She learned that Mary had joined yet another plot to assassinate her. Elizabeth had Mary tried for treason. The judges ruled that Mary had plotted against Elizabeth. Mary was executed on February 8, 1587. She had spent nineteen years as Elizabeth's prisoner. She was forty-four years old. King Philip II of Spain was Catholic. He had already been planning an invasion of England before Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed. Once Mary was dead, Philip judged that Elizabeth had to be removed from the throne. He wanted the Catholic faith restored in England. Up to that point, the explorer Sir Francis Drake had been making Philip angry.

7Elizabeth supported Drake. Drake plundered Spanish ships that were sailing home from new lands in the Americas. He ordered his seamen to raid those ships. They seized large amounts of gold and silver bound for Spain. In 1587 Drake sailed into Cadiz Harbor in Spain. He destroyed many Spanish ships sitting at anchor. After that setback, Philip prepared to attack England and overthrow Elizabeth. In 1588 he sent the Spanish Armada to sea. The fleet's purpose was to invade England. About seventeen thousand soldiers on foot also served Philip from the Netherlands. Those troops were under Spanish rule, and they backed his Armada. Those soldiers were unready, so the invasion could not begin. English sailors were the better seamen, and their ships were more maneuverable. They scattered the Spanish ships and drove them into the North Sea. As the Spanish sailed north, the winds did not favor them. The weather slowly beat them. Elizabeth's troops had triumphed, and her crown had survived another challenge. A map traces the Spanish Armada in 1588. The fleet sailed north toward England. It then went around the coasts of Scotland and Ireland on the way back to Spain.

8Elizabeth built a strong government and a powerful navy. She wanted her beloved country to grow and to gain wealth. She encouraged exploration of new places and trade with foreign lands. Trade in silk, food, and spices gave large help to England's economy. She believed strongly in support for the arts. During her reign she encouraged music, art, and literature. Musicians, poets, writers, and other artists were always welcome at her court. England's arts had reached a flourishing state by 1590. Many people rank William Shakespeare as the finest writer of plays. He grew very popular while Elizabeth ruled. He often brought his troupe of actors to perform at her court. England was on the path to a global empire. Her years later took the name Golden Age in English history. Among countries of the world, England rose until it stood near the top in importance. A picture shows Queen Elizabeth I making Sir Francis Drake a knight. She honored the English explorer for what his voyages achieved. In her later rule, Elizabeth eased the religious fights that had torn the country apart. Protestantism was quietly set in place as England's official religion. Education and the arts, both firmly backed by her, made great strides.

9More people than ever before learned to read and to write. Elizabeth died in 1603 after a reign of forty-four years. She named James VI, son of Mary, Queen of Scots, as the next ruler. That choice brought England and Scotland together. She was highly educated and a keen observer of human nature. Her reign showed allies and enemies the same truth. A woman could rule as an effective monarch and as a successful leader. The English loved her and respected her. They would remember their queen for all the years to come. The Tudor family had no monarch after Elizabeth I. The Tudors had ruled England since 1485. These dates mark the life of Queen Elizabeth I. In 1533 Elizabeth was born to Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. In 1536 Anne Boleyn was executed. In 1544 an order set the succession for the throne. In 1547 Henry VIII died, and Edward became king. On July 6, 1553, King Edward VI died. On October 1, 1553, Mary was crowned queen. In 1554 Mary ordered Elizabeth to be imprisoned. In 1558 Mary died, and Elizabeth became queen. In 1563 Elizabeth was defeated in the French Civil War.

10In 1587 Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed. In 1588 Elizabeth defeated the Spanish Armada. In 1590 the arts began to flourish, largely because Elizabeth supported them. On March 24, 1603, Elizabeth died. James I then became king of England and of Scotland, and the two countries were united. An alliance is a close link between countries or other groups that work together. Heretics are people who reject official or accepted beliefs or practices. Maneuverable means able to turn or change direction quickly and with ease. To annul is to end a thing by official act, or to say it has no legal force. Plundering means stealing everything of value by using force. A reign is the stretch of time when one ruler holds power. Captivating means charming, and able to hold a person's attention. Succession is the order, or the process, by which people inherit a powerful post. To depose is to remove a leader from power in a sudden way. Treason is betrayal, or disloyalty, against one's own government or ruler. Executed means killed, above all as punishment for a crime. An armada is a large fleet of boats, most often warships.

31. Energy Sources: Good Points and Bad Points

1The parts of this book come in this order. First comes the nonstop need for energy. Fossil fuels come next. Power from water follows. Energy from the Sun comes after that. Power from atoms follows. A look toward later years comes next. A word list and an index close the book. The Nonstop Need for Energy. The United States counts as a modern society. Every modern society uses a great deal of energy. To scientists, energy means the ability to do work. Work can take many forms. Moving an automobile along a road counts as work. Sending an airplane into flight counts as work. Making electricity counts as work. Keeping factory machines running counts as work. Energy for the United States comes from many places. Other modern societies draw on many places too. A large share comes from burning fuel. Coal is one such fuel. Gasoline is another. Flowing water supplies some energy. Sunlight supplies some. Wind supplies some. Splitting atoms supplies some. A picture shows machines inside a car factory. Those machines need energy before they can build cars. Every energy source has good points. Every energy source has bad points. People call the good points and the bad points pros and cons. Modern societies face many choices about energy. They must pick a sound way to produce it. Society's needs have to be weighed against care for the environment. The choices are not always simple. A chart tracks energy use in the United States from 1949 to 2005. The unit on the chart is the quadrillion BTU. The four measures are consumption, production, imports, and exports. The figures come from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The report is the Annual Energy Review 2005. More energy is used in the United States than the country produces. What might that gap mean for energy in the United States in the years ahead? In 1955, consumption was 40.21, production was 40.15, imports were 2.79, and exports were 2.29. In 1960, consumption was 45.09, production was 42.8, imports were 4.19, and exports were 1.48.

In 1989, consumption was 85, production was 69.41, imports were 18.77, and exports were 4.66. In 1990, consumption was 84.73, production was 70.79, imports were 18.82, and exports were 4.75. 3In 1993, consumption was 87.65, production was 68.33, imports were 21.27, and exports were 4.26. In 1994, consumption was 89.29, production was 70.72, imports were 22.39, and exports were 4.06. In 1995, consumption was 91.2, production was 71.13, imports were 22.26, and exports were 4.51. In 1996, consumption was 94.23, production was 72.47, imports were 23.7, and exports were 4.63. In 1997, consumption was 94.8, production was 72.46, imports were 25.22, and exports were 4.51. In 1998, consumption was 95.2, production was 72.84, imports were 26.58, and exports were 4.3. In 1999, consumption was 96.84, production was 71.71, imports were 27.25, and exports were 3.71. In 2000, consumption was 98.98, production was 71.29, imports were 28.97, and exports were 4.01. In 2001, consumption was 96.5, production was 71.91, imports were 30.16, and exports were 3.77. In 2002, consumption was 97.97, production was 70.86, imports were 29.41, and exports were 3.67. In 2003, consumption was 98.27, production was 70.14, imports were 31.06, and exports were 4.05. In 2004, consumption was 100.41, production was 70.39, imports were 33.54, and exports were 4.43. In 2005, consumption was 99.89, production was 69.17, imports were 34.26, and exports were 4.64. Fuels from Ancient Life. Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels. Around the world, fossil fuels are a leading energy source. The name comes from the way they formed. They formed from remains of plants and of animals. Those living things died many millions of years ago. Underground, great heat worked on the remains. Great pressure worked on them too. The remains turned into materials we burn as fuel. Fossil fuels supply about 85 percent of the energy the United States uses each year. Many power plants burn coal in order to make electricity. Oil is turned into gasoline. Oil is turned into diesel fuel. Oil is turned into jet fuel. Those fuels move cars. They move trucks. They move airplanes. In most homes, stoves run on natural gas. Water heaters in most homes run on natural gas too. A picture shows gasoline, a familiar fossil fuel. How Oil Forms.

4Marine plants die. Marine animals die. The dead plants and animals fall down to the ocean floor. Dirt mixes with them. Sand mixes with them too. The mix becomes a layer of sediment. Time goes by. Further layers are added. Pressure grows. Buried plant and animal material changes into kerogen. While that happens, the sediment hardens into sedimentary rock. Still more time passes. Still more layers are added. Still more pressure builds. The added pressure turns the kerogen into oil. The new oil starts to rise. It moves through tiny holes in the sedimentary rock. The oil rises until it meets rock it cannot cross. Oil rigs drill through that blocking rock. Pumps then draw out the oil that has collected. A picture shows a close view of coal. A picture shows a pump jack. The pump jack pulls petroleum from an oil well. A main advantage of fossil fuels is abundance. Abundant means they occur in many places. It also means they occur in large amounts. Fossil fuels hold a lot of energy that people can use. Coal is found in especially large amounts. Enough coal remains in the United States for another 200 to 300 years. Natural gas has one special advantage. It burns in a very clean way. Burning natural gas gives off mostly carbon dioxide. It also gives off water vapor. Oil's main advantage is efficient burning. Efficient means little is wasted as oil becomes energy. The refining that makes gasoline also makes diesel fuel. That same refining makes other petroleum products. Some of those products go into crayons. Some go into bubble gum. Some go into eyeglasses. Some even go into artificial heart valves. Fossil fuels are, in essence, nonrenewable sources of energy. Nature cannot make new supplies fast enough to match demand. Many experts expect the world's oil wells to run dry within a few decades. Even sooner, the oil on hand will be too small. It will fail to meet demand around the globe. Fossil fuels give off pollutants. Natural gas is the exception to that. Cars send harmful chemicals into the air. Factories send harmful chemicals into the air.

5Many power plants do the same. Because these fuels are burned, dirty air will remain a problem. A further problem is known as the greenhouse effect. Gases from burned fossil fuels hold extra heat in Earth's atmosphere. The heat held is greater than the heat nature would hold alone. That warming of the atmosphere is called global warming. Carbon dioxide, scientists think, does the most to worsen the greenhouse effect. Natural gas adds to the problem as well. A picture shows pollutants climbing into the atmosphere. Power from Moving Water. In many places, people use water to make electricity. You may ask how water can do that job. The answer is a dam. Picture a dam as a huge wall that is also very wide. Concrete is the usual material. The wall is built across a river. It stops the river from flowing on. Water then gathers in a wide area behind the dam. The gathered water becomes a lake, or a reservoir. Lake water is let out through the bottom of the dam. That water travels very fast. It passes through large machines called turbines. Inside each turbine are blades shaped like fans. Rushing water makes those blades spin. Turbines link to other machines called generators. The generators spin as well. Inside a generator, giant magnets surround a shaft. A huge coil of wire surrounds the shaft and the magnets. Spinning shafts and magnets shift electrons inside the wire coil. Moving electrons make an electric current. Power made this way at a dam is known as hydroelectric power. The word hydro is a prefix. A prefix is the first part of a word. Hydro means water. A picture shows generators inside a dam. Parts of a Working Dam. The labeled parts are the reservoir and the power lines. They include the dam and the generator. They include the penstock and the turbine. Water leaves the reservoir and enters the penstock. The water races downward. On the way, it turns the turbine blades. After that, the water empties into the river. Dams turn out a large share of the electricity people need. More than 2,000 hydroelectric dams stand in the United States.

6Those dams make about 10 percent of the nation's electricity. Around the world, hydroelectric dams make about 20 percent of the electricity. Dams serve other purposes too. One purpose is flood control. A dam can store water that comes from heavy rain. It can store water that comes from melting snow. The stored water is released slowly at a later time. Hoover Dam crosses the Colorado River. The dam forms Lake Mead. Lake Mead is among the largest lakes made by people. A picture shows boat docks on Lake Mead. The lakes open many chances for recreation. People boat on them. People fish on them. Homes draw water from the lakes. Industries draw water from the lakes. Farmers draw water from the lakes. They use it to irrigate crops in the drier months. Holding back floods helps people. The same choice is harder on the environment. A river is meant to flood. Floodwater lays down sediment. Sediment mixes gravel, sand, and topsoil. Sediment left by floods keeps riverside farmland rich. Once a river is dammed, it cannot refresh the soil around it. A picture shows salmon swimming toward the river's source. Dams also cut the path of fish. Some of those fish travel up a river. Some travel down a river. In the Pacific Northwest of the United States, dams have hurt salmon badly. Every three to five years, salmon leave the ocean. They swim up rivers to the places where they were born. They make the trip in order to lay eggs. A dam makes the upstream swim difficult. A dam makes the downstream swim difficult too. Salmon numbers have fallen sharply because of this. The fall has taken place over the past 100 years. Energy from the Sun. Sunlight carries enormous amounts of energy. On a summer day you can feel that energy. The sunlight warms your skin. Scientists made solar cells to catch energy from the Sun. The cells are called photovoltaic cells. Say photovoltaic as FOE-toe-vole-TAY-ik. A solar cell changes sunlight into electricity. When light strikes the cell, some of the light energy is absorbed. Particles inside the cell begin to move faster.

7That faster movement produces electricity. In some places, big panels of solar cells collect sunshine. The panels supply electricity to homes. They supply electricity to businesses. Solar cells have been fitted to cars. They have been fitted to appliances. A picture shows a solar panel powering a phone booth. A picture shows a solar water heater. Towns use many heaters like this one to warm their water. Collectors of solar heat use the Sun to warm water. Collectors of this kind often sit on roofs. Water moves through pipes inside the panels. Radiant energy from the Sun heats that water. Pumps send the hot water into a building. Further pipes carry it. Heat passes out of the water. That heat warms the rooms. Cooled water travels back to the roof. On the roof it is heated once more. A picture shows solar panels on the roof of a house. The panels give the house its energy. Some regions have many days of sun. The southwestern United States is one such region. There, solar cells can make a lot of electricity. Solar panels there can make a lot of heat. The Sun sends free energy toward Earth in abundance. The stream of energy continues through all 24 hours of a day. People far from the sunniest lands still mount solar cells on roofs. They mount solar panels on roofs too. Some roofs belong to houses. Some roofs belong to businesses. The aim is a lower energy bill. Experts say vast sets of solar panels in sunny regions could make enough electricity for a whole country. Catching this energy can help us deal with a diminishing supply. Fresh methods for catching the energy keep being developed. The aim of the new methods is to maximize efficiency. Solar cells bring two main problems. The first problem is the price. Making the cells costs a great deal. That price leaves other plants as a cheaper energy source. A hydroelectric plant costs less. A fossil-fuel power plant costs less. Until the cells can be manufactured at a low price, this free energy stays costly. The cost is in catching the energy. The cost is also in turning it into electricity.

8The second problem is uneven sunlight. Not every part of the world receives abundant sun. Backup sources would be required beside the solar cells. Backups raise the total cost of energy. Some neighbors of solar houses dislike the look. They see rooftop cells and panels as ugly. They believe that look will lower the value of their own homes. A picture shows power plants that could back up solar farms. Power from Atoms. A nuclear power plant releases the energy stored in atoms. The plant uses that energy to make electricity. Every split of an atom lets energy out. An atomic bomb explodes by a chain reaction that is very fast. A nuclear plant uses the element uranium. Uranium is radioactive. The plant runs a chain reaction that is slow. The reaction is kept under control. Energy from broken uranium atoms heats water. The heated water becomes steam. Steam then drives the making of electricity. A coal plant makes electricity in much the same manner. A picture shows cooling towers. The towers hold the plant's core at a safe temperature. A picture shows nuclear waste being handled with great care. The energy from uranium is incredible in amount. One kilogram of uranium can yield more energy than 3 million kilograms of coal. One kilogram equals 2.2 lbs. Three million kilograms equal 6.6 million lbs. Nuclear plants hold another advantage over coal plants. They do not send out gases that dirty the sky. They do not add those gases to global warming. Many people reject nuclear power because of danger. One danger is an accident. A nuclear plant cannot blow up the way an atomic bomb does. It can suffer a steam explosion if the core grows too hot. The core is the part that holds the uranium. Such an explosion would throw out a lot of dangerous radiation. Waste is a second danger. The plants produce this waste material. Uranium can reach a point where it no longer makes electricity. Even then, it stays highly radioactive. The danger lasts for thousands of years. A picture shows wind turbines that could add energy in later years.

9The Years Ahead. In coming years, substitutes for oil will have to be found. Hydroelectric power may be set aside as well. Many people are troubled by what dams do to the environment. They want a large number of dams taken down. Solar energy will probably see wider use. Energy experts say more nuclear plants will need to be built. Growing demand for energy is the reason. A chart compares energy made and energy used by world region in 2004. The unit is the quadrillion BTU. One column records production. Another column records consumption. North, Central, and South America produced 126. That same region consumed 143. Europe produced 51. Europe consumed 86. Eurasia produced 67. Eurasia consumed 45. The Middle East produced 62. The Middle East consumed 21. Africa produced 32. Africa consumed 14. Asia and Oceania produced 105. Asia and Oceania consumed 138. In three world regions, people use more energy than those regions create. Why might that be so? Where do those regions get the extra energy? A second chart shows energy use by type, past and estimated. The years on it run from 1980 to 2030. Oil is one type on the chart. Coal is one type. Natural gas is one type. Renewables are on the chart, including wind and solar. Nuclear energy is on the chart. Part of the chart is history. Part of the chart is projections. With today's rates as a guide, the chart shows world energy use growing. The growth is drawn from now through the year 2030. Looking decades ahead, experts do not expect oil to remain available. What does the chart say about how people will use energy later? These figures come from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The report is the International Energy Outlook 2006. Scientists are studying still more ways to make energy. Wind turbines are one way under study. Geothermal energy is another. A wind turbine makes electricity when wind turns its blades. No fuel is required. The turbines create no pollution. The machines are huge. Birds that live nearby can be killed by them. Geothermal energy begins deep under the ground.

10At that depth the Earth is very hot. Pipes can carry water down to that heat. The water takes the heat in. Hot water from below can warm homes. It can warm other buildings. In many places the underground heat is difficult to reach. Reaching it can also be expensive. A picture shows a geothermal plant. A chart lists the countries that created the most energy in 2004. The unit is the quadrillion BTU. The United States created 70.4. China created 56.0. Russia created 51.7. Saudi Arabia created 24.2. Canada created 18.6. Iran created 12.1. India created 11.1. Norway created 10.8. Australia created 10.6. Mexico created 10.3. Two things are sure. People need energy. Fossil fuels provide most of our energy. Those fuels will not last forever. Renewable substitutes are the key. They matter to the energy future of the whole world. Scientists will go on with their research. Every new source will have pros. Every new source will have cons. Governments will keep arguing over which sources are best. Businesses will keep arguing too. Environmentalists will keep arguing too. While they argue, the need for energy will keep growing. Word List. Energy means the forms of power that people and machines need when they do work. Environmentalists are people who want Earth's ecosystems to stay healthy. Fossil fuels are sources of energy taken out of the earth. Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels. Global warming is the rise of temperatures across the world. The rise happens when air pollution traps heat. Hydroelectric describes electricity that is produced from water. Pollutants are chemicals that harm the environment. Sediment is earth in small bits that floodwater carries. A turbine is a wheel spun by the force of water, air, or steam. Index. The index names carbon dioxide and coal. It names dams and floods. It names fossil fuels and gasoline. It names geothermal energy and global warming. It names hydroelectric power and kerogen. It names natural gas. It names nuclear power, also called atomic power. It names oil and pollution. It names solar energy and steam. It names the Sun and uranium. It names water and wind.

32. Europe’s Big Night of Song

1England's group Bucks Fizz took the top prize in 1981. The show was the Eurovision Song Contest. Their song was Making Your Mind Up. Dana's winning song in 1970 was All Kinds of Everything. Charts across Europe put that sweet ballad in the top spot. I first saw this contest on a television screen in 1970. I watched with my family. My family is Irish. I could not follow the languages the songs used. After every contestant had sung, jurors from other countries voted. They chose their favorite songs. The presenters spoke politely to the jurors in each juror's own language. Television carried the point totals out to Europe's other countries. We waited with excitement. Ireland's entry was the one we hoped would finish with the top score. That first memory of the yearly show has never left me. That night I realized something for the first time. My home, I realized, was a land on the European continent. Ireland's victory that night is why the memory stays sharp. The parts of this account ask what Eurovision is and when it began. They explain how the contest works. They describe the excitement fans call Eurofever.

2They look at national pride and unity. They close with a future that looks bright. At the 2010 contest held in Norway, fans stand together for photos. No song competition in Europe is larger than the Eurovision Song Contest. It is also Europe's most spectacular song competition. A strong national showing fills people with pride. They promote themselves to their neighbors in other countries. Audiences across the continent join the fun. They judge the songs for themselves. Cheesy-looking acts are something friends and relatives enjoy teasing. They argue about the votes. Singers from 1963 stand for a photo before the board of entered songs. Before 2013, the performance order was chosen at random. Today, producers choose the order. The contest started in 1956. Its aim was to help bring European countries together. The Second World War had torn those countries apart. Switzerland hosted the earliest contest. Just seven countries from Europe entered. The show lasted more than an hour and a half. Each of the seven countries sent two entries. Famous singers from each country performed the songs. A live orchestra backed them.

3Early rules said each song must use the official language of its country. Some songs got around that rule so they could appeal to international judges. They used nonsense words that listeners could recognize. Lulu won for England in 1969 with Boom, Bang-a-Bang. Massiel won for Spain in 1968 with La, La, La. The 1974 winner was ABBA, a pop act from Sweden. They sang Waterloo in English. By then, the rule about national languages had been relaxed. ABBA performed Waterloo during the 1974 contest in England. No other contest works quite like this one. Countries vote on one another's songwriting. They also judge one another's performance skills. Each country begins by picking its own song at home. A country may hold a competition on television. A committee may pick the entry instead. Every song must be sung live. Every song must last three minutes or less. The group Twin Twin is one act fans remember. Winning titles have included A-Ba-Ni-Bi, from Israel in 1978. They have included Diggi-Loo Diggi-Ley, from Sweden in 1984. France could have taken a 2014 prize for the strangest song name. The same prize could have gone to the oddest song.

4France's song was Moustache, by Twin Twin. Its subject was a man hoping to grow a moustache. Identical twins called Jedward, known for style, finished eighth during 2011. Their song was Lipstick. They wore jackets that paid tribute to Michael Jackson. During contest week, the acts go to whichever land is the host. They rehearse. Then they compete to reach the semifinals. Two days is the span of those rounds. The twenty-six highest scorers move on to the Grand Final. Prime time is the usual hour for airing the final. Half the points come from viewers, and half come from the jury. Five experts from the music industry also vote. They use a point system. A phone call is one way people at home can send a vote. They can vote by text message. They can vote through the official app. To keep the contest fair, people cannot vote for their own country. Finalists sing once more when the last round begins. Juries in every country still taking part vote a second time. The viewers vote again too. After the votes are in, hosts ask one speaker from each land to announce results.

5On the live broadcast, that speaker reads out the jury score from home. Next, workers add up the total points for each country. The totals are revealed from the lowest score to the highest. In that tense last moment, fans wait to hear the winning name. The winning song is performed once more. The winner receives a glass microphone trophy that fans know at once. Finally, the winning country receives the honor of hosting the next year's contest. Ireland has won seven times. No country has a stronger record across the contest's history. Putting the 1996 show on stage cost 3.5 million dollars. Estimates still said Ireland's economy gained more than 9 million dollars. Norway has lost the most. Norway has also won three times. Four lands in 1969 ended on one shared point total. All four had to be declared winners. Tie-breaker rules were introduced so that would not happen again. Sixty years of the contest were marked during 2015. It is the longest-running yearly television music competition in history. Fans call the excitement Eurofever.

6The show is theatrical. It is flashy. Many viewers love the event. People watching can enter special prize drawings. Fans can download scorecards. They can join the fun at home. The early contests felt serious rather than playful. Women wore ball gowns. Every act in those years was stiff and formal. Lys Assia, singing for Switzerland, was the earliest champion. She won in 1956. She was also the first singer to repeat her entry as the night ended. Emotion overcame her. She forgot her lyrics. She made up the rest of the song as she went. Her winning song was Refrain. In later decades the show became a stage for talent from each nation. Color and style shifted like a bright kaleidoscope. Now, performers wear costumes covered in sequins. Jewels cover the costumes too. The set designs can be very imaginative. The performances can be surprising. Mariya Yaremchuk of Ukraine amazed audiences in 2014. Her song was Tick-Tock. A man ran behind her inside a giant wheel. Playful words helped the Grannies from Buranovo draw notice during 2012. On popular television talent shows, contestants with unusual styles may not reach the final round.

7Eurovision welcomes everyone. Most Eurovision winners do not go on to successful pop careers. There are exceptions. ABBA won the 1974 contest. Switzerland's 1988 singer was Celine Dion. The song that wins is often not the entry people find most interesting. The Russian entry in 2012 was the Grannies from Buranovo. They were the runner-up. Their song was Party for Everybody. Listeners smiled at the Grannies' playful lines. Joy and happiness, those lines claimed, fill each person. Dogs share that feeling. Cats share it too. Honoring diversity is the aim this contest sets for itself. It also acts as a showcase for the wide range of cultures across Europe. Seven countries took part at the start. Eurovision has now grown to more than forty countries. Its audience is more than two hundred million people worldwide. Europeans can use a vote to back the pop partnerships they prefer. A 2006 study by two colleges in London found a pattern. Neighbors often hand points to one another, voting as a bloc. Scandinavian voters can be trusted to back their own neighbors. Eastern European acts getting points from Eastern Europe surprise nobody.

8Points moving between Ireland and the United Kingdom are always watched. Being part of a bloc does not always mean a win. That northern bloc of countries includes Norway. Contest history still treats Norway as the land with the worst luck. Last place has been Norway's finish a record eleven times. It has earned nul points four times. Nul points means no points. Some voting patterns might cause bad feelings between countries. Azerbaijan, next door, placed Armenia at the bottom in 2014. Voters in Armenia answered with their lowest marks for Azerbaijan. The Armenian jury did the same. People thought the reason was resentment. A military conflict between the two countries had ended in 1994. In 2015, both countries again ranked each other last. A list of Eurovision winners from 1956 to 2017 names twenty-seven countries. A repeated win belongs to several of those lands. The countries are Austria, Azerbaijan, and Belgium. They include Denmark, Estonia, Finland, and France. They include Germany, Greece, Ireland, and Israel. They include Italy, Latvia, Luxembourg, and Monaco. They include the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, and Russia.

9They include Serbia, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. They include Turkey, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom. They include the former Yugoslavia. Public broadcasting companies, joined in one big body, operate the show. The group is the European Broadcasting Union, or EBU. A land inside the EBU is allowed to send a song. Israel is a member even though it is not in Europe. Armenia is a member too, though it is not in Europe. After the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991, Eurovision welcomed the new countries of Eastern Europe. Some countries that are not in the EBU have also been invited. Morocco is one of them. Australia is another. Salvador Sobral, singing for Portugal, took the prize in 2017. Sweet and old-fashioned describes the tune that won. Any time period could have produced that melody. A rap performance from Romania lost to this plain melody. It also beat a dancing gorilla from Italy. Could this contest encourage Europe to grow more united? Can it offer hope for a Europe that is more inclusive? The contest is about joyful celebration. Different values and different customs meet with acceptance here.

10Every year its popularity grows. Friends and families come together to watch the big show. They cheer for their favorites. Nothing now in view suggests this lively custom will stop. Francesco Gabbani of Italy shared the 2017 stage with a gorilla that danced. An audience is a gathering that has come to watch or to listen. Sending radio programs, or television programs, out to listeners is broadcasting. People, teams, or businesses chasing the same prize are in a competition. Contestants are people who take part in a competition. Shared ideas and shared customs of a group make up its culture. A culture can also mean one society that keeps customs and ideas of its own. Bringing in many cultures, or many kinds of people, is what diversity means. Experts are people who know a great deal about a subject. Inclusive means available or open to anyone. Matters that involve two nations, or more, are international. Lyrics are the words of a song. To mock is to make fun of someone, often by imitating that person. A trophy is a prize object handed to the winner of a contest.

33. False Hair Across the Ages

1Human hair gives a wig the longest life of any material. They are also easier to cut and style than synthetic wigs. Across recorded history, people have been obsessed with hair.
