Ancient Egyptian culture is one end of that fixation, and modern life is the other. Wigs have played an important part in it. People have worn wigs for many reasons. Fashion is one reason. Social standing is another. Wigs come in many styles. A full wig is one style. A toupee is another. Extensions are a third. From the neck upward, a full wig hides the top of the head and both sides. A toupee covers only part of the head. A toupee's coverage starts at the forehead and stops at the crown's top. Ear to ear is the other span of that same piece. At the back, the person's own hair is still visible. A section of hair, or of fiber, is what an extension is. Pins, clips, or glue attach them to a wig that is already there, or to natural hair. They create a fuller look. They can create a longer look instead.

2Double-sided tape is what holds a toupee to the scalp. Many materials can become a wig. Wool is one. Goat hair is another. Horsehair is another. Straw or grasses can be used. Certain plastics can be used too, such as nylon. For centuries, the natural look of human-hair wigs made them the favorite. It often took the hair of six to ten people to make one wig. Those wigs cost more than the other choices. Wearers of those costly wigs were only the very wealthy. Until the 1700s, a wig was often made for one person alone. That special fit made wigs too expensive for most people. A tight mesh cap was built to the shape of the head, and it had a fabric base. Hair, or some other material, was looped over the mesh. It was tied off. Beeswax, resin, or glue then fixed it to the base fabric. After the hair was attached, stylists could shape it to the fashion then current. Popularity in the 1700s shifted to wigs able to fit any person. Pulling a ribbon tight along the cap's edge gave a good fit.

3Because one wig could fit many head sizes, the price fell. Wigs became more affordable. The tool that weaves a wig is called a ventilating needle. Hair gets pulled through the holes of the base by this needle. It then ties the strands. Ancient Egyptian tomb art shows wigs. Sculpture from that time shows them too. The oldest known wigs date to 1400 bc in Egypt. Looking like their gods was one reason many Egyptians put on wigs. They also wore wigs to cover bald spots. A full head of hair stood for strength. It stood for health too. Thick, braided, fancy hair was what Egyptians believed their gods had. They made wigs in that same style. Even then, the lengths were not all the same. Some wigs reached the neck. Some reached the shoulder. Others fell to the waist. All of them were thick. Curls and braids covered them. Some people added extensions to make a wig even fuller. Beeswax, put on lightly, held the hair's shape much as hairspray does now. Many hairstyles of Elizabeth Taylor appear in the film Cleopatra.

4Each style needed three wigs. Wigs were worn in Egypt by people of every social level. Human hair was the material in the wigs of the king and his family. Ivory and silver decorated those wigs. Hairstylists kept the royal wigs in order. Wealthy people could afford wigs of wool or goat hair. Poor people could afford only straw wigs. Daily life in Asian cultures seldom included wigs. For many centuries, costumes in Japanese theater have depended on wigs. The same is true of Chinese theater. Greek women's wigs in those times may have followed goddess hairstyles, including Aphrodite's. A picture can set the goddess on one side and a woman of the time on the other. False hair was also worn by wealthy people in two world empires that came later. Braids and curls, pinned up, covered the wigs of noblewomen in ancient Greece. Noblewomen of ancient Rome did the same. More braids meant higher social status. A more ornate style meant higher status too. Bald spots were the reason wealthy men and women in Rome put on wigs. They favored blond hair.

5They favored red hair too. Some Romans kept enslaved people who had blond or red hair, so hair would be ready for wigs. A wig could serve a Roman emperor as a disguise. The disguise let them leave the palace without being recognized. They hoped to hear the real thoughts of everyday people. Hair loss troubled Julius Caesar, emperor of Rome from 100 to 44 bc. He was not happy about it. His first try was longer hair in the back, brushed forward over the scalp. That did not work. A recipe against hair loss came next, from his girlfriend Cleopatra, last pharaoh of Egypt. The mix included ground-up mice. It included horse teeth. It included bear grease. That potion did not work either. Caesar decided a laurel wreath was easier. Victory in battle was what the wreath stood for. It also covered his baldness fairly well. Popularity of wigs fell after the Roman Empire ended, and the drop lasted several centuries. King Louis XIII of France made wigs fashionable again in the early seventeenth century. Hair loss started for him at age twenty-three. He feared less respect at the royal court if people believed he was going bald.

6The wigs he chose looked like the hair he used to have, so the loss stayed hidden. Looking like the king was the aim of many noblemen. They began to wear that same style of wig. In this period, full wigs were mainly worn by men. Some men added extensions to make a wig fuller. They added them to make it thicker too. Wigs were also worn by some women whose hair was thinning. Women who still had plenty of hair put extensions into their styles. As clothing at the royal courts grew fancier, hairstyles had to grow fancier too. Demand for wigs rose. Demand for extensions rose too. Women styled both real hair and false hair over a frame on the head, or over a pillow, to build a shape. Lard, which is pig fat, set the style. Powder over the whole style held it in place. Certain styles stood three feet tall, which is 0.91 meters. Model ships sat inside the hairstyles of some women. Months could pass with these styles left in place, because they were so complicated.

7They did not comb the hair in that time. They did not wash it either. Women's fashion in France, and its wild wigs, show up in a cartoon from 1778. The lard that set these styles would spoil as time passed. Nests in the hair were sometimes built by cockroaches. Mice would too. Even rats would. A long stick ending in a claw was what women carried. The stick let them scratch inside the hair without disturbing the style. A wig was worn by almost everyone tied to a royal court in Western Europe by the eighteenth century. So did people in certain professions. Doctors wore this wig as one piece of a uniform. It was part of the uniform for lawyers. Judges wore it. Members of the church wore it. Horsehair was a common material for these wigs. Horsehair was stiff. It was thick. The price was also lower than the price of human hair. These professionals kept the large curled powdered wigs for public wear even after fashion dropped them. Judges in the United Kingdom still wear wigs with their court uniforms.

8Lawyers there do the same. The English court of the eighteenth century appears in one picture. Another shows judges at a meeting at Westminster Abbey. The eighteenth century also brought toupees into fashion. They were still curled. They were still powdered. They were much cooler to wear. They were lighter too. Full wigs were extremely hot. They were also quite heavy. Many people in Europe had given up wigs by the 1850s. To common people, a wig often looked like a luxury the rich alone could pay for. Old wigs were gathered, then sold outdoors for only a little money. Buyers used them as floor mops. They used them as polishing rags too. Sir Edward Willes judged in eighteenth-century Britain, and he fits the idea of a bigwig. Bigwig, in the sense of an important person, is first known from 1703. It appeared in an English journal called English Spy. The biggest wigs belonged to the richest people, and to the most powerful, in that time. They wore the fanciest wigs too. Nylon threads became a wig material in the twentieth century as technology improved.

9Nylon looked like human hair. It cost much less. It also allowed a larger choice of colors. That choice gave people a greater variety of looks. Today, people still wear wigs for many reasons. Some wear them to look fashionable. Some wear them to look stylish. Some wear them simply to change how they look. People who are bald wear wigs to lift their self-esteem. People who are losing their hair do the same. Performers such as clowns may wear a wig as part of a costume. Actors may do the same. Styles have changed with the fashion of each time. Wigs, long or short and fancy or plain, hold an important place in the human story. The next great fashionable hairstyle is still unknown. Hair loss in some people comes from certain illnesses. Doctors may prescribe wigs for those patients. A wig may help a patient feel more positive. It may help the patient respond better to treatment. Gifts of long hair now go to groups such as Locks of Love. That group turns the donated hair into wigs for children after hair loss.

10Some words in this book have special meanings. Obsession is an extreme interest, the kind that fills a person's thoughts far more often than is usual. Court, in this book, is a monarch's inner social circle. Empires means collections of nations or peoples ruled by one person or one government. Ornate means decorated with great detail. Extensions are lengths of hair or of fiber, fixed to a wig or to natural hair by pins, clips, or glue. Professions means paid occupations, especially ones that need training or a specialized education. Fashion means popular or current styles of looks or behavior. Resin is a sticky, fragrant substance that comes from the sap of a tree. Fiber is a thin strand, natural or synthetic, and it is used in fabric, paper, and other goods. Toupees are fake hair pieces that cover part of the head, usually so hair loss stays hidden. Mesh is material made when threads or wires are woven in a loose way. Wigs are coverings for the head, built from hair or from materials that resemble hair.

34. Fire from the Mountains

1Vesuvius and its eruption open the book. People living with volcanoes come next. Where volcanoes form, and why, comes next. Composite volcanoes come next. Shield volcanoes come next. Cinder cones come next. Lava domes come with them. A closing follows. A glossary ends the book. A picture shows smoke rising in a plume from a volcano. Shaking in the region began in 79 ce. Pompeii was a Roman city. Hardly anyone there paid the shaking much notice. Seismic shaking had come before. The city was rebuilt each time damage grew serious. Most quakes, though, stayed small. Habit made the shaking feel ordinary. Love for their beautiful city held the people of Pompeii there. A ground that shook now and then was not enough to make them leave. A fallen building was not enough either. A thin, steady hiss of smoke rose from Mount Vesuvius nearby. Nobody tied that smoke to the trembling ground. Centuries of life in Pompeii had passed with no eruption seen. Trees stood on the mountain's slopes. Flowers stood there. Grass stood there. A thousand years had gone by since the last eruption. Dormant was what most people assumed. Extinct was what some people assumed. August 24 brought the change. The hour was about one in the afternoon. A huge blast shook the land around the mountain. Dust left the summit. Ash left the summit. Melted rock left the summit. Darkness filled the sky. Tephra is the joint name for dust, ash, and stone. The city disappeared under tephra. Ground as far as 16 kilometers from the mountain was covered. That distance is 10 miles. Three o'clock brought lava from the volcano's mouth. Everything in the lava's path was destroyed. Six o'clock found the dust-and-ash cloud very high. The height was 32 kilometers, or 20 miles. Lightning formed from the huge energy inside the cloud. Ash kept falling. Ground lay under 1 meter of it.

2That depth is 3.3 feet. Falling debris grew so heavy that buildings fell. One picture puts Mount Vesuvius behind. Excavated ruins of Pompeii sit in front. Cities around the mountain saw people try to flee. Homes were being demolished. Farms were being demolished. The treasures easiest to carry were gathered. Families were hurried away. Some people tried to walk on the ash layers. Depth of the ash killed many. Heat of the ash killed many. Stones from the dark sky struck and killed others. Ash-clogged air choked many people. Dust-clogged air choked them too. Midnight made the crisis worse. The cloud had grown too heavy to float. Ash was in it. Poisonous gases were in it. Dust hot enough to glow was in it. Smoke was in it. A pyroclastic flow is what the collapsing cloud became. Speed down the mountain reached 500 kilometers an hour. That speed is 310 miles an hour. A picture shows lava, glowing with heat, inside a volcano. A plaster cast of a body appears in a picture. The person had lived in Pompeii. The death happened while Mount Vesuvius was erupting. Pompeii lies not far from that mountain. A surge cloud buried the city completely. Many people died. Ash hardened around the bodies. Mud hardened around them too. Later the bodies themselves broke down. Air pockets remained. Each pocket matched a body's exact shape. Plaster was poured into the holes by scientists. The casts show the look of people at the moment of death. This surge cloud was Vesuvius's first. Moments were enough to scorch people in Pompeii. People in Herculaneum were scorched too. Burial came from the falling cloud. More dust left the volcano. More ash left it. Further surge clouds came after that. When the eruption ended, two cities that belonged to Rome's empire were gone. Burial was complete. They were erased from the face of the Earth.

3More than one thousand years would pass before anyone found them again. What you just read really happened. How could it happen? What could drive an explosion that violent? Danger is real, so why do people still choose a home near a volcano? Reasons are many. Soil near volcanoes is often rich in nutrients. Farming uses that soil. Hot springs are found there. Warm baths can be taken in them. Respect for volcanoes has still been learned. Long ago, science could not predict a volcano. Science could not explain one. Beliefs still included volcanoes. Traditions included them. Lore included them. Indigenous Hawaiian culture tells legends of a goddess named Pele. Say her name PAY-lay. Eruptions, the legends say, came from her anger. Volcanic glass of some kinds carries her name as an honor. Pele's hair is one kind. Pele's tears are another. Pele's tears are little drops of lava. They cool into solid form while they fly through the air. Wyoming holds an extinct volcano called Devil's Tower. Indigenous tribes across the Great Plains treat the place as important. Many of them do. Bear Lodge is the Lakota name. Tree Rock is the Kiowa name. Creation and renewal are honored there as sacred. Ancient Greece shared a belief about volcanoes. Ancient Rome shared it too. Forges for making lightning bolts: that is what people thought volcanoes were. Vulcan, a Roman god, gave volcanoes their word. Lightning bolts were his work. Volcanologists today notice a familiar smell. A blacksmith's forge is what a volcano smells like. Mount Fuji carries meaning in Japanese Shinto tradition. Buddhist tradition gives it meaning too. A stairway toward another world is how Fuji is seen. Konohana's spiritual home is there. Konohana is a deity of Shinto. Pilgrimage in Japan treats it as a sacred center. Art in Japan treats it that way too.

4A picture shows Devil's Tower. Bear's Lodge is another name. Tree Rock is another name. Wyoming is where this extinct volcano stands. Spiritual weight remains for volcanoes in many cultures. Tools now let scientists learn more. Development of a volcano can be studied. Function of a volcano can be studied. The next eruption can even be predicted. The earliest volcanoes showed up 3.5 billion years before now. Hot lava from deep inside Earth covered vast areas. Crust is the name of Earth's hard surface. Enormous sheets of rock make the crust. Tectonic plates is the name of those sheets. Continents are made by some plates. Ocean floors are made by others. Heat just under the plates is extreme. Rock melts in that heat. Magma is the liquid that results. About 1,200 degrees Celsius is the temperature of magma. That is 2,192 degrees Fahrenheit. Magma sometimes climbs to the surface. Cracks in the crust let it seep out. A diagram can label vents. A diagram can label a magma chamber. Plate movement can be drawn with several labels. A volcanic arc can be labeled. A trench can be labeled. Continental crust can be labeled. Oceanic crust can be labeled. Mantle can be labeled in two places. An ocean plate that crashes into a continental plate is forced downward. An active volcanic region is created by that drop. In the most recent ten thousand years, scientists estimate, over fifteen hundred separate volcanoes have erupted. Each year, about thirty-five volcanoes erupt somewhere. Some years the count is about forty. Observers sometimes see only a little smoke. Observers sometimes see only steam. Some volcanoes never really stop. Their eruptions stay very slow. Vesuvius shows the other pattern. Quiet can last thousands of years between blasts. Edges of tectonic plates are the usual birthplace of volcanoes. Thick liquid magma is what the plates slowly float on.

5Directions of movement differ from plate to plate. Crashes happen. Pulling apart happens. Grinding past one another happens. Sliding and rubbing by those huge plates opens large cracks in the crust. Magma breaks through at some cracks. Volcanoes form at those openings. A map can mark the Pacific Ocean. A map can mark the equator. A map can mark the Ring of Fire. Active volcanoes in the world number at least five hundred. Edges of tectonic plates hold most of them. The Pacific Ocean plate's edge is especially crowded. Ring of Fire is the name of that crowded region. Another busy region follows the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. That ridge is a mountain chain under the Atlantic Ocean. Two plates in the Atlantic are drifting apart. Because the plates split, magma can rise through the floor of the ocean. There it builds up. Mountains can grow from that buildup over time. Some grow tall enough to leave the water. Iceland, an island country, sits on large volcanoes. Those volcanoes belong to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Plate edges are not the only home of volcanoes. The islands called Hawai‘i lie amid the Pacific Ocean plate, far from its rim. A hot spot lies beneath them. Hot magma there sits very near the top of Earth's crust. A new island is sometimes the result. The making is very gradual. Tens of thousands of years are required. Wyoming's Yellowstone National Park lies away from any plate edge, on the North American plate. Beneath the park, a hot spot sits under lakes that are underground. It lies under underground waterways too. Ground is heated by the magma. Water is heated by the magma. Hot springs form. Geysers form and send water shooting far upward. A diagram can label Hawai‘i. It can label Kauai. It can label the hot spot. It can label the way the plate moves. Eruption style changes from volcano to volcano.

6Place of formation is one reason. Cause of formation is another. Some eruptions stay peaceful and slow. Other eruptions burst with a power like many atomic bombs going off together. Different kinds of volcanoes come next. Their eruption styles come with them. Mount Vesuvius is a composite volcano. This book already told its story. Southern Italy's west coast is where it stands. Explosive is the word for composite volcanoes. Violence can be extreme. Destruction can follow. Stratovolcanoes is their other name. No volcano type is more common. Large mountains are the usual shape. Sides are steep. Peaks are evenly shaped. A bowl-shaped opening often crowns the peak. That opening is hollow. Magma leaves through it. Hot gases leave through it. Ash leaves through it. A picture can show how striking a composite volcano's shape is. Mount St. Helens after the eruption of 1980 appears in one picture. The same mountain before that eruption appears in another. Washington State is where Mount St. Helens stands. May 18, 1980, was the eruption date. Deaths numbered sixty-three. Hot winds raced down the slope. Forest across 311 square kilometers was flattened. That area is 193 square miles. Thick magma near the surface is typical for most composite volcanoes. Slow movement is typical of that magma. Vents are the tubes that carry magma upward. Unusually thick magma can cool inside a vent. It can harden there. The vent becomes plugged. Magma underneath is trapped. Heat under the plug has nowhere to go. Gases have nowhere to go. Pressure climbs slowly. A critical level is finally reached. Explosion follows. A whole mountain can be destroyed if the blast is violent enough. The 1980 blast at Mount St. Helens obliterated one entire side. The north side was the side destroyed. Huge clouds rise in a composite eruption. Dust is in them. Ash is in them.

7Smoke is in them. Hot gas is in them. Rock is in them. Many kilometers of height are reached. The sky turns black. Ash covers the ground. A debris cloud that grows too dense cannot stay aloft. It falls as a violent surge cloud. Great height is common among composite volcanoes. Ice often covers them. Snow often covers them. An explosion can melt every bit of the ice at once. It can melt the snow too. Water, mud, and rock then flood down the mountain. Speed can reach 100 kilometers an hour. That is 62 miles an hour. A picture shows a huge mudslide. Melted ice and snow were the cause. Crater Lake, in Oregon, is a caldera many people know. It formed when a volcano fell inward on itself. Southern Oregon is home to the Klamath people. A legend about Crater Lake's origin has been passed down by them. The legend says a first coyote loved a star. He found a way to reach her in the sky. His fall back to Earth made a hole. Crater Lake is that hole. Some ash clouds from volcanoes are enormous. Ash and dust from them travel around the world. Sunlight is blocked. The whole planet cools. Tambora, a volcano in Indonesia, erupted in 1815. People far away felt the result. North America lived through a summer that was cold and snowy. Magma stored underground like a lake can empty out of a composite volcano. A huge empty space remains below. The surface has nothing to hold it up. Collapse into the empty chamber follows. A wide basin shaped like a bowl is left. Caldera is the name of that basin. Side to side, a caldera can reach 100 kilometers. That span is 62 miles. Water often fills them later. Large lakes are the result. Huge forests can be destroyed by composite volcanoes. Whole cities can be buried.

8Human deaths can follow. Another danger is their long quiet. Hundreds of years can pass between eruptions. People forget the risk. Homes are built dangerously near the mountain. Bright orange lava may be familiar from a video. It may flow from a volcano's top. It may spray. This lava is very runny. The flow is smooth. The flow is quick. A stream of water is a fair picture of the motion. Land is covered as the lava spreads. Hardening comes slowly, and the rock builds up. A shield volcano is the source of this lava. Gentle slopes are usual. The slopes are smooth. A shield is the mountain's shape. Mauna Loa, in Hawai‘i, is a shield volcano. Mars is the home of Olympus Mons. No larger volcano is known in the solar system. The whole state of Arizona could fit under it. Shield eruptions are usually gentle. Explosion is not the usual style. Roads can still be destroyed by the lava. Homes can still be destroyed. Forests can still be destroyed. Hot gases may sit inside a shield volcano. Steam may sit inside. A spray from the crater can follow. A bright fountain of lava is the result. Lava paths stay stable. Lava paths stay predictable. Scientists can often come very close because of that. Close study becomes possible. Quiet activity can last a long time. Extreme size can grow during those years. The tallest volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa. It stands in Hawai‘i. Its seafloor base is the starting point of a rise of 9,170 meters. That rise is 30,080 feet. Mount Everest is shorter. Even Mauna Loa looks small beside a greater volcano. Olympus Mons, on Mars, is that greater one. Height of this huge Martian shield is 27 kilometers. That height is 17 miles. Some volcanoes never stay active long enough to become large mountains.

9Small bits of lava may be sprayed into the air instead. The spray lasts only a short time. Lava chunks harden. Ash bits harden. Cinders are the lightweight black rocks that result. A pile grows around the vent. The hill has the shape of a cone. A crater tops it. Cinder cones is the name of such hills. A volcano that appears suddenly is new. A cinder cone is the form it often takes. Older, larger volcanoes can hold cinder cones too. The cones pile inside their craters. The cones pile inside their calderas. One eruption is all most cinder cones ever have. Loose rock is what they are made of. Wind erodes them quickly. Rain erodes them quickly. Mauna Kea, in Hawai‘i, shows cinder cones in a picture. A lava dome can be shown in a picture. One dome in Alaska sits on top of a vent. Inside a crater, a scientist keeps watch on a lava dome. Small, brief eruptions also build lava domes. The lava is thick. The lava is pasty. It oozes from the vent. Hardening is quick. More lava may later push up through the dome's center. Expansion follows. The outside cracks. Other volcanic activity is often nearby when these domes form. Craters of larger volcanoes often hold them. Calderas often hold them. Violent explosion is common for lava domes. Composite volcanoes share that habit. A changing Earth has no showier proof than volcanoes. New rock is created by lava leaving a vent. New land is created too. Soil from volcanic ash is extremely fertile. Farming uses that soil. Geothermal energy from volcanoes is used in some places. Power plants run on it. Electricity is produced. Some people even make a home inside a volcano! Rabaul is a port in Papua New Guinea. An active volcano stands close by. Eruptions come from time to time. Volcanic mountains rank among the most recognizable on Earth.

10They rank among the most beautiful. Mount Fuji, in Japan, is one. Mount Rainier, in Washington, is one. Mauna Loa, in Hawai‘i, is one. Living near a volcano is a choice humans often make, and the wonder of it is clear. Danger should never be forgotten. Volcanoes hold forces that rank among the strongest on Earth. Beautiful Mount Fuji, in Japan, appears in a picture. Glossary Accumulates means to pile up over time, or to grow larger. Billowed means swelled and bulged outward when wind pushed. A caldera is a wide basin like a bowl, where land fell into a magma chamber that had emptied. Cinders are light black rocks, or pebbles, made when small flying bits of lava and ash harden. A crater is the bowl-like hollow of a volcano. Lava exits there. Ash exits there. Gases exit there. Debris means leftover scattered pieces after the rest is gone or destroyed. Dormant means quiet across many hundreds of years. Extinct means no eruption for thousands of years, and no sign that one will come. Forges are hot fires where blacksmiths melt metal so it can be shaped. Geothermal describes heat made naturally inside Earth. Geysers are springs that throw jets of hot water and steam. Magma is rock melted to liquid under Earth's surface. Obliterated means destroyed completely. A pyroclastic flow is a very hot mix of rock, water, and gas that races along because gravity pulls it. Seismic describes shaking of the Earth, such as an earthquake. A surge cloud moves fast along the ground. It is superheated. Ash is in it. Gas is in it. Dust is in it. Rock is in it. Tectonic plates are the big rock sheets that form Earth's crust. Vents are openings in the crust where magma and gases come out. Volcanologists are scientists whose subject is volcanoes.

35. First Footprints on the Moon

1All three Apollo 11 astronauts climb onto a raft in the Pacific once splashdown is done. Contents. A walk on the Moon. Gains and losses. Apollo flies again. The rocket leaves Earth. Eagle sets down. One step, one leap, then the sea. Homecoming. Words to know. A walk on the Moon. The date was July 20, 1969. Around the world, half a billion viewers kept their eyes on television. At the same moment, millions followed radio reports. Over the air, a milestone of human history was unfolding. For the first time, astronauts were walking on the Moon of Earth. Only sixty years earlier, powered flights rose barely off the soil. Now they were visiting the lunar surface. Imagination drove that leap in skill. Determination drove it. So did the courage of countless people who chased a dream. In 1903 two American brothers flew a powered aircraft. Their names were Orville Wright and Wilbur Wright. The flight kept going. The pilots stayed in control. No powered flight before theirs had done both. By 1918, airplanes were important to armies in World War I. Forces used them in operations around the globe. Old wishes to fly. From the earliest ages, people have longed to slip free of Earth's gravity and take to the air. Stories and myths spoke of beings who swept across the sky. Greek tales told of Icarus. He was mortal. He aimed for the Sun. Feathers formed his wings, and wax held them. Mercury was a god of Rome. Winged feet carried him fast through the heavens. In Greek belief, Apollo was god of the Sun.

2He was also god of light. A chariot carried him over the clouds. World War II ran from 1939 to 1945. It brought planes that were faster. It also brought planes that were larger. Some could pass 800 miles in an hour, or 1,287 kmph. Some could fly higher than 40,000 feet, or 12,192 m. Scientists wanted to push flight farther. Engineers did too. Outer space was the new boundary. Late in the 1940s, the United States tested rocket planes. They could fly at speeds that were supersonic. President Dwight Eisenhower, in the year 1958, put his name on a law from Congress. The bill formed an agency that stood on its own. Space flight was its work. National Aeronautics and Space Administration is the agency's long name. The short name is NASA. A race in space. Catching up was one of NASA's first aims. The rival was the Soviet Union. That country is now called Russia. Its space program was ahead. The Soviets had launched Sputnik, a satellite made by humans. That launch is what drove the United States to form NASA. The nation poured itself into the contest. People began to call it the space race. The Soviets were the other side. A drawing by an artist shows Sputnik 1. Steps ahead, and steps back. America's earliest program of flights into space was called Project Mercury. By 1961 it had put satellites into space. It had also placed humans in orbit around Earth. Those results moved President John F. Kennedy. Speaking in public, he set a deadline of nine years.

3In that time the country would place a man on the Moon. It would return him safely to Earth. Researchers at NASA knew the promise demanded new technologies. The tools had to be invented. They had to be tried out. Suddenly the team was in another kind of race. The clock was the opponent. John Glenn is shown in a picture. Among American astronauts, he was first to orbit Earth. Mercury showed that NASA could send a single person into space and bring that person back without harm. Leaders then asked about two people, or a larger crew. What if the stay lasted many days? Project Gemini was created to find out. Its chief purpose was practice in space, getting ready for travel to the Moon. The Gemini craft was larger than Mercury's capsule. It was also far more capable. A Mercury capsule, while in orbit, could only change which way it faced. A Gemini capsule could change the orbit itself. Gemini 4 flew in June 1965. On that flight, Ed White stepped outside the craft. That spacewalk was NASA's first. The formal name is extravehicular activity. The short name is EVA. Later in 1965, the Gemini 7 crew stayed in orbit for fourteen days. One year on, Gemini 10 proved a docking. One craft joined another. One engine then shifted both. With every success, NASA's leaders felt surer. They thought the astronauts could start the Moon missions. Those missions would be called Apollo. A picture shows the Apollo 1 crew. Fate would be cruel to them.

4By 1967 NASA planned to launch its first Apollo flight. Even after all the preparation, tragedy struck. On a launch test dated January 27, 1967, fire started inside the Apollo 1 capsule. Gus Grissom could not escape. Ed White could not escape. Roger Chaffee was trapped as well. Flames raced through the cabin. All three died. The nation was stunned. For a time, every launch stopped. NASA studied the accident with care. Pure oxygen in the cabin helped the fire race ahead. Material that could burn was also inside. The cabin air was changed. A mix of gases, closer to the air of Earth, replaced pure oxygen. Nylon had covered seats and other parts. It catches fire easily. Fiberglass that would not burn took its place. The biggest fix was the hatch. Designers rebuilt it. A hand lever could open it. The lever sat inside the craft. Another sat outside. The hatch could swing out in a few seconds. A special device and a seal kept it from popping open by accident. Two photos show the Apollo 1 command module. The left view is before the fire. The right view is after. The blaze started during that launch test. Apollo flies again. Ten months later, a stronger craft left the pad. The craft belonged to Apollo 4. It joined a command section to a service section. Crews shorten that pair to CSM. No pilot was aboard. The flight entered orbit around Earth. It ran without a problem. NASA trusted its work again. More Apollo missions followed. In December 1968 the Apollo 8 crew was sent on a trip around the Moon.

5Half a year later, three people launched on Apollo 10. This was the final rehearsal before a true lunar landing. Crews call the lander the LM. It pulled free of the CSM. Then it flew downward. Two of the crew were inside. The LM came to 47,000 feet from the surface, or 14,326 m. One short scare followed. The LM began to spin wildly. The crew solved it fast. The LM climbed again and docked with the CSM still circling above. Those two crew members went back into the CSM for the ride home. A photograph taken from Apollo 8 shows Earth. Apollo 10 had succeeded. A real landing was the next try. Leaving the ground. The year was 1969, and little time remained to meet President Kennedy's promise. Apollo 11's crew had trained. They stood ready to enter history. Neil Armstrong commanded the flight. Michael Collins piloted the Command and Service Module. Buzz Aldrin piloted the Lunar Module. Launch morning was July 16, 1969. Local clocks read 9:32. The three men entered Columbia, the CSM. With a huge roar, the Saturn V rocket sent them off. The journey was planned for eight days. The route covered 953,054 miles. In kilometers that is 1,533,792. Three minutes after launch, the craft was already 37 miles up, or 60 km. Speed was 6,340 miles each hour, or 10,203 kmph. Near midday the engine of the third stage fired. That burn took Apollo 11 off the path around Earth. The new path pointed at the Moon.

6Earth slipped behind them. The crew started unpacking. Their moon lander, Eagle, sat inside a storage bay. Explosive bolts released Eagle. They also blasted the compartment walls aside. Columbia shifted about 100 feet ahead of Eagle, a gap of 30.5 m, then turned and docked with it end to end. After that, the rest of the outer shell blew away. Still joined, Columbia and Eagle continued toward the Moon. Eagle is down. By the third day, Apollo 11 lay 175,000 miles from Earth, or 281,635 km. The Moon was 48,000 miles away, or 77,248.5 km. Armstrong and Aldrin passed through a tunnel that linked Columbia with Eagle. They made sure the equipment worked. On the fourth day Columbia slowed so lunar gravity could draw it into orbit. Next morning Aldrin entered Eagle and started its engines. Armstrong came aboard sixty minutes afterward. Crews unfolded the legs used for landing. They closed the hatch. Eagle pulled away. Collins flew the CSM off from the LM and kept orbiting. Armstrong fired the engine used for descent. He guided Eagle toward the smooth site already chosen, a place called the Sea of Tranquility. The path was taking them at a crater littered with rocks. Alarms rang. Armstrong seized control and aimed for safer ground. Strain ran high in Eagle. It also ran high among Mission Control, the NASA team on Earth. When the LM at last touched down, thirty seconds of fuel remained. Armstrong told them Eagle had set down. Cheers broke out at Mission Control. A timeline using Eastern Standard Time.

7On July 16, 1969, at 8:32 a.m., the Apollo Saturn V rocket launches. The Saturn V then separates from the booster engine. At 11:16 a.m. that same day, the third-stage engine sends the LM and the CSM into lunar orbit. At 11:56 a.m., the CSM is freed from that stage, turns, and docks with the LM. On July 19 at 12:21 p.m., the CSM and the LM orbit the Moon. On July 20 at 1:11 p.m., the LM separates, heads for the surface, and leaves the CSM in lunar orbit. At 3:17 p.m. the LM lands. At 9:56 p.m. Armstrong steps onto the lunar surface, and Aldrin follows. On July 21 at 12:54 p.m. the LM lifts off. At 4:34 p.m. the LM docks, and Armstrong and Aldrin enter the CSM. The LM is cast off to crash on the Moon. At 11:54 p.m. the CSM turns and starts home. The Service Module is cast off from the Command Module, and the astronauts descend in the Command Module. On July 24 at 11:50 a.m. the Command Module enters the atmosphere, opens parachutes, and splashes down in the Pacific. One step, one leap, then the water. Armstrong and Aldrin clipped on portable gear for life support and for talking during the EVA. At 10:39 p.m. Armstrong opened the hatch. He moved slowly downward until he reached the last rung. During that climb, he switched on a television camera fixed to the ladder. The world could watch. Nearly twenty minutes after leaving Eagle, he set his left foot in the gray dust of the surface.

8He said his step was a small one for a single person. He said the leap was a giant one for all people. Twenty more minutes passed before Aldrin came out and stood with him. They planted a flag of the United States. President Nixon offered congratulations. Armstrong then set the camera to record their work. The pair carried out several experiments. They collected lunar soil. They collected samples of rock. Their time outside lasted two hours and then forty-seven minutes more. Afterward they climbed inside Eagle again. On July 21 the ascent engines fired, and Eagle climbed at 80 feet each second, or 24.3 m. Four hours later it docked with Columbia. Armstrong and Aldrin climbed back in with Mike Collins. July 24 arrived. Columbia's service module was cut loose. Moments later the Command Module began its plunge into air. Moving faster than sound, the CM plunged toward the planet. Rubbing against the air charged the gas around the craft into fiery, glowing plasma. Plasma covered the CM, cut off every radio signal, and caused a blackout of four minutes. A protective shield against heat was all that stopped the capsule from being destroyed by fire. Parachutes were let out to slow the drop toward a Pacific landing zone. The capsule hit the water at 11:49 in the morning by Central Daylight Time. The spot lay about 800 miles southwest of Hawaii. That gap is 1,287.5 km. Crew of the USS Hornet lifted the astronauts out of the craft. Scientists and stitchers. Several women were central to the mission's success.

9Katherine Johnson did the mathematics. Her post was a NASA lab kept apart under segregation, known as the colored computers. Her figures mattered for Mercury. They mattered for Apollo 11 as well. Rita Rapp, a nutritionist, saw that the crew ate well and that leftover food could be disposed of properly in space. Poppy Northcutt, a NASA engineer, calculated the path of the return to Earth. Seamstresses shaped the spacesuits with exact stitches so the wearers stayed warm and safe in the Moon's extreme conditions. Homecoming. A helicopter brought the crew to the Hornet, where a trailer held them in quarantine. The ship sailed to Hawaii. The trailer was placed on a plane bound for Houston, Texas. There the crew remained quarantined for twenty-one days. Huge parades followed in Houston, in Chicago, and in New York City. With the epic flight complete, the astronauts and the NASA team had done a heroic thing. They also widened the talk about what space travel could become. The Apollo missions. On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first people on the Moon. On November 14, Apollo 12 was the second piloted landing. On April 11, 1970, an explosion on Apollo 13 destroyed the Command Module. The crew quit the Moon plan and rode the Lunar Module back to Earth. On January 31, 1971, Apollo 14 made the third lunar landing. On July 26, Apollo 15 made the fourth. On April 16, 1972, Apollo 16 made the fifth. On December 7, Apollo 17 flew the final Moon mission. From July 1966 through April 1968, Apollos 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were tests with no pilots.

10On January 27, 1967, all three Apollo 1 astronauts died in a cabin fire while a launch was being tested. On October 11, 1968, Apollo 7 was the first Apollo flight with pilots, and the first trial of the CSM. On December 21, 1968, Apollo 8 was the first piloted flight to orbit the Moon. On March 3, 1969, Apollo 9 gave the Lunar Module its first piloted trial, in orbit around Earth. On May 18, 1969, Apollo 10 rehearsed a Moon landing but did not land, as preparation for Apollo 11. Words to know. A capsule is the spacecraft section that can detach. People and instruments ride inside it. A compartment is a divided space inside a craft. Ships have them. Trains have them too. To dock is to link two craft while both are in space. A hatch is the door of a ship, a plane, or a spacecraft. Jettisoned means a crew dropped something off a ship, an aircraft, or a spacecraft, often because of danger. Lunar describes whatever belongs to the Moon. A module is a spacecraft piece that can leave the main body and keep working. Plasma is a gas of charged bits that can carry electric current. Quarantined means kept alone so illness cannot spread. Satellites are natural bodies, or bodies people build, that travel in orbit around Earth or another world. Supersonic means quicker than sound. Technologies are tools and machines that scientific knowledge makes possible.

36. Five Wonders Shaped by Nature

1Several continents hold the wonders in this book, and a map marks them. The Grand Canyon sits in North America. South America is named on that same map. Mount Everest is marked near Europe and Asia. Victoria Falls is the mark for Africa. The Great Barrier Reef is the mark for Australia. Paricutin, in Mexico, belongs with this set of places. A crater in Arizona, the Barringer Meteorite Crater, shows another kind of shape in the land. Rocks from space can strike Earth and leave amazing landforms. How can a place earn the name natural wonder? The answer is a natural structure so amazing and so beautiful that people pause and wonder how it formed. Nature, not humans, makes these landforms. A few years is enough for some wonders to appear. Millions of years are needed for others. Many such wonders share our planet. Five of them fill this book. A river carved one of them, a canyon of layers. A young volcano took over a village. A waterfall is breathtaking. A coral reef is immense. A mountain towers. The Grand Canyon opens the tour. Paricutin follows. Victoria Falls comes next. Mount Everest follows the falls. The Great Barrier Reef follows the mountain. A last chapter finds wonders in still more places. Special words and a finding list close the pages. Five to six million years ago, a large plateau lay in the path of the Colorado River. Raised ground is what a plateau is. Say it pla-TOE. Small pieces of that plateau were picked up by the river as time passed. The pieces rode the current all the way to the sea. Water erosion is the name of this process. Say it e-RO-zhun. How much soil and rock leaves depends on two factors. Speed of the water is one. Volume of the water is the other. The kind of rock matters too. Soft rock breaks with ease.

2Limestone is soft in this way. Shale is soft too. Hard rock does not break so easily. Granite is hard. Slate is hard. Softer rock was carried downstream by the Colorado River inside the Grand Canyon. Harder rock stayed. Deep canyons were cut into the rock by this work across millions of years. Arizona, in the United States, is where the canyon lies. What visitors see today is the wondrous shape left by that slow cutting. Rock layers in the walls hold a long record. Across two billion years, geologists can read what happened here. The wall itself is made of these layered rocks. Youngest rock is at the top, where most visitors take a first look. Oldest rock is the bottom layer, close to the river. Some loose rocks on the canyon floor are as old as two billion years. Rocks and the history of Earth are easy to study here. The layers can be seen, and they can be reached. Visits by geologists are common. Among the earliest was John Newberry. His trip to the canyon was in 1858. No scientist before him wrote down the canyon's layers. Many geologic layers were identified by him. Other people had seen the layers first. Reptiles of more than forty-seven kinds live in the Grand Canyon. Harmless is the word for most of them. Snakes still deserve a watchful eye from visitors. Bites on humans are rare. Venom is carried by the Grand Canyon rattlesnake. Venom is carried by the diamondback rattlesnake too. Winter is when rattlesnakes hibernate inside dens. A single den may hold hundreds of them. Living together is rare for rattlers, and the den is one of the few times they do it. Warm spring weather brings the snakes out. Each one then goes a separate way. Live babies are born to females in late summer. The birth area holds the babies for only a short stay.

3Seven to ten days is about how long. A first baby skin is shed after that. A first rattle is added. Food is what they leave to find. Growing rattlesnakes shed at least once each year. Every shed adds a fresh rattle on the tail. A grown diamondback may reach 2 meters, about 6.5 feet. Weight may reach 6.8 kilograms, or 15 pounds. Twenty-five years is a possible lifespan for rattlers. European explorers arrived only after Native Americans had spent over four thousand years in the Grand Canyon and on the land around it. Local animals were hunted by those early groups. Edible plants were gathered. By 1150, most of the first tribes had left. The Havasupai people were the ones who stayed. Some Havasupai still live in the Canyon and work there. Millions of travelers come each year to Grand Canyon National Park. Hiking, rafting, and looking at this majestic wonder are their reasons. Havasu Falls lies on the Havasupai Reservation. Water is still cutting the western Grand Canyon, and the falls show that work. Millions of years of age belong to many of nature's creations. Their start came long before any human lived on Earth. Modern times have produced other creations. Mexico's Paricutin volcano is one of those younger forms. Say the name pah-ree-koo-TEEN. Formation began in a field in 1943. A farmer found a fissure in his cornfield that year. An opening in the ground is what a fissure is. Say it FISH-ur. About 1.8 meters, or 6 feet, was the length of the crack. More openings showed up soon after. Black smoke rose from the holes. Ash stacked on the ground until a cone took shape. Twelve hours or so lifted the cone to 10 meters, or 33 feet. One day lifted it to 50 meters, or 164 feet. Growth did not stop.

4A week brought the height to 100 meters, or 328 feet. News organizations around the world paid attention to this brand-new volcano. Mexico holds Paricutin, between the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean. The eruption year was 1943. Safety for the village was what the people of Paricutin hoped for. A few months later the cone was huge. Lava moved slowly, but it began to reach the town. Leaving became necessary. Homes and farms were left behind. Nine years of lava and ash buried the whole village of Paricutin. San Juan, the town nearby, was mostly buried as well. Almost nothing of the village could be seen at the end. Black rock surrounded a church steeple that still rose above it. Nature's power had a reminder in that steeple. Cinder cones is the name for volcanoes like Paricutin. Among volcanoes, they are the simplest kind. A sudden appearance is how they start. An eruption follows. Dormant years then last for decades or for centuries. Pressure inside Earth drives the lava. A central vent in the ground is where the lava shoots out. Cooling happens as the lava blows into the air. Small pieces are what it breaks into. Rocks and ash, called cinders, are the hard bits that fall. They pile around the central vent until a cone stands there. A crater shaped like a bowl sits at the top of most cinder cones. Rock fragments cover the cone. Youth is why scientists have watched Paricutin since the day it appeared. Height today is about 424 meters, or 1,391 feet. Area covered is 26 square kilometers, or 10 square miles. Powerful forces that shape Earth are better understood because of this growth. Water also formed Victoria Falls, just as water formed the Grand Canyon. Zambia and Zimbabwe meet in Africa near the Indian Ocean, and the falls stand there. No larger mass of falling water exists on the planet.

5The drop is 108 meters, or 354 feet, into a deep pool. Zambia's people call the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya. Say it MOH-see wah TOON-yah. The meaning is the smoke that thunders. The name fits perfectly. Thunder is the boom of water hitting the pool below. Smoke is the vapor rising from the bottom. Color in the mist can be seen from 20 kilometers away, or 12 miles. The Zambezi River is where Victoria Falls stands. Zambia and Zimbabwe, in Africa, share the border that the river follows. Millions of years ago the falls began to form. A shallow crack crossed the river's path in the rock. Shifting parts of the earth, about 150 million years ago, caused that crack. Year after year the river ran across the rock. Softer rock wore away. A cliff was left. The river drops over the cliff now. Hard rock remains next to the softer rock. Plunge pool is the name of the pool at the bottom. David Livingstone, an explorer from Scotland, came to the falls in 1855. People from outside Africa had probably never seen these formations before him. Queen Victoria of England is the person he named the falls for. A more accurate name, many people think, is Mosi-oa-Tunya. Two national parks now include the falls. Zambia holds one park. Zimbabwe holds the other. Almost two million visitors come to the parks each year. Six separate waterfalls make up Victoria Falls. Devil's Cataract is one name. Armchair Falls is another. Horseshoe Falls is a third. The remaining names are Main Falls, then Rainbow Falls, then the Eastern Cataract. Bungee jumping draws people to a bridge at the falls. A full moon keeps the park open late. A rainbow can be enjoyed then. Moonlight passing through the vapor makes the rainbow. Rafts run on the water below the falls.

6Kayaks run there too. Surfing is even possible on the rapids below. Sir George Everest gave his name to Mount Everest. Surveying and geology were his work, and he was Welsh. No mountain on Earth is taller. Few sites are more amazing. Forehead in the Sky is the Nepali name. The Himalaya range is where this magnificent landform stands. Height is 8,850 meters, or 29,035 feet. Nepal and Tibetan China share the border under the peak. Far past that border region lies the Pacific Ocean. Old is how the snowcapped Himalayas can look. For mountains, they are actually quite young. Millions of years ago they formed. Two pieces of Earth's crust slammed together. Rubbing under pressure went on for a long time. The ground crumbled, then rose above the sea. Youth is why the peaks of Mount Everest are still jagged and steep. Endless wind, ice, and snow have not smoothed them yet. Looking at the mountain is beautiful. Living on it is very harsh. An average temperature is about minus 36 degrees Celsius, which is minus 33 degrees Fahrenheit. January can fall to minus 60 degrees Celsius, or minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit. July is the warmest month. Even then, the air only reaches minus 19 degrees Celsius, or minus 2 degrees Fahrenheit. Freezing is a line the temperature never crosses. Ice and snow at the top therefore never melt. Elevation lets storms arrive without warning. Temperatures can fall fast when they do. Every year, storms leave still more snow on Mount Everest. Survival is hard in the extreme conditions on Mount Everest. Animals have trouble. Plants have trouble too. Few animals manage to live on the mountain, and the wild yak is one of them. Weight can pass 454 kilograms, or 1,000 pounds. Height can reach 1.8 meters, or 6 feet. Blood is one reason the yak survives. More oxygen can enter that blood than enters the blood of other animals.

7Little oxygen is in the air on Mount Everest, so this adaptation saves lives. A dense undercoat of soft hair covers the yak. A shaggy outer coat helps it stay warm. Grazing is how wild yaks feed on the high land. Early settlers in the Himalayas held a belief about the peaks. Gods, they believed, made homes there. Climbs of Mount Everest were not attempted for a long time because of that belief. The early 1900s brought British explorers and other explorers from Europe. Climbs started only then. Harsh conditions met the first climbers quickly. Freezing air, powerful winds, shifting weather, and rough terrain were what they found. Stories told about Mount Everest and about the Himalayas describe the yeti, also called the Abominable Snowman. Say yeti YEH-tee. Say abominable a-BOM-in-a-bal. Large footprints are part of stories Sherpas tell. Gnawed bones of yaks are part of those stories too. A scalp and some skins, said to be from a yeti, were carried by Hillary's team. Europe and the United States were where they took them. Scientists decided the scalp came from a goat. They decided the skins came from a bear. Proof that a yeti exists has never been found. Climbers with experience kept coming, hoping to be first on top. Climbers without experience came too. Success waited until 1953. Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first men to reach the top. Hillary kept bees in New Zealand. Norgay was a Sherpa from Nepal. Awards for the climb were accepted by the two men later. Climbers from around the world have risked their lives since then. Their aim is the summit that people call Forehead in the Sky. Australia's coast holds the Great Barrier Reef. Coral formations there can be explored by a diver. Many reefs together make the Great Barrier Reef. Length is more than 2,300 kilometers, or 1,429 miles.

8The northeast coast of Australia is where it lies. Enchanting sea creatures fill it. Sea turtles, sea slugs, and urchins are among them. Dolphins, whales, and sharks are among them too. Birds and reptiles of more than two hundred species inhabit the reef system. A chain, or range, of rock is what a reef is. The rock sits at the water's surface or near it. No coral-reef system in the world is larger. Coral polyps, by living and dying, build reefs like this one. Every tropical ocean has coral reefs. Size like the Great Barrier Reef is found nowhere else. Five thousand to ten thousand years is the age of most established coral reefs. Experts largely agree about the newest growth here. It began six thousand to eight thousand years ago. A first look can make the reef seem like rock. Rock is not what it is. The building material is the hard outer body left by millions of tiny animals known as polyps. Say polyps POL-ips. Anemones and jellyfish are relatives of polyps. Dead polyps become a base, and new polyps grow on the old skeletons. Limestone at the base of a coral reef is those many layers of skeleton. Other living things help build the reef. Algae help. Sponges help. Shellfish help. Most of the structure of this wonder comes from the tiny polyp. Animals are what reefs are made from. Food and shelter for other animals come from reefs. Ocean temperature changes can hurt them. Thousands of species live on this reef. Fish of 1,625 kinds are included. Marine mammals of more than 30 kinds are included. Seaweed of 50 kinds is included. Marine turtles of 6 kinds are included. Breeding is another reason the reef matters. Birds breed there. Sea turtles breed there. Several endangered species breed there too. The humpback whale is one.

9The sea cow is another. Interest and beauty both make the Great Barrier Reef stand out on Earth. Scientists, scuba divers, and tourists all like to go there. A World Heritage Site listing came in 1981 from UNESCO. UNESCO is a department of the United Nations. Protection today is the work of environmentalists together with those groups. Future generations should be able to learn from the reef and enjoy how beautiful it is. Life fills reefs, and the creatures are delicate. Important rules belong to responsible snorkelers and scuba divers. Float above the reef while snorkeling. Standing on it is never the right choice. Pictures are the thing to take. Coral should not be taken home as a souvenir. Fish for a saltwater aquarium should be ones raised in captivity. Fish taken off a coral reef should not fill those tanks. Plastics and other trash should always be packed out. Arizona and the Australian coast are far apart, yet natural wonders are in both places and everywhere between. Millions of years is the age of some. A single lifetime is the age of others. Each one is unique. Size, height, and beauty put these landforms among the greatest places on Earth. Study and recreation will keep drawing travelers, scientists, and people seeking adventure. Generations still to come will visit. Five wonders in this book are only a start. The Northern Lights are another well-known wonder. They are a light show in the skies of the Northern Hemisphere. A massive hole in the Arizona desert is the Barringer Meteorite Crater. Almost a mile is its width, and 174 meters, or 570 feet, is its depth. The world's largest solid rock is Ayers Rock. It rises 862.5 meters above sea level, or 2,830 feet, in Australia. Ha Long Bay is in the Gulf of Tonkin in Vietnam. More than 1,600 limestone islands fill that large bay.

10Words from the five wonders are gathered here. Cinder cones are hills in the shape of cones, built when lava and ash blow into the air and settle around volcanic vents. Dormant means quiet for now, but able to turn active again. Edible means safe for eating. Erosion is rock or soil taken away by nature, whether by water, by wind, or by ice. A fissure is a crack that is long and narrow. Geologists study where Earth came from, what it is made of, how it is built, and what its history holds. To inhabit a place is to live there or to occupy it. Landforms are natural shapes on Earth's surface, including valleys, plateaus, mountains, plains, and hills. A plateau is flat land raised over a large area. A plunge pool is the deep water at the foot of a waterfall. Polyps are small sea animals without backbones, coral among them, with bodies like tubes and mouths circled by tentacles. A Sherpa belongs to a cultural group that lives in the Himalayas. Guiding mountain climbers is common work for Sherpas. A species is a group of living things that look alike in body and can reproduce. A surveyor measures land and names its physical features. Terrain means the natural features of a piece of ground. A finding list points back to names already met. Paricutin, the plateau, the plunge pool, and polyps are on it. Rattlesnakes, reefs, Sherpas, Victoria Falls, and volcanoes are on it. The yak, the yeti, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and the Zambezi River are on it. Australia, cinder cones, coral, and erosion are on it. The Grand Canyon, the Great Barrier Reef, Havasu Falls, and the Havasupai are on it. Sir Edmund Hillary, the Himalayas, David Livingstone, and Mexico are on it. Mount Everest, national parks, Native Americans, John Newberry, and Tenzing Norgay are on it.

1An introduction opens this book. Early balloon days come next. Kinds of balloons follow. Steering follows. A short history of airships begins. The zeppelin is part of it. The first airline follows. The great Graf follows. Flying aircraft carriers follow. The Hindenburg follows. Airships of modern times follow. A closing comes next. A later part asks why a thing can float when the air around it is heavier. A glossary ends the book. A fire is a familiar sight. Smoke from it climbs. A balloon on a string is familiar too, held so it will not drift off. A blimp over a stadium may be familiar. Why do these things float? Lighter than air is the reason. Smoke weighs less than the air beside it. A balloon weighs less than the air beside it. A blimp weighs less than the air beside it. More than two centuries back, a man studied his own fireplace. Joseph Montgolfier was his name. Say it mon-GOLF-yay. Smoke climbing the chimney puzzled him. Sparks climbing with it puzzled him. A gas, he decided, must be made by the burning. Montgolfier Gas was the name he gave it. An experiment followed. Silk was made into a bag. The open bottom was held over the fire. Letting go sent the bag upward. A picture shows him with that silk bag, the one that sparked the idea. Joseph and his brother later built a larger bag. Cloth was one material. Paper was the other.

2The distance around was nearly 12 meters, or 40 feet. A large fire supplied the Montgolfier Gas that filled it. The rise passed 1,800 meters, or 6,000 feet. The trip covered more than 1.6 kilometers, or 1 mile. A drawing shows their balloon. A basket was added for the next show. A duck went up. A rooster went up. A sheep went up. History's first aircraft passengers were these animals. The year 1783 soon brought two other men from France. Humans flew in a balloon for the first time. Twenty-five minutes was the length of the flight. The landing was more than eight kilometers from the start. That distance is 5 miles. Farmers saw the balloon drop into their field. Fright drove them to attack it. Pitchforks were the weapons. The balloon was torn apart. Those early silk balloons were the first balloons heated by air. Hot-air ballooning is now a sport loved widely. People practice it across the world. Safety is far greater than in the Montgolfiers' time. Propane gas powers the burners. Air is heated by those burners. Flame size is under the pilot's control. Up or down follows from a larger or smaller flame. Balloons over New Mexico appear in a picture. A pilot using the propane burner to climb appears in another. Scientists send up gas-filled balloons as well. Weather is what they study. Helium fills some small balloons. Hydrogen fills others. Both gases are lighter than the air around them.

3Instruments ride along. Weather can be studied with them. Weather can be predicted with them. Much larger balloons go higher. Altitude can reach 37 kilometers or more. That height is 23 miles. The edge of space is nearly that high. Atmosphere studies ride on that equipment. Space-object watching rides on it too. A diagram compares sizes. One view is the balloon at the moment of launch. Another view is the balloon at float altitude. Diameter measures 176.6 meters. Volume measures 2.0 million cubic meters. A Boeing 747 stretches 70.4 meters in length. The Goodyear airship called America stretches 58.5 meters. Its volume is 5,740 cubic meters. Helium only partly fills the research balloon at the start. Rising makes it swell to a huge size. Paris, in France, has the Eiffel Tower. The tower's height is 300 meters. A trip all the way around Earth was one last great balloon challenge. The feat was very hard, and many people tried. Weather that turned bad ended flights early. Fuel that ran out ended flights early. Machines that failed ended flights early. Records for distance were set anyway. Records for time were set anyway. A full circle of Earth had still not been done. The year 1999 finally brought success. Bertrand Piccard came from Switzerland. Brian Jones came from Britain. Breitling Orbiter was their balloon's name. No balloon before it had flown around the world. Steering is the weakness of balloon travel.

4Wind chooses the path. Altitude is what pilots can control. They can climb. They can drop. Winds at different heights blow different ways. A chosen direction is still out of reach. Steering ideas began almost as soon as balloons existed. Dirigible was the goal, meaning able to be directed. Today the word dirigible covers any lighter-than-air craft that can be steered. A contest picture shows balloons from many countries. Aero Park in Chicago was the place. July 4, 1908, was the date. Henri Giffard's dirigible appears in a drawing. Powered flight in history begins with that craft. The year was 1852. Henri Giffard was a man from France. His dirigible flew 27.4 kilometers, which is 17 miles. The landing was safe. Steam drove the engine. The engine was his own design. Three horsepower was its output. A lawnmower of today makes about that much. Wind from the front was too much for it. Useful steering against the wind had to wait. Nearly 40 years passed. A gasoline engine finally supplied the needed power. Count Ferdinand Graf von Zeppelin stands at the center of lighter-than-air history. Ships on water were his model for the sky. A rigid frame, he became sure, could be strong enough to matter. Fabric would wrap that frame. Engines would hang on it. Fuel would hang on it. Passengers would ride on it. Cargo would ride on it. Cells inside the frame would hold the lifting gas. Hydrogen was his choice because no gas is lighter.

5Explosion was the danger. Care had to be extreme. Zeppelin was the name he gave the invention. It was a giant dirigible. Rigid airship is the other common name. A picture shows the count. Military service was the count's career. A fleet of zeppelins for the military was his dream. Scouts were one role. Bombers were another. The military would not take up the idea. Private gifts supplied money instead. A large share of his own fortune was spent too. The year 1900 brought the first flight. Luftschiff Zeppelin 1 was the full name. LZ 1 was the short name. Only three flights happened. Money ran out. The ship had to be taken apart. Five years passed before money for another ship could be raised. A short life still proved the idea could work. Floating hangars on a lake served the early ships. The LZ 3 appears in a picture. Nine years after LZ 1, the military was still unconvinced. War use had not been shown. Another money source was required. More zeppelins were the goal. The year 1909 brought a company named DELAG. Airships would be bought. Passengers would travel between cities in Germany. Delicious food was served. Fine champagne was served. Comfortable seats let people watch the land below. By 1914, passengers carried numbered more than 34,000. Distance flown was roughly 160,000 kilometers, or 100,000 miles. No serious trouble marked those flights. LZ 10, called Schwaben, was the first commercial zeppelin that truly succeeded.

6The summer of 1911 brought her nearly 100 flights. LZ 127 carried the name Graf Zeppelin. September 1928 was when the huge new ship first left her hangar. The count was honored by that name. Germany still saw him as a hero of the nation. Nothing like the Graf had been seen. Length was 236 meters, or 775 feet. Three jetliners of the 747 type, set end to end, would still be shorter. The Titanic was only a little longer. The year 1927 had shown an airplane struggling to cross the Atlantic. One year later, an ocean crossing was within the Graf's power. Twenty passengers could ride. Luxury matched only the finest ships of the sea. Sensation followed the Graf wherever she went. The 1920s still held many people who had never seen an airship. An airplane was also new to many of them. People were awestruck when silver ships as big as tall buildings passed overhead. It sailed overhead. Houses emptied as people rushed out. Thousands gathered at each landing. Regular passenger trips ran to Germany and away from Germany. The year 1929 brought a trip around the world. Twelve days was the length. The Arctic was explored with her help. Another kind of first flight waited, and the next lines tell it. Passengers flew between Europe and South America on those first trips. Flying continued until 1937. A museum was what she became after that.

7World War II then began. Germany's Nazi government melted her down. Fighter planes were made from the metal. A landing picture shows her at Lakehurst. Lakehurst is in New Jersey. The landing followed the 1929 trip around the world. Stamps in several countries showed the Graf. Airplanes that leave ships are a familiar idea. Those ships are aircraft carriers. Landing back on them is familiar too. The 1930s gave the U.S. Navy two carriers that could fly. Akron was one name. Macon was the other. Several small airplanes rode inside. Launch could happen in the air. Recovery could happen in the air. Fighter planes appear in a picture. The USS Macon appears in another. Two fighter planes show underneath. A hangar inside each airship stored the small planes. A hook on a wing met a trapeze. The trapeze lowered the plane through a hole. The hole was in the airship's bottom. The engine was started. The hook was released. The plane flew away. Return reversed those steps. Air landings grew so skilled that some planes lost their wheels. Weight was saved. Both Akron and Macon were lost anyway. Bad weather played a part. Human mistakes played a part. Big zeppelins lost the Navy's interest. Smaller blimps for patrol kept flying for many years. Success of the Graf pushed the Zeppelin Company toward a still bigger ship. Hindenburg was the new name. Luxury on her passed every earlier airship. Length was 245 meters, or 803 feet.

8Nearly three football fields match that length. No flying machine since has been larger. Service began in 1936. Passengers were delighted. Watchers were thrilled. Helium was the gas she was designed to use. Hydrogen was the gas she actually held. Helium was very scarce then. Only the United States held enough to fill even a single airship. None was sold for the Hindenburg. Nazi control of Germany was the reason for the refusal. Flames were watched with extreme care by the crew. Sparks were watched the same way. Flames still took the ship. The landing was in stormy weather. Lakehurst, New Jersey, was the place. The year was 1937. Hydrogen took the blame, as everyone expected. Newer evidence points at the covering fabric. That fabric could burn easily. Whatever the cause, passenger zeppelins ended with the fire. The LZ 129, which is the Hindenburg, flies overhead in a picture. Big airships lost most people's interest after World War II. An ocean liner cost less for a sea crossing. Airplanes grew larger. Airplanes grew faster. Fear from the Hindenburg fire lingered. Helium instead of hydrogen did not remove the fear. Interest in flight that is lighter than air never fully died. Spirit of Goodyear, a Goodyear blimp, appears in a picture. Fame among airships probably peaks with the Goodyear blimps. The 1930s joined Goodyear with the Zeppelin Company. Navy zeppelins were built. Navy blimps were built. Advertising blimps were built too.

9Products were promoted, and that work has not stopped. Millions of people see those blimps each year. Other firms use blimps to promote what they sell. Fuji Film is one firm. Metropolitan Life is another. Germany, birthplace of the zeppelin, cares strongly about new airships. The Zeppelin Company is building again. Zeppelin NT is the new ship. NT stands for New Technology. Patrol is one planned use. Exploration is one. Advertising is one. Passenger trips are one. A ticket for an airship ride can be bought again. Almost 70 years had passed since the last chance. Sightseeing over Germany is now sold by the firm that used to operate the Graf. The trips are sightseeing over Germany. A Zeppelin NT cockpit appears in a picture. Takeoff of a Zeppelin NT appears in a picture. More companies have begun building airships. Lockheed Martin has one called the Hybrid Airship. Very heavy cargo can ride. Bulky cargo can ride. Pickup can happen at the factory. Drop-off can happen at the place of need. Roads that are poor, or missing, are where this helps most. The P-791, a hybrid airship, appears in a picture. Lift of more than 450 metric tons is within the P-791's power. Heat was the first lesson. Air grows lighter when it is heated. Some gases are lighter than air even without heat. Floating objects became the goal. Hot-air balloons came first. Dirigibles that could be steered came next. Size grew. Quality grew.

10Travel by air became dependable. Travel by air became safe. People are still fascinated. People are still excited. That feeling has lasted 150 years since dirigibles were invented. The Montgolfier brothers missed one fact. Montgolfier Gas does not exist. Density was unknown to them. Fire heats air. Molecules in that air move farther apart. Density drops. The heated air is then lighter than nearby air. Rising follows. Wood floating on water shows the same idea. Lower density than the water is why the wood floats. A hot-air balloon floats for a matching reason. Hot air inside is less dense than air outside. The balloon is lifted. Passengers are lifted. Other gases can be less dense than air too. Hydrogen became a balloon filling. Helium became a balloon filling. Both weigh less than air, because both are less dense. Hydrogen lifts more than helium does. Hydrogen also catches fire easily. Glossary An airship is a lighter-than-air craft that drives itself and can choose its direction. A blimp keeps its shape by gas pressure inside, not by a stiff frame. Density is how tightly molecules of a material are packed. Dirigible once meant able to be steered. It now names any steerable craft that is lighter than air. Gas is matter free to change both shape and size. Molecules are the tiny bits that build every substance. A zeppelin is an airship whose inside frame is rigid, with cells that hold the lifting gas.

38. Flying Machines With No Pilot

1In Ukraine, a brown bear at a shelter for saved bears comes upon a flying drone. A camera on an aerial drone can map land and survey it. Look up at the sky. Something buzzes past. That object is not a bird. It is not a plane. It is not a superhero. It is an unmanned aerial vehicle. People also call this machine a drone. Drones were once a rare sight. Now their popularity is growing. Their uses are growing too. Making maps is one task these flying robots handle. They can save lives. They can bring packages very fast. Those jobs are only a few of the things drones can do. Drones may look like a fairly new invention. They have been around much longer than some people think. The U.S. military built the earliest form of a drone during World War I. That craft was the Kettering Bug. It was planned as an aerial torpedo. Papier-mache and cardboard went into its body. About twenty years later, more advanced drones appeared. They received the name unmanned aerial vehicles. No pilot rode inside them. A person on the ground flew them by remote control. A person in a nearby mother airplane could fly them too. The first UAVs looked like small airplanes.

2They were fairly large. A few stretched past 6 meters (20 ft.) from nose to tail. Their wings reached nearly 9 meters (30 ft.) across. Building the Kettering Bug cost $400. Charles Kettering developed it with Orville Wright. Radio signals controlled the Queen Bee. It could climb as high as 5,182 meters (17,000 ft.). It could travel as far as 483 kilometers (300 mi.). Its speed passed 161 kilometers (100 mi.) per hour. During World War II, British forces built UAVs mainly so gunners could practice on targets. The British navy called its prototype UAV the Queen Bee. A United States admiral watched a Queen Bee demonstration. He wanted a similar craft for the U.S. Navy. America's UAVs came from the plans of Commander Delmer Fahrney. He gave them the nickname drones. The nickname honored Britain's Queen Bee, the model for the new craft. The name stayed in use. After that, every U.S. Navy UAV was called a target drone. The word drone fit those target craft in more than one way. Among bees, a male worker is known as a drone. Used as a verb, drone means a long humming sound. A UAV in flight makes a hum like that. Across the next eighty years, drones changed into smaller flying machines.

3Early drones looked like tiny planes. Newer ones looked more like small helicopters. Wings were gone. Spinning blades called rotors lifted them instead. Some drones rose on six or more whirling rotors. Rotors made the machines much more agile. These quick craft could swerve. They could switch direction fast. Pilots could aim them at precise places once out of reach. They could also fly nearer the ground. They could hang still in one place. Their size and agility fit jobs that planes found hard. Some of those jobs were impossible for planes. Drones then came into wide use outside the military. Nikola Tesla is known as the Father of Unmanned Technology. In 1898 he invented a boat steered by radio. He showed the boat in New York City. His method was an early form of the technology people use to run drones from far away. Users found drones ideal for pictures taken from high above, like a bird looking down. In earlier years, photos from the air usually came from airplanes. Planes had to stay well above the ground so they would miss obstacles. A close picture of the ground was hard to get. Drones could fly much more slowly. They could also fly much lower. They could pass under clouds that blocked clear photos from planes.

4They could move through tight spaces. Canyons were open to them. Ravines were open to them too. Larger aircraft could not reach those places. People who make films realized their jobs would get much easier with drones. A camera fastened to a drone could record the flight. Special effects were no longer needed to show flying. The footage could show what real flight feels like. Several drones at once also gave views from overhead. Those shots did not get in the actors' way. Crew members were not put in danger. Mapmakers now send drones into far-off land that is hard to cross. The pictures show sharply what that land is really like. Drones can supply fresh photos of glaciers as the ice changes. They can show other landforms that keep changing too. Drones can move near rough land. That skill makes them strong helpers for rescuers. They can help find people who may be lost. They can help find people who may be hurt. A drone can slip beneath the forest canopy. From there it gets a clear look at the ground below. Search and rescue drones do not store video for later viewing. They send a live stream of pictures while they travel.
