5At night they use thermal imaging. That tool senses warmth given off by a person's body. Water, food, or blankets can be released by drone when the need is urgent. The drop lands with better aim than many older methods. The cost stays low. Drones matter especially after a disaster. Earthquakes often make roads impossible to use. Airports can become impossible to use too. Floods cause the same problem. Victims then cannot get the help they need. Drones can also watch disasters that are still underway. A wildfire is one example. A volcanic eruption is another. People can gather the data without standing in danger. A 2015 photo from an aerial drone shows flooding in Bulgaria. A bull elephant meets a drone inside an African reserve. Animals gain from drones, not only people. Watching a huge area, such as a large ranch, takes a great deal of time. It also takes many workers. Drones track roaming animals much faster. They do the job more cheaply too. Drones can locate cattle that have strayed. People have even used them to herd animals back where they belong. Wildlife preserves use drones to watch for danger. They also use drones to follow what animals do. If an animal is in trouble, rangers can reach the exact spot.

6Drone technology makes that fast arrival possible. Researchers use drones to study how animals live in their home habitats. The animals need not be disturbed. Businesses have lately started to test delivery shaped for each buyer. Online sellers want to skip travel on the ground. Local shops want the same thing. They hope to fly small packages from warehouses straight to buyers. In the near future, a pizza you order might not arrive by car. A drone might bring it. In distant parts of the world, drones already carry vital medical goods. Clinics in rural Rwanda, a nation in Africa, depend on these flights. Medical outposts there depend on them too. The drones bring blood for emergency surgery. They also bring medicines that cannot wait. Each drone follows a route set before takeoff. Staff watch that route on computer tablets. Satellite navigation systems guide the flight. At the stop, the drone lets go of its precious load. A paper parachute carries the cargo down to the clinic. This service cut delivery time from hours down to minutes. Countless lives have been saved. A photo captures an emergency medical drop by drone over the Rwandan countryside. The Drone Racing League holds races for drones built for the contest.

7Drones serve serious aims. They have playful uses too. One of the newest playful uses is a race between drones. The league for drone races was started by Nicholas Horbaczewski. The league offers a real flying experience through races that feel like video games. An obstacle course is set inside a large indoor building. An empty shopping mall can be that building. A sports stadium can be that building too. Small drones fitted with lights fly the course. Their speed is nearly 129 kilometers (80 mi.) per hour. Pilots on the ground steer with joysticks. Tiny cameras on the drones send exciting video into headsets. The pilots wear those headsets. The picture makes each pilot feel like a rider on the speeding drone. The league wants every race to feel as thrilling as possible. For that reason, pilots are not asked to bring drones of their own. Race organizers supply the drones for each contest. They also bring a pit crew for the machines. The crew handles repairs. The crew keeps the drones flying. A pilot then need not fear a crash that wrecks a prized machine. Many people expect this new sport to grow more popular. People who like automobile contests may become fans. It may attract fans of video games as well.

8Some sports channels on television have even broadcast drone race contests. The races are held all around the globe. This sport of the future really seems to be lifting off. The 2016 contest drew over one hundred pilots. New York City held the meet. Its title was the National Drone Racing Championships. Safety is not the only worry about drones. Privacy is another worry. A robot overhead that records a private house is unwelcome to most people. Some towns have banned certain drones over neighborhoods where people live. The ban covers drones fitted with smartphones. It also covers drones fitted with cameras. Growing drone use brings fresh problems. Regulators fear that drones may endanger ordinary airplanes with fixed wings. They fear danger to helicopters of a normal size too. Commercial aircraft must file a plan before they fly. No rule forces a drone to file a flight plan. Flight radar does not display these small craft. They are so small that a pilot may not see them until it is too late. Drones flown separately cannot signal one another. They may crash into each other. The Federal Aviation Administration is preparing pilot rules because of those dangers. People often call that agency the FAA.

9As of 2017, anyone who operates a drone must hold a license. The operator must warn an airport about a flight inside 8 kilometers (5 mi.) of that airport. Drones also must not fly near national monuments. They must not fly over big sports events where crowds gather. A disabled drone could put people nearby in danger. A drone out of control could do the same. Even with those risks, drones seem likely to remain. Years ago, people looking ahead made a prediction. They said humans would lean on robots for many tasks. Some tasks were ones people could not do. Other tasks were ones people did not want to do. That old prediction seems to be coming true. Flying robots are taking a larger role in daily life. Drones work together with other advances in technology. The mix offers chances to make lives better. It also lets us view the world from a fresh angle. Sydney, Australia, has seen drones glowing at a festival of the arts. One day, drones may stand in for fireworks. Swarms of tiny drones can carry bright lights in many colors. A program can set them to fly in a formation. The formation can create a dazzling display. These words help with the topic.

10Agility is the power to move fast and with ease. To navigate is to find a route across a long distance. It can also mean steering toward a chosen end point. To collide is to hit another object in a hard, violent crash. A remote control is a tool held in the hand. It runs a machine from far away, such as a television or a toy. Customized describes something changed so it feels more personal. The change can also fit a special need. A drone can be an aircraft with nobody aboard. It can also be a ship run from far away. Rotors are blades that spin. They lift a flying machine and keep it up. The Federal Aviation Administration is a national agency in the United States. It directs every part of civil flying there. A satellite may be a natural body. It may be an object people built. It travels in orbit around Earth or around another body in space. Terrain means the natural features on a piece of land. The word can also mean the ground itself. To monitor is to watch how something moves forward over time. Unmanned means a craft carries no person. It can also mean no person on board is steering it.

39. Freedoms Written Into the Highest Law

1A family photo catches a reaction to court news from 1969. Mary Beth Tinker stands in that photo. Lorena, her mother, stands with her. Paul, her younger brother, stands there too. Mary Beth's junior high had suspended her. A black armband at school was the cause. The book opens on that story. The country's highest law comes next. A later part tells how a list of rights was joined to that law. Protection under those rights is explained after that. Changes made in later years follow. People who still struggle for rights come after those changes. A brief close ends the story. Meanings of hard words come last. Punishment arrived in 1965. Five students in an Iowa district received it. They had worn black armbands at school. The Vietnam War was what the armbands protested. That war ran from 1955 until 1975. Officials ordered the armbands removed. The students left them on. Suspension was the result. Three of those students sued. Their parents joined the suit. The district was the target of the lawsuit. The case climbed through the courts. In 1969 the nation's highest court agreed to hear it. Those judges said the armbands could stay. Their reason was an amendment to the Constitution. An amendment means a change. It can also mean a correction. Wearing the black armband counted as speech, the Court said. The First Amendment guards that kind of speech. That amendment sits inside the Bill of Rights. The Bill of Rights lists the earliest ten amendments.

2Citizen freedoms are what those amendments guard. A grand court building stands in Washington, D.C. It houses the nation's highest court. The Bill of Rights belongs to the Constitution. That document is the country's first law. It is also the highest law. It was created as the United States took shape. Other laws must follow its principles. Earlier, the land was thirteen colonies, not yet one country. Great Britain had planted those colonies on ground seized by force. Native peoples had held that ground. Colonists believed King George III brushed their rights aside. A revolution began in 1775. Eight years of war with Great Britain followed. Independence was the goal. The original Constitution, Bill of Rights included, sits behind glass. Washington, D.C., is where visitors can see that display. The National Archives Building holds it. Founders is the name for colonists who helped form the United States. Wealth described most of them. A strong education described most of them too. Law or politics was the background of many. During the fight with Great Britain, they built a confederation of states. Power at the center of that confederation was weak. King-like power was what they refused to give leaders. States received most of the power instead. A painting shows soldiers of the new country marching toward the British. After the war, the Founders saw failure in their system. They chose to remake it. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was the meeting place in 1787.

3There they wrote exact rules for a different government. More strength for the central government was the aim. Federal government is the name for that center. They still refused it enough strength to strip citizens of rights. Democracy was the form they wanted. In a democracy, elections let citizens pick leaders. Ideas also came from the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Native nations made up that confederacy. Together they ran a government of many states. Each nation kept a government of its own. September 1787 saw the new constitution finished. By the middle of 1788, only two states had not approved it. The Constitution then stood as the law of the land. George Washington became the first elected president. Independence Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was where the Founders argued over the document. We the People are the opening words. All people were not covered by the original text. People held in slavery were left out. Native peoples were left out. Most women were left out. Later amendments, and later laws, widened the circle. Women had no seat at the writing of the Constitution. Many of them still helped the new nation grow. Essays by women took up politics. Gender equality was another subject. Abolition was another. Political talks were hosted by women. Sessions of Congress drew women as listeners. Political rallies were organized by women. Abigail Adams ranks among the most important of them. She was wife to the Founder John Adams. She was also a close advisor to him.

4A letter from her said to remember the ladies. He was then helping to draft the new constitution. North Carolina voted no on the Constitution. Rhode Island voted no as well. They would withhold approval, they said, until rights were listed in a bill. Neither would join the government without that addition. Some Founders called a list of rights dangerous. People might treat any unlisted right as unprotected, they argued. James Madison, a leading Founder, shared that fear. Thomas Jefferson took the other side. A bill of rights was necessary, he said. Both men were Virginians. Virginia's own constitution already held a Declaration of Rights. Bills of rights appeared in several other state constitutions too. Jefferson wanted citizen rights written into the U.S. Constitution. Madison came around. He began drafting a bill of rights. The Virginia Declaration of Rights was one model. His draft proposed twenty amendments. Congress reduced the set to twelve. States received that set in 1789. After receiving them, those two holdout states trusted that rights would be safe. By late 1791, three-fourths of the states had accepted ten amendments out of the twelve. Those ten became the Bill of Rights. Those two Virginians had started out in disagreement. They later joined efforts and helped the Bill of Rights come into being. Five important personal rights sit in the First Amendment. Freedom of speech is one. Citizens may ask government to change laws they reject. Peaceful protest gatherings are allowed.

5Freedom of the press is another First Amendment right. News may be shared by reporters. Opinions may be shared by them too. In the 1700s, public news came only from newspapers and other print. Radio now falls under freedom of the press. Television does too. So does the Internet. A 2017 protest in North Dakota stayed peaceful. Members of the Lakota nation took part. An oil pipeline through sacred land was what they opposed. Limiting a government by listing rights on paper did not start in the United States. England's version passed in 1689. A full century, and more, went by before this country wrote a version of its own. Written protections for civil and political rights now exist in most democracies. Freedom of religion is a further First Amendment right. One official religion is the pattern in many countries. The United States has no official religion. Any religion may be practiced. No religion may be practiced as well. Owning weapons is a right in the Second Amendment. Using weapons is part of that right too. Some readers think the amendment was meant only for militia groups. The National Guard is an example of such a group. Other readers think every citizen may own and use weapons. Housing soldiers by force is blocked by the Third Amendment. British soldiers were allowed to seize private homes in the years leading to the Revolutionary War. A search needs a solid reason under the Fourth Amendment.

6An arrest needs that kind of reason too. The reason must be a belief that a crime was committed. A judge must grant permission before police search someone's property. People accused of crimes are covered by four amendments. Those are the Fifth, the Sixth, the Seventh, and the Eighth. A criminal offense means a crime against the public. It can also mean a crime against a state. The Fifth Amendment blocks a forced trial unless there is solid reason to think the person may be guilty. Court must prove the charge before any punishment. Speed is required by the Sixth Amendment. The trial must happen as soon as it can. The trial must be public. A jury must be present. A civil crime means a wrong against a person. It can also mean a wrong against a company. The Seventh Amendment gives a jury trial for that kind of case too. Cruel and unusual punishments are banned by the Eighth Amendment. Red-hot branding irons were once used on some criminals. Wooden stocks in public places held others. Crowds threw objects at the people in the stocks. Those punishments are banned now. Rights not already written down are covered by the last two amendments. Listing some rights does not erase other rights, the Ninth Amendment says. Only powers named in the Constitution belong to the government, the Tenth Amendment says. Any unnamed power stays with the states. It may also stay with the citizens.

7A timeline of major steps runs like this. The American Revolutionary War started in 1775. The Declaration of Independence won approval from the Continental Congress in 1776. The war ended in 1781. The Constitution was written in 1787. It was approved in 1788. The Bill of Rights joined it in 1791. Slavery was abolished by the 13th Amendment in 1865. The 14th Amendment, in 1868, gave citizenship rights to everyone born in the United States. Naturalized people received those rights too. The 15th Amendment, in 1870, gave the vote to every male citizen. Color did not matter. Race did not matter. Women gained the vote through the 19th Amendment in 1920. The voting age dropped under the 26th Amendment in 1971. The Bill of Rights dates from 1791. Further amendments arrived in the years after that. A new amendment is hard to pass. Congress may propose one. A Constitutional Convention may propose one too. Two-thirds of the state governments must call for such a convention. After a proposal, three-fourths of the state governments must vote yes. That yes vote ratifies the amendment. Ratify means it becomes law. Twenty-seven amendments stand in the Constitution today. The Thirteenth and the Fourteenth rank among the most important after the Bill of Rights. Both followed the Civil War. That war lasted from 1861 to 1865. Slavery in the United States was outlawed by the Thirteenth Amendment. An illustration shows people once enslaved, celebrating that change. Citizenship for all formerly enslaved people came from the Fourteenth Amendment.

8Equal protection of the laws was promised to every citizen. Race was not allowed to block that promise. Voting is among the most important citizen rights. Before the Constitution, land ownership was required for a vote. White men made up most of those owners. By 1856, every white man could vote. Most Black men still could not, until the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870. Women gained the vote through the Nineteenth Amendment. Their organized fight lasted more than seventy years. The amendment passed in 1920. Racial segregation of public schools ended largely because of the Fourteenth Amendment. Oliver Brown lived in Topeka, Kansas, in the 1940s. He was a Black man. He wanted his daughter enrolled at a school close to home. That school served white students. The school said no. The only place offered served Black students. It lay farther from home. Brown went to court. The case reached the Supreme Court in 1954. The full bench agreed. Nine judges sat on it. Racial segregation in public schools broke the Fourteenth Amendment, they ruled. The schools serving white children did not match the schools serving Black children. The ruling is counted among the Court's most important. All Americans are supposed to be covered by the Bill of Rights and by later amendments. Fights for those rights still happen often. California in 2000 was home to Alondra Jones. Her grades made her an honor student. Her high school sat in a low-income area.

9Black students and Latino students made up most of the school. Textbooks were too few. Computers were absent. Filth covered the buildings. Rats moved through the hallways. Another high school, which Alondra visited one day, looked different. Books were there. Computers were there. The buildings were clean and safe. Funding at her own school was far lower than at other schools in the state, she realized. Almost one hundred other students joined her lawsuit. California was the state they sued. The court found a failure of equal protection. The Fourteenth Amendment requires that protection. A good education is a right of every student, the court said. Socioeconomic status must not decide that right. Samantha Elauf was seventeen in 2008. A clothing store in Oklahoma was where she asked for a job. A hijab was the reason the store refused to hire her. Many Muslim women wear that head covering. The store called the hijab a break in its dress code. Samantha sued. The case climbed to the Supreme Court. The year of the ruling was 2015. The Court sided with Samantha. Religion was the reason for the store's discrimination, the Court said. Her First Amendment right was violated. Samantha Elauf and her mother stand before the Supreme Court building. Rights fights by different groups have continued across history. In the United States, the story of each person's rights begins in the Constitution. The story has not ended.

10Most people in the country stood outside the Constitution's protection when it was written. Alondra and Samantha are among those who later fought to guard the rights promised to citizens. Dozens of amendments have widened that protection. Dozens of laws have done the same. Equality under the law is still the aim of advocates. Protection under the law is still their aim too. A few word meanings help. Founders names the men who helped set up the United States and its government. An amendment is a change added to a document. It can also be a change added to a law. The Bill of Rights means those earliest ten amendments. Certain rights are guaranteed there. Freedom of speech means people may share opinions in public. A confederation joins states, provinces, or groups. Its central authority stays limited. Freedoms are political rights. They are also powers to act as one wishes and to think as one wishes. Principles are basic values. They are ideals that steer actions and decisions. The Constitution is the written rule set under United States law. It is also the set of principles under that law. Force is how a revolution drives a government out of power. A different government then takes the place of the old one. Equality means the same rights for everyone. A right is a freedom a person may justly claim. It can also be a power claimed that way. Excluded means shut out from taking part.

40. From a Bronx Party to a Global Culture

1Three performers pose together. At the center is the rap artist Cheryl James. On the right is Sandra Denton. Together they are known as Salt-N-Pepa. On the left is their DJ, Dierda Roper, known as DJ Spinderella. Life in New York City during the 1970s was tough. Jobs were scarce. Poverty followed. Homelessness followed. Crime rose. The city did not give people the resources needed to face these problems. Decades of racism had built extra challenges for people of color. Black people carried those challenges in particular. Most could not afford to leave the city. Many white people did leave. Underserved neighborhoods grew worse. More businesses shut down. Jobs vanished. Entertainment vanished with them. Clubs closed. Movie theaters closed. Boys stand before graffiti in a 1970s New York City scene. Youth in these communities had to invent fresh ways to have fun. They had to invent new ways to express themselves. Their creativity did more than start a new style of music. It started an entire movement. Summer of 1973 brought a request from Cindy Campbell. Her older brother Clive was the person she asked to DJ a party in the neighborhood. DJ means disc jockey. Their neighborhood was the South Bronx, in New York City.

2Black people and Puerto Rican people made up most of it. Jamaica was the country the Campbell family left for the United States. The move had come five years earlier. Clive's nickname was Hercules. On stage he used the name DJ Kool Herc. Fancy equipment was not his. He chose records from his own collection. He connected two turntables to a device that makes sound louder. Records play on a turntable, which is a platform that spins. Success for the party was huge. Neighborhood fame reached Clive within a day. Music that started in the South Bronx on that day later reached listeners worldwide. The people there did not know they were making history. No one had told DJ Kool Herc that a later title would be Father of Hip-Hop. A later photograph shows him performing in England in 2000. His inspiration included a Jamaican tradition called toasting. In toasting, a person talks or chants while a rhythm plays. It grew popular in the 1950s. An older West African oral tradition shaped Jamaican toasting. That tradition belongs to griots, a word said GREE-ohz. A griot is a storyteller. A griot is a poet.

3A griot is a singer. A griot is a historian. Many hip-hop fans treat rappers as griots of the present day. Like griots, rappers tell their community's story. Struggles go into the telling. Successes go into it. The result entertains. It also informs. Community history and culture take shape partly through what rappers do. They help preserve both. A photograph shows a griot from West Africa performing in New York City. Hip-hop is more than music. It is a whole culture. At the start, the community had no clubs. It had no stages. It had no art galleries. Artists carried their creativity into the streets. Four key elements make up the culture. One element is the DJ. Another is breaking. Another is graffiti art. Another is the MC. A DJ's job is to keep music flowing. As one song ends on the first turntable, the second turntable fades a new song in. The music never stops. Few hip-hop sounds are as distinctive as scratching. A DJ makes the scratchy sound by sliding the record back and forth. The record is playing on the turntable while it moves. Early DJs noticed a crowd favorite called the break beat. Drums are all that remain in that stretch of a song.

4Both turntables, for early hip-hop DJs, carried copies of one record. They did it so the break beat could repeat again and again. With these methods, DJs built new music out of old music. Music makers for years afterward drew inspiration from that idea. A photograph from 2002 shows Grandmaster Flash among DJs at an event. Street dancers sometimes hear their art called break dancing. The first of them used another name. They called the dancing breaking. The names they chose included b-boys. They included b-girls. They included breakers. A 1984 photograph shows b-boys in a competition. Dance battles were common. Two breakers took turns, or two crews did. Each side showed its best moves. The crowd gathered around them judged creativity. The crowd judged skill. Writing or drawings on public property are what graffiti means. By the early 1970s, hip-hop culture had taken graffiti on as an important part. Artists painted buildings. They painted subway cars. They painted trains. They painted bridges. Part of the thrill was simple. Thousands of people would see the art every day. Lady Pink is shown working on a painting. The painting honors women in hip-hop.

5Painting on public property breaks the law. Some people saw the painting as destructive. Inside hip-hop culture, graffiti counted as art. Art galleries around the world soon invited graffiti artists to display what they had made. Museums have preserved graffiti art. Art books have preserved it too. Early hip-hop used the name MC for a rapper. The letters stand for master of ceremonies. While the DJ played, the MC talked to the crowd. Soon the talking turned into rhyme that rode along with the music. Rappers are judged on content. They are judged on flow. They are judged on delivery. Good flow means the spoken lyrics stay on the beat. Good delivery means the words come out clearly. Breathing must not break the flow. Many fans add a fifth pillar. That pillar is knowledge. The other four elements are tied together by knowledge. Greatness requires knowing one's own history. It requires knowing one's own identity. It requires knowing the community's history. It also requires knowing hip-hop's history, values, and ideas. That knowledge helps artists grow. Fresh forms of expression grow out of it. Art can then push for change in society. Women have helped shape the culture since the beginning.

6Sharon Green was one of the first. People treat her as the earliest woman to rap. Her career started as a b-girl. She was fourteen. Skill as an MC came quickly. A record deal in 1979 made her the first woman in rap to sign one. National television in 1981 showed her rap group before any other. Few music producers in any era rank as high as Sylvia Robinson. In 1979 she founded Sugar Hill Records. It was hip-hop's first record company. Some of the most familiar early hip-hop records had her help in production. Among them was hip-hop's first hit across the whole nation. Its title is Rapper's Delight. Outside New York, the wider country met hip-hop because of that record. At the time, hip-hop was mostly unknown outside New York City. A portrait shows Sylvia Robinson. Control of hip-hop music has always sat with men. Unfair treatment has met women artists from the earliest days. MC Lyte used hip-hop to empower herself and other women. Queen Latifah did too. Salt-N-Pepa did too. Lady B did too. Lauryn Hill did too. Rap became their platform for talking about sexism. They spoke about sexism inside hip-hop. They spoke about sexism in popular culture.

7A portrait shows Lauryn Hill. Lolita Shante Gooden was fourteen and already one of the strongest rappers then living. She was known as Roxanne Shante. Her 1984 release carried the title Roxanne's Revenge. Women's experience of sexism was the song's subject. It was a huge success. The next year she reached the finals of a freestyle MC competition. In the final rap battle she was the obvious winner. One judge still marked her down, aiming to make her lose. Years later, the judge told her why. He thought a young girl's win would harm hip-hop's reputation as a serious art form. She lost that battle. Two rap albums still came out under her name. Young women in hip-hop later found a mentor in her. The music began as party music. Even early artists still took up serious issues in their songs. Grandmaster Flash was one of the first. Poverty in New York City is the subject of his song The Message. Public Enemy used music to show Black pride. The group also discussed racism. MC Lyte spoke about racism. She spoke about sexism. She spoke about drug use in her community. In the 1990s, few hip-hop groups were more popular than Public Enemy.

8Gangsta rap, a style of the 1990s, came to dominate hip-hop music. The music industry promoted that style above all others. A record deal was often refused to Black artists whose music sat outside that style. Some listeners found the lyrics offensive. As gangsta rap grew more popular, people outside the culture began to treat all rap as offensive. Many others have seen rap as a form of poetry. Rap and traditional poetry share many elements. Rhythm is one. Rhyming is one. Storytelling is one. Few poets of any era are respected more than Maya Angelou. She worked with some of history's best-known rap artists. She inspired them as well. Rap had a path cleared by spoken-word poetry during the 1960s. Performers recited poetry over a beat. One of those groups was the Last Poets, based in New York City. A bongo drum might carry the beat. Jazz music might carry it. Their poems held important social messages. They held important political messages. Black pride was a subject. Racism was a subject. Poverty was a subject. Justice was a subject. Modern hip-hop often looks back to these poets and to what they wrote.

9A photograph shows the Last Poets. Hip-hop music spread across the country in the mid-1980s and the early 1990s. The culture changed with that spread. Newer artists brought new musical influences. They brought more innovation in style. Local radio stations wanted fresh hip-hop. Club DJs wanted it too. Demand grew. Popularity skyrocketed. Large sums started going from record companies into new hip-hop albums. Cities across the country developed styles of their own. Each style was distinctive. Other kinds of music were folded into hip-hop by newer artists. Sampling was one feature of this era. Sampling means a rapper lifts a piece of an existing song, called a sample, into a new one. Samples came from jazz. They came from blues. They came from rock. Movie sound clips became samples for some artists. Nearly 9,000 miles separate the Bronx from New Zealand. The distance is also 14,484 kilometers. Early in the 1980s, hip-hop music crossed that distance anyway. An eager audience was waiting among the Māori. New Zealand's native Polynesian people are the Māori. Black communities in the South Bronx of the early 1970s had faced a similar bind. Large numbers of Māori lived in communities with limited opportunities.

10Financial struggle was greater. Crime was higher. Access to health care was poor. Access to education was poor. They felt absent from mainstream culture in New Zealand. The music struck them with unusual force. Māori bands took it up as their own musical culture. Upper Hutt Posse was one of those bands. A photograph shows the group. Pictures from around the world catch the culture in motion. Hungary hosts a contest where a b-girl from Japan is dancing. A building in Brazil carries graffiti across its walls. One performer from a duo of Muslim rappers is shown in England. As rap grew more popular worldwide, the wider culture was embraced too. Brazil has break dancing now. Morocco has it. China has it. Graffiti art can be seen across that same span. The starting point was a young girl's street party. The place was the South Bronx. The year was 1973. What began there became a global movement. Scarce resources gave rise to musical inventions that rank among the most creative of the twentieth century. They led to forms of artistic expression just as creative. Hip-hop still influences popular culture worldwide. The mark it leaves is a lasting one.

41. From Samhain Night to Candy Night

1An 1890s picture shows a group of children on Halloween. They hold jack-o-lanterns and use them to frighten an adult away. This book traces a fun and scary holiday from its oldest roots to today. It tells how the Celts kept Samhain and how Halloween got its start. It tells about costumes, trick-or-treating, and jack-o-lanterns. It tells about older customs, the holiday now, crowds, and a blend of old and new. A word list closes the book. Halloween is a colorful holiday, and it is a delicious one. People mark it most in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Ireland. Ireland is the place where it first began. On October 31, people dress in all kinds of costumes. Creepy music oozes from Halloween parties and from haunted houses. Trick-or-treaters pour into the streets in search of candy. Monsters, ghosts, superheroes, and princesses celebrate side by side. People of every age join the night. A 1929 photo from Cincinnati, Ohio, shows three girls in Halloween costumes. A boy in Montebello, California, shops for a costume of his own. Today the holiday is most popular in the United States. There it plays an enormous part in culture and an enormous part in business. Hollywood movies feature Halloween, and popular songs feature it too.

2American stores do big Halloween business. Each year, millions of people buy Halloween candy, costumes, and merchandise. The holiday celebrated now is part of an ancient tradition. It began with the Celtic peoples, a name said KEL-tik. About two thousand years ago they lived in Great Britain, Ireland, and northern France. At Stonehenge, in the south of England, druids of today offer a blessing. Each fall the Celts held a harvest festival called Samhain, a name said SOW-in. Samhain shared some features with our New Year celebrations. It also shared features with Halloween as people keep it now. On the Celtic calendar, October 31 was the final day of the year. The Samhain gathering on that date said farewell to the old year. It closed the harvest season. It helped people prepare for winter. The festival had a supernatural side as well. Celtic tradition said that on Samhain eve the doorways stood open. Those doorways lay between the world of the living and the world of the dead. Spirits of people who had died in the past year could cross into the underworld. The Celts believed the dead could appear during this time. They believed the dead could speak with the living.

3To help the dead on the journey, the Celts lit bonfires. They also sacrificed crops and animals. People believed that priests could see the future during the festival. The predictions made at Samhain were important. They helped families plan for the new year. Later, Christianity spread across Europe. The Catholic Church tried to replace the old Samhain festival with traditions of its own. For example, the Church set All Saints Day on November 1. People also knew that day as All Hallows Day. October 31 is the day before All Hallows. It came to be called All Hallows Eve. In time the name was shortened to Halloween. Hundreds of years later, many older Celtic traditions still lived inside the new holiday. The strongest surviving belief was this one. Supernatural activity was expected on the night of October 31. The Halloween customs known today draw on the Celts. They also draw on the Catholic Church and on legends from medieval Europe. A photo shows Catholic churchgoers walking through a town in Poland on All Saints Day. The custom of costumes has changed many times over the centuries. Halloween dress probably began with the Celts, who dressed as animals at the Samhain bonfires.

4In medieval England the costumes took a new turn. People dressed as supernatural beings in the hope of scaring those beings off. Many walked through towns in fairy costumes, witch costumes, and ghost costumes. This practice was called mumming. Townspeople often gave the mummers food and drink. The gift echoed an older Celtic practice of making sacrifices at Samhain. People believed the offerings satisfied the spirits. The spirits would then leave without causing trouble. Today that custom is known as trick-or-treating. Adults give candy to children. A child who receives a treat will, people hope, move on. The child will not play any malicious tricks. In England, a modern druid wears an animal costume during Samhain. Many people carve jack-o-lanterns every Halloween. A carver cuts a face or a design into a pumpkin. A candle, or some other light, is set inside so the carving glows. Jack-o-lanterns are a newer Halloween custom. They are one of the few customs that did not start with Celtic Samhain. They come from an Irish legend about a man named Stingy Jack. Jack was stingy, and he was cruel as well. He liked to trick his friends. When Jack died, his spirit was forced to wander in the dark.

5The wandering was a punishment for his unpleasant character. To light the way, he cut an opening in a turnip and put a candle inside. For that reason the Irish called him Jack-of-the-lantern. Later they called him a jack-o-lantern. The tale of Stingy Jack began one major Halloween custom. Some people still carve turnips at Halloween. In Ireland and in England, people once placed candles and coals in turnips, beets, and potatoes. They cut frightening faces into those vegetables. The faces copied the terrifying look of Stingy Jack, or they were meant to scare him off. During the 1800s, huge numbers of Irish people moved to North America. They carried the jack-o-lantern custom with them. The use of pumpkins, though, began in the United States. In 1846 an American newspaper story described the practice. A poem published separately in that same year described it too. Both told of people cutting faces into pumpkins and setting a candle within. From there the custom spread. Pumpkins make excellent jack-o-lanterns. They are large enough for elaborate designs of many kinds. They are also plentiful in the fall. For many families today, making a jack-o-lantern and setting it out is a beloved Halloween custom. Several Halloween customs that were once popular are less familiar now.

6A number of them link back to fortune-telling at Samhain, a Celtic custom. That custom lasted for centuries in changing forms. For example, people sometimes played games on Halloween night to guess whom they might marry. Holding a candle, a girl might gaze into a mirror. She hoped to see the face of the husband she would one day have. Even bobbing for apples, a classic party game, began as a way to tell fortunes. Players try to lift an apple from a tub of water. They may use only their mouths. The first person to get an apple out was expected to be the first to marry afterward. Fortune-telling has now dropped out of many Halloween games. A guest might still meet a fortune-teller at a Halloween party or inside a haunted house. A photo from the early 1900s shows children in the United States bobbing for apples at a party. The Halloween people keep today is a fairly recent invention. It is often mixed with ancient customs, especially the Samhain bonfire. That mix is clearest in North America, where the holiday was not widely kept until the 1800s. Many of the first European settlers in the New World frowned on Halloween.

7The Puritans are one example. At best, they saw the night as a silly waste of time, and they urged people not to celebrate it. The holiday grew far more popular when huge numbers of Irish immigrants reached the United States in the 1800s. They brought their traditions along. Jack-o-lanterns arrived with them, and so did mumming. Bit by bit, more Americans began to keep Halloween. As the night grew more popular, pranks and vandalism became common. By the 1930s those pranks were a major problem. Some city governments tried to answer the problem. They tried to reshape Halloween into a holiday for families. They organized trick-or-treating and encouraged children to join. In the 1930s and 1940s, the first trick-or-treaters received cookies and fruit. They also received toys and even small change for a pocket. In the 1950s, candy became a popular treat as trick-or-treating spread. The tiny, separately wrapped candy bars common now did not appear until the 1970s. The treats have changed across the years. The excitement of children has not. In the United States alone, more than 41 million children went trick-or-treating in 2014. Those children were between five and fourteen years old. A chart shows where costume ideas come from.

8Other sources account for 10.1 percent. Pop culture accounts for 13.6 percent. Online sources account for 31.4 percent. Friends or family account for 18.1 percent. Ideas found in a store account for 26.8 percent. More Halloween numbers fill out the picture. In 2013, each person in the United States consumed 4.2 pounds of fresh pumpkin. Among dedicated Halloween fans, 5 percent start shopping before September. In 2015, Halloween spending in the United States totaled 6.89 billion dollars. A photo shows children collecting treats at an organized event. The popularity of Halloween is still rising. Each year, more people celebrate, especially in the United States and Canada. Some cities set up community trick-or-treating at malls, churches, and community centers. Children can gather a large amount of candy in a short time. The events also protect them from traffic in the streets. The crowds are not made of children only. Adults are celebrating in greater numbers too. In 2015, buyers planned to spend more on adult costumes than on costumes for children. Many adults, especially young adults, host Halloween parties or go to them. They dress in costume as well. The night is fun for kids, and adults do not want to miss it. Halloween now looks very different from the celebrations of the 1950s.

9It looks different from the celebrations of the 1800s. It looks different from the Samhain festival of the ancient Celts. The customs keep changing, and they mix what is old with what is new. Bonfires stand beside chocolate bars in the story of the night. Turnips once packed with coal stand beside pumpkins lit by candles. Halloween is a holiday that changes as the times change. It offers fun and entertainment for one spooky night each year. Today it is rich with customs from several cultures. People of every age can enjoy those customs. A photo from 1898 shows two girls in the United States dressed for Halloween. A whole industry now surrounds Halloween candy, costumes, and supplies for parties. A survey taken in 2015 produced a startling figure. Shoppers getting ready for the holiday were asked about candy. Of that group, 93.7 percent said they intended to purchase sweets for the night. Those shoppers planned to spend 2.1 billion dollars on candy by itself. They also planned about 28 dollars per household for costumes. Many even planned costumes for their pets. Among people keeping the holiday, 44.8 percent planned to decorate their yards. Another share, 31.5 percent of consumers, planned to host a party or to attend one.

10The average amount spent by people celebrating was 74.34 dollars. The National Retail Federation reported these plans for 2015. Celtic describes the peoples of ancient Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and western Europe, or things linked to them. Pranks are tricks, or jokes played in a practical way. Predictions are guesses about events that might come later. Consumers are people who buy or rent goods or services and then use them. Puritans belonged to a British Protestant group that opposed the Church of England. They came to North America because they sought freedom for their religion. Immigrants are people who move into a new country in order to settle. Supernatural means outside what the laws of nature can explain, and the word often touches religion. Malicious means full of hate and ready to do harm. Medieval describes the Middle Ages, the stretch of European history from the year 500 to the year 1500. A tradition is a belief or a custom handed down year by year and generation by generation. Merchandise means goods that people buy or sell. In some myths, the underworld is the place where the souls of the dead go.

42. From Trading Goods to Spending Money

1Inside: a beginning. Trading goods directly. Currency. Coins. Money printed on paper. What gives money its worth. How money stays genuine. Money you cannot see: checks and credit cards. A closing word. Words to know. A picture makes a point. A bill is worth far more than the sheet it is printed on. A beginning Plain paper has little worth. Paper that is money may equal thousands of dollars. One check may stand for millions of dollars. Every printed bill is worth far more than its paper. The reason is not obvious. People ask where money came from. They ask what makes it so valuable. Money has value because the people who create it and the people who use it agree on that value. The government that issues it agrees. The mint that strikes coins or prints bills agrees. The banks that hold it agree. Shoppers and sellers agree as well. All of them treat money as worth something. The story of money is a fascinating one. People once traded objects that were valuable in themselves. Later they traded objects that stood for those valuables. Technology added another step. It made invisible money. With that money, people can trade goods and materials all over the world. Trading without coins Thousands of years ago, people bartered. They swapped goods in a direct trade. Families near the ocean had fish. They also had salt. Families near the mountains had fruits. They had wood. They had furs. The two groups traded. Barter still happens. Swap the apple in your lunch for another person's candy bar, and you are bartering.

2Barter has problems. You may want someone's goods. That person may not want yours. Many goods are heavy. Many are hard to carry. Many do not last. A picture explains two ideas. Barter let people obtain products they could not make or gather alone. Currency let people trade value without hauling the goods themselves. Currency People invented currency to escape the troubles of barter. Currency means objects that stand for set values. A community might agree that one cow equaled twenty shells. A large fish might equal two shells. Goods could be swapped for currency. Currency could be swapped for goods. Each culture picked its own object to stand for what its goods were worth. The chosen objects were nearly always light enough to carry. They were also rare. People could not simply gather them from the ground. Greater rarity raised the value. So did the extra work of finding the object. Ancient currency took many forms. People used stones that were bright or full of color. They used shells, leaves, and feathers. They used lumps of silver and of gold. They used salt, spices, and gems. Pay for soldiers in ancient Rome came as sacks of salt. Traders from Africa all the way to Asia used rare shells with speckles. Only a handful of islands produced those speckled shells. The ocean they come from is the Indian Ocean. Among Native Americans, some groups used wampum. Wampum is beads made from clam shells. They used it in trade and in treaties. Other Native Americans used feathers from eagles. People in China used bundles of tea leaves.

3Colonists from Europe, living in North America, used leaves of tobacco. This kind of currency was hard to price. A shell much larger than another shell might seem to deserve a higher value. You might also meet someone who thought your shells had no value at all. One fact stands out. No currency anywhere is larger than the one the Yap Islanders use. They live on an island near the equator, close to Indonesia. Their coins are giant stones. A stone can weigh as much as a full-grown Asian elephant. Each stone has a hole. People push a stick through the hole and roll the coin along. Older coins of another kind were stamped with a picture of the king. Coins Ordinary objects made poor currency. One answer was coins struck from metals that are precious. Those metals are rare. Cultures widely treat them as valuable. They are easy to shape and easy to weigh. The first coins were minted, which means produced, 2,600 years ago. The place was Lydia. Today that land sits inside Turkey. Coins then spread quickly from Lydia into nearby Greece. They also spread into Persia, the land now called Iran. The oldest coins were hammered from electrum. Electrum is a natural mix of gold and silver. Those coins were rough and crude. The sides had no patterns. Sizes were not standard. Weights were not standard. Later coins used pure gold, or they used pure silver. Weights became standard. A seal of the king was stamped on one side. The seal confirmed the coin's quality. On many early European coins, one face showed the head of a god.

4The other side carried a seal from the maker. Later coins showed the heads of kings and of rulers. The reverse side carried elaborate symbols. Those pictures helped people tell when a coin was made. They showed where it was made. They showed who made it. Look at modern coins and you can still see faces. Presidents appear. Kings appear. Queens appear. Greek coins carried words. They showed an owl. Athena, a goddess, appeared in a portrait on them. Workers in China melted copper. They poured it into molds. It hardened into coins. A hole went through the center. Thousands of coins could ride on a ribbon. They could ride on a stick. These coins were called cash. They did not use pictures. Words stated the worth, which is the denomination. Only the government was allowed to produce the coins. A string or a stick made Chinese cash easy to carry. How coins are made Coins are harder to produce than they look. After a government decides on new coins, many steps follow. A designer draws both faces of the coin on a large sheet of paper. Sculptors build a large model with depth, not a flat drawing. An engraving machine reads that model and cuts a die. The die is the stamp for the coin. Dies go to mints. A mint is a factory that produces coins. At the mint, blank coins called blanks are cut from a rolled sheet of the proper metal. Laid out, the metal sheet could match five football fields placed end to end.

5The blanks are heated. They are cooled. They are washed. They are dried. The raised rim is formed by a machine known as an upsetting mill. A coin press pushes the die's pattern into the coin. Inspectors look for mistakes. Coins made wrong are melted. The metal is recycled. Armored trucks carry the finished coins out to banks. Money on paper A man in China named Ts'ai Lun invented paper. That was 1,900 years ago. Paper was not money yet. Seven hundred years passed. Then the government in China ran out of copper for coins. Officials turned to printing money on paper. The earliest bills were printed by hand. Wooden blocks covered with ink were pressed onto paper rectangles of one set size. Coins were still around. The lighter paper money grew popular faster. A picture shows early paper money from China. In Europe, a different invention changed money's form. Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press that used movable type. The time was the middle of the 1400s. His press let people print paper money with a machine. Hand printing was no longer the only way. What a bill is worth A coin of gold or of silver has value as metal. Paper money, by itself, is worth very little. Printing one bill costs only four cents in U.S. money. That price covers the paper. It covers the ink. It covers the pay of the person who runs the printer. So why can one sheet be worth a hundred dollars? Why can another be worth only one dollar?

6The government says so. A century ago, the rule was different. For every dollar moving in circulation, the government stored matching gold in a bank. People called this the gold standard. Each dollar stood for its face value in gold. Face value is the number printed on the bill. In those days you could take dollars to the bank and receive the same amount in gold. Banks once stored bars of gold. Those bars stood for the total of everyone's money. Crossing from one country to another has become easy. Changing one nation's money into another's, every time you travel, can be a bother. Most nations of Europe came together as the European Union. A large share of them made their money match, so the euro has the same worth in each of those nations. Each country mints its own euros. The tail side carries a picture. That picture stands for the country that made the coin. Most countries have given up the gold standard. Too many bills are in circulation. The bills stand for more wealth, more goods, and more valuables than all the gold on Earth. Britain left the gold standard in 1931. The United States left it forty years after that. Today a government counts the goods and resources inside the country. It sends out enough money to stand for those goods and resources. A country's money can rise in value next to other currencies. It can also fall. How much the country produces in goods matters to that change. The stock of resources matters too. It depends on how well its businesses do.

7People call this arrangement a floating system for currency. How money stays real Many people agree that only a government should make currency. The government is the one that tracks the real goods and resources behind it. What if private people try to make money themselves? Fake money is called counterfeit. It is worth nothing. No goods or resources stand behind it. Banks will not take it. Stores will not take it. Restaurants will not take it. Companies will not take it. Worse, counterfeit money in circulation damages the value of real money. If fakes are around, you cannot be sure your own money is genuine. Feel can give the secret away. Set a dollar bill beside plain writing paper. Add construction paper. Add cloth. Add tissue paper. Cut each one to the bill's size and shape. Shut your eyes and the real bill feels different. Cashiers who handle piles of money can tell a genuine bill from a fake by touch alone. Bank tellers can do the same. Countries fight counterfeiters with tricks that are hard to copy. Bills use paper made from a secret formula. Cloth in a U.S. dollar is mostly cotton, about three quarters of the sheet. Linen makes up about one quarter. Red fibers and blue fibers are scattered through it. The government keeps the exact recipe secret. A famous maker of soda guards a drink recipe in the same way. A special thread sits below the portrait. It glows under ultraviolet light. Another name for that light is black light. A special pen is used at banks.

8Some stores use it too. On real money the ink shifts from black to yellow. On fake money the ink stays black. The pictures and the printing are planned so that copying is difficult. The portrait is large. It is full of detail. It sits a little off center. Very thin dashed lines build the face. Designs printed on the bill stay tiny. They are also complicated. A serial number on each bill shows when it was printed. The number also shows where. Many bills add colored inks. They add magnetic inks. They add inks that change color when you tilt the bill. Some bills carry holograms. Some carry watermarks. The hidden picture appears if light shines through the bill. Money you cannot hold as cash Most adults have a checking account. The bank records how much that person has saved. The person writes checks. A check is an official note that stands for a set amount. One sheet of paper can stand for a large sum. Many of these accounts also come with a debit card. The card can pull cash from the account at an ATM. It can pay at shops. It can pay at restaurants. A credit card works like a debit card in the hand. It also works like a checking account at the shop. The difference is borrowing. The person is not spending saved money. The bank lends the money. People use credit cards for purchases that cost more than the bank balance. Later they must repay the sum. They also pay a fee called interest.

9Wait a long time to repay, and the interest grows. An automatic teller machine, or ATM, lets people take cash from an account at any hour. A picture shows debit cards and credit cards. Both kinds of card are made of durable plastic. One side is stamped with the person's name. An individual number is stamped there too. So is the name of the bank that holds the account. A magnetic strip along the top stores encoded information about that account. Swipe the card through a reading machine. The machine calls the bank by electronic signal. It asks whether the account holds enough money. When the balance is large enough, the price leaves that person's account. It moves to the account of the store, the restaurant, or the company. One piece of plastic is easier to carry than a stack of bills. The card also bears your name and your information. Stealing that money is harder than stealing bills. Credit cards still hold a danger. People forget that borrowed money must be paid back. Some users act in an irresponsible way. They owe the banks so much that the banks take back the things that were bought. That taking back is called repossession. A plastic card is less visible than cash. It still buys the same goods. Invisible money lets us exchange goods with partners in far countries. Catalogs help. So does the Internet. A credit card can buy goods from a person in another country. It can buy from a company there. Your money is changed, on its own, into a currency that the seller can use.

10A purchase on the Internet, paid by credit card, can move money over an ocean at once. A closing word Go back three thousand years and a person swapped one good directly for a different good. Today they trade with bills. They trade with coins. They trade with invisible money. What kind of money might exist after another three thousand years is still an open question. A picture shows a stock market. People there buy stock. They also sell it. A stock is a piece of a company. The price rises or falls with the company's value. Until that stock is sold, the money inside it is not real money yet. Words to know Barter: to swap goods or services and not use money. Durable: sturdy, and able to last a long time. Encoded: written in a special code. Cash: a common name for paper money. In Chinese, the word also named ancient coins. Floating currency: money whose value comes from the free market. It is not tied to the gold standard. Circulation: the state of being in use, passing from person to person. Counterfeit: a fake, above all of money, built so people mistake it for genuine money. Holograms: special images that look as if they have depth. Mint: a place where coins are made. Currency: money people accept, in whatever form, standing in for goods and for resources. Watermarks: special pictures in paper, including money paper, that show when the sheet is held up to light. Denomination: the face value of one kind of currency.

43. Helping Wild Animals Heal

1A picture shows the Tucson Wildlife Center. The book opens with an introduction. Wildlife rehabilitators come next. Rescue comes next. Rehabilitation comes next. Release comes next. Disaster rescue comes next. A closing follows. A glossary follows. An index ends the book. A wild animal in trouble should be reported to an adult at once. If no trusted adult is nearby, use a phone book. Look up Wildlife Rescue. Animal Rescue is another heading to try. A baby bird hops on the ground. No parent is in sight. What action fits a baby bird that seems orphaned? What if a rabbit cannot seem to hop? What if a raccoon sways from side to side while walking? Many people do not know the right action. They also do not know the action to avoid. Danger may be real for the animal. Specially trained people do know. Wildlife is their care. A raccoon like that should be left alone. Sickness is the likely cause. They can judge whether the rabbit can be helped. They can judge whether a return to the wild is possible. The baby bird can be looked at. The right care, if any is needed, is something they know. You can learn how to help from them too. Topsy is a great horned owl, and she is female. Her age is three months. A fall from the nest brought rescuers. A windstorm caused the fall. Her neck is healing. Her back is healing. Helpers of wildlife have a title. Sick animals are in their care. Injured animals are in their care. Orphaned animals are in their care. Wildlife rehabilitators is the title. Rehabbers is the short name. Rehabilitate means to bring health back. It means to restore the animal. Wild animals are rescued by these rehabbers. Care continues while healing happens. A return to the wild follows recovery, whenever that return is possible. Special training is required. Care is part of the training.

2Feeding is part of it. Housing is part of it. Illness can be treated by many rehabbers. Injury can be treated by many. Safe handling is part of the skill. The animal must not be hurt. The person must not be hurt. A picture shows caretakers with a sea turtle. The right flipper is the injured part they treat. Lisa, a rehabber, treats Tripod. Tripod is a young javelina. A car was what hit him. Need for rehabbers grows as people move into wild land. Farms take land where wild animals lived. Houses take that land. Businesses take that land. Animal homes are destroyed. Food sources are destroyed. Invaded habitats put animals at greater risk. Orphaning grows more likely. Injury grows more likely. Death grows more likely. Most wildlife injuries come from people and what people do. Vehicles, including cars, strike animals. Animals strike objects, and windows are one example. Poisoning causes harm. Hunting that is illegal causes harm. Litter causes harm. Pollution causes harm. Other animals attack and cause harm. Variety is the work of some rehabbers. Mammals are included. Birds are included. Reptiles are included. A single group is the focus of others. Owls may be that group. Bats may be that group. Ocean animals may be that group. Urban wildlife is a common patient. These animals live in cities or in towns. Squirrels are one kind. Raccoons are one kind. Foxes are one kind. Dangerous animals are the work of some brave rehabbers. Bears are included. Mountain lions are included. Bobcats are included. A Florida state wildlife worker appears in a picture. A panther kitten is being examined. The path into this work often starts with volunteering. Teachers are people who already hold special wildlife training. Homes of rehabbers are classrooms. Backyards are classrooms. Wildlife centers are classrooms. Pay does not come to volunteers. Pay does not come to most rehabbers either.

3Personal money is often spent. Food is bought. Medicine is bought. Shelters are bought. Care for wildlife is the motive. Health for the animals is the wish. A wider good is also seen. Healthy habitats follow proper care of wild animals. Illness in people can be prevented. Injury to people can be prevented. A baby red-tailed hawk is held by a volunteer. A bandage comes off in a rehabber's hands. A broken leg was the injury. A fall from the nest was the cause. Need for rescue is not always obvious. Two rules always apply. Do not touch the animal. Call an adult at once. The adult can phone a wildlife rehabber. Wildlife rescue is that person's training. You can watch from a safe spot. Note where the animal hides. Rescuers can then find it quickly. A box can shield a small injured animal. A laundry basket can do the same. Place it over the animal. Predators are kept off until help comes. A rescuer appears in a picture with a koala. Water is given to a koala saved from a fire. Certain behaviors mean stay away. They are clues. Sickness may be present. Danger may be present. A bat on the ground is a reason to stay away. A wild animal that seems tame is a reason to stay away. Too much drool is a reason to stay away. Foam around the mouth is a reason to stay away. An animal that cannot move is a reason to stay away. Extreme anger in the animal's look is a reason to stay back. Nocturnal animals are active at night in normal life. Daytime activity in such an animal is a reason to stay away. The warning is strongest for a raccoon. It is strong for a skunk. It is strong for an opossum. It is strong for a fox. It is strong for a bat. Animal safety comes before anything else.

4Wrong holding can injure a hurt, frightened animal. Death can follow. The wrong cage can injure an animal. Death can follow. Wire cages can break a wild bird's bones. Feathers can be damaged. Escape attempts are the cause. Human scent on a baby can make parents refuse care. Mammals face this risk more than birds do. Smell is stronger in mammals. People need safety too. Pain can make an injured wild animal afraid. A bite may follow. A kick may follow. A scratch, a peck, or a stab may follow. Defense is the animal's goal. Help is not what the animal understands. Disease may live in wild animals. Humans can catch it. Pets can catch it. Rabies is more likely in some species than in others. Bats are on that list. Coyotes are on it. Raccoons are on it. Foxes are on it. Skunks are on it. Rabies kills. Every warm-blooded animal can catch it. Humans can catch it. Treatment must come at once after possible exposure. Homes lose many baby animals that were never in danger. A hopping baby bird may still have parents. Fledgling is the word for a young bird learning flight. Ground hopping is practice before flight. Parents usually watch from far off. You may not see them. Baby rabbits are sometimes "rescued" with no need. Seals are sometimes taken the same way. Fawns are sometimes taken the same way. Quiet rest is normal for these babies. A beach may be the resting place. Grass may be the resting place. Mothers eat nearby. Only trained people can judge the need for human help. The training covers how these animals naturally live. Removal hurts survival if help was not needed. A wound is the reason a baby needs rescue. No wound means no rescue. Taking a wild animal home feels like help to many people. That belief is wrong. Love of wildlife is not the same as skill to care for it.

5Dogs and cats need far less training. Wild animals need much more. The law also forbids taking them home. Picture yourself hurt in an accident. Would any stranger be the right person to take you home? No. A trained professional is the right person. A doctor is one. A nurse is one. A clean place is also needed. The right equipment should be there. The right medicine should be there. Wild animals deserve that same best care. A red panda is examined by veterinarians in a picture. Spring is wildlife rescue's busiest season. Births happen in spring. Babies are weaker then. Survival alone is often impossible. A car that hits the mother can orphan a baby. A hunter can kill the parents. A predator can kill the parents. A checkup is the first step at a rehabilitation center. First aid comes with it. Quarantine follows for the newly rescued. A cage of their own is the place. Sickness then cannot jump to other animals by contact. Notes on each animal are kept in detail. Improvement can be seen in the notes. Medicine times are recorded. Feeding times are recorded. Problems differ widely. Broken bones must be handled before other care. Disease must be handled before other care. Veterinarians do that work. The rehabilitation center comes after, for getting better. Igor is a black vulture. Birdseed was his food. Meat was what his health needed. Bones grew fragile. They broke while he was being rescued. Warmth is a special need of baby animals. An incubator can provide it. Hot-water bottles can go in the cage. Heating pads can go in. Lightbulbs can go in. Extra care is common for the young and injured, so healing can happen. An adult animal may share space once the young one grows stronger. Useful behaviors are shown by the adult. Hunting for food is shown.

6Healing may happen in one place. Recovery may happen in another. One example is a hawk whose wing has broken. A small dark cage may be needed first. Calm helps the start of healing. A flight cage comes after the bone heals. This outdoor space lets the bird exercise. Flight can be learned again. Practice continues in the flight cage. Release waits until healing is enough. Fear of people is normal in most wild animals. Stress rises when home is far away. Stress that grows too high can kill. Contact with people is limited by center workers. Noise is kept low. Towels cover cages. Staring is avoided. In the wild, a stare means a hunt has begun. A puppet can stand in as a mother. One young condor has a puppet for that role. Humans then do not become too familiar. Imprinting on mothers happens early for baby animals. Each day a duckling watches its mother and learns that a duck is what it is. Baby birds get special care from rehabbers. Imprinting on people is blocked. Otherwise the bird grows up believing it is human. Humans, not its own kind, become what it seeks. Raptors are birds of prey. Danger in the wild can follow if they imprint on people. Other birds face that danger too. A hiker may be approached for attention. The hiker may not know the bird expects human contact. Hurt can come to the hiker. Hurt can come to the bird. Return to the wild is often impossible for that reason. Meat is required for meat-eating animals at these centers. Healing depends on it. Strength depends on it. Roadkill is one food source. These are animals just struck by cars or trucks. Mousecicles fill freezers. A mousecicle is a frozen mouse kept as food. Raising food animals saves money at some centers. Quail are raised. Mice are raised. Rats are raised.

7Rabbits are raised. An adult red-tailed hawk receives a mouse from a volunteer. Blindness is almost complete in that hawk. Food must resemble what the animal would eat in nature. Sickness can come from the wrong food. Growth can be thrown off. Store-bought cow's milk is one danger. Many baby animals are badly harmed by it. Death can follow. Natural foods are required for rescued animals. Later survival in the wild depends on that diet. Orphans raised at a center need natural food most of all. A taste for human food may develop. Finding their own food may never be learned. Starvation in the wild may follow. Release back to the wild requires a place. Rehabbers must choose it. The search starts early. Readiness of the animal is not required yet. Food must be plentiful. Water must be there. Shelter must be there. Human contact must be avoidable. Health must be strong enough. Running, climbing, or flying must be possible without trouble. Sight must work. Hearing must work. Food must be findable. Predators must be avoidable. Company of the same kind of animal must be possible. A Tasmanian devil appears in a picture. An exam comes before release. First the animal moves outdoors into a pen, or into a cage. Animals of the same kind share it. Weather becomes familiar outdoors. People become less frequent. Time outdoors at the center leads to release. Young animals, especially orphans, often get a slow release. A pen is set in a safe wild place. The door stays open. Return to the pen is possible. Food is supplied until the animal clearly feeds itself. Adults rescued as adults often get a fast release. Life on their own in nature is already known. A release spot is chosen. Near the finding place is best. Then they are freed. A bald eagle is released in a picture. The rehabber has company as the eagle flies.

8About half the animals at these centers never go back. Sickness is too severe. Injury is too severe. Limbs may be gone. Beaks may be gone. Wings may be gone. Eyesight may be gone. Poor healing in a wing means the bird cannot fly in the wild. Hunting there would fail too. A single eye leaves the same problem. Survival in the wild may be clearly impossible. Survival even at the center may be impossible. A hard choice follows for rehabbers. Pain can make euthanasia the kindest path. The killing is quick. The killing is painless. Suffering ends. An adult female great horned owl appears in a picture. A wing injury keeps her flight noisy. Prey hears her coming. Release can never happen. People are not the only cause of wildlife injury. Natural disasters injure animals too. Wildfires are one. Hurricanes are one. Terri Crisp gives much of her time to this work. Animals hurt by natural disasters are her rescues. A California wildfire raged in 1986. A Shetland pony was saved. She coaxed it into a car. Sea otters were part of her 1989 work. Loons were part of it. The setting was Alaska's Exxon Valdez oil spill. Hundreds of animals were her 1992 work. Hurricane Andrew had hurt them. Noah's Wish is the group she started. Volunteers are trained there. Natural disasters are the danger they answer. A picture shows Terri Crisp with an animal she saved. Earthquakes are among the disasters. Fires are among them. Floods, hurricanes, oil spills, and tornadoes are among them. A huge wave was coming, and many wild animals seemed to know. They ran inland before the Asian tsunami of 2004 reached land. Pets did not fare as well. Farm animals did not fare as well. Working farm animals supported many people in the struck areas. Large numbers were killed. Many more were hurt. Many were left where food was gone.

9The Humane Society International helps those animals. Other groups help too. People who care for the animals are helped as well. Lives are steered back on track. A man appears in a picture from December 2004, after the tsunami. His daughter is in his arms. His dog is with them. Safety is where they are going. Animals that cannot return to the wild still have a job for many rehabbers. Ambassador is the role. Respect for wildlife is the lesson. Local wildlife is what children learn. Adults learn it too. Respect for the land is part of the lesson. Food and shelter can then remain for wild animals. Important work is what rehabbers do. Injured wild animals receive care. Many go back to the wild. You can support that work. Respect wildlife. Phone a rehabber when an animal is in trouble. One call can open a chance. Growing up becomes possible. A free and healthy life becomes possible. A bird of prey appears in a picture as an ambassador. Children learn about animals of their own area. Glossary An ambassador represents a country, a species, or a cause. Coaxing means gentle persuasion that convinces. A fledgling is a young bird still learning flight. A habitat is the natural setting of a plant or an animal. An incubator is a closed space that keeps a baby animal warm. Orphaned means parents are gone. Predators hunt other animals and eat them. Quarantined means kept apart so disease cannot spread. Urban means in a city or town, or near one. Veterinarians are doctors for animals that are not human. They treat illness and injury. Volunteers help or do a service and are not paid. Index Volunteers, and the shorter word volunteer, connect to the numbers 8, 16, and 20. Veterinarians, and the shorter word veterinarian, connect to the numbers 12 and 13. Hurricane Andrew connects to the number 20. Urban wildlife connects to the number 7.

10The Humane Society International connects to the number 21. The tsunami connects to the number 21. Food, and the word foods, connects to the numbers 6, 8, 16 through 18, 21, and 22. Training connects to the numbers 5, 8, and 12. Flight cage connects to the number 14. Substitute parents connect to the numbers 14 and 15. Fast release connects to the number 18. Spring connects to the number 12. The Exxon Valdez oil spill connects to the number 20. Slow release connects to the number 18. Disease, and the word diseases, connects to the numbers 4, 10, and 13. Rules for children connect to the numbers 4 and 9. Respecting wildlife connects to the number 22. Dangerous animals connect to the numbers 4, 7, 9, and 15. Recover connects to the numbers 5, 13, and 14. Terri Crisp connects to the number 20. Release connects to the numbers 5, 16 through 19, and 22. Rehabbers connect to the numbers 5 through 9, 13 through 19, and 22. Contact with humans connects to the numbers 15, 17, and 18. Rabies connects to the numbers 4 and 10. Predators, and the shorter word predator, connect to the numbers 9, 12, and 17. Causes of injury connect to the number 6. Care connects to 4 and to 5. Also to 7. Also to 8. Also to 10. Also to 12. Also to 15. Also to 21. Orphaned connects to the numbers 4 through 6, 11, 12, and 16. Animals that cannot be released connect to the number 19. Baby, and the word babies, connects to the numbers 4, 6, 8, 10 through 12, and 14 through 16. Money connects to the numbers 8 and 16. Animal housing connects to the numbers 5, 8, and 13 through 15. Imprinting connects to the number 15. The Asian tsunami of 2004 connects to the number 21.

44. Hidden Tombs of Egypt's Golden Age

1A map of Egypt marks the Mediterranean Sea, Cairo, Memphis, and the Nile River. It also marks Luxor, once called Thebes, and the Red Sea. Coming pages open on treasure past imagining. They enter a valley of kings. They explain the afterlife. They explain how tombs were built. They move into modern times. They look toward treasure still ahead. Useful words close the book. A photo shows Howard Carter on the left. In November 1922, this British archaeologist found a tomb. The king inside was Tutankhamen, said toot-an-KAH-muhn. The find sat in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Explorers had believed that valley was played out. Better still, the royal seal was still intact. No earlier royal tomb had been found that way. Objects inside numbered more than five thousand. Solid gold made many of them. The golden funeral mask of Tutankhamen became one of Egypt's most famous treasures. Pharaohs buried here outranked him in importance. His tomb was also among the smallest ones. Only four small chambers made it up. The objects were still so many that listing continues. Experts are nearly a century past Carter's discovery, and the list is unfinished.
