2The photo shows that small tomb, four rooms packed with objects beyond price. A tomb map uses KV numbers. KV 62 is Tutankhamen. KV 9 is Ramses IV. Several tombs stay off this map. Some lie farther west. KV 57 is Horemheb. KV 17 is Seti I. KV can stand for the valley itself. Almost every pharaoh of Egypt's golden age has a tomb in this valley. That age is the New Kingdom. Three dynasties ruled then. They were the Eighteenth, the Nineteenth, and the Twentieth. The years run from 1550 to 1080 bc. Thebes, the city now called Luxor, was the capital. It was also the religious center. Temples there honored the empire's pharaohs. Egyptians believed those rulers joined the gods after death. A royal tomb still needed a hidden place. Across the Nile, steep-sided valleys linked together. That network was the right place. Limestone there could be carved into tombs. Steep cliffs helped guards. A single way in helped them too. Robbers were harder to keep out anywhere else. A photo shows Carter at the coffins. He is lifting a covering from the third coffin, the one farthest inside.

3For ancient Egyptians, a pharaoh's tomb mattered for a clear reason. It gave safe passage into the afterlife. The physical body needed protection. People then believed that body could live again after burial. After death, mummification lasted seventy days. The goal was to stop the body from breaking down. Priests took out the inner organs. They mummified those organs. A stone box received them. Nested coffins then held the mummified body. A stone sarcophagus held the coffins. Solid stone formed the sarcophagus. Its weight could reach 9 metric tons (10 T). The tomb had another duty. It guarded the pharaoh's spirit on a trip through the underworld. Priests set protective amulets inside the wrappings. They believed those amulets held powers. Walls and ceilings of a tomb carried spells and prayers. The sarcophagus often carried them too. Long columns held the hieroglyphs and the images. Some writings aimed to bring the body back to life. Others aimed to scare demons away. A soul on its way to the afterlife might need facts. Hieroglyphs supplied those facts. Ancient Egyptians believed the king's soul had a companion.

4The companion was Ra, the Sun god, and the road was the underworld. Wall writings told how the Sun god moved through that dark world. They warned of dangers the soul would meet. Demon-guarded gates were one challenge. Another test was the questioning inside the Hall of Judgment. The writings told how to get past both. A photo shows tomb entrances. Ra's many names appear there, with prayers, images, and hieroglyphs. A royal tomb also stocked whatever a king might need after death. Storerooms held wooden models of gear. Boats were among the models. Chariots were among them. Personal things were stored too. Makeup was one. Clothing was one. Board games were one. Everyday things were stored. Furniture was one. Lamps were one. Treasure was there to enjoy. Expensive gems were part of it. Golden jewelry was part of it. Artwork was part of it. Food was packed. Drink was packed. Carved figures called shabtis filled the tombs by the hundreds. Say shabtis as SHAB-teez. Answerers is the other name. A spell was carved on each shabti. The spell would wake it to serve its master.

5Tutankhamen went into the grave with 413 of these figures. The little statues are wood or stone. They tell us a great deal about what ancient Egyptians believed. A diagram compares tomb layouts. Early tombs bent left once, or more than once. Later tombs ran without a turn. Experts think the change had a purpose. Workers would be less likely to cut into an older tomb by accident. Chambers that many tombs share have names. A is the entrance. B is the passage of Ra. C is the hall of hindering, and a deep well sits in it. D is the chariot hall. Sets of pillars stand there. Chariots themselves have never turned up in that hall. E is the burial chamber. The diagram also contrasts an early design with a later one. Most layouts in this royal valley match one another. An entryway leads to a hall. Egyptians called that hall the passage of Ra. Images there show forms of the Sun god. A deep well is cut through the floor of one room in many tombs. Some experts see the pit as a delay for robbers.

6Some see it as protection if a flood came. Every tomb ended in the burial room. Storerooms often opened off that room, filled with supplies. Similar as they are, no two tombs here are the same. Each one followed the taste of the ruler then in power. That freedom had a limit. Builders started while the king was still alive. Years were needed to finish. Death changed the clock. Only seventy days remained. Mummification would be done then, and burial had to happen. An unfinished tomb forced shortcuts. Paintings might be left half done. Rooms might be left half done. At times the king was buried somewhere else. The tomb he had been building was not the one that held him. Time changed how the valley tombs looked. It changed their layouts too. Early tombs of the New Kingdom were usually the smaller ones. Later tombs were larger. Early tombs usually bent. One turn of ninety degrees was common. Two such turns were common too. Later tombs were straighter. Experts suspect a reason. The valley was growing crowded. A straight dig was less likely to strike a neighbor's tomb.

7Where tombs sat also changed. Older ones usually lay at the bottoms of cliffs. Rain would wash water and earth down over the entrance. Later rulers usually set entrances on slopes that lay lower. A note on Ramses IX tells a rushed story. Experts think death found Ramses IX with only two corridors complete. Workers finished the others afterward. The workmanship looks hurried. Tomb work, experts think, began almost as soon as a new king started to rule. Picking the spot was the important first step. High officials of the court did that picking. Senior workmen did it with them. A bad choice meant they had to stop. A new spot had to be chosen. More than once, cutting had already started when the first spot was abandoned. Limestone bedrock had to receive the tomb directly. Crews began by digging rough passages. Their tools were chisels of copper or bronze. They used wooden mallets. They used hand axes whose blades were stone. A painted line went on the ceiling. That line was the reference for measuring. Walls, ceiling, and floor were built to it. Much of our knowledge comes from writings left behind.

8The writings are from Dier al-Medina. That village stood near the valley. The workers lived there. A photo of Horemheb's unfinished tomb shows early marks and fixes. Red ink is the scribe's outline. A relief is part of the wall. Black ink is the supervisor's correction. Decoration started once the cutting had gone far enough. Plasterers spread white plaster over the surfaces. Scribes drew hieroglyphs. They drew figures. A supervisor came behind them and corrected the sketches. Artists then made the art final. They painted blocks of color. They filled in details. At times, workers cut away parts of a scene. Certain shapes would stand out. Cutting away the background produced raised relief. Details were carved into those raised figures. Paint went on after the carving. Modern care of the valley has its own story. In 1979, the United Nations listed the Valley of the Kings. It was among the first World Heritage sites. Yearly visits to the tombs pass one million. Eighteen tombs open to the public. The set of open tombs rotates. One entry ticket lets a visitor choose three tombs from those that are open.

9Tutankhamen's tomb is the exception. Seeing it takes an extra ticket. Objects first found in his tomb now stay in the Cairo museum. Crowds that never stop have hurt the tombs. Temperature inside shifts quickly. Humidity shifts quickly. Mold now grows on some walls. A hand that touches a wall by accident can harm old paint. It can harm old carvings. The rotating list lets tombs rest from visitors now and then. Repair teams use that quiet time. Visitors are urged to plan before they come. They should choose their tombs ahead of the walk. Tutankhamen's golden funeral mask has traveled to museums around the world. It now stays with every treasure from his tomb. The Cairo museum holds them. Known tombs in the valley today number sixty-three. More than one tomb from the New Kingdom is still missing. Ramses VIII has not been found. Thutmose II has not been found. Several queens of the Eighteenth Dynasty have not been found. Several princes of that dynasty have not been found. This valley is the likely place where those rulers were buried. Archaeological sites rarely rank richer than the Valley of the Kings.

10Experts believe more treasure is still hidden. Afterlife means the life that follows death, once the physical body is gone. Humidity measures moisture held in the air. An archaeologist is a scientist. The subject is remains of ancient cultures. Limestone is a sedimentary rock. It formed from remains of marine organisms. A chamber is a room or another closed space. It may be natural. It may be made by people. Mummification is a way of preserving a dead body. Ancient Egypt practiced it. Chariots were carriages pulled by horses. They had two wheels. Ancient people used them, usually to race or to fight. Pharaohs were the kings of ancient Egypt. A sarcophagus is a coffin or tomb of stone from ancient times. Writing often covers it. Rich ornament often covers it. Dynasties are lines of rulers in one country. The rulers come from the same family. Scribes copy texts by hand. They also record information in writing. They are writers. Hieroglyphs are pictures and symbols that serve as writing. Ancient Egypt is where that system is best known.

45. Hispanic Americans Who Shaped a Nation

1An introduction opens the book. Dolores Huerta comes next, then Lin-Manuel Miranda. Selena Quintanilla-Pérez follows, then Roberto Clemente. Sammy Davis Jr. has a part. Antonia Coello Novello has a part. Ellen Ochoa and Oscar de la Renta follow. Frank Romero and Sonia Sotomayor follow them. A conclusion and a glossary close the book. Immigrants have always helped make the United States special. People were arriving in the early 1600s, before the land was a country. Freedom was what they sought. Opportunity was what they sought. Native peoples lost both freedom and opportunity in that arrival. England sent some of the early colonists. Spain sent some. Other European countries sent some. Today, Hispanic Americans are among the fastest-growing immigrant groups in the United States. The U.S. Census Bureau is the source of that fact. Home countries include Mexico. They include Central America and South America. The Caribbean is included. Spain is included. Population in the United States is about 331 million. The Hispanic share is above 18 percent. The largest Hispanic American group is Mexican American. Second place belongs to Puerto Ricans. Generations have already passed for some Hispanic families. Others have only just arrived. Government is one field they have shaped. Sports is another. The arts, science, and entertainment are others. Those fields are only a sample. One picture shows a man born in the Dominican Republic. He is saying the Pledge of Allegiance. When the ceremony ends, he will be a citizen of the United States.

2Dolores Huerta was born on April 10, 1930. Her birthplace was Dawson, New Mexico. Her profession is activist. Her life’s work has been better conditions on the job. Equal rights for farmworkers have been part of that work. Other laborers have been part of it too. The year 1962 is when she and other activists founded a union. The name was the National Farm Workers Association, or NFWA. Three years later the name changed. It was then the United Farm Workers’ Union, shortened to UFW. Her years as vice president ran through 1999. Grape workers struck with her help from 1965 to 1970. Fairer wages came from that strike. Fairer working conditions came from it too. Labor laws carry her help as a writer. She has also worked to ban pesticides. Those chemicals harm workers. They harm the environment. The year 2012 brought her the Presidential Medal of Honor. She still works hard for people who lack a voice. The word Hispanic mainly means Spanish-speaking ancestry, among people who live in the United States. Latino is a term for a male. Latina is a term for a female. Latinx does not point to one specific gender. Those three words refer to people in the United States whose origins are Latin American countries. Mexico is included. Countries of Central America and South America are included. Race is not what the words name. Color is not what they name. Language is not what they name.

3Lin-Manuel Miranda was born on January 16, 1980. His birthplace was New York, New York. He works as an actor, a singer, a playwright, and a director. Puerto Rican parents raised him. New York City was his home. Each summer he visited grandparents in Puerto Rico. High school is where theater became his passion. College is where he wrote a first musical. The title was In the Heights. Spoken-word raps were in it. Salsa dancing was in it. Broadway later gave the show awards. A movie followed. Hamilton, another musical, changed musical theater. Miranda wrote it. He also starred in it. It became one of the most popular Broadway musicals of all time. Hip-hop tells the story. Spoken word tells it too. Alexander Hamilton is the person in the story. He helped found the United States. Awards have piled up. The MacArthur Genius Grant is one. A Pulitzer Prize honored his writing. An Emmy honored his acting on television. Three Tonys honored his Broadway plays. Three Grammys honored his music. Puerto Rican roots matter deeply to him. Support for that island is work he continues. Selena Quintanilla-Pérez was born on April 16, 1971. She died on March 31, 1995. Lake Jackson, Texas, was her birthplace. She was a singer. Fans called her the Queen of Tejano Music. Say that style teh-HAH-noh. She was Mexican American. She wrote songs as well as sang them. A wide American audience met Latin music through her songs.

4Her career started inside a family group. The music was in Spanish. The style was Tejano. That genre mixes traditions from Spain, Mexico, the Czech lands, and Germany. Accordion and guitar are featured. No woman before her had become a popular Tejano singer. Death came in 1995, only weeks before she would have turned twenty-four. An album in English was her first. It came out after she died. Success was huge. The music still has a lasting impact. People still listen. Recordings in English and recordings in Spanish both came from her, and few singers had done that so early. August 18, 1934, is the birthday of Roberto Clemente. He died on December 31, 1972. Carolina, Puerto Rico, was his birthplace. Baseball was his profession. He was one of the first Hispanic players in Major League Baseball. Right field for the Pittsburgh Pirates became his job in 1955. He kept that job until death in 1972. Fielding was excellent. Hitting was excellent. An All-Star selection came twelve times. Three thousand hits made him the first Hispanic player to reach that mark. Charity took much of his time. An earthquake in Nicaragua caused severe damage. He was flying supplies there when his plane crashed. Death came in that crash. Three months later he entered the Baseball Hall of Fame. He was the first Hispanic American elected there. Census forms in the United States added the word Hispanic in 1970. Earlier counts learned about Hispanic Americans in other ways.

5Questions asked about last names. They asked about language. They asked about place of birth. The U.S. Social Security Administration is the source of that note. Sammy Davis Jr. was born on December 8, 1925. He died on May 16, 1990. New York, New York, was his birthplace. He sang, danced, played music, acted, told jokes, and wrote. Stages held him from age three until he died. He was Black and Hispanic. His heritage was Afro-Cuban. For a long time he hid the Cuban part of his identity. The year 1962 brought the Cuban Missile Crisis. It was a terrifying time. Nuclear war was the threat between Russia and the United States. Cuban soil held the Russian weapons that were aimed at the United States. Prejudice against Cubans was common among Americans then. Davis answered by falsely calling himself Puerto Rican. Childhood performances were inside his father’s vaudeville act. That kind of show often mixed comedy, singing, and dancing. Theaters booked them. Nightclubs booked them. Carnivals across the United States booked them. Service in the U.S. Army showed him racism firsthand. Back on stage, he pushed racism in the country into public view. Tap dancing was one of his skills. Jokes were another. Piano, drums, a trumpet, and further instruments were his to play. Broadway plays starred him for many years. Movies starred him. Records made him a success too. Antonia Coello Novello was born on August 23, 1944.

6Fajardo, Puerto Rico, was her birthplace. She became a doctor. From 1990 to 1993 she was U.S. Surgeon General. She had always known she wanted medicine. She had not dreamed of the nation’s top doctor job. The year 1990 gave her that job. No woman had held it before. No Hispanic American had held it before. The Surgeon General is a doctor who does not see patients. The work is advice that helps the public stay healthy. Her years in the post put much of her effort on children. People of color were a second focus. An immigrant start was not the path for every Hispanic American. The year 1848 made many Mexicans into U.S. citizens. The Mexican-American War was the cause. The border between the two countries changed. A vast stretch of today’s American West was the land that changed hands. The land runs from Texas to California and into parts of Wyoming. Mexicans living there had a choice. They could leave home and live in Mexico. They could become American citizens. Staying was the choice for over 90 percent. Ellen Ochoa was born on May 10, 1958. Los Angeles, California, was her birthplace. She is an electrical engineer and an astronaut. Passions pulled her in many directions. Her campus in the late 1970s was San Diego University. Five times, the major changed. Music was the start. Physics was the degree at the end. NASA looked at that wide range of interests and selected her for astronaut training.

7Her descent is Mexican. The year 1990 made her the first female Hispanic astronaut. March 1993 began a series of trips. Four trips went into space. Hours in space total 978. From 2013 to 2018 she directed the Johnson Space Center. She was the first Hispanic person in that job. She was the second woman in it. Future astronauts learn their work at that center. She calls the astronaut life a wonderful career. She feels very privileged. Her real hope for young people is different. She wants them to find work they care about deeply. The work should be challenging. It should be worthwhile. A 1993 space trip shows her playing the flute. Oscar de la Renta was born on July 22, 1932. He died on October 20, 2014. Santo Domingo, in the Dominican Republic, was his birthplace. Fashion design was his profession. The Dominican Republic of his childhood was colorful and tropical. He expected to become a painter. Spain in 1950 was where he went to study painting. Fashion design caught his interest instead. Training followed. He rose to the top of that world. Paris came first. New York City came next. Citizenship in the United States arrived in 1971. The year 1965 was when he started his own label. A label here means a company whose clothes he designed. Design awards were many. American first ladies wore his clothes. Jacqueline Kennedy was one.

8Hillary Clinton was one. Laura Bush was one. Birth in the United States makes a person a citizen at once. Citizenship also passes from a parent. That parent must already have been a citizen of the United States on the day the child was born. One such parent is enough. An immigrant can also become a citizen by meeting requirements. Age must be at least eighteen. A naturalization test must be passed. History of the United States is on the test. Geography is on it. Government is on it. Next comes the Oath of Allegiance to the United States. After that oath, the person shares the rights of every citizen. Privileges are shared too. Opportunities are shared too. Frank Romero was born in 1941. East Los Angeles, California, was his birthplace. He is a painter. His descent is Mexican. He had been painting for more than forty years. The artist group he entered was called Los Four. The civil rights movement was the setting. Art from Los Four raised awareness of Hispanic culture. It also raised pride in that culture. The year 1974 put their work in a major show. It was the first show of that scale to feature Hispanic artists of the United States. Social conflicts appear often in Romero’s art. Struggles appear often. Size can be huge. More than fifteen murals of his stand around Los Angeles. Length on some of them passes 20 feet, or 6 meters.

9Shows in many countries have included his art. One picture shows him checking a mural. Going to the Olympics is the name of that mural. June 25, 1954, is the birthday of Sonia Sotomayor. The Bronx, in New York, was her birthplace. She is a lawyer and a Supreme Court judge. Her descent is Puerto Rican. A childhood dream was to become a judge. College graduation made her the first in her family to reach that step. The year 1992 made her a federal judge. No Hispanic person had held a federal judgeship in New York State before her. The year 2009 brought her biggest first. She joined the U.S. Supreme Court. No Hispanic judge had sat there before. No court in the country ranks above it. Each year she and the eight other judges pick the cases they will hear. Rulings can change daily life for people across the country. Her years there have included cases on health care. They have dealt with parental rights. They have dealt with gun control. Many more topics have come too. A 2009 meeting considered whether she would join the court. She spoke at that meeting. Success stories are loved in the United States. The lives in this book hold more than private victories. Each Hispanic American here has added something to the culture of the United States. Each has added something to its society. Drive to succeed is part of what they bring. Backgrounds are part of it.

10Beliefs are part of it. Together they help make the country diverse. They help make it unique. More lives belong on the list. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was born on October 13, 1989, in the Bronx, New York. Her office is United States Representative. June 19, 1978, is the birthday of Zoe Saldaña, in Passaic, New Jersey. She is an actress. Jorge Ramos was born on March 16, 1958, in Mexico City, Mexico. He is a journalist and a news anchor. An achievement is something reached by effort. A generation is a span of about 20 to 30 years. It runs from a group of parents to the birth of their children. A citizen belongs officially to a country or to a state. Heritage is a way of life, a tradition, or a trait passed from one generation to the next. Contributed means did something for a person or a cause, or gave something to one. Culture is the way a group thinks, plus the customs it keeps. Hispanic means related to Spanish-speaking countries, especially countries of Latin America. Descent means a person’s origin or background through family, nationality, or culture. Immigrants settle in a country that is new to them, or they come there to live. Diverse means different from one another, or made of different people or things. An opportunity is an opening to take action. Roots are the family story or the cultural story behind a person.

46. How a Young Country Became United

1The Liberty Bell is pictured with this account of a young country. At the Battle of Lexington, colonists are shown in a fight with British soldiers. The Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776 by representatives speaking for the thirteen colonies. Their announcement said the colonies were free. It also said Great Britain no longer ruled them. What had been colonies became a union of states. The United States of America was the name they took. A system of government was still missing. Delegates from the states began writing a plan for that government. War with Great Britain made the writing slow. Five years passed before the plan was in place. Feeling united took much longer than the plan itself. Forty further years would pass. A second war with Great Britain would come before the union felt like one people. The pages ahead follow that long road. The Articles of Confederation open the story. The Treaty of Paris comes after them. Money troubles follow the treaty. The Constitutional Convention comes next. Arguments about land follow the convention. The Louisiana Purchase comes after those arguments. Exploration and war close the account. Special words are gathered at the end. Before the signing, the thirteen colonies had lived under Great Britain's rule. Representatives spoke for those colonies. The Declaration of Independence was the paper that announced the break. A union means the states were joined together. The governing plan was not ready on the day of the signing. The war is the reason the work lasted five years. The first plan did not make the states feel united. Another war would still be needed. During 1777, delegates at the Second Continental Congress took a next step. They agreed to send the new government plan to the states so the states could review it. The paper later took the name Articles of Confederation. The United States was not called a nation in that paper. Thirteen states were described instead as a firm league of friendship. A weak federal government was what the paper created.

2Strong state governments were the other result. The states were glad to hold that power. Indigenous peoples already lived where the original thirteen states were founded. They also lived on lands that bordered those states. The Algonquins, the Abenaki, and the Chippewas were among them. So were the Ottawas, the Hurons, and the Iroquois. So were the Pottawatomies, the Delaware, and the Illinois. So were the Miamis, the Powhatan, and the Shawnee, near the Mississippi River. So were the Cherokee, the Chickasaws, and the Creek. So were the Choctaws and the Seminole. No real power was given to the federal government by the Articles. Freedom to act was missing too. War had left the United States with debts. Only one branch of federal government was created, and that branch was Congress. Taxing people was not a power Congress held. Money to pay the debts could not be raised that way. Later years would show that the missing tax power was a fatal flaw. Other flaws showed up in the years that followed. No single executive stood in charge. A president was chosen, but only to watch over the meetings of Congress. Decisions were beyond that president's power. Changing the Articles was also beyond Congress, even when the union saw that something failed. Any change needed a yes from nine of the thirteen states. Indigenous peoples were pushed off their lands by the original thirteen states. A pattern started there. Westward expansion in the 1800s repeated the pattern. Diplomacy was one way Indigenous peoples resisted the European colonists. Warfare was the other way. Epidemics got in the way of that resistance. The sicknesses came from diseases that Europeans brought. Almost five years passed before every one of the thirteen states accepted the Articles of Confederation. The big fighting of the Revolutionary War stopped in 1781. Two more years passed before the war was truly finished. Peace terms were discussed in Paris, France, by people speaking for the United States and for Great Britain.

3Talks ran from the middle of 1782 until the signing. September 3, 1783, is the day they signed the Treaty of Paris. The war counted as officially finished only after that signature. Two big ideas were set down in the peace treaty. The first idea named the new United States an independent country. The second idea drew the borders of that country. The Atlantic Ocean formed the eastern edge. The Mississippi River formed the western edge. New Orleans stood outside those borders. The Floridas stood outside them too. Spain was in control of those places. Along the north, the border sat at the Great Lakes. It also followed the edges of Quebec and Nova Scotia. A map of the deal shows Canada still held by Britain. Some land is marked as claimed by both Great Britain and Spain. The Great Lakes and the Mississippi River appear on the map. So do states and territories of the United States. New Spain, the Atlantic Ocean, and New Orleans appear as well. A wish for wealth drove most European colonization of North America. In the 1500s, routes of trade between Europe and Asia were badly broken. The Ottoman Turks were fighting various groups in those years. Profitable trade was lost, so many European powers looked for another path. They wanted sea routes west that would still reach Asia. From 1565 to 1625, four powers planted colonies in North America. Spain, Britain, France, and the Netherlands were those powers. Land was split between the United States and Great Britain by the Treaty of Paris of 1783. Rights of Indigenous peoples were ignored. Those peoples had lived on the lands since before recorded history. With the Revolutionary War finished and the Treaty of Paris signed, money trouble hit hard. The government held no money. It also held no power to tax. Pay never reached many of the soldiers. A larger money headache waited. War debts were that headache. More than 76 million dollars was owed.

4Foreign countries were owed part of it. Individual Americans were owed part. State banks were owed part. Leaders had no clear way to gather the money for those debts. In Massachusetts, the money trouble sparked a rebellion. Some farmers had fought for independence and then lost their farms. Prison was their fate because the debts went unpaid. In 1786, about a thousand people marched with Daniel Shays. Shays had been a captain in the Revolutionary War. Springfield, Massachusetts, was the town they marched on. Boston was where they headed next. The army of the United States met them. Shots were fired. Some of the workers were tried, then hanged. Others received no punishment. Leaders saw a clear lesson in Shays' Rebellion. The federal government had to be stronger. A gold coin called a United States Half Eagle dates from 1795. Fifty-five men came to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to face the nation's many problems. May 1787 was the month, and Independence Hall was the place. Their aim was to revise the Articles of Confederation. A stronger federal government was the hope. What they drafted was a constitution. A president would lead the union under that plan. Congress would gain the power to tax. A method for changing the governing paper would exist. Delegates came from twelve of the thirteen states. In his own state, each delegate was a leader with influence. Founders is a name sometimes used for the people who did the most to create the union. Wealthy, educated white men made up the whole group of delegates. In most states at that time, the vote belonged only to white men who owned property. The meeting mirrored that limit. George Washington was the person they chose to run the meeting. People came to call the meeting the Constitutional Convention. Several weeks was how long it lasted. Tempers rose during debates about changes to the Articles of Confederation. Two issues caused the anger. Representation was the first issue.

5Extra representatives in Congress would mean extra power. Two plans were put forward. Population was the base of one plan. A state with more people would receive more representatives. Equal representation for every state was the other plan. Slavery was the second issue. Enslaved people were Black people taken from Africa, or the descendants of those people. Property is how they were treated. Freedom was denied to them. Terrible conditions were common in their lives. Work was forced on them, and no pay came. Southern states wanted slavery kept in place. They also wanted enslaved people included in the count for representation. Rights did not belong to enslaved people. Voting was closed to them. Southern delegates believed the count would help. They wanted their states closer to equal footing with the Northern states. George Washington, like many founders, gained from the labor of enslaved people. That labor happened on his estate. Out of the arguments came the Three-Fifths Compromise. Representation and slavery were both part of it. Two houses of Congress were created for representation. Every state would have the same voice in the Senate. Population would set each state's voice in the House of Representatives. A limit was placed on Congress regarding slavery. For twenty years, Congress could not pass changes that would control slavery. A counting rule was also agreed. Each enslaved person would be counted as three-fifths of a person when representatives were assigned. The president's power was debated as well. Checks and balances were the system they built. Equal power for each branch was the aim. Three branches were suggested. Two houses of Congress would form the legislative branch. A president would form the executive branch. Courts that enforce laws would form the judicial branch. A way to change the Constitution was written into the document itself. Thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution on September 17, 1787. The states then received it for a vote. People all over talked about the plan. They asked if it was a good design for government.

6The Federalists were a group that pushed states to ratify the Constitution. The Antifederalists were a group that pushed the other way. They did not want the plan to become the law of the land. A list, the Antifederalists said, had to be added. The list would name rights the government must not take away. An agreement came at last. Ten changes to the Constitution were part of that agreement. The Bill of Rights is what those changes were called. Free speech was one right the Bill of Rights guaranteed. Freedom to practice religion was another. Other rights were guaranteed too. No democracy already standing in Europe could serve as a model. Europe had none. Examples from some Indigenous nations were used instead. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy was one example. The name sounds like hoh-dee-noh-SHOH-nee. Their government showed how several ideas the delegates liked might work in real life. Women's rights in America had an early supporter in Abigail Adams. Voting in the first presidential election, in 1789, was narrow in most states. Only men who were white and owned land could vote. Since the Civil War, amendments have changed the Constitution more than once. The right to vote grew with those changes. People of every ethnicity can vote now. Women can vote now. Any citizen older than eighteen can vote now. Many people say voting-rights laws still discriminate. They say people of color are hurt unfairly. They say the problem stays serious in many parts of the country today. George Washington became president of the United States of America under the new Constitution. April 30, 1789, was the day he took office. Two terms of four years each were what he served. His presidency ran from 1789 to 1797. Alexander Hamilton was his choice for secretary of the treasury. Hamilton offered a plan for the money troubles. Taxes on imports were part of the plan. The first national bank was part of it too. Faith in the government seemed to return because of the plan.

7The economy grew. John Adams won election as the second president in 1796. His years in office were 1797 to 1801. Thomas Jefferson became the third president in 1801. His years were 1801 to 1809. Land raised another problem for the new country. A huge area had come to the United States after the Revolutionary War was won. Someone had to decide how to divide it. Western lands were claimed by state governments. Indigenous peoples had lived on those lands since before any history was written down. More than one state claimed some of the same areas. A method appeared in the Land Ordinance of 1785. New land would be split into townships and sections. Settlers were to buy many of the sections. The government kept other sections. Public schools received sections as well. Thomas Jefferson designed the Northwest Ordinance in 1787. He was serving as a delegate from Virginia. Rules in that ordinance explained how new states would be made in the Northwest Territory. A promise about colonies was included. Britain had held colonies, but the United States would not. Tecumseh led the Shawnee in a fight. American settlers moving into the Northwest Territory were the people they fought. Homes went up as settlers moved west. A huge westward movement was prepared by the Land Ordinance and the Northwest Ordinance. The early 1800s were the years of that movement. Roads were constructed so the move would be easier. Canals were constructed. Railroads were constructed. Growth of the nation was fast. The new government matched that speed. Debts were paid down. Power in the new government was divided, and that division was set. Prosperity and growth led leaders to make further plans. A wide stretch of land was in French hands. One edge of that land was the Mississippi River. The other edge was the Rocky Mountains. The port of New Orleans was French as well. Trade on the Mississippi River was closed to United States citizens.

8Trade through New Orleans was closed to them too. A message went from the United States to Napoleon Bonaparte, the emperor of France. The message asked to purchase New Orleans. Military losses in Europe had hit Bonaparte. Troops were needed, and so was money. He wanted funds for his war. His offer went beyond New Orleans. The whole Louisiana Territory was offered for 15 million dollars. October 1803 was when the United States bought the Louisiana Territory. The price paid was the price France had asked. The nation doubled in size. Two hundred thousand people were added to the United States. Indigenous nations living there did not agree to give the land away. Nobody asked them. The land area of the United States nearly doubled because of the Louisiana Purchase. Westward expansion grew because of it. In many cases that expansion destroyed Indigenous peoples or forced them from their homes. May 1804 was when President Thomas Jefferson sent explorers out. Two army officers were in charge. Meriwether Lewis was one. William Clark was the other. Forty-five more people traveled with them. A route across the continent was their task. They were also to look over the Louisiana Territory and then report what they found. An interpreter traveled with the group. Her name was Sacagawea, and she was a Lemhi Shoshone girl. Success of the expedition owed a great deal to her help. More than two years passed before they came home. Journals came back with them. Drawings came back. Hundreds of plant and animal samples came back. Groundwork for taking land in the West was laid by this trip. Many Indigenous groups already living there were hit hard. During those same years, France was in a raging war with Great Britain. Jefferson held the United States out of that war. James Madison became president in 1808. Staying out was his hope as well. Staying out proved impossible. Ships of the United States were seized by British ships. French ships seized them too.

9The point of the searches was to block supplies from reaching the enemy. Sailors were seized by the British as well. Those sailors were forced to serve on British ships. Tyranny from Britain had returned for citizens of the United States. A warning went from President Madison to Great Britain in 1812. Searches and seizures of United States ships had to stop, or war would follow. The reply did not satisfy Madison. War was declared on June 18, 1812. Ships enough to fight the British navy were something the United States did not have in the War of 1812. An attempt to conquer Canada, which Britain controlled, failed. Two and a half years of war with Great Britain followed. A peace treaty ending the war was signed by both countries on December 24, 1814. On August 19, 1812, the ship Constitution of the United States defeated the British ship Guerriere. One further battle with the British came after the war had officially ended. On January 8, 1815, Americans won at the Battle of New Orleans. General Andrew Jackson was their leader. He did not know that peace had already been signed. The win was decisive. British dead numbered almost three hundred. American dead numbered fewer than twenty. Control of the western part of the country was made plain. That control belonged to the United States, not to Great Britain. Citizens felt as though the war itself had been won. Neither side had actually won. Perhaps the greatest result was a feeling of unity. Coming late, the victory left the United States of America feeling like one nation at last. A timeline lists steps from an earlier war to this one. The French and Indian War, also called the Seven Years' War, ran from 1754 to 1763. The Sugar Act, the Quartering Act, and the Stamp Act came in 1764 and 1765. The Townshend Acts came in 1767. The Boston Massacre came in 1770. The Coercive Acts, also called the Intolerable Acts, came in 1774.

10The First Continental Congress met in that year. The Revolutionary War began in 1775. The Second Continental Congress met in that year. The Declaration of Independence was signed on July 4, 1776. The Revolutionary War ended in 1781. All thirteen states approved the Articles of Confederation in that year. Shays' Rebellion came in 1786. The Constitutional Convention was held in 1787. Every state ratified the Constitution in 1791. The Bill of Rights was ratified in that year as well. War with Britain began again in 1812. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in 1814, ended the War of 1812. A few words make this nation's story easier to follow. Checks and balances split power across branches of government so that one branch cannot rule the rest. A compromise is a settlement in which each arguing side gives something up. A constitution is the basic law that explains how a state or a nation is governed. Debates are conversations between people or groups who disagree about an issue. Debts are owed things, and the owed thing is usually money. Executive is the word for the branch that leads a nation and puts laws into action. Expansion is growth in size, amount, volume, or scope. Federal describes a government at the center that lets separate states or regions keep some power. Guaranteed means promised, or made certain. Judicial is the word for the branch that tests whether laws fit the constitution. Legislative is the word for the branch that writes laws. Prosperity means success, wealth, or good luck. To ratify is to approve something by an official act. A rebellion is a fight aimed at authority or at power. Representatives are chosen to speak, to vote, or to act for another person or for a group. Seizing means taking hold by force. A treaty is a formal pact of peace or friendship between nations or groups. Tyranny means cruel or harsh acts by someone, or by a group, that holds power.

47. How Human Skin Gets Its Shade

1Lighter skin burns fast when it has no cover. In a crowd, many skin colors often appear together. Singapore, Toronto, and New York City are full of people from many races. You meet people of many ethnicities too. Few places on Earth mix people as widely as these cities do. People there speak different languages. They keep different traditions. Their looks differ as well. Skin ranges in color. It ranges in tone. It ranges in shade. The causes of those differences have been studied by scientists. What they have found might amaze you. Melanin decides most of a person's skin color. Animals carry this pigment. Plants carry it too. Most of it sits in the outer layer of skin. That layer is called the epidermis. Hair holds melanin too. Eyes hold it too. Special cells called melanocytes produce the pigment. At least six genes control melanin. Genes are parts of cells. They guide many sides of looks and of behavior. They are the basic units of heredity. Parents pass them on to their children. Many genes take part, so two parents can have children whose skin tones cover a range.

2Sometimes a child resembles parents and brothers or sisters. Sometimes that child's skin is much lighter. Sometimes it is much darker. Melanin comes in two types. Eumelanin runs from dark brown to black. Pheomelanin runs from red to yellow. Each person makes a different mix of the two. The mix leads to different tones and colors of skin. A larger share of eumelanin makes skin darker. A larger share of pheomelanin makes skin lighter. Skin color also depends on the number of melanin particles. It depends on the size of those particles. Those two factors change skin color more than the balance of the two melanin types. Color in lighter skin also depends partly on what lies underneath. Blood makes skin look pinker. Body fat changes the color as well. Carotene is a red-orange pigment, and it changes skin color too. A zebra's skin is dark because of melanin. The cells that make melanin pass it into only some hairs in the coat.

3A drawing of human skin can show hair, the epidermis, melanin particles, fat, the dermis, and a melanocyte. Sunlight falls on Earth. Part of that light is ultraviolet radiation, which eyes cannot see. People shorten the name to UV radiation. UV radiation can harm cells. It can lead to skin cancer. It can lead to other health problems. Melanin stops harmful UV from passing through the epidermis. Eumelanin, the darker kind, does this job especially well. In darker skin, melanin acts like a sunscreen made by the body. Against UV harm, darker skin has at least double the protection of lighter skin. Melanin also guards the body's store of folate. Folate is a B vitamin. It helps power the building of new cells. UV radiation produces three main kinds of rays. They are called UV-A, UV-B, and UV-C. From A to C, the rays grow shorter. As they grow shorter, they grow stronger. A shorter wavelength can do more damage. UV-C never reaches Earth. UV-A makes up 95 percent of the UV that arrives at Earth's surface.

4UV-A ages cells in the skin. It causes wrinkles. Even so, UV-A is thought to play a part in some skin cancers. UV-B causes a tan. It causes sunburn. It causes most skin cancers. The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center is the source for these facts about UV rays. UV also helps the body. Bare skin in sunlight lets the body make vitamin D. Vitamin D matters for strong bones. It supports a healthy immune system. It supports many other jobs inside the body. Darker skin blocks enough UV to lower vitamin D production. A person with darker skin must stay in the sun longer than a person with lighter skin. The extra time is needed to make enough vitamin D. Eye color depends on melanin packed into the iris. The iris is the colored ring around the middle of the eye. The lightest eyes are a pale blue. The darkest are brown. A darker eye holds more melanin than a lighter eye. Melanin helps guard eyes from sunlight. It guards skin in a similar way.

5Genes set the differences in skin color and in tone. Time in the sun changes skin color too. A suntan is proof of that. UV can push melanocytes to make more melanin. Skin then turns a darker color. Skin type decides whether a person tans or burns. Some lighter-skinned people freckle because only certain melanocytes add melanin after sun exposure. Those people get freckles. They do not get a tan over the whole body. Melanin sets skin color. It also helps shield skin from UV rays. So why do people carry different amounts of melanin? Why do they carry different types? Those differences are why skin colors are not the same. The answer starts far in the past, with the first humans. A high amount of pheomelanin often goes with red hair. It often goes with freckles too. Most scientists place the earliest humans in Africa. Africa's position relative to the equator matters. Over much of Africa, the Sun's rays hit more head-on than in many other regions. About two million years ago, Earth went through a long dry spell.

6Early humans had to find ways to live on dry, open land. Daytime heat meant they needed a way to keep cool as they moved. Scientists place the loss of most body hair at this time in early human life. They also gained the ability to sweat. A map of Earth and UV-B shows where exposure is low and where it is high. The map shows the spread of UV-B in November 2023. UV-B can burn skin that has no protection in as little as fifteen minutes. Closer to the poles, sunlight strikes Earth at a slant. The land there receives less heat. It receives less light. The North Pole is one of those places. The South Pole is another. Closer to the equator, sunlight strikes Earth more straight on. The land there receives more heat. It receives more light. Pigment in skin likely arose in that same period, along with sweat and bare skin. Pigment would have shielded mostly bare skin from UV radiation. It would have protected stores of the vitamin folate.

7Some early humans left at a time between fifty thousand and eighty thousand years before now. They migrated into colder parts of the world. Farther from the equator, sunlight was less intense. UV radiation was weaker there. With less UV, these people no longer needed so much pigment. Losing folate was less of a danger too. The move created a new problem. In the colder lands, early humans could not make as much vitamin D. Melanin in the skin blocked too much sun. Across many generations, their bodies started making less melanin. Skin grew lighter because of that change. Lighter skin allowed the body to make more vitamin D. Drops of vitamin D go from a mother to her infant. Today, many people with light skin still do not get enough vitamin D. Later migrations carried people into still other UV settings. Survival required these human groups to adapt. That long adapting produced the many skin-color variations seen today. Some conditions can change the color of skin. Genes cause albinism. Those genes cut the amount of melanin the body makes.

8This condition often leads to very light skin. Hair may be white. It may be pale blond. People with albinism have less of a shield against UV radiation. Staying out of the sun is especially important for them. Protective clothing matters. Sunscreen matters too. Albinism can change the color of the eyes. It can change the health of the eyes. The eyes are mostly blue. Reddish eyes occur often. So do purple, hazel, and light brown eyes. Vision problems are common. Glasses cannot fix those problems. Albinism appears around the world. Every ethnic background can include people with albinism. Winnie Harlow was bullied in the past because of her vitiligo. She now welcomes her unusual look. Today she is a successful model in fashion. Vitiligo (vit-ih-LY-go) makes skin lose color in patches. Many body parts can be affected. Sometimes only a few parts change. The direct cause is melanocytes that die. It can also be melanocytes that stop working as they should. Nobody knows why that happens. Vitiligo is not dangerous.

9It can still make a person feel uneasy about being seen. Sunscreen is especially important. Skin that has lost melanin burns easily in the sun. Partial loss of hearing is another worry. That can happen if melanocytes inside the inner ear are affected. Thousands of years of migration left many people outside the places their skin color fits best. A person with darker skin may live where UV is low, nearer the poles. That person must take care to get enough vitamin D. A person with lighter skin may live where UV is high, nearer the equator. That person must shield skin from too much UV-B. Humans are good at solving problems. Sunscreen helps with the trouble caused when skin and local UV do not match. Clothing that blocks sun helps too. Extra vitamin D, taken as a supplement, helps as well. People keep changing. The world keeps changing. New solutions will surely keep appearing. Learning how the Sun affects skin makes it easier to keep skin healthy. These words help with the topic. Exposing can mean uncovering something.

10It can mean leaving it open to weather or to sight. It can mean revealing it. A generation is one span of about twenty to thirty years. The span runs from when parents are born to when their children are born. The spans repeat. Heredity is the passing of traits from one generation to the next. Hair color is one example. Eye color is another. The immune system carries antibodies through the body. The antibodies fight infection. Melanin is a dark pigment. Hair gets color from it. Skin gets color from it. Eyes of people and other animals get color from it. Migrated means a person moved on purpose from one region to another. The move was made in order to live there or to work there. Color in an object can come from a substance called a pigment. Ultraviolet radiation is a band of light that eyes cannot see. This invisible band begins where violet light ends and continues toward x-rays. A variation is a different type or form of something.

48. How Movies Make the Impossible Look Real

1Inside: an opening scene. Animation that stops between photos. Scenery thrown from behind. Swapping a color for a new background. Robots that act. Tiny models. Weather made on purpose. Pictures built by computer. A closing word. Words to know. A huge ape stands over New York City. He is on the highest point of the Empire State Building. One enormous hand holds a woman. He sets her gently inside the building. His chest takes a thump. A menacing roar goes out toward a squadron of planes. The planes circle just beyond where he can reach. He hits one plane. It spins down and hits the ground inside a ball of fire. The rest of the planes attack. Bullets fly. Some of them strike. The ape is badly wounded. One last roar leaves him. He releases the building. The street is where he falls. The scene just described comes from the movie King Kong. Many decades have passed since it was made. Without Willis O'Brien, that movie could not have existed. Across the 1920s, and again in the 1930s, he mastered effects for film. Movies he helped build with those effects are still loved by audiences.

2A close view shows the gorilla model from the 1933 film of King Kong. So what counts as a special effect? It is the part of making a movie that builds pictures. It also builds sounds. Those pictures and sounds can make a movie feel real. A superhero can save any person. The rescue can happen in any place. It can happen at any time. An alien craft can race toward Earth at a speed that alarms you. A building can fall apart. A tornado can twist. A dinosaur, gone for ages, can seem alive again. A movie is a run of still pictures. Capture them in a series. Play them back fast, one after another, and they look like motion. Dinosaurs seem to live again in one effects scene. The film is Jurassic Park III, from 2001. Photos that pause, then move What steps let O'Brien bring King Kong to the screen? Several gorilla models came first. Each had a metal skeleton. Joints in that skeleton worked like human knees. They worked like human shoulders. Cotton padded the joints. Foam rubber padded them too. Rabbit skins went on the outside, so the covering looked like the beast's fur.

3Next he watched how gorillas move. Zoos were his classroom. Professional wrestling matches gave him ideas as well. He needed a way for his creature to fight dinosaurs. He needed fights with other huge animals. The place of those fights is Skull Island, home of King Kong. His effects team then built miniature sets full of detail. A street in New York City was one of them. The sets were a backdrop for the models that would be animated. Then came the process he invented. People call it stop-motion animation. Miniature models were photographed a single frame at a time. Each frame put the model in a new position. Developed film, played in order, made the models seem to move. The illusion was that they were alive. One picture shows his ape model and his dinosaur model, locked in battle. The scene belongs to King Kong, the monster film released in 1933. Effects that won notice These films were nominated for an award, or they won it. The award is for Visual Effects. It comes from the film Academy. The group's longer name covers motion pictures, the arts, and the sciences.

4The year beside each title is the year the film came out. You may have seen some of them. 2012 brought Life of Pi, and that film won. 2013 brought Iron Man 3. 2014 brought Interstellar, and that film won. 2015 brought a Star Wars story called The Force Awakens. 2016 brought The Jungle Book. 2017 brought Guardians of the Galaxy, volume 2. 2018 brought an Avengers story called Infinity War. 2019 brought The Lion King. 2020 brought Mulan. Movies have used these tricks for more than 100 years. Some of the earliest came from Georges Méliès, a magician from France. In 1899 he directed The Conjurer. Effects in that film made him vanish. Terror hit some people in the audience so hard that they fainted. Many kinds of tricks have been invented since that day. Scenery from behind Rear projection is one kind of effect. It puts false scenery behind an actor. Picture a person who seems to drive a car along a beach. The beach is filmed before anything else. That beach picture is then thrown onto a screen.

5In front of it stand a driver and a car. The camera films them there. An actor hangs in the air before a green screen. In the finished shot, a busy market will stand where that screen was. Photography that replaces a color Color-replacement photography films a moving actor, or a moving animal. A fall is one example. The action is filmed against a chroma screen that is blue. A green screen can be used instead. Filming of the background happens at a separate time. The pretend fall is then placed over that colored screen. Erase the color, and the background shows through every spot the color had filled. Think of cutting a paper shape of an animal, or of an actor, and sticking it on new scenery. This effect is like that. The difference is motion. The cut-out image moves. The scenery moves too. Most weather parts of television news use this trick every day. A weather anchor stands before a screen of one color. A technician places a map image behind the anchor. Any area that matches the screen's color receives the new image. You will not see that anchor dressed in the screen's color.

6A weather map could appear in the space where a body ought to show. Emmerdale's cast rides wild water before a screen that is green. Wild rapids will replace that screen later. The hit film Jaws, from 1975, used a shark model that was mechanical. Robots that perform A huge shark crunches the boat that belongs to Quint. That image, from Jaws, is hard to forget. So is the creepy sweetness of E.T. Both characters were made with a process called animatronics. The process builds characters out of electronic robots. A crew of effects workers steers the robots. Remote control is the tool. Animators watch how real animals move. They watch how people move. They try to copy those movements with electronics. Because the creatures seem to move as living things move, cameras can film them with actors. Real animals can share the shot. Dinosaurs in Jurassic Park were as frightening as E.T. was lovable. Strong animatronics are the reason. A note on where the name came from. The year 1961 is when this label was coined. Walt Disney made the word. It joins animate with electronics.

7A picture shows one model of a dinosaur built as a machine. Riders on a dragon show how large the creature is. The film is the second part of a Harry Potter story, Deathly Hallows, from 2010. Models built small A miniature model often stands in for a real building. It can stand in for another large object too. On film the model looks full size. A set or a prop can be made extra large. It can be made extra small. People then look tiny, or they look huge. A set is the place where acting happens. A house can be a set. A city can be a set. A jungle can be a set. A prop is an object an actor uses. A chair is a prop. A sword is a prop. Weather made for the camera Films often need weather, or a natural disaster, that effects must create. A violent storm at sea is one example. Actors can stay away from a storm that is real. A real storm would be very dangerous. They can sit safe in a boat. The boat can float in a large pool, or in a pond.

8A machine builds waves that crash. Huge fans build strong wind. Giant sprinklers overhead pour down rain. Life of Pi, directed by Ang Lee and released in 2012, won an Academy Award. The award was for Visual Effects. The storm scene was among the hardest to build. A tiger was created on its own. The storm was created on its own. The two then had to be meshed. Cameras filmed the scene before a blue screen. Film of a real storm can replace that screen later. When a movie needs a snowstorm, flakes can be made in several ways. Bleached flakes of potato are one way. Plastic flakes are another. Powdered detergent for laundry is another. Encanto, from 2021, uses striking computer images. They build the mountain landscape of Colombia. They build abilities that feel fantastical. Pictures made by computer Computer-generated images can build nearly any effect a movie can imagine. A fire can blaze. A wave can tower. A dinosaur can talk. After the pictures exist on the computer, artists can change them. They can move them. They can copy them. They can combine them with other pictures for the film.

9Computers changed the world of movie effects in a deep way. Scenes nobody had thought possible can be made. A whole movie can be built this way. The Polar Express is one example. A closing word Audiences in 1933 felt awe at the effects in King Kong. Audiences now feel the same awe. They watch a volcano erupt inside a city. They watch spaceships fight. They watch a huge ocean liner split apart and go down until it rests on the ocean floor. Viewers today do understand effects a little better than viewers of long ago. Boredom is not the result. Not a chance. The magic on the screen is still a pleasure. People still love to feel fright. They love to feel amazement. They love to be entertained. What remains for these effects? Artists who work with computers want a computer-made human to look fully real. Will they reach that goal? They probably will. With these effects, anything can happen. A picture shows a human character drawn by computer. Words to know Animatronics: the electronics that let a creature model move as if it lived.

10Backdrop: the scenery behind characters in one part of a movie. Color-replacement photography: photography that wipes one color out of the near image, letting a farther image show in that space. Computer-generated images: pictures made with a computer. Developed: processed until it can be used. Illusion: something false that fools you into thinking it is real, or that it really happened. Imaginable: able to be pictured in the mind. Miniature: very small. Models: built copies that resemble the objects they stand for. Movements: the way something moves while it does an action. Process: the order of work used to finish a project. Projected: shown on a screen in a theater or on television. Props: movable things actors handle during a play or a film. Rear projection: a studio trick that puts scenery in back of an actor. Scenery: painted walls, and objects, placed around actors in a play or a film. Special effects: illusions made for movies or television with computers, with cameras, or with props. Stop-motion animation: photos of a model, a small set at a time, after each slight shift, so the model seems to move alone.

49. How the United States Makes Its Money

1Inside: how the money is produced. Banks and the marks from mints. Fake bills. Money worn out, and money saved by collectors. Making one national system. Words to know. Producing the money Life in the United States today depends on money. People could not get by without it. Food is bought with money. Shelter is bought with money. Those are things people need in order to live. Money also buys things people want. Survival does not require every one of those wants. American money is not the same as money in other countries. A currency system of its own belongs to each country. Here the system is decimal. Dollars are one unit. Cents are the other. A large central bank issues every piece of American money. People call it the Federal Reserve. Issuing is not the same as manufacturing. Two other organizations do the making. Coins come from the U.S. Mint. Notes, which means bills, come from a bureau. The bureau's work is engraving, and it is also printing. Faces on the coins, one by one: the penny shows Abraham Lincoln. The nickel shows Thomas Jefferson. The dime shows Franklin D. Roosevelt. The quarter shows George Washington. The half-dollar shows John F. Kennedy. The dollar coin shows Susan B. Anthony. Faces on the notes, one by one: one dollar shows George Washington.

2Two dollars shows Thomas Jefferson. Five dollars shows Abraham Lincoln. Ten dollars shows Alexander Hamilton. Twenty dollars shows Andrew Jackson. Fifty dollars shows Ulysses S. Grant. One hundred dollars shows Benjamin Franklin. Design sets this currency apart from currencies elsewhere in the world. American values are written into the symbols. American history is written into them too. Every coin carries a portrait. Every note carries one. The person shown played an important part in America's past. Banks and the letters on coins Finished notes and finished coins are shipped onward. They go to banks run by the Federal Reserve. That body is America's central bank. A dozen of its banks sit in different parts of the nation. Together they form the national bank system. A private bank can hold a checking account for a person. In a similar way, a private bank holds a checking account at a Federal Reserve bank. Those accounts are how private banks buy notes. They buy coins the same way, whenever customers need them. A teller is the person who cashes a check. A teller also hands out change. Which coins to make is not a choice the U.S. Mint gets to make. Which notes to print is not a choice for the bureau that engraves and prints.

3Neither office has the authority to begin a unit of currency. Neither has the authority to stop one. Yearly coin output from the mint runs from 11 billion up to 20 billion. Daily note output from the bureau is about 37 million. Denomination, meaning which values get made and sent into use, is a decision for Congress. A drawing marks two clues on a coin. One clue is the mint mark. The other is the year. A dollar bill, or a coin, can tell you its birthplace. Every coin receives a mint mark. That mark is a letter, a code for the city of manufacture. A letter P beside the face, on the coin's front, means Philadelphia. A D means Denver. An S means San Francisco. Bills of one dollar printed before 1996 carry a regional seal. The seal names which Reserve bank sent that note out. From 1996 on, a newer seal does that job. A letter and a number sit below the serial number. Banks of origin, with letter and number. Boston is A and 1. New York City is B and 2. Philadelphia is C and 3. Cleveland is D and 4. Richmond is E and 5.

4Atlanta is F and 6. Chicago is G and 7. St. Louis is H and 8. Minneapolis is I and 9. Kansas City is J and 10. Dallas is K and 11. San Francisco is L and 12. Fake notes Criminals started copying notes almost as soon as the printing bureau started making them. Control of those counterfeiters was the reason the Treasury built the Secret Service. The year was 1865. Inside the United States this act is a federal crime. Prison can last as long as fifteen years. Printing grew more advanced. In 1996 the government answered by changing how paper money looks, so it could stay ahead of fakes. Sixty-seven years had passed since the last significant change in that design. Updates have come more often since then. Three twenty-dollar bills show the shift. The top bill has a small portrait inside an oval frame. That design is the twenty from before 1996. The middle bill has a larger portrait, still inside an oval frame. That design ran from 1996 to 2003. The bottom bill has the largest portrait, and no frame around it. A faint eagle appears on that bill. Other differences include the green, which is not one single shade, and the lettering. The bottom design is the twenty as of 2004.

5A later redesign might take Andrew Jackson off the bill. Harriet Tubman might take that place. A diagram labels the parts of a bill. Down the left side, start at the top. You meet a security thread. Next is the type of note. Next is the letter and the number that mark the Reserve bank. Last on that side is the seal of that bank. The portrait sits in the center. Down the right side, start at the top. You meet the treasury seal together with the watermark. Next is the serial number. Next is the number that states the bill's value. That number is printed in ink that shifts color. The word Series is marked as well. Any person can learn a check for fake notes. Three features are the ones to test. One is a watermark. One is ink that shifts color. One is a security thread. A watermark is a faint picture sitting in the bill's background. Ink that shifts color covers the numeral in a corner. Tilt the note up and down and that ink moves from copper to green. A security thread runs from top to bottom through every new note put out since 1996. Size did not change for paper notes in the 1996 redesign.

6Texture did not change either. Older notes and newer notes match on both. Coins have changed design across the years as well. Now and then Congress tells the U.S. Mint to strike a fresh edition of a coin that already exists. Now and then Congress tells the mint to strike a commemorative coin that is wholly new. California joined the Union as the 31st state. It is also the 31st state honored with its own state quarter. From 1999 to 2008, every 10 weeks, the back of the quarter took a new picture so a different state could be honored. The California design shows several things. A man holds a walking stick. He looks toward a large bird and toward a mountain. The word California appears. The year 1850 appears. The name John Muir appears. The place Yosemite Valley appears. The year 2005 appears. Latin words appear: E pluribus unum. Bags of coins are packed by a worker inside a mint. Those bags travel to banks. Metal may be the biggest shift coins have gone through. Early coins of the United States used gold. They used silver. Copper was another metal. The opening year of the mint produced 11,178 cents, all of them copper.

7Silver coins and gold coins were not far behind. Today the mix uses copper, but only a tiny share. Nickel is a tiny share. Zinc is a tiny share. Gold shows up only in coins that are antique. A coin outlasts a bill. Expect a circulating coin to last 30 years. Expect paper money to last 18 months. Worn money, saved money Money does not go on forever. Notes too worn for use are destroyed by Federal Reserve banks. Some of that paper is recycled. Stationery is one product that can be made from it. Used coins are not bought back by the U.S. Mint. Mutilated coins are different. The mint will pay for those, but only what they are worth as scrap metal. Old worn coins can be swapped at Federal Reserve banks for fresh coins that carry the same face value. The old coins then go to the mint. Recycling is their next step. Some American money is never spent. It is never exchanged. It is never recycled. Numismatists keep it in collections. A numismatist is a collector of coins. Notes and coins are held in hope that value will rise. Commemorative coins are also made by the mint, and collectors buy them. A commemorative coin is special. It honors a person, or a place, or an institution, or an event from history.

8Collectors may also keep numismatic coins that began as ordinary standard coins. Rarity sets the value. Condition sets it. Age sets it. One coin's front shows the head of Christopher Columbus, drawn in profile. Words on that side read United States of America. They also read Columbian Half Dollar. The back shows a large sailing ship. It shows two globes, each displaying a different part of Earth. Words there read World's Columbian Exposition. They name Chicago. They give the year 1893. That piece was the first commemorative coin of the United States, and Columbus is the person on it. It was made to line up with the World's Columbian Exposition. Chicago hosted that fair in 1893. Congress is the body that authorizes the mint to produce these special coins. Congress chooses the person or the subject. Congress chooses how many will be made. Circulation is not their purpose. Legal tender is still what they are, so they can be spent. Face value and appraised value are not the same. Take the half dollar for the Hudson, N.Y., Sesquicentennial, dated 1935. Face value is 50 cents. The first sale price was 1 dollar. Today the price runs from 1,000 dollars to 5,000 dollars.

9Coin sales pay for projects that are special. Part of the funding that repaired the Statue of Liberty came from those sales. The coins that paid for it carried a picture of the statue. One system for the whole country At the nation's start, the economy leaned heavily on a mix of coins from other lands. The year 1775 is when the Continental Congress began issuing currency. War costs for the Revolution were the reason. People called the notes Continentals. Value fell fast. Fakes were easy to make. Gold did not stand behind the notes. Silver did not stand behind them either. April 2, 1792, is the day Congress passed the Mint Act. Standardization of currency in the United States began with that law. Coin output has grown since then. A year once meant 1,500 coins. A year now means more than 11 billion. Few currencies in the world now stand stronger than the American dollar. How much money is made here has changed across the years. What kinds are made has changed too. Congress plays a part. The mint plays a part. The bureau that engraves and prints plays a part. Federal Reserve banks play a part. Together, government keeps coins moving. It keeps notes moving.

10It keeps the value of this money safe. An ATM is among the easiest ways to obtain money. Grocery stores in the United States see about 42 billion dollars spent in a month. Designs on money have been changed many times. The new pictures honor people from U.S. history. They honor events too. Security features have been changed so that counterfeiters have a harder time passing fake bills. New rules follow new technology. Further changes in this currency are still ahead. The job of the money will stay the same. People will still buy what they need. They will still buy some of what they want. Using money is now part of ordinary daily life. Words to know Counterfeiters: people who make false currency. Currency: money in any form that people accept. Denomination: the face value attached to one kind of currency. Face value: the number or the words on a coin or a note that say what it is worth. Federal Reserve: America's central bank. Legal tender: money that, inside a country, people must accept when you pay them. Mutilated: damaged in a serious way. Numismatic: describing currency kept because it is rare or because history makes it matter. Precious metals: metals people prize highly because they are rare.

50. How the Yellow Bus Gets to School

1The year in this picture is 1943. The place is an army base. The state is New York. Children there ride to school in a bus pulled by horses. That older kind of transport saved gasoline. It saved tires too. The war at the time was World War II. Sarah steps outside on a winter day that is freezing. She shivers as she walks. The bus stop is one block from her apartment. The cold is sharp, yet waiting outside does not worry her. She knows the wait will be short. The bus arrives right on time. She greets the driver while she climbs aboard. She hardly notices the rest. The bus leaves the stop. It rumbles down the road toward school. This part of her day is something she takes for granted. Sarah sees that yellow bus as a normal piece of the view. Many American students feel the same. They depend on that bus to reach school. Few people pause to ask how the system works. Even so, it is one of the country's most important transit systems. It is also one of the most complex. This kind of transit moves masses of people.

2Getting students to school takes a small army of workers. The buses use every sort of road. Some roll on interstate highways. Others use rural lanes that are not paved. School districts control the pieces that make the system run. Those pieces are the vehicles, the drivers, the mechanics, and the fuel. Each district handles its own. Taxpayer money pays for the buses. The money often comes from local taxes on property. Businesses are taxed on what their property is worth. Homeowners are taxed that way too. They pay the tax to local governments. Those governments buy services with it. Police departments are one service. Fire departments are another. Schools are another. States sometimes add transportation funds for schools. Those funds help pay for busing. The buses support public schools in America. Those schools rest on a principle. Under that principle, an education is owed to every person. Planning the rides to school and back is a huge job. The public school fleet in the United States is enormous. It uses more vehicles than any other mass transit in the country. It also moves more people.

3About 547,000 of these buses were on the road each day in the year 2023. Daily riders made up just over half of the students in public schools. This fleet has more than twice the vehicles of every other mass transit system combined. Several reasons explain the size. The country itself is very large. A huge number of people live in it. Many places have few other ways for students to travel in public. Rural places show this most clearly. Outside the school bus, they often have no public transit at all. Rural routes tend to be complex. They also cover wide ground. Kingman, Arizona, offers an example. The rural buses there cover more ground than the whole state of Delaware. Delaware covers 1,954 square miles. That area is 5,060 square kilometers. Among the fifty states, Delaware is the second smallest. Arizona holds the Kingman Unified School District. That district is far larger. Its area is above 3,000 square miles. That area is 7,779 square kilometers. Take the district as 3,000 square miles. It is bigger than Delaware by 1,046 square miles. The gap is 2,709 square kilometers.

4Planners must keep these long routes efficient. They try to keep daily travel time from growing too large. They set stops that are not too far from homes. Students should be able to walk to a stop. Many districts offer a ride to a clear group. The group is any student living more than 2 miles from school. That distance is 3.2 kilometers. A dangerous walk can also earn a student a seat.
