Crossing a highway is one such danger. Even so, some children still cross in unsafe ways. Around 1910, a Colorado high school had a bus like a stagecoach. Public schools in America started mass rides for students long ago. In the 1800s, many pupils used one-room schoolhouses. Those districts were rural and sparsely settled. Some of those pupils walked. Others rode wagons pulled by horses. Sleds were another way to get there. Districts later found a wagon system more efficient. The wagons collected students. Then the wagons carried them to school. Populations grew, and technology moved ahead. Motor vehicles replaced the horse-drawn wagons. The basic idea stayed the same. Students would still ride in public vehicles.

5Districts set up routes. They lined up large passenger vehicles. The vehicles collected students before school. At day's end they dropped students near home. The big yellow bus familiar now took shape over time. The earliest student vehicles did not look like today's buses. A bus from the 1920s looked more like a long car. Later buses grew so they could hold more students. Yellow was chosen because it is easy to see. Educators wanted other drivers to notice the buses easily. Parents wanted that too. Other drivers could then see a bus and stop in time. Students could board in safety. The law now requires a set color. The color's name is National School Bus Glossy Yellow. Drivers can recognize a school bus in an instant. A photo shows a school bus in 1925. A new goal arrived after that: school integration. Integration brought African American children and white children into the same schools. Before 1954, many schools in America were segregated. Black students were sent to one set of schools. White students were sent to another. Those separate schools were not equal. White students usually got better chances to learn.

6They also got more resources. In 1954 the United States Supreme Court made a ruling. The ruling said African American students had been harmed by segregation's discrimination. Integration then began. A 1954 photo shows a woman and her daughter. The woman is explaining that court ruling. The pair is seated on that court's front steps. The court is in Washington, D.C. For a time, buses mattered a great deal to integration. In the 1970s and the 1980s, districts bused students across old lines. Black students rode to schools that had been white. White students rode the other way. By the 1990s, most districts had stopped that practice. They no longer used busing to undo segregation. A 1973 photo shows white children riding a bus in North Carolina. The ride was part of integration. A 1979 photo shows black children riding a bus in Ohio. That ride was part of integration too. Lately, shutting schools has created a fresh challenge. The process is called consolidation. Several smaller schools join inside one larger building. Sharing a big school can cut costs. Many students can use the same resources.

7Some students must travel much farther, though. The bus system becomes extremely important in those districts. The routes grow larger. They also grow more complex. One rural route in Texas shows how far that can go. In the mid-1990s, some students rode about 100 miles each way. That distance is 160 kilometers. Those students spent more time riding than they spent in class. For students, this bus system is the safest way to travel. The National Safety Council compared buses with private cars. The buses are forty times safer. Districts make drivers take strict safety training. The buses also carry built-in safety features. Emergency exits are one feature. Roofs are reinforced. The way the seats are laid out helps in a crash. Seats sit close together. The backs of the seats are built to absorb a hit. Passengers end up inside a kind of protective box. In most states, belts on these buses are not required. A few states have passed laws that do require them. A flashing stop sign is another safety tool. It warns drivers that students are getting on or off. Cameras let the driver see the inside of the bus.

8They also show what is happening outside. More safety upgrades are likely in the future. When the stop sign swings out, cars must halt. Cars coming from either direction must halt. Belts make riders in private cars much safer. People still debate whether that is true on a school bus. One reason is design. Buses are built to much tougher safety rules. Another reason is the number of riders. A bus often holds more than fifty students. A driver then struggles to check that every belt is on. Some districts are also changing buses to help the environment. One bus in New York runs on an electric engine. That engine does not pollute the air. The bus can go about 120 miles before it must be recharged. That distance is 190 kilometers. Another green change is propane fuel. Propane costs much less than older bus fuel. It pollutes less too. Hybrid buses use electric power and diesel fuel together. In 2007, drivers of those hybrids reported better mileage. The mileage was almost twice that of regular school buses. School buses can also cut pollution in another way.

9They take the place of private vehicles. An average school bus can carry fifty-four students. That removes about thirty-six private vehicles from the road. Those cars would otherwise have driven students to school. Newer green technology adds to that benefit. The result can be cleaner air. A chart compares fuel on a trip of 10 miles. That trip is 16 kilometers. A bus is larger than a car. For one trip of equal length, the bus burns more fuel. Count the passengers, though, and buses use fuel far better. They also pollute far less. Thirty-six family vehicles use 14.4 gallons on that trip. That amount is 54.5 liters. A regular diesel bus uses 1.4 gallons. That amount is 5.3 liters. A hybrid bus, using diesel plus electric power, uses 0.8 gallons. That amount is 3 liters. The bus slows to a stop. Sarah opens her eyes. She is startled to find she had dozed off. She gathers her things. She steps off the bus. The bus pulls from the curb. Its job is done for now. When the school day closes, the bus will be there again.

10It will run the whole trip again, this time in reverse. Rural means a place is countryside, not a city. Discriminated means a person or group was treated unfairly. The reason may be gender. It may be race or age. It may be religion or some other difference. School districts are regions that hold the schools a local group manages. Entitled means a person deserves something or has a right to it. A fleet is a group of vehicles under one owner or one commander. Ships can form a fleet too. Segregated means groups were kept apart. Race is one reason groups have been kept apart. Integration is a process that opens schools and other places to all races. It is the end of segregation. Sparsely means in small numbers, spread thin. The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. Mass transit is public transport that moves many people at once. Buses, subways, and trains can all be mass transit. Transportation is the act of moving people or things from one place to another. A principle is a basic value that guides a choice.

51. How We Learned the Planet Is a Sphere

1In a total lunar eclipse, the Moon's face is crossed by a shadow from Earth. That shadow is noticeably round. A picture named Earthrise entered history in 1968. It is still among the best-known photographs ever made. Three people made up the crew of Apollo 8. No one before them had orbited the Moon. On December 24, 1968, they swung around the Moon a fourth time. Earth was rising over the lunar horizon. They rushed to capture the view. White clouds swirl in the picture. Blue oceans show as well. Both sit above a gray lunar surface that has no life. Night and day are split by a curving shadow on the planet. The sphere of Earth is plain to see. No earlier image had presented that shape so clearly. Thousands of years before any rocket left the ground, people already knew Earth was a sphere. The story of their proof is a chance to use science skills. So is the chance to check the idea for ourselves. Curiosity is a powerful instinct in humans. It has sent questioning minds after problems both large and small in the world around us. Scientists may outdo everyone else in curiosity. A main pursuit of science is to understand the natural world.

2The planet itself might be called the first laboratory. Travelers who crossed land and sea wanted to learn the shape of home. Seen from the surface, the ground can appear flat. Long ago, watchful people still gathered signs that suggested another shape. They started to ask what form the planet truly had. Ideas were put to the test. When a test missed the result they expected, they adjusted the idea. Then they tried again. That cycle is a plain description of the scientific method. The method is an orderly process. A question is posed, and that question is a hypothesis. A test then checks whether the idea is accurate. The aim is a finding that stays true after any number of repeats. It should stay true no matter which person runs the test. For a scientist, this method is the greatest tool. It is what helped show that Earth is round. The cycle can be drawn as six steps. They are question, hypothesis, experiment, analysis, conclusion, and revise. Today, Earth's shape can be checked from high above. Aircraft can do it. Weather balloons can do it. Spacecraft can do it. Before those machines existed, what path led thinkers to a round Earth?

3If anyone puzzled over Earth's shape first, it was likely sailors. Even a watcher on the shore could see what happened to a ship sailing away. The ship did more than grow smaller. It seemed to vanish from the hull upward, as though it were sinking. Human eyesight was not the limit at work. After the ship had slipped past the horizon, a climb up a tall hill could bring the whole vessel back into view. The clue supported a round Earth. As the ship crossed the horizon, Earth's curve hid it piece by piece. A sailor's success depended on knowing that shape. Survival depended on it too. Stars that guide long voyages follow patterns. Only a spherical Earth can explain those patterns. To reject that reality was to risk getting lost. Philosophers brought fame to ancient Greece. It was also famed for sailors who knew their craft. In that era, the word philosopher meant a person who studied science and other subjects. Earth's shape drew the interest of some Greek philosophers. They watched carefully. They thought. They tested. Clues were what they searched for. Aristotle was a genius among those ancient Greeks.

4Around 350 BCE, he saw that travel north or south changes which constellations are visible. Seven stars form the Big Dipper. Together they look like a ladle. From latitude 41 degrees north upward, in the Northern Hemisphere, those stars never leave the sky. Go below 25 degrees south, in the Southern Hemisphere, and the Big Dipper cannot be seen at all. Views like these fit travel along a sphere. They do not fit travel on a flat plane. Lunar eclipses gave Aristotle another line of evidence. Earth's shadow on the Moon stays curved through every lunar eclipse. The shadow is round when the eclipse rides high. It is round when the eclipse sits near the horizon. A spherical Earth is the logical conclusion. About a hundred years afterward, the Greek philosopher Eratosthenes tested the same hypothesis in a new way. His name is said air-uh-TOS-thuh-neez. Sunshine was one of his tools. Shadows were another. He added measurements. He added geometry. Syene was a city in southern Egypt. Its name is said sy-EE-nee. People there reported a noon sight on June 20. The Sun stood straight overhead. They could tell because only on that day did sunlight fall straight down one particular deep well.

5On the same date, at the same hour, Eratosthenes watched a different scene in Alexandria. That Egyptian city lies about 800 kilometers due north of Syene. The distance is also about 500 miles. A tower in sunlight threw a shadow there, and the shadow sat at a slight angle. Straight-down sun over Syene was not straight-down sun over Alexandria. Eight hundred kilometers may feel like a long span. Next to the gap between Earth and the Sun, it is not long at all. Had the world been flat, the Sun's great distance would have placed it directly over both cities. Eratosthenes deduced a spherical Earth from the mismatch in shadows. Egypt is the setting of one image, with sunlight falling straight into a deep well made of stone. He carried the study further. The shadow's angle was part of the work. So was the gap between the two cities. Geometry then yielded Earth's circumference, meaning the distance around the planet. Experts judge his figure fairly close to the true circumference. The real distance is about 40,075 kilometers, or 24,900 miles. More than 2300 years stand between his lifetime and today. High-tech tools were not his to use.

6The result was still impressive. To repeat the experiment, a sunny day is not enough. Two further conditions apply. One site has to sit directly north or south of the other. They must stand at least 322 kilometers apart, which is 200 miles. At each site, a straight marker has to sit perfectly perpendicular to the surface. Observers then measure both shadow angles at one shared moment. At noon, the observer reads angle x, the angle of the marker's shadow. Math can find angle y once angle x is known. For Eratosthenes, the shadow angle at the second site was 0 degrees. At that second site, the noon sun dropped straight into a deep well. The two lines that form angle y must meet at the planet's center. Know the size of one slice, and math can give the circumference of the full circle. Careful minds, working with the scientific method, established that Earth is round. A round form is not unique to Earth. Other planets share it. The Sun shares it. The Moon shares it. Most other large objects in space share it. A telescope makes this easy to see. Unaided eyes can see it too. Gravity is the reason.

7Mass belongs to every physical thing. A huge planet has mass. A grain of sand has mass. Gravity is the way mass draws other mass toward it. A larger mass exerts a stronger gravitational force. Between small objects, that force is too slight to notice. Planets and suns contain enormous mass. Their gravity is therefore immense. From every direction, the pull aims inward at the center. It is powerful enough to compact a planet into a sphere. A sun can be compacted the same way. Crushing a snowball gives a rough picture of the squeeze. Large objects in space mostly end as spheres. On a sphere, every surface point sits as near the center as it can. Some objects lack the mass needed for that squeeze. Asteroids are one example. They are smaller than planets and smaller than moons. Only a few known asteroids carry enough mass, and enough gravity, to become spheres. Feet stay on the ground because of gravity, and that gravity is a function of Earth's mass. Release a rock and it drops. Stand in any spot, and the rock is pulled to the planet's center. The Moon stays in Earth's orbit because of gravitational force.

8Earth stays in orbit around the Sun for the same reason. The rest of the solar system does too. A spherical planet is more than a curious fact. It shapes how people live. It shapes how they build. It shapes how they move. Even a phone call can serve as practical proof. Picture midday in London, England's capital. The friend who picks up lives in Wellington, capital of New Zealand. The friend asks whether the caller knows the hour. It is the middle of the night there. The gap is twelve hours. A globe places these two capitals opposite each other. Sunlight covers one half of the round planet. Shadow covers the other half. Time zones were set up so distant people can manage the hours. They also help people avoid a disruptive call. Gravity presses inward from all sides and forms Earth into a sphere. Big building projects have to reckon with the planet's shape. New York City offers a clear case in the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. Work on it finished in 1964. Two giant towers carry the bridge. Each tower rises 211 meters, or 693 feet. A gap of 1,298 meters separates the towers. That gap is 4,260 feet.

9The towers were not built perfectly parallel. Their tops sit 41.3 millimeters farther apart than their bases. That extra space is one and five-eighths inches. Stability was the goal. Builders therefore allowed for the planet's curvature. The bridge stays firm because of that knowledge of shape. Pilots of airliners must cross a round Earth every day. On a flat map, Madrid in Spain lines up almost due east or west from New York City. A traveler leaving New York might expect the shortest route to Madrid to run due east over the Atlantic Ocean. A glance from the window might instead show ice on the Arctic Ocean. The aircraft is on a path called a great circle route. Over a spherical surface, that path is the shorter one. Time is saved. Fuel is saved. Money is saved. On a flat map, the shortest link between two points is a straight line. A string laid on a globe shows something else. A journey from North America to Europe may pass over the Arctic for that reason. Long-distance navigation of every kind rests on life on a sphere. Sailors have steered by this idea for thousands of years. For decades, pilots of airliners have steered by that same idea.

10Astronauts have done it too. Livelihoods have depended on a round Earth. Lives have depended on it as well. Treat Earth as a sphere, and the world grows easier to understand. Time zones fit that picture. So does travel over long distances. Scientific proof, once recognized and used, opens the way to newer and deeper answers. Working through a question on our own builds scientific skill. That skill lets curiosity choose the next path. It also helps us judge whether another person's ideas are sound. Practice makes thinking sharper. Bass guitar practice makes a stronger musician. Basketball practice makes a stronger athlete. A route to proving Earth's spherical shape sits inside the scientific method. Good questions can be formed with it. Exploration can proceed with it. Observations can be explained with it. Questions and observations can be tested to see whether analysis still supports them. A mismatch with the hypothesis is not the end. The test can be run again. New questions can be asked. Different tests can be tried. Practices that have already been proved can be trusted to yield trustworthy answers. Those answers can send a curious mind still farther.

52. Isaac Newton and the Rules of Force

1A popular legend ties Newton's grasp of gravity to an apple that struck his head. What really happened is quieter. What he saw was an apple dropping ahead of where he stood. That fall led him to understand gravity. Falling fruit seldom catches our interest. Eyes usually go to grander sights, such as a rainbow or a sunset. Isaac Newton cared about natural events on both scales. Careful attention to ordinary events made him ponder the mechanics beneath them. Study and experiment then produced groundbreaking scientific theories. The theories cover light. They cover force. They cover motion. Modern-day physics is built on that foundation. Christmas Day of 1642 was the day Isaac Newton was born. The place was Woolsthorpe, an English village. It sits about 100 miles north of London, a distance of 161 kilometers. His father was a middle-class British farmer. Isaac was that farmer's only child. The father had died two months before the birth. The boy never met him. His mother remarried when Isaac was two. He was sent to live with his grandmother. Her home was in Grantham, a village nearby. Nine years later she lost her second husband. Only then did Isaac live with her again. She sent for him because she wanted help managing her property. The work did not fit him well. Outdoor time pleased him. Still, thinking suited him better than doing.

2Reading beneath an apple tree appealed more than tending herds of cattle. Before long he was back at school in Grantham. Neighbors were impressed by a skill he showed while young. He built working models of machines. Clocks were among the models. Windmills were among them. Study continued. He prepared hard for college. Trinity College had been founded in 1592. Queen Elizabeth I was the founder. Newton enrolled there in 1661. His tie to Cambridge University would last a long time. Students took a traditional course of study. It opened with Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher. In Aristotle's picture, Earth sat at the center of the universe. Nature, for him, was built from basic elements. Earth, air, fire, and water could combine in that account. Beyond Cambridge's walls, a different style of thought had taken hold. The Scientific Revolution, begun in the Renaissance, was moving across Europe. A group of modern philosophers wanted explanations that were more scientific. They also wanted explanations that were mathematical. René Descartes was one such thinker. He pictured the physical world as tiny particles. The particles never stopped moving. Any event in nature, he said, came from particles acting on each other. The newer perspective reached Newton, and he became intrigued. Maybe those physical interactions could be named. Maybe they could be measured. For a long time he had asked why falling objects always head downward.

3He had also asked why light sometimes breaks into different colors. The new way of thinking looked like a path toward the answers he sought. A side account of the Scientific Revolution belongs with this story. Until the sixteenth century, European science leaned heavily on ancient Greek philosophy. Then mathematical and scientific ideas arrived from the Islamic world. The way European scientists investigated nature started to change. Many people trace the revolution's start to Copernicus. He was a Polish astronomer. Math let him propose a new center for the solar system. That center was the Sun, rather than Earth. Ideas passing between cultures did a great deal to feed the Scientific Revolution. One drawing in Newton's notebooks shows calculus being used to solve problems. Course homework lost his attention. Notebooks filled instead with notes he wrote himself. The title he gave them was Certain Philosophical Questions. He learned eagerly. Soon he had mastered the writings of the new thinkers. From that base he built theories of his own. He built calculations of his own. A form of calculus was his own invention. The math is used to analyze curves. It is also used to analyze the areas under those curves. Graduation from Cambridge came in 1665. He was ready to summarize his findings. Mathematical scholars in England were the audience he had in mind. Scholars in other parts of Europe were part of that audience too.

4Fate set a different plan. In August of that year, bubonic plague broke out. The illness was deadly. Officials at Cambridge shut the university for two years. Newton stayed quarantined at home. Experiments and writing were nearly all he had to do. Important theories about light took shape in that same stretch of time. Descartes had called light a type of motion. In his view, the motion traveled through natural substances. Air was one such substance. Water was another. Newton granted that this told how light travels. It did not tell what light is. Experiments with a prism followed in 1666. White light, passed through the prism, separated into bands of color. His notes describe pure white light as colored rays combined. Tilt the path through glass or through water, and one ray shows on its own. The name of that process is refraction. Rainbows, he had discovered, are made this way. A picture of a prism shows the colors being pulled apart. He believed a glass lens would always refract white light to some degree. Anything viewed through the lens would look slightly changed. In 1668 that knowledge became a new instrument. He developed the first reflecting telescope. Mirrors focused the light, and lenses did not. The images came out more accurate. Cambridge opened its doors again in 1667. By 1669 he headed the university's mathematics department.

5The role required lectures. He could pick the topic. He chose his recent work on light. The book Opticks held that explanation. Word of the lectures reached the Royal Society of London. The members asked to examine a model of the reflecting telescope. They were impressed enough to invite him in as a member. A delighted Newton, in 1672, handed them a paper on light and color. Robert Hooke did not share the delight. He was one of the society's leaders. Before Newton, Hooke had been treated as the top expert on optics. His review of the new paper was scathing. Later he charged that Newton had taken ideas from Hooke's own earlier work. Rage followed, and a feud between the two men lasted for life. More harsh reviews from other scholars upset Newton further. A nervous breakdown came in 1678. He left public life completely. A likeness of Newton dates to about 1680. Stepping away from public life gave him time. He could evaluate the work. He could refine it. Interaction between substances still puzzled him. So did interaction between objects. Why will one chemical react with a second chemical, yet ignore another? Why does water seem to climb through a narrow space? Why do the Moon and Earth stay in orbit? A governing principle, he thought, might cover these mysteries. Force and attraction would sit at its center.

6Letters from Hooke, the old rival, started a discussion. The subject was the elliptical path of planets. Hooke said the paths fail to be circles because two influences are out of balance. One influence is attraction. The other is the velocity of a moving object. Momentum pulls one way. The attraction toward nearby objects pulls the other way. The contest is a tug-of-war. Hooke had the right idea. Proving the statement was difficult. Newton supplied the proof. His tool was calculus. Both Earth and the Moon follow elliptical orbits. Elliptical means oval-shaped. Velocity and gravity are not quite equal, and that mismatch makes the ovals. With elliptical orbits understood, calculus could do finer work. Planetary motion could be predicted more accurately. Lunar motion could be explained more accurately. Their real movement could be shown. Modern missions to the Moon, among other efforts, were informed by that knowledge. A diagram places the Sun, Earth, and the Moon, and it traces each orbit. Halley's Comet is named for an astronomer who solved a puzzle of three sightings. The comets of 1521, of 1607, and of 1682 were a single comet. It comes back near Earth every seventy-five years. The next return is projected for 2061. Edmond Halley learned of the calculations Newton had made. A visit followed in 1684. Halley asked Newton to demonstrate the principles at work.

7What Newton sent was a short essay titled De Motu. The words mean On Motion. Most of the essay concerns how planets move. Newton still thought the account fell short. Force and attraction, across all of nature, were not yet explained well enough. He went on refining both the ideas and the calculations inside De Motu. Two and a half years after that visit, the year 1687 brought his masterpiece. The book carried the title The Principia. Its full name is Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. It was a landmark. The scientific world was rocked by it. His stature grew in country after country. Three laws of motion are set out in the book. Law one concerns a body, or an object, that is at rest. It stays at rest unless some force acts on it. Floating objects in outer space illustrate the point. No force is acting on them. A second part of the law covers an object that is already moving. Without a force acting on it, the motion continues unchanged. Picture an astronaut throwing an object. The object travels in a straight line. Direction stays the same. Speed stays the same. Change waits on some interfering force. Gravity from a planet could be that force. A bump from space debris could be that force. Resting or moving, an object has inertia. Inertia is the tendency to continue whatever it is already doing.

8More than one force usually acts on an object. Whether motion starts, or changes, depends on how those forces balance. Equal forces leave a resting object unmoved. They leave a moving object on its same path. Unequal forces start a resting object into motion. They can also change a moving object's speed. They can change its direction. A bowling ball and a soccer ball can both be thrown. The throws are not alike. Mass is far greater in the bowling ball. Raise one behind the head, and the thrower might tip over backward. Law two sets out how mass and motion connect. The matter inside an object is what mass measures. Put a great force on an object with less mass, and you get more motion. That extra motion is acceleration. The same force on a more massive object yields less acceleration. Throw a soccer ball and a bowling ball with equal force. The soccer ball goes faster. It also goes farther. Less mass is the reason. Law three states a pairing. Each action is paired with a reaction of equal size in the opposite direction. Daily life is full of examples. Riding a skateboard is one. A foot pushes, and the wheels carry the board ahead. A harder kick raises the board's speed. Forward motion is the reaction. The foot's backward push is the action matched to it.

9A picture catches a skateboarder demonstrating that third law. A chart asks what a person weighs in different places. On Earth the mass is 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On Earth the weight is 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On the Moon the mass is still 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On the Moon the weight is 7.5 kilograms, or 16.5 pounds. On Jupiter the mass is again 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On Jupiter the weight is 107 kilograms, or 236 pounds. Mass is not the same thing as weight. Mass means how much matter an object contains. Any object that has mass pulls on every other mass. The strength of that pull depends on the masses involved. Mass itself does not change. Weight does, because weight depends on gravity. Your weight is how strongly Earth attracts you. The Moon's mass is smaller than Earth's. Standing on the Moon, you would feel less attraction. Your weight would drop. Jupiter's mass is larger. Standing there, the attraction would be stronger. Your weight would rise. The chart invites a look at how weight and gravity relate. Some scientists resisted the ideas Newton offered. Many others came to treat them as a great achievement. Young mathematicians flocked to Cambridge, hoping to learn more. Newton turned into something of a celebrity. A friendship grew with Charles Montagu.

10Montagu later became a powerful politician. Across the next few years, Newton's focus drifted. Politics drew him, and science drew him less. In 1696, Montagu made him Warden of the Mint. Cambridge was behind him by 1701, when he moved to London. Pay for the post was good. Earlier wardens had been less active. Newton oversaw the making of coins in a direct way. Election as president of the Royal Society came in 1703. Knighthood came in 1705. No scientist had been knighted before him. Later years were spent refining Principia. He revised that greatest work. New papers did not appear. Death came in 1727. Wealth and wide fame were his by then. Queen Anne had performed the knighting. A knighthood remains a high honor now. Jousting is not part of it. Armor is not required. Theories were only part of Newton's work. Mathematics let him demonstrate how each theory operated. Notes taken with care, and calculations made with care, carried him far. A bookish boy from a village became one of the greatest scientists ever known. He also became one of the most influential. Our picture of the universe was changed for good. Woolsthorpe Manor was once the family home. An apple tree still grows there. Did that tree inspire the gravity theory? Nobody knows. What is known is that he liked to read in its shade.

53. Japan's Quiet Giant

1Ocean wind hits this mountain and is forced to rise. Unusual cloud shapes form because of that. People call one shape a cap cloud. Contents. A calm peak. A national treasure. Fire under the rock. Plants and animals. A holy sign. Climbing the slopes. Many gifts in one place. Words to know. Religious shrines of great importance stand on the land nearby. Cherry blossoms stand there too. A calm peak. Earth's tallest peaks are famous for fierce wind. Cold is part of their fame. Steep cliffs of rock are part of it. Ice is part of it. Visitors often meet a harsh scene. They often meet a scene that does not welcome them. The highest mountain in Japan does not feel that way. Scientists class it as a volcano that is still active. What it offers instead is peace. It also offers calm. For most of each year, snow lies on top. Many people place it among the loveliest mountains known. Lots of people in Japan see more than stone. They see a symbol of the nation. They see ground set aside for worship. Through the past it has stirred human imagination. It still does. A national treasure. The summit rises 3,776 meters over the country around it. In feet, that is 12,388.

2The site is about 100 kilometers from Tokyo, on the southwest side. The same gap is 60 miles. Honshu is the island beneath it. No island in Japan is larger. The Pacific lies roughly 46 kilometers away, or 29 miles. A national park holds the peak at its heart. The park's name is Fuji-Hakone-Izu. Say the name in three beats. First comes FOO-jee. Next comes HAH-koh-neh. Last comes EE-zoo. The park was established in 1936. Landforms shaped by volcanoes fill the park. Hot springs are there. Coastlines are there. Islands are there. During 2013, UNESCO acted. It belongs to the United Nations. It gave the mountain the standing of a World Heritage Site. Protection is part of the standing. Conservation is part of it. UNESCO chose the peak because of its cultural weight for people in Japan. A map shows the location. How the cone was built. Old Fuji erupted and covered Komitake with lava. New Fuji erupted later and covered both older volcanoes with lava. The outline is a cone. Three enormous plates of crust meet here. The Pacific Plate slides underneath the Philippine Plate. Heat farther down melts stone. Volcanic action comes from that melt. A Buddhist legend tells another origin. An earthquake, it says, raised the mountain in 286 bce.

3The real growth took far longer. The base may be 65 million years old. What people see today grew mainly as lava stacked higher. Hundreds of thousands of years passed during that stacking. Eruptions in a span of 2,200 years add up to more than seventy. The greatest blast written down took place in the year 864. Writers mark that year with ce. The latest large blast took place in 1707. A massive earthquake had come less than two months before it. Volcanic ash fell in huge clouds upon Edo. The modern name of Edo is Tokyo. Villages nearby were wiped out. Farmland nearby was wiped out. Famine followed. It lasted ten years. Since then the volcano has stayed dormant. Scientists still judge it active. They look for another eruption someday. The base stretches roughly 50 kilometers from side to side. That width is 30 miles. One side of the crater sits about 500 meters from the other side. That width is 1,600 feet. Japan was hit by a huge quake in the year 2011. Afterward, scientists feared this peak might erupt. When a large quake hits near a volcano, an eruption often is signaled. Gauges recorded more volcanic action. The blast did not arrive.

4Tokyo is among the biggest cities anywhere, and the volcano is close. Officials put fresh safety measures to work. More than a million residents might have to leave quickly. A new plan lays out that escape. Watching continues with care. A warning system stands ready. Lava would threaten people if an eruption came. Ash riding the wind would threaten them. Hot rocks mixed with gases can rush downhill. That rush would threaten them too. When the sky is clear, Tokyo can see the mountain. Plants and animals. Many sorts of plants grow on these slopes. Climb in elevation and the habitat turns colder. Each higher band is colder than the band under it. Temperature helps decide which plants a vegetation zone can hold. The mountainous zone grows several trees. Beech grows there. Oak grows there. Maple grows there. Cedar grows there. Fir grows there. A thick forest fills part of this zone. The forest is Aokigahara. Say ou-kee-gah, then HAH-rah. Another name for it is Sea of Trees. The Asagiri highland is in this zone too. Say ah-SAH, then gee-ree. Grass covers that highland. Cattle ranches use it. At lower altitudes, hemlock grows. Fir grows there as well. Farther up, birch takes over in places. Larch takes over in places.

5Past about 2,200 meters, trees do not grow. That height is 7,218 feet. Snow is common in the alpine zone. Readings stay under zero. Moss can live there. Lichen can live there. The mountain is home to thirty-seven mammal types. The Japanese serow is one type. It is a goat-antelope. Say suh, then ROHS. Japanese deer live on the mountain. An Asiatic black bear appears only at times. Japanese squirrels show up more often. Foxes show up more often. They occupy many habitats. The range runs from the base to nearly the upper end of the subalpine band. Serows keep to forest in the mountainous zone. Bird types that breed around the base number more than a hundred. Mixed habitats are the reason. A few kinds remain all year. Other kinds migrate through the area. Some live here in summer. Some live here in winter. Amphibians are few. Reptiles are few. One tree frog is part of that small group. Insects reach their peak numbers in the mountainous zone. Many sorts of butterflies are among them. Japanese paradise flycatchers keep to the slopes down low. A male's tail may grow to three times his body length. A picture shows a Shinto shrine. The shrine honors this mountain's spirit. A holy sign.

6Japan holds the peak as its sacred symbol. People have seen a sacred mountain here for as long as Japan has had residents. Near 800 ce, early people built a shrine close to the base. They wanted the shrine to quiet a god. They believed that god made the volcano erupt. Two faiths lead religious life in Japan. Shinto is one. Buddhism is the other. Each faith holds the mountain sacred. Shinto practice says a goddess makes her home on it. She is Konohana Sakuya Hime. Hear the name in parts. Koh-noh-HAH-nah comes first. SAH-koo-yah comes next. HEE-meh comes last. She is goddess of trees when they flower. Cherry blossoms are the sign linked to her. Shrines raised for her sit in more than one place. Some sit at the base. Some sit on the summit. Some sit on the crater floor. Buddhists give the summit a special word, zenjo. The word points to meditation brought into a perfect state. Both faiths treat the climb as important. Worshippers go up as a religious pilgrimage. Where the name came from. Certainty is missing. A folktale from Japan links the peak to life without end. The tale uses fu-shi. Say foo, then SHEE. The meaning is not death. Another trail of thought leads to Fuchi.

7She was a goddess of fire. Her people were the Ainu. The Ainu are described as Japan's earliest people. Names used in Japan today include Fuji-san. They include Fujiyama. They include Fuji no Yama. San is a word for mountain. Yama is a word for mountain too. Katsushika Hokusai made art from 1760 until 1849. Say kaht-SOOSH-kah, then HAWK-sie. He took the peak as a mark of life that lasts forever. Between 1826 and 1833 he cut a set of woodblock prints. He described the set as thirty-six views. No Japanese artwork is better known. He added ten prints to the set later on. In 1834 he produced a further set. That set holds one hundred views. One print carries the title The Great Wave off Kanagawa. The mountain appears behind the wave. Around the world, that picture ranks with the most famous art ever made. Seen from a distance, many people report, the beauty grows. Close up, much of the face is bare rock left by the volcano. Dust lies on it. Climbing the slopes. Tourist sites in Japan rarely draw a bigger crowd than this peak. It may also be the mountain that the most people climb. In a year, climbers can number four hundred thousand.

8Japanese visitors make up close to two out of every three. Judged by hard mountain craft, the path is not a hard one. Special gear is not needed. Going up feels more like a long backpack walk. It feels less like a technical climb. The challenge is real even so. Rocks cover the trails. Weather turns often. Wind shows up again and again. Pavement reaches the halfway line. Public rides go as far as the 5th station. The station's height is 2,305 meters, or 7,562 feet. Four main trails leave from that point. Hours to the top depend on the trail chosen. The short end is four hours. The long end is ten hours. Descent takes about half the climbing time. Lakes often build a stunning picture, and one view is a sunset mirrored in the water. Climbing is officially open from the start of July, or from mid-July, until mid-September. Trails stay open in that window. Services stay open. Weather is fairly mild. Snow has usually melted. Crowds come with the season. At some points, people have to queue and wait their turn. Winter brings very hard conditions. The advice is to leave winter climbs to people with the deepest experience. Reaching the top is not the only aim.

9Lakes beside the route please visitors. Shrines please them too. Shiraito Falls is a favorite stop. It is counted with the most beautiful falls in Japan. Mount Tenjo is close. Photographers use it for a fine look at the higher summit. Many gifts in one place. Worldwide, the peak stands as a mark of peace. It stands as a mark of calm. Because the volcano is active, it also marks the power in nature. It marks danger as well. For some, a look at the mountain becomes a spiritual moment. Beauty that will not hold still inspires people who paint. It inspires people who take photographs. It inspires people who write poems. Habitats here suit many plants. They suit many animals. Those same habitats draw hikers. They draw people who love wild nature. So many gifts reach so many kinds of people. Little wonder the peak is loved as few places on Earth are loved. Special sights. On a few days each year, the top aligns with the Sun at sunrise. It can also align at sunset. Light flashes in a star shape, and the moment is dramatic. The name for it is Diamond Fuji. Across a lake, the flash can reflect. The reflected pair is called a Double Diamond Fuji.

10If the Moon aligns with the top, the sight is called a Pearl Fuji. Words to know. Alpine points to high peaks and to whatever lives higher than trees can grow. Sacred points to a god, a faith, or a spiritual aim, and it can mean holy. Altitude is a measure of height, starting from sea level or from the ground. A shrine is a place set apart as a holy honor for a person or for a god. Conservation is care that keeps historical or cultural things, buildings, and sites from being lost. The summit is the highest spot a mountain has. A tourist visits a place in order to enjoy it or to learn about it. Dormant means resting, with the ability to act again. A famine is food falling terribly short across a wide region. A volcano is a break in the planet's crust. A mountain often holds that break, and a crater may ring it. Gases can spill out. Ash can spill out. Lava can spill out. A habitat is the home setting a plant or an animal uses in nature. A pilgrimage is a trip toward a holy site or another site set apart, and a shrine may be the goal.

54. Jupiter, the Planet That Keeps Changing

1Sections of this book follow. A Night of Surprise. Where Jupiter Sits and What It Is. The Stuff Inside Jupiter. A Weather Report. Moons Around the Giant. Rings You Cannot See from Here. Robot Visitors. Watching It Yourself. What Comes Later. Words and Topics. A sketch is dated August 7, 1985. A Night of Surprise. Night-sky watching with a telescope is a pleasure of mine. Most objects, I have learned, look the same on every visit. Surprise broke that pattern one night in August 1985. Jupiter was in the eyepiece. A pencil sketch of the planet was underway. Then I noticed the stripes. They are swirly and full of color. They were moving. They were changing while I watched. Excitement from that discovery is still with me. Finishing the sketch grew harder because of it. July 1994 brought another change, and again I watched it happen. A comet had broken into big chunks. Its name was Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. That night was the last night those chunks collided with the planet. Several dark bruises marked the impact spots. I drew those as well. Seeing them through a telescope felt wonderful. Jupiter holds the title of largest planet in our solar system. Night-sky brightness puts it near the top as well. Skip the telescope, and it could pass for a star. Surprises keep turning up. I think no planet is more exciting. A sketch is dated July 16, 1994. Where Jupiter Sits and What It Is. Distance from the Sun is about 484 million miles. That is 779 million kilometers. Earth is five times closer to the Sun than Jupiter is. Counting outward, Jupiter is planet number five. Earth is planet number three. A single trip around the Sun takes Jupiter 12 Earth-years. The distance is that great. Giant of our solar system is a fair title. Diameter across the middle, the equator, is about 89,000 miles.

2That is 143,000 kilometers. Picture Earth as a small grape. Jupiter would then be a large grapefruit. A name note belongs here. Ancient Rome supplied the name. More than 2,000 years have passed since then. Romans treated Jupiter as king over the other gods. Jove was another name for him. His weapon was a thunderbolt. In their stories, Saturn ruled the universe before anyone else. That name now belongs to another planet. His children overthrew him. Jupiter was one of those children. Neptune was one. Pluto was one. Marriage joined Jupiter to the goddess Juno. Mars was born to them. Vulcan was born to them too. A diagram of our solar system shows Mars, Earth, Venus, and Mercury. The Sun is marked. Jupiter and Saturn are marked. An asteroid belt is marked. Uranus and Neptune are marked. Jupiter's path around the Sun runs between Mars and Saturn. Where does Earth sit compared with Jupiter? One turn on its axis takes Jupiter 9 hours and 55 minutes. No other planet spins faster. A day there lasts only that long. 9 hours and 55 minutes. Earth's own spin raises a question. How long is one full turn on its axis? A hint asks how long one day lasts. A note on origins: Jupiter formed inside a vast cloud made of gas and of dust. The Sun formed in that cloud too. Every other planet in our solar system did as well. The time was 4.6 billion years ago. A picture shows a younger solar system than ours. Dusty disks orbit the central star. Planets are thought most likely to form in those disks. A size comparison lines up Venus, Mercury, Earth, and Mars with the Sun and Jupiter. Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune appear as well. The drawing sets each planet beside the others so sizes can be compared.

3A question asks how many Earths, set side by side, could stretch across Jupiter. Middle widths and usual gaps from the Sun are listed next. Mercury's middle is 3,032 miles, or 4,879 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 35,980,000 miles, or 57,910,000 kilometers. Venus has a middle of 7,521 miles, or 12,104 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 67,240,000 miles, or 108,210,000 kilometers. Earth has a middle of 7,926 miles, or 12,756 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 92,960,000 miles, or 149,600,000 kilometers. Mars has a middle of 4,222 miles, or 6,794 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 141,620,000 miles, or 227,920,000 kilometers. Jupiter has a middle of 88,846 miles, or 142,984 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 483,780,000 miles, or 778,570,000 kilometers. Saturn has a middle of 74,898 miles, or 120,536 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 890,750,000 miles, or 1,433,530,000 kilometers. Uranus has a middle of 31,763 miles, or 51,118 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 1,784,860,000 miles, or 2,872,460,000 kilometers. Neptune has a middle of 30,775 miles, or 49,528 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 2,793,100,000 miles, or 4,495,060,000 kilometers. The Stuff Inside Jupiter. Earth has a solid surface you can walk on. Not every planet is like that. Jupiter is mostly a huge ball of gases and of liquids. Hydrogen is the main material, as in the Sun. Helium is the other main material. Those two are the lightest chemical elements. Water is present too. Ammonia is present. Methane is present. Clouds of gas make the stripes I saw through my telescope. The stripes are swirly. Colors include reddish, whitish, and yellowish. Zones are the stripes that look bright and wide. They are clouds of gas. Belts are the stripes that look dark and thin. They are clouds of gas too.

4Belts and zones both travel around the planet. Their winds do not agree. Zones blow from west to east. Belts blow from east to west. A note on elements: they are the simplest materials known. Natural elements number 92. Every other material is a mix of those elements. A note on molecules: nothing smaller still counts as that material or that substance. Atoms are the smaller particles. A molecule needs at least two of them. Water is written H2O. Each water molecule holds two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen. A drawing labels H, H, and O. Layers of Jupiter are shown in a diagram. Hydrogen is in the gas atmosphere. Helium is there too. So are methane, ammonia, and water. A ball of rock and of ice sits at the center. Liquid metallic hydrogen is a layer. Liquid hydrogen is a layer. Scientists think these layers stack inside the planet. Under the thin, cloudy atmosphere, gases become liquids. Clouds overhead press down with great weight. Gas molecules are forced very near one another. Molecules sit nearer one another in liquids than they do in gases. Farther down, liquid hydrogen starts to act as a liquid metal. That metallic hydrogen moves through the planet's interior. At the very center, the deepest part, rock and ice may form a core. That core may be bigger than Earth. Scientists are still unsure what the core is really like. A Weather Report. Have you heard today's weather from Jupiter? I heard an average temperature near minus 236 degrees Fahrenheit. That is minus 149 degrees Celsius. The cold is serious. Highest cloud tops can be a different story. Heat might reach 1,500 degrees Fahrenheit on the cloud tops that face the Sun most directly. That is 800 degrees Celsius. Winds today blow out of the north.

5Speed is about 400 miles an hour. That is 650 kilometers an hour. Hundreds of swirling storms cover the planet. They resemble gigantic hurricanes. Do not get caught in one. Largest of the storms is the Great Red Spot. Its width could hold three Earths side by side. A telescope on Earth can see this storm. More than 300 years of raging have not stopped it. Giant storms are part of the weather, and the Great Red Spot is the famous example. Huge lightning flashes are part of it. Winds of hundreds of miles an hour are part of it. Seeing the planet from space is a subject of its own. Many sharp photographs of Jupiter have come from the Hubble Space Telescope. Other planets have been photographed too. Galaxies and other deep-space objects have been photographed. Fine detail is possible because Earth is far below the telescope's orbit, under the atmosphere. Photos from the ground can blur because of that atmosphere. A high orbit avoids the blur. The year 1990 is when astronauts set the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. They rode the space shuttle Discovery. Later shuttle missions added new equipment. Equipment updates left it working as late as 2025. A picture shows that orbiting telescope above Earth. Huge lightning flashes have been reported. They light the storm clouds. Would you pack a picnic for a day like that? Moons Around the Giant. At least 95 moons of many sizes orbit Jupiter. Sixteen of them are more than 6 miles wide. That width is 10 kilometers. Four moons are the largest. Their names are Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. An Italian astronomer found them in 1610. His name was Galileo Galilei. Say it GAL-uh-LAY-oh. These huge moons are known as the Galilean satellites. A pair of binoculars is enough to see them.

6Ganymede is said GAN-uh-meed. It is Jupiter's largest moon. It is also the largest moon in the whole solar system. Mountains cover the surface. Valleys cover it. Craters cover it. Ice mixed with rock is there too. Callisto is said kuh-LIHS-toh. Many craters cover it. Comets made them when they crashed into the moon. Asteroids made them too. An ocean of salty water may lie under the surface. Europa may hide a similar ocean. Europa is said yu-ROH-puh. Ice covers the surface. Deep cracks run through that ice. Large chunks are split apart. They resemble icebergs on Earth. These icebergs are the size of cities on Earth. Under the cold, cracked ice, a deep ocean of warm water may wait in the dark. Scientists think alien creatures might live in that ocean, if the ocean is real. Io is said EYE-oh. More than 300 volcanoes mark the surface. Sulfur dioxide gas leaves in hot plumes. Bubbling flows of melted rock shoot out too. That rock is lava. Chemicals in the lava flows paint the surface in different colors. Yellow appears. Red appears. Orange appears. Green appears. A note on those volcanoes: rock and other material pour out of the deep interior in such quantity that Io has turned inside out many times. Loki is one of those volcanoes. Its heat output beats the combined output of all volcanoes on Earth. Sizes and usual gaps from Jupiter come next. Io's diameter is 2,264 miles, or 3,643 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 262,000 miles, or 421,600 kilometers. Europa's diameter is 1,940 miles, or 3,122 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 416,900 miles, or 670,900 kilometers. Ganymede's diameter is 3,270 miles, or 5,262 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 664,900 miles, or 1,070,000 kilometers. Callisto's diameter is 2,996 miles, or 4,821 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 1,170,000 miles, or 1,883,000 kilometers.

7A discovery that changed ideas: Galileo lived from 1564 to 1642. Important finds came first from him, using a tool his age had only just gained. The tool was the telescope. In 1610 that telescope showed him Jupiter's four largest moons. Many people then believed something else. They thought the planets revolved around Earth. They thought the Sun did too. Moons going around Jupiter were the first evidence against that belief. Not everything moves around Earth. Other scientists grew more willing to accept a different path. The Sun is what Earth circles. The other planets circle it too. Rings Around the Giant. Saturn once seemed to be the only planet with rings. From Earth, a telescope can see rings around that planet and no other. Surprise came in 1979. The Voyager spacecraft flew near Jupiter. Rings around the planet showed up in the camera pictures. Four rings showed in those Voyager pictures. They are much thinner than Saturn's rings. Saturn's rings are made partly of large ice chunks. Dust in tiny bits is what Jupiter's rings are made of. The idea is that meteoroids struck the moons. Dust was thrown into space. That dust collected into rings. A craft passing close to this giant planet can see the main ring. Tiny particles that make the ring create a fuzz around it. Robot Visitors. Many spacecraft have been launched toward Jupiter by NASA. NASA means National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The agency belongs to the United States. These robot explorers send pictures back to Earth. Other information rides along. Radio waves carry the reports. Signals that reach a radio ride on that same kind of energy. They carry signals to televisions too. Two craft led the way. One was Pioneer 10. The other was Pioneer 11. Jupiter had never been photographed from so close before those pictures.

8The years were 1973 and 1974. Those photos showed clouds more colorful than people had believed. The clouds were also more complex. Much of our knowledge arrived from several NASA craft. Pioneer was one. Voyager was one. Ulysses was one. Galileo was one. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 made finds in 1979. Rings were one find. Lightning was another. Auroras were another. Auroras are colorful shows of light. On Earth, aurora borealis is the northern lights. Aurora australis is the southern lights. Energy particles leave the Sun and hit gas in the atmosphere. That meeting creates Jupiter's auroras. Big features on the moons were another Voyager find. Volcanoes are among them. Ice is among them. Craters are among them. The year 1992 brought Ulysses near Jupiter. It passed close again from 2003 to 2004. How strong Jupiter's surrounding magnetic field is was one measurement. Charged particles trapped by that field were studied. No spacecraft before Galileo had orbited Jupiter. Circling lasted from 1995 to 2003. The mysterious planet was studied. Its moons were studied. A small probe was released. The probe parachuted into the atmosphere. Instruments measured wind speed. They measured how much of different chemicals the atmosphere held. Watching It Yourself. To the eye, Jupiter could be mistaken for a bright star. Look toward the south in the sky if you want to find it. Only certain times of the year work. Exact place and time can be found in a local newspaper. Check the weather section or the astronomy section. An astronomy magazine can help. A website can help. Binoculars reveal the four largest moons. Night by night, you can watch them change position around the planet. A telescope of medium power shows the belts and the zones. The Great Red Spot shows too. Night follows night, and each of these looks different.

9Sketching what you see is fun. A certain kind of telescope lets you use a camera instead, and take photos. A chart for March 24, 1997, says Rise time is 3:35 a.m. PST. Set time is 2:03 p.m. PST. The horizon is marked E, SE, S, SW, and W. A refracting telescope is labeled with its lens and its eyepiece. A reflecting telescope is labeled with its mirrors. Two telescope designs matter most. One is the refracting telescope. The other is the reflecting telescope. A large lens in the refracting kind focuses light rays from an object. The focus is a point inside the telescope. Mirrors do that focusing job in the reflecting kind. Either kind is viewed through an eyepiece. The eyepiece shows you where those light rays meet. What you see is the object, made larger. What Comes Later. A big ball of surprises is a good description of Jupiter. That is why the planet stays exciting. New knowledge about this huge world keeps arriving. The next discovery cannot be predicted. Many new plans aim at Jupiter and at its moons. One plan would send a spacecraft from the United States and from Europe. The landing target is the moon Europa. The craft would melt through the icy surface. Study would turn to the ocean scientists believe may lie inside Europa. Ocean life on this moon might be discovered. Plenty remains to look forward to. Something new about this giant of surprises might someday be yours to find. A closing note: spin on Jupiter is slowing. Gravity from its moons is pulling on it. Earth is going through the same change because of its own moon. Words to Know. Asteroids are small rocky objects. They revolve around the Sun. An astronomer is a scientist. The subject covers planets. It covers stars. It covers galaxies.

10It covers other objects in the universe. Learning about whatever is out in space is the field called astronomy. An atmosphere is a layer of gases. It can surround a planet, a star, or a moon. An axis is an imaginary line. A planet, or another object, turns around that line. A comet is an object in space made of ice and dust. Near the Sun, it grows a long, bright tail. Craters are holes in the ground. Objects from space strike and leave them. To find a diameter, draw a straight line. Pass the line through the middle of a circle. Or pass it through the middle of a sphere. Stop where the outside edge is. Around a planet's middle, an equator is a circle that is only imagined. Helium is often a gas. Among chemical elements, only one is lighter. Hydrogen, often a gas, is that lighter element. Around a magnet, or around a planet, a magnetic field is the region where the force reaches. Magnetic force can be felt there. Meteoroids are particles of metal or of stone. They travel through space. An orbit is the path one celestial body follows around a larger one. A planet or a moon can follow that path. The Sun can be the larger body. Electric force and magnetic force make patterns. Those patterns are radio waves. They carry information in radio broadcasts and in television broadcasts. Take the Sun. Add every celestial body that travels around it. That is the solar system. Topics include Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. Spacecraft listed are Discovery, Galileo, Pioneer, Ulysses, and Voyager. Galileo Galilei is listed. The Great Red Spot is listed. Jove is listed.
