55. Languages That May Die Out

1A world map marks languages talked about in this book. Mandan belongs to North Dakota and South Dakota, in the United States. Hawaiian belongs to Hawaii, in the United States. Taíno belongs to the Caribbean Islands. Languages of Aboriginal peoples and of Torres Strait Islander peoples belong to Australia. Swahili belongs to the coast of East Africa. Languages of Inuit peoples and of Aleut peoples belong to the United States, Canada, and Greenland. Maori belongs to New Zealand. Languages resemble living things. They grow when people use them to share ideas. They spread. They change. Sometimes a language fades. It can die out completely. The Linguistic Society of America says more and more languages are becoming endangered. An endangered language may die out soon. Anthropologists are scientists who study cultures. They sometimes set endangered languages beside endangered species. Without care and protection, the languages may go extinct. Often only a few elders still speak one. Young people no longer learn it. A chart groups languages of the world by how endangered they are. Fifty-seven percent are safe, or the data are missing. Those languages are not about to go extinct. Ten percent are vulnerable. Adults speak these languages. Children speak them too. Most of that speech happens in one place, such as home. Eleven percent are definitely endangered. At home, the language is not the first one children learn.

2Nine percent are severely endangered. Grandparents and elders speak it. Parents may understand it. Parents do not use it with one another. They do not teach it to their children. Ten percent are critically endangered. Only a portion of the language remains with some grandparents and elders. Four percent went extinct between the 1950s and 2003, the year the study ended. No speakers remain. More than 7,000 languages exist in the world. Linguists are experts on language. They predict that 3,500 languages will die out by 2100. That share is half of every language on Earth. Every two weeks, about one language dies out. Linguists work hard so languages will not vanish. Speakers of endangered languages work hard too. Edwin Benson belonged to the Mandan people. The Mandan are one of three tribes on the Fort Berthold Reservation. North Dakota, inside the United States, is where that reservation lies. Mandan people now live in many communities around the world. Long ago they lived on wider tribal land along the Missouri River. That land is where North Dakota and South Dakota stand today. Benson died in 2016. Part of his people's culture died with him. He had been the last person who spoke Mandan with full ease. The language had been spoken for centuries. Before he died, he helped build Mandan dictionaries.

3He helped make recordings too. Fluent speakers now teach intense language classes to young students. Linguists hurry to record last speakers such as Benson. They write down what those speakers know. The shared aim is to keep these vital pieces of culture from being lost for good. Languages have faded across human history. They have disappeared too. Sometimes an outside culture conquers a people. Then the losers' language can be wiped out very fast. The Taíno (tah-EE-noh) of the Caribbean Islands are one case. They met the men of Christopher Columbus in the 1490s. Those men had just reached the Americas. Columbus and his men forced many Taíno into slavery. They crushed Taíno traditions. They crushed Taíno culture. They also carried diseases the Taíno could not fight. Millions of Taíno and other native peoples died quickly from those illnesses. Within fifty years, nearly every Taíno person was dead. Almost the whole culture died. Almost the whole language died. People with Taíno heritage still lived on. Some Taíno words entered other cultures. English took in canoe, barbecue, hammock, and hurricane. A rock carving made by the Taíno is called a petroglyph. In more recent times, Aboriginal peoples of Australia lost much of their old way of life. Torres Strait Islander peoples suffered the same loss. The first arrival on that continent may date back sixty-five thousand years, researchers think.

4They formed hundreds of nations. Each nation had its own culture. Each had its own language. In 1788, colonists sailed in from England. Foreign disease soon hit indigenous people in Australia, as it had hit the Taíno. Soldiers killed many of them. Settlers killed many too. Researchers think the indigenous population fell from 300,000 to 75,000. The fall took place within 150 years after the British colonists landed. Outside pressure made languages fade. Old parts of many cultures faded. Some went extinct. Linguists think about 250 indigenous languages were spoken in Australia before Europeans arrived. Today people in Australia use only 60 of them in regular life. From the 1870s through the 1960s, governments in the United States and Canada ran boarding schools. Many Native American children were sent to those schools. Many First Nations children were sent too. The children had to speak English. Speaking a native language brought punishment. At times one culture is assimilated into another. Assimilated means taken in, or absorbed. Outside force can cause the shift. Benefits offered by the other culture can cause it too. The first culture often drops its own language. Money and trade can drive the change. People may gain by using the language of partners they trade with. They may use the language of people they do business with.

5After a while, that outside language can become everyday speech. Swahili people form a small ethnic community. They live along East Africa's coast. Across the wider region, Arab traders took up Swahili for business. They used it for politics. Other African peoples did the same. As Swahili spread, it picked up many words from Arabic. Kenya has made Swahili its official language. It is the official language of Tanzania. More speakers meant less room for older local languages. The language of the Dahalo in Kenya was pushed aside. The language of the Zaramo in Tanzania was pushed aside. Other languages were pushed aside too. In Kenya, a child reads a book called Brother Rabbit. The book is in Swahili. Assimilation from another culture has also changed Hawaiian. Hawaiian is listed as severely endangered. Hawaii is the only state in the United States with two official languages. The two are English and Hawaiian. Late in the 1800s, these islands in the Pacific came under United States control. Bit by bit, younger native Hawaiians shifted to English. English became the daily language of school. It became the daily language of business. A report from the U.S. government looked at 2011. That year, only about 6 percent of Hawaii's people spoke Hawaiian at home. Hawaii then had more than 1.3 million people.

6Popular culture helped push these language shifts. Modern technology helped too. Young speakers may be hit again and again by music, films, and news. The flood arrives in some other culture's language. The extra pressure wears the endangered language down further. The Internet can also help keep endangered languages from disappearing. Other media can help too. They can share a language with many more people. Today some public schools teach through Hawaiian the whole day. Students in those schools do not start English until fifth grade. Why care if a language disappears? One reason is that words help form who we are. The ideas inside the words do the same work. Language is a deep part of culture. It is a deep part of identity. It ties people to their communities. Speech gives people a way to make sense of the world. When a language vanishes, descendants of its speakers usually suffer. Important pieces of history are often lost. Religion can be lost. Values can be lost. Daily ways of living can be lost. Some ideas cannot be said in any language except their own. Each language belongs to the time and the place that shaped it. Hebrew stopped being a language of daily life almost two thousand years ago. People still used it in Jewish religious practice.

7They still used it in some writing. During the nineteenth century and the twentieth century, Jewish leaders restored Hebrew as speech. No other dead language has made so successful a return. In some cities, street signs use Hebrew and English together. Shop names do the same. Linguists go all over the world to record languages in danger. They write down what they find. They want a record before a last speaker says a last word. Speakers of one language may hold wide knowledge that no other group has. The knowledge can be scientific. It may cover plants of the home region. It may cover animals. It may cover patterns in the weather. Far northern lands have been home to Inuit peoples for many generations. Say Inuit as IN-yoo-it. Aleut peoples have shared that cold region. Say Aleut as A-lee-oot. For most of the year, dark and cold surround them. Their languages hold dozens of words for kinds of snow. They hold dozens of words for kinds of ice. Inuktitut (i-NOOK-tuh-toot) is one of those languages. Central Siberian Yupik (YOO-pik) is another. In Juneau, Alaska, a teacher holds alphabet cards for the Tlingit (TLING-kuht) language. The cards are a tool for teaching this language, which is critically endangered, to new speakers. A boy in Nunavut, Canada, studies letters at a school for Inuit children.

8Through stories told aloud, Inuit elders passed knowledge onward. Each generation taught the next in a traditional language. That expert knowledge has helped scientists who study climate. They understand better how the Arctic has changed across time. Inuit people can describe ice and snow that used to be common. Those kinds no longer form. They can also tell how shifts in the environment affect animals. Some of these northern languages are endangered now. Researchers want this knowledge kept. Most endangered languages today share a few traits. First, they usually belong to a small ethnic group. Second, most are oral languages. People have spoken them, yet writing them down was never a strong tradition. Third, other cultures press on them. Those cultures are often stronger in money and trade. Together, these traits can put a language at risk. Field linguists travel widely to list the languages closest to disappearing. They make recordings of them. Some linguists work on the Enduring Voices Project. Partners include National Geographic Society and Living Tongues Institute of Endangered Languages. Recording a fluent speaker helps protect the range of human knowledge. Researchers want to save vocabulary. They want to save pronunciation. They want to save grammar. A library of materials is how they do it. Linguists record people using the language during ordinary tasks. Someone may sing a song.

9Someone may cook a meal. Someone may put up a house. From those recordings they build living dictionaries. The pages show how the speakers talk about the world around them. In New Zealand, two children point at a sign written in Maori. That sign shows a place name longer than any other on Earth. Children in many countries take immersion classes, as students in Hawaii do. Communities use the classes to bring an endangered language back. Every lesson is taught only in the language people hope to keep. A Polynesian people native to these islands speaks Maori, and the language is endangered. About 125,000 people speak it. New Zealand has 4.7 million people. Many children now take Maori immersion classes. The goal is daily use of Maori by very young children. If the young learn the language, its chance of surviving is much higher. The film Moana tells of a Polynesian girl. She sets off on a quest over the ocean. In 2017 the film was dubbed into Maori. Local movie theaters showed that version. Linguists sit with one of the last people who speak Kanakanavu (kah-nah-kah-NAH-voo). The language is critically endangered. A mountain village in Taiwan's south uses this tribal language. Saving a language means guarding knowledge so it does not vanish. Human experience should not vanish either. Chinese keeps spreading across the world.

10Spanish keeps spreading. English keeps spreading. That spread makes it harder to stop other languages from disappearing. Linguists know that saving Maori takes more than learning words by heart. Saving Mandan takes more than that. Saving any endangered language takes more than correct sounds. The real work saves a culture. It saves a way of living. That way of living can teach us more about being human. These words help with the topic. Assimilated means drawn into something else and made part of it. Extinct means gone from existence. It means wiped out entirely. Fluent means able to use a language with ease, smoothness, and accuracy. Bombarded means hit by a huge, repeating flood of things, such as questions or complaints. Heritage is a way of life, a custom, or a trait handed down across generations. A culture is a particular society with its own ideas and customs. Immersion is a way to teach a language that is new to the learner. Only that language is used. Documenting means saving notes or photos about what happened. Indigenous means native to one particular place. Endangered means at risk of dying out fully. To preserve is to care for something and keep it for later. Erosion is the wearing away of something. It can also be a slow destruction.

56. Lives Spent Making Peace

1What you will meet in these pages: an opening. Wangarĩ Muta Maathai. Nelson Mandela. Martin Luther King, Jr. Óscar Romero. Mairead Corrigan and Betty Williams. A peacemaker's work that can be yours. Further paths. Words to know. Opening Someone who makes peace tries to bring wars to an end. Conflicts are part of that work. So are disagreements that split people, groups, or countries. Respect for this work is wide. Argument can be wide too. A peacemaker may refuse to choose either side, and that refusal stirs debate. Violence can reach these people. Belief itself has cost some of them their lives. Awards for this work are many. None is better known than the Nobel Peace Prize. The pages ahead follow several people who labored for peace. A Nobel Prize reached many of those lives. Each year the world gives this international prize. The giving started in 1901. The money that comes with it is 1.3 million dollars. Winners divide that sum into equal shares. The prize also includes a medal made of gold. A diploma comes with it too. One picture catches Wangarĩ Muta Maathai as she sets a tree into the soil. Wangarĩ Muta Maathai April 1, 1940, is the birthday of Wangarĩ Muta Maathai. Ihithe, a village in Kenya, was her home. Teachers saw a gifted student. An invitation came from a Catholic boarding school. In that school she climbed fast, until she led her class. Graduation led her to the United States. Biology gave her two degrees there. Kenya saw her again when she took an advanced degree, a Ph.D., at the University of Nairobi. East Africa had not had a woman earn a Ph.D. until she did. She cared deeply about whether the environment stayed healthy.

2Her studies let her notice trouble. They also let her invent fixes. Deforestation was clear to her. Humans were cutting away too many trees. Harm followed for the environment. Waterways went dry. Farm crops failed. Desert moved into land that once held healthy forest. A seat in Kenya's Parliament went to her husband. His promise had been jobs for more Kenyans. A plan formed in her mind. Two problems would get one answer. The new work would heal the land at the same time. A second picture shows a 2005 ceremony in Kenya. She is planting. U.S. Senator Barack Obama stands with the group. Tree planting was the work she created. Seeds went into ground all over the country. Women made up most of the hired planters. People came to call the effort the Green Belt Movement. A goal sat inside the name. Planters would raise a green belt, meaning a strip of trees, along a line 8,000 kilometers long. About 5,000 miles is the same distance. That tree line was supposed to push back the damage of a desert on the move. Planting was not the last task of the Green Belt Movement. Laws that guard the environment mattered to Maathai. Voting lists grew with the movement's help. Changes in government were demanded. Protests rose against actions that would hurt the land. Arrest came for Maathai again and again. Beatings came too. Supporters were arrested and beaten. They were trying to block the sale of public land. They were trying to block building there. A clear reason kept them going. Put buildings on forest and more trees come down. Protest continued. The year 2004 brought her the Nobel Peace Prize. No African woman had won it earlier.

3No environmentalist had won it earlier. Cancer ended her life in 2011. A picture shows her beside others as they take up worries about Kenya's environment. Nelson Mandela July 18, 1918, is the birthday of Nelson Mandela. Mvezo, in South Africa, was the place. Rolihlahla Mandela was the name given at birth. School is where he took the name Nelson. Law was his study. Politics became his active work. Late in the 1940s, South Africa put a system in place and called it apartheid. The sound is ah-PAR-tide. Races were kept apart. Contact between people who were not white and people who were white had to stay limited. Political power did not belong to the first group. Native Black people formed 75 percent of the population. Their schools were poor, or they had none. Their houses were poor. Servant work or laborer work was all that most of them could get. A picture shows Nelson Mandela. A Black political group had Mandela's labor for many years. Apartheid was the enemy. Peaceful protest was answered with violence. A ban from the government stopped the group's protests. Mandela's choice was to answer violence with violence. A new military wing took shape with his help. Weapons were obtained for it with his help. The year 1962 brought his arrest. Prison followed. A life sentence arrived in 1964. Other countries, at the same time, pushed South Africa to drop apartheid. Inside the nation, protests against the system were led by Black people and by white people. F. W. de Klerk was president, and he was a white man. Ending apartheid became a path he started. More than twenty-five years had passed in prison. Freedom then came from de Klerk.

4One picture returns Mandela to his former cell on Robben Island. The year of that visit is 1994, four years after release. Another picture, from 1990, shows de Klerk at the left, walking beside Mandela. Changing the government of South Africa became work the two men shared. Elections arrived in 1994 because of them. Every citizen could take part, a first for the country. Race was no longer a block. Both men received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. The honor was for opening elections that were free and fair to every South African. April 1994 made Nelson Mandela president. He was the first Black person in that office. He understood the office as a chance to lead the country toward full equality of races. A new constitution was written under his lead. Law took it up in December 1996. Advisors around him came from every race, and he was known for that. Plenty of white South Africans had fought the idea of political power for others. Many of those people changed their view because of him. Death came for Nelson Mandela in 2013, at the age of 95. Martin Luther King, Jr. January 15, 1929, is the birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. Atlanta, Georgia, was the city. School trained him as a minister. One reason was a belief he held. Leaders in Black churches, he thought, ought to direct the movement against discrimination. Southern cities of the United States were segregated in that era. Separation kept Black Americans away from white people. Treatment marked them as inferior. Separate bathrooms were forced on Black people by white people. Separate water fountains were forced on them too. Voting was not allowed. A try at the polls brought intimidation.

5A picture shows him addressing his Montgomery congregation. From that congregation in Montgomery, Alabama, he asked people to fight discrimination. Joining a civil rights group was part of the ask. The group is the NAACP. Those letters stand for National Association. They also stand for Advancement of Colored People. Voting was the other ask. Police, in 1955, arrested Rosa Parks, a Black woman. Her seat on a bus in Montgomery was one she would not surrender to a white man. King backed what she had done. He led a movement whose tool was a boycott of the city bus system. A boycott means you will not use something, and the refusal is how you make your point. A lawsuit grew out of the boycott, and the NAACP filed it. Alabama's segregation laws were declared illegal by the U.S. Supreme Court because of that case. After the boycott, a picture shows Rosa Parks on a bus that is integrated. People then counted him as a central civil rights leader in the United States. Speeches of his moved listeners so far that some treated him as leader of the Black population of the nation. More Black citizens got onto voting rolls with his help. Restaurants were integrated with his help. Other work followed. Active life as U.S. citizens, for all Black people, was the goal. Violence was sometimes aimed at him. Arrest happened. Prison happened. Threats against his life happened. Quitting was not his choice. Violence was not his answer. July 1964 is when President Lyndon Johnson put his name on the Civil Rights Act. From then on, segregation was a federal crime. A picture shows him delivering the speech people tie to a dream. The Nobel Peace Prize of 1964 was his.

6It honored resistance to segregation that stayed nonviolent. Memphis, Tennessee, was the place on April 4, 1968. A white man fired the shot that killed him. Tribute came in 1983 from the U.S. Congress. The third Monday of January became Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. Listeners still hold words from August 28, 1963. He spoke of holding a dream on that day. In the dream, sons of people once held as slaves could sit with sons of people who had owned slaves. One table would hold them as brothers. Óscar Romero August 15, 1917, is the birthday of Óscar Romero. El Salvador was his country. A Catholic family raised him. Age 13 is when he entered a special high school aimed at the priesthood. Studies continued in San Salvador once high school ended. Graduation made him a priest. A picture shows the clergy collar he wore. Rutilio Grande, priest and friend, died at the government's hands in 1977. Speech about human rights had made leaders dislike Grande. They feared that people seeking rights would put the government's power at risk. The death shook Romero. Poverty became something he spoke against. Social injustice became something he spoke against. Other human rights violations, killings by the government among them, became something he spoke against. His urging was that people keep teaching love and not grow weary of it. Love, he said, is the force able to overcome the world. The Violence of Love is the book that carries those words. Several military dictatorships seized power across the following years. Control of the government sat with the military. People of El Salvador struck back at military control. Out of that fight came the Salvadoran Civil War.

7Opponents of the dictatorship were hunted by the military. They were killed. Only government-approved words could appear in the newspapers. Radio carried Romero's speeches instead. He spoke the names of the missing. He spoke the names of the harmed. He spoke the names of the killed. A target was what that honesty made him. Reliable news of the war still reached Salvadorans. Print was closed to that news. A picture places Archbishop Óscar Romero in a gathering at Church of Divine Providence. San Salvador is the city. 1979 is the year. March 1980 brought a speech about whose orders to follow. God's orders, he said, mattered more than orders from government or from military leaders. Soldiers were asked to lay weapons down. They were asked to refuse orders that broke human rights. A shot killed him once the speech was finished. Sainthood came from the Catholic Church in 2018. Another picture shows him sending a mass out over the air in March 1980. Death followed not long after. Mairead Corrigan and Betty Williams January 27, 1944, is the birthday of Mairead Corrigan. Belfast, in Northern Ireland, was the city. May 22, 1943, is the birthday of Betty Williams, in that same city. Their childhood fell in years when the Catholic Irish Republican Army, the IRA, killed people and spread terror. Driving the British from Northern Ireland was the aim. Protestant groups replied with the same kind of violence. Both sides lost hundreds of dead. Thousands more were injured. August 1976 is when Betty Williams met Mairead Corrigan, after a crash. An IRA member's car swung out of control. Protestant troops backed by the British had shot him. Loss of control sent the car into a family.

8Corrigan's sister was the mother, and she was hurt. A niece of Corrigan was killed. Two nephews, both young, were killed. The crash had a witness in Betty Williams. She made a vow to do whatever she could so peace would return. A petition was her start, calling for the fight to stop. Television, the day after the crash, carried Corrigan's criticism of IRA violence. Two nights after that, television showed Williams talking about her petition, and Corrigan saw it. A phone call invited Williams to the funeral. About 10,000 women followed the two of them in a protest demonstration. The graves of the victims were the destination. Friendship followed. Feelings about violence in their country bound them. An organization, they decided, could help build peace in Northern Ireland. Ciaran McKeown, a popular journalist, joined them. Peace People is the group they founded. A booklet was written and handed out under the title The Price of Peace. Marches were organized under the name of peace. The marchers numbered in the thousands. A picture shows Betty Williams. Travel took Corrigan and Williams through countries across the world. Peace for Northern Ireland was their message. Their lives drew threats. The goal still held them steadfast. Summer 1977 was ending when violence tied to the conflict in Ireland had fallen past the halfway mark. The Nobel Peace Prize of 1976 went to Williams and to Corrigan. Work with Peace People did not stop. Survivors of attacks got help. Victims of violence got help. Rallies raised money. So did other fundraising. Communities in areas struck by poverty could rebuild buildings that bombs had broken. Millions of dollars went into the programs. One of those programs brought terrorists to hand over weapons. Further awards for making peace reached both women.

9March 17, 2020, is the day Betty Williams died. A picture shows the two women on a peace march. A peacemaker's work for you The world grows better where peacemakers work. Your effort can do that too. Arguments among friends are a place to start. School is a place to start. Your community is a place to start. That is how a person becomes a peacemaker and changes something. Student conflicts can grow into violent feelings. Violent actions sometimes follow. Peer mediation programs exist in some schools. Students with training guide the others toward working out differences. Talk, plus respect, can settle a conflict, and people learn that. Solving stays in the students' own hands. Friends who practice talking through trouble practice keeping peace. A picture shows students in peer mediation finding a peaceful compromise. Starting such a group begins with a teacher willing to help. Training in mediation usually comes first for the teachers. Volunteers then supply a small set of student mediators, either chosen or nominated. Training for most middle school mediators runs 12 to 15 hours. Conflict gets a definition in that training. Communication is practiced. Listening is practiced. The role of an effective go-between is practiced. An argument gives teachers a choice to offer. One path is a peer mediator. The other path is the principal. Students always decide. Those who pick mediation sit with a trained student guide. Compromise is what the discussion teaches each person. A meeting can run like this. First the mediator asks if the students in the argument want the problem solved. A yes sends all of them to a spot reserved for solving problems. A no from one student, or from both, means mediation cannot go on.

10Agreement is required: no name-calling while the problem is solved. Interrupting is also off limits. Truth-telling is required. Each person tells what took place. Each person tells how it felt. Both are asked for fixes. A fix that both can like is the search. Congratulations from the mediator close the meeting. Time and energy go, for many people, into standing against war. Injustice draws that same effort. Others may be inspired by you to act as peacemakers. Every effort, whether large or small, leaves the world more peaceful. Results that show up Do the programs work well? Some schools say far fewer students are suspended because of fights. One survey found success in the eyes of more than 8 middle schools out of every 10. Paths for more reading The Nobel Peace Prize is one subject worth following further. Peer mediation programs are another. Terms inside this book, and the words defined below, can guide a search. Students sit together in one picture, using peer mediation. Problems get discussed. Compromises get found. Words to know Apartheid: the South African policy that was unfair to anyone outside the white population. Discrimination: unfair treatment of people. Mediation: a way of settling differences between people or between groups. Boycott: refusing to join in something so that a point gets made. Protested: gave voice to strong disagreement or disapproval. Congregation: people gathered as a church group. Segregated: split along lines of race. Controversial: the cause of much disagreement. Threatened: in danger of being harmed. Violations: times when laws are broken or rules are not followed. Demanded: asked for in the tone of a command. Dictatorships: governments seized by a leader the people never approved.

57. Macedonia's King of Many Lands

1A map shows Alexander's empire at its largest in 323 BCE. Macedonia and the Caspian Sea are named. The Black Sea, Taxila, and Asia Minor are named. The Hydaspes River, Persia, and Babylon are named. The Mediterranean Sea, Alexandria, and the Persian Gulf are named. The Euphrates River, India, and Egypt are named. The Nile, the Red Sea, and the Arabian Sea are named. Both the empire and a route of exploration appear. More than 2,300 years ago, Macedonia, a Greek state, was the birthplace of a prince. Power came later, when that prince was king. People came to call him Alexander the Great and the greatest leader yet seen. Nations and kingdoms fell to him, some near Greece and some far away. Violent oppression was one of his methods. Forcing his culture onto defeated people was another. Education had been deep. A hunger for knowledge had grown in him. Empire and power were goals. Curiosity, some historians think, also pushed him. No Macedonian before him had gone so far, and he wanted to pass that mark. Parts of Europe, Africa, and Asia would lie inside his kingdom. A birth in Macedonia opens this book. Training for leadership follows. Kingship follows that. A journey, the conquest of Asia, and a legacy close the account. King Philip II, Alexander's father, is where the story starts.

2A son usually receives a king's title from his father. Philip did not wait for that path. He took the throne from a young nephew. Macedonia's king was the result. A strong will, plus a fierce army, put Macedonia under his control. Greek states around it came under his control as well. Olympias, Alexander's mother, held a firm plan. Her son, she decided, would be king someday. Her own place would be safe if he were. The year 359 BCE is when Philip II became Macedonia's king. Affection from Olympias was lavish. She told Alexander the crown would be his. Eighteen years was how long the horse Bucephalus stayed with Alexander. Drive for power came to Alexander from both parents, and much of his later greatness grew from that inheritance. Intelligence showed early. At age twelve, a beautiful but nervous horse was refused by his father. Alexander saw the cause. The horse feared its own shadow. Turning the head away from the shadow calmed the animal. Control came easily after that. Riding came easily too. Bucephalus was the horse's name. Say it byoo-SEF-uh-luhs. For the rest of Alexander's life, this horse mattered deeply. Philip was often gone while Alexander grew up. Tutors and teachers were hired to ready the boy for kingship. Horse riding and hunting were part of training for young noblemen of Greece.

3Swords, javelins, and bows were part of it too. Hard battles lay ahead for Alexander and his boyhood friends. Readiness was required. Manhood tests of Macedonia were passed as he grew. A wild boar was killed by him. A man was killed by him in combat. A philosopher named Aristotle became one of his teachers. Knowledge brought Aristotle respect. Culture became something Alexander could understand and value, with Aristotle's help. Art became something he valued too. Science, philosophy, history, politics, and ethics were all taught. Love of reading was sparked. Love of learning itself was sparked. Stagira, Greece, is Aristotle's birthplace, and a statue of him is displayed there. Much of Asia was held by the Persian Empire. Greece counted Persia as an enemy. Greek cities in Asia Minor had been destroyed by Persia years before. Control of the area had been taken. Philip wanted a war with the Persians. Regaining control and conquering Asia were his aims. Leadership duties started while Alexander was still young. A small revolution was stopped by him at sixteen, during a time Philip was away. While still a teenager, he led soldiers during battles his father was fighting. Kingship was the future he was raised for. Then Philip took another wife. Pure Macedonian blood was not Olympias's.

4A baby with the new wife could change the line. She was Macedonian. Alexander might lose the place of chosen heir. A daughter was born to the new queen in 336 BCE. Philip was killed not long after that birth. Soon afterward, Alexander's mother had the baby killed. The baby's mother was killed as well. The crown was then Alexander's. His father's army was rallied at once. Conquest of Asia was his wish, as it had been Philip's. A strong army was not enough. Support from the people was needed too. Macedonia had the backing of most Greek city-states. Philip had never won the approval of some of them. His son in charge did not calm that wariness. Fighting back could block Alexander's plans. Rule over Greece could be denied. Conquest of Persia could be denied. Support from many Greek states was still gained. Persuasion was the tool. Force often traveled with the persuasion. Opposition remained in some Greek states and in territories around Macedonia. Rebellion was their wish. The army crushed them. Mercy was not Alexander's way as a leader. Rebels were made into an example. Some were killed. Others were sold into slavery. Submission of every Greek city-state was locked in by that extreme punishment. A year after he became king, he was ready to push farther.

5Macedonian control beyond Greece was the aim. A map of the region names the Black Sea and Macedonia. Pella is named, and so is Asia Minor, then part of the Persian Empire. The Aegean Sea, Thebes, Delphi, Corinth, and Athens are named. The Mediterranean Sea is named. Some of the strongest capitals of the Greek city-states appear on that map. Equipment was added to strengthen the troops. Body armor, shields, and helmets were included. Daggers and enormous spears were included. Cavalry numbers were increased. Foot soldiers were sent in a tight formation called a phalanx. Cavalry would go first. Enemy soldiers still standing would be crushed by the phalanx. Vision could be shared, and troops could be rallied, because Alexander led with strength. Example was his method. Battle always found him in front of his men. Rough moments found him beside them. Instincts were sharp. How to attack, when to attack, and where to attack were clear to him. Spring of 334 BCE was when he left for Asia Minor. Turkey is the modern name of that land. A spear thrown into the ground was his bold claim on the land. Tight groups in the phalanx held thousands of his soldiers. About sixteen rows of men made each phalanx. Spears were often 6 meters long, or 20 feet.

6The first fight with the Persian army came soon, at the Granicus River. Darius III, the Persian king, was absent from the lead. Training was strong on both sides. Cities along the Mediterranean Sea were the way he hoped to take the Persian fleet. Syria and Lebanon are those lands today. Surrender came from some cities. Tyre refused in 332 BCE. Seven months of resistance followed. Brutal defeat came at the end. The Mediterranean coast was the path after Tyre fell. Later that same year, 332 BCE, he reached Egypt. A different man killed Darius in 330 BCE, before Alexander arrived. That killer was later executed by Alexander. King of Persia was the title people then gave Alexander. A mosaic from ancient times shows Darius fighting Alexander at the Battle of Issus. Far from Macedonia, daily life began to change. Persian customs were taken up. Two local princesses became his wives. Low bows, the Persian form of honor, were what he began to expect from Macedonians. Many Macedonians disliked the new behavior. Other soldiers copied him. Say it hy-DAS-peez. Elephants were used in battle by soldiers of this area. Some harm to the Greeks was done by Porus's elephants. Panic took the elephants when the fighting grew too intense. They pulled back. Surrender was Porus's choice. No later battle of Alexander's was as large. Unrest among the soldiers was great. Farther travel could not be won from them. Turning back was the agreement. Babylon was reached. A fever struck him in the spring of 323 BCE. June of that year was when he died there. Power and exceptional leadership both belonged to him. Aristotle became his teacher in 343 BCE. A revolt on Macedonia's eastern border was stopped by him in 340 BCE. Philip was killed in 336 BCE, and Alexander became king of Macedonia. Tyre was captured in 332 BCE, and Egypt was invaded and welcomed him.

10Darius and the Persians were defeated at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE. Darius was killed in 330 BCE. Central Asia was still being conquered in 327 BCE, and India was entered. Porus was defeated at the Battle of Hydaspes in 326 BCE. Death in Babylon came in 323 BCE. Words from his story are gathered here. Cavalry means soldiers who fight from horseback. It can also mean soldiers who fight from armored vehicles. City-states are cities, or urban areas, that behave as countries of their own. Destined means set ahead of time, or sure to happen. Ethics are moral rules that steer how a person acts. Executed means killed, above all as punishment for a crime. 1A father and his son share a car that is steered from a distance. The picture shows them enjoying that car together. The book starts with a new record. Next comes the start of radio control. 2Children have played with them for decades. Adults have too. Herbrich’s jet is faster than most of those machines. The fun, though, is just as real. The experiments led him to a famous hall. The hall was Madison Square Garden in New York City. The year of the show was 1898. Curious people in the crowd were shocked. They were also delighted. The craft floated in a big tank. The tank had been built for the show. Silent orders from Tesla made the small boat travel. It moved around the tank in a graceful way.

Another was World War II, from 1939 to 1945. In those years, radio control fit large machines best. Electric motors needed bulky equipment. The batteries were huge too. Some builders even placed transistors inside radio-controlled toys. A new hobby had begun. Robots, boats, and many other vehicles now run by radio. People have created hundreds of types. The mechanics are not all the same. The basic technology is shared. A transmitter sends the radio signals. People also call that device a remote control. The signals travel on one chosen frequency. 4It watches all the time for the transmitter. The signals get decoded. Electric current then goes to the motors. Those motors move the vehicle and steer it. Batteries power the transmitter. Batteries power the receiver too. Radio is a kind of electromagnetic energy. Visible light is that same family of energy. Radio energy moves as waves you cannot see. The waves pass through the air. They also pass through most walls. Wave size changes the form of this energy. Frequency changes it too. Frequency means how many waves pass in one second. Some radio waves are longer than a football field. Some are about as long as a person. Their frequency runs from 1 million waves each second to 100 million. Light is electromagnetic energy as well. Microwaves are too. X-rays are too. Those forms have much shorter wavelengths. Their frequencies are much higher than radio. An early radio-controlled model car was a Ferrari P4. The model was built at one-tenth scale. It was among the first cars of this kind ever made. An Italian company called El-Gi created it. The year was 1969. Toy makers started selling radio-controlled cars in the mid-1960s. Cars sold today are smaller. They are also more powerful. Gasoline can power them. Electricity can power them. A fuel called glow fuel can power them too. Drivers nickname that mix nitro.

5It is a high-performance fuel mixture. Basic cars in many toy stores cost little. They are easy to maintain. Serious drivers buy hobby-grade cars instead. A price in the hundreds of dollars is common. Kits let many people build those cars. Every part arrives boxed together. Drivers can swap parts. They can paint the body. They can add accessories. Bigger engines go into some kit cars. Bigger motors go into others. Ready-to-run cars are a different choice. Those cars are also called RTR cars. They arrive already assembled. Three cars powered by nitro race around a track in one picture. The cars are at the top. Off-road buggies appear below them. The buggies catch big air on jumps. The event was a national contest for radio-controlled cars. It took place in Kingsville Township, Ohio. The date was August 10, 2013. Kit cars and ready-built cars come in many shapes. They come in many sizes too. Touring cars are one group. Ford Mustangs are among the models. Chevy Camaros are among them. Porsche 911s are among them. Off-road vehicles are popular. Large tires come with them. Heavy-duty shock absorbers come with them too. Almost any ground will do. Uncut lawns are fine. Vacant lots are fine. Dirt fields are fine. Some of these vehicles look like classic monster trucks. Some look like sporty pickup trucks.

6Some look like buggies. Racing is the favorite part for some owners. Friends may race in a vacant lot. They may race in a park. Other drivers enter organized contests. The tracks can look like real speedways. Organized classes sort the cars in several ways. Size is one way. Class is another. A kit-built car is marked apart from other cars. Power source is marked too. An electric motor is one source. A gasoline-powered engine is another. Touring cars form one racing class. Sports cars form another. Off-road vehicles form another. Some of those are two-wheel drive. Some are four-wheel drive. Some contests are straight-line races. A drag strip is a usual site. An airfield is another. Oval tracks with a closed course are used as well. Truck-pulling and tractor-pulling events are among the most exciting off-road meets. The trucks drag sleds. A light sled is 35 pounds. A heavy sled is 100 pounds. That is 16 to 45 kilograms. The load is like an average-sized bulldog. It is also like a German shepherd. The letters RC can also be written R/C. Either form can mean remote-controlled. Either form can mean radio-controlled. A wire may link some remote-controlled vehicles to a controller. Most modern ones do not need a wire. They send messages on radio frequencies. Radio-controlled planes did stunts at a contest in 2009.

7Bob Motta lives in Danbury, Connecticut. He remembers the moment the flying hobby took hold. The time was the 1960s. His first radio-controlled plane was an F4 Corsair. It was a replica of a Navy plane from World War II. Motta is 66 now. World War I models are what he mostly pilots. The progress of these planes amazes him. Electronics got much smaller, he says. After that, the hobby really took off. Sky time is the joy for many hobbyists. The aircraft might be a plane. It might be a blimp. It might be a helicopter. Most new pilots start on training planes. People call those planes trainers. A trainer is meant to be simple. It is meant to make flight easy. Foam is a common building material. Foam keeps the plane light. A crash is less likely to wreck it. Computer networks now link some radio-controlled cars. A driver can use a wireless connection. A smartphone can be the controller. A tablet can be the controller. Wireless computer networks already speak in radio waves. That is why these systems work. Some vehicles use the link to a computer for extra jobs. One example is the Rover Revolution. It looks like a robot. It rolls on four wheels. Two cameras are on board. A microphone is on board. A speaker is on board.

8The driver can watch video. The driver can talk. The driver can listen. All of that happens while the rover moves. A pilot who can handle a trainer often moves on. The next step is often a sport plane. Complicated aerobatic maneuvers are possible in those planes. A special wing design is common. Flying upside down is easier with that wing. Motta has heard from pilots of real 747s. They told him model airplanes are harder to fly than real planes. The model pilot must stay on the ground. Every sense has to be used. Whatever goes up has to come down. Replicas of war planes are a favorite for many pilots. The real planes flew in World War I or World War II. Hobbyists call the models warbirds. Some come as kits. Some come as RTF models. Germany’s three-wing war plane is one popular warbird. The real aircraft flew during World War I. Pilots can also build a plane of their own. Motta recalls spending hundreds of hours on one plane. A crash does not end the parts. He saves every piece that is not damaged. Those pieces become spares for other planes. Almost-Ready-to-Fly planes are sold today. People shorten that name to ARTF. Motta compares the build times. An older project could take two hundred hours. An ARTF plane can be ready in about twenty.

9The finished plane, he says, can look respectable. It can look good too. A boy in China flew a mini helicopter in 2013. He steered it through an obstacle course. The flight was part of a contest. A plane already takes skill. A helicopter asks still more of the pilot. Mini helicopters make the first lessons easier. Indoor practice is especially helpful. The small craft still teach many skills. Those skills are needed for bigger helicopters. Quadrocopters have another name. People also say quadcopters. Four blades spin on them. They can fly in every direction. An autogyro looks partly like a plane and partly like a helicopter. A propeller pulls or pushes the craft forward. The propeller may sit at the front. It may sit at the back. Blades on top are not powered. Forward motion makes them spin. The spin keeps the autogyro in the air. A delivery drone in the form of a quadcopter appears in a test. It carries a package. 10The flight takes an organ to a team that will transplant it. Package delivery is another new use. Some companies have started that work. Television crews use drones at big events. Athletic events are covered that way. Entertainment events are covered that way too. A hundred years ago, this power seemed like magic. It is quickly becoming part of ordinary life. Playing with it is still a blast. Aerobatic describes hard or thrilling moves an aircraft makes in flight. A remote control is a handheld device. It can run something from far away, such as a television or a toy. Drones are aircraft or ships with no crew on board. A person operates them from somewhere else. A replica is a copy of something. Electromagnetic radiation is energy that travels as electromagnetic waves. Shock absorbers are parts tied to a vehicle’s wheels. They make a rough surface feel smoother. To maneuver is to move something around or guide its motion. A transistor is a small electronic part. It controls how electricity flows in a device. Mechanics are the details of how a thing works. 1Visitors like the long look from the high deck of the Empire State Building. Later pages follow a landmark that reaches into the sky. They follow two partners who made a winning team. They follow a hotel cleared away until a hole remained. They follow workers who became the city's favorite sight. They follow a rush toward the top. They follow the claim that Al Smith had been right. Useful words are explained at the end. Manhattan Island holds the tower near its center. New York City is the city around that island. Travelers who come from every part of the world take delight in it too. Construction years were 1930 and 1931. After that, the tower was a landmark known in many countries. Forty-one years passed while no building on Earth stood taller. No other skyscraper kept that height title for so long. Manhattan's skyline still shows the tower standing high. 2The film and the count showed the tower working as a giant lightning rod. Sunrise reaches the roof about a half hour sooner than the street. LED lights at the crown are driven by computers. Then comes Massachusetts. Pennsylvania is the fifth. A map of this lookout includes the Atlantic Ocean. About 80 miles (129 km) is as far as the view can reach. Offices fill 2.7 million square feet (250,838 sq m). The whole structure weighs 365,000 tons (331,122 mt). One nickname calls it the world's most famous office building. Another nickname calls it America's favorite building. The Seven Wonders of the Modern World include it. The base measures 79,288 square feet (7,366 sq m).

3One photo places Alfred E. Smith on the left. John J. Raskob stands on the right. Low-income families were the start for both men. Later life still held great achievements for each of them. Hard work helped him as well. Rich friends stood around him. Those friends would put money into the skyscraper as an investment. Smith grew famous because he ran to be president of the United States. The contest ended in a loss. He talked very well. The press received exciting stories about the building from him. Side by side, the two men made a winning team. They had already picked the ground they wanted. A problem came with that ground. The Waldorf-Astoria Hotel already occupied the spot. The team purchased the hotel. Opening year for the Waldorf-Astoria was 1893. No hotel in New York was bigger at that time. None was more luxurious either. Pulling the grand hotel down was hard. Its size was one cause.

4Another cause was a plan that the hotel should endure across a long span of time. Demolition was the job of some six hundred people. They kept working through the day. They kept working through the night. An enormous hole was dug next. Solid bedrock was the depth they had to reach. The massive skyscraper would rest on that rock. Digging and blasting carried the crews downward. The bottom lay 40 feet (12.2 m) under the street. Dump trucks, a whole fleet of them, carried off the diggings. Those loads numbered 28,529. Earth filled the loads. Stone filled them too. So did what remained of a hotel that had once been proud. Barges waiting on the East River took the loads. Tugboats moved the barges toward the ocean. Out there, the loads were dumped. When five months had passed, a gaping hole was all that was left. Huge cranes shifted giant beams into position. April 7, 1930, was the first day of construction. A skyscraper presses hardest at its base. Vertical columns were set in that low part. The columns numbered 210. Each one weighed 44 tons (39 mt). Beams that ran across came after the columns. Crews joined those beams to the columns. A strong grid of steel was the result. People on the ground stopped as the grid climbed.

5Sidewalks filled with the crowd. Their eyes stayed on the steelworkers. Those workers kept their balance on beams that were narrow. Newspaper reporters named this the city's best show. The papers gave the men a nickname, sky boys. Danger was so great that sickness changed the day. A crew of four went home together if even one man was ill. Men on a crew had to know one another fully. They had to trust one another fully. A stranger stepping in could make the work unsafe. Rivets were the fasteners that locked the steel beams. The heater made each rivet red hot. Coals that burned in his bucket did the heating. He then threw the rivet through the air. The catcher dropped it into the hole waiting in the beam. The bucker-up pressed one end of that hot rivet. A metal bar was the tool he used. The riveter struck the opposite end. An air hammer delivered the blow. The enormous beams were then bonded tight. Crews from the Mohawk Nation did this job best. These Native people were from New York State. They could place one rivet every minute. Water boys also walked those high beams. Some of them were only sixteen years old. Buckets of cool water for drinking went with them to the crews.

6A few thought beam work would be fun. They learned a strict habit very quickly. Eyes had to stay on the beam end under their feet. A look downward was not allowed. Say that name as gahnah-WAH-geh. A restaurant sign there honored the workers. The words were The Greatest Ironworkers in the World Pass Through These Doors. One picture shows a Mohawk ironworker setting a girder on a New York building site. Smith and Raskob wanted the skyscraper finished in a great hurry. Floors therefore rose at an incredible pace. Four-and-a-half floors were added every week. By summer the grid of steel had climbed to floor forty. The outer wall was gaining on it. 7Columns of windows went up. Columns of metal plates went up beside them. Columns of stone went up as well. Each of those pieces came ready to set in place. Higher on the tower, crews closed in the outside at one floor a day. Inside jobs continued while the outside climbed. Plumbers were among the inside workers. Electricians were among them. Carpenters were among them. August swelled the workforce. More than 3,500 people could be on the site during one day. More than sixty kinds of jobs were filled. Pipe was required by the plumbers. Bricks were required by the bricklayers. Supplies were required by every worker. In that era, wheelbarrows moved the supplies. A building so large made wheelbarrows too slow. Tracks were laid as the answer. The tracks circled each floor. They even ran inside the elevators. Supplies, once delivered, went straight into big carts. Workers shoved the carts along the tracks. Elevators carried the carts upward. Crossing a floor was then quick. Injuries came often with so many people working. The builders put a hospital of their own inside the building. Autumn found the crews on the tower's smaller upper floors. The work then moved faster. Hours of labor for the whole job came to 7 million. Steel that crews set and riveted weighed 57,000 tons (51,709 mt).

8The windows numbered 6,400. Limestone set in place measured 200,000 cubic feet. That volume is 5,663 cubic meters. Bricks set in the walls numbered 10 million. Plaster put on the surfaces weighed 10,000 tons (9,072 mt). Radiators put in numbered 6,700. Sinks and toilets put in numbered 2,500. Pipe put in stretched 51 miles (82 km). Elevators put in numbered 67. Their shafts stretched 7 miles (11 km). The finished building weighed 365,000 tons (331,122 mt). Some smaller floors near the top rose at a pace of one floor a day. Lunch turned into a problem because the crew was huge. Too many people wanted food at the same time. Workers began returning late. The builders would not allow lateness. Late returns slowed the job. Cafeterias on the site were the answer. The first sat on floor 3. Another sat on floor 9. Another sat on floor 24. Two more opened as the tower grew. Floor 47 received one. Floor 64 received the other. The contractors, who were the builders, had a schedule they were meant to keep. They kept it. They planned each part of the work. They also recorded each part. They counted the bricks that went in. They measured the plaster that went on. Plans this careful can make a smooth job seem certain. The job was not fully smooth.

9One idea failed in a huge way. Al Smith wanted airships to stop at the spire. That spire rises above floor 86. Dirigibles is another name for those airships. At the time, they were seen as the modern way to travel. His plan for passengers was simple. They would leave a dirigible by walking down a plank. They would step onto floor 102. An elevator would take them down. Fifth Avenue would be only minutes away. The plan sounded wonderful. The first airship drew near the mast. Wind at the mast was too strong. Wind around this skyscraper is always that strong. The airship idea was abandoned. Thousands of watchers stood in the street for one failed try. Columbia was the dirigible they saw. Taking mail off the roof was beyond what it could do. The year of that try was 1931. Special holidays bring shows of light to the building. A new system of LED lights makes the shows. Sixteen million colors belong to that system. May 1, 1931, was the day the doors opened. The first steel columns had gone in a little over a year earlier. How fast the world's tallest building went up set a record. That record still stands. Landmark status arrived just after the fiftieth birthday. The law says the appearance must stay as it has always been.

10On the skyline of New York City, people still notice this most famous office building. Smith said the tower had been made for generations still to come. He was absolutely right. An architect is someone who designs buildings. Demolish means to destroy a thing completely. The thing is usually a building or another large object. Art deco is a bold style. It belongs to decorative art, to design, and to architecture. Its time is the 1920s and the 1930s. Strong lines mark the style. Geometric shapes mark it too. To invest is to place money in a business chance. A later profit is the hope that chance offers. Rivets are small pieces of metal. They clamp things together. Barges are boats whose bottoms are flat. They carry freight. A canal or a river is where they usually go. A skyscraper is a building of great height. Bedrock is the solid rock layer under the ground's surface. A spire is a pointed crown. A tower or another building can have one. Steel is a strong metal. Iron and carbon are what it is made from. Cafeterias are rooms where meals are served. The serving happens at a counter. 60. Maria Tallchief, Star of American Ballet

1On September 29, 1999, an awards ceremony took place in Washington, D.C. The honor was the National Medal of Arts. A president of the United States gives this medal. It is the highest honor that president gives to one artist for outstanding achievement. The artists who receive it come from many fields. Those fields include music and visual art. They include singing, writing, and filmmaking. Maria Tallchief was one honoree that year. She was a tall, elegant dancer. Half a century before the medal, she had shaken the world of ballet. She became the first Native professional ballerina. She was also American ballet's first prima ballerina. The tale starts on Oklahoma land set aside for Native peoples. When she won the medal, she joined a very small group of artists. The parts of her story move from her early years to New York, where a star was born. They then turn to her years in Chicago as a master teacher. They close with the legacy she left. Quiet and shy describes Betty Marie as a girl. Her birthday was January 24, 1925. Elizabeth Marie Tall Chief was her full name. People nicknamed her Betty Marie. She belonged to the Osage nation. Speakers say that name as OH-sayj. Fairfax, Oklahoma, on the Osage Reservation, was her birthplace. In the Osage language, the family was called Ki He Kah Stah Tsa.

2Her father was Alexander Tall Chief. He was full-blooded Osage. Osage land yielded oil while Alexander was still young. Those profits brought wealth to many members of the tribe. Grown up, Alexander held a large amount of property in Fairfax. Ruth Porter was the name of Betty Marie's mother. Ruth's family were low-income settlers. They had come from Scotland and Ireland. Ruth saw a musical gift in Betty Marie. She saw the same gift in Betty Marie's sister, Marjorie. Ruth encouraged both girls to develop that gift. She arranged piano lessons for them from an early age. She arranged dance lessons too. In 1933, Betty Marie was eight. Her mother decided the girls needed more chances to learn. Their father agreed that chances in Fairfax were limited. Los Angeles became the family's new home. Lessons in dance were arranged for the girls before any house was bought. Ballet was one subject the sisters learned at that school. They studied tap dancing. They studied tumbling. They studied acrobatics. They studied Spanish dancing. A picture from 1930 shows Betty Marie on the left and Marjorie on the right. Their mother stands with them. Before long, the sisters were performing at rodeos. They also performed at county fairs. Their shows included a staged Native dance. They wore feathered headbands. They wore buckskin costumes. They wore bells.

3They wore moccasins. The dance made both girls uneasy. It was not authentic. It stressed stereotypes many people held about Native peoples. In ceremonial Osage dances, only men are active dancers. Women make a ring around the dancing men. Those women step a short way sideways, then return. They move in time with the drumbeat. Ceremonial Native dances were against United States law while the sisters were growing up. Grandma Tall Chief regularly led the girls to Osage ceremonies. Those dances went on in secret. The yearly Osage In-Lon-Schka dance still continues. It is no longer secret. Photography is not permitted. Vaslav Nijinsky's sister was Madame Bronislava Nijinska. He was one of the greatest male dancers of the twentieth century. Speakers say her name brah-nuh-SLAH-vuh nuh-JIN-skuh. At age twelve, her father gave her a short order. She should follow one star. He insisted that she pursue piano or dance. He did not want her to pursue both. Choosing dance was something she wrote about later. She wrote that dance was the true start of her life. Madame Nijinska accepted her as a pupil not long after that choice. Nijinska was her first important ballet teacher. Betty Marie studied with her from 1937 until 1942. Power in movement was one lesson of those years. She learned grace. She learned feeling. When high school ended in 1942, she felt sure this art was her path.

4She later explained her choice in her own book about her life as America's prima ballerina. She loved music. She felt that music grew inside her. Her hands on an instrument could not show it in the same way. The music ran through her body. During her teen years, ballet was still a young art inside the United States. Russian dancers were the only famous ones in ballet then. A Russian troupe, Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, performed this art. Speakers say that name ROOSS DU MOHN-tee KAR-loh. The company toured the world. People all over the United States met ballet through this company's tours. The company was based in New York. Los Angeles saw the company arrive in 1938. Betty Marie attended all of their performances. She was amazed. She readied her ballet shoes ahead of the 1944 show called The Song of Norway. In her final high school year, the company's leader watched her dance. He recognized her talent. New York was her destination once she had graduated. Several dance companies rejected her. Hiring came at once from Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo. Her professional career began without an audition. She then took the name Maria Tallchief. George Balanchine began creating dances for that troupe two years after Tallchief arrived. His name was George Balanchine.

5He had studied ballet in Russia. Many people count him among the most important choreographers of the twentieth century. Classical ballet was graceful and flowing. Balanchine built on that base. American ballet gained a fresh style from his work. The new style asked dancers to be very strong. It asked them to be quick. It asked them to be streamlined. It asked them to be athletic. Balanchine's choreography came alive through Tallchief's dancing. She became his muse. A muse is a person's greatest source of inspiration. Each of the two artists respected the other's gift. They married in 1946. The marriage itself went on for only five years. They kept working together for decades. They practiced ballet for as long as fourteen hours a day. Tallchief later wrote about dancing in Firebird. She compared the roar inside City Center to a stadium just after a score. In 1948, Balanchine worked as a visiting choreographer for the Paris Opera Ballet. France was where she traveled with him. She became that company's first American dancer. The next year, Balanchine helped found the New York City Ballet. Plenty of people in New York felt no need for a ballet company based in America. They changed their minds when they saw Tallchief dance. The ballet was Balanchine's Firebird, in 1949. That role made Tallchief famous.

6New York City Ballet's first prima ballerina was Tallchief. Thirteen years was how long she kept that title. She held it until 1965. In 2006 she spoke at a diversity celebration held by the Producers Guild of America. She said a wish to move and to dance seems born into American Indian people. She said this is the way they are. She said they show happiness in dance. She said they show sorrow in dance too. Some of Balanchine's loveliest roles were made with Tallchief in mind. Those roles included parts in Swan Lake. They included parts in Scotch Symphony. One part was a sugar-plum fairy in the ballet called The Nutcracker. Her Sugar Plum Fairy helped ballet win more fans across the United States. During her years there, she traveled on tour with New York City Ballet. The tours reached nineteen different countries. She also danced on television. The film Million Dollar Mermaid gave her a brief part as a ballerina. That film came out in 1952. American Ballet Theatre also invited her to dance as a guest. Erik Bruhn partnered with her in Swan Lake. He partnered with her in many other ballets. Wherever she performed, audiences covered her with praise. Those audiences kept asking to see another performance. The reviews from critics were full of strong praise. They praised her strength. They praised her musicality.

7They praised her technical precision. Tallchief had a fiery presence on stage. Her steps were light. She danced in a regal way. She also danced in a free way. That combination made her unlike the other dancers. She never failed to speak her mind. People respected her intelligence. They respected her honesty. In Balanchine's Swan Lake, her part was the Swan Princess. She publicly rejected unfair images of Native people. She supported the nonprofit group America for Indian Opportunity. A 1965 talk with the Des Moines Register let her explain her art. She said a ballerina receives steps and then makes them her own. One shared role still changes, because every dancer adds something of her own. As an American, she believed in great individualism. She said that was the way she was brought up. In 1965, Tallchief was forty-one. She grew tired of performing. All the trips her work demanded wore her out as well. Her marriage to Henry Paschen had taken place nine years before that move. He was from Chicago, Illinois. They had a daughter together. Tallchief retired from dancing. She moved to Chicago so she could give time to her family. Chicago Lyric Opera Ballet made her its creative director in 1975. The year 1980 was when she started the Chicago City Ballet. She believed a major ballet company belonged in Chicago.

8She led that company, in the creative role, through 1987. A number of students she taught later built strong careers in ballet. Her only child, Elise Paschen, danced beside her in Chicago. After she stopped performing, she also worked to keep Balanchine's dances as he had made them. He died in 1983. She felt strongly that dancers should perform his ballets as he first intended. Tallchief and several other dancers from his companies filmed parts of those ballets. Future students could learn from those recordings. In 1996 she was added to a national hall that honors women. People know it as National Women's Hall of Fame. That hall honors extraordinary achievements by women. The same year, she received a Kennedy Center award. This prize honors artists who have given outstanding things to the culture of the United States. Chicago was the city. The date was April 11, 2013. She was eighty-eight. People around the world honored the life she had lived. They also honored the work she had done. A timeline of her life marks 1925 as the year of her birth on January 24. It marks 1933 as the move to Los Angeles with her family. It marks 1937 as the start of dance lessons with Madame Nijinska. It marks 1942 as her high school graduation. In that same year she left for New York City and entered Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo.

9It marks 1944 as the year George Balanchine joined that company. It marks 1948 as the year she joined the New York City Ballet and became its first prima ballerina. It marks 1949 as her performance in Firebird. It marks 1956 as her marriage to Henry Paschen. It marks 1959 as the birth of her daughter, Elise. It marks 1965 as her retirement from performing at age forty-one and her move to Chicago. It marks 1980 as the founding of the Chicago City Ballet. It marks 2013 as the year she died in April. In the United States, Maria Tallchief broke a new path. The United States had never had a prima ballerina before her. A fresh style of ballet drew inspiration from what she did. Professional ballet had not had a Native star before her. She opened its doors to ethnic groups that had been underrepresented. Grace was one gift she used to push ballet ahead. Her talent helped too. Her achievements helped as well. A fellow dancer, Jacques d'Amboise, once spoke about her. Speakers say his name ZHAHK dahm-BWAHZ. He said one word fit her. The word was grand. He said she was absolutely grand. In 1964, she and Jacques d'Amboise performed at the White House. The event was a state dinner.

10In 1999, President Clinton gave her a National Medal of Arts. He said she had taken an art form from Europe and made it belong to America. In his view, it was right that a Native American woman was the one who did it. An achievement is an accomplishment reached through effort. Inspiration is a good influence. It can spark a creative idea or a creative act. An audition is a tryout performance by an actor, a dancer, or a musician. The performer hopes to win a new role or position. Being exact, or accurate, is what precision means. A reservation is land where the United States once compelled Native peoples to live. Authentic work follows an original or traditional form. Such work is not a false copy. A stereotype is a too-simple picture of a group, and that picture is often unfair. Those images are often unfair or untrue. Ballet is a form of dance. This dance joins exact formal steps with set movements. A choreographer chooses the style of a dance. That person also arranges the steps and moves. A streamlined form can slip easily through water or through air. A trailblazer is the first person to do something new. That person inspires others to follow. To be inducted is to be chosen as a member of a group.

61. Napoleon and the French Empire

1By 1812 the French Empire stood at the height of its power. A map of that year marks the French Empire. It marks French allies and French enemies. It also marks countries under French control. Napoleon orders French troops across the Neman River. The order sends them to invade Russia in 1812. Napoleon Bonaparte ruled France. He felt sure of himself. He stands among the most notable military leaders in history. By 1810 he had taken control of much of Europe. Many armies had marched against him. He had beaten most of those armies. He had built an empire in Europe. The empire was not going to last. In 1812 he chose to invade Russia. Trade linked Russia with Great Britain. Great Britain was the main enemy of France. Russia was about to join the British against the French. Napoleon wanted to guard his empire. Blocking that alliance meant marching his huge army into Russia. He saw little reason to doubt a victory over Russia. The choice would become the greatest error of his career. Corsica was his birthplace in 1769. The island is French and lies in the Mediterranean Sea. His family belonged to the Italian nobility. France had taken the island from Genoa, an Italian republic, one year before his birth. The family remained on Corsica after the takeover. He attended grade school on Corsica. Two army schools in France gave him later training.

2In 1785 he finished school as an army lieutenant. France's people rebelled against the king in 1789. The French Revolution brought the monarchy to an end. Kings had ruled France for centuries before that break. The Revolution stood on several ideals. One ideal was brotherhood among all male citizens. Another was freedom from unfair treatment by the government. Many people believed the Revolution would improve France. Early in 1793, revolutionaries killed King Louis XVI. His death opened a bloody stretch called the Reign of Terror. In that stretch, Queen Marie Antoinette was executed. Many other powerful nobles were executed too. So many officials died that France lacked strong leaders. The gap let an ambitious man picture himself in charge. Napoleon believed he was that man. Toulon was where he went in 1793 to battle British troops. Toulon is a city in the south of France. Great Britain and other nations in Europe wanted the Revolution stopped. They wanted the French monarchy restored. They feared revolutionary ideas would spread. Those ideas might threaten their own kingdoms. Napoleon forced the British out of Toulon. The victory made him a general. He was twenty-four. A picture shows his campaign with troops in northern Italy's Piedmont region. Some people inside France also wanted the kings brought back. These royalists started an uprising in Paris in 1795.

3The Directory called on Napoleon to stop it. From 1795 to 1799, France was led by a small circle of men called the Directory. After he succeeded, the Directory put him at the head of France's army. In 1796 he married Joséphine de Beauharnais. Say the last name BOH-ar-nay. She was a widow. She had two children. Her first husband had been a general. He was killed during the Reign of Terror. France already knew Napoleon's skill in command. His ambitions grew larger. He set out to control the whole nation. Napoleon went on winning battle after battle. The Directory's 1796 order sent French troops under him into Italy. The task was to push Austrian armies out of the country. Italian armies were to be pushed out too. He won a run of battles. He took Italy for France. He came home to France as a hero. Two years later, in 1798, he led a small army into Egypt. He hoped to cut Britain's commerce with the Middle East. He won several fights in Egypt. Then ships of the British navy beat a French fleet at the Battle of the Nile. The loss blocked his plan to move the army over the channel into England. In 1799 he overthrew the Directory. He made himself first consul of the republic. He took the powers of a dictator.

4In 1804 he placed the crown on his own head and became emperor. France had only recently thrown off its kings. An emperor now ruled the country. A picture shows him in an emperor's crown and robes. The scene is the coronation ceremony in Paris in 1804. In running the government he was as full of energy as he was in battle. He was just as focused. He changed how the government worked. He set up a national bank. He tried to repair trouble in the economy. He worked on the courts. He worked on higher education. The Napoleonic Code may have been his most important change inside France. The code put France's laws into an organized system. It took rights away from women. Husbands gained more power. Fathers gained more power. Male citizens received equal rights under the code. They received freedom of religion. The code said a job should go to a person because of merit. The code also brought enslavement back. France had abolished enslavement earlier. He shut down the old way of collecting taxes. Elected collectors had done that work. He picked new collectors. Each one received a salary. He watched spending by the government very closely. He wanted tax money used in the way he chose. The changes supplied enough money for his wars, which never seemed to stop. In 1815, inside the Tuileries Palace, a picture shows him at work on a letter.

5Admiral Horatio Nelson was Britain's great commander at sea, a kind of Napoleon on the water. His first name is said huh-RAY-shee-oh. On the mainland of Europe, Napoleon kept winning. At sea, Nelson blocked his hopes. Nelson led the British fleet at the Battle of the Nile. He led it again at an even larger sea fight in 1805. In October of that year, brilliant tactics let him crush a fleet of French and Spanish ships. Spain was on France's side at the time. The battle is called Trafalgar. Spain's southwest coast was the site of the battle. After that victory, Napoleon no longer had a real hope of invading England. He wanted to build a European empire and rule it. The nations of Europe rejected French control. They fought him with everything they had. For twelve years the Napoleonic Wars tore across Europe. The years were 1803 to 1815. He signed up enormous numbers of soldiers. Many of them came from lands he had conquered. He poured France's resources into the fighting. His force was called the Great Army. In time it numbered about 680,000 men. France's enemies built alliance after alliance. Each alliance tried to end his ambitions. On land he beat them. The empire kept growing. He set friends in place as rulers of conquered countries.

6He set relatives in those roles too. He hoped the new rulers would make those countries into allies. Money kept crossing the sea to British merchants. He tried to stop that flow. He banned the countries of mainland Europe from trading with Britain. French ships closed off ports all over Europe. The closures made the ban hold. In December 1805 he won a victory that ranks among his greatest. People call that fight Austerlitz. Say it AW-stur-lits. The ground is now inside the Czech (CHEK) Republic.
