He commanded 68,000 soldiers. He defeated 90,000 Russians and Austrians. In 1810 the French empire stood at its largest. Holland had been added. Parts of today's Germany had been added too. He worried because he had no heir. He divorced Joséphine. In 1810 he married Archduchess Marie Louise of Austria. In 1811 she had a son. The boy was named Napoleon too. The marriage did not make Austria an ally of France. A painting shows Marie Louise beside her husband and their son. Both father and son carried the name Napoleon. A seated Napoleon directs French troops at the Battle of Borodino. The enemy is the Russian army. The date is September 7, 1812. Invading Russia in 1812 was the worst military blunder of his career. Russia had broken his trade ban with Great Britain again and again.

7Czar (ZAR) Alexander I of Russia was about to side with Britain. Napoleon chose to move first. June 1812 saw him enter Russia at the head of over six hundred thousand soldiers. He hoped the win would come quickly. Russian forces would not stand for one huge battle. They pulled back ahead of the French. They burned crops as they left. French troops then found no food on the land. They found no supplies either. The Russian army finally stood and fought on September 7. Borodino was the nearby town. Say it bor-uh-DEE-noh. Losses were terrible. About 45,000 Russian soldiers died. About 30,000 French soldiers died. One picture shows Napoleon leading French troops who are cold and hungry. They are falling back from Moscow. He chased the Russian army farther into the country. His own army shrank. A lack of supplies made it weaker. He entered Moscow in the middle of September. The city was almost empty. Czar Alexander I would not meet him in battle. The czar had cleared supplies out of Moscow. He ordered his army to burn much of the city. The fires started after the French arrived. By the middle of October, food was nearly gone. Winter was coming. Napoleon turned the army toward home. Russian forces kept attacking the French during the withdrawal. About ten thousand soldiers were all who got back to France.

8The ruin in Russia was the start of Napoleon's end. In 1814, armies from a group of nations closed in around Paris. They made him give up the throne. He was sent away to Elba, an island of Italy. Early in 1815 he got away. He gathered a new army. Allied armies from across Europe close in on Napoleon's men at the Battle of Waterloo. His last defeat came there. The battle was fought in Belgium on June 18. He faced a mixed army of Austrians, British, Prussians, and Russians. That loss brought the Napoleonic Wars to a close. For a time, France's monarchy was put back in place. Later, a government with wider representation replaced it. He was sent away to St. Helena, a remote island held by Britain. The island lies in the South Atlantic Ocean. He spent the rest of his life there. Death came in 1821. France later received his body. The burial was in Paris. His ideas still shape modern politics in a major way. Many countries borrowed pieces of his civil code. The countries lie in Europe, in Latin America, and in the Middle East. They used those ideas as a base for their own laws. His legacy also includes a new way of making war. In that way, every part of a nation is turned toward the war.

9Support from the public is not required. Military schools worldwide have studied how he fought battles. They have studied how he planned campaigns. Later wars have used those lessons. He was ready to spend lives to reach his ambition. He was ready to spend resources too. Estimates put the dead across Europe at three million to six million because of his actions. His actions left France in ruins. The Duke of Wellington of Britain commanded the allied army at Waterloo. Asked to name the greatest general of every era, he picked Napoleon for the present, for earlier times, and for any time at all. The tomb of Napoleon stands in Paris, France. A list of dates traces Napoleon's life. In 1769 he was born on Corsica. In 1785 he left military school as a second lieutenant. In 1793 he put down a revolt inside France. He was raised to brigadier general. In 1796 he married Joséphine de Beauharnais. The year 1804 is when he placed the crown on himself as emperor of France. Russian forces and Austrian forces fell to him in 1805 at Austerlitz. In 1810 he divorced Joséphine. He married Archduchess Marie Louise of Austria. In 1812 he invaded Russia and met a terrible defeat. In 1814 he gave up the throne. He was exiled to the island of Elba. In 1815 he escaped Elba and raised an army.

10He lost at the Battle of Waterloo. That same year he was exiled to the far-off island of St. Helena. In 1821 he died on St. Helena. His body was brought back to France afterward. These words help with the topic. An alliance joins two or more groups or countries. They agree to work as partners and to fight on one side. An empire gathers nations or peoples under one ruler or one government. Exiled means a person was forced out of the home country. Punishment is a common reason. Politics is another. An ambition is something a person badly wants to reach. It may be a goal or a dream. An ideal is a guiding principle. It is a standard of what seems perfect. Blockaded means a route through a place was shut. Merit is a strong quality that earns praise or a reward. A casualty is a person hurt, killed, or missing. War, an accident, or a disaster can cause it. A monarchy is rule by one person who was not elected. A king is one example. A queen is another. A czar was a man who ruled Russia before the Russian Revolution of 1917. A revolution pulls a government from power by force. A different government takes its place. An emperor is a man at the head of an empire.

62. Nikola Tesla and the Electric Age

1Crowds at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago stared at electric displays. Tesla and Westinghouse had built those displays. The sight amazed people. This book calls its first part The Magician. Then Tesla meets Mr. Edison. Ditch digging comes next. A battle over currents follows. Radio days come after that. A great tower has its own part. A lasting influence closes the story. A glossary explains key words. In one laboratory picture, Tesla sits and reads. Artificial lightning fills the room. He looks calm. One day a dark-haired man with a mustache opened his laboratory. The room was in New York City. He asked a group to watch an experiment full of electricity. Nikola Tesla was that man. Guests took their seats. Tesla walked to a wooden platform without rushing. He sat in a chair. A generator sat under the platform. It could make millions of volts. Tesla flipped a switch. Wild streaks of light jumped across the room. The scene looked like a lightning storm indoors. Some streaks even hit Tesla. The show ended. Tesla left the stage without a wound. Clapping filled the room. The crowd had watched a man sit inside a storm of light and walk away fine. That calm figure, and that wild light, are the picture of the magician at work. New technology often became a spectacle in Tesla’s shows. He was a scientist, not a magician.

2The show had a point. A newly found kind of electric current could be safe. That current is alternating current, or AC. The discovery changed the world. In time it would run modern industry. It would also light whole nations. Tesla was a visionary as well as a scientist. Established scientists of his day met a challenge in him. His inventions were astonishing. His ideas were astonishing too. Many experts give him a large share of the credit for later devices. Smartphones are on that list. Wireless communication is on it. Television is on it. Robots are on it. Radar is on it. Other amazing devices are on it too. Genius in science did not make him a strong businessman. He died without money. Other people made millions of dollars from his work. A lightning storm was raging when Tesla was born. The year was 1856. The place is the country of Croatia today. It lies in Eastern Europe. As a boy he studied hard. His father served as an Eastern Orthodox priest. A large library filled the home. Tesla read those books eagerly. His mother gave him a love of inventing. In spare hours she built small appliances for the house. Electricity caught his interest while he was still a boy. He wanted to be an electrical engineer. Years of study and work followed. He found a better way to make electricity.

3Alternating current made that way more efficient. It also made it safer. In 1884 he sailed for the United States. He was twenty-eight. His second day in America took him to an office in New York. The office belonged to Thomas Edison. Tesla carried a letter. A European friend of Edison had written it. The writer greeted Edison warmly. The writer claimed to know two great men. Edison was one of them. The young man in front of him was the other. Edison was an inventor. Business skill sat beside that inventing skill. In those years, people treated Edison as the parent of the electrical age. A lighting system was among his creations. Incandescent lamps were part of it. Power stations that used direct current were part of it. Direct current is also called DC. DC power was dangerous. High voltage never let up. Cities raised poles for the lines. The wires on those poles were bare. A touch could electrocute a person or an animal. Electric trolleys in Brooklyn made the danger plain. Sparks flew from the lines when a trolley passed. People had to dodge the fiery bolts. Dodging happened so often that Brooklyn’s baseball club borrowed the idea. The club’s name became the Dodgers. Edison’s first bulb that truly worked was modest. Sixteen candles would equal its light. Tesla spoke plainly to Edison. Direct current, he said, was weak.

4He added that it cost too much. Lighting a city, Tesla said, would take hundreds of DC generators. Alternating current, he said, could deliver power for less money. Edison did not trust AC power generation. He still gave Tesla a job. A prize was attached. Tesla would receive $50,000 if he raised the voltage of Edison’s DC system. The system was the one in New York City. Tesla took the challenge. Long hours followed. Tesla wanted to win. Sleep was rare. Meals were small. After a few months he reported success. Edison would not pay the $50,000. He said the offer had been a joke. A full American, Edison said, would understand an American joke. Anger took hold of Tesla. He quit. He stormed out of the office. News of his achievements spread anyway. Investors soon came to him. They asked for a lightbulb that wasted less energy. Electricity is a flow of charged particles. Those particles are electrons. The flow can take two forms. One form is alternating current. The other is direct current. Direct current travels one way. Drawn on a chart, it is a straight line. Long distances are hard for it. Energy is lost along the way. Raising or lowering its voltage is also hard. In alternating current, electrons rush back and forth. The direction changes sixty times each second. Transformers can shift AC to a lower voltage.

5They can shift it to a higher voltage. Long-distance travel becomes efficient because of that. Tesla did invent that highly efficient lightbulb. Payment came as shares of stock. A share is a piece of ownership. The company soon became worthless. The investors got rich once the bulb was sold. Little cash ended up with Tesla. A short life list helps place the events. On July 10, 1856, Tesla was born at midnight. A lightning storm was raging. In 1873 he was 17 and nearly died of cholera. His father made a promise. Recovery would mean engineering school. On June 6, 1884, Tesla reached America. Work for Thomas Edison began. Poverty then pushed him into ditch digging. The job was for Edison’s light company. Pay was $2 a day. Luck turned when the crew chief made an introduction. The man was A. K. Brown. Brown worked at the Western Union Company. In March 1885, Tesla founded the Tesla Electric Light Company. In 1891 he built a special coil. It made alternating current at high voltage and high frequency. On May 1, 1893, his AC generators lit the Chicago World’s Fair. Tesla had told Brown about the AC ideas. Brown was impressed. He put money into those power-generation ideas. The workshop sat only a few blocks from Edison’s office. Tesla built every part an AC power station needed. The motors that made the electricity were among those parts.

6In 1895 he experimented with radio waves. In 1898 he showed the first robot. It was a boat steered from afar. On January 7, 1943, he died. He was 86. George Westinghouse became a major backer. Several train improvements had come from Westinghouse’s own inventing. He was one of the richest businessmen in America. He was sure alternating current was the coming way. He bought every one of Tesla’s patents. The price was $60,000. In today’s money that is about $1.4 million. He also gave 150 shares of stock in his own company. Royalties were part of the deal. A royalty is an ongoing payment. The payment depended on how much power the AC motors could make. Tesla spent the money quickly. A new laboratory was the result. Bringing electric power to the whole United States became their project. Anger rose in Edison. Westinghouse was putting AC generators in rural places. Those country places sat outside the reach of Edison’s DC system. Westinghouse sold the power at a cheap price. The low price cut into Edison’s business. Edison could lose a great deal of money. He tried to harm Westinghouse’s good name. He warned the public. Alternating current, he said, was dangerous. A big chance then came to Westinghouse. The 1893 World’s Fair needed lights. Westinghouse won that work. Chicago was the host city. He asked Tesla to install the AC generators.

7Large AC generators were part of Tesla’s design for Westinghouse. Pictures show machines of that kind. Opening day put a famous hand on a button. The hand belonged to U.S. President Grover Cleveland. One hundred thousand incandescent lamps flashed on. The crowd answered with delighted oohs and aahs. People called the fair the City of Light. It burned with a brilliant glow. The lesson was clear. AC took less wasteful effort than DC. The danger was also smaller than Edison had claimed. A new contract followed. Westinghouse would build AC generators for a power plant. The plant was planned at Niagara Falls, New York. Years of conflict with Edison had a cost. Westinghouse’s company nearly went bankrupt. Tesla wanted to save the firm. Tesla destroyed the agreement he had put his name on. Westinghouse paid him once. The fee was $216,000. In return, the patents could be used forever. Across later decades Tesla lost millions of dollars. Westinghouse grew richer. Victory in the current fight freed Tesla for a new problem. Open air, with no wires, was the path he wanted for electricity. He built a special coil of wire for that work. The coil made alternating current. The current had high voltage. It also had high frequency. The first neon lights came from work with that coil. The first fluorescent lights did too. The same device made the first X-ray photographs.

8November 1890 brought a result that had seemed impossible. An AC current crossed the air and lit a vacuum tube. Radio waves became the next experiment. They were another way to send signals with no wires. Early in 1895 a long test was nearly ready. The signal would cross fifty miles by radio. New York City would send it. West Point, in New York, would receive it. Disaster came before the test. Fire started by accident. Nothing of the laboratory survived. Coils built in later years can still perform a related trick. Power jumps the air and lights a neon tube. A 1901 picture shows Guglielmo Marconi. Early radio equipment surrounds him. The timing of that fire could hardly have been worse. In England, during that same period, Marconi had his own goal. He wanted radio waves to carry electrical signals. In 1901 a signal from Marconi crossed the Atlantic Ocean. Radio carried it. Many ideas inside that feat belonged to Tesla. Fame on a huge scale followed. Money arrived so he could start a radio company. Thomas Edison was among the givers. Edison was Tesla’s rival. Tesla’s answer was calm. He called Marconi a good fellow. He said Marconi should continue. He counted seventeen of his own patents inside Marconi’s system. Disappointment followed. Official credit for the radio went to Marconi. The U.S. Patent Office made that choice.

9Tesla answered with a lawsuit. He could not keep the case going. Failed project after failed project had used up his fortune. Cash was too tight. The year 1943 finally brought a different ruling. The U.S. Supreme Court gave Tesla the invention. The court called him the father of radio. A tower at Wardenclyffe, New York, was Tesla’s next great hope. A finished tower might have changed the world. It was never finished. Wireless work still filled his time. In 1901 he started the tower on Long Island. He hoped it would be powerful. Electronic telephone calls might leave it. Pictures might leave it. Stock market reports might leave it. Weather information might leave it. He described a fully wireless Earth in a striking way. The planet, he said, would become a huge brain. Every part of that brain could respond. Money ran out before the tower was done. Someone else took over the land. Workers pulled the tower down. Tesla died in 1943. He was eighty-six. His home was a hotel room. Westinghouse had paid for the room. Fortune after fortune had gone into projects that failed. Credit he deserved for research and inventions often never arrived. Even so, his effect on technology was huge. He helped shape the modern world. Alternating current, in his hands, powered modern cities. Rural places that had lacked electricity were changed too. X-rays, radar, radio, and robots all showed up in his tests.

10Those tests pointed toward the future. His hope for a wireless world did come true. The Internet carries his mark. Wireless communication carries it too. People now treat both as ordinary. A love of making things set him among the giants of modern science. He once described an inventor’s feeling. No thrill in a human heart, he said, matches that moment. The moment comes when a creation of the brain unfolds into success. A coil is rope or wire wound so it forms one loop or several loops. Experiments are tests a scientist runs. An investor is a person or a group. Money goes into a business in hope of profit. Patents are official papers. They let someone earn from a new idea. A visionary pictures what is coming and imagines it in a rare way. Voltage tells how hard electricity pushes. The unit is the volt. Current means electrical energy that is moving. To do something efficiently is to use time or supplies well. Electricity is energy that appears when charged particles move. An engineer plans a machine and may also build it or fix it. Buildings and bridges can be part of that work. A generator takes motion and gives back electricity. An invention can be a new device. It can also be a new way of doing a job.

63. One Hiker, Two Thousand Miles

1My hike crossed many kinds of land, from steep mountains to the rolling fields of Pennsylvania shown in a photo. My name is Ben. I am a psychotherapist, and my work is in western Massachusetts. I help people who are healing from emotional distress. The work matters deeply to me, yet sometimes I need a break. When I do, I walk in the forest so I can regroup. In 2015 the job overwhelmed me so fully that I needed a longer rest than usual. I decided the time had come to meet a dream from childhood. I would walk the whole length of the Appalachian Trail. That trail, often called the A.T., is almost one hundred years old. In 1921 Benton MacKaye stood on a mountaintop in Vermont. He worked as a conservationist, a planner, and a forester. He imagined a grand trail linking the Appalachian Mountains in the eastern United States. The path would follow the highest ridgelines. Builders finished the trail in 1937. From then on, the A.T. has been the longest footpath in the world that is kept for hiking alone. A map of my walk marks October 1, 2016, far to the north, and April 4, 2016, at the southern start. A canoe is required to cross the Kennebec River, and that crossing is an official piece of the trail in Maine.

2The map names Mount Katahdin and the country of Canada. It names Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, New York, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. It names Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland, West Virginia, and Virginia. It names Tennessee, North Carolina, and Georgia, with the United States holding the whole route. Mahoosuc Notch, in southern Maine, was the hardest mile, a jumble of slippery boulders. My sneakers wore out just before I entered New Jersey, so I swapped the old pair for a new pair. A rocky stretch in Pennsylvania hurt to walk. I kept brushing my teeth, even while I was on the move. The A.T. starts on Springer Mountain in Georgia and runs north for more than 2,000 miles, or 3,000 kilometers. It crosses fourteen states of the United States and finishes on Mount Katahdin in Maine. Many hikers call the A.T. the Green Tunnel, because it passes through so much thick green forest. The path also crosses farmland, runs beside rivers, and even cuts through backyards. Walking an entire long trail inside a single year is called thru-hiking. Most thru-hikers start in spring and head north, as I did, because the south is already warm. Each year, thousands try to finish an A.T. thru-hike, but only a few hundred succeed. I write as one of those fortunate few who completed this grueling and demanding endeavor.

3A few facts about the trail are worth keeping. Its length is 2,190 miles, or 3,524 kilometers. A full thru-hike takes about five million steps. The highest point is Clingman's Dome, on the border of North Carolina and Tennessee. The dome stands 6,643 feet above sea level, which is 2,025 meters. The climbing up and the dropping down equal a vast effort. Imagine hiking Mount Everest from the ocean up and back down, and doing that sixteen times. Earl Shaffer, whose middle initial is V, was the first thru-hiker and later the oldest. He finished first in 1948, when he was thirty. He finished again in 1998, when he was eighty. The fastest thru-hike on record took 45 days, 22 hours, and 38 minutes. Getting ready was the key. I spent several months preparing in an intense way. Wherever I could, I walked with a full backpack, and I practiced often in bad weather. To learn the supplies I would need, I took a job at a store that sold outdoor gear. I tried to set aside as much money as I could. One practice walk crossed the Brooklyn Bridge with my pack full of supplies. I also practiced pitching my tent inside my apartment. After those months, I was ready. I took the train from New York City to Atlanta, Georgia, then got a ride to the trailhead.

4On April 4, 2016, I took the first step, and the thru-hike was underway. The next few days were among the hardest, because body and mind both had to acclimate. The gear list was long. I carried a sanitary kit, toothbrush, toothpaste, and a towel. I carried a hat, gloves, a bandanna, underwear, and long underwear. I carried a T-shirt, shorts, pants, a long-sleeved shirt, and a balaclava. I carried hiking sneakers, camp shoes, camp socks, sock liners, wool socks, and gaiters. I carried a headlamp, a smartphone, headphones, a GPS tracker, and spare batteries. I carried a backpack, a tent, and trekking poles. I carried a sleeping bag, a sleeping pad, and a sitting pad. I carried a down jacket, a rain jacket, a poncho, a rain skirt, and a pack cover. I carried waterproof bags, a bag for food that also served as a bear bag, and rope. I carried a camping stove, fuel, and a lighter. I carried water bottles, a water filter, and tablets for purifying water. I carried a first-aid kit, a repair kit, and a very small pocketknife. I carried earplugs. With a day's food, some stove fuel, and a liter of water, the pack averaged 21 pounds. That weight is 9.5 kilograms. All the gear together cost nearly 2,500 dollars.

5McAfee's Knob, in Virginia, draws more photographs than any other spot on the Appalachian Trail. From the time I first heard of the A.T. as a child, the idea of its trail community fascinated me. Picture a whole community that never stops moving. People travel at different speeds across 2,190 miles of unbroken trail, a distance of 3,524 kilometers. The path itself is only a few feet wide. Fascinating hikers of every age choose the A.T. each year. They come from many cultures, and they bring many different abilities. I met many veterans who had lately come home from overseas. Many people were walking in order to recover from trauma and from tragedies. Every person I met had a reason for being on the trail, and every person had a story. Some thru-hikers traveled in a group. I chose to walk alone most days, because I liked meeting new people and keeping my own pace. If loneliness arrived, I could find friends among the other hikers. The A.T. let me hold a balance between solitude and good company. One of the hardest parts of the hike was simple. I had to hike on every single day. Most thru-hikers subsist on food that is cheap, light, easy to cook, and slow to spoil. On an ordinary day I woke when the Sun rose.

6I walked until I met the distance I had set, and I reached camp just before sunset. Shelters were usually small, like one in Pennsylvania, and often crowded, like one in the Smoky Mountains. How far I walked each day depended on weather, on terrain, on my goals, and on how tired I was. I tried to camp where there was a lean-to, a source of water, and an outhouse. If not, I pitched my small tent. When a shelter had no space left, I pitched the tent, as I did in a forest in Vermont. On rainy days I shaped the whole day around one aim. I needed to reach a shelter in time to claim a spot, because bad weather fills shelters fast. Sometimes rain lasted several days in a row, and I could not dry out fully until a town. Every few days I walked into a nearby town to refill my food, shower, and wash clothes. I learned that rest and fresh supplies mattered as much as the walking itself. Safety matters more than anything else on the hike. Along the way I met black bears, snakes with venom, and ticks that carry disease. A hiker must know how to act around unpleasant animals. That knowledge is critical if a person is to stay safe in the woods.

7Stay calm, act with respect, and keep a safe distance. Anything that smells of food is hung on bear poles, so bears are not drawn into camp. The thru-hike lasted 181 days. On an average day I covered 12.1 miles, a distance of 19.5 kilometers. I filtered every drop of water, and I was careful about hygiene so I would not fall ill. To avoid hypothermia I stayed dry and I stayed warm. The right shoes helped me avoid injury, and so did resting when rest felt necessary. I kept my gear in order so I would be ready if an emergency came. Contact with people I love mattered for safety. It also eased the homesickness of months spent alone in the woods. Fierce heat dried up most water sources in New York, so I filtered water from puddles. I felt happy most of the time. Even so, a large challenge was this: the hiking was not always fun. Often I was very hungry, worn out, and sore, and sometimes I was simply bored. The best help was the trail community, the people around me. I leaned on them. At times the path felt as if it had no end, yet it stayed beautiful, as a photo from North Carolina shows. The finish was hard, just as the start had been. Fall was fully underway, nights were turning cold, and I was hungrier than I had ever been.

8The mountains of northern New England were, without question, the hardest climbs. My speed dropped by half as I traversed the steep White Mountains of New Hampshire. The rocky ranges of southern Maine cut my speed in the same way. After almost six months of walking, I reached the top. Mount Katahdin was the summit I reached on October 1, 2016. Those last days were difficult, yet they did not feel like the first days. I felt like a different person from the one who had begun. Never before had I felt so strong, so confident, and so proud of what I had done. Sports were a rare part of my childhood. After the thru-hike I could, for the first time, call myself an athlete. A photo taken after more than 2,000 miles, or 3,000 kilometers, shows the change. I am clearly thinner than at the start, and I am dirtier too. After the hardest night of the whole adventure, I looked out on beautiful views of the Roan Highlands in Tennessee. Since the finish, many people have asked which memories I like best. The memories I hold dearest are the ones in which a challenge that seemed insurmountable turned beautiful. One night I camped alone on a mountaintop with no trees.

9Hard wind and heavy rain made the tent fall in. I grew frustrated, and I grew afraid. At 3:00 in the morning I stopped trying to sleep. I packed my things, ate breakfast, and began to walk. What came next was the most amazing sunrise I had ever watched, and I watched it alone on that peak. A challenge that first looked impossible had, with time, become something incredible. People also ask how the hike was possible. I answer that I crossed the whole Appalachian Trail the way any large task is done. I took one step, and then another step. They ask, as well, why I did it. Looking back, the reasons I continued were not the reasons I had at the start. Love and support from people on the trail, and from people at home, wrapped around me. I never truly wanted to quit. I am writing these pages several months after the thru-hike ended. My knees still ache from the five million steps, and I do not know how long that pain will last. I also spent six months away from people I love. A reader may ask whether the trip was worth the cost. Across five million steps, I pursued a dream by moving forward one pace at a time. Nobody can take that achievement from me.

10I stepped outside my comfort zone, and I healed a heaviness that had sat in my heart. I made plans and saved money, and I learned how to live on a tight budget. I learned to prize every object in my pack, because my life depended on those objects. The difficulties were real. In the end, the thru-hike was worth doing, and it was an experience of invaluable worth. I often remember the beautiful places, including Mount Katahdin in Maine. To acclimate is to grow used to a new climate or a new situation. A footpath is a narrow track made for walking. Hygiene means keeping clean in order to stay healthy. Hypothermia is a drop in body temperature low enough to be dangerous. Insurmountable describes a thing that cannot be beaten or completed. A lean-to is a small shelter whose sloping roof is held up by rocks, posts, or trees. Solitude is what a person feels when alone. To subsist is to keep on living, or to keep on existing. Summited means arrived at the top of a mountain. Terrain means the natural shape of a piece of land, including the ground itself. Thru-hiking means walking a long trail from its start to its end inside one hiking season. Traversed means moved across a place, or through it.

64. One Hour Inside a Great Art Museum

1A straw hat sits on Vincent van Gogh in Self Portrait with a Straw Hat. Thousands of other famous works share the museum with that painting. A huge staircase draws a sigh from a student looking up. The doorway above belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. New York City is where the building stands. Ms. Kessler teaches English, and she set an assignment. A tour with a guide is what the class must take. An essay has to follow the tour. Three artworks from the visit must be described in the essay. The task feels pointless in the beginning. Maybe, the student thinks, art is nothing but paintings hung on walls. Both feet drag on the climb. The room just inside the door is called the Great Hall. People of every age fill that room. People from many backgrounds fill it too. Many different languages rise from the crowd. Adults in groups draw sketches of the fine art in front of them. Children draw sketches as well. A young woman is talking to a circle of listeners. The student steps into that circle. She says that Jada is her name. Art history is what she studies at a college close by. She also guides tours for the museum. Four city blocks is the length she gives for the building. More than two million objects, she says, are kept there. Those objects reach from ancient times to the present day.

2She will lead the group through the entire museum. The walk is planned for one hour. Only a few artworks can be shown along the way. Millions more will remain unseen. Egyptian art comes first on the route. American art comes later. Arms and armor fill a hall after that. Greek and Roman art follows the armor. Art of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas comes next. Modern and contemporary art follows those galleries. A closing moment ends the visit. Special words are gathered at the end. Jada seems pretty cool. Art is something she cares about deeply. The student wants to understand that excitement. Around 15 BCE, builders completed the Temple of Dendur. Egyptian art fills the first galleries on the tour. Glass cases of mummies line the path Jada follows. An enormous room opens ahead, and its ceilings are high. A real temple of stone rests on a raised platform. Water in a pool wraps around the Temple of Dendur. Light pours in through a huge wall of windows. Jada describes a change to the Aswan Dam in 1933. The dam was made taller that year. Massive floods then hit the Nile River. For part of each year, the temple sat underwater. Destruction was a real threat. During the 1960s, the Aswan Dam was rebuilt. The site then faced a danger that would not go away. People chose to preserve the temple so its history would survive.

3Piece by piece, workers took the Temple of Dendur down. Ships carried the pieces to New York. Inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the pieces were joined again. A chieftain, Jada explains, dedicated the temple to Isis, an Egyptian goddess. His two sons received the same dedication. The Nile was where those sons drowned. Picture writing covers the facade of the building. That writing is called hieroglyphs, and it is the Egyptian way of writing with pictures. Princes appear in the pictures, bringing gifts. The pharaoh appears as well, bringing gifts. The gifts are acts of worship offered to gods and goddesses. Two carving styles hold these hieroglyphs. On the outside walls, the pictures are cut down into the stone. Sunken relief is the name of that style. On the inside walls, the pictures stand out from the surface. Raised relief is the name of that style. Electricity lights rooms today. Long ago, the only lights were the Sun, candles, and oil lamps. Inside a dark room, raised relief was easier to see. Feeling the carving was easier too. English graffiti marks the temple. From the seventeenth century through the nineteenth, travelers cut their names into the walls. Spray paint did not exist yet. A darkened hallway is the path Jada takes next. American art waits in the wing at the end of that hall.

4The group steps into an enormous room. Stained glass rises three stories and lights the space. A beautiful stairway climbs toward further galleries. American paintings hang in those galleries, and American furniture is shown there too. Even the stairs, Jada says, carry a history. They once belonged to the Chicago Stock Exchange Building. That building was among the first skyscrapers in America. The year 1894 is when it was built. Colorful windows on the gallery walls make the student stop. One window of stained glass comes from the famous Tiffany Studios. The years 1923 and 1924 are when it was made. Another gallery holds an enormous painting the student already knows. In 1851, Emanuel Leutze painted Washington Crossing the Delaware. George Washington appears with his troops. They are crossing the Delaware River while it is full of ice. The night shown is Christmas of 1776. American history class is where the student met this painting before. That night brought a surprise attack, with George Washington at the head of his troops. A camp of British supporters was the target. Misleading is the word Jada uses for the painting. Several historical inaccuracies sit inside it. An American flag is painted in the scene. When the battle happened, that flag had not been adopted yet. The uniforms shown are not the right kinds. Washington is standing in the boat. A boat that size would have capsized under a standing man.

5Jada says Leutze chose these details on purpose. A stronger reaction from viewers was his aim. She asks everyone to look with a critical eye. Questioning the content is part of that look. Understanding the history is the other part. Other paintings in the Met, she says, are worth finding. Some were made by Black painters as a response to Washington Crossing the Delaware. Some were made by Indigenous painters as a response. America looks more complex in those paintings. The canvas of Washington Crossing the Delaware is very large. A long walk brings the group to a hall of arms and armor. Knights in armor sit on horses in armor, and they seem to charge at the visitors. A glass case is the next stop. Inside is a large French suit made of steel. The date is around 1600. Yellow silk still lines the inside of the helmet. Red leather straps look nearly new. Battle was one time kings wore armor. Tournaments were another. This particular suit, Jada says, was worn in battle. A matching saddle belonged with it. A matching chanfron belonged with it too. The chanfron is the armor piece that covers a horse's head. Walking in the suit is hard to imagine. Fighting in it is harder still. Heavy is how it looks. Heavy is what it is. The full weight is 77 pounds, which is 34.9 kilograms.

6A room of helmets from Japan comes next. Samurai warriors once wore them. Material, size, and shape all differ from helmet to helmet. A bright red flame marks one helmet. A tiny figurine on that helmet holds a sword. The sixteenth century is the date Jada gives. Wisdom has a Buddhist guardian, and the figurine on top stands for that guardian. Hidden history, once known, changes how the student understands these objects. Their purpose grows clearer. More than 17,000 works sit in the Greek and Roman collection. A marble statue shows a woman who is an Amazon warrior. Battle has left her wounded. Shiny marble statues line a long hallway in the Greek and Roman galleries. Most of them, Jada explains, are copies made by Romans. Greek sculptures from several hundred years earlier were the models. Metal sculptures were often melted. Weapons and coins were made from that metal. Few metal sculptures remain. The white color of the marble is not how they once looked. Bright paint once covered ancient marble statues and temples. Reds, blues, and yellows were among those colors. A small room called a cubiculum is the next stop. Its painted walls traveled to New York City from Boscoreale, a village in Italy. The name sounds like boh-skoh-re-AH-le. Brilliant colors fill wall paintings of an outdoor sanctuary. Jada turns to the date August 24, 79 CE. Mount Vesuvius erupted on that day.

7Italy is home to this famous volcano. Enormous amounts of ash poured out. Nearby villages disappeared under the ash. Death and destruction on a massive scale followed. Layers of ash buried Romans who had been living ordinary days. Whole cities were preserved by that same ash. Buildings survived, and so did artwork, including the cubiculum walls. The paintings, Jada says, go back to 70 BCE. More than one hundred years separate them from the disaster. Decorations on the cubiculum walls are the work of ancient artists. Their method was fresco. In fresco, paints made with water go straight onto plaster. Leaving the cubiculum, the group enters new galleries. The art there is from Africa, from Oceania, and from the Americas. Islands in the Pacific Ocean make up Oceania. These galleries feel unlike the rooms before. Light is not the same. Sound is not the same. The design of the exhibits is not the same. Wooden boats of giant size hang overhead. Masks cover the walls in many shapes. Many colors and many materials appear in those masks. Jada pauses and asks for some thought. She wants the group to examine its own ideas of conventional beauty. A specific purpose shaped many objects across the Met. Everyday life is where they were useful. Prettiness was not the main goal. Beauty of its own kind still belongs to each object. A slit gong stands among the works.

8Its height is 14 feet, or 4.3 meters. Among musical instruments, it is one of the largest in the world. An African art gallery holds a figure of a man. The student stands before it. Massive is how the figure seems. Its real height is only about 3.5 feet, or 1.1 meters. Jada names the wooden sculpture an African power figure. Nails cover the body. The way he stands is commanding. His mouth hangs open. He could be a leader calling out orders. Wisdom and a sharp mind seem to live in his eyes. The Kongo peoples, Jada explains, are the makers. A round cavity is set in the stomach. Medicines used in ritual once filled that space. A beard of organic materials was once part of the figure. Rot took those materials away. Nails that held the beard are still there. Old age and wisdom, Jada says, were what the beard meant. Legal agreements were one use of this sculpture, as a symbol. Ending conflicts was another use. Healing illness was a third. Special sculptors produced African power figures. Ritual leaders produced them too. Modern and Contemporary Art galleries come next on the tour. Works there date from 1900 through today. Upstairs, a large canvas stops the group. The paint looks flung by a child in a tantrum. Jada names the American artist Jackson Pollock as the maker of a famous work.

9A movement called abstract expressionism grew with his help. Shapes and patterns, rather than people or things, carry the feeling in that style. An emotion or an attitude can come through the paint. Usual subjects were rejected by Pollock and other abstract expressionists. Usual methods were rejected too. Paint was poured by Pollock. Paint was splattered. Paint was thrown. The canvases stayed on the ground. An artist's stand was not used. Heavy cloth pulled tight on a frame is what a canvas is, and it is a surface for painting. Pretty landscapes, Jada says, are not required for art to be good. People who look realistic are not required either. It helps to learn where a work comes from. It helps to learn what stirred the artist. It helps to notice the effect the art has. A viewer can decide what to think from those clues. The year 1950 is when Jackson Pollock painted Autumn Rhythm (Number 30). Visitors like to gather on the museum steps. Tired legs are the student's problem by now. Famous artists line the last part of the walk. Vincent van Gogh is one of them. Claude Monet is another. A giant staircase leads downward. The Great Hall is waiting at the bottom. The tour has ended. Amazement is what the student feels at all that was seen and learned. One hour felt like travel around the world.

10It also felt like travel into the past. The importance of art had been misunderstood until this day. Outside, New York City crowds the senses with sights. Sounds crowd them too. Smells crowd them as well. A break seems necessary. The student sits on the broad front steps of the Met. Ideas for the essay should be written while they are still fresh. A rough drawing or outline is what a sketch is. To preserve a thing is to care for it and keep it for later years. A sanctuary is a safe place, and it is also the protection that place gives. Sculptures are works of art with depth, made from materials that bend or from materials that are hard. A cavity is an empty space held inside something solid. Conventional describes what is common, traditional, or accepted by most people. To symbolize is to let an object, a picture, a sign, or an act stand for an idea. A facade is the front face of a building. Galleries are rooms or buildings where art is kept for the public to see. Inaccuracies are details that are wrong. The hard part comes now. Every artwork felt amazing. Picking only three for the essay will not be easy. One choice is already clear. A return visit will happen. The next visit will last longer. The next visit will be for the student alone.

65. Partners That Share the Wild

1A school of yellow tangs cleans a green sea turtle. Algae is what they take off. The book opens with an introduction to shared living. Finding food while giving protection comes next. Help with keeping clean follows. Sharing a home comes after that. Teaming up to locate food is another part. Hitching a ride follows. Pollinating and fertilizing come next. Spreading seeds comes after that. A short close ends the book. Hard words are explained last. A crocodile holds its mouth open for a small bird. Leftover food stuck in the teeth is what the bird cleans away. Wild life is hard. Food can run short. A good home is difficult to locate. Pests stay pests. Something is nearly always trying to eat you. Many wild species answer that pressure with an unusual partnership. Two species that are nothing alike may each do a separate job. Each job helps the other. Scientists call this a symbiotic relationship. Safety from predators may be one partner's gift. A thorough cleaning may be the other's. Symbiosis is a word from ancient Greek. The Greek pieces mean with and living. The year 1877 is when scientists first used the word for wild species. They were describing lichens. A lichen is a complex living thing. Color sometimes marks it. Fungus is one part. A kind of algae is the other. The two parts labor together. Partnerships like these have been found in many places since that year. Deep oceans hold some. Dry deserts hold some. Mountains and forests hold some too. The pairs can look unlikely.

2A venomous sea anemone may live with a brightly colored clownfish. Anemone is said uh-NEM-uh-nee. A tall tree may live with a rodent that stays on the ground. A partnership of this kind can exist in a home. A pet dog may offer love. Companionship may come with it. Protection may come with it too. Food is what the dog receives back. Attention is part of the return. A safe place to live is part of it too. Both sides gain. In the wild, such pairings are fascinating. They can also decide life or death. Bees would struggle to live without flower nectar. Flowers would struggle to spread without bees to carry pollen. Starlings may stay close to a red deer. Insects on the deer's body are the prize. These partnerships are not always even. The ones that last thousands of years, or millions, last for a simple reason. Each species gains enough to make the deal worth keeping. Some scientists think such ties help explain Earth's many kinds of plants. They think the ties also help explain the wide range of wildlife. Different species rely on one another. Examples of the many kinds come next. In nature, unlike living things labor side by side. It helps to know someone is watching your back. Clownfish need every bit of help they can get. Colorful ones in the Indian Ocean are one case. Predators are the danger. Hiding in the tentacles of a venomous sea anemone is one defense. Anemones look like plants.

3They are sea animals. Rocks or other surfaces are where they attach. Prey is expected to come to them. A small fish or a shrimp that brushes the soft tentacles meets a toxin. The toxin freezes the prey in place. The anemone pulls that prey to its mouth and eats it. Clownfish are treated differently. They have learned how to build immunity to the venom. A touch or two on the tentacles starts the process. A pause follows. The touch is repeated over and over. Slowly, mucus builds as a shield on the skin. A cautious clownfish with stripes hides among those tentacles. Harmful contact is blocked by the mucus. The fish can move through the tentacles and stay unhurt. If a predator comes to eat the clownfish, the fish can dive into those safe arms. The larger hunter is often killed by the anemone. The anemone may eat from that kill. The clownfish may eat from it too. Ostriches and zebras in Africa often eat in the same place. Each helps the other watch for hunters. Sight is the ostrich's strength. Hearing is the zebra's strength. Together they are far more likely to notice a lion sneaking close. Other predators are noticed sooner too. Escape can start earlier. Impalas and baboons in Africa share a similar deal. Hearing in impalas is superb. Sight is superb. Smell is superb. If danger is sensed first, alert posture warns the baboons. Shaking horns warns them too. Loud screams from the baboons then drive hunters off. Teeth that look intimidating help.

4Ostrich groups and zebra groups often feed as neighbors. Each warns the other when hunters draw near. Some animals need a partner for spots they cannot clean. On many reefs, a small silvery fish does that work. It is called a cleaner wrasse. The little wrasse opens a cleaning station. Big fish wait their turn with patience. Why not simply swallow the wrasse? The wrasse swims in a special pattern. Some have likened it to a hypnotic dance. The dance settles the bigger fish. In time the mouth opens and the wrasse is allowed in. The wrasse shoots in and out of the mouth. It does the same at the gills. Fungus is eaten. Parasites are eaten. Dead skin and other debris are eaten. A giant moray eel may have teeth and mouth cleaned by one tiny wrasse. The wrasse gains a snack. The bigger fish is left clean, and left healthy. A similar cleaning is offered to tortoises by some of Darwin's ground finches. The place is the Galapagos Islands. A tortoise that wants cleaning stretches its neck. It stretches its legs. Finches swoop in. They peck off parasites the tortoise cannot reach. The tortoise leaves cleaner. The finches leave with fuller stomachs. They cling to the neck of a giant tortoise, and to its legs, picking off ticks. Sharing a house is hard. It is harder when the roommate is nothing like you. High cliffs along the New Zealand shore hold two very unlikely roommates. One is a slow reptile, lizardlike, called a tuatara.

5The name is said too-uh-TARR-uh. Building a nest is usually more effort than a tuatara wants. The other roommate is a fast bird called a sooty shearwater. They share one home. Each uses it at a different hour. Daytime in the burrow is usual for the tuatara. Night is when it goes out. While home, it eats bugs and parasites that bother the neat shearwater. The shearwater hunts by day. Night brings it back to the shared burrow. Inside, it loosens the dirt. Its droppings draw insects the tuatara likes to eat. The two seldom meet. A home is still shared, and so is a useful partnership. A tiny burrowing owl nests under the ground in a burrow someone else abandoned. Neighbors get a warning if a predator comes. These owls are the smallest in North America. Digging holes is beyond them. A safe hiding place is still required. Small bodies fit burrows once used by prairie dogs. Burrows of gopher tortoises fit too. An empty burrow chosen by a tiny owl may sit beside the old owner's home. Each animal calls out if a predator nears. Mice of the forest gain when they share space with beetles of the burrow. While the mouse sleeps, the beetle works through the fur. Fleas are the snack. Other burrow bugs are eaten when the mouse is gone. The beetle feeds well. The mouse keeps a home without those bugs. Ocean animals share houses too. Every species is playing for survival. Survival is harder if danger cannot be seen.

6Snapping shrimp on the seafloor face that problem. They are nearly blind. They dig burrows in the seabed. Moving sand to shape a home leaves them open to hungry hunters. A clever partner spots trouble well. That partner is a goby fish. As sand is dug out, gobies hover near the shrimp's antennae. They serve as lookouts. A tail flick is the warning when danger is close. The tail touches the antennae. The shrimp is told to hide. Burrows are shared in return. Night brings the fish a safe bed. A handy hiding spot comes with it. For these sea partners, the deal works well. A goby and a snapping shrimp join to make a home. A huge grizzly and a small red squirrel rely on each other. High in the Rocky Mountains of America, three living things depend on one another if they are to thrive. One is the grizzly bear. Another is the red squirrel. The third is the white bark pine. Pine nuts from that tree are rich in calories. The squirrel eats some nuts. Other nuts are buried. Smell lets the bear find the buried nuts. After the meal, droppings scatter some seeds. New trees sprout and grow. Later bears and later squirrels will have more nuts from those trees. Most small fish stay far from sharks, and that is wise. A slim fish called a remora does the reverse. It works to get as close to sharks as it can. A special organ sits on its head. The organ works like a suction cup.

7The fish can stick to a shark's underside. One small remora may cling to a shark's belly, travel with it, and share the meals. Remoras can swim alone. They often do. Sticking to a shark can be the simpler way to travel. Another large animal can serve the same way. Once stuck on, the remora goes where the shark goes. Scraps that slip from the strong jaws are sometimes eaten. A service is sometimes given back. Parasites are eaten. Host animals are helped to stay clean. Some hermit crabs of the Mediterranean Sea wear a strange hat. The hat is a sea anemone along for the ride. Long tentacles on the anemone carry venom. A hard shell protects the crab from them. Predators are kept off the crab by the anemone. Extra meals are the anemone's pay. Scraps the crab leaves are eaten. A small African bird often skips the search flight. It rides a hippopotamus and looks for insects there. Bugs are picked from the skin and eaten. The bird gains a meal and a ride. The hippo is cleared of pests. Several birds together may sit on that broad back. Bug cleaning is the return for the ride. A long-nosed bat feeds at an agave plant rich in pollen. Nectar is taken too. Where these bats live, agaves depend on them most for pollination. Cacti depend on them most as well. Bats do more than feed spooky tales. For many plants worldwide, a bat is a path to survival. A sweet meal is the plant's gift to those winged partners.

8Pollinators are the group these bats belong to. Pollen is carried from male parts of plants to female parts of other plants. Fertilization can follow. The plants can then reproduce and grow. Night is when bats often work. They like to push their heads deep into a flower's center. Sugary nectar is drunk. Pollen rich in protein is eaten. Leaving the flower, a bat is often dotted with sticky pollen. The next flower visited receives that pollen. Plants gain a steady trade of pollen from flower to flower. Bats gain a steady supply of nectar and of tasty pollen. Honeybees rank among the busiest pollinators on Earth. Like bats, they enter flowers for nectar. Flecks of pollen often cover them as they leave. The next stop wipes the pollen off. Hummingbirds work in a very similar way. Female yucca moths are choosy about egg sites. They like to place hundreds of eggs across several yucca flowers. The eggs get safe homes. The flowers gain as well. Pollen is spread as the moth flits from bloom to bloom. A honeybee can carry pollen from one dandelion to another while it gathers nectar. High in a Brazil nut tree, pods cluster together. A tree, or any plant, needs a way to send seeds to new ground. Otherwise growth stays in one spot. Survival odds improve if seeds travel far. Unusual partners help many plants scatter seeds. One striking case is in the Amazon rainforest. It joins the Brazil nut tree with a rodent called an agouti.

9An agouti is about as big as a cat. The tree is huge and tall. Height can reach 200 feet. That is 61 meters, or even more. Seedpods are about the size of grapefruits. They are hard. They are tough. A fall to the ground usually does not crack them. The fall can start at 100 feet. That is 30.5 meters, or from even higher. Tough pods can be cracked by the small agouti's strong jaws. New Brazil nut trees can sprout from droppings the agouti leaves behind. Few forest animals have teeth and jaws strong enough for that thick shell. The agouti is one of them. Some seeds are eaten. Others are buried far from the parent tree, which scatters them through the forest. In time the seeds become trees. The long cycle starts again. Mistletoe in the desert needs help to move its seeds. A small songbird that is black does that work. The bird likes to eat those seeds. Berries hide them. The beak splits berry skin away. Undigested seeds fall wherever droppings are left. Without symbiotic partnerships, the world would look very different. Many species would face predators and pests with less help. They would be more likely to stay stuck in small patches of habitat. Blooming and spreading would be less likely. Food choices would be fewer. Scientists are still learning how these special ties work. New ones are still being found. On shoreline cliffs in New Zealand, sooty shearwaters and tuataras keep a special living arrangement.

10Bugs stirred up by grazing impalas become an easy meal for baboons. A warning call is the payback if danger comes near. Each partnership differs a little. The benefit to each species differs a little too. One thing is shared. Each partner receives something useful in return. Survival becomes more likely. Fish, birds, humans, and many other living things can reproduce. Longer and healthier lives become more likely too. A few word meanings help. To distribute is to spread things, or to scatter them, across an area. Pollen is the male cells of a flower. It often looks like a fine yellow dust. Fertilized means male and female reproductive cells have joined. A new animal or a new plant can result. A refuge is a safe place. Comfort or protection can define it too. A species groups living things that share a body plan and can produce young together. Interdependent means each side needs the other. People can need one another this way. Groups can. So can organisms sharing an ecosystem. Symbiotic describes a helpful tie between different kinds of organisms. Frightening is one sense of intimidating. It can mean overwhelming. Venomous means able to inject venom. That poisonous fluid can be delivered by a strike, a bite, or a sting. Mucus is a thick, slippery liquid made in a body. It guards tissues and keeps them wet. A parasite may be a plant or an animal. It grows on another living thing and takes food from it. Vulnerable means easy to harm.

66. People Who Follow the Funnel

1A funnel cloud is being filmed by storm chasers. This book follows people who chase wind. Tornado Alley comes next. Tornado weather follows. The question of prediction comes after that. Damage is described next. Chasers at work come after the damage. Hard words are explained at the end, along with the topics the book covers. Who chooses to chase a storm? Most people seek shelter when weather turns nasty. High winds are part of a chaser's work. Funnel clouds are part of it. Lightning is part of it too. Some chasers make films. Some take photographs. A spectacular image of a tornado is the goal. Most chasers, though, are scientists. Meteorologists who study weather are in that group. They step into a tornado's path on purpose. The information they gather can sharpen predictions. Lives can be saved by that information. Danger is real. Thrill may seem to be part of it. Severe weather makes these people extra careful. Tornado comes from a Spanish word, tronada. Thunderstorm is what tronada means.

2Cyclone is another common name. Twister is another. Whirlwind is another. A tornado that forms over water is a waterspout. A picture shows one taking shape above the water. Each year, hundreds of these storms tear through the middle of the United States. Cars can be flipped. Roofs can be ripped from houses. Crops can be ruined. Most of the winds reach about 160 kilometers in an hour. That is about 100 miles in an hour. The strongest storms are sometimes called super tornadoes. Their winds run from 402 kilometers in an hour to beyond 482. In miles, that span is about 250 to 300. Everything in the path of a super tornado is destroyed. Fewer than two in every hundred tornadoes blow harder than 322 kilometers in an hour. That is 200 miles in an hour. Each year the United States sees more than 800 tornadoes reach the ground. More than half of all tornadoes on Earth hit a central belt called Tornado Alley. Iowa is one state in that belt.

3Nebraska is one. Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas are others. Most chasing happens in these states. Spring is the season in the southern Great Plains. Late summer is the season farther north. A photograph records tornado damage in Illinois in 1925. No state in the country has been spared a tornado. The middle of the country tends to see stronger ones, and more of them. Texas holds the record for the most touchdowns. On March 8, 1925, a tornado ranked among the nation's worst. Missouri was hit. Illinois was hit. Indiana was hit. Its path along the ground measured 352 kilometers. That distance is 219 miles. Three hours and thirty minutes was how long it lasted. Deaths numbered more than 600. Homes were lost by about 10,000 people. Meteorologists learn by watching tornadoes and by gathering data. Much is still unknown. Most of the weather needed to build a tornado is understood. What is not understood is why some funnel clouds reach the ground. Those that do become tornadoes.

4Others never touch down. Warm air that is moist, sitting low, is the first ingredient. Cool dry air higher up is part of it. A cold air mass must collide with a warm air mass. Diagrams show the steps of formation. A tornado watch means the setup is right for a tornado. Radio updates should be heard. Television updates should be watched. A tornado warning means one has been seen nearby. Go indoors at once. The moment of a strike cannot always be known. Clues exist. Funnel clouds may appear in the sky before they reach the ground. Other times, formations called wall clouds appear. Severe storms or supercells can follow wall clouds. A severe storm does not always make a tornado. Each tornado's data teaches chasers more. Meteorologists still cannot forecast a tornado the way they forecast sun or rain five to seven days out. They can say when the setup is right. A watch can then be issued. A few safety steps matter.

5Get into a house or some other building. A basement is the place to go. If no basement exists, use the lowest floor. A hallway is a good room. An interior room is a good room. Windows should be avoided. A desk, a table, or some other sturdy furniture should be used as cover. Outdoors, with no safe way inside, find the nearest low spot. A ditch is one example. Arms and hands should cover the head. A picture shows a storm shelter in a mobile-home park in Alabama. Meteorologists read Doppler radar to follow storms. Wind direction can be found with it. Fast-spinning air inside thunderstorms can show up early. Precise wind directions can be found as well. People can get about 20 minutes of warning. That span may sound short. A warning ahead of time can save lives. Doppler radar also shows how severe a storm is. The storm's exact place can be pinned down. Its likely length can be judged. Ten minutes is an average tornado.

6Some last only seconds. Some run on for hours. F-scale ratings measure tornadoes. Theodore Fujita, a scientist, invented the measuring method, and the scale carries his name. Destruction is what the ratings are based on. An F0 is weak. An F1 is weak too. An F5 is a monster. Winds in an F5 reach 420 to 512 kilometers in an hour. In miles, that is 261 to 318. An expert sets the rating by studying damage after the hit. The rating cannot be known with real accuracy beforehand. Only the aftermath allows it. People inspect what the tornado broke. An F0, the weak class, has winds of 64 to 116 kilometers in an hour, or 40 to 72 miles. Branches break. An F1, also weak, has winds of 117 to 180 kilometers in an hour, or 73 to 112 miles. Trees snap. Shingles come off. Other roof surfaces come off too. An F2 is strong. Winds run 181 to 253 kilometers in an hour, or 113 to 157 miles.

7Large trees are pulled up by the roots. An F3 is strong as well. Winds run 254 to 332 kilometers in an hour, or 158 to 206 miles. Cars are flipped. Roofs of houses are torn away. Walls are torn away too. An F4 is violent. Winds run 333 to 419 kilometers in an hour, or 207 to 260 miles. Houses are leveled. Cars are thrown about. An F5 is violent as well. Winds run 420 to 512 kilometers in an hour, or 261 to 318 miles. Houses are ripped from their foundations. Large objects are thrown hundreds of feet. Real tornadoes have never given scientists a verified check of these Fujita wind speeds. True speeds at ground level are unknown in most cases. Getting close enough to measure is too hard. Two buildings can look equally damaged even when the wind that hit them differed by a lot. Chasers must read radar reports if they hope to find a tornado worth studying. Weather data is watched as storms build.

8They hunt for a storm with a chance of spinning up a tornado. An educated guess helps. So does advice from chasers with more experience. That mix can put a team five miles from the hit instead of 50. Closeness lets them gather the data that improves later predictions. Ordinary people also help the National Weather Service by looking out for these storms. Local police in that alley learn how to spot a tornado. Emergency personnel learn that skill too. Chasers watch a tornado take shape. The job can feel like hurry, then wait. Professionals may hunt storms for about 10 days to gain one minute of watching a tornado. Collecting data takes that same long hunt per minute. Filming does too. Warren Faidley is widely known as a chaser, a photographer, and a filmmaker. He says a whole year has sometimes passed with no tornado in sight. When one appears, he wants the best pictures he can get. A safe distance still has to be kept. Winds above 322 to 483 kilometers in an hour can toss cars like toys.

9In miles, that is 200 to 300. Knowing when to leave is the trick. The path has to be judged too. People left without homes by fires, tornadoes, and other natural disasters can get help from the American Red Cross. Chasers treat the work as serious. They believe the mission matters. Winds near the ground may matter more in forming a tornado than earlier thinking allowed. A smaller eye, meaning the center, spins faster. Plenty is still unknown. More data is gathered with hard work. That data helps everyone understand whirling storms. Lives can be destroyed by them. Whole towns can be torn apart in only a few minutes. A few word meanings help. Doppler radar is a tracking system. It reports where storms, clouds, and precipitation are, and how fast they move. F-ratings are numbers. They say how destructive a tornado is, and how dangerous. A funnel cloud is shaped like a funnel. It hangs under the base of a thundercloud.

10Meteorologists study the air around Earth, the climate, and the weather. Supercells are thunderclouds that rotate. They reach high and often make tornadoes. Tornado Alley is not an official name. It labels a central stretch of the United States where touchdowns are frequent. A tornado warning is the alert used once a tornado has been seen close by. A tornado watch is the alert used when conditions favor one. Wall clouds are smaller clouds under a supercell's main cloud. They make little rain, or none. A waterspout is a tornado over water. Topics in the book include devastation. They include Doppler radar, F-ratings, and the F-scale. They include funnel clouds and meteorologists. They include the National Weather Service and safety. They include severe storms and storm chasers. They include super tornadoes and Texas. They include Theodore Fujita and Tornado Alley. They include the warning and the watch. They include the United States and the updraft. They include wall clouds, Warren Faidley, and winds.

67. Plates, Places, and Ways of Cooking

1Friends and family gathered for a meal often mark something important. The meal can be a central part of a country's culture. A question is worth asking. Where do the ingredients in a favorite meal come from? A store today can hold foods from many countries. Corn from Peru may be there. Peaches from China may be there. Salmon from Norway may be there. Hundreds of years ago, the choice was narrower. People could eat only foods that grew or lived naturally where they were. Each region built its own dishes. Each region built its own style of cooking. That style is called cuisine, said kwih-ZEEN. Trade began to reshape the cooking of each region. Travel did too. People met foods from elsewhere. They met spices from elsewhere. Even inside one country, cuisine can differ quite a bit today. A country's cooking can teach a great deal about its culture. Rice grows well where the climate is warm and wet. Many parts of Asia have that climate. Many cuisines in Asia therefore treat rice as a staple.

2Rice might be waiting on an Indian dinner table. It might hold stewed meat or vegetables. It might hold a bread called naan, said NAHN. Chicken often appears in the meal. Lamb often appears. Legumes often appear. Sauces based on yogurt often appear. One popular dish is biryani, said bee-ree-AH-nee. It is rice with meat and onions. Hot spices go in. Raisins may top it. Dried apricots may top it. Nuts may top it. A picture pairs the word Asia with plates of biryani. China, an East Asian country, also sets rice out for dinner. Southeast China may serve the rice with meat. Slightly cooked vegetables may join it. A mild, sweet sauce may join it. Southwest China often serves meat and vegetables another way. The sauces there are hot and spicy. A market scene is set in China. Travel on to Thailand, said TY-land, in Southeast Asia, and dinner might be shrimp. The shrimp sits in a green curry sauce. Rice comes with it.

3Curry paste flavors many dishes in this region. Coconut milk does too. Lemongrass does too. Garlic does too. Cooks often blend several tastes in a single dish. Sweet is one taste. Sour is one. Salty is one. Bitter is one. Hot is one. Pictures show green curry beside the regional notes. A short note concerns Japan. Japan cares about eating some foods at the moment of peak freshness and flavor. The practice is part of the country's cuisine. It is part of the country's culture. Most foods can be found all year. Many local markets still choose to sell only what is in season. The Japanese word for season is shun. It is said SHOON. It also points to the moment a food tastes best. Southeast of Thailand lies a region called Oceania. Australia is part of that region. Great Britain colonized Australia in the 1700s. Because of that history, many of the same foods appear in Australian cooking. Dinner might be a meat pie. Beef or chicken is cooked inside a flaky crust.

4Vegetables come with it. People from Thailand have influenced the cooking. People from Vietnam have influenced it too. Curry is popular. Stir-fry is popular. A picture labels this region Oceania. Lovos are underground ovens. Heated stones make the heat. In Fiji, meats and vegetables are wrapped in palm leaves or banana leaves and cooked in a lovo. Fiji lies east of Australia. Oceania is a spread of small islands, and this is one of them. Shipping fresh meat there is expensive. Canned meat is common. Corned beef is one example. Miles of coastline supply plenty of fish. Cassava goes into nearly every dish. Taro goes into nearly every dish. Both are vegetables similar to potatoes. The hot, wet climate suits many fruits. Bananas grow well. Pineapple grows well. Dinner might be kokoda, said koh-KOHN-dah. The dish is raw fish. Coconut cream is served with it. Fresh lime juice is served with it. Long, cold winters come to some places in Eastern Europe. They come to some places in Northern Europe.

5Dinner there can look very different from dinner in Fiji. In a colder climate, fruits and vegetables grow for only a short time. Poland keeps them by pickling. The food goes into vinegar. It can also go into salty water. A long winter is easier to outlast once the food has been pickled. Meat is often prepared for winter too. It may be dried. It may be smoked. It may be salted. It may be pickled. A dinner plate might hold smoked sausage. It might hold rye bread. It might hold potatoes. It might hold pickled cabbage. A picture labels this region Europe. Beet soup is popular in eastern European countries. Sour cream often sits on top. Naples, in Italy, is where the modern pizza was created during the 1700s. Tomatoes and cheese sit on a flat round of dough. Southern Europe belongs to a region called the Mediterranean. The climate is warmer. Many fruits grow there. Many vegetables grow there. Tomatoes show up in many dishes.

6Olives show up. Peppers show up. Lemons show up. Onions show up. In Italy, pasta alla Norma might be the dinner. It is a popular pasta dish. Fried eggplant is in it. Tomatoes are in it. Garlic is in it. Cheese is in it. The same kind of dish can turn up in many countries. Dumplings are one example. From place to place, they may look a little different. A dumpling is a cooked piece of dough. Sometimes a filling sits inside. The filling may be sweet. It may be savory. Flour often makes the dough. Potatoes often make it. A filling can mix meat. It can mix cheese. It can mix fruits. It can mix vegetables. It can mix nuts. Dumplings come in more than 140 kinds across the world. Northern Africa also sits in the Mediterranean. Couscous, said KOOSS-kooss, is used in many dishes. Olives are used. Almonds are used. Dates are used. Cinnamon is used. Sweetness from dried fruit enters savory cooking in Morocco.

7Figs are one such fruit. Apricots are another. Dinner might be lamb tagine, said tah-ZHEEN. It is a stew of lamb and prunes. The stew is cooked in a tagine pot. Farther south, in Central Africa, tomatoes appear in many dishes. Cassavas appear. Plantains appear. Peanuts reached this region when traders carried them out of Brazil. The arrival was in the 1600s. Peanuts now go into many sauces. The sauces mix them with foods found naturally in the region. Yams are one of those foods. Okra is another. A popular dish is fufu, said FOO-foo. Smashed cassava is mixed with water. The mix is formed into balls. The balls are dipped in peanut soup. A picture labels this region Africa. Rainbow cuisine is a name sometimes given to the food of Southern Africa. The name points to how diverse it is. Colonizers from France influenced the cooking across history. Colonizers from the Netherlands did too. Enslaved peoples from India influenced it. Enslaved peoples from Malaysia influenced it. Popularity still belongs to ingredients Indigenous peoples of the area have long used.

8The Zulu are one of those peoples. Potatoes are among the ingredients. Leafy vegetables are among them. Corn is among them. Beans are among them. In South Africa, a common dish is bobotie, said buh-BOO-uh-tee. It mixes meat with dried fruits and nuts. Eggs and milk top the dish. An outdoor food market is shown in Morocco. Across the Atlantic Ocean lies Brazil, a large country in South America. The cooking there is equally diverse. Indigenous peoples of the region shaped it over time. Colonizers from Portugal shaped it. West African peoples who had been enslaved also shaped the cooking. Black beans are common ingredients. Rice is common. Peppers are common. Fruits such as mangoes are common. Papayas are common. Dinner might be feijoada, said fayzh-WAH-duh. It is a stew of beans. Beef is in the stew. Pork is in the stew. A picture labels this region South America and shows feijoada. Peru, in the north of the continent, holds several landscapes.

9Coastlines are there. Rainforests are there. Mountains are there. The mix lets many fruits grow. Many grains grow. Many vegetables grow. Peppers are among them. Corn is among them. Tomatoes are among them. Plantains are among them. Mangoes are among them. Avocados are among them. Potatoes are among them. Ceviche, said seh-VEE-cheh, is a popular dinner. It is raw fish. Fresh lemon juice is served with it. Fresh lime juice may be served with it instead. Pictures show ceviche. The United States holds many landscapes and many climates. Those differences help shape cooking from region to region. History added more influences. Native peoples shaped regional cooking. Enslaved peoples from Africa shaped it. Colonizers from Europe shaped it. People who immigrated from every part of the world shaped it too. Mexican cooking influenced the cuisine of southwestern states. Arizona is one of those states. Texas is one. French cooking helped shape cuisine in the South. African cooking helped. Spanish cooking helped. Caribbean cooking helped. Cuisine in Hawai‘i drew on recipes and cooking methods from several traditions.

10Japanese cooking was one. Filipino cooking was one. Korean cooking was one. Chinese cooking was one. Portuguese cooking was one. Polynesian cooking was one. Nearly every country's dishes can be located somewhere in the United States today. Food tied to one country can now turn up far from home. A French restaurant might stand in China. An Ethiopian restaurant might stand in Brazil. An Italian restaurant might stand in Australia. A new food can feel like a short visit, a couple of hours long, to some other country. Cuisine can teach a country's history. It can teach the country's culture. It can teach the landscape. It can even teach the weather. Fun can come from tasting foods that traveled from far away. Tasting new flavors can be fun. A new favorite dish might be waiting. Dinner brings an Indonesian family to the table together. Other plates in view include rellena. They include fish and chips. They include lamb tagine.

68. Seeing Color in Another Way

1A person who sees every color can pick out a red crayon with ease. Red-green color blindness makes that same choice much harder. This book starts by asking which colors you notice. It asks where color itself comes from. It explains the way color vision works. Rods and cones get their own look. Several kinds of color vision deficiency are explained. Challenges come next, then tests, then tools that help, then treatment. Daily life closes the story, followed by special words. Picture a box of crayons. Gray, blue, and yellow, in many shades, may be all that a person with color blindness sees there. CVD is another name for color blindness. The letters stand for color vision deficiency. Some colors remain visible for most people who have CVD. The world simply does not look the same to them as it does to other people. A top picture can show the crayon box in full color. A bottom picture can show the same box as red-green color blindness changes it. Full-color vision makes the red crayon easy to find in that box. Red-green color blindness changes which crayon looks which color.
