2Gray shades can stand in for colors other people name as red or green. Blue can still appear. Yellow can still appear. The difference is in the colors, not in whether a crayon is there. CVD does not mean every color vanishes for most people who have it. A small shift in how the world looks is the common experience. The chapters that follow stay with that shift, from the eye's parts to daily life. Every color of the rainbow is hidden inside white light. A wavelength is what makes one color differ from another. Color that we see on an object has a clear cause. Some wavelengths are absorbed by the object. Other wavelengths are reflected. Red wavelengths bounce off a strawberry, which is why it looks red. Most other wavelengths are taken in by the fruit. Several parts of the eye work as a team. Incoming light is gathered by the cornea, which starts the focus. The iris can open the pupil or close it. More light enters, or less light does. A hole at the center of the eye is the pupil.

3Light goes through that hole. Focusing is finished when the lens changes its shape. At the back of the eye, rods and cones line the retina's wall. What is seen gets registered there. Messages about the view travel along the optic nerve to the brain. Eyes do not treat every wavelength in the same way, and that is why color is seen. Light that enters an eye is focused by the lens onto the retina. Tissue in a thin layer at the back of the eyeball is the retina. Rod cells and cone cells that sense light are triggered there. Signals leave those cells for the brain. Images are built by the brain from the signals. No cells in the eye are more sensitive than rod cells. Very dim light is still enough for them to let you see. Colors cannot be separated by rod cells. Color vision is the job of cone cells. Three kinds of cone cells exist. Blue light is absorbed by one kind. Green light is absorbed by another.

4Red light is absorbed by the third. Thousands of colors become visible when these three main colors combine. CVD appears if one or more kinds of cone cells fail to work. Which cones are affected decides the type of CVD. How badly they are affected decides it too. Humans see more colors than most animals do. Blue and yellow shades are all that dogs can see. Red is invisible to bulls. A few animals see more colors than humans. Some birds are in that group. Bees are in it. Butterflies are in it. Wavelengths that humans cannot see are visible to them. Vision in a honeybee is not the same as vision in a human. The most common color-vision problem is red-green CVD. It shows up most often among white people with family roots in the north of Europe. Men are affected at a rate of one in twelve. Women have it less often. Green cone cells are the usual source of the problem. Green objects and yellow objects can look reddish because of that. Red cone cells can cause red-green CVD as well.

5Then red, orange, and yellow can look green or black. Telling some colors apart is hard for people with red-green CVD. Clear sight is still possible. Some of the light sensed by red cones is also sensed by green cones. That shared range is why vision stays clear. A comparison can show full-color vision beside red-green CVD, with red, yellow, and green labeled in each view. Missing blue cone cells can cause blue-yellow CVD. Blue cone cells that work poorly can cause it too. This kind of CVD is fairly rare. Worldwide, about one person in ten thousand is affected. Men and women have it equally often, which is unlike red-green CVD. Blue cone cells are entirely absent in some people who have the blue-yellow form. Green is how blue looks to them. Violet or gray is how yellow looks. More often, the blue cones still work a little. Telling yellow and red apart from pink becomes difficult. The most serious form is complete CVD. It is very rare. Two or more of the three cone types have problems in this form.

6Extra sensitivity to light is common when two or more cone types are missing. Seeing clearly can be hard. Bright light makes the problem worse. Most or all of their seeing depends on rod cells. Low light is the only setting where rod cells work. Worldwide, about one person in thirty thousand lacks all three cone types. Black, white, and gray are the only shades in a world seen without working cone cells. A view of full color can be set beside blue-yellow CVD and beside red-green CVD. Blue-yellow CVD is not the same problem as red-green CVD. The cone type that fails is different. Complete CVD is different again, because more than one cone type fails. Rarity is greatest when every cone type is missing. Shades of black, white, and gray are then the whole view. Light that is too bright can hurt when cones are missing and rods must do the work. Low light is where those rods can help. Each form of CVD changes color in its own way. Challenges can meet people who have CVD. Color-coded facts on maps can be hard to read.

7Classwork can be hard for children with CVD. Yellow chalk on a green chalkboard is hard to read when the CVD is the red-green kind. Art projects raise a color-choice problem for every type of CVD. Science projects raise the same problem. Safety can be affected too. Red or yellow is a common color for fire hydrants, chosen so they stand out. Warning lights on cars often use those colors. Emergency equipment often uses them. Full-color vision makes those bright colors obvious. CVD can make them easy to miss. A sunburn can go unnoticed without color vision. A rash can go unnoticed. Meat that is undercooked can go unnoticed. A career choice can be shaped by CVD. Full-color vision is required for geologists. It is required for airline pilots. Other jobs grow harder without it. 3Planners placed twenty-seven events into nine categories. The nine groups included Bungee Jumping and also Eco-Challenge. In-line Skating was a group. Skateboarding was a group. Skysurfing was a group. Sport Climbing was a group. So were Street Luge, Biking, and the events held on water. Photos mark sky surfing in 1997, ice climbing in 1999, and street luge in 1999. Reporters who had covered sports for a long time scoffed. One writer joked that this was an Olympics performed with no hands. Even so, no one could dismiss the athletic fire. No one could dismiss the creativity the athletes showed. Young fans devoted to extreme sports loved the meet. Organizers set the date again for the following year. They cut the word Extreme down to the letter X. The year after that was 1997. A winter version opened at Big Bear Lake, California. Skiing filled most of the card. Snowboarding did too. Winter and summer versions each last four days. Both have continued strongly from then until now. For a long stretch they moved among different places in the United States. Winter events were staged in Aspen, Colorado. Later, winter moved to Minneapolis in Minnesota. The summer shift came in 2014. Los Angeles in California was left behind.

4Austin, Texas, took over. ESPN does more than display extreme sports at the meet. It also seeks a profit. Extreme athletes buy a great deal of gear. They buy clothing. They buy music. They buy video games. Advertisers pay the network for a path to those consumers. Some of the payment is for ads on TV. Some is for other advertising. A number of the athletes have earned money too. A sponsor is a business that pays an athlete. The athlete uses that company's gear. Logos go on the clothes and on the equipment. A handful of pro stars hold sponsor contracts. Some of those contracts pay millions of dollars. Tony Hawk is among them. Most athletes make much less. Some make nothing, especially at the start of a career. Kelly Slater is shown surfing. The meet is the ninth X Games. The year is 2003. Companies that sell surf gear have paid him millions in sponsorships. Two more scenes show the wider map. In 2000, athletes in Thailand try to qualify for the Asia events. In 2018, a skier launches a big jump at the Norway meet. The home base of the games is the United States. ESPN has tested several expansions abroad. France has hosted. Brazil has hosted.

5Australia has hosted. So have other countries. From 1998 until 2005, Asia played host. Thailand was one stop. Malaysia was another. South Korea was another. China was another. They returned in 2014 and again in 2015. A China edition began in 2019. A Norway edition has run strongly since 2016. No foreign meet has proved as successful as the games inside America. Most of the action happens inside America. A worldwide field still shows up. Athletes from many countries enter qualifying rounds. Their hope is a spot in the X Games. Meets held abroad, plus qualifying days and demonstrations, help promote the games to a worldwide audience. Sophie Rodriquez of France is shown competing. The place is Oslo. The year is 2016. Where do the athletes live? At the 2019 meet in Minneapolis, Americans made up most of the invited field. Even so, many competitors travel in from other parts of the world. ESPN is the source of that count. The menu of events shifts every year. Early programs included surprises. Skydiving was one. Jumping on water skis with bare feet was one. Racing on super-modified shovels was one. In the barefoot jump, a speedboat pulls a skier who has no skis. The skier performs tricks. Then the skier leaves a ramp and hopes to come down upright.

6In shovel racing, riders rebuild a snow shovel. The result is a sled that can go at super speed. The sled can go very fast. It can also crash in a major way. Organizers refresh the lineup as each year arrives. From the opening games in 1995, just two sports remain. One is skateboarding. The other is BMX biking. Four questions decide what is dropped or added. Does a large group of fans care deeply? Is it viewed as a true sport that demands skill and effort? Are companies willing to back it with advertising and with sponsorships? Can it be held without a trip to a special site? A small word list from the athletes. These athletes enjoy wordplay. Some of their inventiveness sits in the names of stunts. A digger is a bad fall while a trick is being tried. A whip tips a Moto X machine until the bike is flat while it is still flying. A kiss of death is a handstand in the middle of a Moto X jump. A nothing means the rider lets go of the bike completely, on a BMX jump or a Moto X jump. A rail grind puts a skateboard, a snowboard, or a pair of skis onto a metal rail for a slide.

7A Superman is a trick on a BMX bike or a Moto X bike. The rider kicks back while gripping the handlebars and seems to be flying. Competitive jumping with bungee cords was another event that faded. It seemed closer to play than to sport. Competitors jumped off a platform. Long cords that stretch were wrapped around their ankles. They dropped, sprang upward, and added twists and flips. Judges scored the moves. Surfing was removed. Wakeboarding was removed. Both demand locations that are hard to find. A small set of main sports now carries most of the events. Skateboarding sits at the center of that set. Summer 2018 included six events for skateboards. Vert is short for vertical. Riders shoot up and down ramps and throw tricks. Street sends skaters through a park. Steps, rails, ramps, and slopes stand in the way. Judges grade technique. They also grade style. Leticia Bufoni of Brazil is shown in the street contest. The city is Sydney. The year is 2018. The country is Australia. The winter meet has fewer choices. In 2018 it offered only four sports. They were skiing, snowboarding, snowmobiling, and biking on snow. Slopestyle takes skiers and snowboarders down a hill.

8Tricks happen on ramps, on rails, and on other built features. Snowmobile sessions include races. They also include trick events. Snow BikeCross sends athletes racing and doing stunts. Their bikes started as motorcycles. Builders changed them so they run on snow. While these games evolved, the Olympic Games tried to borrow some of the appeal. Younger fans were the target. Events that grew popular here were added there. Halfpipe contests for skateboarders are one example. Halfpipe contests for snowboarders are another. Plenty of athletes enter both gatherings. An Olympic athlete is part of a national team. An athlete here is not. Each one competes alone. Sponsors provide the pay. A more surprising addition is the set of events for major-league gamers. Since 2017, eGamers have joined. They are competitors with high skill at video games. Letting them in has been controversial. Many people ask how a gamer can seek the same medals as an extreme athlete. Names that rose here. Through this meet, a whole generation of extreme athletes became legends. Newer names are still climbing. A few stand at the top and have shaped the history of these sports. Brighton Zeuner rides a skateboard. She won the women's park event at age thirteen. The meet was Minneapolis.

9The year was 2017. Chloe Kim rides a snowboard. At seventeen she took gold in the women's halfpipe at the Winter Olympics of 2018. She already owned six medals from these games. Nyjah Huston rides a skateboard. From 2009 to 2016 he dominated the summer street contest. His prize money is greater than that of any other skateboarder. Travis Pastrana rides Moto X and also races rally cars. Across fifteen years in the motorsport events he collected seventeen medals. Eleven were gold. A workshop for action sports. To someone new to extreme sports, these athletes can look a little wild. They launch to astonishing heights. A board or a bike of some kind stays with them. Then they land in a graceful way. Or the crash is spectacular. Trying tricks brings road rash. It brings bruises that are black and blue. It brings broken bones. A crowd can feel awe when a huge stunt seems to land with no effort. Fans rarely notice how many years of practice fill each day. Athletes experiment again and again until a goal is reached. Tony Hawk says the 900 took him thirteen years of practice before a clean landing. These daredevils are bold in the extreme. Reckless is the wrong word for them.

10Mastering fear, and then succeeding, leaves a strong feeling of empowerment. Snow BikeCross shows that same drive. These games helped move extreme sports into ordinary public view. Audiences love watching an attempt that looks impossible. Both the misses and the landings prove a point. The human mind can be astonishing. The body can be astonishing. The spirit can be astonishing. Words to know. An athlete trains to race, play, or perform, and needs strength plus speed plus skill. Passionate describes intense feeling or belief about a person or a thing. Promote means to put an idea forward and hope others accept it. Extreme sports carry more risk, more thrill, and harder tests than ordinary sports. Stunts are daring physical feats, often staged as entertainment. An obstacle is anything that blocks progress or movement.

72. Steam, Mills, and a New Way of Life

1Late in the 1800s, linen was made on a roving frame. A woman in an English factory did that work. About 1764, the Scottish inventor James Watt took on a repair job. The machine in need of repair was a Newcomen steam engine. Mines that filled with water already depended on engines like it. Miners used them to pump the water clear. Those engines were not new. Decades had passed since they were invented. Watt redesigned the engine. Fuel went further in his version. Running it also cost less. Later years brought still more changes to the steam engine. Watt stayed part of that work. Other inventors joined in. Steam could then drive machines of many sorts. Looms that wove cloth could run on it. Locomotives could run on it too. The redesigned engine was a single advance among many. That group of advances is what sparked the Industrial Revolution. The older Newcomen design had prepared the ground. From the middle of the 1700s through the middle of the 1800s, new technology remade Great Britain. The wider world changed after that. Nearly every part of daily life felt the shift. Work was done in new ways. People lived in different places. Travel could cover greater distances. Clothing was not what it had been. The foods people ate changed as well.

2New machines were a leading cause of the Industrial Revolution. They were not the only cause. The East India Company was another. Traders formed that company in England in the year 1600. Over time it held military power. It held political power as well. A large private army belonged to it. Cotton products from India were among the goods it brought in. Those goods stayed cheap. Indian laborers received little pay for their work. In Britain, cotton goods won extreme popularity. Around the middle of the 1700s, Indian territories came under the company's control. Raw cotton in India was then within Britain's direct reach. Britain imported that cheap cotton. The aim was to finish goods at home for still less money. A scene from 1799 shows a battle in India's Kingdom of Mysore. Soldiers serving the British East India Company face local troops. An 1815 map of the British Empire marks many overseas places. Canada is on that map. Newfoundland is on it. Bermuda, the Bahamas, Jamaica, British Honduras, and Trinidad are on it. Gibraltar and Malta are on it. Sierra Leone, Ascension Island, Saint Helena, and Cape Colony are on it. Mauritius, India, Ceylon, New South Wales, and Tasmania are on it too. Late in the 1700s, colonies in the West Indies sat under British control.

3Colonies in North America and South America did too. Canada was part of that reach. Wool came from those lands. Silk came from them. Lumber came from them. Coal lay in large supply inside Britain. Iron did too. Resources of that kind mattered for industrialization. Farmers had found new ways to grow more food. The population rose because of that extra food. During those same years, lords who held wealth bought up wide tracts of common land. Small farmers had once worked that land. Many people could no longer raise their own food. They had to seek jobs in cities. In the 1700s, cloth and clothes formed the largest industry. People call that work textile production. New inventions transformed it before they transformed other trades. Until the Industrial Revolution, most clothing was sewn at home. Village workshops were the other common place for that work. Cloth-making often stayed inside one family. The family split the jobs. Yarn might be spun from cotton. It might be spun from flax. It might be spun from wool. Cloth was then woven on a hand loom. The work moved slowly. Even a skilled worker found it tedious. Late in the 1700s, a run of new inventions raised the efficiency of spinning. Weaving grew more efficient as well.

4Richard Arkwright worked as both an industrialist and an inventor. In his design, a waterwheel turned a machine that spun thread. Strong cotton thread came off that machine. No ordinary workshop could hold an invention of that size. He put up a large mill at Cromford, in Derbyshire. Hundreds of workers soon had jobs at Cromford Mill. More factories followed from Arkwright's hand. Other makers of textiles copied the pattern. Many people treat Cromford Mill as the earliest modern factory. An 1840 engraving records how Bridgewater Factory looked. Factories altered the way goods were produced. They also altered what a working life felt like. Water power ran the earliest factories. A river had to flow nearby. A factory that ran on steam had no such limit. It could stand in almost any spot. A cluster of them grew up near Manchester. That city lies in the north of England. Cheap coal could reach Manchester along the Bridgewater Canal. Sitting near the coast made overseas trade easier. Raw materials could come in. Finished products could go out. A population boom followed the new mills and factories. About 25,000 people lived in Manchester in 1773. Fifty-two mills stood there by 1802. Inhabitants numbered about 95,000. By 1851 the city had sprawled past 300,000 people. A new nickname stuck to it: Cottonopolis.

5Factory rooms were usually loud. Space inside was tight. Light was poor. A workday ran from twelve hours to sixteen. The week ran six days. Paid vacations did not exist. Sick days did not exist. Safety regulations did not exist. Owners kept strict rules. Some beat the people who worked for them. Some used a whip. Children met that treatment most often. A fine could follow a whistle. Opening a window could bring a fine too. The manufacturing process was split by a method called division of labor. One person handled only one part of the work. Production moved faster under that system. Owners could offer low wages. Little skill was required. Factories grew more complex as the Industrial Revolution went on. The huge machines were dangerous to run. Some of the full-time hands were only four years old. Their families worked beside them. Early in the 1800s, some British factories had a striking mix of ages. More than half the workers were younger than fourteen. A child's pay could fall as low as one-tenth of an adult wage. Some children earned no wages. Room and board were their only return. Adults were too big for certain jobs. A child could crawl under a textile machine and gather thread that had dropped.

6Adults were often hurt. Children were often hurt. Coal mines employed children as well. Gas could explode at any time. A shaft could fall in. Trappers in the mines could be as young as five. Their job was to open and close doors. Fresh air entered when the doors moved. Older children shoved and hauled heavy tubs of coal. Women did that hauling too. The tubs traveled dark, narrow tunnels. Public outrage pushed the British Parliament to act. A series of laws followed. The laws cut how many hours a child could work. They lifted the youngest age allowed for work. Enforcing the laws was hard. For many children, a factory was the only place to earn money for food and a place to live. A mine was the other place. School in Britain cost money before the 1800s. Rich children learned at home. Governesses and tutors did the teaching. Churches ran Sunday schools that poor children could attend. A poor family could also pay for a small private school. Those informal classes met inside a teacher's house. The Factory Act of 1833 added a rule. A child working in a factory was to get two hours of schooling each day. Charities opened free schools in working-class neighborhoods. People knew them as ragged schools.

7Fresh printing methods put more books within reach. Fresh papermaking methods did the same for newspapers. Prices for both fell. Literacy rose. Charles Dickens was born in 1812 and died in 1870. In his day he was Britain's most popular writer. At age twelve, he saw his father sent to prison. Debt was the cause. Dickens was the oldest son. He had to take a job in a blacking factory. Blacking means shoe polish. Three years passed before he could go back to school. Readers still love his novels and stories. Oliver Twist is one title. Hard Times is another. A Christmas Carol is a third. His pages showed how hard the Industrial Revolution could be. Children stood at the center of that picture. He also argued that society needed reform right away. A gain in one field pulled other fields forward. Cheap coal, for instance, sped up the making of cast iron. Once iron cost less, stronger tools were built from it. Stronger machines were built from it too. Firms needed better ways to move goods. Canals were dug. Roads were improved. Heavy raw materials had to travel. Finished goods had to come in and go out. Engineers built steam locomotives so coal could be hauled. A railway opened in 1825 between Stockton and Darlington.

8British engineer George Stephenson led the building. His son Robert worked with him. The track stretched 25 miles, or 40 kilometers. No earlier railway had carried a passenger car. Riding a locomotive was among the most exciting changes of the Industrial Revolution. Some people found it frightening. A few critics thought a human body might melt if the speed grew too high. Opening day in 1825 put members of the public on a train. The line was the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Chemical production moved forward, and many industries gained from it. Scientists learned how to mass-produce sulfuric acid. They learned how to mass-produce sodium carbonate, also called soda ash. Textile makers used sulfuric acid when they bleached cloth. They used it when they dyed cloth. The same acid could lift rust off iron. It went into fertilizer as well. Glass needed soda ash. Soap needed it. Paper needed it. The year 1824 brought Portland cement. Building gained an important advancement. Construction gained one. Transportation gained one. The Thames Tunnel was built with Portland cement. No underwater tunnel in the world had come before it. The tunnel opened in 1843. A chart follows coal output in the United Kingdom from 1800 to 1900. The figures are in millions of tons. Through the 1800s, coal production climbed quickly.

9The Industrial Revolution needed that fuel. Change did not stay inside Great Britain. Mainland Europe felt it first. North America felt it next. Britain was reluctant to hand over its inventions. It was reluctant to share its wealth and its power. Sending machines abroad was forbidden. Sending techniques abroad was forbidden. Profit was too large to ignore. Secrecy around the new technologies did not last. William Cockerill had been born in England. He was an expert at making iron. He carried the new technology into Belgium. An ironworks there was opened by his son. France then picked up the methods. Germany did too. The rest of Europe followed. Samuel Slater had studied how textile machines were designed. That study came before he left Britain for the United States. He rebuilt the machines from memory. People nicknamed him Slater the Traitor. A spinning mill rose in Rhode Island in 1793 under his direction. That mill helped start the American Industrial Revolution. Much of the money behind early factories came from rich people who traded in enslaved people. Technological improvements drew money from the same trade. Shipping enslaved people made many British port cities powerful. Those cities also handled raw materials from plantations in the Americas. Cotton was one material. Sugar was another. Tea was a third.

10A law in 1807 abolished that trade in Britain. A broad judgment is shared by many historians. During the Industrial Revolution, the overall standard of living rose for most people. Average income went up. Affordable goods could be chosen from a selection, and that choice was new. Mass-produced clothing sat in the selection. Household items sat there too. So did other goods. Harm came with the gains. Air was polluted by fossil fuels used in manufacturing. Water was polluted by them. Chemicals used in manufacturing polluted both. Life was harsh for poorer people. Work was harsh for them. Children carried the heaviest burden. Big cities grew overcrowded. They grew filthy. Some of those problems eased as the Industrial Revolution moved forward. Sanitation in cities got better. Sewage systems got better. Laws were passed so working lives would improve. Workers formed unions by joining together. The push for fair treatment later reached further groups. Women were one of those groups. Modern society rests on groundwork laid by the Industrial Revolution. Conveniences we rely on today rest on it too. A phone is one such convenience. A car is another. A photograph from 1909 was made in Macon, Georgia. The setting is a mill that made textiles. Young boys climb on the machinery to do their jobs.

73. Stock Cars Built for Speed

1Sections in this book follow this order. Roaring Start. Parts on the Way to Victory. Out in Front of the Others. Beneath the Hood. Tires That Truly Burn. A Flag of Checks. Words to Know and Topics. One picture shows racing of stock cars during 1953. Another shows racing at Bristol Motor Speedway. Roaring Start. The cars streak past. Speed climbs past 200 miles in an hour. This kind of racing began in the 1940s under the name NASCAR. Those letters mean the National Association. That group governs Stock Car Auto Racing. Drivers in that era used everyday cars from the road. Another name for them is stock cars. Dirt was the surface of the tracks. The sport did not stay there. It grew into a major contest. The machines now are custom-built. They are superior cars. A present-day NASCAR car still has four wheels. Windows are there. An engine is there. A seat for the driver is there. Likeness to a normal road car mostly ends at that list. Each piece is engineered on purpose. The goal is fast travel. Another goal is surviving the pounding of a race. A third goal is the driver's safety. Pictures show a modern race car of this type, and they show its interior.

2Martinsville Speedway is in Martinsville, Virginia. Race meets take place all around the United States. Shapes of the tracks are not all alike. Length can be under one mile. Length can reach three miles. Distance for a single race may run from 250 miles up to 600 miles. The cars keep looping. Their speed goes beyond 200 mph. Inches are all that separate a car from its rivals. Success then depends on strength. It depends on durability. It depends on speed. Equipment for the drivers and for the cars makes each race safer. Fine tuning touches every part, so the vehicle can perform at its peak. A careful balance is required. Driver safety sits on one side. Speed sits on the other. Strength serves safety. Inventors keep creating lighter materials. Those materials make the cars better. Safety is the first concern. Heat inside one of these cars can reach 150 degrees Fahrenheit. That reading is 65 degrees Celsius. Space travel led NASA to invent many materials. Those materials now shield drivers from fierce heat. Vents are built into the driving suits. Cool, dry air flows in through them. Hot, humid air next to the skin is pushed out. Temperature inside the suit falls by 24 degrees. Heat-blocking blankets guard the cockpit.

3Heat comes from the engine. It comes from the exhaust. It comes from the transmission. The blankets lower temperature inside the car by 40 degrees. A picture shows the racing helmet and the Hans device. In a crash, that device protects the neck. Kevlar insulates and also bounces heat away. Nomex does the same work. Clothing that resists fire is made from these materials. Gloves are part of that clothing. Socks are part of it. Underwear is part of it. NASA is the source of these details. Gary Nelson speaks to the media in a 2006 photo. NASCAR had given him the vice president role. His department covered research. It also covered development. Parts on the Way to Victory. Each year brings fresh methods. Racing teams introduce them. So do the companies that build cars. They are pushing the edge of performance. Millions of dollars go into the search. Wind-tunnel tests are one expense. Engine design is another. Development of the car is another. Small gains from that spending can open a path to the championship. Here is a surprise. For every race, each team builds a car that is brand new. The work can take weeks. Completion starts with the frame. The engine follows. The body follows that.

4Electronics are installed next. Steering is installed. The driver's seat is installed. At that point the car is close to ready. Testing comes after. The crew takes the car apart and inspects it. They put it back together in time for race day. A crew labors on the car their driver will use. The garage sits at Daytona International Speedway. Highly skilled engineers design these cars. Mechanics build them. They work in teams. Four main pieces make up each car. The frame is one. The engine is one. The body is one. The tires are one. Chassis is another name for the frame. The word sounds like CHAH-see. Protection of the driver is one duty of the frame. Forming the car's main structure is the other duty. Rolled steel tubing, thick and strong, makes the roll cage. That cage is the frame's guard around the driver. The remaining frame uses rolled steel tubing that is thin. A crash makes it crumple. A hit against a wall does the same. Engine, body, and wheel axle all fasten onto this frame. Keeping those pieces joined is the purpose. A diagram labels the engine, the frame, the axle, and the tires. Further labels mark the seat, the body, and the paint.

5Kevin Harvick drives a NASCAR car along the inside lane. Talladega Superspeedway is the track. It is in Talladega, Alabama. Fabricators, two of them, assemble the body. Welding joins sheet metal that has been rolled thin. Primer covers the shaped body. Primer gets the surface ready for color. Sanding follows. Colors of the sponsor go on next. A logo from that sponsor covers the car. The car's number is added. The team's name is added. Decals from several advertisers are added too. Out in Front of the Others. The outer form is meant to resemble regular cars from the road. Designers also shape it for conditions that change. Track conditions are one factor. Car speed is another. Shifting aerodynamics is a third. Aerodynamics names how air moves as it passes the vehicle. NASCAR's rules on shape are strict. A template, which is a model, goes to every design team. The model keeps them inside limits. Those limits cover height. They cover width. They cover shape. They cover airflow. One image is the 2006 Dodge Charger sold as a production car. Another is a Dodge Charger redrawn for this kind of racing. Raise the downforce, and grip increases. Extra grip helps the car work through corners. Drag increases at the same time.

6Speed is what drag takes away. Downward pressure comes from the rear spoiler. Stability gets help from that pressure. During a spin, the side skirt stops air from slipping underneath. How air travels around the car matters deeply in this sport. That airflow can add downforce. It can also reduce downforce. Downforce is energy in the air that presses the car onto the racing surface. The air dam has a matching job. It stops air that tries to pass beneath the vehicle. Rules about how these cars perform exist for clear reasons. The contest should excite the fans. It should keep drivers safe. It should stay competitive for the teams. Large objects that fly loose are a danger. The Earnhardt bar helps shield the driver against them. A rollover can throw a driver out. The window net holds the driver in the car. Harnesses cross a seat that fits the body closely. Together they secure the driver. A fire extinguisher rides in the car. Downforce is not left to chance. NASCAR decides how much a car must have. The decision depends on the track type. It also depends on the race series. If a car spins, roof flaps pop up. Their job is to prevent a flip.

7A typical engine of this sport is shown sitting in the chassis. Power from that engine is extreme. The design is a V8. Eight cylinders form a V. Measured size is 5.87 liters. In cubic inches, that is 358. Output can climb to 800 brake horsepower. The short name is bhp. A typical car on the road produces 150 bhp. Placement is under a hood, at the front. Most road cars put the engine in that same spot. The stock-car theme stays intact because of it. Designs of the body are regulated. Engine output is regulated as well. Some races use restrictor plates inside the engine. Those plates reduce how much horsepower can be produced. A turbo system is banned. A fuel-injection system is banned too. George Metrick, an official with NASCAR, studies a restrictor plate. The look happens during inspection before a race. The site is Talladega Superspeedway. At that track, NASCAR demands the plates. One picture presents a modern engine from this sport. A block of cast iron sits at the engine's core. Blocks of that kind have served engines for decades. Even so, technology and modifications have raised what the modern version can do. The gain is dramatic. Testing of this engine is intense. Tuning is precise.

8Running at 200 mph for longer than three hours is within its ability. Output has to stay at the maximum. The engine must run in an efficient way. It must run in a reliable way. Radical new elements show up in these power plants. A few short years may be all it takes before road cars include those developments. Mechanics are shown swapping in a fresh engine. Tires That Truly Burn. Layers of rubber build each tire. Fabric is layered in. Steel belts add strength. The build must stand extreme speed. It must stand extreme temperature. Blowouts are the risk being prevented. Incredible strength is required. California Speedway is where one photo shows a tire just mounted. Daytona International Speedway is where another photo shows a tire torn to shreds. Air is what fills a tire on a road car. Nitrogen is what fills these race tires. Extreme heat makes air expand. Pressure then shifts, and the tire grows unstable. Nitrogen bears the harsh conditions of a race more successfully. Tire pressure stays steady. So does performance. One view shows the tire mounted on its wheel. A cutaway view shows the interior. Grip on the track is built into these tires. Very high speed through a corner becomes possible.

9Stress on a tire during a race is extreme. Track shape creates some of it. Downforce creates more. Sheer speed creates more. About 150 miles is the life of each tire. Because speed decides the sport, a pit stop must replace all four tires. Crews can do that job in under 15 seconds. Jeff Gordon appears in a photo during a pit stop. Talladega Superspeedway is the track. Crossing the finish line as the winner is what the checkered flag announces. A Flag of Checks. Designers never stop seeking airflow changes. Some changes aid cornering. Some changes lift speed. Asphalt tracks today carry these cars at incredible speeds. A future version of the sport may use cars that hover over the surface. Fascination with speed is certain to last. So is fascination with vehicles that can arrive the fastest. Words to Know. Aerodynamics studies the movement of air as it passes an object's shape. An axle is a steel bar. It runs between the wheel on the left and the wheel on the right. Bhp means brake horsepower. It measures all the power an engine can give for high performance. The chassis is the frame. It binds the car and shields the driver. A component is one part. It combines with other parts and works beside them.

10Cylinders are tubes inside the engine. Fuel is compressed there and then ignited. Downforce is air pressing a car down. That press helps the car stay on the track. Drag is the push of air against a moving car, slowing it. Fuel injection delivers fuel. The fuel arrives at the cylinders by a more direct path. A logo is a small design. It stands for a company, a product, or both. NASCAR names both an organization and the events it runs. The full name is the National Association. It governs Stock Car Auto Racing. Nitrogen is a gas. It makes up 78 percent of the atmosphere of Earth. A sponsor is a company. It gives money to a racing team. In return it gets advertising space on the stock cars. Stock cars are ordinary automobiles. They are the sort used on city streets. A turbo is a turbine inside a housing. The turbine is a fan. It increases horsepower. Topics in this book include Jeff Gordon, Kevin Harvick, and Gary Nelson. 74. Stone Dragon on China's Northern Edge

1In every season, millions of visitors come to the Great Wall. The wall is a landmark known in many countries. Pages ahead look at this remarkable landmark. They look at a wall that seems to flow. They look at its separate sections. They look at why a wall was wanted. They look at the building work. They look at what a visit is like. They look at how the wall inspires people. A list of useful words ends the book. In 1987, a world body made a choice about this wall. The United Nations named the Great Wall of China a World Heritage Site. Among human-made features on Earth, few are more famous. It also belongs to the New Seven Wonders of the World. The engineering is a remarkable feat. The design is a remarkable feat as well. Construction projects rarely get more challenging than this one. Taken together, the many sections are China's largest draw for tourists. Their combined length beats the distance from the North Pole to the South Pole. A long record of China sits in the wall. That record is a rich one. Work on it began more than two thousand years in the past. The story it tells includes shifts in power. It includes shifts in technology. It includes shifts in how people lived. The span runs from ancient days to now. An old Chinese mix of art and science is called feng shui.

2Say it FUNG SHWAY. That system governed the wall's design. Its principles offer advice on arrangement. Things should sit in a way that follows flowing energy. A curve was chosen, rather than a straight line. Harmony with the shape of the land was the aim. Builders set the wall on China's northern border. In China, many people see the wall as a dragon asleep. The west holds the tail. That western place is Gansu Province. Say Gansu as GAHN-soo. The east holds the head. That eastern place is Liaoning Province. Say Liaoning as lee-OW-ning. The Yellow Sea lies near that head. From tail to head, deserts ring the dragon's body. Steppes ring it too. Mountains ring it. Lakes ring it. Rivers ring it. Fertile lowlands ring it. Beaches ring it as well. Part of the wall lies near Beijing. Say Beijing as bay-ZHING. Beijing is the capital of China. A map marks Hushan Great Wall as the eastern end. It marks Jaiyu Mountain Pass as the western end. Mongolia appears on the map. Inner Mongolia appears too. So do Beijing, the Yellow Sea, and China. A key points out important sections. The border of Inner Mongolia is marked. A scale on the map reads 150 km (93 mi.). Badaling is one section that remains well preserved.

3It sits about 70 kilometers (43 mi.) northwest of the capital, Beijing. The Great Wall is not a single wall. Separate sections, many of them, make it up. Some of those walls run parallel to one another. Four of the main sections lie inside a range of 121 kilometers (75 mi.) from Beijing. In 2007, a vote placed the Great Wall on the list known as the New Seven Wonders of the World. The section people know best is Badaling, said BAH-dah-ling. It is also the section kept in the best shape. Steep mountains northwest of Beijing are where it winds. The winding stretch is about 12 kilometers (7.5 mi.). Watchtowers there number forty-three. East of that, Mutianyu is a scenic portion. Say Mutianyu as MOO-tyen-yoo. High mountains are what it spans. The length is 2.25 kilometers (1.4 mi.). Watchtowers there number twenty-two. Translated from Chinese, that name is Long Wall of Ten Thousand Li. A li is a unit used in China. One li is about half a kilometer. One li is also about a third of a mile. Ten thousand li therefore comes to about 5,000 kilometers (3,100 mi.). For a long time, people believed the wall was not much longer than that figure. A new measure took place from 2007 to 2012. Scientists did the measuring. Advanced technology was their tool. They learned the real length is over four times the old figure.

4Add every section, and the total is about 21,196 kilometers (13,171 mi.). Jinshanling lies northeast of Beijing. Say it JIN-shahnling. This section is well preserved. It runs about 10 kilometers (6 mi.). Watchtowers there number sixty-seven. In earlier times, soldiers slept inside some towers. Other towers held hay. Other towers held weapons. Windows appear on some watchtowers. Archers used those windows to shoot at enemies. Simatai sits just east of Jinshanling. Say Simatai as SU-mah-tie. This part runs about 5 kilometers (3 mi.). Workers have done a great deal of restoration here. The ground is extremely steep. Watchtowers number thirty-four. Mandarin Duck Lake has the towers split about evenly, half along each shore. Inner Mongolia's southern edge is roughly the line the wall follows. Today that region governs itself as part of China. During the building years, peoples who were not Chinese held most of the control. Long ago, the Mongol people stood as enemies of China. Keeping them outside was why the wall was constructed. Chinese culture was also shielded from influences beyond the wall. Invaders still got through at times. Getting through was made hard, though. Ancient days held small groups of nomadic people. They lived in lands that are now China, and near those lands. Wild animals gave them food. Wild plants gave them food. Clothing came from those same wild sources.

5Other needs came from them too. A change started around 4000 bc. People on richer soil began to grow crops. They began to tame animals. They settled in one place. Village walls went up around them. Northern nomads might raid, and the walls were meant to stop that. Andrew Howat, a British artist, painted a scene called Great Wall of China. In it, Chinese soldiers take aim at invaders. One picture marks the time after Qin held every part of China. Zheng was then emperor, the earliest one the new country had. By 500 bc, China held many states. Each state was independent. Those states fought one another. States in the north also fought enemies farther north. More walls went up during that period. By 221 bc, one powerful state held all of China. That state was Qin. Say Qin as CHIN. Zheng was the new emperor. Say Zheng as ZHUNG. He wanted enemies kept away from China. His order put workers onto border walls. The length he called for was almost 4,828 kilometers (3,000 mi.). Some experts treat this project as the beginning of the Great Wall. Zheng died in 210 bc. Neglect followed his death for about one hundred years. Parts of it fell apart. A later emperor then called for a new stretch. That stretch measured 483 kilometers (300 mi.) along the borders.

6From ad 386 until 1279, emperor followed emperor with fresh orders. Some orders said to repair old parts. Some orders said to raise new parts. During the middle years of the 1200s, enemies were not held out. Mongols invaded from the north. Genghis Khan led them. Their hold on China lasted over one hundred years. Maintenance of the wall was not something they did. In 1368, the Mongols were driven out. The emperor who followed wanted them kept outside. He had the wall built again. So much had already crumbled that the task was huge. For roughly the next 275 years, emperors rebuilt the Great Wall. They also expanded it. A large part of the wall people see today was raised in that span. A large part was repaired in that span. Since that span ended, the work has mostly been repair. Genghis Khan also conquered Mongol tribes one by one. He formed the Mongol Empire. Many countries sat inside his empire. Together they covered a huge area of Asia. A picture of hang-tu building shows three steps in order. First, a frame made of wood was built, and earth was packed into it. Second, they made the wall taller. Third, the frame came off. The Great Wall grew in stages. Those stages covered thousands of years. Soldiers labored on the wall. Convicts labored on it.

7Prisoners taken in war labored on it. Peasants labored on it. Other people labored on it too. Often they worked because they were forced. Every wall was made by the hang-tu method. Rammed earth is the other name for it. Packed earth was pounded down inside a frame. The frame might be wood. The frame might be bamboo. Deserts had no earth to use. Packed sand was used instead. Shrubs were used instead. The earliest walls were mainly earth. One earth wall stands in the far western part of the Great Wall. A later time in China's history is the Ming dynasty. Its dates are 1368 to 1644. During those years, many sections took on the face they show today. People still built with hang-tu methods. After that, brick went over the earth. Stone went over it in other places. The cover made the walls look uniform. Workers shaped large bricks in wooden molds. Then kilns baked the bricks. After each brick was set, mortar went into the spaces between. Harsh conditions fell on so many builders that a myth started. People said the mortar held bones of dead workers, ground into powder. Historians in recent times found the true extra ingredient. Sticky rice was that ingredient. A cutaway of a Ming wall labels the parts. At the top are a crenellation and a parapet.

8A paved surface runs along the top. The outer face is brick or stone. Earth and stones fill the inside. A stone base sits underneath. A caption gives Simatai a measure of its own. The length is 5.4 kilometers (3.3 mi.). Beacon towers there number thirty-five. Every year, over ten million people travel to China so they can see the Great Wall. Watchtowers along the sections reach an amazing 25,000. Outposts reach 15,000. Put every section together, and the length is about 21,196 kilometers (13,170 mi.). No chain of structures built anywhere has run longer. The widest section measures about 9 meters (30 ft.). The tallest part of the wall measures about 8 meters (26 ft.). Sea level is where the wall sits at its lowest. The highest point stands more than 500 meters (1,600 ft.) above that. A visitor fortunate enough to tour the wall has a choice to make. Badaling is the section people visit most. Closeness to Beijing is one reason. It is also the safest section for walking. The Great Wall Museum stands there. Nine exhibition halls fill the museum. Their topics are history, construction, art, and culture. Badaling can be crowded. Souvenir shops crowd it as well. Most other sections draw fewer tourists. Those sections are much steeper too. A challenging climb is what to expect. Visitors can walk. They can climb.

9They can take pictures. A guided tour can explain the wall's history. It can explain the construction. Cable car rides exist at some sections. Mutianyu offers a toboggan ride. People who hike the mountainous sections should be in good physical condition. A picture from the 2008 Olympic Games shows a woman lifting China's flag. North of Beijing, bicycle racers go past the wall during a race for cyclists. The Great Wall of China remains a remarkable landmark. People around the world still find it inspiring. They still find it fascinating. Beijing was host to the 2008 Summer Olympic Games. The Games always give honor to the host country's history. They always give honor to that country's culture. A representation of the wall stood out in the Opening Ceremony. One course for cyclists made loops between two passes. Those passes were Badaling and Juyong. Say Juyong as JOO-yoong. Fabian Cancellara is a cyclist from Switzerland. He won a gold medal. He also won a silver medal. Afterward he talked about the wall. The labor of building it supplied him with inspiration. It supplied him with strength. An enormous stretch of human history has passed in front of the wall. Early farmers belong to that stretch. Warring states belong to it. Powerful empires belong to it. So does modern-day China. Many people are working so the wall will be preserved.

10They want it to keep telling part of Earth's story. They want coming generations to hear that story. A convict is someone a court found guilty of a crime. That person serves a sentence in prison. Prisoner is another name. Culture is the set of ideas held by one group of people. Customs of that group belong to culture too. A feat is an amazing action. It can also be an amazing accomplishment. Harmonious means the parts relate, combine, or work as one. The result is a pleasing effect. Kilns are ovens with a special job. They burn materials, bake them, or dry them. Clay, brick, and glass are materials they handle. Nomadic means shifting from place to place. No lasting home is part of that life. Parallel describes things that lie or move in one shared direction. An equal gap stays between them. Raiding is an attack that comes as a surprise. It may be an invasion aimed at one purpose. Restoration is the work of bringing something back. The goal is the condition it had at first. Steppes are grasslands that are flat and dry. Summer there can be very hot. Winter there can be very cold. To wind, as a verb, is to travel a curving line. The course can bend many times. Uniform means matching. It can also mean nearly the same.

75. Stone Mountains for the Dead

1Workers have found more than 100 pyramids in Egypt. This book explains those monuments and the people who raised them. It describes ancient Egypt, the building of a pyramid, and the care of a body. It names famous pyramids in Egypt and pyramids in other lands. A closing section and a word list finish the book. Egypt lies at the northeastern corner of the continent of Africa. The civilization of ancient Egypt once made its home there. Ancient Egypt stands among the most fascinating cultures that have ever existed. Thousands of years ago, Egyptians studied agriculture and irrigation. They practiced architecture and engineering, and they practiced much besides. They raised great structures, and the pyramids are among those works. Study of the pyramids can teach a great deal about this amazing civilization. About seven thousand years ago, Egyptians began to settle on the banks of the Nile River. Village life was how they started. Over time the villages joined into larger groups, and those groups became tribes. By about 3200 BCE, one king had united the tribes. People called that king the pharaoh. Most pharaohs were men, yet powerful women ruled Egypt in later dynasties. Life in ancient Egypt depended on the Nile, a river that gives life. The river supplied fish and birds for food. It supplied water to irrigate the crops. It also served as a waterway, so boats could travel and carry goods. For thousands of years the Nile has stayed a busy waterway.

2Paintings inside a tomb show scenes of the next life. The ancient Egyptians believed that life continued after death. They believed the next life would resemble the life they already knew. They believed they would need the same sorts of tools and objects. For that reason, many people were buried with a collection of their belongings. No burial in ancient Egypt was more lavish than the burial of a pharaoh. Belief held that the pharaoh was the child of the Sun god, called Re or Ra. During life on Earth, the pharaoh was known as Horus. After death, the pharaoh was joined with Re. The new pharaoh, taking the dead ruler's place, became the new Horus. Egyptians believed a pharaoh could live forever and go on blessing the people. For that to happen, the body had to be preserved so the spirit would remain alive. They built pyramids to honor pharaohs who had died. Each pyramid held the ruler's body, together with riches and treasures for the next life. The pyramid also guarded the tomb and those treasures against theft. It stood, too, as a monument to the pharaoh's greatness. A pyramid's shape stands for rays of the Sun falling on the Earth. Ancient Egyptians believed a dead pharaoh climbed to heaven along those rays. A pharaoh planned the building long before death was expected, because the work took many years. A large pyramid might need as many as twenty years.

3Thousands of people were required. Some were skilled, including architects who designed the whole form on the pharaoh's orders. Special knowledge was needed to cut stone out of a quarry and to shape it. After the pyramid stood, skilled sculptors and painters decorated it. A scribe listed every material the work required. The scribe wrote in hieroglyphics, the writing of ancient Egypt. Hieroglyphics are rows of small pictures, and each picture stands for an idea. Old carvings still show samples of that writing. A large crew was needed to haul each heavy stone on a sledge. Beyond the specialists, other workers had to move those stones. Some stones traveled by boat from the quarry to the building site. Other stones were loaded onto sledges, which are large sleds made of wood. Workers then dragged the sledges over the desert sand. Until not long ago, historians thought much of this hard labor was forced on enslaved people. In 1990 a tourist in Egypt came upon the remains of an ancient city. Builders of the pyramids at Giza were once thought to have lived in that city. Evidence there suggests the builders were not enslaved. They were skilled craftspeople, about 15,000 of them. Written records suggest that workers were treated well during the job. Farmers are also thought to have helped, especially in the flood season, when fields could not be worked. Farmers counted on floods to lay down fertile soil for crops.

4Because the pharaoh was believed to be a god's son, farmers thought the ruler could promise good floods. They were glad to serve, and the fertile soil from the floods was their return. A pyramid's site had to be picked with great care. The ground had to be rocky, strong enough for the immense weight of the finished monument. Stones in the Great Pyramid each weighed as much as two tons, or 2000 kilograms. A car weighs about that much. Heavy stones were sailed along the Nile River. A pyramid also had to stand near the river, so some stones could move by water from quarry to site. The site had to lie on the west bank. The Sun sets in the west each night, and the dead were believed to dwell in the west. The exact facing of the pyramid had to be set with equal care. Each side had to point to true north, south, east, or west. An astronomer-priest was called to watch the stars and to find true north. While the pyramid was actually going up, many ceremonies took place. The rites were meant to win the gods' help for the endeavor. Several kinds of stone went into the building. Local limestone formed the core. Finer limestone, carried from far away, formed the outer shell. Granite from still farther away was used for the coffin, called a sarcophagus. That same granite decorated the burial chamber.

5Once place and position were chosen, workers made the ground level. Only then did the real labor of raising the pyramid begin. A picture shows the tomb of King Tutankhamun, known as King Tut. The inside of a pyramid was planned to fool thieves and to keep them from the burial chamber and its treasures. If that chamber sat at ground level, or under it, workers set the chamber first. They then raised the pyramid around it, layer upon horizontal layer. Ramps leaned against the sides. Huge stones were dragged up those ramps and set in place. Passages and rooms included dead ends and empty chambers. The maze was meant to confuse anyone who tried to loot the tomb. Enormous stone slabs blocked the way into the real tomb. A drawing shows the tunnels and passages inside a pyramid. A reader can build a small pyramid at home. Sugar cubes will work, and so will cubes shaped from clay. The model may have steps, or flat sides, or a shape the builder invents. Ancient Egyptians used a special method to ready an important body for burial. The method is called mummification, and it kept a body whole for thousands of years. The body went to an embalmer, who took out the inner organs and preserved them in canopic jars. Each jar lid had the shape of a guardian god. The body was then left to dry for forty days. After drying, it was washed, rubbed with oil and spices, and packed with preservatives.

6Many layers of linen, soaked in resin, were wrapped around it so the form would hold. A decorative mask was set on the head, and the whole body was laid in a sarcophagus. Every sarcophagus was painted in an ornate way. Thieves hunting souvenirs damaged one mummy shown in a picture. Burial of a pharaoh came with an elaborate ceremony. The decorated coffin and the canopic jars were carried to the pyramid. Priests and priestesses led a parade of mourners. Servants came behind them, carrying goods for the next life, including food, clothes, and furniture. Before the burial, a priest opened the mouth of the dead pharaoh. People believed this act let the person breathe, eat, and speak in the life to come. The coffin was then set in the tomb and sealed inside the pyramid, in a chamber built to keep it safe. Pharaohs were buried with servant statues called shabtis. People believed a shabti would come alive in the next world and serve the pharaoh again. A picture shows a group of these shabtis. The Sphinx watches the pyramids and the other buildings at Giza. The earliest pyramid was made for King Zoser at Saqqâra. People call it a step pyramid because the sides rise like giant stairs. Later pyramids used smaller steps. In time the form changed to pyramids with straight sides, such as the Great Pyramid at Giza.

7That pyramid was built about 4,500 years ago for King Khufu. It stands 147 meters tall, or 482 feet, and it holds about 2,300,000 blocks of stone. The Great Pyramid belongs to a larger group of pyramids at Giza. King Khufu, his son Khafre, and his grandson Menkaure built them. Other buildings stand around those pyramids. Queen Meritites and Queen Hetepheres have pyramids there. Stone mastabas, tombs of mud brick, hold the rest of the royal family and members of the court. The Sphinx guards the whole site. It is a limestone figure with a king's face and a lion's body, and it stands for the Sun god. Looters have taken the treasures from every ancient Egyptian pyramid. Very few tombs remain intact. Archaeologists have found only one burial of an Egyptian king still whole. That burial is the tomb of King Tutankhamun. It lies in the Valley of the Kings, and it was dug underground rather than set inside a pyramid. Because the tomb was still whole, it has taught archaeologists a great deal about ancient Egyptian culture. Egyptian archaeologists study objects from the tomb, which was found in 1922. People in the Americas built pyramids too. The first rose in Central America and in the northwest of South America. Before long, pyramid building spread into North America as well. Several cultures of the New World that raised pyramids are described here. The Maya, and other peoples of Central America, built stepped pyramids.

8Stairs decorated with sculptures and with writing climbed to temples at the top. Some of these pyramids held tombs of kings, and some did not. Chichén Itzá is one of the best-known Mayan pyramids. It was rebuilt over an older pyramid, and the pyramid seen today was raised just before 1100 BCE. A map marks pyramid sites in the New World, and a picture shows Chichén Itzá. The older pyramid, built 100 years earlier, held a stone jaguar. The jaguar was painted red, and its eyes were jade. For the Maya, the jaguar symbolized the fertility of the Earth, and people worshipped it as a god. The Aztecs, another people of Central America, built the Great Pyramid Temple. They most likely raised it in the 1300s. It stood in their capital, Tenochtitlán, on an island in Lake Texcoco in Mexico. Aztec belief said the Sun god needed blood from human hearts in order to stay strong. Without that blood, the Sun would die and the world would end. Prisoners captured in war were sacrificed, and those killings were a regular part of Aztec life. The sacrifices happened at the Great Pyramid Temple. Peoples of northwestern South America also raised pyramids with flat tops and with steps. The Moche, who flourished from 100 BCE to 800 CE, built the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. After a gap of 600 to 700 years, pyramids were raised by the Inca.

9In the Inca empire, the Temple of the Sun was the shrine held most sacred. The temple was a pyramid, and a huge disk of gold inside it stood for the Sun god. The Inca believed their rulers descended directly from the Sun. A picture shows the Pyramid of the Moon at Teotihuacan in Mexico. Another picture shows the pyramids at Meroë in Sudan. Builders in other cultures around the world have used the pyramid form. The pyramids at Meroë show exchange between cultures. That exchange linked ancient Egypt with Nubia, an empire and one of Africa's earliest civilizations. When two cultures exchange in this way, each helps the other change, grow, or take shape. Pyramids in the Nubian style were built from 700 BCE to 300 BCE. They joined Egyptian forms of culture with other influences from Africa. Pyramid designs also appear in parts of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. Modern buildings in many countries use the pyramid shape, including works in France, England, and the United States. A pyramid of modern times was raised in Egypt to honor President Anwar Sadat, who was assassinated in 1981. People are working to preserve the pyramids of ancient Egypt and to protect pyramids elsewhere. Pollution, the spread of cities, tourism, and other troubles threaten the pyramids at Giza. The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza still stands. It is the single survivor among the seven famous wonders left from ancient times.

10Every pyramid and every tomb is a wonder that deserves to be preserved. Study of pyramids teaches us about ancient cultures that were complex and fascinating. It teaches what people of those times were able to accomplish. It also teaches how those cultures honored their leaders and how they worshipped their gods. Each year, millions of tourists from around the world visit the pyramids at Giza. An embalmer is a person who treats a dead body with chemicals so it will not rot quickly. Mastabas are tombs of ancient Egypt. They are oblong, built of mud brick, with a flat roof and sides that slope. An endeavor is a serious effort to carry out a hard task. Mummification is the ancient Egyptian way of preserving a dead body. Enslaved describes someone kept in slavery, owned by another person or forced to work for that person. Pharaoh is the title of a ruler in ancient Egypt. Hieroglyphics are pictures or symbols that stand for words, syllables, or sounds. Ancient Egyptians and other peoples used them instead of letters of an alphabet. A quarry is a place where stone, marble, or slate is dug out for building. A sarcophagus is a coffin or a tomb, often of limestone, and often carved and richly decorated. Historians are people with expert knowledge of the past. Lavish means extravagant, or very generous. A scribe was a writer by trade, paid to record information.

76. Stone Ruins of Great Zimbabwe

1A person on a hilltop wall looks out over the striking land around Great Zimbabwe. The ruins of that once-magnificent city spread across a wide area. Rolling hills fill the land. Huge piles of boulders rise in many places. Massive stone walls stand across the landscape. In some spots, the walls reach 11 meters. That height equals 36 feet. The ruins cover 728.4 hectares. That area equals 1,800 acres. About 1,400 American football fields, set side by side, would cover nearly the same ground. The ruins offer a glimpse of life at Great Zimbabwe from the eleventh century to the fifteenth century. The empty city also holds many mysteries that no one has solved. The account ahead starts with the size of the place. It then tells why the nation takes pride in the ruins. It describes a city of stone. It describes an empire that grew rich. It explains how people raised the walls. It asks who built the city. It ends with the work of protecting Great Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe's southeastern area is where these mysterious ruins stand. Zimbabwe is a nation in southern Africa.

2Mozambique lies next to it. South Africa lies next to it as well. Zambia is another neighbor. Botswana is a neighbor too. Lake Mutirikwi is a landmark nearby. The town of Masvingo is nearby too. A map of this part of Africa marks Zambia and the Mozambique Channel. It also marks Harare, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Masvingo. Botswana and South Africa appear on that map as well. In the late 1800s, the land now called Zimbabwe was a colony under British control. People called the colony Southern Rhodesia. Zimbabwe gained independence from Britain in 1980. Their new country needed a fresh name. For a long time, this ancient city made the nation proud. They chose to name the country after that famous ancient city. At the city's north end is the Hill Complex. Three main sections stretch across the ruins. One section is the Hill Complex. Another is the Great Enclosure. The third is the Valley Ruins. The Hill Complex measures about 100 meters long. That length equals 328 feet. It measures about 45 meters wide.

3That width equals 148 feet. A steep hillside at the site's northern edge lifts this section high. The rest of the city looks beautiful from that height. They also see the valley around it. Six upright posts stand on the hill. Sculptures of birds top those posts. Experts think the Hill Complex may have been the city's spiritual center. They also think it may have been the home of the kings. A site is the place where something is found or where an event happened. Something spiritual connects to the spirit, to the soul, or to a divine being. To say a place functioned as something means it served that purpose. Religion in the city probably centered on the Hill Complex. It was also probably the place where the kings lived. Experts think the people of Great Zimbabwe lived in the Valley Ruins. The city's wealthy residents likely lived in the Great Enclosure. Some stretches of wall rise 11 meters. That height equals 36 feet. A three-story building is about that tall. In some places, the walls are up to 6 meters thick.

4That thickness equals 20 feet. The walls curve without a break. In some places they are quite smooth. In some places they are decorative. Curves in the Great Enclosure's walls show what the builders preferred. The builders favored rounded shapes. They did not favor angular shapes. Visitors find the Great Enclosure on the site's south side. Workers built it in the 1300s. The city was at its most successful then. South of the Sahara Desert, no ancient African structure is larger. An oval is the shape of the Great Enclosure. Around the outside, it measures 250 meters. That distance equals 820 feet. The builders used about one million stones. Just inside the outer wall, an inner wall forms a narrow passage. The passage leads to a tower shaped like a cone. The tower's purpose is unknown to archaeologists. They also do not know why people built the Great Enclosure. It is possible that the enclosure was a royal palace. The Valley Ruins occupy the ground that separates those two stone areas. Many smaller houses fill that valley area.

5Those houses are made from a mix of clay and gravel. People call that mix daga. In the fourteenth century, a powerful empire had this city at its center. The number of residents may have passed ten thousand. Some researchers estimate a population as high as twenty thousand. Stone buildings may have housed the empire's wealthy people. Those stone buildings are found in the Hill Complex. The Great Enclosure has stone buildings as well. Peasants likely lived in daga structures through the valley. Someone here may have carved a woman from soapstone. The people grew crops. They raised cattle. They also took part in a large trade network. The city lay on a busy trade route. Ports on the Indian Ocean connected, along this route, with other African regions. People of Great Zimbabwe mined gold from the hills around the city. They traded that gold for goods from West Africa. They also traded it for goods from the Middle East. They even traded it for goods from China. A sculpture that may come from Great Zimbabwe mixes two kinds of features.

6Some features belong to an eagle. Other features belong to a person. The city was once very rich. It was once very powerful. Around the midpoint of the fifteenth century, the city stood empty. Some people think too much farming ruined the land around the city. Others think the people moved so they could follow trade routes that had shifted. Why this great city collapsed is still unknown to scholars. The most famous artworks recovered from Great Zimbabwe are eight soapstone bird statues. Workers found them in the Hill Complex. The sculptures may have stood for royal authority. They may instead have stood for the ancestors of the kings. The bird statues sat on top of columns. They likely served as protectors. Those sculptures gave Zimbabwe the idea for its national symbol. The symbol appears on the country's flag. It also appears on the country's coins. The Great Enclosure's walls took an estimated million bricks, or even more. Most walls at Great Zimbabwe are made of stones shaped like bricks. The builders cut those stones from the huge boulders around the city.

7Fire was used to heat the boulders. Cold water came next, poured over the hot stones. That process made the stones split. The granite boulders they used split along straight lines by nature. Those lines made the rock excellent for shaping into bricks. The builders stacked the brick-shaped stones one on top of another. In most brick walls made today, mortar holds the bricks together. Mortar is a substance like cement. Mortar was not part of the building method at Great Zimbabwe. Each wall is a bit thicker at the bottom than at the top. That shape made the towering walls stable. Huge boulders form part of the Hill Complex walls. They also used cut stones. Some of the more careful walls are as smooth as walls people make today. Another striking feature of the ancient walls is their path. They form curves. They do not form straight lines. A characteristic is a feature that helps identify a thing or a group of things. Researchers are not sure why the people built such massive walls. It seems clear that the walls were not designed to hold up weight.

8Defense against enemies may have been one reason for the walls. They may have built them to give the ruling class more privacy. The walls may also have displayed the king's power. Exploration of these ruins by Europeans started late in the nineteenth century. They did not believe builders from the local African community could have made such a city. Wood found at the site had come from the far north. That wood led some Europeans to think another civilization had built the city. They pointed to people who lived along the Mediterranean Sea. Proving that idea took them decades of effort. Objects at the site pointed to local builders, yet the explorers paid those objects no mind. Their search harmed sections of the site. They destroyed other parts during that search. What they hoped to find were signs of a culture from far away. Shared ideas and customs of one group of people make up that group's culture. Artifacts are objects that humans made or used long ago.

9Finally, in 1905, an archaeologist studied the artifacts from the site. His study showed that local Africans were the builders. Scientists who study what ancient cultures left behind are called archaeologists. In 1892, artists drew how the Great Enclosure was laid out. They also show artifacts found near the site. Several tribes say the people of this ancient city were their ancestors. A descendant comes later in the family line of a person or a group from earlier times. Today, most people credit the Shona with building that ancient city. For many centuries the Shona have made their home in that area. Some artifacts match items the Shona used in a later time. Tools from the ruins look much like tools Shona people used in the nineteenth century. Many people say a Shona phrase is the source of the word Zimbabwe. That phrase means stone houses. Traditional clothing is still worn by Shona people today. At night, starlight falls across these ruins. In 1986, a United Nations organization named the ruins a World Heritage Site. The organization works in education, science, and culture.

10People know it by the short name UNESCO. Because of that title, nearly every country accepts the importance of the site. They see it as worthy of admiration. They also see it as worthy of protection. Time has still harmed the site. Visitors arrive from many countries. Those visits add to the need for repair. Plants may cover many structures that are still standing. Weather has also worn the site down. More funding is needed to study the ruins. More funding is needed to preserve them. More staff are needed for that work as well. Roughly a thousand years have passed since the oldest walls here were raised. Good care could keep them standing for another thousand years. Heritage is a way of life, a tradition, or a feature passed down from one generation to the next. What is left of old buildings, or of other old structures, is called ruins. An enclosure is an area that something surrounds and seals off. Daga is a building material. Daga can also be described as clay mixed with mud.

77. Storms Made of Dust and Sand

1A sandstorm in China surrounds people who are walking. The year is 2008, and they are marking a festival. In September 2009, residents of eastern Australia watched the color of their world change. Strong winds had lifted dirt that was dry as bone. The storm rolled toward the east. It grew into a moving cloud of dust. The cloud was more than 500 kilometers (311 mi.) wide. It was 1,000 kilometers (621 mi.) long. Dust settled over towns. It settled over cities. Sky and land turned a strange reddish orange. Australians said the 2009 sky looked like a scene from a film about disaster. Meteorologists said that region had not seen so bad a dust storm in nearly seventy years. Drivers could not see well, so they slowed down. They switched on their headlights. Airlines called off flights because the conditions were hazardous. Doctors told people with asthma to remain indoors. They gave the same warning to people with other health problems. When the dust finally settled, a huge mass had fallen into the ocean. The mass was about 2.5 million metric tonnes (2.75 million tn.). Meteorologists label this dramatic Australian storm an SDS event. The letters stand for sandstorm or dust storm. These fierce weather systems seriously threaten human health. They threaten the land itself.

2Thunderstorms often create powerful winds. Other strong weather that stirs the atmosphere does the same. When a hard gust crosses dry ground, it shoves bits of earth ahead. It can also lift those bits into the air. Earth plus wind is the simple recipe for an SDS event. These events happen most often in arid parts of Earth. Deserts are arid. So are other places that get little rain. Such land covers about 40 percent of all the land on Earth. A 2016 map from the United Nations Environment Programme shows regions at risk. A sandstorm is shown blowing across Jordan. Jordan is a country in the Middle East. People sometimes treat every SDS storm as the same kind. Some meteorologists separate the kinds. Other scientists do too. Sandstorms, as the name says, happen where the ground is sand. The Gobi Desert in Asia is one of those places. Another sandy region is the Middle East's Arabian Desert. A strong gust lifts the upper layer of sand. A sandstorm stays near the ground. It seldom climbs higher than 15 meters (49 ft.). Dust is lighter than sand, so a sandstorm usually carries dust as well. A dust storm can start wherever the soil is dry. Land dried out by drought is especially likely.

3With no moisture, dirt does not cling together. It crumbles into smaller bits of dust. Those bits are smaller than grains of sand. They are lighter. Wind can therefore move dust farther than sand. It can move dust faster. Dust storms often lift dust 10 kilometers (6 mi.) or more into the atmosphere. A haboob is one particular kind of SDS event. Violent weather is the cause. A haboob can form anywhere SDS conditions already exist. It begins when a powerful weather front sends down very cold, very fast wind. A thunderstorm can be that front.
