Downward gusts can scoop up a great load of sand and dust. The wind builds giant walls of that material. A wall may stand 457 to 1,524 meters (1,500 to 5,000 ft.) high. The wall can hide the Sun. Seeing ahead becomes very hard. Day can look like night, so people also call haboobs black blizzards. One storm can cover a huge area. The width can reach 160 kilometers (100 mi.). The storm can travel 320 kilometers (200 mi.). Now and then it goes even farther. Some have crossed the Pacific Ocean. Haboobs arrive with thunderstorms. Cold air drops from high in the sky down to the ground. The drop drives sand and dust up to great heights. In Arabic, habb means wind.

4It can also mean to blow. Haboob means blowing with fury. Each year, storms carry orange dust out of the Sahara Desert. The dust crosses the Atlantic Ocean and reaches North America and South America. About 2,600 kilometers (1,616 mi.) separate those lands. How often an SDS event happens depends on place and on conditions. How severe it is depends on those things too. Sandstorms and dust storms usually come in the driest season. In much of China, and in other parts of Asia, that season may run from November to April. In the Sahara of North Africa, the events come most often from June to September. Summer brings haboobs often to Arizona and the wider American Southwest. Heavy rain is frequent then. In 2012 a massive haboob crossed Phoenix, Arizona. A sandstorm or a dust storm can make ordinary life miserable. Blowing dust pushes people indoors. High wind can cut off electric power. Drivers face serious risk as well. Dust that suddenly blinds them can cause crashes. Officials tell drivers to leave the road and wait until the storm passes. In 2014, drivers in Kuwait faced those dangers during a sandstorm. Kuwait is in the Middle East. The worst harm from an SDS event often shows up after the sky clears.

5Dirty air is linked to about three million deaths worldwide each year. The World Health Organization, called WHO, estimates that SDS events make some of those people sick. Counting the people harmed directly by sand and dust is difficult. As a safeguard, WHO says to wear a mask outdoors during an SDS event. The advice covers anyone who must walk or work outside. People with asthma are asked to stay inside. People with lung trouble are asked to stay inside. People with heart trouble are asked to stay inside. Bacteria are another major threat. Viruses are a threat. Fungal spores are a threat. Grains of sand and dust can carry all of them. Once the grains are in the air, breathing them in is easier. Research shows that SDS events can carry grave infections across long distances. Thousands of meningococcal meningitis cases in North Africa have been linked to these storms. The first part of the name is said muh-nin-juh-KAH-kuhl. The second part is said meh-nin-JY-tiss. This bacterial illness attacks the brain. It attacks the spinal cord. It can cause death. In the American Southwest and in northern Mexico, some dust storms carry fungal spores. The spores cause valley fever. Chest pain can be a sign. Coughing can be a sign. Rashes and infections of the breathing system can be signs.

6In some cases valley fever ends in death. In 2010, a woman in Beijing, China, shields herself during a sandstorm. Not every dust storm is bad news. Saharan dust lifted by wind each year weighs about 18 million metric tonnes (20 million tn.). The dust crosses the Atlantic. Much of it comes down in South America. Some comes down near the Amazon River. African dust brings nutrients the Amazon region does not have. The Amazon's thick rainforest depends on that dust. Farmland and the food grown on it face a different danger from these storms. The lands most at risk have few plants to stop erosion. Erosion can mean water or ice carrying soil away. It can mean wind blowing soil away. Roots of trees usually pin soil down. Roots of bushes and of grasses do the same. Without those roots, one storm can strip the soil. Dry weather can turn the top layer of soil into dust. Plants need that layer. Nutrients in it let them grow. After wind removes the topsoil, bare ground remains. Crops cannot be grown there. The Dust Bowl in the United States during the 1930s is an extreme case. The case reveals the harm these dusty winds can bring to farmland.

7Farmers on the Plains suffered a harsh drought through the whole decade. Those states lie in the middle of the country. From 1934 onward, huge dust storms made life even harder. The Dust Bowl was one major cause of the Great Depression. In those years, many Americans went hungry. Many had no home. In the hardest-hit places, animals died because they could not breathe. Dirt buried houses halfway. Some 2.5 million people were gone from Dust Bowl country by 1940. They hoped to begin again somewhere else. The U.S. government answered with programs for rural places. Farmers were taught better ways to guard the soil. The lessons also covered how to slow erosion. Another serious SDS threat is deserts spreading outward. The name for that spread is desertification. Each year, topsoil along a desert's edge dries up and blows off. The desert grows. Storms that come often and hit hard speed the process up. A loss has been reported by China's State Environmental Protection Administration. China loses nearly a million acres of fields every year. Desertification pushes residents out of some lands in Asia, in Africa, and in the Middle East. Farmers must leave. Villagers must leave. Fields and gardens cannot grow food once the soil is no longer healthy. In 2014, a farmer in Yemen herds animals during a drought.

8Yemen is in the Middle East. The World Meteorological Organization, called WMO, watches sandstorms and dust storms worldwide. It warns that these storms are growing more numerous. They are growing stronger. Officials fear the rise is a worrying sign of climate change. Slow climate change, over a long time, is natural. Across that long time, energy coming from the Sun shifts. Right now Earth is warming at a frightening pace. Most scientists say certain human actions are the cause. Destroying forests on a huge scale is one major example. Burning fossil fuels is another. Oil and coal are fossil fuels. If world temperatures keep climbing, the danger stays. Stronger SDS events, and more of them, remain a steady threat. Scientists are also fascinated by dust storms on other planets. Mars is one of those planets. Some Martian storms grow large enough to circle the whole planet. Telescopes on Earth can see them. Dust on Mars can spoil a space mission to the Red Planet. It clings to machines. It covers solar panels that refill electric batteries. An artist pictured the look of blowing dust on Mars. WMO officials urge towns and countries to prepare more carefully. One way to cut future harm is to protect land that is easily damaged.

9The main step is to reduce erosion. People and governments fight desertification by planting. They plant new forests on land that is at risk. Rows of trees and shrubs, set in the right places, work as windbreaks. A windbreak can stop a strong wind. It also keeps dirt in place. It keeps moisture in place. Farmers in West Africa plant trees and look after them. The trees help hold soil. They help hold crops. They help stop the Sahara from moving onto more farmland. The work has brought back millions of acres of trees that hold the desert off. Sharper forecasts can limit damage too. Closer watching of the storms can do the same. Like other weather reports, a forecast warns people that a storm is coming. People can then take care ahead of time. Watching the storms also gathers useful data. The data show where storms form and how they form. They show how storms behave and what they do. The Great Green Wall includes a tree planted by a woman. That project fights desertification along the Sahara. Dust from a Sahara sandstorm turned snow orange. The snow lay in Russia and in eastern Europe. Climate scientists have recorded more sandstorms. They have recorded more dust storms. The increase covers the last fifteen years.

10They also report that dry regions are growing at a worrying rate. Higher temperatures worldwide are feeding more thunderstorms. The winds are stronger. Those winds bring SDS events more often. More sand lies ahead for the globe's driest regions. They are set for more dust and more storms. Slowing the conditions behind this rise will take large efforts by many nations. Fresh ideas will be required. Plans that last many years will be required too. These words help with the topic. Arid means very dry. Asthma is a condition of the lungs that makes breathing hard. Encroaching means creeping into a place beyond the usual or allowed limit. Erosion is rock or soil taken away by water, by wind, or by ice. A gust is a short, strong burst of wind. A haboob is a large sandstorm or dust storm. Violent weather over dry land creates it. Hazardous means full of risk or danger, above all to life or health. To inhale is to draw breath in. A meteorologist studies the air around Earth, along with climate and weather. Parched means dried out badly by heat or by a lack of water. Respiratory describes breathing, or the body parts used to breathe. Vulnerable means easy to damage or easy to attack.

78. Stubby, the Dog Who Went to War

1A map shows the Western Front of World War I. Stubby was a small dog. He was very strong. The season was fall. The year was 1917. A young recruit served in the U.S. Army. A difficult problem faced that recruit. World War I was raging. Private James Robert Conroy was the recruit's name. He was about to ship off to Europe. He would join America's British allies. He would also join America's French allies. The problem was his pet. The pet was a bull terrier. That bull terrier was young. Conroy needed a way to get his pet onto the ship. The picture shows a small dog with great strength. Fall of 1917 was the time of this problem. The raging war was the reason for the trip. Europe was where the ship was going. The British were among America's allies. The French were among America's allies too. Conroy's rank was private. His full name was James Robert Conroy. The young bull terrier had to get onto the ship. Shipping off was Conroy's next step. The pet made that step hard. The picture shows that small size. The picture also shows that strength. The Western Front is the place named on the map. World War I is the war named on the map. One question fills this part of the story.

2How could Conroy take his young bull terrier onto the ship? Conroy was a soldier in the 102nd Infantry Regiment. That regiment was part of the Yankee Division. The division was based in New England. During basic training, he noticed a dog at the Yale University football stadium. The stadium is in New Haven, Connecticut. The dog kept hanging around. Conroy adopted the dog. He named him Stubby. The name probably came from the dog's tail. That tail was a little stump. Conroy soon found that Stubby was a natural-born soldier. The dog easily learned the bugle calls. He learned how to march with the men on the drill field. He even learned how to salute. He sat back on his hind legs. He raised his right paw to his brow. Military skills were still not enough. They would not get him to France with Conroy. Pets were banned on troop ships. Conroy asked a sailor for help. The sailor served aboard the Minnesota. That ship would carry the regiment to the war. Before the ship left for France in September, the seaman hid Stubby. The hiding spot was the coal bin of the engine room. After the ship sailed, Conroy and Stubby were reunited. The dog enjoyed the voyage. The voyage lasted nearly a month.

3A later account described shipboard life for Stubby. It was one soup bone after another. The 102nd Infantry Regiment landed in France in early October. Conroy then had a new problem. He had to get Stubby off the ship. His friends distracted some nearby officers. Conroy hid Stubby in his army overcoat. He walked casually down the ship's gangplank. Stubby made it ashore without being detected. By this time he had become the regiment's unofficial mascot. Some of Conroy's friends made Stubby a set of metal identity tags. Those tags are known as dog tags. Official approval was still missing. Several stern-faced officers finally discovered Stubby. The soldiers feared he would be taken away. Stubby saved the day. He charmed the officers by saluting them. His skill at the salute won him many fans. Stubby's role as mascot was confirmed in early 1918. The regiment had a new commander, Colonel John H. Parker. The colonel issued an order. Stubby would remain with Conroy. The soldiers made a joke about that order. They said Stubby was the only member of the regiment who could talk back to Parker. They said he could get away with it. The way Stubby went to war was unusual. He was still just one of thousands of dogs. Both sides in World War I used dogs.

4Some twenty thousand dogs served with the Allies. They pulled carriages that carried machine guns. They carried messages. They stood guard. They killed rats in the filthy trenches. Mercy dogs searched for wounded men on the battlefield. Ambulance dogs did that searching too. Stubby was always happiest at the side of James Robert Conroy. With so many canine recruits, standing out was hard for any one dog. Stubby would still stand apart from every other dog. The trenches of World War I were filthy. They were dangerous as well. By late 1917, the Great War had been dragging on for three years. Great War was the name used at the time. The loss of life on the battlefields in France was beyond belief. The destruction was beyond belief too. The causes of the war were complicated. This part was clear. Millions of soldiers were dying. Many people on both sides wanted the conflict to end. No end was in sight. The war had become a stalemate. Germany led one side. The Allies, including Britain and France, stood on the other. The United States was sending a large force to Europe. That force would aid the British. It would also aid the French. The Yankee Division was part of that force. Conroy and his fellow soldiers were sent to the Lorraine region.

5Lorraine is in northeastern France. There they underwent further training. Experienced French troops led that training. The men were preparing for a German attack. The attack was expected in the spring. The German push began on March 21, 1918. It began with a poison-gas attack. Both sides in the war used poisonous gases. The gas caused terrible damage to exposed eyes. It damaged exposed throats. It damaged exposed lungs. Gas masks were what soldiers put on for protection. Stubby had his own mask. A French officer made it. Stubby's sense of smell was keen. He could detect the smallest hint of gas seeping into Allied lines. Whenever he smelled the deadly gas, he ran up and down the trenches. He barked. He nipped the men. The faithful mascot's warning alerted the soldiers. They then put on their protective masks. Stubby learned a fact about the gas. It settled into low areas of land. One time, he found a soldier asleep in an underground bunker. A gas attack was just starting. The alarmed dog realized the danger the man was in. He woke him up. He barked until the soldier put on his mask. Hearing that was sharp also saved lives. Stubby could hear incoming artillery shells long before the men around him.

6He would warn everyone to take cover. He did similar work when German soldiers left their trenches to attack. He alerted dozing soldiers whenever he heard them sneaking. Stubby was active on the battlefield. He ran to any American who called for help. A soldier who could walk got a guide back to the Allied lines. The guide was Stubby. If the man was too badly wounded to stand, Stubby stayed by him. He barked until medics arrived. The medics carried the man to safety. Stubby's own injury came in April 1918. He went out beyond the trench after an artillery barrage. Another shell landed nearby and exploded. Conroy heard Stubby give a low howl of pain. Shell fragments tore into his chest. They also tore into his left foreleg. Conroy carried Stubby in his arms to a first-aid station. There the dog was put into an ambulance. The ambulance sent him to a field hospital. The hospital was flooded with wounded men. Stubby was so popular that treatment was never in question. Word came that the beloved mascot would survive his wounds. That news lifted the regiment's spirits. June brought him back to duty. The regiment by then looked on him as a hero. The men of the 102nd made him a jacket of a military type.

7They decorated it with his medals. Those awards included a Purple Heart. The Purple Heart marked his wound in action. September 1918 added another accomplishment. Stubby confronted a German soldier. The man may have been mapping the layout of the American trenches. The intruder tried desperately to quiet the barking dog. He used pleas of Kamerad. That word means comrade. The plea did not work. The man dashed for his own lines. Stubby ran him down. He sank his teeth into the soldier's leg. The angry dog held on tight. He held on until the soldier was taken prisoner. Capturing the German soldier brought Stubby a new title. He was made an unofficial sergeant. Conroy was just a corporal. The dog's rank now sat above Conroy's rank. The German had been wearing an Iron Cross medal. As an added honor, that medal was pinned to Stubby's army coat. A photo shows Stubby in his military jacket. He poses next to James Robert Conroy. Among Stubby's many fans was President Wilson. The terrible war finally ended in November 1918. It ended with the surrender of Germany. By that time, Conroy and Stubby had served in four major military offensives. They had also served in seventeen battles. The Yankee Division saw more fighting in the war than any other American division.

8The total was 210 days. While they waited to be sent back to America, Stubby met the U.S. president. The president was Woodrow Wilson. The two shook hands. Wilson was the first of three presidents who would pay Stubby their respects. On his return to the United States, the war hero had a place of honor in many parades. Conroy and Stubby arrived back in April 1919. For the next few years, the newly famous dog was the center of attention. He lapped it up. The American Legion inducted Stubby. He became a star at its parades. He became a star at its conventions too. The YMCA also made Stubby a member. The group said he was entitled to three bones a day for the rest of his life. It also promised a place to sleep. In 1920, Stubby was an honored guest at the Republican National Convention. At that meeting, Warren G. Harding was nominated for president. Harding won the presidency. He then asked Stubby to visit the White House. Stubby also paid visits to the next president. That president was Calvin Coolidge. On July 6, 1921, General John J. Pershing added another medal to Stubby's collection. Many places with no-pet rules made exceptions for Stubby. The New York Times reported one case. The city's exclusive Hotel Majestic had allowed Stubby to stay overnight with Conroy.

9Perhaps the greatest tribute took place on July 6, 1921. The city was Washington, D.C. The occasion was a ceremony for members of the 102nd Infantry Regiment. General John J. Pershing presided. People knew him as Black Jack. During the war he had commanded U.S. forces in Europe. During Stubby's turn in the spotlight, Pershing praised him. He praised heroism of the highest caliber. He praised bravery under fire. The general then pinned a solid-gold medal to Stubby's uniform. The Times observed the happy hero's response. He licked his chops. He wagged his diminutive tail. Stubby marches before a crowd in a 1922 photo. The event was the American Legion parade in New Orleans, Louisiana. Conroy and Stubby stayed side by side for good. When Conroy attended law school in 1921, Stubby went along. The school was Georgetown University. In true Stubby manner, he became the mascot of the Georgetown football team. At football games he entertained crowds. He butted the ball around the field with his nose. By the mid-1920s, Stubby was approaching old age for a dog. He was winding down. He died in his sleep in 1926. He was cradled in Conroy's arms. His final honor came from the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

10The museum recognized him as a war hero. His preserved body stands in a display case. He looks as if he is on alert. Beside him is a mannequin of a World War I soldier. The figure stands for the many men who owed their lives to this brave dog. A few words from his story have special meanings. Allies means people or groups that join with others for a common cause. Sergeant means a military rank above corporal and below lieutenant. It is the highest rank for a noncommissioned officer. Artillery means large guns that fire heavy shells over long distances. Stalemate means a draw or a deadlock, a contest in which neither side can gain an advantage or win. Canine means of or about dogs. Diminutive means very small. Trenches means long ditches dug to protect soldiers near the front lines from enemy fire. Distinguish means to become well known because of excellence. Mascot means a person, an animal, or a thing that is a symbol of an event or an organization. Tribute means an act or a statement that shows gratitude or respect. Regiment means a military unit that consists of two or more large groups of soldiers. World War I means the 1914 to 1918 war of the Allied Powers against the Central Powers.

79. The Air Around Earth Is in Danger

1Inside: an opening. The air around Earth. The ozone layer. Finding the ozone hole. Chemicals that open that hole. How the world answered. A warming planet. Gases that hold heat. A debate across nations. What a person can do. A closing word. Words to know. Topics in this book. A satellite picture shows the layers of air around Earth. Opening A protective blanket wraps Earth. That blanket is the atmosphere. Many gases mix together to make it. Three of those gases matter most. Nitrogen is one. Oxygen is one. Carbon dioxide is one. Survival for living things depends on those gases. Harmful rays from the Sun are filtered by this blanket. Heat is kept from racing away into space too fast. Life on Earth stays inside a narrow band of conditions. The amount of gas has to be right. The temperature range has to be right. The balance of sunlight has to be right. Proper conditions for life are kept in place with the atmosphere's help. The air around Earth Five layers divide the atmosphere. Move upward and the conditions change. Farther from the surface, the air grows colder. It also grows thinner. The troposphere is the layer nearest the ground. Clouds form there. Precipitation falls there. Next comes the stratosphere. It reaches about 50 kilometers above the ground. That height is 31 miles. Passenger jets on commercial routes cruise near 11 kilometers of altitude. That distance is 6.84 miles. They ride in the calmer, lower part of the stratosphere. Above that sit the mesosphere and the thermosphere. Those layers begin at 50 kilometers.

2They continue past 90 kilometers above the surface. In miles, the span is 31 to 56. The exosphere is the outermost layer. It is very thin. A shield made of ozone Oxygen gas has a special form, and that form is ozone. Each of the five layers holds a different amount. A great deal sits in the upper stratosphere. People treat that band as its own sublayer. They call it the ozone layer. The Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays are taken in by that sublayer. Protection is the reason it is called good ozone. All matter in the universe is built from tiny particles called atoms. Earth has ninety-four natural substances. Scientists call those substances elements. No two elements share the same kind of atom. Atoms join, and the things on Earth are the result. A combination of atoms is a molecule. The oxygen we breathe has two oxygen atoms in one molecule. The symbol is O2. Ozone is an oxygen molecule with three atoms. The symbol is O3. Ordinary oxygen molecules are broken apart by UV rays. Two separate atoms are what remain. Those atoms can join other oxygen molecules. Ozone is the result. Inside this layer, ozone is always being made. Destruction never pauses. In ordinary conditions the total barely shifts. The balance does not tip very far either way. Ultraviolet light, called UV, does both jobs. It creates ozone. It also destroys ozone. Creation starts when UV splits O2, the gas we call oxygen, so that two lone atoms remain. Each of those atoms is written O. One of those atoms may join an oxygen-gas molecule.

3Ozone, with three atoms, is what forms. UV can also alter ozone that already exists. It pulls away one oxygen atom. That freed atom then reacts with a molecule of ozone, written O3. The ozone splits into two molecules of oxygen. Those two are O2 plus O2. Sunlight is a mix. Some of the light we can see. Some we cannot. Wavelengths differ. The colors we can see run from the red end to the violet end. A long wavelength carries less power. They make red light. Shorter wavelengths are more powerful. They make blue light. They make violet light. Keep shortening the wavelength and the light turns invisible. Ultraviolet light is powerful, and it cannot be seen. Skin cancer can come from it. Eyes can be damaged. Plants can be hurt. Ocean life can be killed. Some biologists think extra ultraviolet light is bleaching color from corals around the world. Rainbow colors are the range people can see with their eyes. Those waves are the longer ones. The shorter waves, called ultraviolet, stay unseen. Creation and destruction of ozone never stop. Because of that, the amount in the ozone layer stays fairly constant. Harmful UV is kept from Earth's surface by the layer that forms. Ozone also forms close to the ground. Plants are harmed by this kind. Animals are harmed by it. People call it bad ozone. Cars release chemicals called pollutants. Factories do the same. On a hot day, sunlight starts a reaction. The pollutants meet oxygen, and harmful ozone forms at ground level. Polluted air can mean limits on time spent outdoors.

4A warning goes out if ground-level ozone climbs to a dangerous height. People who have trouble breathing are told to remain indoors. Finding the hole Scientists working in Antarctica, back in the 1970s, measured a rise in ultraviolet light reaching Earth. Satellites later confirmed a change. In some places the ozone layer was absorbing less UV than in earlier years. Maps from those satellite readings showed a gap. The gap sat above the South Pole, inside the ozone. The year 1994 found ozone down to half the level measured in the 1970s. Signs showed the hole above Antarctica spreading past the polar region. The spread was heading for the equator. More people live in that direction. People were under threat. So was the environment. A small piece of math belongs here. Lose one percent of the ozone in the stratosphere, and UV-B light at the ground rises by two percent. A chart then asks what the rise would be if the ozone loss were ten percent. Destruction of ozone is greatest near the North Pole and the South Pole. Winter is the season, because polar regions have strong winds and low temperatures. Warmer months let the ozone layer rebuild. Winter at Antarctica, the South Pole, falls during summer in the Arctic, the North Pole. An instrument goes up from Antarctica, launched by scientists there. Measuring the ozone layer is its job. Charts from NASA record how much ozone is present each day. The lowest level ever recorded came in 2006. Chemicals that open the hole Scientists looked for reasons the ozone levels were changing.

5Factories, they learned, were sending out chemicals known as CFCs. The longer name is chlorofluorocarbons. Those chemicals can destroy ozone. Chlorine, an element inside CFCs, was the main problem. Air conditioners used CFCs. Insulating foams used them. Spray paint used them. Large amounts of chlorine were released into the atmosphere on a regular basis. Another chemical, bromine, can destroy ozone too. Bromine sits in substances called ODCs. Those letters mean Ozone Depleting Chemicals. Match the amount of bromine to the amount of chlorine in CFCs, and the bromine destroys forty-five times as much ozone. Fire-control chemicals often contain ODCs. Planes drop chemicals onto forest fires to slow them or to stop them. Harmful chemicals that break ozone apart can come from nature. An eruption is one example. CFCs rise into the stratosphere. ODCs rise there too. Sunlight breaks those molecules apart. Chlorine atoms come free. Bromine atoms come free. Those atoms then break ozone molecules apart. One atom of chlorine is enough to wipe out 100,000 molecules of ozone. Drift beyond the air is what ends the process for chlorine and for bromine. Natural sources of chemicals can destroy ozone as well. An eruption sends hydrochloric acid far upward, into the stratosphere. Up there the acid separates, and chlorine gas is the result. That gas breaks ozone apart. Some loss does come from eruptions and from other events in nature. Most of the damage still comes from CFCs and ODCs made by industry. How the world answered The link between ozone loss and these chemicals was known.

6Many countries kept producing them anyway. The chemicals were so useful that people did not want to give them up. Fixing a problem this large took governments working together. In 1987 those countries signed the Montreal Protocol. The agreement called for cutting production of CFCs and of ODCs. A later ban would finish the job by 1996. This counts as a success. It was the first time many nations took on an environmental issue at a global scale. From 2000 onward, the atmosphere has held less and less CFC. ODC levels have fallen as well. Years may pass before anyone can say whether the ozone layer will recover fully. People who study this, in many nations, pass along the satellite findings. Those satellites watch the atmosphere. A warming planet Engineers moved fast. They built other chemicals to replace CFCs and ODCs. The hope was to help the ozone layer recover. Some of those replacements are friendly to ozone. They are also powerful greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide is one greenhouse gas. Methane is another. Released into the atmosphere, they trap heat near Earth's surface. Glass in a greenhouse traps heat the same way. That trapped heat is known as the greenhouse effect. A rise in these gases, in the view of some scientists, has made the air around Earth warmer little by little. A hotter Earth could melt polar ice that sits on land. That ice could break off into the sea. Ocean water levels would climb. A hundred years of records show a warmer Earth, by one degree. The change can look small.

7Scientists are still concerned. A warming trend that persists could push the temperature higher and higher as time goes on. A hotter Earth may melt the polar ice caps. It may warm the oceans. Ice that melts on land would make the oceans rise. Land near the coast would flood. Habitats of living things would be destroyed. Weather patterns would change on a warmer Earth. Those changes could destroy more habitat. Some plants could die. Some animals could die. Living things that cannot move would be trapped. Corals in the ocean are one example. They would be doomed. Sea life that needs coral reefs for shelter would die too. Sea life that needs those reefs for food would die as well. Gases that hold heat Four greenhouse gases add to global warming when they enter the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is one. Methane is one. Nitrous oxide is one. Fluorocarbons are one. Most scientists give carbon dioxide the blame for roughly three quarters of the warming increase. That share is 76 percent. Machines with gas-powered motors make carbon dioxide. Power plants make it too. They burn fossil fuels. Coal is one of those fuels. Oil is one. Natural gas is one. Cars release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Planes do. Trucks do. Trains do. More warming may follow that release. The trends seen now, most scientists say, come from these four gases. About 13 percent of the warming traces back to methane. Swamps produce it naturally. Livestock produce it when they pass gas. Rotting garbage produces it too. Third place among the contributors belongs to nitrous oxide.

8Fertilizers are where most of it is found. Nitrogen in fertilizer is important food for plants. Mix that nitrogen with soil and nitrous oxide is produced. Animal waste also produces it as the waste decomposes. Fluorocarbon gases are the last contributor. They also help destroy ozone. Nature almost never makes them. They are almost entirely made by people, so making them can be stopped. A picture shows rotting garbage at a landfill. Methane, a greenhouse gas, comes off that garbage. Sharing car rides would cut the carbon dioxide that gas-powered cars and trucks release. So would public transportation. A debate in the world Not everyone agrees about how serious global warming is. Some people say a rise of one percent is no cause for worry. Others think the problem will grow worse. They think people should act now, so later warming can be prevented. Their belief is that greenhouse gases should be reduced before it is too late. Cutting those gases may also slow the loss of the ozone layer. Heat gain down low has a cooling result higher up. That cooling sets up conditions for still more breakdown of the ozone layer. Learn how to make fewer greenhouse gases, and further damage to the ozone layer might be avoided. No final answers exist for global warming. The search for working solutions involves scientists on every continent. They say everyone gains if the understanding goes as far as it can. The subject is how to release fewer greenhouse gases. A bicycle instead of a car helps cut greenhouse gases. A skateboard helps.

9A scooter helps. What a person can do Governments have taken steps to cut chemicals that destroy ozone. Industries have taken steps too. They cooperate in programs that measure the ozone layer. They cooperate in programs that monitor it. Each person can protect the atmosphere as well. Less driving means less ground-level ozone. A mower powered by hand can replace a mower that burns gasoline. Guarding ozone high in the atmosphere means trying not to release CFCs. It means trying not to release ODCs. Chemicals that cool old refrigerators should be recycled. Chemicals that cool old air conditioners should be recycled. Foam packaging should be avoided when that is possible. Industries that still use CFCs can be asked, in a letter, what they are doing. The same letter can ask about ODCs. The question is what alternatives they are seeking. A picture makes one comparison. Buses and trains treat high ozone more kindly than driving alone does. A closing word Factories release chemicals. So do certain products people use. Part of the protective blanket around Earth is being destroyed by those chemicals. The same releases may be warming the atmosphere. Governments all over the world have acted, and some chemicals are now banned. More action is still needed if future harm is to be prevented. The ozone trouble has taught many lessons. Certain chemicals have to be controlled. Scientists work toward shared goals. Politicians do too. Concerned citizens do too. Perhaps the largest lesson is about our actions right now. We need to think about them. We need to ask how they will affect our well-being later.

10We need to ask how they will affect the health of our planet. Words to know Atmosphere: the gas that surrounds a body in space, such as Earth. Global warming: a rise in Earth's temperature, large enough to change the climate. Atoms: the smallest particles of elements that can exist on their own. Greenhouse effect: heat trapped inside Earth's atmosphere by gases. Chemicals: substances made by a chemical process, or used in one. Molecules: what you get when two or more atoms lock together. They are the tiniest complete bits of a substance. Constant: steady, and not changing. Pollutants: things that make something no longer pure. Contributor: a donor, or a supplier, of something. Precipitation: water falling to the ground. Hail is one form. Sleet is one. Rain is one. Snow is one. Mist is one. Decomposes: breaks down by decay. Ultraviolet: having to do with unseen light energy. Fossil fuels: organic substances such as coal and oil, found underground and used as sources of energy. Topics you can look up Invisible light. Antarctica. Methane. The atmosphere, including the exosphere, the mesosphere, the stratosphere, the thermosphere, and the troposphere. Molecules. The Montreal Protocol. Nitrogen. The North Pole. Oxygen. Ozone, including atoms, the hole, breathing, and the layer. Bromine. Ozone Depleting Chemicals, the ODCs. Carbon dioxide. Chlorine. Satellites. Skin cancer. The South Pole. Damage. Ultraviolet light, called UV, including UV-B. Visible light. Elements. Fluorocarbons. Fossil fuels. Volcanoes. Global warming. Wavelengths. Greenhouse gases. Further reading can follow global warming. It can follow the ozone hole. It can follow CFCs.

80. The Curious Life of Albert Einstein

1These parts make up the book, in order. Deeply Hidden Things comes first. A Talented, Curious Boy comes next. The Patent Office follows. The Miracle Year follows that. A Rising Star comes next. The Uses of Fame follow. Coming to America comes next. Einstein's Influence follows. A Life Well Lived ends the story. A glossary comes after. An index comes last. Einstein warned that knowing facts is not the same as knowing the right action. The warning said knowledge of what exists does not by itself open a door to what should be done. Age five was when Albert Einstein first met a magnetic compass. His father was the one who showed it. The floating motion made the boy curious. He wanted the meaning of that motion. His father spun the casing again and again. The needle refused to spin with it. Why? The answer was beyond a child that young. Wonder stayed with him anyway. Mystery stayed too. Years later he wrote down the lesson of the compass. Behind ordinary things, he said, something deeply hidden must exist. The boy who wondered grew into a scientist who still wondered. Finding that hidden something became his life's work. Curiosity kept driving him. Because he followed it, people's picture of the universe changed for good. Hard problems drew him. Great discoveries followed. Violin playing stayed with Einstein from boyhood into adult years. Happiness, in his view, needed little. A table would do. A chair would do. Fruit in a bowl would do. A violin would do. Birth came on March 14, 1879. The place was Ulm, a small town in Germany. Munich, a bigger city, became home the next year. Maja, a younger sister, was born there. She grew into his closest friend in childhood. Family shaped his life in a strong way.

2Pauline, his mother, played piano. Violin lessons were her idea when Albert turned six. The strict shape of those lessons did not please him. Playing itself did please him. The violin stayed beside him for all the years after. Parents once worried about a speech habit of his childhood. The habit is common in children. Words said aloud were often said again, very quietly, to himself. He seemed to be testing whether they sounded right. The habit faded as he grew. Public speaking later became a skill he did well. A picture shows him beside his sister Maja. Engineers in the family shaped him too. His father worked as an electrical engineer. Two uncles did that work as well. Math reached him early through them. Science reached him early through them. Algebra's basics arrived as a game they made. Science books arrived from a family friend. Hours could pass while he pored over those books. Geometry was the book he liked most. Deep concentration was already his as a child. A hard problem held him until he felt finished. He wanted every possible answer considered. Teaching, Einstein believed, should arrive like a gift of real worth. It should not arrive like a heavy duty. Math talent showed at once in school. Science talent showed at once. A mind of his own showed at once too. He challenged the teaching style of his instructors. Strict discipline ran German schools of that time. Strict discipline ran much of German life too. Army sergeants were what the teachers seemed like to the young student. Drill was their method. Students had to memorize information. Students had to memorize facts with no life in them. Creative thought was what Einstein wanted instead. A stamp from the United States later honored that creative mind.

3Seventeen was his age when a top university accepted him. Europe held few scientific schools as fine. Curiosity again chose his path. How things worked interested him. Why they worked interested him. Routine lectures were often skipped. A laboratory got his time instead, while his own ideas grew. Professors mostly agreed about their brilliant student. A bright future was possible. Obeying orders was the condition they named. Imagination, he held, outranks mere knowledge. The future was not something he spent time picturing. It arrives soon enough, he felt. The year 1900 brought the end of school and a surprise. Work was hard to find. Brightness as a student had been real. A diploma from one of Europe's finest universities had been real. Independence had made him unpopular. Curiosity had done the same. The teachers who might have opened jobs were the ones he had bothered. A teaching post would have left him free. Further study could have filled that freedom. Missing that post felt like a setback. Quitting was not his choice. Ideas still needed thinking and testing. Time was what he lacked, and a place. The year 1902 supplied both. Bern is a city in Switzerland. A patent office there hired him. The task was odd. New devices arrived, seeking a patent. He had to test each claim. Did the device really work as the inventor promised? Curiosity had room again. Old ideas could be questioned. Day one brought a boss's rule. Treat every inventor's claim as wrong, the boss said, the moment an application is in hand. Patents of his own were part of Einstein's record. A compass was the subject of one patent. Iron in large amounts did not throw that compass off.

4Metal ships took it on as standard gear. Submarines took it on as standard gear. A refrigerator pump was another patent. Quiet was one gain. Safety was another gain. Pay that arrived on a schedule left him free for private ideas. Work hours that stayed regular left him free too. Spare hours went to friends. Those friends shared his hunger for the science questions of the day. Olympia Academy was the name they chose. Evenings often ran late for the eager group. Cafes held their talk and their social time. His apartment held those meetings too. Steady work plus strong friendship was the soil for new ideas. Science would be changed by those ideas. Three years at the patent office had passed by 1905. Curiosity had grown the whole time. New theories received a huge share of his thought. Confidence finally felt high enough to share the work. Papers went to the top German science journal of the day. The papers laid out his ideas. March 1905 saw the first paper in print. Four more papers followed soon. Light was the subject of the first paper. Both its nature and its behavior were explained. Molecules and atoms were proved real in the second paper and the third. Motion of those tiny bits of matter was described too. Space, time, and moving objects were linked in new ways by the last two papers. Water offers a picture now known to many people. Two hydrogen atoms sit in one water molecule. One oxygen atom sits there too. The letters H, H, and O can stand for them. Proof that atoms and molecules exist was Einstein's. Astonishment was the scientists' response to his writing. Two centuries of thinking about the universe were challenged. The challenge fit inside six months.

5A second surprise was the writer's job. He was not a physics professor at a great university. He was a patent clerk, curious and 26 years old. A career in science then shot off in many directions. Attention from other scientists gave him energy. Fresh chances gave him energy too. Speaking invitations arrived, for science meetings. Explaining the new ideas was part of those invitations. Congratulations came from the 1905 physics winner of the Nobel Prize. Max Planck, a famous physics professor, went further. Students in Planck's classes began to hear Einstein's ideas. Miracle year became the later name for 1905. University classes taught by Planck included those theories. Patent-office work continued until 1909. A full-time university job arrived that year. He accepted it. School after school followed for a few years. The search was for the best home for his research. Older ideas were still being developed. Older ideas were still being refined. The labor was hard. A wrong track was what he often feared. The ideas felt so new, and so strange, that he feared for his own mind. He said the fear was of losing it. The year 1915 brought a discovery. Earlier ideas could finally be joined into a single system. General theory of relativity was the name he gave it. Excitement returned among scientists worldwide. A wider public would soon hear the ideas. The reach would pass anything he had expected. British scientists ran a test in 1919. A star's position was measured while a solar eclipse was underway. A correct theory would put the star's apparent place in one spot. The true place would be another spot. The star showed up almost exactly in Einstein's predicted place. Person of the Century was a title a magazine later gave Einstein.

6Eclipse results filled newspapers across the world. A paper in Britain announced a revolution in science. A new account of the universe was the claim. A paper in Germany called him a new celebrity of world history. A total change in how nature is understood: that was the paper's view of his ideas. Fame of the highest kind arrived overnight. A drawing of the eclipse test is not drawn to scale. B is the label for where the star seems to sit. A is the label for where the star truly sits. The Sun is in the drawing. Earth is in the drawing. Starlight bends because of the Sun's gravity. The bend is why the star seems to sit at B. The true place is A. Pleasure was not universal, even after this success. Careers had been built on ideas Einstein had shown to be wrong. Some scientists did not want the new theories believed. A laboratory test would be hard to arrange. Dislike also had a cruel source. Einstein was Jewish. He lived where prejudice toward many groups was on the rise. Criticism did not knock him off his path. Perfect theories were not what he claimed to have. Each new paper still brought more people to see why the work mattered. Value, not mere success, was the kind of person Einstein urged others to become. Fame brought heavier demands. Interviews were wanted. Photographs were wanted. Speeches were wanted. Fresh writing was wanted. Mixed feelings followed all that distracting notice. Research time was what the demands ate. Usefulness was clear to him even so. Other minds could be opened by fame. A bigger audience could meet his ideas. Causes he cared about got attention because of that fame. War was one deep belief.

7Avoid it whenever avoidance is possible. World War I brought a letter against Germany's entry. The year was 1914. Only three scientists signed. Einstein was among them. A different letter supported entering the war. More than 100 scientists signed that one. The 1930s brought a series of articles from him. General readers were the audience. The series title begins with the words The World and finishes as I See It. War was a topic. Liberty was a topic. Progress was a topic. Education was a topic. Science was not the only topic. Antiwar work got his active help. Peace groups that crossed borders got his work. Writing carried his antiwar beliefs. United States magazines gave him credit for helping make the atomic bomb. He rejected that credit. Other people used his science to build the bomb. He himself did not join the project. A letter of his went to President Franklin Roosevelt. Destruction the bomb could cause was the warning. Views of his changed across a long life. Pacifism did not change. Pacifism says violence is never the answer. Pacifism says war is never the answer. Inequality was another subject his fame served. Fair treatment for every person was what he supported. New York in 1921 brought news reporters to greet him. Elsa, his wife, arrived with him. Schoolwork and daily living share one strong motive, Einstein said. Pleasure in the work is that motive. Pleasure in the result is part of it. Knowing the result helps the community is part of it. Peace had promoters, Einstein among them. Germany still slid toward war in the 1930s. Tolerance from the German government had covered him until then. Criticism of government plans had been allowed. He knew the tolerance would end. The Nazi Party was rising.

8Spoken attacks on Nazi politics put him in danger. Jewish heritage put him in danger too. Germany was left behind in 1933. The Institute for Advanced Study became his workplace. The workplace sat in Princeton. Princeton is in New Jersey. New Jersey is part of the United States. The year 1949 brought a meeting at his Princeton home. Jawaharlal Nehru came. Nehru was prime minister of India. Sailing was a pleasure. Lake Carnegie, at Princeton, often held his boat. A house near the office became the family home in New Jersey. Princeton's tight community soon included them. Visitors from other towns asked where the great man lived. Townsfolk answered with a question: Are you expected? Strangers were kept from bothering him at home by that question. Twenty-nine more years of work followed. New areas were where he tried to stretch his ideas. Losing touch was what some people read into the effort. Little attention went to that criticism. A further theory was his hope. Old ideas and the newest theories would be joined by it. Hard work continued. Miracle-year discoveries were never matched again. Discoveries of the general theory of relativity were never matched again. Demand for him never stopped. Speeches continued. Articles continued. Regular meetings with other scientists continued. Helen Dukas, his secretary, went over matters with him. Her work beside him ran from 1928 to his death in 1955. Few people, he believed, truly see by their own eyes. Few people truly feel by their own hearts. Useful products grew from his curiosity. Light's nature was one source. Light's behavior was part of that source. New control of light was what later scientists built from those ideas. Television cameras grew from that technology. Remote controls for home electronics grew from it. Flat-screen computers grew from it.

9Laser light was first thought of by Einstein. Compact discs, called CDs, use that technology now. Digital video discs, called DVDs, use it. Store checkout equipment uses it. Atoms and molecules, once proved real, changed everyday goods. Some goods were created from that proof. Some goods were improved by it. Shaving cream is one. Toothpaste is one. Computers are one. Portable phones are one. A framework for studying space objects comes from Einstein's theories. The Helix Nebula is one such object. New theories still feel his influence. Ideas about how the universe began trace back to his work. Ideas about what space is like trace back to his work. Ideas about black holes, those strange objects, trace back to his work. Mystery, he once said, is the most beautiful experience open to us. Understanding a little of that mystery each day is enough, he said. Death came on April 18, 1955. Curiosity had kept him working up to then. Nature's greatest mysteries were the target. Thinking about time changed because of him. Thinking about space changed. Thinking about energy changed. Thinking about matter changed. Those four things are the universe's foundations. Glossary Algebra is math that lets symbols, usually letters, stand in for numbers that are unknown. A patent is a paper giving an inventor the right to earn money from an invention. Physics studies matter and energy by science. Astounded means amazed or surprised in a great way. Pore means to read while paying very close attention. Atoms are matter broken into tiny pieces. A compass finds direction. North is where its needle always aims. A revolution throws down older ideas, or older ways of doing work. Molecules are the smallest bits of a substance that can still be known as that substance.

10Theories are explanations that might be true. The universe means everything that exists in space. Mysterious describes what is not easy to understand. Index The word mysterious is tied to number 10. Mother is tied to number 5. Miracle year is tied to numbers 10, 11, and 19. War is tied to numbers 15 through 17. Magnetic is tied to number 4. Violin is tied to number 5. Laser light is tied to number 20. Universe is tied to numbers 4, 11, 13, 21, and 22. Laboratory is tied to numbers 7 and 14. Job is tied to numbers 8, 12, and 17. The United States is tied to numbers 16 and 17. Inventor is tied to number 8. Uncles are tied to number 6. Solar eclipse is tied to number 12. General theory of relativity is tied to numbers 12 and 19. Sister is tied to number 5. Father is tied to numbers 4 and 6. Scientific theories are tied to number 10. Family is tied to numbers 5, 6, and 18. School is tied to numbers 7, 8, 12, and 17. Revolution is tied to number 13. Fame is tied to numbers 15 and 16. Research is tied to numbers 12 and 15. Curiosity is tied to numbers 4, 7 through 9, 10, 20, and 22. Curious is tied to numbers 4, 5, and 11. Princeton, New Jersey, is tied to numbers 17 and 18. Criticism is tied to numbers 14, 17, and 19. Peace is tied to numbers 16 and 17. Patent office is tied to numbers 8, 10, and 12. Born is tied to number 5. Papers are tied to number 10. Beliefs are tied to numbers 15 and 16. Olympia Academy is tied to number 9.

81. The Great Dam in Black Canyon

1On a guided tour, people step inside Hoover Dam. The tour shows the machinery that makes the dam work. Coming pages start with desert water. They ask why anyone built a dam here. They measure a huge structure. They follow the construction. They follow a visit. They follow how the Southwest changed. A word list ends the book. Stand on the west side, and Arizona is the land across the dam. Kayaks are a common sight on Lake Mead. In summer, parts of the U.S. Southwest often climb past 100°F (38°C). Yearly rain in much of the region stays below 10 inches (25.4 cm). Even so, millions of visitors arrive each year. Fishing draws them. Boating draws them. Water-skiing draws them. Swimming in a vast, cool lake draws them. The land around that lake is dry and baked by sun. The 1930s are what made the lake possible. That is when Hoover Dam went up. The Southwest of the United States was transformed. Water reached desert that had been parched. Power reached it too. This iconic landmark let cities spread. It let farms spread. It let recreation spread. The Colorado River is where Hoover Dam stands. Around it lies the Mojave Desert, said moh-HAH-vee. The state line of Arizona and Nevada runs through this spot.

2The distance to Las Vegas, Nevada, is about 30 miles (48 km). The dam lies to the southeast of that city. Black Canyon was the government's choice. Tall walls and a narrow gap defined the canyon. Solid bedrock was there. Solid walls were there. Nothing weaker could hold a structure so huge. No earlier dam stood on the Colorado River. Hoover Dam therefore had to be extremely large. The river's control rested on this one dam. Only a very tall canyon would do. A watershed map names Nevada, Utah, and Colorado. It names Lake Mead and California. It names New Mexico, Arizona, and the Colorado River. The Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of California appear as well. One photo shows Black Canyon with no dam yet. Another recalls 1905. Floodwater from the Colorado spread across much of Imperial Valley. The Salton Sea came into being. Control of that water took two years. The river bends its way across the southwestern United States. Life-giving water reaches a land that would otherwise stay dry. For centuries, people have made homes on the Colorado's banks. Crop irrigation used that water. In earlier times the supply fluctuated. Spring snowmelt swelled the river.

3Farms often went under floodwater. By the later part of the year, only a trickle remained. Crops died. Settlers who came early grew discouraged. The water would not stay steady. A search began for control of the river. The year 1901 brought the Alamo Canal. A private company built it. It lay just north of Mexico's border. The plan was to turn the Colorado westward. Imperial Valley, in California, would receive irrigation. Farms then did very well. The year 1905 brought a severe flood that undid the gain. Control gates on the canal were ruined. Much of Imperial Valley was ruined with them. Residents of Imperial Valley asked for a bigger canal. Arthur Powell Davis served as chief engineer. His agency was the government office that handles western water. He believed a river dam would work better. More people could receive more water. He studied the Colorado first. Congress heard his findings in 1918. A decade later, Congress approved the building of Hoover Dam. A canal was approved with it. Imperial Valley would get irrigation from that canal. Spending won approval from President Hoover in 1930. The Great Depression was already underway. Its start came only eight months before the project was approved. Hard times in the economy gripped the United States.

4Work was gone for millions of people. Southern Nevada drew 21,000 arrivals in total. Construction jobs were the magnet. President Hoover pushed to employ as many people as he could. He told crews to begin before the support was ready. Houses were missing. Water fit to drink was missing. A hospital was missing. Other facilities were missing. Early on, camps held some workers and their families. Electricity did not reach the camps. Running water did not reach them. Tents were the homes. The Colorado River was the bathtub. Hoover Dam counts as an arch-gravity dam. A sketch labels downstream, gravity, arch, and upstream. At the time of building, no dam on Earth was taller. The engineering feat was amazing. Six companies had to join their skills. The design shows a gravity dam. It also shows an arch dam. Weight is what a gravity dam relies on. Stored water pushes, and that weight pushes back. An arch dam bends upstream. Canyon walls then take most of the water's push. Squeezing follows. The dam compresses and gains strength. Inside the power plant, moving water is converted into electricity. Lake Mead, the reservoir, holds the stored water. Lake Mead is a lake that people made.

5No larger one exists in the United States. Measurements of Hoover Dam fill one diagram. Thickness at the top is 45 feet (13.7 m). Intake towers number four. Each one rises 395 feet (120.4 m). They control water headed for the power plant. From foundation rock up to the crest, height is 726.4 feet (221.4 m). Across the top of Black Canyon, width is 1,244 feet (379 m). Weight passes 6,600,000 tons (5,987,419 mt). Thickness at the base is 660 feet (201 m). A second map shows how the river was diverted. Arizona and Nevada are labeled. Diversion tunnels, a rock barrier, and cofferdams are labeled. Dry ground was required at the site. The Colorado had to be sent around it. That huge job started in May 1931. Dynamite opened the rock. Each side of the canyon received two tunnels. River water would use those tunnels to pass the site. Concrete then lined the finished tunnels. Danger in the tunnels was extreme. Rocks fell on the crews. Fumes filled the air. Vehicles that burned gasoline, working underground, made the fumes. Up on the surface, other crews raised barriers. Water could not leak through them. Cofferdam is the name. One cofferdam stood upstream of the site.

6One stood downstream. The upstream cofferdam would push the river into the tunnels. The downstream cofferdam worked beside a rock barrier. Water would not be allowed to run back up the canyon. The work area would stay dry. During those same months, high scalers worked the walls. Loose rock came off. Grooves were cut for the dam to lock into. The men often dangled far above the water. Wooden swings held them. Heat reached 120°F (49°C). Jackhammers were their tools. Dynamite was used as well. Several other builds happened alongside the dam. Boulder City rose so workers could live there. A hospital was part of the town. Other facilities were part of it. Tracks for trains went in near the site. Deliveries of supplies used those tracks. A road linked Boulder City with the dam. A power line went in too. Its length was 222 miles (357 km). San Bernardino, California, was one end. Black Canyon was the other. Construction needed that power. High scalers perhaps faced the roughest work on the whole project. Rocks that fell took dozens of lives. Tools that fell took lives too. Deaths from industrial accidents came to almost one hundred men. Ready tunnels let pumps empty the work area.

7Solid bedrock had to lie under the dam. A cover of silt and stones sat on that rock. The cover was 135 feet (41 m) deep. June 6, 1933, saw the last of it dug away. Tunnel work had started about two years before that day. Concrete could then go in. Huge buckets carried the wet mix downward. Block-shaped molds received it. Form is the name of each mold. Crews smoothed the surface. They drove out air bubbles. They finished that step before hardening began. Fresh layers followed. Steel pipes, narrow ones, ran through the forms. Cold water inside them chilled the concrete fast. Hardened concrete let workers pull the wooden form apart. The same form was rebuilt above the block just finished. A new block was poured there. The stack continued. Columns grew until they hit their final height. Grout closed the gaps between columns. The picture of the method is simple. Blocks of concrete, piled up, became the columns. Spillways came after the main dam. These passages would steer high water around the structure. A Colorado flood would have a path that spared the dam. The power plant was built next. Four intake towers were built with it. Flow toward the power plant would be under their control.

8February 1, 1935, marked the end of the work. Plugs went into the diversion tunnels. Until then, those tunnels had carried the Colorado past the site. Behind the dam, the water rose. It spilled over the cofferdam. Lake Mead took shape. The workforce, by the end, numbered more than 21,000 men. A typical day saw 3,500 of them. Cost of the project was $165 million. In today's money, that is $3 billion or more. Concrete in the dam, the power plant, and the other structures could pave a road. San Francisco would stand at one end of that road. New York City would stand at the other. Cement used in construction passed 5,000,000 barrels. A single day might use 7,500 barrels. It might use as many as 10,800. On September 30, 1935, President Roosevelt led the dedication. He praised the dam as the greatest anywhere in the world. The public has been invited in since 1937. Each year, millions come. Tours of the dam and the power plant draw close to a million of them. Displays fill the visitor center. Natural history of the region is one subject. History of the dam is another. Construction is another.

9Visitors often leave impressed. Spectacular is a word they use. Amazing is another. Incredible is another. Lake Mead allows fishing in every season. Boating, picnics, and hikes are available in every season too. Nine wilderness areas lie in the region. Animal types number five hundred. Plant types number nine hundred. Inside the visitor center, the view down on Hoover Dam is a bird's-eye view. Tours with guides add details from behind the scenes. Las Vegas in 1930 was a stop on the railroad. Residents numbered only about 5,000. Population swelled once Hoover Dam stood finished. By 2013, the count was over 600,000. Across the southwestern United States, the Colorado supplies more water than any other source. Control of that river began with Hoover Dam. History had not seen the river controlled before. Irrigation that farmers could trust reached Arizona. It reached Nevada. It reached California. Drinking water came from the dam as well. Electricity at a price people could pay came too. Growth followed in Los Angeles. It followed in San Diego. It followed in Las Vegas. It followed in Phoenix. It followed in other southwestern cities. Thousands of men found jobs on the project. In a very hard time, the dam stood as a symbol of hope.

83. The Iron Giant of Paris

1People often call the sight of the Eiffel Tower breathtaking. More than 125 years ago, four men shared a wild idea. Their goal was the tallest structure on Earth. The height would be 300 meters, or 984 feet. Building it would use upwards of 18,000 metal pieces. Holding those pieces would take 2.5 million metal pins. The men said the finished work would be attractive. They said it would stand through high winds. Plenty of people believed the dream could not be done. Others believed it would look ridiculous. The dream could be done. The look was not ridiculous. Today the result is one of Earth's best-known landmarks. It is also one of the most loved. That landmark is the Eiffel Tower. A list of facts sets out the tower's size. Height without the antenna is 300 meters, or 984 feet. The antenna adds 24 meters, or 79 feet. Counting the antenna, height is 324 meters, or 1,063 feet. There are 108 stories and three platforms. Those platforms stand 57 meters, 115 meters, and 276 meters above the ground. In feet, those heights are 187, 377, and 906. Weight is 10,100 metric tons, or 11,133 tons.

2The iron alone weighs 7,300 metric tons, or 8,046 tons. Visitors have numbered over 250 million. Among monuments people pay to enter, it is the most visited in the world. Work finished in 1889. New York's Chrysler Building passed the tower that year. Since then, a small number of other buildings have taken the title. The tower remains remarkable even so. Four gigantic beams form the legs. The beams bend gently inward. They join into a single tower up top. Wrought iron is the metal. Strength is one quality of this iron. Ease of shaping is another. A new coat of paint goes on every seven years. Dark red was an early color, and dark yellow came after it. It later became brown. The latest color is bronze. Twenty-five painters need over a year to cover the whole surface. A map puts the tower in Paris, near the Seine River, the Champ de Mars, and Avenue Gustave Eiffel.

3France lies between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. Paris, France's capital, is the tower's city. The 1889 World's Fair was the reason it was built. Say Champ de Mars as shahm duh MARS. Travelers from around the world come for the huge landmark. Nearby sights draw them too. Art and culture fill the streets around the tower. Museums are there. Gardens are there. Palaces are there. Monuments are there. Cultural centers are there. The area also holds upscale hotels, restaurants, and stores. Old buildings stand beside new ones. He did not make the first drawings. Maurice Koechlin and Emile Nouguier did. Say Koechlin as mor-EES kay-KLAHN.

4Say Nouguier as ay-MEEL NOO-gee-ay. Both men were chief engineers in Eiffel's company. They entered the design in a contest. A contest asked for something decorative to mark the World's Fair of 1889. Their plan was a very tall tower. Four iron beams, slightly curved, would form it. Crossed metal strips would build each beam. Horizontal metal beams would tie the four main beams together. The ties would run along all four sides. The company already knew tall bridge work. A structure 300 meters tall, or 984 feet, would still be a daring achievement. They asked a French architect, Stephen Sauvestre, to join them. Say his name stay-FAHN soh-VES-truh. He was to keep the tower attractive. He was also to keep it structurally solid. Gustave Eiffel had already designed hundreds of metal works in many countries before this tower. His life ran from 1832 to 1923. A railway station was among those works. An observatory was among them. Many bridges were among them. Their plan won against 106 other projects. Building started soon after. January 26, 1887, was the day ground was broken. Just over two years later, the huge work was done.

5The finish date was March 31, 1889. Wrought iron pieces in the tower number 18,038. Their weight is 7,300 metric tons, or 8,046 tons. Eiffel chose wrought iron on purpose. He wanted proof that metal could match stone for strength. Metal's weight is lower than stone's. Bolts held the sections together at first. More than one hundred workers assembled them at Eiffel's factory. Each section was about 5 meters long, or 16 feet. The sections then traveled to the site. July 1888 already showed the tower's second horizontal band in position. Late November showed a tower close to finished. At the site, the bolts came out. Special metal pins took their place. Workers heated each pin before it went in. Cooling made the pin shrink. The shrink created a very tight fit. The pins totaled 2.5 million. A team of four workers set each pin. As many as three hundred men were on the site during construction. Stone and cement form the foundation, also called the base. Gravel is the layer under it. The base was set at one exact angle. That angle was meant to hold it if strong winds came.

6Each level was made flat with special care before the next level went on. Scaffolds, which are temporary wooden platforms, were used. Small steam cranes helped put the tower together. For the tools of that time, the methods were astonishing. The speed was astonishing too. The tower became a lesson in engineering. On a hot day, sunlit metal expands more than shaded metal. The tower can lean as much as 18 centimeters, or 7 inches, because of that. One elevator in the tower covers about 103,000 kilometers in a year. That distance is 64,000 miles. Going around the equator two and a half times would cover the same distance. French achievements were what the World's Fair celebrated. Opening day was May 6, and closing day was October 31, both in 1889. Exhibits filled more than eighty structures. Europe sent exhibits. North America sent exhibits. South America sent exhibits. The Champ de Mars was where those structures stood. Eiffel and his team trusted the design. Agreement was not universal. Some feared a tower so tall would fail in the wind. One math professor went further.

7He said even a shorter tower would collapse under strong winds. A different worry came from other people. After building had started, a group tried to halt the project. The first floor is 57 meters up, or 187 feet. A glass floor is there. Walkers feel as if they are stepping on air. Interactive displays about the tower are on that floor. Shows project city views onto three walls. Restaurants and shops are there. A piece of the first spiral staircase remains. It once led to Eiffel's office. Every winter since 2004, an ice-skating rink has been part of the first floor. At floor two, the height is 115 meters, equal to 377 feet. Souvenir shops are on it. Restaurants are on it. Story windows there tell how the tower was built. A glass window gives a plunging look straight to the ground. A glass elevator carries visitors. Many angles of the tower open up during the ride.

9The top, 276 meters up or 906 feet, offers a stunning look over Paris. Two levels share that view. One level has a roof. The other is open. Day or night, the view is there. Any weather still allows it. Eiffel's restored office is on the top floor. Panoramic maps are there as well. They show directions and distances to other large cities. Outstanding photos are possible on all three floors. From the top, Paris spreads out in a grand view. Visitors can also enter the restored office. Wax figures show Gustave Eiffel talking with Thomas Edison. Eiffel stands on the right. Edison stands on the left. The countdown that welcomed the year 2000 was shown on television worldwide from the tower. Gustave Eiffel and his team, if alive now, would surely feel pleased. Joy has reached people worldwide because of their engineering wonder. Close to seven million people visit each year. Dozens of novels have used the tower in the plot. Dozens of movies have done the same. More than thirty replicas have been inspired by it. Dazzling light shows take place there.

10Fireworks shows take place there. One astonishing show marked the start of the year 2000. A person in Paris cannot miss this famous landmark. Someone in almost any district of Paris can see it. It still soars over Paris, which is what Mister Eiffel intended. Some words in this book have special meanings. An achievement is an accomplishment earned by effort. An architect is a person who designs buildings. Plunging has to do with falling fast, or with a slope that is steep. Collapse means to fall apart or to fall down. Installed means equipment or software was put in place and set up for use.

1People cut marks into a clay tablet so they could track rations and goods. A sharp tool cut the images into the clay. A map of this early world marks the years 5000 to 2150 bce. They also found bricks. They also found pottery. From these objects, researchers could tell how those ancient people lived. Farming villages were already there as early as the year 5000 bce. Its pictures show life in early Mesopotamia. Sumer is the land these Ubaid people settled before anyone else. Until they built settlements, the Ubaid kept traveling. Other Sumerian tribes did the same. They were nomadic hunters and gatherers. They searched for food. They searched for water. Later, the Ubaid learned how to remain in a single spot. They drained marshes. Rich soil let them raise crops. Irrigation canals carried water into places that were dry. River clay was the material for their pots. Reeds from shallow water were woven into baskets. The river's riches met their personal needs. Those riches also gave them goods to trade with travelers. Busy trade paths from Asia and from Europe ran across Sumeria's rich plains.

3Traders supplied items the Ubaid could not grow. Traders also supplied items the Ubaid could not make. Copper lion heads were common protective figures on Mesopotamian buildings. Uruk's ziggurat still has its stone base in the spot where builders first set it. A clay tablet from about 2350 bce lists grain given out each month. The writer used cuneiform script. Pictographs of Mesopotamia showed up first in the city of Uruk. In writing, a pictograph is a symbol. Trade at Uruk helped this early writing grow.

4Business dealings at Uruk helped the writing grow as well. People marked simple images on clay tablets. The marks added up workers' rations. The marks also kept a record of goods. Those picture marks later became the writing called cuneiform. In that system, symbols stood for sounds. They did not stand for objects. People could use those sound symbols to write in any language. Using sounds instead of pictures brought several benefits. Writers could shuffle one group of symbols and spell many different words. Because of that, fewer symbols were needed. The system also made abstract ideas easier to express. Those ideas would be hard to show as pictures. Wedge-shaped cuneiform on clay tablets shows how Sumerians lived in that age. One official was a leader of the plow. Another was a leader of the law. Other leaders followed the same pattern. Three main classes made up society in Mesopotamia. One class was free people. A second class was semi-free people. A third class was enslaved people. Life among Sumer's lower classes is mostly unknown. Most Sumerian women were wives. Most were mothers. Homes and children were in their daily care. School was closed to most girls.

5Girls from a wealthy family were the exception. Women in Sumer held more rights than women did in Mesopotamia's later cultures. They could own property. They could run businesses. His mother was the Sumerian mother-goddess Ninsumun. Uruk's huge protective wall is credited to Gilgamesh. That wall still stands today. During 2003, scientists from Germany located a tomb in the riverbed of the Euphrates. They thought the tomb belonged to Gilgamesh. The epic's description of a tomb matches this find quite closely. Ancient poems from Mesopotamia, gathered together, make up the Epic of Gilgamesh. The poems tell of an ancient king's battles. They tell of his struggles. They tell of his achievements. He strives to gain immortality. Many people also think no older work of literature still survives. Stone tablets with single poems date to about 2100 bce.

6In the story, Gilgamesh wears the skins of lions he killed. As the Sumerian city-states grew, they began to fight one another for control of the region. They were thriving while those fights increased. Battles grew steadily more frequent. A battle in the year 2525 bce is the earliest Sumerian war described in detail. The city-states of Lagash and Umma fought that battle. Pictures and words cover a tall stone column known as a stele. Speakers say stele as STEE-lee. The carvings show soldiers carrying swords into battle. The soldiers also carry spears. They also carry shields. Wheeled carts carried the army leaders. Pairs of onagers pulled the carts. An onager is a native species of donkey. Materials for making arms arrived along the trade routes. Smiths learned how to melt copper together with tin. Both metals are soft on their own. Together they make a harder substance. People called this alloy bronze. They used bronze for swords. They used it for spear tips. Tin, however, was rare. Traders from central Asia could supply it. Traders from Europe could supply it too. Cutting off trade routes kept weapons out of an enemy army's hands. One damaged fragment of a stele ranks among the oldest historical records known. The fight of Lagash against Umma is what that fragment records. A map of Sargon's Akkadian Empire marks the Caspian Sea twice in its labels.

That empire continued until the year 2150 bce. Westward, its farthest reach was the Mediterranean Sea. It reached Arabia in the south. It reached Iran in the east. No deity in Mesopotamia was more widely loved than Inanna. Quiet years under the Akkadian Empire changed life in this land. The earliest system for sending messages began in Mesopotamia. Workers inscribed clay tablets with messages in cuneiform. They then wrapped each tablet in a clay envelope. A seal belonging to the sender was pressed on the clay wrapper.

8It was also marked with the name of the person who should receive it. It showed where that person could be reached. No one but the receiver could read the message. Someone had to crack the clay wrapper open to reach the message inside. A central government enforced laws. It enforced regulations. Trade networks expanded. Commerce boomed.
