Place value in numbers was another idea these people worked out. The way people measure time uses this same old system. People use numerical base systems when they count certain objects. When they count dozens of eggs, they use base twelve. Twelve eggs equal one dozen. When people count time, they use base sixty. Ancient Mesopotamians devised that system. Sixty seconds make one minute. Sixty minutes make one hour. The earliest pottery wheels have been found in Sumer. Sumer has also yielded the oldest wheels used for travel. Modern life still depends on wheels. Near 3500 bce, Sumerian potters started shaping clay bowls with a flat round tool. That wheel lay level and turned on a center pin. A spin of the wheel let the potter form a bowl whose rim stayed even.

9The bowl could also have even surfaces. About three centuries after that, Sumerians found another job for wheels. Wheels made it easier to move objects. Wheels made it easier to transport people. They tested many ideas, and then they tried a fresh setup. A single axle carried one wheel at its left end and another wheel at its right end. Loads became much easier to haul with this new device. Little strength was needed to roll that cart over the ground. The design may have been copied by people in other lands. Soon, people used wheels across the world. About 2150 bce, this empire came to an end. A severe drought struck it. An invasion by the Gutians struck it too. Speakers say Gutians as GOO-tee-uhnz. These Gutians were wandering people who came out of northern mountains. Bands of Gutian fighters often struck the kingdom's distant edges. As a result, trade slowed. Fields lay untended. In the end, the city of Akkad fell to these wanderers. The Akkadian Empire collapsed. Running a society this complex was something the Gutians barely knew how to do. The web of canals was allowed to break down. They brought on a terrible famine. Their rule of Sumer lasted 125 years. Later ages gave this hard time the name Dark Age of Mesopotamia. Mesopotamia did not return as a thriving empire until the seventeenth century bce.

10King Hammurabi reigned then. People called the new empire Babylonia. A statue shows Gudea. He was a Gutian prince. His rule in Lagash ran from 2144 to 2124 bce. Nomadic means moving from place to place with no permanent home. An alloy is a metal made by combining two or more metals. Phonologic describes the study of speech sounds inside one language or across several. A city-state is a city or an urban area that behaves like a country of its own. Pictographs are symbols or pictures that stand for words or ideas. Civilizations are organized societies. They have a stable food supply, a government, a social structure, and a culture. They also have written language and religion. Smelted means melted or fused by extreme heat. Buying goods and selling them is what the word commerce means. A stele is a tall piece of rock set upright, either a slab or a column. Designs or words on it usually honor a person or an event. Another spelling is stela. Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped characters. Several areas of the ancient Middle East wrote with this script. A ziggurat is a rectangular structure of ancient Mesopotamia. Steps rise up its sides. A temple sits at the top. In myth, a demigod is half human and half divine.

85. The Land Called India

1A map of this country sits in Asia. China lies nearby. So do Afghanistan, Bhutan, Pakistan, and Nepal. New Delhi is marked. Bangladesh and Myanmar, also called Burma, are marked. Mumbai is marked. The Arabian Sea is marked. The Bay of Bengal is marked. The Andaman Islands are marked. The Indian Ocean is marked. Sri Lanka is marked. The Nicobar Islands are marked. India’s place is Asia, and most of the country is a peninsula. The northern border has several neighbors. Pakistan is one. China is one. Nepal, said nuh-PAHL, is one. Bhutan, said boo-TAHN, is one. Bangladesh, said bahng-gluh-DESH, lies east of India. Myanmar, said mee-AHN-mar, lies east as well. Just south of India is an island nation. That nation is Sri Lanka, said SHREE LAHNG-kuh. The Arabian Sea lies to the southwest. The Bay of Bengal lies to the southeast. Islands belong to India too. The Andaman Islands, said AHN-dah-mahn, are one group. The Nicobar Islands, said NEE-koh-bar, are another. Say DEL-ee and you have the sound of India’s capital. The capital’s name is New Delhi. It sits inside the older city of Delhi. Delhi reaches far back in time. Construction of New Delhi belongs to the early 1900s.

2British India needed a capital, and this city was made for that role. India was still inside the British Empire. Delhi feels like a maze. Streets are small. Bazaars are crowded. New Delhi offers a contrast. Avenues have room. Shopping centers are modern. Suburbs joined to Delhi now make a huge metropolitan region. The population there is more than twenty million. New Delhi itself is just a slice of that urban spread. Mumbai, said mum-BY, is the other giant in the race. Each city wants the title of largest in the country. The two population totals sit close. Both totals climb year by year. Bombay was the name British speakers used. They could not pronounce Mumbai. The year 1995 put the original pronunciation back. A huge port earned the city a nickname. People called Mumbai the Gateway of India. A monument uses that nickname. The year 1911 placed the monument at the harbor mouth. British monarchs were making a first visit. India was their colony. Freedom came about forty years afterward. The highest British official in the government left by that same gate. An island holds the city. Mainland India has a west coast. The Arabian Sea lies between that coast and the island.

3Women in one picture wait at a well. Indoor plumbing is missing from many homes in the countryside. West Bengal is one Indian region where that is true. Head count in India has passed 1.2 billion. China is the only country with more people. Growth continues. Big cities are numerous. Countryside towns and villages still hold most people. Rural houses usually lack plumbing indoors. About half also lack electricity. Classes once split Indian society. The split was called the caste system. A person’s social group brought strict rules. Foods of the group were traditional. Customs of the group were its own. Work of the group followed an old pattern. Lower castes suffered terrible treatment from the castes above them. The system is now against the law. Its grip on society is still strong. Half of India’s workers live by agriculture. Cattle are raised. Water buffalo are raised. Other animals are raised too. In many regions, meat from a killed cow is against the law. Cows are sacred in Hinduism. Some other faiths in India agree. Plows are pulled by cattle. Travel can depend on cattle too. Meat comes from sheep. It comes from goats. It comes from chickens.

4Crops feed people inside the country. Crops also leave the country as exports. The biggest harvests include rice. They include wheat. They include sorghum. Spices sit with those crops. Vegetables sit with them. Shoppers across India buy fresh produce every day. Power supply lags behind need. Population size is the reason. Cities often lose power. Cities often ration power. Rationing limits when power may be used. Pay for an average worker is among the lowest on Earth. Poverty is the condition of many people. Education still runs high for a large number of Indians. Science employs many of them. Technology employs many of them. Shops and crowds jam many city streets. Old Delhi shows one such street. A map of landforms names the Indus River. It names the Himalayan Mountains and Mount Everest. It names New Delhi. It names the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Thar Desert. It names the Ganges River and the Chota Nagpur Plateau. It names the Sundarban and the Deccan Plateau. It names the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats. Say him-uh-LAY-uhz for the Himalayas. Those peaks make the northern border. No mountains anywhere are higher. Asia’s other lands are cut off by them.

5That separation is why people often call India a subcontinent. Northern India holds a low plain. The name is the Indo-Gangetic Plain, said in-doh-gan-JE-tik. Long ago, rivers flooded over and over. Each flood left sediment. The rich soil is the result. Northern India holds the Ganges River. Say GAN-jeez. Hinduism treats the river as sacred. Travelers who follow Hinduism come from every region. They step into the water. The plain’s south side meets raised country. That country is the Deccan Plateau, said DE-kuhn pla-TOH. Over half of India is this high ground. Low hills are included. Coasts are included. Residents are many. Soil is rich. Crops like the climate. Westward, dryness increases until the land is the Thar Desert. Dunes of sand never stay put. Area is about 200,000 square kilometers. The same area is 77,000 square miles. Three seasons cover most of the country. Hot and dry is one. Hot and wet is one. Cool and dry is one. March opens the hot dry season. May or June closes it. Temperatures run high. Winds run strong. Dust storms arrive. Monsoon is the name of the hot wet season. The start is May or June. Hard winds arrive from the south.

6Rain is very heavy. Afternoon is when it usually falls. Most days get that rain. About three-fourths of yearly precipitation usually comes in this season. Floods reach many regions in some years. Late October stops the rain. Cool, dry weather takes over. October 2 marks a birthday. The person is Mohandas Gandhi, said moh-huhn-DAHS GAHN-dee. His leadership brought independence from British rule. Prayer services are held. Ceremonies are held. Father of the Nation is the title of honor. Autumn brings Diwali, said dee-VAH-lee, a festival built on lights. Five days is the length. Small candles are lit. Firecrackers go off. Sweets are gifts for family. Friends receive them too. Links to Diwali cross many faiths. Spring brings Holi, said HOH-lee. Colors name this festival. A Hindu holiday was the origin. Many religions take part now. The party marks winter’s end. People throw colored water. They throw colored powder. Singing is part of the day. Dancing is part of it. Special foods are part of it. Mess is common. Baths close the day. Clean white clothes follow the baths. Water guns are popular with children. So are balloons full of colored water. August 15 is Independence Day. The celebration remembers freedom from Great Britain.

7The year was 1947. Kites of many colors go up. Freedom is what the kites mean. Civilization here is ancient. Around 321 bce, one ruler held most of the people. Their land is the India of today. The 700s ce brought invasions by several Muslim empires. A kingdom near Delhi was the result of one invasion. Rule by Muslims continued into the 1600s. Shah Jahan, a Muslim ruler, left a landmark still famous today. It is the Taj Mahal, said TAHZH muh-HAHL. Beauty is its fame. After his wife died, the Shah built this mausoleum for her. The same centuries sent Europeans out to explore. A Portuguese sailor reached India in 1498. He was Vasco da Gama, said VAHS-koh DAH GAH-mah. Control of the future India passed to the British Empire by 1858. Resistance gained Mohandas Gandhi around 1920. Violence was not his method. Protest without violence, he showed, could matter. Twenty-seven years passed before independence. A free democracy was born in 1947. Conflict has not disappeared since then. Worry about population has not disappeared. Good changes have still arrived. The first woman to serve as prime minister took office in 1966. She was Indira Gandhi.

8A woman president came forty-one years afterward. The year was 2007. Rabindranath Tagore won a Nobel prize for poetry. Birth was in Kolkata in 1861. Home was where most of his lessons happened. England came after he turned 17. Writing poured out of him. Poems were included. Plays were included. Short stories were included. Paintings were his too. Some poems received music he composed. A knighthood was given. He gave it back. Colonization by England was what he protested. Wild animals here include many species. Large cats are among them. Wild lions and wild tigers share this one country. Nowhere else do both live wild. Leopards of two kinds live here as well. Rarity marks both kinds. Scarcity is even greater for the snow leopard. Its home is the Himalayas. A famous reptile is the cobra. Poison is its weapon. A threat makes the hood spread wide. Mice and rats are the hunt. Those animals stay near people. Bites therefore happen at times. King cobras are one cobra type found here. Strength made the Indian elephant prized in earlier times. Forests were cleared with that strength. Logs were lifted. Crops were hauled. People were carried. Work today still calls on some elephants.

9Wild herds remain in most regions. Loss of habitat puts them at risk. Crops are still loaded onto some elephants. Other labor still uses them. Along the Bay of Bengal, swamp forest grows thick. The trees are mangroves. The place is the Sundarban, said SHOON-dar-bahn. Few habitats are like it. Sea turtles live in it. Sharks live in it. Crocodiles live in it. Bengal tigers have their greatest stronghold there. Swimming is how those tigers take prey in the swamp. A male can reach 3 meters from end to end. That length is 10 feet. Mass can reach 230 kilograms. That mass is 500 pounds. Scientists keep up hard work to guard this endangered tiger. Crowds like to meet at the India Gate. The gate is in New Delhi. Local people come. Visitors from other countries come. People and many kinds of animals fill this large country. Feeding them all is a challenge. Giving them homes is a challenge. Rare natural beauty must be kept safe at the same time. Among the nations, India still carries great weight. A fact list gives a snapshot. Population is 1.4 billion. Land covers 2,973,193 square kilometers. That equals 1,147,956 square miles.

10New Delhi is the capital city. Hindi is the primary language. Hinduism is the primary religion. The rupee, said ROO-pee, is the currency. Central Intelligence Agency published the figures in February 2022. The World Bank is a second source. Bazaars are markets. Rows of small shops fill them. A peninsula is land that stretches out long. Water wraps nearly all of its edge. The caste system locks social rank in place. Birth sets the rank. Profession sets it too. Snow, rain, sleet, and hail are all precipitation falling from the sky. A mangrove is a tree of the tropics. Swamps suit it. Shallow salt water suits it. Sacred describes a link to religion or to the spiritual. A mausoleum is a tomb built large. Several tombs can share one structure. Sediment is small pieces of dirt and of rock. Water can move those pieces. Wind can move them. Ice can move them. A monsoon is a storm tied to a season. The rain it brings is heavy. A subcontinent is one large portion of a continent. A Muslim follows Islam. The Sundarban is swamp packed with forest. India and Bangladesh both contain it. The Bay of Bengal lies beside it.

86. The Long Road West from Chicago

1This book follows Route 66, a road that carries drivers across the whole American West. It tells how the highway began and how songs, shows, and films used it. It points out roadside sights, including Cadillac Ranch, a ranch of bottle trees, and a blue whale. It describes giants, dinosaurs, and the effort to save the road. A word list ends the book. Picture the year 1957. You have just lowered the top of a convertible painted a bright cherry red. Sunlight flashes across the car's shiny metal fins. Rock and roll pours from the speakers. Nothing but open road waits ahead. Could the drive improve? You doubt it, until an ice cream cone three stories high comes into view. Sprinkles cover the cone, and your mouth waters. Should you stop? Then a cheeseburger as huge as a bus appears. A quick lunch can come first. When night arrives, you park beside a hotel room built in the shape of a teepee. Inside are a bed, a bathroom, and a shower. The day on the road has been spectacular. No one can say what the next day will bring. If this trip sounds like a dream, or like a made-up journey, that guess is wrong. The drive is a real one, down the highway Americans have loved best.

2That highway is Route 66. A road map of the United States looks a great deal like a spiderweb, and the web is intricate. Huge highways zigzag from one coast to the other. They crisscross from Canada down to Mexico. They link nearly every city that lies between. Travel is simple. A person gets into a car and starts driving. A hundred years ago, a trip across the country was much harder. Most roads were only small trails of dirt. Cars were new inventions. They often broke down, sank into mud, or blew a tire on jagged rock. A driver who ran out of gas had no luck left. Only a few gas stations stood in the wild country. A traveler who needed sleep had a single choice. Set up a tent at the roadside. During the 1920s, the government of the United States built a new highway plan. Roads received numbers so cities and states would connect more effectively. The first road paved along its full length ran 2,400 miles, or 3,862 kilometers. It stretched from Chicago to Los Angeles. People named it Route 66. Many came to call it the Main Street of America. A severe trial arrived for that road not long after it opened. The crash of the stock market came in 1929.

3Large numbers of people lost their money, their jobs, and their homes. The dire time that followed is known as the Great Depression. In those same years, drought followed drought. Giant dust storms wrecked farms on the Great Plains. Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico suffered the worst of it. People named this phenomenon the Dust Bowl. All at once, many families had to leave home and search for a better life. A great number believed that paradise waited in the West, above all in California. Thousands packed what they owned and made the long trip. They traveled a new road called Route 66. Many trusted that road to carry them away from trouble. They hoped it would lead them toward work and toward riches. A famous novel tells that story. John Steinbeck published The Grapes of Wrath in 1939, and the book is now a classic. It follows a family leaving Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl years. The family drives Route 66 in search of work in California. Steinbeck named Route 66 the mother road. He also named it the road of flight. During the 1930s, California gained 1.2 million new residents. More than half a million of them left because life was so hard in the Dust Bowl years.

4On December 7, 1941, Japanese forces bombed naval ships of the United States. The ships lay at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The next day, the United States entered World War II. Soldiers, workers, and supplies had to move quickly. They were mobilized from many parts of the country toward military bases in the West. Their route was Route 66. The journey was long, and wartime travelers needed food, gasoline, and a place to sleep. Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels sprang up along the road to serve them. Life in America was hard, yet business along Route 66 was booming. The war ended in 1945, and Americans celebrated. Soldiers came home, started families, built houses, and bought cars. Many wanted to drive those new cars toward the West. They hoped to see the Grand Canyon and the Pacific Ocean, traveling by way of Route 66. The years after World War II were glory days for the highway. Shiny blue roadsters rolled along it. So did convertibles of cherry red, coupes of bubble-gum pink, and yellow Checker cabs. Route 66 was no longer only a path to some other place. It had become the place people wanted to be. In 1946 a song titled Route 66 rose to the top of the hits. Its best-known line invited listeners to go find fun on that highway.

5The line helped fix the road's place in popular culture. The Nat King Cole Trio sang the first version of the song in 1946. In 1960 a television show took the same name, Route 66. It followed two friends who crossed the country in a Corvette. They had no single destination. They were hunting for adventure on the road. The show stayed on the air from 1960 to 1964. By 1970 a newer highway had bypassed most of the original Route 66. Mentions of the old road still showed up in American popular culture through the century's end. Move ahead to the year 2000. John Lasseter, the director at Pixar Animation Studios, drove Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the imaginative buildings he passed. He loved the colorful art installations as well. He chose to turn those sights into a film. Disney and Pixar released the movie Cars in 2006. Lasseter sent a team along Route 66 to study the road for the film. Some of the roadside art they found became the seed of characters in Cars. Landmarks from the highway appear in the movie too. The Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, for example, turned into the Cozy Cone Motel. Cars succeeded so fully that many families who watched it took vacations of their own on Route 66.

6That new interest helped the old route grow popular once more. A rusty tow truck in Galena, Kansas, gave artists an idea. The truck became the movie character Tow Mater. A map of stops runs from Chicago to Los Angeles across Illinois, Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Canada lies to the north, Mexico to the south, with the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean at the coasts. The Gemini Giant stands in Wilmington, Illinois. Paul Bunyon stands in Atlanta, Illinois. The Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower stands in Collinsville, Illinois. The Red Rocker stands in Fanning, Missouri. The Blue Whale stands in Catoosa, Oklahoma. Slug Bug Ranch stands in Conway, Texas. Cadillac Ranch stands in Amarillo, Texas. The Wigwam Motel stands in Holbrook, Arizona. Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch stands in Oro Grande, California. The Cabazon Dinosaurs stand in Cabazon, California. Chicken Boy stands in Los Angeles, California. Museums, motels, and shops unlike any others appear in every state the route crosses. Unusual art, old gas stations, and lively theaters line the road as well. Travelers can also watch live shows. At Lookout Point, New Mexico, a visitor can see a real Native American dance ceremony. At Vinita, Oklahoma, the Will Rogers Memorial Rodeo is held.

7One promise holds. A traveler will not feel bored on Route 66. Cows graze in the pasture that surrounds Cadillac Ranch. Ten Cadillacs were set nose-down in a field in 1974 by alternative artists who came from San Francisco. The rear bumpers point up at the sky. Over the years the cars have worn many bright coats of paint. One of the easiest to notice came in 1990, when every car was painted pink. Today the cars show every color of the rainbow, because visitors have covered them with graffiti. Close by, the VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, plants five colorful Volkswagen Beetles in the ground. Elmer Long is a folk artist who looks at garbage and sees a forest. He built Bottle Tree Ranch from bottles that had been used before. He also used car parts and objects of every sort, including jawbones of buffalo. Seeing the forest is only half the visit, because music fills the place too. Wind off the desert blows through the open bottles and makes a medley of tones. As a boy, Elmer Long saved bottles and other things people had thrown out. What gift suits a woman who already has everything? Hugh Davis answered that question with a blue whale for his wife, built for an anniversary.

8The whale measures 80 feet, a length of 24.4 meters. For many years children loved to slide and dive from the whale into the swimming hole below. Visitors can now climb inside and look out through tiny windows in the head. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma, has a boardwalk that follows its spine. Pictures along the highway show Chicken Boy in Los Angeles, California. They show the Gemini Giant in Wilmington, Illinois, and Paul Bunyon in Atlanta, Illinois. Giants truly fill the land along Route 66. A California factory named International Fiberglass made thousands of colossal statues from fiberglass. The factory sold the statues to businesses on Route 66 so the businesses could advertise. Workers at the factory built unusual costumes for the giants. The costumes turned them into cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and even chickens. Food statues are among the largest figures on the route. Oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones of humongous size make a hungry kind of ride. Near Collinsville, Illinois, a rider may glimpse the biggest catsup bottle on Earth. That bottle is the Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower. Dinny cost 300,000 dollars to build, and the builders used materials from roadside construction. Dinosaurs have died out almost everywhere else on the planet.

9They have not died out on Route 66, where tall prehistoric creatures of many shapes greet travelers. Dinny stretches 150 feet, equal to 45.7 meters. He is likely the biggest dinosaur made of concrete in America. He lives in a dinosaur park at Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to draw guests to his restaurant nearby, the Wheel Inn. The park grew famous, and the 1985 film Pee-wee's Big Adventure even showed it. Mr. Rex, a Tyrannosaurus rex as tall as three stories, is a favorite at Cabazon Dinosaurs. Fame brought traffic, and the traffic was heavy. Congestion wore the highway down. From 1956 through the 1980s, the government of the United States built new interstates around Route 66. Those fast highways have many lanes. As more travelers picked the interstates, shops and services on Route 66 suffered. Peeling paint, faded signs, and windows boarded shut became ordinary sights. In 1999 the United States Congress passed a law meant to protect Route 66. The government began to offer money. Towns and businesses could use the money to help pay for saving important landmarks. In 2008 the World Monuments Fund called Route 66 endangered. The fund made plans to draw tourists, including a map that uses virtual reality. A photo shows the Red Rocker of Route 66 in Fanning, Missouri.

10Today the old road is growing popular again. People come back to enjoy its playful art and its creative spirit. The surest way to feel that spirit is to drive the road and live a classic American journey. Mobilized means that troops and supplies were made ready for war or for other action. Bypassed means gone past, or avoided, often to make a job faster or simpler. A phenomenon is a striking event, or a person or thing admired for an unusual quality. Congestion means a state of being crowded, blocked, or overly full. Dire means terribly bad. A resurgence is a return of growth, or of popularity, after a fall or a quiet time. Endangered means at risk of disappearing completely. Fiberglass is a light but strong material made from thin threads of glass. Those threads are sometimes set inside a substance much like plastic. A road trip is a car journey, usually across a long distance. A stock market is a system, or a place, where people buy, sell, and trade stocks. A highway is a main road linking towns or cities. Installations are artworks, often large and unlike older art, built from mixed materials. Sometimes the artwork is a whole room or a whole building.

87. The Mud Mosque of Djenné

1Each week, an open-air market meets beside the mosque. Djenné is one of the oldest towns in Africa south of the Sahara. People pronounce the town name je-NAY. A religious building in the town is unlike any other. People call it the Great Mosque of Djenné. Muslims worship in buildings called mosques. Muslims follow the religion of Islam. Islam ranks among the largest faiths on Earth. More than one billion people follow Islam. Five ideas form the base of the religion. A statement of faith is one idea. Prayer is a second idea. Fasting is a third idea. Charity is a fourth idea. A journey to Mecca is the fifth idea. Mecca is the city where Islam began. Followers of Islam travel to Djenné's famous mosque when they want to learn about their faith. They also visit so they can worship. This mosque is the largest mud-built structure on Earth. South of the Sahara, few buildings matter more than this one. The account that follows begins with trade routes. It then turns to a place for worship. It tells about the first mosque on this ground. It tells about a later mosque linked with Amadu. It describes the mosque people see today.

2It explains walls formed from mud. It explains how builders raised the mosque. It shows why the building matters to the town. It closes with the mosque in the present and in the years ahead. Mali is the country of this small town. Mali lies in West Africa. The town stands on a floodplain. The Niger River borders that plain. The Bani River borders it as well. People can reach the town only by boat. In the thirteenth century, the location made a strong link to Timbuktu. Timbuktu lies 483 kilometers to the north. That distance equals 300 miles. Timbuktu was a major stop on trade routes across the Sahara. Traders left the coast and traveled north toward Timbuktu. Their path passed through Djenné. The town grew because of that traffic. Islam spread along the same desert routes that carried goods. Islam had reached Mali in the ninth century. Mansa Musa was a Muslim king of Mali. During the 1300s, Islam gained greater influence under his rule. As years passed, students of Islam gathered in Djenné. In 1896, an artist drew the mosque as workers rebuilt it. Followers of Islam in Djenné needed a place to worship.

3Work on this mosque started in the thirteenth century. The mosque visitors see today is not the first building on this ground. King Koi Konboro ruled Djenné when the first Great Mosque was built. He built it during the thirteenth century. He placed the mosque where his palace had stood. He used materials from the local area. He followed a traditional design. He added towers that rose high. He added large walls around the building. Rain damaged the mosque as years passed. The mud washed away. By the 1800s, wear had left Djenné's great mosque in poor condition. In the 1800s, a tribal leader from West Africa took control of Djenné. His name was Seku Amadu. He let the first mosque fall into even worse condition. In 1834, Amadu began a new mosque. The new building was plainer than the old one. Workers raised it on a site nearby. The job lasted two years. They finished the building in 1836. In 1893, soldiers from France took the city. The mosque Amadu had built was already in ruins by then. The French put a school in its place. Workers finished the mosque visitors see now in the year 1907.

4Workers built it on the ground of the original Great Mosque. That 1907 project was the last time the whole mosque was constructed. Repairs still change the building from year to year. Yearly repairs mean the present building does not match the first mosque. Palm-wood bundles called toron are not only decoration. During the yearly restoration, workers climb by using the toron. The Great Mosque of Djenné looks plain next to mosques in Egypt. It also looks plain next to mosques in India. It looks plain next to mosques in Turkey as well. Its walls are tall. Its walls are brown. Builders made the walls from mud. The Sun baked that mud until it was hard. The hard mud gives the building a smooth surface. The surface looks sculpted, as if a carver had shaped it. At regular spaces, bundles of palm-wood sticks poke out from the walls. People call those sticks toron. These wooden bundles brace the walls. The prayer wall is called the qibla wall. Speakers say qibla as KIB-luh. The qibla wall faces east. It faces toward Mecca. The wall looks over the city's marketplace. The city of Mecca stands in the Middle East.

5People regard Mecca as the place where Islam began. Three towers rise from the mosque. Each tower has a boxlike shape. People call the towers minarets. An ornate ostrich egg crowns each tower. The egg stands for purity. The egg also stands for fertility. A golden ostrich egg, shaped as if carved, sits atop each minaret. Religious leaders go up the stairs five times daily. They call local Muslims to prayer. The mosque chooses a man to stand by the minarets and give that call. Visitors enter by climbing stairs. The mosque has six sets of stairs. As many as three thousand worshippers can fit in the big hall. Ninety wooden pillars span the closed space and carry the roof. The roof covers half of the mosque. Vents let hot air leave the hall. Removable caps made of ceramic sit on those vents. Worshippers use the remaining half as an outdoor hall. An arched passageway surrounds that courtyard. From the passageway, visitors can watch activity inside. The Great Mosque of Djenné covers 5,625 square meters. That area equals 60,547 square feet. No mud-brick building anywhere is larger. Many people count it among Africa's greatest works of architecture.

6The year 1988 brought this mosque the title of World Heritage Site. The walls measure 41 to 61 centimeters in thickness. That thickness equals 16 to 24 inches. Smooth mud forms the walls. The tallest minaret reaches 16 meters. That height equals 52 feet. The building has three minarets. Eighteen decorative projections stand along the main wall. The mosque rests on a raised platform. The platform is 3 meters high. That height equals 9 feet. The raised base helps the building avoid floods. Builders of the Great Mosque of Djenné used traditional materials from the region. Mud was the material they relied on. They formed bricks from mud. They made mortar from mud. They made plaster from mud. Locals baked mud in the sun to produce bricks. They called the bricks ferey. They used mud mortar to bond the bricks while the walls rose. They coated the walls with mud plaster. The coating leaves a smooth surface that looks shaped by hand. 1The book is arranged in these parts. Opening. The Man Who Jumped. Another Mark for Joe. Still More Marks. Closing Words. Words to Know and Topics. Pictures name three spacefarers. 1A mosaic set in the floor of an ancient Christian church shows a donkey. Visitors who come through the Siq meet the Treasury first. You have agreed to take an amazing adventure. 2The city lies about 185 kilometers, or 115 miles, southwest of Amman, the capital of Jordan. Ancient trade routes linking the Middle East, Asia, and Africa pass through Petra. The Street of Facades leads toward the city center, and tombs cut from rock line the street. Visitors next reach the Theatre, which could seat four thousand people. Then come the Royal Tombs, the burial places of kings. The Colonnaded Street runs through the center and leads to Petra Museum. The museum holds more than six hundred artifacts. From the museum, a hiker with energy can climb about eight hundred steps cut in the rock.

4Those steps reach the Monastery, called al-Deir in Arabic, one of the largest monuments in Petra. In 1993 the site was protected as an archaeological park. Jordan's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities manages the park. Ancient trade roads around the city are part of the park. The Theatre was cut from solid rock, and centuries have left it with extensive damage. A walking route runs east to west from the Visitor Centre to the Monastery. 5Little by little they became successful traders. They took control of routes that tied parts of the Middle East to Asia and to Africa. In time the traders grew rich, built Petra, and settled. Petra was their capital, and it is thought to have been founded around 300 BCE. The city flourished from the first century BCE onward. It became a center of culture, and a center of people, goods, and money. While Petra thrived, the Roman Empire was pushing east into the Middle East. The empire had its center in ancient Rome, in Italy. Across several centuries it grew until it held all the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. In 106 CE the Romans took Petra without a fight. The Romans held Petra for three hundred years.

6They then shifted the heart of their trade to the north and moved much of that trade onto water routes. Petra grew less important as a place of trade.
