A huge earthquake in 363 CE wrecked much of the water system and nearly half the city. That quake was likely an important reason for Petra's decline. Another large earthquake struck in 551. Early in the 600s, Arab forces gained control of this region. By the end of that century, Petra's last residents had gone. After the decline, only the Bedouins knew the city. Bedouins are Arab nomads who lived in the area. The wider world stayed unaware until the Crusades, which ran from 1095 to 1291.

7In those years, Christian countries of Europe invaded. They tried to seize Jerusalem and the land around it, and in the end they failed. After the Crusades, Europeans did not know of Petra again until the early nineteenth century. A Swiss explorer, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, heard of the ancient city of stone and set out to find it. In 1812 he made a short visit, and his reports opened the way for other outsiders to come and study Petra. The buildings fall into two kinds: structures that stand free, and monuments cut from rock. Free-standing buildings were raised from the bottom upward. Rock-cut monuments were carved from the top downward. Unfinished monuments prove the point, because only their tops are carved. Nobody knows for certain how the Nabataeans cut those monuments, which are Petra's most remarkable works. Scholars think the carvers did not use wooden scaffolding, since few trees grow in the desert nearby. One idea is that they cut away large blocks of sandstone, one level at a time. The cuts would leave huge steps, and carvers could stand on the steps while they worked.

8A second idea is that strong rods fixed in the rock held a wooden board. Carvers stood on the board, and after a level was done they set pins lower on the face and shifted the board. Scientists still hunt for clues that would explain the building methods. Stairs, water channels, and other features were also carved by hand into the natural forms of the cliffs and canyons. The unfinished monuments have been important to scientists who study how carving was done at Petra. Nabataean buildings mix many styles. The mix reflects influences from Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, India, and Egypt. Petra is the tourist site people in Jordan visit most. In 2015, more than four hundred thousand visitors made the trip. Tickets are sold to travelers at the Visitor Centre. They enter by way of the Siq, riding a horse cart or walking, or riding a horse, a donkey, or a camel. A person can see Petra in two days, but several days are better. The soft sandstone can be worn down by wind, by water, and by salt. Wind brings that salt inland from the Red Sea.

9Large crowds of tourists threaten the city as well. Touching the stone wears it away, and so does sitting on it or walking on it. In 1985 the Rose City was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a status that supports protection and conservation. Hundreds of artifacts are displayed in Petra Museum. Thieves have carried off many other objects across the centuries. At sunset on the winter solstice, sunlight falls on the central podium of the Monastery. Little is known about the Nabataeans, yet two facts are certain. First, they worshipped the Sun. The proof is in the light. On the winter solstice, and at certain other times of year, the Sun strikes the main buildings or lines up with them. That alignment happens for 80 percent of those buildings. Second, they were incredibly inventive in the way they brought water into the desert. More pieces of the water system keep being found. Radar lately found a network of water channels under the ground. Scientists also found fountains and gardens that were once lush. Research that continues will surely show more about these ancient people. It will show how they lived, and how they thrived, in their majestic city of rock.

10Antiquities are objects or buildings that come from ancient times. A decline is a long downward slide in amount, in quality, in value, or in strength. An aqueduct is a channel made by people so that water can move from one spot to another. A facade is the front face of a building. Nomadic describes people who shift from place to place and keep no lasting home. Archaeological describes work that studies what ancient cultures left behind. A reservoir is a large tank or lake where water is gathered and kept. People may use that water for drinking or for growing crops. Architectural describes the design of buildings and the way they are put up. Civic describes matters of a city, of being a citizen, or of community life. Scaffolding is a temporary set of platforms that holds workers while they build, repair, or decorate. Conservation means keeping safe the historical and cultural things, buildings, and places people value. A solstice is one of two days in the year when the Sun stands farthest from the equator.

91. The Writer Who Grew Up on the Prairie

1A map marks the places Laura lived. Pepin, in Wisconsin, was home from 1867 to 1869, and again from 1871 to 1874. Madison is that state's capital. Independence, in Kansas, was home from 1869 to 1870. Topeka is that state's capital. Walnut Grove, in Minnesota, was home from 1874 to 1876, and again from 1878 to 1879. St. Paul is that state's capital. De Smet, in what became South Dakota, was home from 1879 to 1894. Pierre is that state's capital. Mansfield, in Missouri, was home from 1894 to 1957. Jefferson City is that state's capital. Iowa appears too, with Des Moines. Nebraska appears, with Lincoln. Illinois appears, with Springfield. Oklahoma appears as well. The book opens with an introduction. Prairie life and the big woods come next. Hard times follow. Dakota Territory comes after that. Laura as a young woman follows. Happiness at Rocky Ridge comes next. The Little House stories come after that. Hard words are explained last. Near dawn, three-year-old Laura Ingalls woke. Pa asked, gently, if the girls wanted a picnic at the Indian camp. Mary, the older sister, leaped from bed with Laura. Both were excited. Days with Pa were rare. Farm chores usually filled his time. A lunch was packed. The girls followed him over a wide, rolling prairie.

2Warm wind moved Laura's hair. Insects sang in the rippling grass. Birds sang there too. The Osage had left camp for the season. Lunch was eaten near the fire pits. Colorful beads were gathered from the grass. Walking home, the girls saw a sunset. Pink and gold stained the sky. Inside the little log cabin, Laura stopped short. Ma was in bed. A doctor stood nearby. Ma asked the girls to meet a new baby sister. The voice was tired, and it was proud. This memory is among the earliest and strongest Laura Ingalls Wilder kept. Two forces in it later shaped her famous novels. Family closeness was one. Love of wild, open country was the other. Birth came on February 7, 1867. The place was the northern woods at Pepin, Wisconsin. Laura was child number two. Mary was first. At age two, Laura watched Ma and Pa Ingalls load a covered wagon. Independence, Kansas, was the aim. Many more moves would follow in her childhood. The family were settler-colonists. White families like theirs were some of the first to settle the American West. The Kansas cabin left vivid memories. The stay lasted only about a year. The land was Osage land, and the family had settled there by mistake. They had to go.

3Wisconsin was the return. For centuries before white settlers came, the Osage had lived in that part of Kansas. Late in the 1800s, the U.S. government used violence to push the Osage off those lands. Indian Territory was where they were sent. That territory is today's Oklahoma. At age four, Laura watched the prairie fall behind the wagon. She felt sad. Baby years in Wisconsin were too early for her to remember. The return revealed another wonderful world. Dark, wild, and mysterious is how the big woods felt. Outdoors was where Laura wanted to be. Snowballs flew between her and her cousins. Firewood had to be gathered. Other chores waited. Long winter nights brought Pa's fiddle. That music belonged to the happiest days of her childhood. Hard times came next. Laura later described the packing. Goods from the little house went into the wagon. Beds stayed behind. Tables stayed. Chairs stayed. Pa could build replacements. Restlessness defined Pa Ingalls. Open prairie was what he missed. Minnesota was the move he planned for the young family. Trouble started before departure. Scarlet fever struck Laura. Every blanket the family owned was wrapped around her. She was settled in the back of the wagon. At age seven, she watched a silent, snow-covered home disappear. Minnesota put Laura and Pa back on open prairie, and that made them glad.

4The first shelter was a sod house. Dense mats of grass roots formed its walls. From far off it looked like a low hill. A creek bank was where that hill rose. Later Pa built a house of wood. Wheat was planted near Walnut Grove. School began for Laura and Mary. Reading pleased Laura. Writing pleased her. Reciting pleased her. Another baby was on the way. Happiness lasted a few months. Then hardship hit. Grasshoppers arrived in swarms the size of thunderclouds. The wheat was eaten. With the crop gone, the family shifted into Walnut Grove. Odd jobs kept them going. Even young Laura cleaned in a hotel and waited on tables. Fever then took the new baby brother, Freddie. Spirits rose a little in 1877, when Grace was born. Hard times continued. Mary became ill. Eye nerves were damaged, either by that illness or by a stroke. The cause was never certain. Blindness lasted the rest of Mary's life. Pa chose to head west and start again. A photo from about 1880 shows the sisters. Laura is on the right. Carrie is on the left. Mary stands with them. A train at Walnut Grove carried the family west. Pa had gone ahead to work in Dakota Territory.

5They were joining him. At age eleven, Laura told what she saw. The train was huge and smoking. The cars were decorated in an ornate style. Wheat fields rushed past as a golden blur. Mary listened to every word. The stop had no town yet. Only a railroad halt was there. The Ingalls family, with a few other white families, became the first citizens of a future town. That town would be De Smet, in South Dakota. Some of the earliest buildings were Pa's work. The first store was one of them. More settlers came. A homestead a few miles out of town was acquired. Pa built a cabin there. He built a stable. He built a garden. Winter sent the family to rooms above the store in town. School would be closer for the girls. The U.S. government urged white settler-colonists westward. Homesteads were offered. They were nearly free places to live. The ground had been taken from Native people. Native people were not counted as citizens then. Laura lived on land that belonged to Native people. Like many white settler-colonists, she held racist views about them. Her books often leave those peoples out. They often show them in a negative light. White settler-colonists are praised.

6Wintering in town proved lucky. Blizzard followed blizzard. Snow blinded the way to school. Food trains could not get through. Some families nearly starved. Hours were spent grinding raw wheat by hand until it became flour. Almanzo Wilder, a young man, walked through the snow. He went to the only farm already established nearby. He brought back every bit of wheat that farmer could spare. Settlers' lives were saved. Laura would hear of this good man again. Laura later wrote that pain ends. Love, she wrote, lasts forever. The long winter finally broke. The family went back to the homestead. The Dakota prairie was in bloom. The farm began to thrive. The new town did too. Mary learned of a college in Iowa for students who were blind. Attending mattered more than anything to her. Laura was old enough to teach. Her pay could help with Mary's college costs. Her teaching job was twelve miles out from De Smet. The place was a small settlement. At sixteen, she said goodbye with courage. A whole semester away from home was what she dreaded. The first school week ended with a surprise. Almanzo Wilder drove up to the schoolhouse. This was Almanzo, already known for helping De Smet survive. A beautiful sleigh, pulled by horses, carried him.

7Weekend rides home were his offer. Long drives over the prairie turned friendship into love. One night he asked Laura to marry him. Her answer was yes. She called him Manly. His homestead, outside De Smet, became their home. A daughter, Rose, soon arrived. Bad luck then hit in a string. Hail destroyed the wheat. A dangerous infection struck both Laura and Manly. Laura got fully well. Manly's limp lasted the rest of his life. A baby boy was born. He lived only two weeks. Fire then burned the house to the ground. Laura was still a settler. She looked for a place to begin again. She found it before long. A photo from 1885 shows her beside Almanzo Wilder. The picture was made soon after the wedding. Before the twentieth century, vaccines were few. Medicines that worked were very few. Disease was common, and it was serious. Illness touched many people in Laura's family. For that time, this was not unusual. Laura later wrote that life's sweet, simple things are the true ones. A visitor once handed her a gleaming red apple. It had come from the Ozark Mountains. At twenty-seven, she set out again by covered wagon. East was the new direction. She was heading for the country that grew that apple.

8Near Mansfield, Missouri, she and Manly bought a plain farm. The Ozark foothills were the setting. The ground was rough. It was wooded. It was rocky. Laura knew at once it was home. Years went into chopping trees. Rocks had to be hauled for years. Plowing took years. Building took years. Planting took years. Rocky Ridge became a beautiful farm, and a prosperous one. After a life of moving, she was content. Rose had inherited Pa's restless spirit. She was intelligent. She was ambitious. San Francisco was where she moved. Journalism there earned her respect. One summer, Laura visited her grown daughter in California. Letters to Manly described towering redwoods. They described a glittering city. They described the Pacific Ocean in thunder. Rose earned her living by writing. Writing was what Laura had always loved. Farm life was comfortable by then. Could Laura do the same work? Back home, memories poured onto paper. Some nights she wrote until morning. Manly had built her a small desk. A whole book grew from her early years under Wisconsin's tall trees. The title has two parts. The first part is Little House. The second part is in the Big Woods. A publisher received the manuscript from Rose. At sixty-four, Laura expected little to come of it.

9The decade was the 1930s. Cars existed. Electricity existed. Radio existed. Who would care about heavy chores in a dark forest? Readers treated it as a sensation right away. Howling winter wind came alive on the page. A crackling fire came alive. Pa's fiddle, with its joyful skip, seemed to play again. Meeting wild animals felt thrilling again. A simple rag doll's joy, for a settler girl in a rough log cabin, was called up. Letters overflowed the mailbox at Rocky Ridge. Young readers begged for more. Kansas prairie years became another book. Its title is Little House on the Prairie. Walnut Grove years became a book too. Its title puts On the Banks first, and of Plum Creek after. De Smet's terrible winter became a book. The title is The Long Winter. The town's recovery became a book whose title is Little Town on the Prairie. Around 1940, a photo shows Laura Ingalls Wilder smiling. She is signing copies of her books. Fan letters were a pleasure to answer. Readings and signings were a pleasure to travel to. Coming home to Manly still made her happiest. Rocky Ridge Farm was that home. Both lived into their nineties. Laura died in 1957. The books continued. A television series followed in 1974. Stories of settler life still hold young readers.

10Her life is now part of the history of the United States. A few word meanings help. Evoked means a feeling was called up. A memory can be called up that way. A picture in the mind can be called up that way. Receded means something moved back. It pulled away from where it had been. A sensation is great excitement. It can also be a person or a thing that causes that excitement. Hardship is pain. It is loss. It can be the thing that causes either. A homestead was land from the U.S. government. Settlers who farmed it received the property, especially in the 1800s. People who move to a new place and stay are called settler-colonists. They claim ground and treat it as theirs. Income is money from work. It can come from another source too. A stroke is a fast loss of how the brain works. Blood that should reach the brain is interrupted. That interruption is the cause. A prairie is a wide flat plain. Grasses cover it. Vivid means very bright. It means strong. Prosperous means successful. It means well-off. A publisher is a person, or a company, that offers writing to the public. Print is one way. The Internet is another.

92. The Young Pharaoh's Unanswered Death

1A photo shows the British archaeologist Howard Carter at work. He is studying the golden sarcophagus while the digging goes on. He is the man who found King Tut's tomb. Coming pages tell how Tut was found. They describe his homeland. They describe his family. They describe the boy who ruled. They describe a dynasty's end. They describe the tomb. They name suspects. They study the body. They ask whether the mystery is solved. Useful words come last. The year of the find was 1922. Say archaeologist as AR-kee-OLL-oh-jist. The king was Tutankhamun, said toot-an-KAH-muhn. Most people call him King Tut. More than 3,300 years separate his reign from the present. Pharaoh, said FAIR-oh, was his title, and he received it at age nine. The reign lasted almost ten years. Then death came suddenly. Opening the coffin started a long question. How did this young king die? An archaeologist works by looking at evidence. Questions come with that evidence. Where was Tut's home? Who were his family and his friends? Did enemies surround him? Those answers may unlock a harder question. Why did death come to King Tut while he was still so young? A picture imagines his living face. The funeral mask sits behind him. For thousands of years, ruling families governed ancient Egypt. Dynasty is the word for one of those families. Historians sort the dynasties into three large periods. The three periods are known as the Old Kingdom, then the Middle Kingdom, then the New Kingdom. Membership in the 18th Dynasty belonged to King Tutankhamun.

2That dynasty was the first of the New Kingdom. The New Kingdom opened around 1550 bce. Belief in the gods was a major part of life in ancient Egypt. People worshipped many gods. They worshipped many goddesses. Tut's life, and maybe his death, sits inside that religious history. A reader has to know the history to follow him. A map shows ancient Egypt. At the start of the New Kingdom, two gods stood among the most important. One was Ra, said RAH. The other was Amun, said AH-muhn. Ra was god of the Sun. Pictures often gave him a falcon's form. Amun was a god who created. Pictures usually gave him a man's body and a tall crown. Late in the New Kingdom, some Egyptians shifted their worship of the Sun. They named this god Aten, said AH-tuhn. The picture was a golden disk of the Sun. Nobles gave Aten more importance. Other gods received less worship. Religion still filled daily life, and the rules bent. For most people, Aten was simply one more god in a crowd. Their beliefs did not feel threatened. The change came with a young pharaoh. His name was Amenhotep IV, said ah-muhn-HO-tep. He was Tut's father. A caption shows Amenhotep IV. Hundreds of gods and goddesses existed. Most people still chose a small group to worship. Help with a career was one reason for the choice. Thoth watched over writing and knowledge. Seshat watched over writing and measurement. Ptah watched over people who made things by craft.

3Amenhotep IV started his reign in 1352 bce. Egyptian art gives him a long face. It gives him thin calves. It gives him a belly that protrudes. He grew up inside the newer Aten faith. He believed it fully. In his view, Aten was a god for every person in the world. He held that Aten made the world when time began. He held that Aten ruled that world alone. People have called him the world's first monotheist. A monotheist believes in a single god. About five years into the reign, official religion changed all at once. The shift was complete. Egyptians were told they could worship Aten and no other god. The pharaoh took a new name, Akhenaten, said ahk-eh-NAH-tuhn. The name means He Who Serves Aten. Temples of many older gods were shut. He tried to have those temples destroyed. People were upset, and the priests of the older gods were among them. In several regions, locals tried to halt the wrecking of their temples. The pharaoh's army was able to hold those people down. A new capital city was also his project. He shifted the capital away from Thebes. The new city's name was Akhetaten, said ahk-eh-TAH-tuhn. The name means Horizon of Aten. People today call that area Amarna. The wife he favored most was Queen Nefertiti, said neh-fer-TEE-tee. His mother died, and Nefertiti was likely stepmother to the young prince. The prince was Tutankhaten, later called Tutankhamun. Nefertiti's death came in her early thirties.

4Birth came to King Tut in that new capital. The year was about 1345 bce. His name was Tutankhaten. The name means the Living Image of Aten. Not long ago, researchers used genetic tests on mummies. They were looking for his parents and his grandparents. DNA came from bones. One mummy may be Akhenaten, and that mummy may be the father. The result included a chart of the boy king's relatives. His mother was a sister of Akhenaten. Which sister is not clear. Seventeen years was the length of Akhenaten's rule. Two rulers filled the three or four years that followed. After those rulers, Egypt's throne sat empty again. Tutankhaten, age nine, became pharaoh. A temple at Amarna supplied a carving of a family group. Akhenaten is there. Nefertiti is there, and she may be Tut's stepmother. Three of their children are there. Wealth shaped Tut's life. He wore jewelry. He wore clothing of linen. He wore oils that were perfumed. He wore makeup. His tomb held all of those things. A pharaoh was expected to hunt. Members of the royal court hunted with him. A bow was the usual weapon. A chariot was the usual seat. Chariots went into the tomb. Bows went into it. Board games went into it. The afterlife was the reason. He married his half-sister. At least two daughters were born. Neither daughter lived. The court included several servants. One attendant who stayed near him had served the family for a long time. Service began when Tut's grandfather was king.

5Other servants handled even the smallest tasks. Some of those servants were younger than the king. A cupbearer was one of them. Filling drinking cups was the job. The young king's cup came first. A caption names him King Tutankhaten. Youth left the military work to other people. Political work of the court went to other people too. Two men were deeply involved. Ay was the chief advisor. Horemheb, said HOR-ehm-heb, led the army. Both had served Akhenaten. Both strongly disliked the religious reforms Akhenaten had made. They wanted the old ways of worship brought back. Ending Aten's worship was the change they urged on King Tut. Amun, they said, should be chief god again. Tut did restore him. The king also took a new name, Tutankhamun. Living Image of Amun is what that name means. Historians know who pushed the changes during this reign. Ay and Horemheb did the pushing. Youth meant the king followed orders. Back to Thebes went the royal court. Amarna, a city given to Aten, was abandoned. It was left to rot under the Egyptian sun. Death came to King Tut in 1327 bce. His age was about nineteen. No official record says how he died. Workers mummified the young pharaoh. Burial was in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Near Thebes, this valley was a cemetery for royalty, and it was large. No child of Tut was alive. Egypt still needed a king. Ay took the throne. Long experience in the court was the reason.

6He also married the woman Tut had left as a widow. Ay's own rule lasted just four years. He died in 1323 bce. Horemheb became pharaoh next. Pharaohs carried more than one name. Birth gave them one name. Becoming pharaoh brought further names. Those names often sat inside an oval. The oval is a cartouche, said car-TOOSH. A photo shows archaeologists digging in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Horemheb sent men to destroy the temples of Aten. Statues of Akhenaten were smashed. Statues of his family were smashed. Statues of King Tut were smashed too. Later, workers pulled stone blocks out of the city's buildings. Wall art covered those blocks. The blocks were reused in building projects at Hermopolis. The Nile separates Hermopolis from Amarna, with Hermopolis on the far bank. What remained of Akhenaten's capital had been splendid. It was shattered, then covered by drifting sand. People forgot it. Horemheb's rule lasted twenty-seven years. He died in 1295 bce. His death ended the 18th Dynasty. In the 1800s, many archaeologists from Britain and from Europe traveled to Egypt. They came to study Egyptian writing. The writing is called hieroglyphics, said hy-ur-uh-GLIFiks. Walls carried it. Monuments carried it. The writing revealed a great deal about how pharaohs lived and what customs they kept. Archaeologists learned what a pharaoh's tomb was meant to hold. Whatever that person would need after death was supposed to be inside. Profit drew some diggers. They opened many tombs. Disappointment always followed. Robbers had arrived first. The Rosetta Stone has a story of its own.

7Napoleon's army arrived in 1798 with orders to seize Egypt. One soldier found a flat black rock. Three languages were carved on its face. Two were forms of ancient Egyptian. The third was Greek. Scholars spent the next twenty-five years translating the other languages. The Greek text was one key. Coptic, a later Egyptian language, supplied the other key. A breakthrough came from one scholar. He realized the old writing used symbols for sounds. The symbols did not stand for whole words. Discovery of the Rosetta Stone remains among the most critical finds in archaeology. By the early 1900s, archaeologists had settled on a belief. No tomb in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, they thought, was still unknown. Carter's search for Tut went on for more than five years. Luck did not come. In 1922 he asked for one more season of pay. The man funding the search agreed. Later that same year, Carter reached a tomb that was almost intact. Artifacts were plentiful. Thrones were there. Jewelry was there. Weapons were there. Statues were there. A large mask of gold covered the mummy. Three coffins nested around the body. The coffin farthest inside was gold. The gold weighed about 242 pounds (110 kg). The find caused a sensation. History's most famous pharaoh became Tut. Foreign archaeologists worked under Egyptian rules. An intact tomb meant every artifact had to remain in Egypt. Carter disputed the government's view. Intact, he claimed, was the wrong word for this tomb.

8England was where he hoped to send half the treasure. Not a single object left Egypt. The funeral mask of gold stayed. The jewelry stayed. The statues stayed. Today the Egyptian government partners with researchers from other countries. Artifacts from the tomb are allowed to travel on tour. Egyptians still make the final decision about this treasure. Dying young was common in ancient times. In ancient Egypt, a typical life ran about thirty years. Many people never reached that age. Even so, some historians suspect murder. Ay guided many of Tut's decisions. Horemheb guided many of them too. Both men became pharaohs after Tut died. No natural heir stood ready for the throne. Seizing power had a deadline. It had to happen before a child of Tut survived. It had to happen before Tut himself became an adult. Researchers have named two servants as possible killers. One is the cupbearer. The other is the personal attendant. Few people could enter the king's bedroom. Killing the pharaoh was within either man's reach. Tut's tomb includes a wall painting that shows Ay. For years, a blow to the head was the leading idea. People thought that blow killed Tut. X-ray studies of the mummy supported the idea. One study was in 1968. Another was in 1978. The images showed damage in the skull. Experts called the damage strong proof. A heavy object, they said, had hit the back of the head. In 2005, a team in Cairo, Egypt, set out to test that claim.

9Dr. Zahi Hawass led the group. He is a top archaeologist in Egypt. The tool was an advanced X-ray method. It is called CT scanning, also called CAT scanning. A CT scanner shoots many X-rays. The angles differ. A computer turns that information into pictures. The pictures show much more detail than a regular X-ray machine. A photo shows Dr. Zahi Hawass beside Tut. The mummy has not yet entered the scanner. Hawass reported that the skull was damaged after death. Mummification was the likely moment. The scans also showed several problems in the body. A cleft palate was one. A club foot was another. A further clue concerned the cause of death. Shortly before he died, a leg had broken. The break had not healed properly. Hawass said an infection may have followed the injury. Death may have followed within a few days. Between 2007 and 2010, Hawass and fellow researchers studied the remains once more. Genetic tests were the method. Two important conditions appeared that had not been seen before. One was repeated attacks of severe malaria. Malaria by itself probably would not have killed Tut. Great weakness may have followed. The other was bone deterioration in the left foot. Both parents may have passed the condition down. The parents were siblings. That family link may have made the harm worse. Scientists have also shown the face of King Tut's mummy. A question remains. Did the young king die from several troubles stacked together? Physical problems could be part of it.

10An accident could be part of it. A disease could be part of it. Infection from a broken leg could be part of it. Something else could be the cause instead. Some people on Hawass's team offered another reading of the leg. Embalming, some of them said, might be when the leg broke. Carter's team draws blame from other experts. They say the break came when the mummy was lifted from its inner coffin. That lifting happened years ago. Newer science and DNA evidence make theories easier to prove. Experts can still read the same evidence in different ways. What is your reading? A photo shows Carter's team taking artifacts out of the tomb. An archaeologist is a scientist who studies what ancient cultures left behind. Genetic describes heredity. It also describes variation in living things. Hieroglyphics is a writing system of pictures or symbols. Those marks can stand for words, for syllables, or for sounds. Ancient Egyptians used it. Other peoples used it too. It is not an alphabet of letters. An artifact is any object humans made or used long ago. Depicted means represented. It can mean portrayed. Deterioration is the process of growing worse as time passes. A monotheist believes there is only one god. Dynasties are ruling lines that stay inside one family in a country. Mummified means made into a mummy. A pharaoh is a ruler of ancient Egypt. Embalmed means a dead body was treated so decay would stay away. Protruding means sticking out.

93. Tiny Germs: Help or Harm?

1A sneeze can push air from the mouth at 120 kph, which is 75 mph. The parts of this book come in this order. An opening comes first. A part asks what microbes are. A part explains the immune system. A part names four groups of microbes. Bacteria have a part of their own. Viruses have a part of their own. Fungi have a part of their own. Protozoa have a part of their own. A part shows how infection travels. A part explains outbreaks and epidemics. A part explains vaccines. A part explains antibiotics. A closing part ends the story. A glossary lists word meanings. An index lists key words. Achoo! Illness often announces itself with a sudden sneeze. That first clue is called a symptom. A cough may come along. A tired body may come along. A throat that hurts may come along. Those clues usually mean an infection has started. A tiny germ, called a microbe, brings the infection. Someone may say a bug was caught. The words mean a microbe got inside. So what is a microbe? In early times, nobody could explain sickness. No doctors worked then. No medical schools existed then. Death often followed a sickness that seemed small. Death often followed a wound that seemed small. Death often followed an infection that seemed mild. Science had not yet studied health. Science had not yet studied disease. Some people who believed in curses blamed a witch. Some people thought a punishment had fallen on them. The real cause of any illness stayed hidden. The path an illness took from one person to another stayed hidden. Nobody knew a way to stop a disease. Nobody knew a way to treat a disease. Long study and many discoveries changed that picture. Many kinds of microbes, we now know, can make a person sick. Questions are still worth asking. What counts as a microbe? In what places do microbes live? Does every microbe do harm? Can facts about microbes help a person stay well? Can those facts help stop disease before it starts? Leeches were once a doctor's tool for treating sickness. A microbe is a living organism, tiny enough to be almost invisible. Seeing one takes a microscope with strong power. Such organisms surround people on every side. They travel in the air that fills the lungs. They stick to each surface a hand meets. Skin carries them. Shoes carry them. Bodies hide them on the inside.

2Microbes show up in every place! Once inside a body, they increase their numbers fast. The increase happens inside cells. Each cell is one small unit of living matter. Health depends on cells. Growth depends on cells. Cells lock together. The fit is close to the way puzzle pieces lock. Blood is built from cells. Bone is built from cells. The stomach is built from cells. Skin is built from cells. Muscle is built from cells. The number of cells inside one person reaches the trillions. Every cell has a job that matters. Those jobs guard health. Microbes that push in where they are not wanted can block a cell's work. Disease can follow some of those invasions. The flu virus is one kind of microbe. Strep bacteria are another kind. Ophryoscolex protozoa are another kind. Yeast fungus is another kind. Louis Pasteur (pass-TUR) earned modern medicine's deep thanks. The Germ Theory of Disease was proved by him. Harmful microbes, that theory says, cause disease when contact happens. Heat was the tool in his greatest find. Food went into a canister that was sealed. He raised the heat to one chosen temperature. He held that heat for one chosen length of time. Many organisms inside died from the heat. Pasteurization is the name of this heating. Fresh milk goes through pasteurization now. Canned food goes through it too. Try this math minute. Milk can reach 145 degrees Fahrenheit, or 62.8°C, and stay there for 30 minutes. Milk can instead reach 163 degrees Fahrenheit, or 72.8°C, and stay there for 15 seconds. The hotter way finishes sooner. By how many seconds? Harmful microbes meet a body system built to block them. That system is the immune system. Its parts each matter alone. Together the parts make one defense. The defense is a team. Cells of many types belong to it. Glands belong to it. Tissues belong to it. Body structure is formed by all of them working as one. Try this math minute. Every 20 minutes, some microbes can double how many there are. Begin with a single microbe. After 4 hours, what number will you have? A hint: at 0 minutes, the count is still 1. Memory gives this system its strongest weapon. It already knows the microbes it must seek. Problem-causers are the ones it picks out. It recalls which defense worked in the last attack. Then the fight begins again. A childhood case of mumps leaves a memory in the system.

3A childhood case of measles leaves a memory too. Mumps rarely returns for a second illness. Measles rarely returns for a second illness. One drop of blood holds white cells in a count from 7,000 up to 25,000. Invading microbes are attacked by those cells, and the attacks differ. Antibodies come from some of those white cells. The chemicals of a microbe are the target. Those chemicals are neutralized. Other white cells close in around the microbe. Destruction follows. How, then, are troublemakers kept out? Skin on the outside is a shield. The shield wraps the whole body. A cut needs cleaning. A scrape needs cleaning. Disinfect the opening. Cover it with a bandage. A microbe then has a harder time entering and starting an infection. Under the skin, white cells hunt microbes. Blood vessels are their roads. Each day they locate millions of harmful invaders. Each day they destroy those invaders. White cells stand as the natural foe of microbes that cause disease. Microbes fall into four groups. One group is bacteria (back-TEER-ee-uh). Bacteria cover every place and every thing. They are hard to kill. Barren ice is a home some of them can thrive in. Extreme heat is a home others can thrive in. Good bacteria exist, just as good microbes of other kinds exist. Harmful bacteria exist too. No other organisms on Earth come in more types. Count the population, and bacteria rule! Here is a fun fact about food. Yogurt gets help from several kinds of bacteria that change milk. Sour cream gets that same help. Lactose is what these bacteria eat. Milk sugars are what lactose means. Lactic acid is what they release. Milk curdles because of that acid. The milk turns more solid. Yogurt tastes tangy and sour because of the acid. Sour cream tastes that way too. Intestines hold one helpful kind of bacteria. Food is broken down with their help. Digestion uses their help. Life without them would not work. A painful throat can come from nasty strep bacteria. A fever can come from them. A headache can come from them. An upset stomach can come from them. Neck glands can grow tender and swollen because of them. Pus shows up as white spots at the back of the throat. When study is the goal, scientists may choose to raise bacteria themselves. A picture can show strep bacteria in a dish. A gel fills the dish. Food comes from the gel.

4A safe setting comes from the gel. Very bad sickness can also come from food poisoning. The usual cause is harmful bacteria. Uncooked foods carry those bacteria on the outside. Uncooked foods carry them on the inside too. The right cooking heat kills them. Surfaces used for making food each day carry other bacteria. Hands carry bacteria too. An upset stomach is a common result of food poisoning. Vomiting is a common result. Diarrhea is a common result. Many food-poisoning cases trace back to bacteria called salmonella. Viruses (VY-russ-es) do not leave the body easily. Human cells are a place a virus will enter. Cells of other animals are a place it will enter too. Cell after cell gets the virus in a quick spread. Infection is the result. Sickness in people is a result of viruses. Death is a result some viruses can bring. A careful immune system may still miss a virus. Mutate is a skill a virus has. To mutate is to change what it seems to be. The change lets it pass unnoticed. Finding the virus grows harder. Stopping the virus grows harder. Flu comes from a virus. Chicken pox comes from a virus. HIV comes from a virus. A common cold comes from a virus. An influenza virus can be pictured at a magnification of 295,000x. Health is another goal some scientists hope viruses might serve. Control passes to the virus once it is inside a cell. The cell is told what to do. Picture a cell whose multiplying will not stop. A scientist might send in a virus with a different order. The order would be to slow that growth. Cancer is the disease this idea might fight, and study of it continues. In cancer, cell growth runs out of control. A chart can separate a common cold from the flu. Headaches stay away in a cold. Headaches show up in the flu. Fever stays away in a cold, or stays mild. Flu fever climbs high, from 102 to 104˚F, and lasts for days. Muscle aches and tiredness show up only sometimes in a cold. They show up with the flu. A sore throat shows up with a cold. It shows up only sometimes with the flu. A runny nose shows up with a cold. It shows up only sometimes with the flu. Sneezing shows up with a cold. It shows up only sometimes with the flu. Coughing shows up with a cold.

5Coughing shows up with the flu. Chills stay away in a cold. Chills show up with the flu. Fungi (FUN-guy) include a wide mix of types. Mushrooms are fungi that look like plants. Body invasion can come from harmful fungi too small to see. The infections they cause are common. The infections irritate. Ringworm is one infection of this kind. Athlete's foot is another. Skin can show an itchy red ring from ringworm. The ring looks a bit like a worm. Feet get attacked on the bottom by athlete's foot fungi. The space between the toes gets attacked too. Itching follows in the sore skin. Cracking follows. Peeling follows. Protozoa (pro-toe-ZOE-uh) are simple living things. One cell is all each protozoan has. Streams are a common home. Ponds are a common home. Dirty water is a common home. Drinking water calls for care. Nausea can follow if protozoa enter the body. Vomiting can follow. Mouth infections can follow. Malaria can move from person to person by mosquito. West Nile virus can move that way too. One serious protozoa illness travels in saliva. The saliva is from a bite. The mosquito that bites is already infected. Blood receives the protozoa through that bite. Malaria is the disease that follows. Hot tropical climates are where malaria shows up most. High fever is one result. Weakness is another result. Delirium is another result. Hundreds of thousands of deaths each year come from this infection. Think of a packed place. A person nearby may sneeze. A person nearby may cough. Germs are leaving that person, and you know it. Home is where you wish that person had stayed. Contact with someone infected, meaning sick, spreads most diseases. Body fluids hold many of the microbes that cause infection. Saliva is one fluid. Blood is one fluid. Nasal mucus is one fluid. Passing an infection from person to person is easier because of those fluids. Air can carry germs from a cough. An object can carry germs too, if you handle it. A sick person may have touched it and left it contaminated. An insect may catch a harmful microbe first. Another animal may catch it first. A human can receive that infection next. Rabies can come from mammals that are infected. Dogs are one example. Raccoons are one example. Skunks are one example. Chickens may carry salmonella. Birds may carry it. Fish may carry it. Reptiles may carry it. West Nile virus is another gift infected mosquitoes can give, along with malaria.

6Avian flu of a serious kind can move from sick birds. Lyme disease follows the bite of a tick that is infected. A tissue is a help in keeping germs from traveling. Speed is on the side of spreading disease. Dozens of people can catch an illness from one sick person. Hundreds more can catch it from those dozens. The sick person may not know about the illness yet. Even so, others can already be infected. A healthy carrier is a name sometimes used for this person. No signs of disease show. Infection of others still happens. Finding such a person is hard. Isolating such a person is hard. Treating such a person is hard. An outbreak is a shared disease in a small group in one place. An epidemic means the outbreak has raced onward and reached many people. A pandemic is that epidemic racing out to big groups across the world. One town is no longer the expected limit of a local outbreak. Hitchhikers are a fair picture of microbes that carry disease. People's trips become the microbes' trips. Quick travel comes from buses. Quick travel comes from airplanes. Quick travel comes from other modern ways of moving. Any person met on the trip can catch the illness from a sick traveler. A new outbreak can then start in a different place. Shots are unpopular. Shots still matter. Planning ahead is what a vaccine does, so a disease can be blocked. The immune system is what a vaccine trains. Recognition of a harmful microbe is part of the training. Fighting that microbe off is the other part. Tiny weakened bits are the stuff of many strong vaccines. The bits may come from the virus itself. The bits may come from the bacteria itself. Smallpox microbes reached the Americas with Europeans. Smallpox microbes reached the Americas with Africans. Exposure to that disease had never happened for any Native American. Immunity was missing. Millions died from smallpox because of that gap. Nine out of ten people died in the largest Native cities of South America. The same share died in Central America. About two hundred years back, a new thought appeared in England. A virus might be used to block a disease. A mild disease might be used to block a worse one. Farm workers were among the patients of Dr. Edward Jenner. Cowpox, a mild pox, was what many of them caught. Deadly smallpox, in severe form, was also what he treated.

7A pattern became clear to Dr. Jenner as time passed. Cowpox in the past meant smallpox never arrived later. Why? Deadliness puts smallpox among the worst diseases on Earth. It spreads with ease. Many thousands of people died in smallpox epidemics. Related diseases: that is what Dr. Jenner decided cowpox and smallpox must be. Cousins in one family is a fair picture of the link. Natural immunity, he grew sure, could come from having cowpox. Smallpox would then be less able to take hold. His plan was to give the weaker disease on purpose. The gift would come before any meeting with smallpox. Fewer deaths from smallpox might follow. A test required healthy people willing to volunteer. Cowpox sickness was what they would accept. Waiting would show the result. Help came, amazingly, from real volunteers. Mild sickness followed for a while in the people who received cowpox. Quick recovery followed. During the sickness, the pox microbe became known to their immune systems. A way to fight it was built. A picture can set cowpox beside smallpox. Mouth is one way to give a vaccine. A nasal spray is another way. An injection is another way. The link Jenner proposed between the two diseases turned out to be right. Cowpox virus was given in his test as a guard ahead of time. Deadly smallpox did not arrive later for those people. A weak form of a disease was used to block a stronger, similar form. Thousands of lives were saved by that choice. Credit for stopping smallpox around the world goes to Dr. Jenner. About seventy-five years after his remarkable test, Louis Pasteur took the next step. Weakening microbes was something he learned to do. Putting those weakened microbes into the immune system was something he learned too. Learning could happen, as it had in the cowpox test. A defense would be waiting if the real disease struck. Several vaccines for prevention grew from Pasteur's tests with weakened microbes. The flu shot is one example. Large groups of people could receive those vaccines. Fighting is natural for some microbes. Other kinds of microbes are the ones they fight. Killing can be the result. Healthy cells stay unharmed. Helpful microbes stay unharmed too. Strong medicines are a natural product of these special killer microbes. Antibiotics is the name of those medicines. Only the infection that was targeted gets the attack. Strength is a mark of antibiotics.

8Worry followed a later discovery. Survival after antibiotic treatment sometimes belonged to the very strongest microbes. Failure of an antibiotic has several causes, research showed. A small identity change can let a tough microbe hide from the drug. Overuse is another cause. Misuse is another cause. Resistance can then grow in the microbes. Fighting back is something the microbe has learned. Research on microbes continues. Research on antibiotics continues. New antibiotics are a goal. Different antibiotics are a goal. More effective antibiotics are a goal. Stronger and deadlier microbes are what those drugs must face. The year 1928 brought a find by Dr. Alexander Fleming. Bacteria died because of a common mold from bread. The first antibiotic in the world grew from that find. Penicillin is its name. Wide use still belongs to penicillin more than to any other antibiotic. Travel appeals to microbes. Crowds appeal to them. Home is the right place when you are sick. Other people should be kept at a distance. Rest matters. Harmful microbes meet a stronger body when you stay home and rest. Other people stay safer from your infection too. A cold calls for a tissue over the mouth and the nose during a sneeze. A cough calls for the same cover. The tissue then belongs in a trash can. No tissue nearby means a cough into the side of the arm. Cupped hands can cover the nose and the mouth instead. Hand washing should follow as soon as it can. Food should not be shared during sickness. Cups should not be shared. Plates should not be shared. Crowded places let germs, meaning harmful microbes, move with ease. A strong immune system is required if you want to stay well. Nutritious foods in a balanced diet are part of that strength. Fruits belong in the diet. Vegetables belong in the diet. Water should be drunk in large amounts. Fresh air helps. Exercise helps. Enough sleep each night helps. Knives need water and soap after raw meat is cut. Cutting boards need the same wash. Cooked food must never touch raw meat. A dented can is not food to eat. A swollen can is not food to eat. Food from the floor is not food to eat. Soap and water, used to stay clean, fight microbes better than any other daily act. Touch passes along eighty percent of diseases. Unwashed hands are the reason for much of that spread. Hand washing by everyone could shrink how far disease travels.

9The bathroom is one time to wash. Touching an animal is another time. Making food is a time to wash, both before and after. Eating is a time to wash, both before and after. Twenty seconds is the least time for the soap. Humming Happy Birthday twice takes about that long. Lather should cover the whole hand. Fingernails need lather underneath. A rinse comes next. A clean towel should dry the hands. Brushing clears bits of food from teeth. Flossing clears them too. Cavities come from bacteria in the mouth. Rotting food is what those bacteria feed on. The mouth is an easy door for infection into the bloodstream. A well person needs a doctor visit one time each year. Problems can be stopped early by a regular checkup. Every shot you need should be received. Wild animals should not be touched outdoors. A bite is possible. A scratch is possible. Bugs that carry disease may ride on the animal. Camping calls for insect repellent. Hiking calls for it too. Mosquitoes are kept away. Ticks are kept away. Water must be purified before you drink it. Water must be chlorinated before you drink it. Almost every thing has microbes in it, on it, or around it. Harm is absent from most microbes. Disease can still come from some of them. Speed is possible once a disease starts to spread. Vaccines are one tool for blocking disease. Antibiotics are another tool. More than two hundred years of work produced those tools. Scientific discovery was part of the work. Medical research was part of the work. Modern medical practice was part of the work. Countries join their efforts. Organizations join their efforts. Single doctors join their efforts. Control of many diseases is the aim. Erasing many diseases, to eradicate them, is also the aim. Total removal of every harmful microbe will never happen, even with all this work. Infection's causes can still be learned. Control can still be helped. Healthier living can still be learned. Glossary An antibiotic is a medicine that comes from microbes and fights infection in the body. A cell is the smallest unit able to work on its own inside an organism. Contaminated describes something made unsafe, or made no longer fit to use. A disease is a body condition that alters normal function. An epidemic is disease moving fast through a community. Eradicate means to wipe something out completely. The immune system carries antibodies through the body in the fight against infection.

10An infection is sickness that starts when microbes move in. Invading describes an aggressive entry meant to conquer, weaken, or injure. A microbe is an organism seen only with special tools, often one that passes disease along. A microscope is a tool for looking at objects that are tiny. Mutate means to change in a lasting way. An organism is a living thing, whether a person, another animal, a plant, or a microbe. An outbreak is disease that spreads in a quick burst. A pandemic is disease that spreads fast across the whole world. Resistance is being able to push back against something. A symptom is a sign that points to illness. A vaccine is medicine built from a disease that is weak or dead, so the body can learn to fight stronger forms of that same disease. A virus is an organism too small to see that infects the body, and the word also names the sickness that follows. Index West Nile virus is tied to number 13. Viruses, and the shorter word virus, are tied to numbers 5, 11 through 14, and 16 through 18. Vaccines, and the shorter word vaccine, are tied to numbers 16 and 18. Strep throat is tied to number 10. Smallpox is tied to numbers 16 through 18. Protozoa, and the word protozoan, are tied to numbers 5 and 13. Penicillin is tied to number 19. Pasteurization is tied to number 6. Louis Pasteur is tied to numbers 6 and 18. Microbes, and the shorter word microbe, are tied to numbers 4 through 9, plus 13, 14, 16, 18, 19, and 22. Malaria is tied to number 13. Edward Jenner is tied to numbers 17 and 18. Infections, and the shorter word infection, are tied to numbers 8, 11 through 15, and 18 through 20. The immune system is tied to numbers 7, 8, 16, and 18. The germ theory of disease is tied to number 6. Fungi are tied to number 13. Alexander Fleming is tied to number 19. Epidemics, and the shorter word epidemic, are tied to numbers 15 and 16. Cowpox is tied to numbers 16 through 18. Chicken pox is tied to number 11. Bacteria are tied to 5, then to 9, then to 10. Also to 14. Also to 16. Also to 19. Also to 21. Antibiotics, and the shorter word antibiotic, are tied to number 19.

94. Traits Passed from Generation to Generation

1A picture shows members of one family. They look alike because inherited traits are shared among them. The book opens with an introduction. Farming comes next. Breeding animals comes after that. Animals that live in zoos come next. Solving crimes follows. Health follows that. A conclusion closes the main text. Useful words are gathered at the end. Many young people ask what work they will want. Being a doctor is one idea. Being a detective is another. Working among animals is another. Genetics is the one thing these jobs share. Genetics is a science field. It studies the way living things hand traits forward. The handoff runs onward, parent group to child group. A trait is a feature of a living thing. Color of hair is a trait. Length of a finger is a trait. Shape of a nose is a trait. Knowing genetics matters in a lot of work. Farming is one kind of that work. Breeding animals is another kind. Curing diseases is another kind. Stopping illnesses before they start is another kind. Solving crimes is another kind. Genetics counts as a new science. Even so, people were already using genetic techniques very early. The early date is 5000 BC. The aim was better crops. The aim was also better animals. Selective breeding is one of those techniques. Scientists pick plants that carry traits they want.

2Quick growth is one such trait. Fruit that looks attractive is another. Those plants are then bred with other plants that carry the same traits. Selective breeding makes sure the wanted traits move to the next plants. The crops that result grow faster. They also make better fruit. A supermarket can offer many kinds of tomatoes. Selective breeding of tomato plants produced those kinds. Wheat is another common crop raised with genetic techniques. Soybeans are another. Corn is another. Genetics will let farmers raise plants with more protein. It will also let them raise plants with less oil. A picture shows many tomato varieties. All of them were bred out of one wild variety. Scientists use genetic techniques on animals as well. One result is chickens that lay a greater number of eggs. Another result is cows that grow faster. Those cows also give more milk. Farming gains from genetics can sound wonderful. Faster crops that also taste better seem easy to want. More milk from cows seems easy to want too. Some people answer with a warning. They say genetic changes to crops and animals will harm genetic diversity. Breeding for only a chosen set of traits has a cost. Many other useful traits of plants and animals may vanish for good. A thin range of genes can also leave crops and animals open to danger.

3One virus might then wipe out a whole species. A picture shows piglets from selective breeding. They grow up faster than wild piglets that are their cousins. Supporters of genetics in farming want food production improved. Opponents worry about effects nobody can yet predict. Those effects might touch the environment. They might touch human health. People who breed animals use some genetic techniques that plant scientists use. Selective breeding is one shared technique. Hybridization is another. Crossbreeding is another name for hybridization. It means breeding different varieties. It can even mean breeding different species. The goal is to join the best characteristics of both parents. A female horse can be bred with a male donkey. The offspring is a mule. A mule is a hybrid. Horses are one parent type. Donkeys are the other. A mule is tough in the way a donkey is tough. A mule is agile in the way a horse is agile. Mules make very good animals for work. A picture places a donkey at the top. A horse is on the left. A mule is on the right. Plenty of dog breeders raise dogs only so the dogs can be shown. Other breeds are shaped for a set purpose. Hunting is one purpose. Herding is another. Guarding is another.

4Spaniels were among the earliest dogs used for hunting. Spain is where springer spaniels were bred at the start. Cocker spaniels began there as well. The prey included water birds such as ducks. It also included land birds such as pheasants. A breeder first decides which traits a dog should have. Parents are then chosen so those traits will pass to the offspring. A picture shows border collies. They are excellent at herding. Herding is another trait people choose to breed into certain dogs. Herding dogs guard cattle. They also round the cattle up. They do the same with other livestock. Border collies are popular herding dogs. People also like Australian shepherds for herding work. The breeding has been so successful that herding continues without lessons. Owners of border collies often report a funny habit. The dogs try to herd cars. They try to herd people as well. The border collie breed took shape hundreds of years ago. Its first job was herding cattle and sheep. England and Scotland meet at a border, and that border was the workplace. The Australian shepherd came from several herding breeds. The border collie was one of those breeds. English settlers carried border collies with them to Australia. Shepherds of this type are still used widely in Australia. Australia keeps its cattle on fields that are open.

5Its other livestock live on open fields as well. Some dogs are bred to guard. The Doberman pinscher is one common guard dog. The German shepherd is another. Louis Dobermann, a watchman in Germany, was the first to breed the Doberman. The time was the late 1890s. The breed gained a reputation for danger. Breeders in later years worked hard on a different temperament. They wanted the Doberman calmer. They wanted it friendlier. Many dogs are hybrids. A hybrid here is a cross of two breeds or more. Some people think hybrids make the best pets. Their reason is that each parent can pass a strong quality into the same pup. A picture shows mutts. A mutt can gather strong qualities from a wide mix of breeds. Another picture shows giant pandas. Captive-breeding programs have helped them. Zoos do research on animals. Zoos also teach people. Zoos also entertain people. Genetics is part of the research at some zoos. The research aims at a future in which animal species still survive well. Genetics matters a great deal in protection. Many species that are endangered receive that protection. Many species that are threatened receive it too. Zoo scientists have a technique for raising the numbers of endangered species. The technique is called captive breeding. It means breeding animals that live in captivity.

6A zoo is one kind of captivity. The purpose is to keep genetic diversity inside a species. Some young born in captivity are later set free among wild animals. Those young bring different genes into the wild group. The wild animals then have a better chance to survive. This kind of captive breeding works only under one condition. After release, the animals must live on their own. They must also produce young on their own. Captive breeding is in use for certain species that are endangered. It is in use for certain species that are threatened. The red wolf is one. The gorilla is one. The giant panda is one. The cheetah is one. The rhinoceros is one. A second kind of captive breeding serves species that are nearly extinct. Those species cannot live in the wild. A protected place gives them a chance to produce young. Captive breeding matters. It still cannot take the place of animals that live and breed in the wild. Zoo workers also try to teach the public. They teach why habitats of endangered species must be protected. They teach the same lesson for threatened species. Rhinoceroses need that protection. Tigers need it too. Without it, later generations of people would meet those animals only in books. Crime work has changed as well. A magnifying glass is no longer the only tool.

7Police now use genetics. Detectives use it. Lawyers use it. DNA is part of that work. Every gene holds DNA. DNA carries a code. The code sets an organism's genetic traits. Fingerprints differ from person to person. DNA differs in that same way. Every organism has DNA of its own. A picture reminds us that detectives now hold more clues than before. Police take fingerprints from criminals. Those prints go into a database. A print found where a crime happened can be compared with prints already stored. DNA is unique, as a fingerprint is unique. Using DNA to solve crimes is therefore called DNA fingerprinting. One advantage is large. A fingerprint does not have to be found. A DNA fingerprint can come from a tiny bit of skin. It can come from one hair. It can come from a drop of fluid. Blood is one such fluid. Saliva is another. A criminal can hardly avoid leaving some trace. The trace may be skin, hair, or fluid. A person leaves microscopic traces of DNA in every place he or she goes. Picture an investigation that finds skin cells. The cells are under a victim's fingernails. Investigators can read the DNA in those cells. They can also take a DNA sample from a suspect. A match between the two samples moves the case forward.

8The case then moves nearer to an answer. A picture shows a lab agent at work on DNA evidence. Agencies that enforce the law are building DNA databases. The collections resemble files of fingerprints. DNA fingerprints of people convicted of crimes sit in those databases. Other evidence from crime scenes is stored there too. DNA has also freed people. Those people had been convicted of crimes they did not commit. Many crimes have been cleared with help from DNA fingerprinting. The first use was in 1985. Some people still worry. Contamination might hurt the accuracy of a DNA test. Misuse of the tests is another worry. Even with those worries, the method is likely to stay. It will stay while it helps name criminals. It will stay while it helps solve crimes. Health workers use genetics too. Medical scientists use it. Health-care scientists use it. Genetics helps them diagnose diseases. It helps them treat diseases. It helps them prevent diseases. It also helps them develop new medicines. Many genes that cause particular diseases are now being found. Finding the gene behind a disease helps scientists build medicines. It helps them build vaccines. The medicines and vaccines may cure the disease. They may prevent it. Genetics counselors use genetics as well. They help parents estimate odds. They help people who may become parents.

9The odds concern passing genetic disorders to children. That information helps parents choose if they will have children. They also think about care. Caring for a child with a genetic disorder is part of the decision. Some genetic disorders are fairly common as inherited conditions. Cystic fibrosis is one. Huntington's disease is one. Breast cancer is one. In 2000, scientists finished the Human Genome Project. That project is a full map. It shows where every human gene sits. The human gene count is about twenty-four thousand. The genes sit in a set order on our chromosomes. Powerful computers spent ten years on the count. They also spent those years locating every gene. Many diseases come from genes that are missing. Many come from genes that sit in the wrong place. A picture shows a scientist at a computer screen. The scientist is comparing DNA fingerprints. Genetics, as a field, offers many chances for jobs. It is an exciting branch of science. It is also a branch that is still relatively new. Fresh developments arrive almost every day. Fresh job chances arrive almost every day too. Plant breeding is tied to genetics. Animal breeding is tied to it. Medicine is tied to it. The study of crime is tied to it. Other fields are tied to it as well. A library can offer more on this science.

10So can the Internet. Captive breeding means breeding animals that already live in captivity. The young may later be released into the wild. A habitat is the natural environment of a plant or an animal. A hybrid is offspring. The parents are of two different types, breeds, or species. A characteristic is a feature. It helps identify a thing or a group of things. Hybridization is a breeding process. Two different species are bred so characteristics of both can combine. Diversity means a wide variety. Many different things make up that variety. DNA is a code. A living thing's genetic message is what it holds. The long name is deoxyribonucleic acid, and DNA is the short form. Selective breeding means chosen plants or animals are bred together. The purpose is to improve traits their offspring inherit. The purpose can also be to control those traits. Genes are the basic units of heredity. Traits move through them, from parents on to their offspring. A species is a group of living things. Members look physically similar. They can reproduce. Genetics is the science of how traits pass onward. The pass runs from parents to the young that follow. A trait is a feature or a quality. An animal, a plant, a thing, or a group can have one.

95. Two Minutes at a Soldiers' Cemetery

1Only one handwritten copy of the Gettysburg Address carries President Lincoln's signature. It is the fifth version. This book moves from a war inside families to Lincoln's role in the Civil War. His words come next. A close reading follows. Life after the battle comes after that. Hard words are explained at the end. Brothers and sisters quarrel so often that people barely notice. Now picture a real war. You fight for one side. A brother or a sister fights as your enemy. Two parts of one country fought a long war called the American Civil War. The soldier across the field was sometimes a familiar face. Men of one town chose opposite sides. Men of one family did the same. Officers had trained together in wars that came earlier. They had even fought as allies before. Close friends stood against each other for the first time. Northern states made up the Union. Southern states made up the Confederacy. Fighting raged from 1861 until 1865. The dead numbered 620,000 men. Gettysburg was among the most famous battles. Lewis Armistead had a close friend before the fighting. Eighty-seven years earlier, he said, the founders had started a new nation on this continent. Liberty was its birth. The nation was pledged to one idea. All men are created equal.
