96. Two Skeletons and a Fight Over Bones

1A map asks where the dueling dinosaurs once walked. The book tells how the bones were found. It then tells how people fought over them. It asks who the fossils belong to. Hard words are explained last. Clayton Phipps poses beside a fossil he found in Montana. In 2006, he and Mark Eatman hunted fossils on a neighbor's land. The land was in eastern Montana. Dinosaur fossils are common in that area. Eatman soon spotted a huge pelvis. It stuck out of a canyon wall. Phipps then found an enormous thighbone close by. He began to think a full skeleton might be there. Digging started. The bones belonged to a horned dinosaur that ate plants. A couple of weeks later, a surprise appeared. It was a meat eater's claw. Horned dinosaurs do not have claws. The find was clearly important. Two fossil skeletons, almost complete, had been buried as a pair. The animals had died together. A plaster cast shows the pose. One animal was a carnivore. The other was an herbivore. They lay side by side. Their tails crossed. The skeletons left the ground still locked in blocks. Rock and soil made those blocks. Matrix is the name for that material. A laboratory received the blocks. Once the matrix was cleared, fifteen teeth from the meat eater were found stuck in the plant eater.

2An attack on the plant eater was the clear reading. Cracked ribs marked the meat eater. Its skull was crushed. Those injuries suggest a kick from the plant eater. The evidence points to a mutual killing. Each animal also mattered on its own. The plant eater is about as big as an elephant. It seems to be a horned dinosaur unknown before. The meat eater is about as big as a polar bear. In many ways it resembles a small Tyrannosaurus rex. Scientists might use it to decide a question. Is this kind of dinosaur new? Or is it only a young T. rex? Most fossil finds are missing bones. These two skeletons are not. Each skeleton's bones were still joined. They were not scattered apart. Preservation is so fine that patches of skin remain. Skin almost never turns up as a fossil. Museums nationwide might be expected to rush for such rare specimens. They did not. The Montana Dueling Dinosaurs show a debate inside paleontology. A great deal of research has stalled because of it. Two questions stand at the center. Should these bones be the world's? Do they instead belong to whoever held that land?

3Who should be permitted to collect them? An artist's picture suggests how the pair may have looked. To see why scientists and museums are not scrambling to buy the fossils, begin with the finders. Mark Eatman learned fossil hunting from Clayton Phipps. Phipps works as a commercial fossil hunter. Commercial collector is another label. Independent collector is another. Garfield County is home to both men. That county, in Montana, is where the pair was found. About 1,200 people live there. They are spread over roughly 4,800 square miles. That area is 12,432 square kilometers. Ranching or farming is how most of them live. Incomes, on average, are low. Many families struggle to get by. Dinosaur bones are among the few resources the area has in plenty. Fossils fill the eastern portion of Montana. They fill the western Dakotas too. Hunters such as these two ask landowners before they search. Sale money is split with those owners. Each find pays Phipps and Eatman. For a landowner, a discovery like this pair may arrive only once in a life. The hope is money enough to feel secure. Michael Triebold founded a center for dinosaur work in the Rocky Mountains. Its name is the Dinosaur Resource Center.

4He has said that private land carries a simple rule. The person who owns the ground owns the fossils. That owner may handle them however the owner chooses. Many scientists wanted these specimens open for study. Phipps offered them to three museums. None bought them. The asking price was 15 million dollars. A museum could not pay that sum alone. A second objection was raised. Commercial hunters had done the digging. The diggers were not scientists with academic training who worked for a museum or a university. The museums feared the dig had been done poorly. Care in digging matters. Fossils can be damaged as they leave the ground unless handling is extremely careful. Details have to be written down. Position in the ground matters. The stuff around the bones matters. Nearby fossils matter too. Clues can hide in those details. Paleontologists use the clues to rebuild how an animal lived. They use them to rebuild how it died. A sloppy dig can lose precious data for good. David Trexler, a paleontologist, has put the warning in plain words. A fossil can be collected only one time. A mistake cannot be undone. Digging fossils free is slow work. A great deal of time is required. The greatest care is required.

5Done properly, the work usually leaves bones where they lie at first. Whole blocks of matrix are lifted out. Plaster jackets wrap the blocks so the trip to a lab is safe. Maps are made during the dig. Photographs are taken. Soil samples are collected. As much information as possible is saved. At the lab, preparation is careful. Matrix comes off first. Cleaning follows. Repair follows. Strengthening follows. The fossils are then made ready to store, or to show. A university student is pictured cleaning part of a fossil tree found in Germany. That tree once stood in a forest. The forest is 290 million years old. Another picture shows a paleontologist in a lab. A tool frees a fossil from surrounding rock. The book poses a hard question. Should any person be allowed to collect fossils and prepare them? Should training be limited in some way? If a limit is set, should only academic training count? Who gets to decide? Good digging skills can be learned away from colleges and universities. Some commercial hunters may match university-trained paleontologists. Some may surpass them. Even so, some paleontologists distrust reports of careful commercial digs. They suspect the reports exist mainly to push prices higher. Some scientists and some institutions refuse to buy specimens.

6Proper collection does not change their refusal. Paying for fossils, they think, invites more people into commercial hunting. David Trexler works at the Two Medicine Dinosaur Center. He repeats the warning. Collection happens once. No second chance follows a mistake. Robert Bakker, also a paleontologist, says this dig met professional standards. He says the opposition is bias. Academic paleontologists, in his view, are biased against commercial hunters. How common dinosaur fossils are is another point of debate. Some people call them scarce. In that view, only scientists with formal training should dig them up and study them. Others call them so common that most would erode away. Wind would wear them down. Water would. Other forces of nature would do the same. That erosion would follow if collection were left to only a handful of trained scientists. Burial can last beyond 160 million years. Once weather reaches the fossil, it can disappear quickly. Both sides care where a find like this pair ends up. Some academic paleontologists oppose commercial collecting because of a risk. A wealthy private collector might buy the bones. An institution that would keep them open for ongoing study might lose the chance. Science rests on a principle. Evidence should stay available for other scientists.

7With dinosaur bones, new finds need to be set beside old specimens. They also need to be set beside finds still to come. Another question is posed. Suppose you found an amazing dinosaur worth thousands of dollars, or even millions. Would you give it to a museum? Would you try to sell it? How much would the final home matter to you? Students are shown searching for fossil remains. The place is Dinosaur Provincial Park. It is in Alberta, which is in Canada. Several endings are possible. Purchase by a museum is one path. Display and research could both follow. A generous buyer might give them to a scientific institution. Someone collecting in private might permit study first and display the fossils later. A private collector might show them only in private and block study. Access refused at first is sometimes granted later. Other family members may inherit the fossil. Decades can pass. Generations can pass. Nothing guarantees that later chance. Private land held these two dinosaurs. Current law in Montana gives them to the landowners. The owners may do what they wish. Museums would not buy, so the fossils went to auction. The month was November 2013. The expected price ran from 7 million dollars to 9 million.

8No bid reached the auction house's minimum. Another question is posed. Which people should have the right of ownership? Should museums and universities be the only owners of the important ones? Should wealthy private citizens buy them for private collections? The choice of who decides is left open. A fossil called Sue is famous worldwide. She is on display in Chicago, Illinois. The Field Museum is the place. She is a Tyrannosaurus rex. She is the largest ever found. She is the best preserved. She is the most complete. In the United States, limits on fossil collecting apply only on public land. Even there, the limits apply only sometimes. Some laws control archaeological remains. Those remains are linked to humans. They are too recent to count as fossils. Rules about fossil collecting are not always clear. They are not always the same from place to place. On private land, the landowner owns what is found. Keeping the fossils is allowed. Getting rid of them is allowed. An auction to the highest bidder is allowed, no matter the buyer's plans. Other countries write different rules. Germany requires a professional paleontologist to inspect each fossil that is collected. A find that matters to science becomes government property.

9The finder receives a fee. A find that does not matter goes back to the finder. Keeping it is allowed. Selling it is allowed. Some people in this debate want the United States to copy Germany's policy. Others call that a mistake. Strict rules, they say, would cost a lot to enforce. The rules would be inconvenient. They also say a policy like Germany's would break the property rights of citizens in the United States. One fossil has helped scientists link feathered dinosaurs with birds living now. Picture a hike, and a fossil at your feet. Should it go home with you? Should the find be reported? Should it be left alone? Children are usually curious about nature. Adults are too. Picking up rocks can be fun. Picking up fossils can be fun. Other objects can be fun to pick up as well. Such objects record the planet's history. Geological cycles are part of that record. Many forms of life are part of it. A great number of those forms are extinct. The Black Hills Institute studies geological research. It reports a striking share. Important fossils have a striking finder. Amateurs account for more than four-fifths of them. This dinosaur pair will not be the last amazing discovery in a reader's lifetime.

10Many more will surely be made. Academic scientists will make some. Commercial hunters will make some. Ordinary people on nature walks will make some. What will become of those fossils? A few word meanings help. An amateur takes up an activity for enjoyment. A hobby is another way to describe it. Pay is not the reason. Excavating means uncovering something. It means digging it out. A fossil is what remains of a plant or an animal after it has turned to stone. An auction sells goods or property by letting buyers bid. The highest offer wins. Paleontology studies fossils of plants and of animals. Private means not public. It can mean not meant to be shared. Biased means unfair support for one opinion. It can mean unfair support for one group, or for one set of beliefs, over another. To regulate is to control an amount, a rate, a speed, or a behavior. The aim is that something works properly, or follows laws and rules. Commercial describes buying and selling. A debate is a discussion. The people or groups in it hold different opinions. Specimens are examples kept for comparison. Study is another use. Display is another. Dueling means a fight between two.

1Sections come in this order. A Bright Beginning. Heat and Danger. A Surface Full of Wonders. Spacecraft That Went There. Last Thoughts. Words and Topics. A photo shows the planet Venus. Ancient Chinese speakers named it Tai-pe. Say that name tie-PAY. The meaning is beautiful white one. Ancient Romans gave the name we use today. Venus was their goddess. Love and beauty were her domain. No other planet carries the name of a female figure. Long ago, people did not know the truth about this world. Venus is a planet.

2A hard, rocky surface covers it, as on Earth. Towering mountains rise there. Vast plains spread out. Volcanoes of enormous size stand there. Craters cut deep. Many other interesting features appear as well. Telescopes let scientists study Venus. Space probes did the same. Because of that work, we know far more than ancient people knew. Hostility is extreme. Heat there is more than six times the heat of the hottest place on Earth. Beauty is one part of this bizarre world. Beast is the other part. A view shows Venus once the clouds are stripped away. A diagram places the Sun and then Venus. Venus is second in order from the Sun. Heat and Danger. Seven other planets share our solar system. Among them, Venus sits nearest to Earth. Second from the Sun is Venus. Third from the Sun is Earth. Size is another likeness. Venus comes closest to Earth in size. Solid, rocky surfaces like Earth's belong to three planets. Venus is one. Mercury is one. Mars is one. Every remaining planet is a gigantic ball. Gas and liquid make up those balls. Likeness to Earth is only partial.

3Venus differs sharply from the planet we live on. Average temperature is 870 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 465 degrees Celsius. Clouds as thick as soup wrap the planet and hold heat in. The heat begins at the Sun. Some of that heat reflects upward off the surface. Thick clouds hold the reflected heat in. Glass or plastic on a greenhouse holds heat the same way, so plants stay warm. The name for this heating is the greenhouse effect. Clouds belong to the atmosphere of Venus. Atmosphere means the gases that make the air around the planet. That air holds a great deal of carbon dioxide. Trapping heat is something carbon dioxide does very well. Droplets of sulfuric acid ride in many of the clouds. This compound is oily. It ranks among the strongest acids. Skin burns easily from it. Metals dissolve in it. Sometimes sulfuric acid falls from the clouds in drops that act like rain. Layers of air can weigh a great deal. Large amounts of water can weigh a great deal in the same way. Weight creates pressure. The atmosphere of Venus is so heavy that pressure on the surface is tremendous.

4Standing there, if you could, would end in a crush. A greenhouse effect also comes from Earth's atmosphere. Venus has the stronger effect. No other feature on Venus takes a man's name. Near the north pole, the top of this range stands 7 miles up. That is 11.3 kilometers. Mount Everest is the highest place on Earth. Maxwell Montes stands more than 1 mile higher. That extra height is 1.6 kilometers. Thousands of huge volcanoes mark Venus. Some are more than 150 miles wide. That width is 240 kilometers.

It hardened. Long, winding channels look like riverbeds. Scientists think flowing lava carved them, millions of years in the past. Streaming water probably did not carve them, as water does on Earth. Heat on Venus is so high that water would turn to vapor and join the air. A cooler Venus in the past might have held water on the surface. That remains a possibility. Deep craters mark the planet. Safe viewing of such an event must be indirect. Special glasses made for eclipses are another safe choice. Spacecraft That Went There. Telescopes on Earth could not settle what the surface was actually like. Opaque clouds hide whatever lies beneath. That surface was almost unknown to scientists until robotic space probes went there. 7Miles from the Sun: Venus stands at 67 million. Miles from the Sun: Earth stands at 93 million. A year is the time a planet needs to orbit the Sun, counted in Earth days. Venus needs 225. A shuttle carried the Magellan probe into space. The shuttle's name was Atlantis. The year 2005 brought the Venus Express probe. The European Union launched it. Instruments on Venus Express let scientists study the clouds further. The surface got further study too. In 2010, Japan's launch sent up the Akatsuki orbiter.

9Lightning was one subject. Volcanoes were the other. An illustration shows the Venus Express probe. The European Union launched it in 2005. Last Thoughts. Stargazers noticed Venus thousands of years ago. Everything else in the sky was outshone, apart from the Sun and the Moon. A special place of honor seemed required. The honor came as a name. It came from a goddess of ancient times, linked with love and with beauty. Science is how we honor Venus today. Much light has been shed on this bright point overhead. Science has made the picture clear. Venus is a very special world. It is also a strange one. No planet in the Solar System is hotter. Some of the largest mountains found on any planet are here. Some of the largest volcanoes are here too. Sulfuric acid is what falls as its rain. Earth once seemed a fair match for Venus. That idea is now known to be wrong. Another planet could hardly be less like ours. Hostility is severe. Life of the kind we understand cannot exist there. Venus still holds a beauty that is strange and its alone.

10Beauty and beast together: that is Venus. Words to Know. Atmosphere is a layer of gases. The layer surrounds a planet. Radar finds objects, or keeps track of them. It sends out radio waves and picks them up after they bounce off an object. The equator is an imaginary line. On Earth it circles halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. Robotic describes a device programmed to perform tasks. Hostile means very unfriendly. Sulfuric acid is a strong acid with an oily quality. Oxidizing sulfur dioxide produces it. Melted rock is what lava is. It flows as liquid from an opening in a surface. Tropical relates to the region around the equator. Heat and humid air mark that region. Rock pieces from outer space are meteorites. Metal pieces are meteorites too. They have landed on a planet after coming from outer space. Opaque means not see-through. Light is blocked. Topics include Aphrodite Terra and carbon dioxide. The greenhouse effect is listed. Magellan is listed. Maxwell Montes is listed. Pioneer is listed. Sulfuric acid is listed. Venera is listed. Venus Express is listed.

98. Watching the Sky with Telescopes

1Puerto Rico once held the Arecibo Observatory. It ranked among the largest centers for astronomy research. Collapse came in 2020. After that, the site was taken offline. Parts of this book follow. An Opening. The First Telescopes That Gathered Light. The Way a Telescope Works. Telescopes of Recent Times. Telescopes Above Earth. Telescopes That Hear Radio Waves. Astronomy Still Ahead. Words and Topics. A comet pictured here is NEAT. Another name for it is C/2001 Q4. An Opening. People full of questions have watched the sky across thousands of years. They wondered about whatever they saw. Only the unaided eye could supply those observations. About four hundred years ago, the telescope was invented. Knowledge of space then leapt forward in a huge way. From that point, telescopes changed. They became powerful tools. Stars can be viewed with them. Planets can be viewed. Other objects in space can be viewed. Telescopes come in two major kinds. One kind gathers light from objects that are far away. It also magnifies the images that light forms. People call it an optical telescope. Light-gathering telescope is another name. The second kind collects radio waves that arrive from space. A radio telescope is its name. Those waves cannot be seen. They can be turned into pictures we are able to study. One drawing stands for an optical telescope. Another stands for a radio telescope. Ahead you will meet the history of these tools. You will see how they work. You will see how scientists, and other people, use them on far-off objects in space. A word note explains the name. Telescope comes from Greek. Tele means far off, or distant. Skopos means to watch, or to look at. An early telescope is shown as an example. The First Telescopes That Gathered Light. Glass lenses had to be developed before a telescope could be invented. A lens is glass with a curve. It bends light. It also focuses light. Italian makers of glass developed early eyeglass lenses used for reading.

2Most historians give the first combination of lenses for distant viewing to a Dutch maker. His name was Hans Lippershey. He lined up two lenses. Light from the second lens was magnified by the first. Distant things then looked much nearer. The year 1608 is when Lippershey built his earliest rough telescope. He named it The Looker. Other people were trying lens combinations in that same period. Even so, he was first to seek a patent. Armies found the invention important. Warfare gained a large advantage from it. Dutch forces could watch enemy troops moving, and they could do so from far away. One year after that invention, an Italian man worked hard on a telescope of his own. His aim was objects in space. Galileo Galilei improved greatly on Lippershey. He also improved on other Dutch lens makers. Magnification in his telescopes reached five times. Later it reached thirty times. Distant space objects were what he observed. Because of this early labor, people know him as the Father of Astronomy. Important sights he recorded are listed here. Craters mark the Moon's surface. Mountains mark it too. He saw four moons of Jupiter. Phases of Venus showed that Venus orbits the Sun. Sunspots mark the Sun's surface. He found the Milky Way to be a galaxy of stars. Earlier thought had called it a cloud of cosmic dust. He saw Neptune. He did not realize it was a planet. A hard problem faced Galileo. As a professor of astronomy, his job required one taught picture of the solar system. Earth sat in the middle of that picture. The Sun had to be described as circling Earth. Every planet had to be described that way too. What he observed pushed him toward another theory. That theory might fit the sky better. In that theory the Sun sits at the center. Planets revolve around the Sun. Teaching this upset the Roman Catholic Church. Church teaching said God had built the universe with Earth as the hub.

3Galileo's theory moved humanity out of the center of the universe. Earth became just one planet among others. Those planets turn around one star among many. The Church banned his theory. A life sentence in prison followed. Old age was already his. Serving the sentence at home was permitted. He stayed under house arrest until life ended. Other scientists walked the path Galileo had opened. They improved the telescope. Still more about space objects came into view. Famous British scientist Isaac Newton was among the first. He found that a curved mirror, once polished, could gather light from objects. Lenses used by Lippershey and by Galileo did similar gathering. A lens telescope splits light into a rainbow of colors. The mirror telescope Newton built collected light and skipped that color split. A mirror could also be built larger than a lens. Those advantages made Newton's telescope superior. Telescopes that relied only on lenses fell behind. Technicians are shown in 1984 inspecting the mirror of the Hubble Space Telescope. The Way a Telescope Works. Lenses do not all magnify images in one same manner. Every optical telescope gathers light toward a point. A lens in some of them bends light inward until it meets at one center. Those are refracting telescopes. A curved mirror in others bounces light inward until it meets at one center. Those are reflecting telescopes. Three basic parts make a refracting telescope. A tube is one. Two lenses are the others. Correct distance between the lenses is held by the tube. Dust is kept out by the tube. So is stray light that would ruin the picture. Farther from the eye sits the bigger lens. Convex is its shape. That means the middle is thicker than the outer edge. Light enters through this lens and bends to a point. That point is the focal point. An image forms there, of whatever the telescope points toward.

4The smaller lens is the eyepiece. It magnifies the image before the image enters the eye. A far object then looks larger. It also looks closer. A convex lens appears in a picture of a magnifying glass. Labels on a refracting telescope name the focal point. They name the convex objective lens. They name the concave eyepiece lens. Four basic parts make a reflecting telescope. A tube is one. Two mirrors are two more. A lens is the last. Mirrors and lens are held in place by the tube. The primary mirror is large and concave. The curve sinks inward. A bowl's inner surface has that same curve. Light is gathered by this mirror and reflected to a second mirror. The second mirror is flat. It is mounted at an angle. It is much smaller. Because of the angle, more incoming light can pass by without distortion. Up to the eyepiece goes the bright picture bounced off the concave mirror. That lens is mounted on the side. Labels on a reflecting telescope name the eyepiece lens, the focal point, the flat mirror, and the concave mirror. Advantages belong to reflecting telescopes when they are set beside refracting ones. The most important advantage is cost and ease. Making a large concave mirror, and polishing it, is easier. The price is also lower than the price of a big convex lens. A light-gathering lens wider than 10 centimeters is hard to make. Four inches is that same width. Larger mirrors are easier to make. They also gather more light. More light means astronomers can observe a greater number of dim objects. Distant objects in space become visible too. A typical telescope for home use has labels. They name the optical tube, the viewfinder, the eyepiece, the dew shield, the focus knob, and the tripod legs. A math pause gives a result of 8.3 minutes. Light is very fast. One second carries it 300,000 kilometers. That distance is 186,000 miles. The Sun stands 149,000,000 kilometers from Earth.

5That distance is 93,000,000 miles. How many minutes does light need to leave the Sun and arrive at Earth? A telescope image shows Alpha Centauri in white. Distances in space are so huge that astronomers made a unit for them. They call it a light-year. Light travels at 300,000 kilometers each second. That rate is 186,000 miles each second. A light-year is how far that light goes in one year. Nearest stars to Earth include Proxima Centauri. It lies 4.2 light-years off. Alpha Centauri lies 4.3 light-years off. Telescopes of Recent Times. New telescopes keep being built larger. This is true for the refracting type. It is true for the reflecting type. Ireland's scientists, in the 1840s, constructed a big reflecting telescope. Across, the mirror measured 1.8 meters. That is 5.9 feet. At the time, the size seemed incredible. As telescopes grew, people made special buildings to hold them. Those buildings are observatories. They began to appear all around the world. Many stood on mountaintops. City lights and their glare were left behind. Wisconsin gained an observatory in 1897, built by the United States. Inside stood a refracting telescope bigger than any built before or since. Width of its extraordinary light-gathering lens was 40 centimeters. That is 15 inches. Early in the 1900s, new observatories rose for giant reflecting telescopes. Larger size was possible. More power was possible than refracting telescopes could offer. Astronomers wanted to see farther into space, and then farther still. Farther sight needed more light, including light that is dimmer. Two large reflecting telescopes helped southern California emerge. Astronomy gained a major base there. Research did too. One telescope stood at the Mount Wilson Observatory. That site is near Los Angeles. Diameter of its mirror was 2.5 meters. That is 8 feet. Astronomers used this powerful tool to help prove a big idea. Many galaxies exist well past our own Milky Way Galaxy. The Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson measures 2.5 meters, or 8 feet.

6A building houses the telescope at Mount Palomar. When the telescope is in use, the dome opens. Mount Palomar was the second major observatory in California. Opening year was 1948. Mount Wilson's mirror was only half as wide. Distant planets looked much clearer through this powerful telescope. Galaxies looked sharper too. Space objects never seen before were revealed. Reflecting telescopes kept growing. Some mirrors had diameters around 10 meters. That is 33 feet. Set one of those mirrors on edge beside a building, and the top would line up with a fourth-story window. Light-gathering power of these mirrors was tremendous. Still greater distances in space came into view. A modern tool of rare power pairs two large reflecting telescopes. They act as one telescope of extraordinary power. In some ways the setup works like binoculars. That likeness gave it a name. People call it the Large Binocular Telescope. LBT is the short name. Mount Graham in Arizona is the location. Images from the LBT are sharper than images from the Hubble Space Telescope. The gain is more than nine times. Each of the two mirrors measures 8.4 meters across. That is 27.5 feet. Together, their light-gathering power equals one mirror nearly 12 meters across. That is 37 feet. The top picture shows the Large Binocular Telescope and its two mirrors. Distant space objects can be seen more clearly than ever. The bottom picture shows workers looking tiny beside the huge mirror. An orbiting Hubble image, on the left, shows a ring of baby stars. They circle galaxy NGC 4314. Distance is about 40 million light-years. On the right, a telescope based on land shows those baby stars as a blur. Telescopes Above Earth. Telescopes that stand on land share one serious limit. Light from far objects has to cross Earth's atmosphere on the way in. Gases wrap the planet in that atmosphere. Height of the blanket is 50 kilometers. That is 30 miles.

7It surrounds our planet. The gases never stop moving. Light that passes through becomes distorted. Images of stars blur. Other space objects blur too. The blur happens before a telescope is even reached. It resembles looking at an object under the surface of a clear pool. A second problem involves very weak light from some distant objects. That light cannot penetrate Earth's atmosphere. Scattering happens before any telescope is reached. Computers have reduced some of the blur the atmosphere causes. They can predict how much movement will occur. They adjust the curve of a mirror. Sharper images result. Even with those adjustments, astronomers know a hard truth. Severe limits will always remain for land-based telescopes that try to view distant space objects. The Hubble Space Telescope offered a way past the problem. The only real solution was to place telescopes above Earth's atmosphere. Orbiting satellites were developed. Space stations were developed. A chance then existed to put a telescope into orbit, higher than the atmosphere. Scientists designed that orbiting telescope. Launch of the first one came in 1990. Edwin Hubble, famous as an American astronomer, is the person honored in the name. It is the Hubble Space Telescope. Orbit height is 515 kilometers above Earth. That is 320 miles. The planet's atmosphere is far below. From that position in space, distant objects are seen clearly. Images are formed with a mirror 2.4 meters across. That is 7.8 feet. Computers ride on the spacecraft. Other equipment rides there too. Light images are changed into radio waves and sent to Earth. Ground stations receive those waves. They change them back into images. Scientists on Earth can view the images. Other people can view them too. Objects never seen before became visible because of the Hubble Space Telescope. Many open questions about the universe gained answers from its evidence. Discoveries from Hubble include these breakthroughs. Black holes gained their first solid proof. Planets beyond our own solar system were shown to be real.

8A rocky planet like Earth was found for the first time beyond our solar system. Dust disks, the material from which planets form, turned out to be common around other stars. Ancient galaxies were viewed for the first time. Their age is over 10 billion years. Views of stars and of supernovas let astronomers work out how old the universe is with better accuracy. A comet was seen up close hitting a planet for the first time. Jupiter was struck by Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. Images still come back to Earth from the Hubble Space Telescope. Space now also holds a telescope with far more power. Construction of the James Webb Space Telescope began in 2004. Launch into space came in December 2021. Just past six months after launch, early pictures from this amazing telescope went out to people everywhere. Visible light waves are gathered by the Webb Telescope. Low-energy infrared waves are gathered too. Side to side, the mirror measures 6.5 meters. That is 20 feet. A shield blocks radiation from the Sun. A tennis court would match the shield in size. Compared with the Hubble Telescope, it can gather ten times the light. The start of time can be studied much more closely with Webb. Clues about how the first galaxies formed are the goal. It also watches how galaxies have changed as time passed. Dust clouds can be looked into. New stars forming there can be observed. Planetary systems forming there can be observed. In only its first few years, Webb expanded scientific knowledge about space by a great amount. Space scientists wait eagerly for the next discoveries. The general public waits too. Telescopes That Hear Radio Waves. Another telescope type is the radio telescope. It does not collect light from far objects and then magnify that light. It gathers radio waves that cannot be seen. Distant formations in space send those waves out. You might say these telescopes listen to space. Optical telescopes, by contrast, look into space.

9If optical telescopes are our eyes on space, radio telescopes do the job of ears. Most radio telescopes are large dishes made of metal. The shape is a dish. Radio waves are collected by the metal and reflected to an antenna. The antenna sits at the dish's center. An average-sized dish measures about 25 meters across. That is 82 feet. One dish, though, was immense. Puerto Rico, an island in the Caribbean Ocean, was its site. Diameter was 305 meters. That is 1,000 feet. Scientists have also linked many radio telescopes in one place. A site in New Mexico is an example. A computer receives signals from twenty-seven radio telescopes. One big radio signal is built from them. The Puerto Rico telescope worked for fifty-three years. Collapse came in 2020. Radio astronomy began in 1933. Karl Jansky, an engineer from America, discovered radio waves from space by accident that year. He built a radio antenna 33 meters long. That is 100 feet. A Ford Model-T supplied four tires that held it up and let it rotate. His aim was interference on phone lines. Those lines were laid along the bed of the Atlantic Ocean. Static radio waves from thunderstorms showed up. A hissing sound from far off in space showed up too. At first he thought the hiss was radiation from the Sun. Later he decided the waves came out of the Milky Way Galaxy's center. The find was purely an accident. Other scientists took several years to grow interested enough to build radio telescopes of their own. A radio telescope's collected waves travel to an amplifier. The amplifier magnifies the faint signals. It increases their strength. Amplified signals then go to a computer. The computer turns the signals into an image. Shape in the picture follows the radio waves that left their source. Different colors are assigned to various parts of that image. The colors stand for different strengths of radio waves inside the picture.

10A picture shows Karl Jansky's radio antenna, the one that rotated. Astronomy Still Ahead. Land-based telescopes will keep growing in size. Their technology will grow more specialized. Hawaii holds the Pan STARRS 1 telescope. PS 1 is its short name. A powerful digital camera on it tracks asteroids. It tracks comets that might threaten Earth. One-sixth of the sky can be mapped every month. A newer telescope, Once PS 4 starts its work, its power will be four times the power of PS 1. Little doubt remains about the best future view of space objects. That view will happen in space, beyond the interference Earth's atmosphere creates. Agreement is wide among scientists on the ultimate telescope. The Moon would be the building site. Plans are underway for an observatory on the Moon's surface. Very little atmosphere covers the Moon. Interference with light from distant space objects would be minimal. Mysteries of space are being revealed slowly. The finds of the newest telescopes are still unknown. These keen eyes aimed at space can show those finds to us directly. A picture shows Earth as it looks from the Moon's surface. Words to Know. An amplifier is equipment. It makes sounds louder. Light rays meet at a focal point. They can also spread from that point. Lenses have focal points. Curved mirrors have them too. Concave describes a shape or a surface that curves inward. Observatories are places for scientific watching of things in nature, including objects studied by astronomy. Convex describes a shape or a surface that curves outward. Distorted means changed so it is no longer accurate. An optical telescope gathers light. Emitted means sent out from a source. A radio telescope collects radio waves that come from space. Topics include Galileo Galilei, Karl Jansky, Hans Lippershey, and Isaac Newton. The Milky Way Galaxy is listed. The Sun is listed. Telescopes listed include the Hooker, the Hubble, the Large Binocular, and the James Webb.

99. What a Trip to Mars Would Take

1Mars One plans to grow a hydroponic garden inside part of a rocket meant for Mars. The book asks whether the trip is close. A bigger rocket is the next problem. Gravity must be brought along. Cosmic radiation is a danger. Dust waits on the surface. Food is missing, though water is not. Living packed together is another test. Cost comes next. Plans that might succeed, or fail, close the story. Hard words come last. A drawing shows a ship that could reach Mars. It comes from Inspiration Mars. That project is a private foundation, and it is nonprofit. Scientists have talked about astronauts on Mars for what feels like forever. So far the United States has sent only rovers, one after another. From 1969 to 1972, astronauts flew to the Moon and back six times. The Moon is the nearest neighbor. Mars then looked like the clear next stop in the solar system. The open question is the date. Something is still holding the trip back. Distance to Mars changes with the date you pick. Earth circles the Sun faster than Mars does.

2Every twenty-six months, Earth swings through the gap that separates the Sun from Mars. Earth may share the Sun's near side with Mars. It may sit on the far side. It may be anywhere else along its orbit. A Mars trip brings problems no astronaut has faced. Mars is vastly farther than the Moon. On average the gap is more than five hundred times as large. Arriving in one piece will be hard. Staying alive there will be hard. Humans will have attempted nothing greater in technology. There is welcome news. Serious planning for a mission is finally underway. Many people want to go. You might be one of them. The obstacles are worth listing. How long would your trip last? Red Planet is the nickname. Reddish minerals full of iron in the soil are the reason. The closest approach is still about 55 million kilometers. That is 34 million miles. The typical gap is about 240 million kilometers. That is 140 million miles. One direction alone would last seven months, or as many as nine. Time on the surface must be added.

3Ships for a journey that long and that far must be larger than any ship flying now. NASA is the U.S. space agency. Spelled out, NASA is National Aeronautics and Space Administration. A huge NASA rocket is under construction. Its name is the Space Launch System. SLS is the short name. A private firm, SpaceX, is building a giant of its own. Falcon Heavy is that rocket's name. The new SLS is planned to outpower the Saturn V. Saturn V is the rocket that carried crews to the Moon. Building the International Space Station took more than thirty flights. ISS is the short name. Pieces had to be delivered and joined. You cannot simply board one of those new rockets and leave for Mars. Neither rocket can serve alone as a Mars vehicle. A Mars ship must be larger still. The crew area must be roomier. Experts say the job is so big that several ships would be needed. Crew would ride in some. Supplies would ride in others. A habitat would ride as well. SLS and Falcon Heavy could lift separate pieces into orbit around Earth.

4Assembly would happen there. Fuel would be saved. The ISS was built that way, so the method is known. Readiness is what is missing. Gravity is another problem. The lack of it is the real trouble. Gravity lets people walk. It lets someone pour milk. It lets someone shoot a basket. Everyday acts depend on it. Health and fitness depend on it too, because bodies must push against it. A ship in space would have no gravity. Muscles then shrink. Bones grow weak. Nine months of that would leave a person wrecked. Artificial gravity is the proposed fix. A round section of the ship would spin. Centrifugal force would imitate gravity. A diagram shows that section turning without a stop. People standing on the inner surface would keep circling the center. Walking there would feel like a downward pull. To those people, the outward push would feel like gravity. Space is full of electrically charged particles. They race about in huge numbers. The Sun sends some. Space between the stars sends others.

5On Earth a magnetic field pushes those particles away, so the danger stays off us. A Mars ship would be struck the whole way. Engineers are looking for shields for long journeys. One idea wraps crew space in a tank of water. Incoming particles would be soaked up. Water weighs a lot. The ship's mass would jump. More mass means more fuel burned. A magnetic shield of the ship's own might work better. The ship would act like a tiny Earth. Researchers in many countries are trying to design that system. The work now sits with engineers. One NASA drawing sets fuel tanks and shields in a ring around the outside. Crew inside would be guarded from radiation. Arrival will not feel like a picnic. No magnetic field guards Mars. Radiation therefore remains a problem there. Underground is the only escape. A surface habitat would need shielding as heavy as the ship's. Dust, dirt, and rock cover this barren world. Huge dust storms, violent ones, often roar across it. You and your machines would both be threatened. No larger dust storms exist in the solar system.

6Farmland is a poor description of Mars. What would travelers eat? A short stay, followed by a return, allows food to be packed. That is the plan NASA has for the first missions. A person who means to stay and call Mars home would need another plan. Crop plants grown in a hydroponic solution are the best bet. Lots of water would be required. Mars seems able to help. Water appears plentiful. Some sits at the poles as ice. Some lies deep under the ground. Drinking water could come from it. Indoor farming could use it. Other jobs could use it. Some might even be sprinkled on the dust. Shoppers may have seen produce marked as grown without soil. Hydroponic farming uses big tanks of water. Nutrients are mixed in. Lettuce is a common crop grown this way on Earth. Tomatoes are common. Peppers are common. Cucumbers are common. A colony on Mars would surely add many other crops. Biosphere 2 studied how living things behave in a closed space. Long confinement can create a serious problem.

7Tension grows when people stay that close for so long. Arguments start. Fights can start. Small annoying habits are easy to ignore in ordinary life. Inside a sealed place, over many months, those habits swell. Severe conflict can follow. People hoping to go would need careful screening for compatibility. Friendly relations still could not be promised. In the 1990s, eight carefully picked people were sealed inside an artificial world in Arizona. The lock-in lasted two years. Four were men. Four were women. Biosphere 2 was the experiment's name. It was built to copy life on Mars. By the finish, the volunteers hardly spoke to one another. Cost can be answered in a short way: a great deal. The longer answer depends on the mission you imagine. A round trip with a surface stay of weeks, or of months, has been priced as high as 500 billion dollars. The unit is billions, not a smaller count. That price is one reason no mission has launched yet. A real mission will probably be shared. The United States would join several other nations.

8One privately owned company has another plan. Mars One is based in the Netherlands. It wants SpaceX's Falcon Heavy to lift spacecraft parts. The parts would meet in low orbit around Earth and be joined. Mars One says the mission can be done for 6 billion dollars. That sum is still large. Set beside 500 billion dollars, it looks like a bargain. An artist pictured a settlement built by Mars One. The shape of a trip is coming together. What is the timetable? NASA speaks of a possible round trip near 2033. Three ships would be joined in orbit around Earth. Two would leave first, carrying a habitat and supplies. The third would carry the crew. Weeks or months on the planet would be spent exploring. Soil samples would be gathered. Dennis Tito, an American billionaire, hopes to reach Mars before NASA. His plan is called Inspiration Mars. Two people would fly past in 2018, loop the planet, and return. If Mars still sounds like paradise, Mars One may be the fit. The hoped start is 2024. Several dozen people would go.

9A lasting colony is the aim. Four people would go first. Four more settlers would follow every two years. The required age is eighteen. After that, a seat might be possible. One limit matters. Every such trip is one way. No Mars One colonist should expect a ride home. Would people accept a deal like that? Many would. By 2014, hopeful applicants numbered more than two hundred thousand. Those chosen face eight years of training. If the plan holds, they then embark. Connected domes would be home. Living rooms and work rooms would fill the domes. Hydroponic farming would have space too. Tasks would be varied. Health effects of a life on Mars would be studied. The planet's geology would be studied. Signs of life today would be sought. Signs of ancient life would be sought too. Biosphere 2 offers warnings beyond personal conflict. Crops failed in that Arizona test. Oxygen ran short. Those people could step outside into Arizona's fresh air. Mars would offer no such exit. Danger has not stopped the people pressing Mars One. They want the trip.

10They want to be picked. A few word meanings help. Hydroponic describes plants grown with no soil, in water that carries what they need. Barren means plants are missing. A colony is a group settled in a new land while still tied to the home they left. Mass is how much matter something holds. On Earth, weight is how it is measured. Compatibility means getting along, or working together, without conflict. An orbit is the path a smaller space object takes around a larger one. To embark means to board a ship, a plane, or some other vehicle. It can also mean to begin something new. Radiation is a strong, dangerous energy. Nuclear reactions release it. A feat is an act that amazes, or a great accomplishment. To simulate is to copy the look of something, or its condition. Gravity is the natural pull of objects toward one another. Objects pulled toward Earth's center are one example. A habitat is a structure for living where people normally could not live. Under the sea is one such place.

100. What Makes a Price Go Up or Down

1During the COVID-19 pandemic, shoppers hunted for paper goods. Toilet paper was one item they wanted. Paper towels were another. Store shelves were often bare. Some scientists say shopping can switch on parts of the brain. Those parts make a person feel truly excited. They can also bring a feeling of happiness. A new movie has just premiered. You badly want a T-shirt that shows a favorite character from it. Then you see the price tag. The shirt costs a great deal, and it is still only a T-shirt. Another part of you feels no price would be too high. The want is that strong. Parents are likely to disagree. Weeks or months later, the shirt may be on sale. You might even look for it online. Buying it on sale is unlikely. A newer movie's merchandise would be the better purchase. The question is worth a pause. Who gets to decide what a T-shirt costs? Whose job is it to set that price? Buyers, including you, fill an important role in setting prices. The goods and services involved run from T-shirts to sandwiches.

2They run from haircuts to airplane tickets. Choosing to buy is an interaction with the seller. A market is the place, physical or virtual, where buyer and seller meet to do business. In a market, money moves from buyers to sellers. Goods and services move the other way. Prices can differ widely, even for things of the same kind. Return to the T-shirt. The character on it is only one factor in the price. The place where the shirt was made matters. The material matters. The stores that sell it matter. The people who appear in its advertisements matter. More factors sit in the price as well. A seller is free to ask any amount, whether the thing sold is a shirt, a good, or a service. Whether a buyer will pay that price is a separate question. Sellers design signs in big letters. They use bright colors. The aim is to catch interest and draw people into a store or onto a website. Economists try to explain how prices work.

3Economics is their field. It studies buying, selling, and wealth. They look for patterns. Laws of supply and demand help them describe why costs in the market change, and how. Supply is the quantity of a good or a service on hand. Demand means how much of it people want. Those two forces set the price of everything. Products such as lollipops fall under that rule. Computers do too. Services such as dog grooming fall under it. Doctor visits do too. Because supply and demand keep shifting, prices change often. The link also runs backward. A shift in price can make supply fluctuate. It can make demand fluctuate. Was the movie behind that T-shirt a hit at the box office, or a failure? Popularity changes what the related merchandise costs. A hit lets sellers keep asking top price for connected goods. A film that does worse in theaters than expected pushes sellers another way. Price cuts on that merchandise grow more likely. Supply is not fixed. Demand is not fixed. Price is not fixed.

4The three stay intertwined, each shaping the others from moment to moment. Picture lunchtime, and a strong craving for a chicken sandwich. A local restaurant has made chicken sandwiches the special. Two sandwiches cost the price of one. The deal is a welcome one. Here the sandwich price fell, and demand rose. Hunger plus a free extra sandwich leads you to take two instead of one. The lower price created a spike in demand. A special deal can excite buyers so much that they lose track of the true cost. Now look at the same sandwiches from the seller's side. What pushed the restaurant to advertise a two-for-one offer? Maybe too many chicken patties sat in the kitchen. They had to be sold by a certain date, or they would spoil. The supply of patties was a little too large. More patties were on hand than people wanted. That situation is called a surplus. A surplus in the market often sends prices down. Sellers, in general, want the highest price the market will allow. Profit is the gap between the selling price and the cost of making the good or service.

5Buyers, in general, want to pay as little as possible. Tension between those aims helps balance supply and demand. Price an item too high, and demand will often fall. Imagine arriving to find chicken sandwiches at one hundred dollars each. Another restaurant would probably get your lunch trade. Demand for the sandwich would drop as the price climbed. Price an item too low, and demand is likely to jump. Imagine the same sandwiches at one dollar each. You might buy every sandwich you could eat, and some for friends. The restaurant would likely run out very fast. At a movie theater, people will pay a large sum for snacks such as popcorn. Over a longer span, both extremes left buyer and seller worse off. In the first scene, an overly high sandwich price drove demand down. The restaurant missed the sale. The customer went home with nothing. In the second scene, the price was too low and the supply ran out. Many customers likely left disappointed, with no chicken sandwich left to buy.

6Sales may also have failed to pay for what the sandwiches cost to prepare. A table shows how supply and demand move together and affect price. If supply stays the same while demand increases, the price increases. If supply stays the same while demand decreases, the price decreases. A larger supply, with demand unchanged, pushes the price down. A smaller supply, with demand unchanged, pushes the price up. The price of one chicken sandwich at a local restaurant rests on a complex set of calculations. Many factors must be counted. The restaurant pays suppliers for chicken patties. It pays for buns. It pays employees. It pays to keep the restaurant running, including energy bills and rent. It must also judge what other nearby restaurants charge for the same sandwich. It must judge whether customers will actually pay the price being asked. Balancing every factor that touches a price is difficult. Prices fluctuate often as a result. Holiday season offers another view of supply, demand, and price.

7The next time your area marks a holiday, watch seasonal goods. Holiday-themed candy is one example. Before the holiday, that candy usually costs much more than it does after the holiday has passed. The ideas of supply and demand suggest a reason. A graph of chicken sandwiches sets demand against supply. Price runs from low to high. The crossing point is market equilibrium. Buyers and sellers both gain when supply and demand sit in a more even balance. That balance is called market equilibrium. For the imagined chicken sandwiches, equilibrium is a price at which every sandwich sells. The seller never runs out. Customers will buy exactly as many sandwiches as the restaurant has. They want no more and no fewer. Concert tickets offer another scene to ponder. An international pop band plays your city once every summer. Popularity keeps rising. The band stays in the same stadium, so the supply of tickets stays fixed. Each new year is likely to push a ticket's equilibrium price higher. Greater popularity raises demand for a seat at the show.

8Scarcity can be stated in a short form. Scarcity balances a supply that has limits against a demand that does not. Abundance is the opposite of scarcity. Scarcity shapes daily choices. Money, for most of us, is a scarce item. The supply of it is not unlimited. Everything we want cannot be purchased. A choice has to be made about the goods and services that matter most. We decide which ones we can skip. Toilet paper prices shot upward in 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic was starting. Businesses sold out quickly. Some customers hoarded toilet paper. Other people could not find any to buy. A common household item had suddenly become scarce. A fading trend can shake supply and demand for the goods tied to it. Fidget spinners are one example. Preferences differ from person to person. Values differ too. Buying habits shift because of those differences. That is why supply and demand keep changing what goods and services cost. How much is too much for a concert ticket? A fan's answer depends on personal circumstances.

9It depends on preferences. It depends on enthusiasm for the band. Emotions play a large economic role in the marketplace. Two bands can play the same stadium. Each show can offer the same number of tickets. Ticket prices can still differ sharply. The difference tracks what fans are willing to pay. Perceptions matter as well. A perception is the way a buyer views and judges a good or a service. Buyers often pay more for what they see as valuable or cool. Each buyer runs that calculation differently. Personality is one basis. Budget is another. Sooner or later, most people need someone to cut their hair. What they will pay for it varies widely. Some hunt for the cheapest cut they can find. A salon visit is worth a much higher payment to other people. Sneakers show the same spread. Nike's Air Jordan sneakers take their name from the basketball player Michael Jordan. Since 1985 they have appeared in many editions. Those editions are often very expensive. Plain sneakers usually cost far less than sneakers a famous athlete has endorsed.

10Some buyers see value in that endorsement. They will pay extra for the celebrity factor. Another kind of buyer hunts for footwear at the lowest price. Values and circumstances make every buyer different. A shopper can pick one product, or another product, or nothing at all. As a consumer, you hold power over supply and demand. Daily life puts you, and everyone you know, into economic markets again and again. Pause over the goods and services your family buys on a regular basis. The next time one of those prices rises or falls, notice your own reaction. Did demand, meaning how much you wanted the item, change because the price changed? Why would that happen? Price can also hint at the supply available for the things you buy. What would you conclude? A purchase joins a much larger conversation. A bus ticket is such a purchase. A swim lesson is one. A house is one. An apple is one. Every one of these purchases joins the tug between supply and demand.

101. When the Ocean Sends a Giant Wave

1In this book: a huge wave in the Indian Ocean. Tsunamis in earlier times. What sets a tsunami off. Places that face the greatest danger. Ways people get a warning. How to stay alive. A closing word. Words to know. Topics you can look up. A picture shows the center of the 2004 quake that sent out a tsunami. Another picture shows Banda Aceh, Indonesia, after the Indian Ocean wave of 2004 swept much of that city away. The wave in the Indian Ocean December 26, 2004, brought a powerful quake. It shook the seafloor near Sumatra, in Indonesia. Villages nearby felt the ground move. Those people did not know what would follow. Within minutes, a huge wave would flood their homes. That kind of wave is called a tsunami. A tall wall of moving water wiped out whole towns. Hours later, the water had struck thousands of miles of shoreline. Indonesia was hit. So were India, parts of Africa, Thailand, Bangladesh, Malaysia, the Maldives, Myanmar, and Singapore. Other places were hit as well. Day after day, the world was stunned. The reported number of deaths kept climbing. Early reports named 20,000 deaths. New reports named 100,000. The count later stood at 226,000. The true number of deaths may never be known.

2Mud and wreckage buried many bodies. The sea carried other bodies away. Scientists think fewer people would have died if more of them had understood the danger. They also needed to know how to escape. Pictures show Banda Aceh before the tsunami and after it. One picture shows the wooden raft a survivor used. People who lived through it Stories of loss stood beside stories of amazing survival. A man who lived in Indonesia was carried far out to sea. He pulled himself aboard a raft made of wood. Coconuts kept him fed. Rainwater kept him from dying of thirst. After two weeks, a ship found him. Some people ran ahead of the water. Some were carried inland by the wave itself. Others lived by clinging to trees. Others climbed onto the roofs of strong buildings. The best chance belonged to people who moved uphill the moment the shaking started. Experts say only two places are truly safe when a tsunami hits. One is higher ground. The other is land farther inland. Looking back at tsunamis The word tsunami comes from Japanese. It means harbor wave. Japanese fishermen were the first to use it that way. They would sail home and find their towns destroyed. Unusually large ocean waves had done the damage.

3While those fishermen were out on the water, they had not noticed the waves at all. A tsunami can bring terrible ruin. Large ones are very rare, which is fortunate. In a typical span of 100 years, the world sees about six major tsunamis. Krakatoa, a volcano in Indonesia, blew apart in 1883. The blast set off a tsunami. That wave killed 36,000 people. A picture shows Krakatoa erupting in 1943. Alaska had a landslide in 1958. Rock crashed into Lituya Bay. The splash built a wave 1,720 feet tall. That is 524.26 meters. Chile's coast shook in 1960. The quake set off a tsunami. Parts of South America were devastated. Hawaii was devastated. Japan was devastated too. What starts these waves Most tsunamis begin when the ocean floor quakes. An underwater landslide can start one. A volcanic explosion can start one. A meteor hitting Earth can start one. A quake in the ocean, or near it, does not always make a tsunami. Strength matters. The kind of movement in Earth's crust matters too. On the Richter scale, the quake must reach at least 6.75 before a tsunami can result. The 2004 Indian Ocean wave came from what scientists call a mega-earthquake. Its magnitude was 9.0. How the scale works The Richter scale is how people describe an earthquake's force.

4A reading of 2.0 is too weak for anyone to feel. A reading of 4.5 can be measured by seismographs everywhere on Earth. Each step up the scale makes the force grow fast. Step from a reading of 5.0 to a reading of 6.0 and the force grows by ten times. A report of 7, then of 8, then of 9, should be read with care. Each whole number is 10 times as strong as the number just below it. Ordinary waves and tsunami waves Wind-made waves reach the beach fairly close together. In shallower water, the bottom of a wave rubs the ocean floor. That rubbing slows the bottom. The top of the wave then spills onto land. A tsunami behaves in a similar way. Its bottom drags on the seafloor and slows. Its top spills onto the shore. A tsunami is taller than a surface wave. Its crests sit farther apart. For that reason, a much greater amount of water comes ashore at once. Some people call a tsunami a tidal wave. It can rush in the way a very high tide does. Tides are not the cause. A tsunami is also unlike the ordinary surface waves that wind makes.

5Those wind waves tend to roll up the beach in a circling motion. A quake happens when pieces of Earth's crust suddenly slip past each other. They slip along a fault. If the seafloor shifts up and down, the water above it shifts too. An enormous bulge of water forms. That bulge is a tsunami. Far from land, the wave is almost impossible to see. Compared with surface waves, it is very wide and very low. A map names pieces of Earth's crust. They are the North American Plate, the Eurasian Plate, the Philippine Plate, and the Arabian Plate. Also shown are the Indian Plate, the Pacific Plate, the Australian Plate, the African Plate, and the Antarctic Plate. A key marks land that stands above sea level. It marks faults. A star marks where the December 2004 tsunami began. The letter N shows north. A diagram shows one plate of Earth's crust pushing beneath another plate. Pressure builds where one plate sticks to the other. The land above bulges. An earthquake is that pressure letting go. People can picture it as a pop. The land then jumps. Water above the fault line surges. The water rises into a tsunami. Waves travel outward from the fault line. A map marks where the earthquake began.

6It labels India, the Indian Ocean, Indonesia, Australia, and Antarctica. Numbers on that map tell how many hours the 2004 tsunami needed to reach land. One question the map asks is how long the wave took to arrive in Australia. A tsunami can race as fast as a jet airplane. Its speed can be 200 to 500 miles in an hour. That equals 321 to 643 kilometers in an hour. As the wave spreads across thousands of miles, it does not lose its strength. Think of ripples moving over a pond. Crossing the Pacific, from one side to the other, can take less than one day. Shallow water near shore changes the wave. It grows much taller. It also loses speed. Before it arrives, the sea draws back. Then the sea rushes in past the usual shoreline. Water pours inland. It can run a long way up rivers and streams that meet the ocean. These waves often arrive as a group. People who watched the Indian Ocean tsunami said the opening wave was the smaller one. The wave after it was larger. Some people lived through the first wave. They stopped running. The bigger second wave caught them. A drawing shows a tsunami meeting the shore. The top of the wave moves faster than the bottom.

7Friction against the ocean floor holds the bottom back. The drawing marks the runup, the shore, the ocean, sea level, and the ocean floor. Where the danger is greatest The highest risk sits on low coasts in places where quakes are common. One famous belt of volcanoes is the Ring of Fire. It circles the whole Pacific Ocean. Volcanoes and frequent earthquakes go together. Both come from movement in Earth's crust. Indonesia is another place where the crust moves often. Nobody can name the exact hour of the next quake. Nobody can name the exact spot either. People can still judge when a region is overdue. A map labels North America, Asia, South America, the Pacific Ocean, Australia, and the Indian Ocean. It traces the Ring of Fire. N marks north. A picture shows a warning sign. Signs of this kind line western American shores. They tell people that a tsunami is a danger there. Systems that warn people No practical method can save buildings from a tsunami's ruin. An early warning can still save lives. A quake at sea usually leaves some time before the wave reaches land. Banda Aceh, in Indonesia, was not that lucky. Only a few minutes passed between the shaking and the wave.

8India was about three or four hours away. Sri Lanka was about that far in time as well. That gap would have been long enough to radio a warning ahead. Governments and scientists are building warning systems for later tsunamis in many parts of the world. A picture shows a buoy in the Pacific Ocean. More buoys like it will be set out. Scientists will use them to watch for tsunamis. The buoys will also help warn places that are at risk. America's Pacific shore already runs a system that warns of these waves. Seismographs along that coast pick up earthquakes. An Alaska quake of 6.8 brings a tsunami warning. In the western United States, the warning level is a quake of 7.5. Buoys fixed in place at sea can sense how fast a tsunami is moving. They can also sense which way it is going. They radio those facts back to shore. Seaside towns hear the news by radio. Loud sirens sound as well. Highway signs mark places where the risk is high. Those signs point out routes for leaving. How to stay alive People who live in a risk zone should remember these rules. Learn the safe routes for leaving. Make an emergency plan with your family.

9If a tsunami warning goes out, follow the order to leave. Do not spend time trying to save belongings. You might have hours. You might have only minutes. It depends on where the quake struck. When the ground shakes, go to higher ground at once. Everyone in the house should know to leave. Do not wait until you see the wave coming. Running from a tsunami that is already there should be the last choice. Go on foot. Cars can jam the roads very fast. A jam wastes minutes you cannot spare. Do not remain in a small building near the coast. Most houses cannot hold against a tsunami's force. Keep away from rivers that meet the coast. A tsunami can travel far inland by following a river channel. Remain in the safe place until officials say it is all clear. Wave number one is not always the tallest. A later wave can still be the one that finishes the danger. A picture shows an elephant clearing wreckage in Banda Aceh. The wreckage was left by the devastating tsunami of December 2004. A last word Quakes and tsunamis remind us how powerful nature is. The reminder can be frightening. People cannot stop these events. People can get ready for them.

10Knowing the right actions can save lives. So can a warning that arrives early. Words to know Buoys: floating objects held in place in water, including the ocean. Some send information from that place back to scientists. Richter scale: a measure from 1 to 10 of how strong an earthquake is. Sirens: machines that make a sharp, loud sound to warn people in an emergency. Devastating: bringing ruin. Tidal: having to do with tides. The pull of the Sun and the Moon raises tides on the ocean twice each day. Earthquake: the shaking of Earth where pieces of the crust meet. Evacuation: moving people out of a dangerous place. Tsunami: a huge sea wave, or a set of them, started by the earth moving under the ocean, as in a strong quake. Fault: a crack in Earth's crust. Movement happens along that crack. Magnitude: how great something is in size or in intensity. Topics in this book Africa. Major tsunamis. Alaska. Meteors. Areas at risk. The Pacific Coast. Buoys. The Pacific Ocean. Chile. The Richter scale. The death toll. The Ring of Fire. Earthquakes. Sri Lanka. Earth's crust. Surface waves. Faults. A survivor. Volcanoes and volcanic eruptions. Hawaii. A wall of water. India. Warnings. The Indian Ocean. Indonesia. Japan. A landslide.

102. Who Should Hold the North Pole?

1Tall ships work in the Arctic’s Beaufort Sea. Towers on those ships drill for oil. An introduction opens this book. Geography comes next. Then the book asks why the North Pole has value. Indigenous peoples of the Arctic have a part. Another part asks who wants the North Pole. A conclusion follows. A glossary explains important words. The words North Pole may bring one picture to mind. You may picture a cold, empty spot in the middle of nowhere. Cold is true. Remote is true. Empty is not. The North Pole and the land and sea around it hold many natural wonders. That wider area is the Arctic region. A hard question follows. Ownership is the hard question. One answer gives the treasures to separate countries. All people might share them. The planet itself might hold them. Several countries want pieces of the Arctic past their own borders. They are competing for those pieces. The grab for Arctic resources will touch the North Pole. The rest of Planet Earth will feel it too. Ice covers the sea around the North Pole. A viewer in outer space can see that ice. The North Pole sits in the Arctic Ocean. It is the northernmost place on Earth. Sea ice surrounds it. That ice forms the Arctic ice cap. Seasons change the size of the cap. Temperatures rise, and temperatures fall. Since 1981 the cap has been shrinking overall. Every ten years, the loss comes to 3.2 percent.

2Scientists have evidence for the cause. They point to climate change. Weather patterns on Earth change and then stay changed. That is what the phrase means. Five countries ring the North Pole. Norway is one of them. Russia is one of them. Canada is one of them. The United States is one of them. Greenland is one of them. Each one controls a band of sea. The band reaches 200 nautical miles out from the coast. That distance is 230 miles, or 370 kilometers. Inside the band, the country or region controls resource rights. Water can be used to make energy. Wind can be used too. Minerals are included. Fish are included. Past that boundary, the waters are international. Minerals lie on the seafloor out in the high seas. The International Seabed Authority writes the rules for taking them. People shorten that name to ISA. The ISA belongs to an agreement among countries. Under that agreement, international waters should help all people. They should not help only separate countries. Patterns in Earth’s climate have not stayed still. A full century holds that shift. Inside the latest twenty years, the hottest ones on record cluster. Warming is not equal in every place. Air around the globe is warmer by about two degrees. A century holds that rise. Scientists are nearly united on one important cause. Carbon dioxide in Earth’s atmosphere is that cause. Human actions make the gas. Factories burn coal for power.

3Cars use petroleum products. Carbon dioxide and other gases hold the Sun’s heat. The heat cannot escape into space. Scientists tie this warming to human activity for a clear reason. The climate is heating about ten times faster than in older warming periods that happened naturally. Effects differ from place to place. Some places will face droughts. They will also face extremely high temperatures. Rain will increase in other places. Hurricanes will increase there too. Coral reefs out in the sea will die. Coral cannot live in high temperatures. In the Arctic, glaciers are melting. Polar ice caps are melting. Sea levels are rising. Each September, scientists measure sea ice. They catch it at the lowest level of the year. A map can show the 2020 minimum in white. A dashed white line shows the average from 1981 to 2010. The yearly loss of ice is 31,000 square miles. South Carolina covers about the same area. By early 2014, many nations had ratified the agreement. Ratified means approved. One hundred sixty-five countries had approved it. The European Union had approved it too. A country that has approved the deal then gets ten years. In that time it may file a request. The request is allowed if the country believes it deserves areas past its exclusive economic zone. People shorten that zone’s name to EEZ. If the request is approved, a bigger result follows. Every resource in the larger area belongs to that country.

4A country might want more territory for that reason. The band of 200 nautical miles from a coastline has a name. It is an exclusive economic zone. Exclusive means not shared by others. Economic means tied to buying and selling. A zone is a marked area. A special purpose can set it apart. A set of rules can set it apart too. Some stretches of the Arctic Circle have no owner once those zones end. That is true at least for now. North of the Arctic Circle lies the Arctic region. Natural resources there are abundant. Petroleum is one resource people depend on most. Petroleum includes oil. It also includes natural gas. The supply sits under Earth’s surface. Reaching it is easier now than in the past. Melting of the Arctic ice cap is the reason. About 10 percent of oil used worldwide now comes from the Arctic region. It supplies 25 percent of the world’s natural gas. Experts think still more of both fuels may turn up later. The place would be near the North Pole. The time would be the future. The Environmental Protection Agency has warned about petroleum-based energy. It causes a lot of pollution. That pollution, they say, is what mainly drives climate change. A large share of climate scientists want it cut. They think countries must stop using petroleum-based energy at once. Even so, most energy people use still comes from goods made of petroleum.

5More than half of our energy comes from them. They are nonrenewable. That means they will run out someday. The day could arrive in forty to fifty years. Many countries are therefore scrambling for new petroleum supplies. Other energy sources could lower that dependence. Wind is one. Solar power is one. Electric power is one. Shipping routes are another promise of the Arctic. They sit beyond the natural resources. Warmer months are the only season for most of those paths. By then, sea ice has melted in large amounts. If melting continues, the open season could grow. A large part of the year might allow ships through. One recent voyage shows the change. A ship went from northern Russia to China in February. No ship had done that before. Getting natural resources in the Arctic is a dangerous business. Few other regions of the globe make the job this risky. It costs more too. The climate can defeat ordinary tools. Gear built for this place has to be used. In some cases it must still be invented. The gear has to work in extreme cold. It has to work in wet conditions. Moving materials to such a remote place costs a great deal. Moving people costs a great deal too. Workers in that remote place need higher wages. Accidents raise a further problem. Search-and-rescue stations may be far away. More lives may be lost. Equipment may suffer greater damage. The environment may suffer greater damage too.

6Spilled oil does not come up easily. A sea otter can end up coated in oil. Ordinary clean-up tools cannot handle an Arctic oil spill. Sea ice makes the job much harder than liquid water does. The U.S. Energy Information Administration supplied these points. Scientists name a further kind of value. Environmental groups name it too. The Arctic matters to humans. It also matters because of its natural environment. A wide variety of life lives there. Tundra vegetation is part of that life. Caribou are part of it. Polar bears are part of it. Whales are part of it. Seals are part of it. Taking more from the Arctic could throw the environment off in many ways. Extinction already threatens polar bears. Polar ice melt is the reason. Many scientists expect most polar bears to die out. The years they name run from 2050 to 2100. Drilling for petroleum worries scientists for another reason. Caribou populations could be hurt. Bird populations could be hurt. Roads make noise and other disruptions. Trucks do too. Power lines do too. Drilling does too. Migratory patterns might change. Mating patterns might change. Autumn tundra in Arctic Canada feeds a grazing caribou. Her calf feeds beside her. Indigenous peoples are about 10 percent of the people who live in the Arctic. Forty distinct Indigenous ethnic groups have homes there. The Saami are one group. Say that name SAH-mee. The Inuit are another group.

7Tribes, nations, and groups in the Arctic are not all the same. A likeness still joins them. Cultures and survival rest on Indigenous knowledge. That knowledge grew over thousands of years. People watched the Arctic’s unique environment. Traditions grew that reflect those surroundings. Inuit people, long ago and today, depend on wildlife. Caribou are part of that wildlife. Seals are part of it. Walruses are part of it. Whales are part of it. Every part of these animals is used. Bones are used. Teeth are used. Fat is used. Skins are used. The resources supply food. They supply clothing. They supply boats. They supply tools. Because daily life depends so deeply on the environment, climate change hurts these peoples in a special way.
