Melted ice makes hunting harder. The animals that matter to their way of life are harder to reach. Some Indigenous peoples risk hunger. Hunting supplies much of their food. Environmental change also makes water less safe to drink. Four countries have asked for territories larger than the ones they hold now. The four are Norway, Russia, Canada, and Greenland. The EEZ alone is not enough for them. Some claims reach the North Pole itself. Along the Arctic, Russia’s coast stretches about 4,300 miles. That is 7,000 kilometers. No other country on the Arctic Ocean has a longer coast. A small research ship went out from Russia in 2007. It dropped to the sea bottom. That bottom was at the North Pole.

8Soil samples came up. Water samples came up. They came from an underwater land feature. The samples came from the Lomonosov Ridge. Scientists wanted that ridge counted as part of Russia. They wanted Russia to own it. Any natural resources at that site would then be Russia’s. A wider seabed claim came from Russia in 2021. The added area was 705,000 square kilometers. The same ridge reaches Canada on the other side of the Arctic Ocean. Canada’s Arctic coast is the second longest. Canada says that underwater mountain ridge is part of its seabed. Denmark wants the ridge too. The reason is a historic relationship with Greenland. A map of the North Pole neighborhood uses color for depth. Bright blue means shallower water. Dark blue means deep water. The Lomonosov Ridge shows as a bright blue line. The North Pole sits just to the right of that line. The ridge is 1,110 miles long. That is 1,800 kilometers. Canada and the United States do not agree about the Beaufort Sea. That water lies north of western Canada. It also lies north of Alaska. Mineral rights sit inside all these arguments. Control of shipping routes sits there too. Russia wants more territory for military reasons as well. Norway may want that too. Other nations may want it. They worry about a future need to defend Arctic resources. They also want strong sites for military bases. A war between countries of the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere is the case they picture.

9Arctic routes would cut the travel distance. Military planes could reach targets sooner. Military ships could too. No decision has been made yet. Each country thinks its reasons for a larger territory are good ones. The arguments keep the countries at odds with one another. Another way to plan the changing Arctic might still be found. Earth’s axis has two ends. The South Pole is the far one. Extreme cold is true there too. An international agreement blocks ownership of Antarctica. It also blocks use of Antarctica’s resources. The continent is reserved for scientific research. It is reserved for peaceful purposes only. Military activity is not permitted. Should those same guidelines cover the Arctic region? Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station has a dome over it. The station is in Antarctica. The dome is 165 feet tall. That is 50 meters. Look ahead fifty years. Look ahead one hundred years. Should a single country hold the Arctic region, North Pole included? Some people say Indigenous groups deserve a larger place in these debates. Their Indigenous knowledge deserves that place too. Six Arctic Indigenous groups hold a special seat. The Arctic Council names them permanent participants. Nations and other groups are urged to work as partners. Arctic concerns are the shared subject. Solving those problems is the aim. Indigenous groups speak by way of the Arctic Council. Policies that affect the Arctic are part of that voice.

10Laws are part of it too. Countries that want a wider hold on the Arctic face serious choices. Peaceful cooperation is one path. Competition for control is another. Which path will win? Climate change is a threat. Arctic wildlife matters. Should those facts shape the choices? What choice should those Arctic countries make? A picture shows an Inuit woman cooking outdoors. The ground is tundra. Arctic Indigenous peoples depend on the environment for daily life. Their cultural traditions depend on it too. Petroleum is a natural liquid under the ground. Fuel is made from it. Many other goods are made from it too. Arctic describes the North Pole’s surroundings. The Arctic Ocean belongs to that area. Climate change is a weather shift that lasts, for the whole Earth or for one region. A remote spot is far away or cut off. Resources are useful supplies. People value them. Cooperation is joint work toward one shared aim. A route is a path from a starting point to another point. A dispute is an argument. Territory can be land or water that one state or country controls. A geographic area can carry the same name. Extinction is the end of a species, with no members left alive. International describes a matter that takes in two nations or more. Tundra is cold Arctic ground without trees. The soil stays frozen. Minerals are solid materials from nature. Living things are not their source.

103. Wings of Cloth and Air

1Contents. A record ride. What this sport is. How the wing stays up. Learning to pilot. Who may fly. Staying safe. Contests. Stunt flying. Races over land. Hike-and-fly races. A dream made real. Words to know. A 2016 picture shows three pilots from Brazil. They are on a paragliding flight that broke a record. A record ride. The day was October 13, 2016. Five people from Brazil put on their gear. They left the ground. No motor carried them. No engine of any kind carried them. Simple canopies of cloth held them aloft. After 32 kilometers, two flyers could not find enough lift. That distance is 20 miles. Those two could not keep going. The other three stayed in the air. They crossed the countryside of Brazil. Hour after hour they glided farther. Nearly twelve hours passed. The distance then was just over 564 kilometers. That is 350 miles. They came down to the ground. Those three pilots held a new world record. The record was for paragliding a long way. A hang glider is built with a solid frame. Its wings make a V shape. A paraglider is lighter than that. It is also simpler. The pilot has a soft harness.

2The wing is flexible cloth in an elliptical shape. What this sport is. All through history, people have stared at the sky and wished. They wanted flight like a bird's flight. Airplanes do give people flight. The riders are jammed inside heavy machines. The engines make noise. Sailplanes, also called gliders, are quieter. Even so, a plane must tow them up. Neither experience is truly birdlike. Paragliders bring people close to a bird's freedom. Hang gliders bring them close to that grace. A flyer can leave the ground under personal power. Hours can pass high above the land. Only nature's forces keep the flyer up. Gear for the sport. The equipment is easy to carry. Often the weight is under 16 kilograms, or 35 pounds. A pilot can unpack and prepare for launch in less than ten minutes. The wing, or canopy. Tough synthetic cloth makes the wing. A standard wing has two layers. Cells lie between those layers. The cells inflate and trap air. Harness and risers. The harness feels like a soft chair. Straps lock the pilot in. Thin straps called risers join the harness to the lines. Helmet. A helmet that leaves the face open resembles gear skiers wear.

3A full-face helmet adds a bar that guards the chin. Radio. Pilots carry a radio so they can speak with other pilots and with people still on the ground. An emergency makes that link important. The variometer, also called a vario. Pilots use this tool when they need to locate air that climbs. That rising air is essential for staying aloft. The vario measures speed up and down. It gives altitude. It gives ground speed too. Reserve parachute. This piece of safety gear is essential. It is a last resort. A pilot uses it when the wing collapses and does not open again. A pilot faces the wing and brings it up. Pilots call that stance the reverse launch. They use it when the wind is strong. Facing the wing makes it easier to manage. How the wing flies. Once the gear is ready, the pilot runs downhill. The wing trails behind and is pulled along. Moving air enters the wing. The fabric cells trap that air. Above the pilot, the wing fills. It climbs much as a kite climbs. The air lifts it. The pilot is lifted gently as well.

4Once airborne, the pilot leans back into the harness. Lines tie that harness to the wing overhead. To remain up, and to climb, the pilot searches for rising air. The air must rise faster than gravity pulls downward. Thermals are one help. A thermal is a column of hot air moving up. Warmth from the Sun makes it. Ridge lift is another help. Wind strikes a fixed shape in the land and is turned upward. A mountain can do this. A hill can do this. A dune can do this. Two paths upward. Thermal flying lets experienced pilots climb many thousands of meters high. They can cross hundreds of kilometers. They can remain aloft for hours. Brakes give them control. Those brakes are held in the hands. A pull on them reshapes the soft wing. Pilots also lean their bodies from one side toward the other. The shift makes a turn easier. With no rising air, gravity lets the glider sink gently. Brakes set the speed of that descent. The goal is a safe landing. Once the pilot's feet touch ground, a short run brings a stop. Gavin McClurg. In 2013 he set the U.S. record for distance in a paraglider.

5The flight covered 386 kilometers, or 240 miles. It ran from Idaho to Montana. Some of the largest ranges in the American West lay under him. He is an experienced sailor as well. He also kite surfs. He also kayaks. He calls paragliding the most intense adventure sport he knows. He calls it the most pleasurable one too. A picture shows him high over Alaska. Becoming a pilot. Students learn beside a licensed instructor. A training program is the path. At a flying school, a typical full-time course takes ten days. Some take two weeks. Students handle their equipment outside. They study flight rules. They study theory. Most schools hand out all the needed gear. Most have practice hills. Carrying the glider comes first. Setting it up comes next. Then students learn to kite it. Kiting means controlling the glider while still on the ground. That step prepares a launch. After that, students launch. They fly. They land safely. A license for solo flight requires teachers to watch a set number of flights. Thirty-five is a common minimum. Some schools ask for more. In Austria, a boy is pictured flying with a partner.

6Who is allowed to try. The sport is accessible to people with many kinds of physical ability. Countries do not share one age rule. Under eighteen, a young person must always have a parent say yes. Younger teenagers usually need a parent in the lessons. That parent usually flies with them. Even younger children can go tandem. On a tandem flight, the instructor takes a passenger along. Beginners can learn this way. Kids who are not old enough to fly alone can try the sport. Anyone who is curious can try it too. Staying safe. Flying sports carry some risk. Paragliding is one of them. Careful habits can greatly lower the chance of getting hurt. Pilots should inspect gear before they launch. They should judge the place they leave from. They should judge the place they mean to land. They must notice obstacles they could meet. Power lines are one kind. Other buildings and structures are another. Weather matters most of all. Wind that is too strong makes flight dangerous. Wind that is too gusty does too. A storm front can collapse a canopy. Other turbulent air can do the same. Pilots may then have to deploy the reserve parachute.

7When conditions are wrong, the safe choice is not to fly. Extra chances are not worth taking. Advanced training helps many pilots stay safer. In the air, they practice emergencies that are simulated. Over a lake they recover from stalls. They recover from spins. They recover from spiral dives. They recover from collapses. If the canopy or the lines tangle them, they can open the parachute. If the parachute does not open, the lake is still below. A rescue boat can collect them. Falling into the water can spare them a serious injury. Contests. After training, and after pilots know how to stay safe, almost no limit remains. As skills improve, many pilots want a test. Competitive flying is that test. Acro. Aerobatic events are one kind of contest. Pilots perform maneuvers that are difficult and dramatic. The Acro World Tour is one stage for them. Other tournaments are like it. The strongest pilots put on bold shows in the sky. The shows prove mastery of the wing. They prove control. Named stunts include the deep spiral. They include the helicopter. They include infinity tumbling. That last maneuver is a hard trick.

8The pilot makes forward somersaults in a series that does not break. The wing turns with the pilot. A picture shows an acro pilot moving through somersaults. In 2001, Spain's sky is crowded with fliers at a Paragliding World Cup. Races across the land. Pilots also enter cross-country events. A meet can be a race. It can be a test of distance. It can be a test of accuracy. During a race, the aim is the shortest time on a course through the air. The course begins at a start. It ends at a finish line. Markers called turn points divide the route. The crest of a ridge can be one turn point. Photos taken from the air can show that a pilot passed each section. A GPS receiver can show the same thing. In an accuracy meet, the pilot tries to land nearest a target circle on the ground. In an open-distance meet, the longest flight is the goal. Hike-and-fly races. Hike-and-fly is a third kind of contest. The X-Alps is one example. Its slogan says it is the toughest adventure race anywhere. Every second year, pilots come to Europe from all over the world.

9They test themselves above the largest mountain chain on the continent. Flying is only half of the X-Alps. They travel the Alps, starting on the north side and ending on the south side. They mix paragliding with hiking. Every other kind of transportation is forbidden. A usual route may pass through five countries or more. It may run past 1,000 kilometers, or 621 miles. Christian Maurer of Switzerland. Friends call him Chrigel, said KREE-gul. The name Chrigel the Eagle followed him. He began this sport when he was nine. Today many people rank him among the most skillful pilots in the world. As of 2023 he had taken the X-Alps eight times. No one else had won it that often. Coasts often give excellent chances to fly. The wind can stay steady. The ridges can be soarable. A dream made real. For people who practice the sport, no feeling beats paragliding. More and more people in countries around the world are becoming pilots. Accessibility is the key to that growing popularity. This is the easiest way to reach the air. It is the simplest way. It is the most affordable way. The basics of flight can be learned in just a few days.

10A light pack can hold all the equipment. With proper training, almost anyone can do it. Proper equipment is needed as well. When the weather cooperates, hours in the sky are possible. An old human wish is no longer only a wish. Birdlike flight is finally possible. Words to know. Accessible describes something easy to reach, easy to use, or easy to do. A maneuver is an action that needs skill, care, or a plan. Accuracy means landing or measuring in a way that is exact. Paragliding names a sport. A person leaves a high place, glides, and wears a parachute on the body. Aerobatic describes daring aircraft moves that thrill a crowd. Simulated describes a practice copy of a real event. Airborne means moving while held up by air. A somersault turns the whole body in a full circle. The knees stay bent. It can happen on land or while airborne. Aloft means up in the air, often high. A canopy is a big parachute. It slows a falling person. Tandem means two people, or two objects, acting as a pair. Inflate means to fill with air.

104. Words That Won a War

1Cecil Trosip, a Navajo code talker, is at a radio on Saipan in July 1944. Saipan is an island set in the Pacific between Japan and Hawaii. A second picture, from February 19, 1945, shows troops of the United States unloading supplies at Iwo Jima. That date, February 19, 1945, is when this account begins. A platoon of Marines from the United States leaps out of a landing craft. They fight their way through the surf. The beach they want is on the island of Iwo Jima, out in the Pacific. Japan lies not far away. Japanese forces answer with a hail of gunfire. What to do is unclear to the platoon leader. Where to go is unclear too. He uses the radio to ask his commander for instructions. Should the enemy learn the platoon's plans, everything will be lost. The marines stay confident. A secret weapon is with them. It is a team of Navajo radiomen. Say Navajo as NA-vuh-hoh. Their training is to transmit messages by a code. No outsider can decipher that code. They call themselves Dine', said dih-NEH. Dine' means The People. World War II, in 1942, was a fight spread over the whole globe. The United States was one of many nations pulled into the fighting. Messages had to move if troops were to stay supplied. Messages also kept them safe.

2Messages kept them ready to fight. Commanders of the United States faced a serious problem. Enemy listeners intercepted coded notes sent from unit to unit. Then the enemy decoded those notes. Breaking codes of the United States was a special skill of the Japanese. Many American casualties followed in some cases. Philip Johnston noticed newspaper stories about those radio-code troubles. Childhood for him included years on the Navajo reservation. The Navajo language was one he learned there. Few people outside that isolated tribe could understand Navajo, and he knew it. He also knew Navajo was hidden in a special way. Speech was its only form. No written symbols matched the spoken words. Top-secret communication fit those traits perfectly. News of the encryption trouble left him sure he had an answer. One photo shows Philip Johnston in 1944. Another, from 1904, shows him near age twelve, standing in the center. His family moved him to the Navajo reservation in 1896. He wrote to military authorities in California. His idea was a code built on Navajo. Leaders doubted the plan at the start. A test was what they finally allowed. He had to prove Navajo messages could travel fast. He had to prove they could stay secure. Success would make the military of the United States willing to try the plan. A map sets the Navajo Nation among Utah, Nevada, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico.

3Las Vegas, Flagstaff, and Albuquerque are marked on that map. No reservation in the United States is larger than the Navajo Nation. Its area is 27,000 square miles, or 69,930 square kilometers. That area is about equal to West Virginia. The smaller Hopi reservation is surrounded by this territory. People have sent hidden messages since ancient times. Steganography was an early method, used to physically conceal a message or to mask it. How the hiding worked was known only to the sender and the recipient. Invisible ink sometimes concealed the words. Once applied, that ink seems to vanish. Heat could bring it back into sight later. Chemicals could do the same. The message was then clear. A picture can show the true message turning up in white after the invisible ink is revealed. Some steganographic tricks were stranger. Ancient Greeks used one. A messenger's head was shaved. Words were tattooed on the skin. Hair was left to grow until it covered the words. He then traveled to the person who was meant to read it. That person shaved the head and read. Cryptographic methods are what most modern systems use. The message stays in plain sight. What stays hidden is the meaning. Wrong hands may hold the message. Understanding still requires the code. Substitution is one way to encode Send help now.

4Each letter is swapped for a different letter in the Caesar Cipher. Julius Caesar, emperor of ancient Rome, was a user of this letter swap. It works by shifting the alphabet. This example moves every letter three places left. Normal order starts A, then B, then C, then D, then E, then F, then G. Next come H, then I, then J, then K, then L, then M. It goes on N, then O, then P, then Q, then R, then S, then T. It finishes U, then V, then W, then X, then Y, then Z. After the shift, the row opens X, then Y, then Z, then A, then B, then C, then D, then E, then F. It next has G, then H, then I, then J, then K, then L, then M. It ends N, then O, then P, then Q, then R, then S, then T, then U, then V, then W. Send help now turns into PBKA EBIM KLT. Scrambling the letters is another method. The Rail Fence Cipher is one example. Letters of the words alternate on two or more lines, and the lines are then joined. One line is S, then N, then E, then P, then N, then W. E D H L O is the other. Send help now then reads SNEPNW EDHLO.

5When World War II began, cryptographers in the American military kept switching techniques. Coded American slang was one try. Failure followed again and again. A good number of Japanese students had studied in the United States. American English was familiar to them. Code breakers in Japan cracked the notes nearly as fast as Americans could transmit them. A Native people's language had been used before. In World War I, several Native languages carried messages for the United States, and the messages got through. Soldiers who were Cherokee helped the 30th Infantry Division pass battlefield messages. This happened at the Somme, in the battle called the Second. Men of the Choctaw, from the army's 36th Infantry Division, used a code as well. Important battles in France went to Allied forces with help from that code. Comanche codes helped in addition. A photo shows the Choctaw Telephone Squad from World War I. A question follows those successes. During World War II, why move to Navajo? Adolf Hitler holds most of the answer. Germany was under his rule from 1933 to 1945. He knew Choctaw had worked for the United States in the earlier war. He meant to block a repeat. After World War I he sent German students into the United States. Their studies were the languages of different Native peoples. Military leaders in the United States knew about that plan.

6Japan, they also knew, had sent students to learn those languages too. For a short time the armed forces tried something else. Servicemen from other groups were trained to serve as code talkers. Those groups had small populations. Eligible speakers were therefore scarce. Navajo numbers were larger. The men were willing to help. Older rules had refused Navajo recruits who lacked English. Speaking Navajo suddenly counted as an asset. A German student would struggle to learn it. A Japanese student would struggle too. The language family of Navajo is Na-Dene, said nah-de-NAY. Writings on Na-Dene were scarce in that period. Marines of the United States felt sure of one point. Outside the United States, nobody would understand the Navajo code. The United States has a long record of mistreating Native peoples. Johnston still recruited twenty-nine men. They made an all-Navajo platoon of marines. Work with the Field Signal School produced a coding system. Their own language was the base. Two parts made up the system. Part one used a Navajo translation of English words, and each word stood for a letter. Bear, in Navajo, is shush. Shush stood for the letter B. More pairs appear on a code list. The letter A is wol-la-chee, meaning ant. The letter B is shush, meaning bear. The letter C is moasi, meaning cat. The letter D is be, meaning deer.

7The letter E is dzeh, meaning elk. The letter F is tsa-e-donin-ee, meaning fly. Everyday military words had codes too. A commanding officer was hash-kay-gi-na-tah, a war chief. A squad was debeh-li-zini, a black sheep. A dive bomber was gini, a chicken hawk. A battleship was lo-tso, a whale. Bombs were a-ye-shi, eggs. An enemy would have been confused. Part two gave 211 Navajo words fresh military meanings. Looks often guided the choice of word. So did the job a thing did. An observation plane was called an owl. Shark, as a Navajo word, meant destroyer. An iron fish was the name for a submarine. From an early age these servicemen had been taught to listen. Stories of their people were learned that way. Memory was a strength. Listening was a strength too. A strong oral tradition belongs to Navajo. Memorizing the new vocabulary was no trouble because of that. A photo shows two Navajo soldiers passing orders on a field radio by means of the code. Some of the soldiers already knew one another from the same reservation. The two in the photo were cousins. A short period of training left Johnston's plan ready to test. Time trials were run by the signal corps. Speed of the radio messages was measured. Accuracy was measured too. The results astounded the testers. Seconds were enough for work that took other coders half an hour.

8Adoption of the code by the military was immediate. More code talkers were put into training. Service appealed to many Navajo men. Altogether, the Navajo code talkers who served in the Pacific numbered over four hundred. Their service was brilliant. Six of them worked through one of the war's biggest battles. That battle was Iwo Jima. More than eight hundred messages went out and came in. Combat was at full heat. Not one message was wrong. Keith Little was one of the six. He described what he gave to the battle. His language, he said, was his weapon. Countless lives, he said, were probably saved by that language. A 2009 book signing shows Keith Little speaking beside other Navajo code talkers. He died in 2012. He was 87. Several Pacific battles of World War II depended on these code talkers. The code made no sense to the Japanese. Surrender by Japan to the United States came on September 2, 1945. The code stayed a government secret after that day. It was kept in case a later war needed the code and the men again. Speaking about what they had done was not allowed. Years of silence followed. Loyalty and patriotism stand out even more because of what came next. Life after the war was hard.

9Jobs were scarce for many former soldiers. Discrimination often met Native peoples. Citizenship had been extended to all Native peoples by the United States in 1924. Individual states still denied many groups the vote. A guarantee of the vote for all Native peoples did not arrive until forty years later. In New Mexico in 1948, a photo shows Native peoples signing up to vote, a first for them. Lawmakers signed the Code Talkers Recognition Act in 2008. The act speaks of years when Indians were pushed away from practicing their native culture. A few brave men, it says, used their cultural heritage. Language was that heritage. They used it and helped change history's course. President George W. Bush is shown shaking hands with John Brown Jr. That 2001 event awarded the Congressional Gold Medal to Navajo code talkers. A report says one of the code talkers spoke at the ceremony. He said that just maybe he had become a citizen of America. Secrecy around the program finally ended in 1968. The world then learned what these men had contributed. President Clinton signed a law in December 2000. The original twenty-nine Navajo code talkers were the ones named for the Congressional Gold Medal. At the United States Capitol in 2001, President Bush handed out medals. Four of the five survivors from that original group received them. Success of the code owed much to the Navajo language.

10It also owed much to the honorable actions of the men. That success helped the United States win the war. It remains, to this day, the only spoken military code nobody has ever broken. Some words in this book have special meanings. Casualties are people wounded or killed in a war, an accident, or a disaster. Intercepted means a message was caught and taken on its way between two places. Navajo can mean a member of a Native group in the Southwest, and it can mean their language. Code talkers are Indigenous soldiers who used a native language as a code in World Wars I and II. Cryptographic has to do with a cipher or a code used to read or write secret messages. A recipient is the one who receives something. Reservation is the name for land the government of the United States once made Native peoples live on. Decipher means to work out the meaning of something hard to understand, which is also to decode it. A translation is words moved from one language into another. Discrimination is unfair treatment tied to gender, to race, to age, to religion, or to other differences. To transmit is to hand something along from person to person. Encryption means a message is coded so the meaning stays secret.

105. Yo-Yo Ma and His Cello

1High-school singers joined Yo-Yo Ma on stage in Chicago, Illinois, in 2012. His story begins long before that concert. The year 1955 and the city of Paris, France, mark his birth. Both of his parents had been born in China. Yo-Yo was seven when the family left France for the United States. Those early years set him on a path toward rare skill and wide respect as a musician. He also became one of the most respected. His mother was a singer. His father was a violinist. His father was a music professor too. His father had taught at a Chinese university before the family moved. His next teaching post was at a famous school of music in the city of Paris. Once they lived in New York City, his father started a group for young players called the Children's Orchestra Society. The society taught classical music to children. The account ahead follows that early start. It follows his rise as a young star. It follows trouble with his back. It follows three cultures that shaped him. It follows the Silk Road project. It closes with his own view that his success was an accident. From his earliest years, both parents pushed him toward music.

2A violin came into his hands when he was just three. By his own account, the sound he made on it was awful. Talent, he believed, was something he lacked. His older sister is Yeou-Cheng. Speakers say her name YOO-CHANG. Anger led him to break more than one violin, his sister says. The start was rough. He would soon show a large supply of talent. The violin lasted only a few months in his hands. Music did not stay out of his life for long. About a year later, the family went to hear music performed in the city of Paris. There he saw a huge instrument. It was a double bass. Learning that huge instrument became his wish. From end to end, a double bass measures about 6 feet. That height equals 1.8 meters. For a small child, his parents felt, that size was far too big. They agreed to let him play the next-largest stringed instrument instead. That instrument was the cello. Speakers say cello as CHEL-oh. A 1961 photo shows Yo-Yo at age six and Yeou-Cheng at age ten. The photo catches them playing for Denver Symphony members while a practice session paused.

3By the time Yo-Yo started cello, Yeou-Cheng was already strong on the violin. Their parents pushed both children to play hard music. Hard music was required, both inside that children's group and elsewhere. Three suites by Bach were in his memory by the age of five. Bach was a classical composer. Difficult music fills much of what Bach composed. Yeou-Cheng says their father used to tell her something about hard work. A hard job, their father told them, can be split into easier pieces. Those smaller parts were easier. Their mother, Yo-Yo says, pushed them to know every note deeply. Once the notes were that secure, worry about them faded. Feeling inside the music could then take their full attention. In 1962, Leonard Bernstein introduced a young player to an audience. Bernstein was America's most famous conductor. He presented a seven-year-old cellist from a Chinese family. The boy was playing old French music. Bernstein said the boy was playing for his new American compatriots. President John F. Kennedy was there, among the American listeners. A year after that concert, brother and sister performed together on a program called The Tonight Show. Most children that young are just starting a recorder, yet Ma was already well known.

4Fame already placed him among the leading cello players anywhere. Performance gifts belonged to his sister as well. She left music once it was obvious that her brother outshone everyone else at home. Medicine is her profession now. She also directs the children's music group her father began. The 2012 trip to Sweden included Jill Hornor. Emily Ma came too. So did Nicholas Ma. He received a Polar Music Prize there for his musical work. High school ended early for him, at age fifteen. A solo role opened for him with the Harvard Radcliffe Orchestra. That same year he played at a wedding for the first time. He still loves playing weddings. He attended Juilliard. Few schools of music anywhere rank above Juilliard. Soon, however, he dropped out. He switched to Harvard University. There he studied classics. He studied anthropology. He studied German literature. Ma kept studying music. He kept playing cello along with his other studies. He wanted more in his days than cello alone. His first college summer was spent performing at a music festival. He met Jill Hornor there and fell in love.

5She was a college sophomore. She ran the festival. Later college summers were spent at that same festival. He played music there. He got to know Jill. They later married. They had two children. Back trouble bothered Yo-Yo Ma while he was still young. Graduation forced him to pause the career at once. An operation was what the doctors said he must have. His spine bent the wrong way, and the operation was meant to correct that curve. The surgery was risky. A failed operation might have ended his ability to play. Skipping the operation could have meant pain in his back for life. He thought the risk was worth taking. He went ahead with the surgery. The surgery was successful. For six months afterward, a cast covered his body. Walking about was impossible for him then. He was even less able to play the cello. Getting well again was extremely hard. As soon as the cast came off, people wanted Ma again at once. Concerts soon took him to countries across the globe. He often booked concerts years in advance. Age twenty-three was when his first album was made. Albums since that first one number more than seventy-five.

6His Grammy Awards number fifteen. Among classical players still living, few have sold more recordings. Makers finished his usual cello in the year 1733. It is worth 2.5 million dollars. In 1999, Ma left that cello in a taxi by accident. The driver returned it. After that, Ma recorded a message. Every taxi in New York played the message he had recorded. Riders were told to take their belongings when the ride ended. Ma has said that part of him is always charging ahead. He calls himself the curious kid. He says he is always going to the edge. Listeners in many countries count him among the finest players alive. Many events that history remembers have included his playing. He played for the hundredth birthday of the Statue of Liberty. He performed at a memorial when one year had passed since the 9/11 attacks. He took part when the Olympic Games of 2002 opened. He played at President Obama's inauguration. Classical music now treats him as a central person. The wider culture of the United States treats him as a central person too. In 2011, he performed with the Silk Road Ensemble. Dancer Charles Riley, known as Lil Buck, performed with them.

7Ma's Chinese heritage matters deeply to him. His French childhood matters too. His American adulthood matters as well. His playing carries the mark of all three cultures. Fresh ideas from unfamiliar cultures have filled his whole career. European music in the classical style was his starting point. He then branched into bluegrass. He branched into Argentine tango. He branched into jazz. He also played traditional music from China. He played traditional music from Japan. He played traditional music from Brazil. He says that people who open themselves to new cultures understand music better. They also understand people better. Older albums let him hear how his playing shifted. His music changed as he met new styles and took them in. Classical pieces fill most of the albums under his name. Other musical styles appear in his work as well. He made his own recordings of tunes from Cole Porter shows staged on Broadway during the 1930s. He recorded John Williams's themes for Star Wars. He recorded the theme for E.T. He recorded the theme for Jurassic Park. Film music of his own making fills several soundtracks. He has recorded with bluegrass musicians.

8He has recorded with jazz musicians. Groups of musicians in many countries have recorded with him. When the Winter Olympics of 2002 opened, he played beside the pop artist Sting. Those games were in Salt Lake City, Utah. During 2011 the Silk Road Ensemble joined him for a concert in New York's Central Park. That mix of backgrounds had always mattered to his music. In 1998 he launched the Silk Road Ensemble. The blend has always mattered to his music as well. Players in the group come from twenty countries. Composers from those countries take part too. Together they build music from customs found in many lands. Traders once traveled a route known by that silk name. Centuries ago, that route crossed the continent of Asia. It united cultures across the whole continent. The Silk Road project is not only a musical ensemble. It is also a nonprofit group. Linking people across cultures, through music and through art, is the nonprofit's work. He still guides the nonprofit in seasons when he is not on stage with the players. He is its artistic director. He helps plan programs that teach music from around the world. He helps plan programs that perform that music.

9Many successful musicians give credit to hard work. Others give credit to natural talent. Why he became so widely loved as a musician is something Yo-Yo Ma says he cannot explain. He also does not know why other talented performers do not reach the same level. He once said, I'm an accident. Many separate pieces, he says, add up to the success he has had. Those things include his parents. They include his sister. They include various teachers. They include Paris. They include New York. They include his experience of performing at a young age. They include meeting his wife. They include raising his children. Change any single one of those pieces, he feels, and worldwide fame might never have arrived. Missing that huge double bass at age four, he believes, would have sent his life another way. In 2001, he prepared to perform in Germany. He has said that every day he makes an effort. He moves toward what he does not understand. He says this wandering leads to learning that happens by accident. That learning keeps shaping his life. Human societies, their cultures, and where they began are the subject of anthropology.

10People who perform as one company, whether they act or play music, form an ensemble. Classical can mean European music of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Symphonies and operas are examples of this older music of the West. Heritage is what one generation hands to the next, such as a way of living, a custom, or a trait. An inauguration is the ceremony that places a person into office by oath. Working side by side with others on one project is collaboration. Musicians in a large group who play at the same time form an orchestra. They often perform classical music on stringed instruments. Compatriots are people who live in the same country or are its citizens. A composer is a person who writes music. Short classical pieces gathered into a set are called suites. The pieces have different forms. A shared key is a common choice for those pieces. Players are expected to perform the pieces in one set order. A conductor directs an orchestra, a choir, or another ensemble. A group's shared ideas and its customs are its culture. The word can also point to one society that keeps ideas and customs of its own.

106. Young Players in a Big League

1British Columbia, a province of Canada, gave a totem pole to the Little League Organization. In 1951, a Little League team in British Columbia became one of the earliest outside the United States. The parts of this book come in this order. An introduction opens it. Next comes the start of baseball. Then comes the history of Little League Baseball. The path to the championship follows. The 2006 Little League World Series comes next. A closing section follows. A word list and an index finish the book. Introduction. An announcer describes Josh Lester taking a short lead. Lester is off first base. Japan leads by a score of 1 to 0. The inning is the third. Behind the bleachers, the sun is going down. Players begin to notice a bright glow. The glow comes from lights above the field. The grass has a smell unlike the smell at home. It is as if the field waited a full year for the kids to return. Cody Walker steps up to bat. The pitcher he faces is Go Matsumoto. Two fine pitching jobs have already been seen today. For the United States team, Kyle Carter has pitched at his best. A picture shows Cody Walker swinging the bat. Back home in June, the stands held only about 50 people. The month now is August. Almost 5,000 people fill the seats. Still more people watch on national television.

2Weekend practices helped bring the boys here. Stretching exercises helped too. The 2006 Little League World Series is the event these boys are in. The next pitch is on the way. Each game brings excitement. This game is the one for the championship. These players no longer stand for only their own team. They no longer stand for only their state. They now stand for the whole United States. The ball is gone from the park. No one doubts that it left the field. Cody Walker has just hit a home run. The home run scores two runs. The United States moves ahead, 2 to 1. The moment is huge for this young player. It is huge for his teammates too. That hit turned out to be the play that decided the game. Cody's team comes from Columbus, Georgia. The team went on to win the championship by a score of 2 to 1. Spectators saw players leap with joy. Families leaped too. Gloves sailed through the air. Caps sailed through the air. A scene like this returns every summer. The place is Williamsport, Pennsylvania. Some of the strongest youth teams in the world come to play. The event is the Little League World Series. The series is popular now. How did Little League Baseball arrive at this point? A picture shows teammates from Columbus, Georgia. They celebrate the 2006 Little League World Series championship.

3A picture shows an early professional game of the Washington Senators. The catcher reaches to tag the runner. Baseball Begins. Experts still do not share one date for the birth of baseball. Games with a ball and a stick go far back in many countries. Baseball resembles some older games. Cricket is one of those older games. Rounders is another. Both cricket and rounders come from Britain. Even so, baseball uses rules of its own. It uses equipment of its own. The printed word base-ball first showed up in 1744. That printing shows the game already existed then. During the Civil War, baseball became popular. The war took place in the mid-1800s. Soldiers treated the game as a diversion. They played during free time. A picture shows a crowd at the professional World Series of 1907. The clubs were the Detroit Tigers and the Chicago Cubs. Professional baseball got its start near the end of the Civil War. People organized the first major league in 1871. In 1876 that league became the National League. By the 1890s the game was so loved that it was called the national pastime of the United States. A second major league formed in 1901. The new league was the American League. The first World Series was played in 1903. That series pairs the champion of the American League with the champion of the National League.

4The Boston Americans defeated the Pittsburg Pirates. The teams needed eight games. That win put the Boston Americans first among baseball teams in the United States. History of Little League Baseball. Kids have been eager to play baseball ever since the game began. Before homes had television, many children hurried back from school. They crowded around a radio. They listened to the games of teams they loved. Sometimes a child pretended to be a star. One friend might be named Mickey Mantle for the game. The other child might claim to be Jackie Robinson. Farm families saved a piece of land for a baseball diamond. In cities, kids played stickball in the street. A broomstick served as the bat. A mailbox could be a base. A tree could be a base too. Empty lots were turned into fields. A win felt wonderful. Playing a sport beside friends felt just as important. The games were fun. They were not very well organized. A picture shows kids in a pickup baseball game. A picture shows Carl Stotz. Another picture shows Carl Stotz posing with players. The pose is from before a Little League World Series game in the early 1950s. Then Carl Stotz changed things. As a boy, Carl was left out by older kids. The older kids refused to let Carl play baseball. Grown up, he wanted every young boy to get a chance.

5The chance he wanted for them was baseball. He hoped a formal league would teach boys strong ideals. Sportsmanship was one ideal. Fair play was another. Teamwork was another. Kids used to knock on doors to ask friends out to play. On a team, they could play games that were scheduled. A coach could help them play better. Stotz formed Little League Baseball in 1939. He formed it in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. Only thirty players were in the league. Only three teams were in it. Local businesses sent donations. Stotz managed the Lycoming Dairy team. Two brothers were invited by Stotz to coach the other teams. One of those teams was Lundy Lumber. The other was Jumbo Pretzel. Each team had thirty dollars. That money bought uniforms for every player. Mothers sewed team names onto the uniforms. Gloves had to be shared. The only catcher's mask had to be shared too. Their field was a vacant lot. In 1947, twelve teams entered the first Little League tournament. Years later, that tournament grew into the World Series. The Maynard Midgets were from Williamsport. They beat Lock Haven Little League for the championship. About 2,000 fans showed up. They came even though August was hot. From that day, a great tradition began. A picture shows fans cheering at a tournament game in 1955. Word of the league traveled. Teams formed quickly across the country. Any boy aged 9 to 13 was allowed to play.

6Race did not bar a boy. Religion did not bar a boy. Color did not bar a boy. Until 1974, girls could not take part. A picture shows a Girls Little League team lined up for a photo. By 1948 the league had ninety-four teams. Little League teams today include about 2.7 million children. Some of those teams are in the United States. Others are in countries around the world. A picture shows the team from Chinese Taipei. The photo is from the mid-1980s. The team is preparing to play. The Path to the Championship. More than 100,000 teams now take part. They compete in separate divisions. Age is what places a player in a division. The best-known division is called Little League. Players on those teams are 11 and 12 years old. Each local team belongs to a district. A district gathers teams from one area. In June, each district picks its best players. Those players form an all-star team. An all-star team has no more than 14 players. Someone is chosen as the all-star coach. Someone is chosen as the manager. In July the all-star teams enter many tournaments. The tournaments cut down the number of competitors. A picture shows a batter on the Saudi Arabian team. He swings at a pitch. The swing comes during a win over Whalley Little League. That win was part of the 2006 World Series tournament.

7By August, the Little League Baseball Division is down to 16 teams. Those 16 have earned the trip to Howard J. Lamade Stadium. The stadium is in Williamsport. They come for the Little League World Series. Teams drop out game by game. At the end, two teams are left. One finalist comes from outside the United States. Little League play reaches 80 countries beyond the United States. The other finalist comes from the United States. Those two teams play a single game. The winner is the Little League World Series champion. The 2006 Little League World Series. Teams in the 2006 series traveled a long way to Williamsport. Saudi Arabia was one faraway source of a team. Russia was another. They arrived in late August. Kawaguchi City, Japan, took the International Championship. The team it beat was from Matamoros, Mexico. The final score was 3 to 0. Go Matsumoto was Japan's star. He hit a home run in that championship. He later entered as a relief pitcher. His team faced a bases-loaded jam. Nobody was out. His pitching ended the jam. A picture shows Matsumoto on the mound. In the United States Championship, Columbus, Georgia, won. The team that lost was from Beaverton, Oregon. The score of that game was 7 to 3. Georgia then had to carry the United States banner. Japan would be the opponent in the World Series Championship.

8Georgia did carry the banner. A picture shows Kyle Carter. He speaks with his catcher on the mound. Other teammates stand there with him. The opponent in the picture is Japan. People called Kyle Carter a pitching phenom. Eleven batters struck out against him. Only three hits came off his pitches. Matsumoto's pitching held the score close. Georgia still came out ahead. The series title went to the United States. It was the second straight year for a United States title. The result was a real feat. Before that final, Kawaguchi City had not lost. Successful Little Leaguers. Plenty of Little League World Series players later became pros. Some grew up to play baseball. Some grew up to play hockey. Some grew up to play football. Gary Sheffield has been named a Major League Baseball All-Star nine times. He played in the Little League World Series in 1980. Derek Bell was a teammate of Sheffield in that 1980 series. Bell later reached the Major League World Series. He played then for the Toronto Blue Jays. Chris Drury was in the Little League World Series in 1989. Stephane Matteau was in it in 1982. Pierre Turgeon was in it in 1982 as well. Ray Ferraro was in it in 1976. Later, all four reached the National Hockey League as hockey players. Brian Sipe was once the quarterback of the Cleveland Browns.

9He played in the Little League Baseball World Series in 1961. A picture shows Gary Sheffield. A picture shows Chris Drury. Wilson Alvarez is shown as a former pitcher in Major League Baseball. Sean Burroughs is shown as a third baseman. He played for the Tampa Bay Devil Rays. Jason Varitek is shown as a catcher for the Boston Red Sox. Conclusion. The Little League World Series is still growing. It is still changing. Tournament games in 2006 drew more than 300,000 people. Television carried those games across the United States. Josh Lester is the second baseman from Columbus, Georgia. He fielded the final out of the championship. Cheers broke out in the crowd. The chant was USA, USA. A picture shows Georgia celebrating the 2006 win for the USA. Georgia's players acted in true Little League spirit. They invited the Kawaguchi City players to join them. The two teams took a victory lap around the field together. After decades of growth, the goal of Little League is unchanged. The goal is a game that teaches useful principles. Players can carry those principles as good citizens of the world. An announcer then speaks to the crowd. Ladies, gentlemen, boys, and girls are asked to return next year. Another exciting Little League World Series will be waiting. Readers who want more can look up Little League Baseball. Little League Softball is part of that story too.

10World Series history can be looked up as well. That history includes records. It includes more famous players from earlier years. Word List. Organized means put into groups and guided by leaders. A competitor is a person or a team you play against. A pastime is a hobby or a free-time activity. Divisions are smaller groups inside one larger body. Scheduled means a starting time has been set. Eager means excited and full of interest. Spectators watch an event, yet they do not play in it. Equipment means the tools people use for work or for play. A feat is an action that amazes people, or a fine accomplishment. A tournament is a run of games or competitions. The run decides a final champion. A goal is a result someone hopes to reach. Index. The index names Chris Drury. It names the old printed word base-ball. It names Derek Bell. It names Kyle Carter. It names the championship. It names the Civil War. Under divisions it names the American League and Big League. It names Little League and Major League. It names the National League and Tee Ball. It names Japan. It names Josh Lester. It names Go Matsumoto. It names professional baseball. It names Gary Sheffield. It names stickball. It names Carl Stotz. It names the tournament. It names Cody Walker. It names the World Series.

107. Yusuf, Commander Who Honored the Faith

1A map of the Middle East from 1137 to 1193 shows the world of Salah al-Din. The Caspian Sea lies to the north. The Tigris River and the Euphrates River cross the land. The Mediterranean Sea borders the west. Aleppo, Tikrit, Baalbek, Damascus, Baghdad, Jaffa, Jerusalem, and Cairo are marked. Hattin is marked too. The Syrian Desert and the Arabian Desert cover wide dry ground. The Persian Gulf and the Red Sea meet these lands. Asia, Europe, Egypt, and Africa come together near this region. The book moves through his life in order. It begins with the Muslim world and his early years. It then tells how he rose to power and how he fought the Franks. It describes a fierce opponent and the time after the truce. It ends with the reasons people called him an honorable leader, plus a word list. Jerusalem ranks among the oldest cities on Earth. Salah al-Din lived in the Middle East almost nine hundred years ago. While he was young, this Muslim spent his days studying the faith. He followed its teachings with care. As an adult, he became a famous Muslim military leader. Few commanders of that faith are better known in history. The world of his birth was complex. Three religions hold Jerusalem holy. Those religions are Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The city holds many buildings that followers treat as sacred. Other sacred sites fill the city as well.

2Muslims ruled Jerusalem for centuries. Muslims, Christians, and Jews all made the city their home. In 1099, Christians from Western Europe conquered Jerusalem. That conquest came decades before Salah al-Din was born. The conquerors had promised safety to the residents. Instead, they killed thousands. Salah al-Din would later take Jerusalem back for Muslims. His birth came in 1137, or possibly in 1138. His Muslim family lived in Tikrit, in Mesopotamia. Tikrit stood many miles from Jerusalem. His father was a wealthy chief. The family left Tikrit while Salah al-Din was still an infant. They traveled west to Aleppo, in northern Syria. Sultan Zengi led that area. The area belonged to a Muslim Turkic empire. When Salah al-Din turned six, his father went to work for Zengi. The family moved again. They lived in Baalbek and in Damascus. At age seven, Salah al-Din began school at a mosque. He learned the Five Pillars of Islam. The pillars are faith, prayer, fasting, alms, and pilgrimage. Alms means money or food for people in need. He studied science and math. He studied poetry and religion. He studied Muslim history and Muslim culture. He hoped to become a scholar. Training for war interested him less. The name Salah al-Din is a nickname given in honor. It names a man who brings honor to the faith. His given name was Yusuf. In the West, people often shorten that name to Saladin. Each pillar shapes daily Muslim life.

3To show faith, Muslims say that Allah alone is God. They say that Muhammad is his messenger. To pray, Muslims turn toward Mecca. They pray five times a day. The hours are dawn, noon, afternoon, evening, and night. Fasting belongs to the holy month of Ramadan. From first light until dark, Muslims do not eat. They do not drink during those hours either. Almsgiving is a duty. Muslims give a portion of their income to people in need. Pilgrimage means a journey to Mecca when the trip is possible. A Muslim makes that journey once in a lifetime. Muslim society puts great weight on a spiritual life. A bond with Allah, or God, matters deeply. Muslims learn to be fair and generous. They learn to be loving and merciful. They learn to be noble and humble. The year 1146 changed his life. Zengi died. Nur al-Din was Zengi's second son. Part of the father's kingdom passed into the hands of Nur al-Din. Damascus gained a new governor, and that governor was Salah al-Din's father. His uncle Shirkuh became a military general. At age fourteen, Salah al-Din joined the army of Nur al-Din. A few years later, he became the sultan's chief aide. Riches and power both belonged to the sultan. He still lived with honor and simplicity. He ruled in a fair way. He used his wealth to help his people. Nur al-Din became the model for how Salah al-Din would live.

4Salah al-Din went on learning. In his late twenties he traveled to Egypt with his uncle Shirkuh. They went on several military expeditions. The goal was to keep Egypt out of Frankish hands. The Franks were Christians from Western Europe. Egyptian politics were confused at that time. Shirkuh became the ruler of Egypt. He died nine weeks later. In 1169, Salah al-Din became the new ruler. He was thirty-one years old. He also took command of the Syrian troops in Egypt. He made a vow to free Jerusalem from the Franks. He vowed to free the land around the city as well. He improved the economy of Egypt. He built schools. Scholars from Europe and from Asia came to those schools. He ordered workers to build the Citadel of Salah al-Din in Egypt. The work ran from 1176 to 1184. The citadel was meant as protection from Christians of Western Europe. Crusades were wars called by popes. The popes asked Christians of Western Europe to fight in the Middle East. Their aim was to end Muslim control. They wanted the holy city of Jerusalem. They also wanted other lands already taken. In 1095, Pope Urban II gave the order that began the First Crusade. An enormous palace could have been his home. He chose a small and simple house. He gave away most of the palace riches. People gave him loyalty because he was strong.

5They also stayed loyal because he was gentle and generous. Nur al-Din died in 1174, only a few years later. Salah al-Din believed he was the best person to rule. He led an army into Syria. For nine years he fought the brothers of Nur al-Din. During that fight he ordered respectful treatment of enemies. His men did not loot villages. They did not burn villages. They did not chase an army that was pulling back. They did not treat captives without mercy. He was skilled at politics and at war. His fame grew for being firm, virtuous, and generous. By 1185 a wide region was under his control. That region included Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. It also included northern Mesopotamia. Northern Mesopotamia is the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris. In 1187, Salah al-Din opened a war on the Franks. The Franks had taken Jerusalem eighty-eight years earlier, in the First Crusade. He planned to drive the invaders out. He planned to win back the holy city. He planned to help the spread of Islam. At that time the Franks were fighting among themselves. They disagreed about who should rule Jerusalem. Raynald of Châtillon took control of trade routes. His name is said sha-tee-YOHN. He was hostile toward Muslims. Guy of Lusignan became king. His name is said loo-zee-NYON. Before Raynald, Arab traders and Frankish traders crossed one another's lands in peace.

6Once Raynald was in charge, he broke treaties with Salah al-Din. He attacked Muslim trade caravans. He raided towns along the coast. In early July 1187, the army of Salah al-Din captured the town of Tiberias. The army surrounded the castle. The Crusader force King Guy gathered numbered twenty thousand soldiers. He hoped to take Tiberias back. On the march, Salah al-Din's army forced Guy's troops against two hills. The hills are called the Horns of Hattin. The Franks fought hard. Salah al-Din's army still defeated them badly. King Guy was taken captive. Later, Salah al-Din chose to let Guy live. Raynald was killed. Raynald had broken the truce between Salah al-Din and the Crusaders. Salah al-Din then took the castle at Tiberias. A battle map for 1187 to 1192 shows Tyre, Acre, and Tiberias. It shows Hattin, the Sea of Galilee, and the Dead Sea. It shows Jerusalem, the Syrian Desert, the Arabian Desert, and the Mediterranean Sea. The Franks fled to the fortress at Tyre so they could rebuild their forces. Salah al-Din chose to deal with Tyre later. He turned to the task of retaking Jerusalem. His army attacked the holy city. Two weeks later, on October 2, 1187, the city was his. He had met his goal at last. Jerusalem was back under Muslim control. For the Crusaders, that loss was a crushing blow. The Christian capture of Jerusalem in 1099 had been cruel and vengeful.

7His capture was not like that. No Christian holy place was destroyed. Many reports said that few people were killed. After the capture, Christians could still visit their shrines in the city. Europe was shocked that Muslims now held Jerusalem. European leaders at once called for a Third Crusade. King Richard I of England raised an army to win the holy city back. People called him Richard the Lionheart. Other European kings raised armies too. Richard became the person who led that effort. Salah al-Din tried to capture Tyre, the strongest Frankish fortress still standing. He did not succeed. At about that same time, he set King Guy free. Guy and his supporters went to Acre, which Muslims controlled, and they attacked. By the time Salah al-Din reached Acre, Crusaders from Europe were already there. He could not defeat them. The fight at Acre lasted 638 days. Muslims held the inside of the fortress. Christians surrounded those Muslims. The army of Salah al-Din surrounded the Christians. Leaders of the Third Crusade arrived in the spring of 1191, and their armies came with them. Philip Augustus, from France, was the first leader to arrive. A few weeks after that landing, Richard the Lionheart reached the war. Richard was a brilliant commander. Only one month after he arrived, he forced the Muslims at Acre to surrender. During August 1191, Frankish troops under Richard moved south, with Jaffa as their aim.

8Archers serving Salah al-Din struck those troops without a pause. Long years of war had weakened the army of Salah al-Din. He could not stop Richard from taking cities on the coast. He moved his own army to Jerusalem instead. He worked to strengthen the city against Frankish troops. The Franks never launched that attack. Richard saw that his army was not large enough to take the holy city and hold it. His choice to turn away marked the end of the Third Crusade. On September 2, 1192, a brother of Salah al-Din spoke with Richard. They discussed the terms of a truce. Salah al-Din let the Franks keep the coast between Tyre and Jaffa. The rest of the land, including Jerusalem, would remain Muslim land. Christians would still be allowed to visit holy places. His honorable conduct won lasting respect from the Christian world. It also won lasting appreciation. After the truce was signed, Salah al-Din returned home to Damascus. Only six months later he died, on March 4, 1193. He was fifty-five. Money and luxury had never mattered much to him. He had given everything away, so nothing remained for a proper burial. His son later built a building in Damascus, and Salah al-Din was buried there. After his death, his family kept ruling Egypt and the nearby lands. That rule lasted until 1250. Then a different empire gained power. For centuries after that, Jerusalem stayed mostly under Muslim rule.

9The building that holds his tomb was raised in 1193. It was restored in 1898. A statue in Damascus today shows Salah al-Din on horseback. Damascus is in South Syria. While he lived, people respected his intelligence. They respected his skill in politics and in war. Muslims honored him for uniting them. They honored him for driving the Crusaders out of Jerusalem. The Crusaders were his enemies, yet they held him in high respect too. Across two continents, people knew him as fierce in battle. They also knew that he showed mercy. He lived during the Middle Ages in Europe. Some people call that same era an Islamic Golden Age. Empires kept changing. They fought one another without mercy. Even so, one of the most respected leaders of that age is remembered for the opposite. Just before death, he spoke to his oldest son. He said his greatness came from winning men's hearts through gentleness and kindness. During his life he showed what an honorable leader can be. He still offers that example today. These dates mark the life of Salah al-Din. In 1137 or 1138 he was born in Tikrit, in Mesopotamia. From 1152 to 1169 he served under Nur al-Din, the Syrian ruler. In 1169 he became ruler of Egypt and commander of Egypt's Syrian troops. In 1174 Nur al-Din died, and Salah al-Din began work to unite the Muslim states.

10In 1185 he succeeded in uniting those states. On July 4, 1187, the Battle of Hattin was fought. On October 2, 1187, he took Jerusalem again after a battle of two weeks. In 1189 the Third Crusade began. On July 12, 1191, the battle at Acre ended. On August 4, 1192, the Battle of Jaffa ended. On September 2, 1192, he and Richard the Lionheart agreed to a truce. On March 4, 1193, Salah al-Din died in Damascus. A shrine is a holy place, or a small space that holds religious objects. It may honor a person or a god. A caravan is a group of people traveling together, often with animals or vehicles. To loot is to steal during a war, a riot, or another destructive event. A sultan rules a Muslim country in a role much like a king or an emperor. A mosque is a place where Muslims worship. A truce is an agreement that both sides will stop fighting. A Muslim is a person who follows Islam. A vengeful person wants to hurt someone back for a wrong. A pilgrimage is a trip to a shrine or another special sacred place. A virtuous person shows goodness and a clear sense of right and wrong. To raid is to strike by surprise for a set purpose. Sacred means holy, or tied to a god, a religion, or a spiritual aim.
